Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

Majjhimanikāye

The Middle Length Discourses

Uparipaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Upper Fifty

1. Devadahavaggo

1. The Devadaha Chapter

1. Devadahasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta

1. Evaṃ [V 4.0001][P 4.0001][M 4.0001] me sutanti devadahasuttaṃ. Tattha devadahaṃ nāmāti devā vuccanti rājāno, tattha ca sakyarājūnaṃ maṅgalapokkharaṇī ahosi pāsādikā ārakkhasampannā, sā devānaṃ dahattā “devadaha”nti paññāyittha. Tadupādāya sopi nigamo devadahantveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Bhagavā taṃ nigamaṃ nissāya lumbinivane viharati. Sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetūti pubbe katakammapaccayā. Iminā kammavedanañca kiriyavedanañca paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ vipākavedanameva sampaṭicchantīti dasseti. Evaṃ vādino, bhikkhave, nigaṇṭhāti iminā pubbe aniyametvā vuttaṃ niyametvā dasseti.

1. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Devadaha Sutta. Therein, regarding the name 'Devadaha': kings are called 'devas,' and there, the Sakyan kings had a pleasant, well-guarded royal lotus pond. Because it was the lake (daha) of the devas (kings), it became known as 'Devadaha.' Based on that, the town also came to be known as Devadaha. The Blessed One, depending on that town, was dwelling in the Lumbinī grove. 'All that is due to past action as a cause' means: because of the condition of action done previously. By this, it is shown that they, rejecting both feeling concurrent with kamma and functional feeling, accept only feeling that is resultant. By the phrase 'Thus speaking, O monks, are the Nigaṇṭhas,' what was stated previously without specification is now shown with specification.

Ahuvamheva [P 4.0002] mayanti idaṃ bhagavā tesaṃ ajānanabhāvaṃ jānantova kevalaṃ kalisāsanaṃ āropetukāmo [V 4.0002] pucchati. Ye hi “mayaṃ ahuvamhā”tipi na jānanti, te kathaṃ kammassa katabhāvaṃ vā akatabhāvaṃ vā jānissanti. Uttaripucchāyapi eseva nayo.

Regarding the question, 'Were we in the past?': the Blessed One, knowing their state of ignorance, asks this merely with the wish to lead them to defeat. For if they do not even know, 'We were in the past,' how then will they know whether kamma was done or not done? This same principle should be understood in the subsequent questions as well.

2. Evaṃ santeti cūḷadukkhakkhandhe (ma. ni. 1.179-180) mahānigaṇṭhassa vacane sacce santeti attho, idha pana ettakassa ṭhānassa tumhākaṃ ajānanabhāve santeti attho. Na kallanti na yuttaṃ.

2. 'If that is so': in the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta, this means, 'if the statement of the great Nigaṇṭha is true.' Here, however, it means, 'if there is your ignorance regarding these points.' 'It is not proper' means 'it is not fitting.'

3. Gāḷhūpalepanenāti [M 4.0002] bahalūpalepanena, punappunaṃ visarañjitena, na pana khaliyā littena viya. Esaniyāti esanisalākāya antamaso nantakavaṭṭiyāpi. Eseyyāti gambhīraṃ vā uttānaṃ vāti vīmaṃseyya. Agadaṅgāranti jhāmaharītakassa vā āmalakassa vā cuṇṇaṃ. Odaheyyāti pakkhipeyya. Arogotiādi māgaṇḍiyasutte (ma. ni. 2.213) vuttameva.

3. 'With a thick application': with a heavy application, repeatedly smeared with poison, and not like one smeared with rice-scum. 'With a probe': with a probing splinter, or at least with a small cord. 'He would probe': he would investigate whether it is deep or shallow. 'Antidote-charcoal': the powder of scorched myrobalan or emblic myrobalan. 'He would place it': he would insert it. 'Healthy,' and so on: this has been explained in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ, sallena viddhassa hi viddhakāle vedanāya pākaṭakālo viya imesaṃ “mayaṃ pubbe ahuvamhā vā no vā, pāpakammaṃ akaramhā [P 4.0003] vā no vā, evarūpaṃ vā pāpaṃ karamhā”ti jānanakālo siyā. Vaṇamukhassa parikantanādīsu catūsu kālesu vedanāya pākaṭakālo viya “ettakaṃ vā no dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ, ettake vā nijjiṇṇe sabbameva dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissati, suddhante patiṭṭhitā nāma bhavissāmā”ti jānanakālo siyā. Aparabhāge phāsubhāvajānanakālo viya diṭṭheva dhamme akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya jānanakālo siyā. Evamettha ekāya upamāya tayo atthā, catūhi upamāhi eko attho paridīpito.

'Just so': here is the connection of the simile. For just as for one pierced by an arrow, the time when the pain is manifest is at the time of being pierced, so for them there should be a time of knowing, 'Were we in the past or not? Did we do evil kamma or not? Did we do such-and-such evil?' Just as the time when the pain is manifest is at the four times of cutting open the wound, and so on, so for them there should be a time of knowing, 'Has this much of our suffering been worn away? When this much has been worn away, will all our suffering be worn away? We shall be established in the state of purity.' Just as there is a time of knowing comfort later on, so there should be a time of knowing for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states in this very life. Thus here, by one simile three meanings are illustrated, and by four similes one meaning is illustrated.

4. Ime pana tato ekampi na jānanti, virajjhitvā gate salle aviddhova “viddhosi mayā”ti paccatthikassa vacanappamāṇeneva “viddhosmī”ti saññaṃ uppādetvā dukkhappattapuriso viya kevalaṃ mahānigaṇṭhassa vacanappamāṇena sabbametaṃ saddahantā evaṃ sallopamāya bhagavatā niggahitā paccāharituṃ asakkontā yathā nāma dubbalo sunakho migaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā sāmikassa abhimukhaṃ karitvā attanā osakkati, evaṃ mahānigaṇṭhassa matthake vādaṃ pakkhipantā nigaṇṭho, āvusotiādīmāhaṃsu.

4. But these Nigaṇṭhas do not know even one of these points. Just as a man, though not pierced by an arrow that went astray, might give rise to the perception, 'I have been pierced,' merely on the strength of his adversary's word, 'You have been pierced by me,' and thereby come to suffering; just so, believing all this merely on the authority of the great Nigaṇṭha's word, and being rebuked by the Blessed One with the simile of the arrow, they were unable to reply. Just as a weak dog, having roused a deer, makes it face its master and then itself retreats, so too, they, casting the doctrine upon the head of the great Nigaṇṭha, said, 'The Nigaṇṭha, friend...' and so on.

5. Atha ne [V 4.0003] bhagavā sācariyake niggaṇhanto pañca kho imetiādimāha. Tatrāyasmantānanti [P 4.0004] tesu pañcasu dhammesu āyasmantānaṃ. Kā atītaṃse satthari saddhāti atītaṃsavādimhi satthari kā saddhā. Yā atītavādaṃ saddahantānaṃ tumhākaṃ mahānigaṇṭhassa saddhā, sā katamā? Kiṃ [M 4.0003] bhūtatthā abhūtatthā, bhūtavipākā abhūtavipākāti pucchati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Sahadhammikanti sahetukaṃ sakāraṇaṃ. Vādapaṭihāranti paccāgamanakavādaṃ. Ettāvatā tesaṃ “apanetha saddhaṃ, sabbadubbalā esā”ti saddhāchedakavādaṃ nāma dasseti.

5. Then the Blessed One, rebuking them together with their teacher, said, 'There are these five things...' Herein, 'of the venerable ones' means of the venerable ones in regard to those five things. 'What faith in a teacher concerning the past?' means: what faith in a teacher who is a past-proponent? He asks: 'That faith which you who believe in the doctrine of the past have in the great Nigaṇṭha—what sort is it? Is it based on fact or not on fact? Does it have a factual result or a non-factual result?' The same principle should be understood in the remaining phrases. 'With justice' means with a supporting reason, with a cause. 'A refutation' means a counter-argument. By this much, he shows what is called the 'faith-cutting doctrine,' saying, 'Do away with this faith; it is the weakest of all.'

6. Avijjā aññāṇāti avijjāya aññāṇena. Sammohāti sammohena. Vipaccethāti viparītato saddahatha, vipallāsaggāhaṃ vā gaṇhathāti attho.

6. 'Through ignorance and unknowing' means: because of ignorance, because of unknowing. 'Through delusion' means: because of delusion. 'You have faith' means: you believe perversely, or you adopt a perverted grasp; this is the meaning.

7. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyanti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākadāyakaṃ. Upakkamenāti payogena. Padhānenāti vīriyena. Samparāyavedanīyanti dutiye vā tatiye vā attabhāve vipākadāyakaṃ. Sukhavedanīyanti iṭṭhārammaṇavipākadāyakaṃ kusalakammaṃ. Viparītaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ. Paripakkavedanīyanti paripakke nipphanne attabhāve vedanīyaṃ, diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aparipakkavedanīyanti [P 4.0005] aparipakke attabhāve vedanīyaṃ, samparāyavedanīyassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evaṃ santepi ayamettha viseso – yaṃ paṭhamavaye kataṃ paṭhamavaye vā majjhimavaye vā pacchimavaye vā vipākaṃ deti, majjhimavaye kataṃ majjhimavaye vā pacchimavaye vā vipākaṃ deti, pacchimavaye kataṃ tattheva vipākaṃ deti, taṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana sattadivasabbhantare vipākaṃ deti, taṃ paripakkavedanīyaṃ nāma. Taṃ kusalampi hoti akusalampi.

7. 'To be experienced in this very life' means kamma that gives its result in this very existence. 'By striving' means by effort. 'By exertion' means by energy. 'To be experienced in a future life' means kamma that gives its result in a second or third existence. 'To be experienced as pleasant' means wholesome kamma that gives a desirable object as its result. The opposite is 'to be experienced as painful.' 'To be experienced when ripened' means to be experienced in a ripened, completed existence; this is a designation for 'to be experienced in this very life.' 'To be experienced when unripened' means to be experienced in an unripened existence; this is a designation for 'to be experienced in a future life.' Even so, there is this distinction here: kamma done in the first period of life that gives its result in the first, middle, or last period; kamma done in the middle period that gives its result in the middle or last period; and kamma done in the last period that gives its result right there—this is called 'to be experienced in this very life.' But that kamma which gives its result within seven days is called 'to be experienced when ripened.' That can be wholesome or unwholesome.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – puṇṇo nāma kira duggatamanusso rājagahe sumanaseṭṭhiṃ nissāya vasati. Tamenaṃ ekadivasaṃ nagaramhi nakkhatte saṅghuṭṭhe seṭṭhi āha – “sace ajja kasissasi, dve ca goṇe naṅgalañca labhissasi. Kiṃ nakkhattaṃ kīḷissasi, kasissasī”ti. Kiṃ me nakkhattena, kasissāmīti? Tena hi ye goṇe icchasi, te gahetvā kasāhīti. So kasituṃ gato. Taṃ divasaṃ sāriputtatthero nirodhā vuṭṭhāya “kassa saṅgahaṃ karomī”ti? Āvajjanto puṇṇaṃ disvā pattacīvaraṃ ādāya tassa kasanaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Puṇṇo kasiṃ ṭhapetvā therassa dantakaṭṭhaṃ datvā mukhodakaṃ [V 4.0004] adāsi. Thero sarīraṃ paṭijaggitvā kammantassa avidūre [M 4.0004] nisīdi bhattābhihāraṃ olokento. Athassa bhariyaṃ bhattaṃ āharantiṃ disvā antarāmaggeyeva attānaṃ dassesi.

Herein, these are the stories. It is said that a poor man named Puṇṇa lived in Rājagaha, dependent on the merchant Sumana. One day, when a festival was proclaimed in the city, the merchant said to him: 'If you plow today, you will receive two oxen and a plow. Will you play at the festival, or will you plow?' 'What is the festival to me? I will plow.' 'Then take whichever oxen you wish and plow.' So he went to plow. That day, the Elder Sāriputta, having arisen from the attainment of cessation, reflected, 'Whom shall I support?' Seeing Puṇṇa, he took his bowl and robe and went to his plowing place. Puṇṇa, having stopped plowing, gave the Elder a tooth-stick and offered water for his face. The Elder, having tended to his body, sat down not far from the workplace, looking out for the bringing of the meal. Then, seeing his wife bringing the meal, he showed himself to her right in the middle of the path.

Sā sāmikassa āhaṭabhattaṃ therassa patte pakkhipitvā puna gantvā aññaṃ bhattaṃ sampādetvā divā agamāsi. Puṇṇo ekavāraṃ kasitvā nisīdi. Sāpi bhattaṃ gahetvā āgacchantī āha – “sāmi pātova te bhattaṃ āhariyittha, antarāmagge pana [P 4.0006] sāriputtattheraṃ disvā taṃ tassa datvā aññaṃ pacitvā āharantiyā me ussūro jāto, mā kujjhi sāmī”ti. Bhaddakaṃ te bhadde kataṃ, mayā therassa pātova dantakaṭṭhañca mukhodakañca dinnaṃ, amhākaṃyevānena piṇḍapātopi paribhutto, ajja therena katasamaṇadhammassa mayaṃ bhāgino jātāti cittaṃ pasādesi. Ekavāraṃ kasitaṭṭhānaṃ suvaṇṇameva ahosi. So bhuñjitvā kasitaṭṭhānaṃ olokento vijjotamānaṃ disvā uṭṭhāya yaṭṭhiyā paharitvā rattasuvaṇṇabhāvaṃ jānitvā “rañño akathetvā paribhuñjituṃ na sakkā”ti gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā taṃ sabbaṃ sakaṭehi āharāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe rāsiṃ kāretvā “kassimasmiṃ nagare ettakaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ atthī”ti pucchi. Kassaci natthīti ca vutte seṭṭhiṭṭhānamassa adāsi. So puṇṇaseṭṭhi nāma jāto.

She, having placed the meal brought for her husband into the Elder's bowl, went back again, prepared another meal, and came late in the day. Puṇṇa, having plowed one round, sat down. She too, bringing the meal, approached and said: 'Master, your meal was brought early in the morning, but on the way, seeing the Elder Sāriputta, I gave it to him. It became late for me while I was cooking and bringing another meal. Do not be angry, master.' 'Good lady, what you have done is good. By me, the Elder was given a tooth-stick and water for his face early in the morning. By him, our almsfood has also been partaken of. Today, we have become partakers of the recluse's duties performed by the Elder.' Thus he gladdened her mind. The place plowed once became pure gold. After eating, as he was looking at the plowed area, he saw it shining, and getting up, he struck it with his stick. Realizing it was red gold, he thought, 'It is not possible to enjoy this without informing the king,' and went and reported it to the king. The king had it all brought by carts and made into a pile in the royal courtyard. He asked, 'Who in this city has this much gold?' And when it was said, 'No one,' he gave him the position of a great merchant. He became known as Puṇṇa the Merchant.

Aparampi vatthu – tasmiṃyeva rājagahe kāḷaveḷiyo nāma duggato atthi. Tassa bhariyā paṇṇambilayāguṃ paci. Mahākassapatthero nirodhā vuṭṭhāya “kassa saṅgahaṃ karomī”ti āvajjanto taṃ disvā gantvā gehadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Sā pattaṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ tattha pakkhipitvā therassa adāsi, thero vihāraṃ gantvā satthu upanāmesi. Satthā attano yāpanamattaṃ gaṇhi, sesaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pahosi. Kāḷavaḷiyopi taṃ ṭhānaṃ patto cūḷakaṃ labhi. Mahākassapo satthāraṃ kāḷavaḷiyassa vipākaṃ pucchi. Satthā “ito sattame divase seṭṭhicchattaṃ labhissatī”ti āha. Kāḷavaḷiyo taṃ kathaṃ sutvā gantvā bhariyāya ārocesi.

There is also another story. In that same Rājagaha, there was a poor man named Kāḷavaḷiya. His wife cooked sour leaf-gruel. The Elder Mahākassapa, having arisen from the attainment of cessation and reflecting, 'Whom shall I support?', saw that man, went, and stood at his house door. She took the bowl, put all of the gruel into it, and gave it to the Elder. The Elder went to the monastery and offered it to the Teacher. The Teacher took just enough for His own sustenance; the rest was sufficient for five hundred monks. Kāḷavaḷiya also, having come to that place, received a small portion. Mahākassapa asked the Teacher about the result of Kāḷavaḷiya's deed. The Teacher said, 'On the seventh day from today, he will receive the merchant's umbrella.' Kāḷavaḷiya, hearing these words, went and told his wife.

Tadā ca rājā nagaraṃ anusañcaranto bahinagare jīvasūle nisinnaṃ [P 4.0007] purisaṃ addasa. Puriso rājānaṃ disvā uccāsaddaṃ akāsi “tumhākaṃ me [M 4.0005] bhuñjanabhattaṃ pahiṇatha devā”ti. Rājā “pesessāmī”ti vatvā sāyamāsabhatte upanīte saritvā “imaṃ harituṃ samatthaṃ jānāthā”ti āha, nagare sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ cāresuṃ. Tatiyavāre kāḷavaḷiyassa bhariyā aggahesi[V 4.0005]. Atha naṃ rañño dassesuṃ, sā purisavesaṃ gahetvā pañcāvudhasannaddhā bhattapātiṃ gahetvā nagarā nikkhami. Bahinagare tāle adhivattho dīghatālo nāma yakkho taṃ rukkhamūlena gacchantiṃ disvā “tiṭṭha tiṭṭha bhakkhosi me”ti āha. Nāhaṃ tava bhakkho, rājadūto ahanti. Kattha gacchasīti. Jīvasūle nisinnassa purisassa santikanti. Mamapi ekaṃ sāsanaṃ harituṃ sakkhissasīti. Āma sakkhissāmīti. “Dīghatālassa bhariyā sumanadevarājadhītā kāḷī puttaṃ vijātā”ti āroceyyāsi. Imasmiṃ tālamūle satta nidhikumbhiyo atthi, tā tvaṃ gaṇheyyāsīti. Sā “dīghatālassa bhariyā sumanadevarājadhītā kāḷī puttaṃ vijātā”ti ugghosentī agamāsi.

At that time, the king, while touring the city, saw a man sitting on a stake of impalement outside the city. The man, seeing the king, cried out loudly, 'O lord, send me your meal!' The king, saying, 'I will send it,' remembered when the evening meal was brought and said, 'Do you know of anyone capable of taking this?' They had a reward of a thousand announced in the city. On the third time, the wife of Kāḷavaḷiya accepted. Then they presented her to the king. She, having taken on the guise of a man and being armed with five weapons, took the food bowl and left the city. Outside the city, a yakkha named Dīghatāla, who dwelt in a palm tree, saw her passing by the foot of the tree and said, 'Stop, stop! You are my prey!' She replied, 'I am not your prey; I am a royal messenger.' 'Where are you going?' he asked. 'To the man sitting on the stake of impalement.' 'Will you be able to carry a message for me too?' 'Yes, I will be able.' 'You should announce: "Dīghatāla’s wife, Kāḷī, daughter of King Sumanadeva, has given birth to a son." At the foot of this palm tree there are seven pots of treasure; you may take them.' She went on, proclaiming aloud, 'Dīghatāla’s wife, Kāḷī, daughter of King Sumanadeva, has given birth to a son!'

Sumanadevo yakkhasamāgame nisinno sutvā “eko manusso amhākaṃ piyapavattiṃ āharati, pakkosatha na”nti sāsanaṃ sutvā pasanno “imassa rukkhassa parimaṇḍalacchāyāya pharaṇaṭṭhāne nidhikumbhiyo tuyhaṃ dammī”ti āha. Jīvasūle nisinnapuriso bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā mukhapuñchanakāle itthiphassoti ñatvā cūḷāya ḍaṃsi, sā asinā attano cūḷaṃ [P 4.0008] chinditvā rañño santikaṃyeva gatā. Rājā bhattabhojitabhāvo kathaṃ jānitabboti? Cūḷasaññāyāti vatvā rañño ācikkhitvā taṃ dhanaṃ āharāpesi. Rājā aññassa ettakaṃ dhanaṃ nāma atthīti. Natthi devāti. Rājā tassā patiṃ tasmiṃ nagare dhanaseṭṭhiṃ akāsi. Mallikāyapi deviyā vatthu kathetabbaṃ. Imāni tāva kusalakamme vatthūni.

Sumanadeva, seated in the assembly of yakkhas, heard her proclamation and, being pleased, said, 'A human brings us pleasant news. Summon her! I give you the treasure pots in the place covered by the round shadow of this tree.' The man seated on the stake of impalement, having eaten the meal, realized at the time of wiping his mouth that it was the touch of a woman and, with lust arisen, bit her topknot. She cut off her own topknot with her sword and went to the king. The king asked, 'How is it to be known that the meal has been eaten?' She replied, 'By the sign of the topknot,' and after explaining the matter to the king, had the wealth brought. The king asked, 'Does anyone else have such wealth?' 'No, lord,' they replied. The king made her husband, Kāḷavaḷiya, the treasurer-merchant in that city. The story of Queen Mallikā should also be told. These, for now, are the stories concerning wholesome kamma.

Nandamāṇavako pana uppalavaṇṇāya theriyā vippaṭipajji, tassa mañcato uṭṭhāya nikkhamitvā gacchantassa mahāpathavī bhijjitvā okāsamadāsi, tattheva mahānarakaṃ paviṭṭho. Nandopi goghātako paṇṇāsa vassāni goghātakakammaṃ katvā ekadivasaṃ bhojanakāle maṃsaṃ alabhanto ekassa jīvamānakagoṇassa jivhaṃ chinditvā aṅgāresu pacāpetvā khādituṃ āraddho. Athassa jivhā mūle chijjitvā bhattapātiyaṃyeva patitā, so viravanto kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatti. Nandopi yakkho aññena yakkhena [M 4.0006] saddhiṃ ākāsena gacchanto sāriputtattheraṃ navoropitehi kesehi rattibhāge abbhokāse nisinnaṃ disvā sīse paharitukāmo itarassa yakkhassa ārocetvā tena vāriyamānopi pahāraṃ datvā ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmīti viravanto tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne bhūmiṃ pavisitvā mahāniraye nibbattoti imāni akusalakamme vatthūni.

Furthermore, the young man Nanda misbehaved with the Theri Uppalavaṇṇā. As he got up from the bed and was going out, the great earth split open and gave him an opening; right there he entered a great hell. Nanda the cattle-butcher, too, after having done the work of a cattle-butcher for fifty years, one day at mealtime, not getting any meat, cut out the tongue of a living bull, had it roasted on coals, and began to eat it. Then his tongue was severed at the root and fell right into his food bowl. Screaming, he passed away and was reborn in hell. Nanda the yakkha, too, while traveling through the sky with another yakkha, saw the Elder Sāriputta sitting in the open air at night with his newly shaven head. Desiring to strike him on the head, he informed the other yakkha. Though restrained by him, he delivered the blow and, screaming, "I'm burning! I'm burning!" he entered the earth right at that spot and was reborn in a great hell. These are the stories of unwholesome kamma.

Yaṃ [V 4.0006] pana antamaso maraṇasantikepi kataṃ kammaṃ bhavantare vipākaṃ deti, taṃ sabbaṃ samparāyavedanīyaṃ [P 4.0009] nāma. Tattha yo aparihīnassa jhānassa vipāko nibbattissati, so idha nibbattitavipākoti vutto. Tassa mūlabhūtaṃ kammaṃ neva diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ na samparāyavedanīyanti, na vicāritaṃ, kiñcāpi na vicāritaṃ, samparāyavedanīyameva panetanti veditabbaṃ. Yo paṭhamamaggādīnaṃ bhavantare phalasamāpattivipāko, so idha nibbattitaguṇotveva vutto. Kiñcāpi evaṃ vutto, maggakammaṃ pana paripakkavedanīyanti veditabbaṃ. Maggacetanāyeva hi sabbalahuṃ phaladāyikā anantaraphalattāti.

Whatever kamma is done, even near the time of death, that gives its result in another existence—all that is called 'to be experienced in a future existence.' Herein, the result that will arise from an un-declined jhāna is said to be 'a result that has been made to arise' in this present life. As for its root kamma, the position that it is 'neither to be experienced in the present life nor to be experienced in a future existence' is not investigated. Although it is not investigated, it should be known that this kamma is indeed 'to be experienced in a future existence.' The result of fruition-attainment in a future existence, arising from the first path and so on, is said to be a quality that has been made to arise in this present life. Although it is said thus, the kamma of the path should be understood as 'to be experienced when ripe.' For the volition of the path itself is the swiftest of all in giving fruit, because of the immediacy of its fruit.

8. Bahuvedanīyanti saññābhavūpagaṃ. Appavedanīyanti asaññābhavūpagaṃ. Savedanīyanti savipākaṃ kammaṃ. Avedanīyanti avipākaṃ kammaṃ. Evaṃ santeti imesaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīnaṃ kammānaṃ upakkamena samparāyavedanīyādi bhāvakāraṇassa alābhe sati. Aphaloti nipphalo niratthakoti. Ettāvatā aniyyānikasāsane payogassa aphalataṃ dassetvā padhānacchedakavādo nāma dassitoti veditabbo. Sahadhammikā vādānuvādāti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇā hutvā nigaṇṭhānaṃ vādā ca anuvādā ca. Gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchantīti viññūhi garahitabbaṃ kāraṇaṃ āgacchanti. “Vādānuppattā gārayhaṭṭhānā”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – parehi vuttena kāraṇena sakāraṇā [P 4.0010] nigaṇṭhānaṃ vādaṃ anuppattā taṃ vādaṃ sosentā milāpentā dukkaṭakammakārinotiādayo dasa gārayhaṭṭhānā āgacchanti.

8. 'To be experienced much' refers to kamma that leads to the realm of perception. 'To be experienced little' refers to kamma that leads to the realm of non-perception. 'To be experienced' refers to kamma with its result. 'Not to be experienced' refers to kamma without result. This being so, when, through exertion, there is no attainment of the cause for these kammas—such as those to be experienced in this very life—to become those to be experienced in a future existence and so forth, they are called 'fruitless.' 'Fruitless' means without fruit, useless. To this extent, having shown the fruitlessness of exertion in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, it should be understood that what is called the 'doctrine of cutting off exertion' is thus shown. ‘Arguments and counter-arguments among fellow practitioners’ means the arguments and counter-arguments of the Nigaṇṭhas, which are well-reasoned because of what was said by others. They come to a blameworthy state—that is, they come to a state blameworthy by the wise. Alternatively, there is also the reading: “Having come to arguments, to blameworthy states.” Its meaning is: those who, being well-reasoned by virtue of what was stated by others, having encountered the argument of the Nigaṇṭhas, and causing that argument to dry up and wither, come to ten blameworthy states, such as being doers of difficult deeds.

9. Saṅgatibhāvahetūti niyatibhāvakāraṇā. Pāpasaṅgatikāti pāpaniyatino. Abhijātihetūti chaḷabhijātihetu.

9. 'Cause of association' means the cause of a fixed destiny. 'Those of evil association' means those of a fixed evil destiny. 'Cause of birth' means the cause of the six kinds of birth.

10. Evaṃ [M 4.0007] nigaṇṭhānaṃ upakkamassa aphalataṃ dassetvā idāni niyyānikasāsane upakkamassa vīriyassa ca saphalataṃ dassetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha anaddhabhūtanti anadhibhūtaṃ. Dukkhena anadhibhūto nāma manussattabhāvo vuccati, na taṃ addhabhāveti nābhibhavatīti attho. Tampi nānappakārāya dukkarakārikāya payojento dukkhena addhabhāveti nāma. Ye pana sāsane pabbajitvā āraññakā vā honti rukkhamūlikādayo vā, te dukkhena na addhabhāventi nāma. Niyyānikasāsanasmiñhi vīriyaṃ sammāvāyāmo nāma hoti.

9. Having thus shown the fruitlessness of the Nigaṇṭhas' exertion, now to show the fruitfulness of exertion and energy in the teaching that leads to liberation, the Buddha says, 'And how, monks,' and so on. Herein, 'not afflicted' means not overpowered. The human existence is called 'not overpowered by suffering'; that is, suffering does not afflict or overpower it. But when one engages even that existence in various kinds of difficult practices, one is said to afflict it with suffering. Those, however, who have gone forth in this teaching and are forest-dwellers or dwell at the roots of trees and so on, are not said to afflict themselves with suffering. For in the teaching that leads to liberation, energy is called 'right effort.'

Thero [V 4.0007] panāha – yo issarakule nibbatto sattavassiko hutvā alaṅkatappaṭiyatto pituaṅke nisinno ghare bhattakiccaṃ katvā nisinnena bhikkhusaṅghena anumodanāya kariyamānāya tisso sampattiyo dassetvā saccesu pakāsitesu arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, mātāpitūhi vā “pabbajissasi tātā”ti vutto “āma pabbajissāmī”ti vatvā [P 4.0011] nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā vihāraṃ nīto tacapañcakaṃ uggaṇhitvā nisinno kesesu ohāriyamānesu khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, navapabbajito vā pana manosilātelamakkhitena sīsena punadivase mātāpitūhi pesitaṃ kājabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vihāre nisinnova arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ na dukkhena attānaṃ addhabhāveti nāma. Ayaṃ pana ukkaṭṭhasakkāro. Yo dāsikucchiyaṃ nibbatto antamaso rajatamuddikampi piḷandhitvā gorakapiyaṅgumattenāpi sarīraṃ vilimpetvā “pabbājetha na”nti nīto khuragge vā punadivase vā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayampi na anaddhabhūtaṃ attānaṃ dukkhena addhabhāveti nāma.

10. The Elder, however, said: "A person who is born in a wealthy family, being seven years old, adorned and prepared, sitting on his father's lap, when the community of monks, having finished their meal in the house and being seated, is giving the anumodanā, and the three accomplishments are shown, when the truths are explained, he attains Arahantship. Or, when asked by his parents, 'Dear one, will you go forth?', and he replies, 'Yes, I will go forth,' he is bathed, adorned, and led to the monastery. Having learned the contemplation of the five parts ending with the skin, while seated, as his hair is being removed, he attains Arahantship right at the razor's edge. Or, a newly ordained one, with his head anointed with realgar and oil, the next day eats the rice-meal carried on a pole sent by his parents and, while just sitting in the monastery, attains Arahantship. This one is not said to afflict himself with suffering. This, indeed, is a person of the highest honor. One who is born in a slave girl’s womb, at the very least wearing a silver ring, his body smeared with just a little goraka and piyaṅgu perfume, is led forth with the words, 'Let him go forth.' Whether at the razor’s edge or the next day, he attains Arahantship. This one, too, does not afflict his unafflicted self with suffering."

Dhammikaṃ sukhaṃ nāma saṅghato vā gaṇato vā uppannaṃ catupaccayasukhaṃ. Anadhimucchitoti taṇhāmucchanāya amucchito. Dhammikañhi sukhaṃ na pariccajāmīti na tattha gedho kātabbo. Saṅghato hi uppannaṃ salākabhattaṃ vā vassāvāsikaṃ vā “idamatthaṃ eta”nti paricchinditvā saṅghamajjhe bhikkhūnaṃ antare paribhuñjanto pattantare padumaṃ viya sīlasamādhivipassanāmaggaphalehi vaḍḍhati. Imassāti paccuppannānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ mūlabhūtassa. Dukkhanidānassāti taṇhāya. Sā hi pañcakkhandhadukkhassa nidānaṃ. Saṅkhāraṃ padahatoti sampayogavīriyaṃ [M 4.0008] karontassa. Virāgo [P 4.0012] hotīti maggena virāgo hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “saṅkhārapadhānena me imassa dukkhanidānassa virāgo hotī”ti evaṃ pajānātīti iminā sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā kathitā. Dutiyavārena tassa sampayogavīriyassa majjhattatākāro kathito. So yassa hi khvāssāti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – so puggalo yassa dukkhanidānassa saṅkhārapadhānena virāgo hoti, saṅkhāraṃ tattha padahati, maggapadhānena padahati. Yassa pana dukkhanidānassa ajjhupekkhato upekkhaṃ bhāventassa virāgo hoti, upekkhaṃ tattha bhāveti, maggabhāvanāya bhāveti. Tassāti tassa puggalassa.

Righteous happiness, so-called, is the happiness in the four requisites, arisen from the Sangha or from a group. 'Not infatuated' means: not infatuated by the infatuation that is craving. Indeed, greed should not be made in that regard with the thought, 'I do not abandon righteous happiness.' For, having determined, 'This is for this purpose,' one who partakes of ticket-food or a rains-residence robe arisen from the Sangha, in the midst of the Sangha, among the bhikkhus, grows through virtue, concentration, insight, path, and fruition, like a lotus among the leaves of a water lily. 'Of this' means: of that which is the root of the five present aggregates. 'Of the cause of suffering' means: of craving. For that craving is the cause of the suffering of the five aggregates. 'One who exerts effort' means: of one who makes conjoined effort. 'Dispassion arises' means: dispassion arises through the path. This is what is meant: 'He understands thus: "For me, through the exertion of effort, dispassion for this cause of suffering arises."' By this, the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge is explained. By the second turn, the state of neutrality of that conjoined effort is explained. Regarding 'So yassa hi khvāssa,' this is the condensed meaning: That person, for whom dispassion for a certain cause of suffering arises through the exertion of effort, exerts effort in that regard; he exerts effort by means of path-exertion. Furthermore, for whom dispassion for a certain cause of suffering arises from looking on with equanimity while developing equanimity, he develops equanimity in that regard; he develops it by means of path-cultivation. 'Of him' means: of that person.

11. Paṭibaddhacittoti chandarāgena baddhacitto. Tibbacchandoti bahalacchando. Tibbāpekkhoti [V 4.0008] bahalapatthano. Santiṭṭhantinti ekato tiṭṭhantiṃ. Sañjagghantinti mahāhasitaṃ hasamānaṃ. Saṃhasantinti sitaṃ kurumānaṃ.

11. 'A mind bound' means: a man whose mind is bound by desire and lust. 'Of intense desire' means: a man of strong desire. 'Of intense longing' means: a man of strong aspiration. 'Standing together' means: a woman standing together. 'Laughing loudly' means: a woman laughing a great laugh. 'Smiling together' means: a woman making a smile.

Evameva kho, bhikkhaveti ettha idaṃ opammavibhāvanaṃ – eko hi puriso ekissā itthiyā sāratto ghāsacchādanamālālaṅkārādīni datvā ghare vāseti. Sā taṃ aticaritvā aññaṃ sevati. So “nūna ahaṃ assā anurūpaṃ sakkāraṃ na karomī”ti sakkāraṃ vaḍḍhesi. Sā bhiyyosomattāya aticaratiyeva. So – “ayaṃ sakkariyamānāpi aticarateva, ghare me vasamānā anatthampi kareyya, nīharāmi na”nti parisamajjhe alaṃvacanīyaṃ katvā “mā puna gehaṃ pāvisī”ti vissajjesi. Sā kenaci [P 4.0013] upāyena tena saddhiṃ santhavaṃ kātuṃ asakkontī naṭanaccakādīhi saddhiṃ vicarati. Tassa purisassa taṃ disvā neva uppajjati domanassaṃ, somanassaṃ pana uppajjati.

Just so, bhikkhus, here is the explanation of the simile: A certain man, being infatuated with a woman, provides her with food, clothing, garlands, ornaments, and so on, and has her dwell in his house. She, transgressing against him, consorts with another man. He thinks, 'Surely I am not providing her with suitable respect,' and so he increases the respect shown to her. She transgresses all the more. He thinks, 'This one, though respected, still transgresses. While living in my house, she might cause me harm. I shall drive her out.' Then, in the midst of an assembly, having made a declaration of 'enough!', he dismisses her, saying, 'Do not enter my house again!' She, being unable by any means to establish intimacy with him, wanders about with actors, dancers, and the like. When that man sees her, sorrow does not arise in him; on the contrary, joy arises.

Tattha purisassa itthiyā sārattakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno attabhāve ālayo. Ghāsacchādanādīni datvā ghare vasāpanakālo viya attabhāvassa paṭijagganakālo. Tassā aticaraṇakālo viya jaggiyamānasseva attabhāvassa pittapakopādīnaṃ vasena sābādhatā. “Attano anurūpaṃ sakkāraṃ alabhantī aticaratī”ti sallakkhetvā sakkāravaḍḍhanaṃ viya “bhesajjaṃ alabhanto evaṃ hotī”ti sallakkhetvā [M 4.0009] bhesajjakaraṇakālo. Sakkāre vaḍḍhitepi puna aticaraṇaṃ viya pittādīsu ekassa bhesajje kariyamāne sesānaṃ pakopavasena puna sābādhatā. Parisamajjhe alaṃvacanīyaṃ katvā gehā nikkaḍḍhanaṃ viya “idāni te nāhaṃ dāso na kammakaro, anamatagge saṃsāre taṃyeva upaṭṭhahanto vicariṃ, ko me tayā attho, chijja vā bhijja vā”ti tasmiṃ anapekkhataṃ āpajjitvā vīriyaṃ thiraṃ katvā maggena kilesasamugghātanaṃ. Naṭanaccakādīhi naccamānaṃ vicarantiṃ disvā yathā tassa purisassa domanassaṃ na uppajjati, somanassameva uppajjati, evameva imassa bhikkhuno arahattaṃ pattassa pittapakopādīnaṃ vasena ābādhikaṃ attabhāvaṃ disvā domanassaṃ na uppajjati, “muccissāmi vata khandhaparihāradukkhato”ti somanassameva uppajjatīti. Ayaṃ pana upamā “paṭibaddhacittassa domanassaṃ uppajjati, appaṭibaddhacittassa natthetanti ñatvā [P 4.0014] itthiyā chandarāgaṃ pajahati, evamayaṃ bhikkhu saṅkhāraṃ vā padahantassa upekkhaṃ vā bhāventassa dukkhanidānaṃ [V 4.0009] pahīyati, no aññathāti ñatvā tadubhayaṃ sampādento dukkhanidānaṃ pajahatī”ti etamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ āgatāti veditabbā.

In this simile, the bhikkhu's attachment to his own person is to be seen as like the man's period of infatuation with the woman. The period of caring for his own person is to be seen as like the period of providing her with food, clothing, and so on, and having her dwell in his house. The state of affliction of his own person, by way of disturbances of bile and so on even while it is being cared for, is to be seen as like her period of transgression. Reflecting, 'She transgresses because she does not receive suitable respect,' and then increasing the respect shown, is like reflecting, 'My person becomes thus because it does not receive medicine,' and then applying medicine. Her transgressing again even when the respect is increased is like the person's renewed affliction by way of the disturbance of the other humors when medicine is being applied for one of them, such as bile. The expelling of her from the house after making a declaration of 'enough!' in the midst of an assembly is like the eradication of the defilements by means of the path, after becoming indifferent to the person, making one's effort firm, and saying, 'Now I am not your slave, not your worker. In this beginningless saṃsāra I have wandered attending only to you. What use have I for you? Let it be cut off or let it be broken!' Just as for that man, seeing her wandering about and dancing with actors, dancers, and the like, sorrow does not arise, but only joy arises, even so for this bhikkhu who has attained Arahantship, seeing his own person afflicted by way of disturbances of bile and so on, sorrow does not arise. Rather, only joy arises with the thought: 'Indeed, I shall be freed from the suffering of maintaining the aggregates!' This simile, it should be known, has been presented to clarify this meaning: 'Sorrow arises for one with a bound mind; it does not exist for one with an unbound mind. Knowing this, one abandons sensual desire for a woman. In the same way, this bhikkhu, knowing that the cause of suffering is abandoned by one who exerts effort or by one who develops equanimity, and not otherwise, accomplishes both and abandons the cause of suffering.'

12. Yathā sukhaṃ kho me viharatoti yena sukhena viharituṃ icchāmi tena, me viharato. Padahatoti pesentassa. Ettha ca yassa sukhā paṭipadā asappāyā, sukhumacīvarāni dhārentassa pāsādike senāsane vasantassa cittaṃ vikkhipati, dukkhā paṭipadā sappāyā, chinnabhinnāni thūlacīvarāni dhārentassa susānarukkhamūlādīsu vasantassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

12. 'As I dwell happily' means: dwelling with whatever happiness I wish to dwell. 'Of one who exerts' means: of one who sends forth the mind towards Nibbāna. And here, this was said in reference to a person for whom the pleasant practice is unsuitable—whose mind is distracted when wearing fine robes and dwelling in a pleasant lodging—but for whom the difficult practice is suitable—whose mind becomes unified when wearing rough, torn-and-tattered robes and dwelling in places like a charnel ground or at the foot of a tree.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ, usukāro viya hi jātijarāmaraṇabhīto yogī daṭṭhabbo, vaṅkakuṭilajimhatejanaṃ viya vaṅkakuṭilajimhacittaṃ, dve alātā viya kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ, tejanaṃ ujuṃ karontassa kañjikatelaṃ viya saddhā, namanadaṇḍako viya lokuttaramaggo, ussukārassa vaṅkakuṭilajimhatejanaṃ kañjikatelena sinehetvā alātesu tāpetvā namanadaṇḍakena ujukaraṇaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno vaṅkakuṭilajimhacittaṃ saddhāya sinehetvā kāyikacetasikavīriyena tāpetvā [M 4.0010] lokuttaramaggena ujukaraṇaṃ, usukārasseva evaṃ ujukatena tejanena sapattaṃ vijjhitvā sampattianubhavanaṃ viya imassa yogino tathā ujukatena [P 4.0015] cittena kilesagaṇaṃ vijjhitvā pāsādike senāsane nirodhavaratalagatassa phalasamāpattisukhānubhavanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idha tathāgato sukhāpaṭipadākhippābhiññabhikkhuno, dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññabhikkhuno ca paṭipattiyo kathitā, itaresaṃ dvinnaṃ na kathitā, tā kathetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Imāsu vā dvīsu kathitāsu itarāpi kathitāva honti, āgamanīyapaṭipadā pana na kathitā, taṃ kathetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Sahāgamanīyāpi vā paṭipadā kathitāva, adassitaṃ pana ekaṃ buddhuppādaṃ dassetvā ekassa kulaputtassa nikkhamanadesanaṃ arahattena vinivaṭṭessāmīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Herein, 'Just so' is the statement connecting the simile with its subject. It should be understood thus: like an arrow-maker, the yogī who fears birth, aging, and death should be understood. Like a crooked, bent, and warped arrow-shaft, the crooked, bent, and warped mind should be understood. Like two firebrands, the bodily and mental energy should be understood. Like the sour gruel and oil used by one straightening an arrow-shaft, faith should be understood. Like the straightening rod, the supramundane path should be understood. Like the arrow-maker's straightening of a crooked, bent, and warped arrow-shaft by anointing it with sour gruel and oil, heating it over two firebrands, and using the straightening rod, so too, the straightening of this monk's crooked, bent, and warped mind by moistening it with faith, heating it with bodily and mental energy, and using the supramundane path should be understood. Like the arrow-maker's experiencing of prosperity after piercing the enemy with the arrow thus straightened, so too, the experiencing of the bliss of fruition attainment by this yogī—who has reached the supreme plane of Nibbāna, in a pleasant lodging, after piercing the host of defilements with the mind thus straightened—should be understood. Herein, the practices of the monk with pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge and of the monk with difficult practice and slow direct knowledge have been taught by the Blessed One. The practices of the other two have not been taught. To teach them, He began this discourse. Or, when these two have been taught, the others are also considered taught. However, the practice leading to the path and fruit, which is insight, has not been taught. To teach that, He began this discourse. Or alternatively, the practice together with that which leads to the path and fruit has indeed been taught. However, to show a meaning not yet shown, that is: 'Having shown a previously unrevealed arising of a Buddha, I shall bring to a conclusion with Arahantship the teaching on the renunciation of a certain clansman'—to show this meaning, the Blessed One began this discourse. The rest is clear in all places.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses (Papañcasūdanī)

Devadahasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta is concluded.

2. Pañcattayasuttavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Pañcattaya Sutta

21. Evaṃ [V 4.0010] me sutanti pañcattayasuttaṃ. Tattha eketi ekacce. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti paribbajupagatabhāvena samaṇā jātiyā brāhmaṇā, lokena vā samaṇāti ca brāhmaṇāti ca evaṃ sammatā. Aparantaṃ kappetvā vikappetvā gaṇhantīti aparantakappikā. Aparantakappo vā etesaṃ atthītipi aparantakappikā. Ettha [P 4.0016] ca antoti “sakkāyo kho, āvuso, eko anto”tiādīsu (a. ni. 6.61) viya idha koṭṭhāso adhippeto. Kappoti taṇhādiṭṭhiyo. Vuttampi cetaṃ “kappoti uddānato dve kappā taṇhākappo ca diṭṭhikappo cā”ti. Tasmā taṇhādiṭṭhivasena anāgataṃ khandhakoṭṭhāsaṃ kappetvā ṭhitāti aparantakappikāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tesaṃ evaṃ aparantaṃ kappetvā ṭhitānaṃ punappunaṃ uppajjanavasena aparantameva anugatā diṭṭhīti aparantānudiṭṭhino. Te evaṃdiṭṭhino taṃ aparantaṃ ārabbha āgamma paṭicca aññampi janaṃ diṭṭhigatikaṃ karontā [M 4.0011] anekavihitāni adhivuttipadāni abhivadanti. Anekavihitānīti anekavidhāni. Adhivuttipadānīti adhivacanapadāni. Atha vā bhūtamatthaṃ adhibhavitvā yathāsabhāvato aggahetvā vattanato adhivuttiyoti diṭṭhiyo vuccanti, adhivuttīnaṃ padāni adhivuttipadāni, diṭṭhidīpakāni vacanānīti attho.

2. The Pañcattaya Sutta begins with 'Thus have I heard.' Herein, 'some' means certain ones. 'Ascetics and brahmins' means: they are ascetics by way of having undertaken the wandering life, and brahmins by birth; or alternatively, they are regarded by the world as 'ascetics' and 'brahmins'. Because they speculate upon and variously speculate upon the future and grasp it, they are called 'speculators on the future'. Or alternatively, because they have a speculation about the future, they are also called speculators on the future. And here, by the word 'anta' (end), as in passages such as 'Friend, the personal identity is one end,' a 'portion' is intended here. 'Kappa' (speculation) means craving and views. And this has been said: 'As to "kappa," in summary there are two "kappas": the kappa of craving and the kappa of views.' Therefore, because they stand speculating on a future portion of the aggregates by way of craving and views, they are called 'speculators on the future'—thus the meaning should be understood here. Of those who stand thus speculating on the future, their view follows after the future by way of arising again and again; therefore, they are called 'those whose views follow after the future'. They, holding such views, concerning, based on, and depending on that future, while making other people adopt their views, declare various kinds of terms of assertion. 'Of various kinds' means of many sorts. 'Terms of assertion' means terms of designation. Or alternatively, because they proceed by overpowering the true meaning and not grasping it in accordance with its real nature, views are called 'assertions'; the expressions of these assertions are 'terms of assertion'. The meaning is: words that indicate a view.

Saññīti saññāsamaṅgī. Arogoti nicco. Ittheketi itthaṃ eke, evameketi attho. Iminā soḷasa saññīvādā kathitā, asaññīti iminā aṭṭha asaññīvādā, nevasaññīnāsaññīti iminā aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, sato vā pana sattassāti iminā satta ucchedavādā. Tattha satoti vijjamānassa. Ucchedanti upacchedaṃ. Vināsanti adassanaṃ. Vibhavanti bhavavigamaṃ. Sabbānetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ [P 4.0017] vāti iminā pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā kathitā. Tattha diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati, tattha tattha paṭiladdhaattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhavūpasamanti attho. Santaṃ vāti saññītiādivasena tīhākārehi santaṃ. Tīṇi hontīti saññī attātiādīni santaattavasena ekaṃ, itarāni dveti evaṃ tīṇi.

21. “Percipient” (saññī) means endowed with perception. “Without illness” (arogo) means permanent. “Some hold” (ittheke) should be parsed as “thus some” (itthaṃ eke); the meaning is just that. By this, sixteen doctrines of a percipient self are stated; by “non-percipient” (asaññī), eight doctrines of a non-percipient self; by “neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient” (nevasaññīnāsaññī), eight doctrines of a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self; and by “of a being that, however, exists” (sato vā pana sattassa), seven doctrines of annihilationism. Therein, “of an existing being” (sato) means of one that is present. “Annihilation” (ucchedaṃ) means cutting off. “Perishing” (vināsaṃ) means disappearance. “Non-existence” (vibhavaṃ) means cessation of existence. All these are just synonyms for one another. By “or Nibbāna in the present life” (diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā), five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life are stated. Therein, “the presently visible state” (diṭṭhadhamma) is called the directly experienceable state; this is a designation for the individual existence obtained in this or that state of being. Nibbāna in the presently visible state is “Nibbāna in the present life” (diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ); the meaning is the pacification of suffering in this very individual existence. By “or existing” (santaṃ vā) is meant existing in three modes, by way of “percipient,” and so on. “There are three” (tīṇi honti) means: the doctrines beginning with “the self is percipient” are one by way of an existing self, that is, eternalism; the other two—the annihilationist view and the view of Nibbāna in the present life—make three.

22. Rūpiṃ [V 4.0011] vāti karajarūpena vā kasiṇarūpena vā rūpiṃ. Tattha lābhī kasiṇarūpaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, takkī ubhopi rūpāni gaṇhātiyeva. Arūpinti arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ vā, ṭhapetvā saññākkhandhaṃ sesaarūpadhamme vā attāti paññapentā lābhinopi takkikāpi evaṃ paññapenti. Tatiyadiṭṭhi pana missakagāhavasena pavattā, catutthā takkagāheneva. Dutiyacatukke paṭhamadiṭṭhi samāpannakavārena kathitā, dutiyadiṭṭhi asamāpannakavārena, tatiyadiṭṭhi suppamattena vā sarāvamattena vā kasiṇaparikammavasena, catutthadiṭṭhi vipulakasiṇavasena kathitāti veditabbā.

By 'or having form' (rūpiṃ vā) is meant having form either through the body born of parents or through a kasiṇa-form. Therein, the one who has attained meditative absorption takes the kasiṇa-form as self; the reasoner takes both forms as self. By 'formless' (arūpiṃ) is meant that both attainers and reasoners declare thus, positing as self either the sign of a formless attainment or the remaining immaterial states, having excluded the perception aggregate. The third view, however, proceeds by way of a mixed grasp, while the fourth proceeds by way of reasoning alone. In the second tetrad, it should be understood that the first view is stated by way of one who has attained absorption; the second view, by way of one who has not attained absorption; the third view, by way of kasiṇa preliminary work of a small measure, such as a winnowing basketful or a saucerful; and the fourth view, by way of an extensive kasiṇa.

Etaṃ vā panekesaṃ upātivattatanti saññītipadena saṅkhepato vuttaṃ saññāsattakaṃ atikkantānanti attho. Apare aṭṭhakanti vadanti. Tadubhayaṃ parato āvibhavissati. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – keci hi etā satta [M 4.0012] vā aṭṭha vā saññā [P 4.0018] samatikkamituṃ sakkonti, keci pana na sakkonti. Tattha ye sakkonti, teva gahitā. Tesaṃ pana ekesaṃ upātivattataṃ atikkamituṃ sakkontānaṃ yathāpi nāma gaṅgaṃ uttiṇṇesu manussesu eko dīghavāpiṃ gantvā tiṭṭheyya, eko tato paraṃ mahāgāmaṃ; evameva eke viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ appamāṇaṃ āneñjanti vatvā tiṭṭhanti, eke ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Tattha viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ tāva dassetuṃ viññāṇakasiṇameketi vuttaṃ. Parato “ākiñcaññāyatanameke”ti vakkhati. Tayidanti taṃ idaṃ diṭṭhigatañca diṭṭhipaccayañca diṭṭhārammaṇañca. Tathāgato abhijānātīti. Iminā paccayena idaṃ nāma dassanaṃ gahitanti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena jānāti.

“This, however, some surpass”—this is briefly stated by the word 'percipient' (saññī), meaning those who have surpassed the group of seven perceptions. Others say there are eight. Both will become clear later. Herein is the concise meaning: for some are able to transcend these seven or eight perceptions, while others are not. Among them, only those who are able are referred to. For some of them who are able to surpass, it is as when, among people who have crossed the Ganges, one might go to Dīghavāpī and stop, while another might go further to a great village. Similarly, some stop, saying, “The base of infinite consciousness is infinite, imperturbable,” while others stop at the base of nothingness. Herein, to show the base of infinite consciousness, it is said, “some, the consciousness-kasiṇa.” Later, it will be said, “some, the base of nothingness.” ‘Tayidaṃ’ means this: this view, the condition for the view, and the object of the view. “The Tathāgata directly knows” means: he knows with distinguished knowledge that “By this condition, this particular view is held.”

Idāni tadeva vitthārento ye kho te bhontotiādimāha. Yā vā pana etāsaṃ saññānanti yā vā pana etāsaṃ “yadi rūpasaññāna”nti evaṃ vuttasaññānaṃ. Parisuddhāti nirupakkilesā. Paramāti uttamā. Aggāti seṭṭhā. Anuttariyā akkhāyatīti asadisā kathīyati. Yadi rūpasaññānanti iminā catasso rūpāvacarasaññā kathitā. Yadi arūpasaññānanti iminā ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇañcāyatanasaññā. Itarehi pana dvīhi padehi samāpannakavāro ca asamāpannakavāro ca kathitoti evametā [P 4.0019] koṭṭhāsato aṭṭha, atthato pana satta saññā honti. Samāpannakavāro hi purimāhi chahisaṅgahitoyeva. Tayidaṃ saṅkhatanti taṃ idaṃ sabbampi saññāgataṃ saddhiṃ diṭṭhigatena saṅkhataṃ paccayehi samāgantvā kataṃ. Oḷārikanti [V 4.0012] saṅkhatattāva oḷārikaṃ. Atthi kho pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhoti etesaṃ pana saṅkhatanti vuttānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma atthi. Atthetanti iti viditvāti taṃ kho pana nibbānaṃ “atthi eta”nti evaṃ jānitvā. Tassa nissaraṇadassāvīti tassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇadassī nibbānadassī. Tathāgato tadupātivattoti taṃ saṅkhataṃ atikkanto samatikkantoti attho.

Now, elaborating on that, he says, “Those venerable ones,” and so on. “Or whatever of these perceptions” refers to these perceptions spoken of thus: “If of form-perceptions.” “Perfectly pure” means free from defilements. “Supreme” means the highest. “Foremost” means the best. “Declared unsurpassable” means spoken of as incomparable. By “If of form-perceptions,” the four form-sphere perceptions are described. By “If of formless perceptions,” the perceptions of the base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness are described. By the other two phrases, the case of one who has attained and the case of one who has not attained are described. Thus, these are eight in terms of divisions, but in substance, there are seven perceptions, for the case of one who has attained is indeed included in the previous six. “This is conditioned” means all this that has come under perception, together with that which has come under views, is conditioned, made by the coming together of conditions. “Coarse” means that precisely because it is conditioned, it is coarse. “But there is indeed the cessation of formations” means that for these formations, which are said to be ‘conditioned,’ there is what is called Nibbāna, designated as ‘cessation.’ “Having known, ‘This exists’” means having known thus, “That Nibbāna indeed exists.” “One who sees the escape from that” means one who sees the escape from that conditioned state, one who sees Nibbāna. “The Tathāgata has surpassed that” means he has transcended, completely surpassed that conditioned state—this is the meaning.

23. Tatrāti tesu aṭṭhasu asaññīvādesu. Rūpiṃ vātiādīni saññīvāde vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Ayañca yasmā asaññīvādo, tasmā idha dutiyacatukkaṃ na vuttaṃ. Paṭikkosantīti paṭibāhanti paṭisedhenti. Saññā [M 4.0013] rogotiādīsu ābādhaṭṭhena rogo, sadosaṭṭhena gaṇḍo, anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sallaṃ. Āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vātiādīsu paṭisandhivasena āgatiṃ, cutivasena gatiṃ, cavanavasena cutiṃ, upapajjanavasena upapattiṃ, punappunaṃ uppajjitvā aparāparaṃ vaḍḍhanavasena vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ. Kāmañca [P 4.0020] catuvokārabhave rūpaṃ vināpi viññāṇassa pavatti atthi, sese pana tayo khandhe vinā natthi. Ayaṃ pana pañho pañcavokārabhavavasena kathito. Pañcavokāre hi ettake khandhe vinā viññāṇassa pavatti nāma natthi. Vitaṇḍavādī panettha “aññatra rūpātiādivacanato arūpabhavepi rūpaṃ, asaññābhave ca viññāṇaṃ atthi, tathā nirodhasamāpannassā”ti vadati. So vattabbo – byañjanacchāyāya ce atthaṃ paṭibāhasi, āgatiṃ vātiādivacanato taṃ viññāṇaṃ pakkhidvipadacatuppadā viya uppatitvāpi gacchati, padasāpi gacchati, govisāṇavalliādīni viya ca vaḍḍhatīti āpajjati. Ye ca bhagavatā anekasatesu suttesu tayo bhavā vuttā, te arūpabhavassa abhāvā dveva āpajjanti. Tasmā mā evaṃ avaca, yathā vuttamatthaṃ dhārehīti.

23. Herein, ‘therein’ (tatra) refers to those eight doctrines of the non-percipient. The phrases beginning ‘Having form…’ should be understood in the very way explained in the doctrine of the percipient. And since this is the doctrine of the non-percipient, the second tetrad is not stated here. ‘They decry’ (paṭikkosanti) means they ward off, they repudiate. In the phrases beginning ‘Perception is a disease,’ ‘disease’ (rogo) is in the sense of affliction; ‘boil’ (gaṇḍo) is in the sense of being faulty; and ‘dart’ (sallaṃ) is in the sense of having penetrated. In the phrases beginning ‘coming or going,’ ‘coming’ (āgati) is in the sense of rebirth-linking; ‘going’ (gati) is in the sense of death; ‘passing away’ (cuti) is in the sense of shifting; ‘reappearance’ (upapatti) is in the sense of arising; and ‘growth, increase, expansion’ (vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ) is in the sense of growing successively after arising again and again. Although it is true that in the four-constituent existence there is an occurrence of consciousness even without form, it does not occur without the remaining three aggregates. But this question is spoken in terms of the five-constituent existence. For in the five-constituent existence, there is no such thing as an occurrence of consciousness without these aggregates. Herein, a sophist argues: “From the statement beginning ‘apart from form,’ it follows that form exists even in the formless existence, and consciousness exists in the non-percipient existence, and likewise for one who has attained cessation.” He should be told in return: “If you reject the meaning for the shadow of the letter, then from the statement beginning ‘coming or…,’ it would follow that consciousness, like birds, bipeds, and quadrupeds, goes by flying up and goes on foot, and grows like a cow's horn, creepers, and so on. And the three existences that have been spoken of by the Blessed One in many hundreds of suttas would, due to the non-existence of the formless existence, be reduced to only two. Therefore, do not speak thus; hold to the meaning as it has been spoken.”

24. Tatrāti aṭṭhasu nevasaññīnāsaññīvādesu bhummaṃ. Idhāpi rūpiṃ vātiādīni vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Asaññā sammohoti nissaññabhāvo nāmesa sammohaṭṭhānaṃ. Yo hi kiñci na jānāti, taṃ asaññī esoti vadanti. Diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbasaṅkhāramattenāti diṭṭhaviññātabbamattena sutaviññātabbamattena mutaviññātabbamattena. Ettha ca vijānātīti viññātabbaṃ, diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbamattena pañcadvārikasaññāpavattimattenāti ayañhi ettha attho. Saṅkhāramattenāti oḷārikasaṅkhārapavattimattenāti attho. Etassa [P 4.0021] āyatanassāti etassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa[V 4.0013]. Upasampadanti paṭilābhaṃ. Byasanaṃ hetanti vināso hesa, vuṭṭhānaṃ hetanti attho. Pañcadvārikasaññāpavattañhi oḷārikasaṅkhārapavattaṃ vā appavattaṃ katvā taṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ. Tassa pana pavattena tato vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti dasseti. Saṅkhārasamāpattipattabbamakkhāyatīti oḷārikasaṅkhārapavattiyā pattabbanti na akkhāyati. Saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattipattabbanti saṅkhārānaṃyeva avasesā bhāvanāvasena sabbasukhumabhāvaṃ pattā saṅkhārā, tesaṃ pavattiyā etaṃ pattabbanti attho. Evarūpesu hi saṅkhāresu pavattesu etaṃ [M 4.0014] pattabbaṃ nāma hoti. Tayidanti taṃ idaṃ etaṃ sukhumampi samānaṃ saṅkhataṃ saṅkhatattā ca oḷārikaṃ.

24. Herein, 'tatrā' (therein) is a term in the locative case referring to the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Here too, the phrases beginning with 'rūpī' ('possessed of form') should be understood in the manner already stated. 'Non-perception is delusion' means this state of being without perception is a ground for deep delusion. For of one who knows nothing at all, they say, 'This one is non-percipient.' 'Merely by the formations of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized' means merely by what is seen and cognized, merely by what is heard and cognized, and merely by what is sensed and cognized. And here, 'one cognizes' (vijānāti), therefore it is 'to be cognized' (viññātabbaṃ); 'merely by what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized' means merely by the occurrence of perception at the five sense-doors. This is the meaning here. 'Merely by formations' means merely by the occurrence of gross formations. 'Of this base' means of this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. 'Upasampadaṃ' (attainment) means acquisition. 'Byasanaṃ hetaṃ' (this is a calamity) means this is its destruction; 'vuṭṭhānaṃ hetaṃ' (this is an emergence) means it is the cause for emerging from that state. For that attainment must be entered upon by causing the non-occurrence of perception at the five sense-doors or the non-occurrence of gross formations. But it is shown that by their occurrence, emergence from that state happens. 'It is said to be attainable by the attainment of formations' means that it is not said to be attainable by the occurrence of gross formations. 'Attainable by the attainment of residual formations' means that the remainder of the formations themselves, which through the power of development have reached a state of utter subtlety—by the occurrence of these, this base is attained. For when such formations are occurring, this is what is called attainable. 'Tayidaṃ' is to be divided as 'taṃ idaṃ'. This attainment, although it is subtle, is conditioned; and because it is conditioned, it is gross.

25. Tatrāti sattasu ucchedavādesu bhummaṃ. Uddhaṃ saranti uddhaṃ vuccati anāgatasaṃsāravādo, anāgataṃ saṃsāravādaṃ sarantīti attho. Āsattiṃyeva abhivadanti lagganakaṃyeva vadanti. “Āsatta”ntipi pāṭho, taṇhaṃyeva vadantīti attho. Iti pecca bhavissāmāti evaṃ pecca bhavissāma. Khattiyā bhavissāma, brāhmaṇā bhavissāmāti evamettha nayo netabbo. Vāṇijūpamā [P 4.0022] maññeti vāṇijūpamā viya vāṇijapaṭibhāgā vāṇijasadisā mayhaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Sakkāyabhayāti sakkāyassa bhayā. Te hi yatheva “cattāro kho, mahārāja, abhayassa bhāyanti. Katame cattāro? Gaṇḍuppādo kho, mahārāja, bhayā pathaviṃ na khādati ‘mā pathavī khiyī’ti, konto kho, mahārāja, ekapādena tiṭṭhati ‘mā pathavī osīdī’ti, kikī kho, mahārāja, uttānā seti ‘mā ambhā undriyī’ti, brāhmaṇadhammiko kho, mahārāja, brahmacariyaṃ na carati ‘mā loko ucchijjī’ti ime cattāro abhayassa bhāyanti, evaṃ sakkāyassa bhāyanti”. Sakkāyaparijegucchāti tameva tebhūmakasaṅkhātaṃ sakkāyaṃ parijigucchamānā. Sā gaddulabaddhoti daṇḍake rajjuṃ pavesetvā baddhasunakho. Evamevimeti ettha daḷhatthambho viya khīlo viya ca tebhūmakadhammasaṅkhāto sakkāyo daṭṭhabbo, sā viya diṭṭhigatiko, daṇḍako viya diṭṭhi, rajju viya taṇhā, gaddulena bandhitvā thambhe vā khīle vā upanibaddhasunakhassa attano dhammatāya chinditvā gantuṃ asamatthassa anuparidhāvanaṃ viya diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhidaṇḍake pavesitāya taṇhārajjuyā bandhitvā sakkāye upanibaddhassa anuparidhāvanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

25. Herein, 'tatrā' (therein) is a term in the locative case referring to the seven annihilationist doctrines. 'Uddhaṃ saranti' (they recall upwards) means that 'upwards' is a term for the doctrine of the future round of rebirths; the meaning is that they recall the doctrine of the future round of rebirths. 'Āsattiṃyeva abhivadanti' (they declare only attachment) means they speak only of clinging. There is also the reading 'āsattaṃ', which means they speak only of craving. 'Iti pecca bhavissāma' (Thus, after death, we shall be) means 'Thus, after death, we shall be.' 'We shall be khattiyas,' 'We shall be brahmins'—in this way the method should be understood here. 'Vāṇijūpamā maññe' (I consider them like merchants) means they appear in my knowledge as being like merchants, having the character of merchants, similar to merchants. 'Sakkāyabhayā' means 'out of fear of the existing body.' For they fear the existing body just as these four, it is said, fear what is not to be feared: 'Great King, four fear what is not to be feared. Which four? Great King, the earthworm, out of fear, does not eat the earth, thinking, “May the earth not be exhausted!” Great King, the crane stands on one foot, thinking, “May the earth not subside!” Great King, the kikī bird lies on its back, thinking, “May the sky not fall!” Great King, the brahmin Dhammika does not practice the holy life, thinking, “May the world not be cut off!” These four fear what is not to be feared.' 'Sakkāyaparijegucchā' (loathing of the existing body) means they loathe that very existing body which is reckoned as belonging to the three realms. 'Sā gaddulabaddho' (that dog tied with a leash) means a dog tied by a rope passed through a stick. Herein, the existing body, reckoned as the states of the three realms, should be seen as a firm post or a stake; the person holding wrong views is like the dog; wrong view is like the stick; craving is like the rope. Just as a dog, tied by a leash to a post or a stake, unable to break it and go free by its own nature, runs round and round, so should be understood the running round and round of the person holding wrong views, who is bound to the existing body by the rope of craving passed through the stick of wrong view.

26. Imāneva pañcāyatanānīti imāneva pañca kāraṇāni. Iti mātikaṃ ṭhapentenapi pañceva [V 4.0014] ṭhapitāni, nigamentenapi pañceva nigamitāni, bhājentena pana cattāri [P 4.0023] bhājitāni. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ kuhiṃ paviṭṭhanti. Ekattanānattavasena dvīsu padesu paviṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ.

26. 'Imāneva pañcāyatanāni' (these five bases themselves) means these five causes themselves. Thus, when laying down the matrix, five were laid down; and when concluding, five were concluded; but when analyzing, four were analyzed. The question is asked: 'Where does the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life enter?' It should be understood that it enters into two places by way of unity and diversity.

27. Evañca catucattālīsa aparantakappike dassetvā idāni aṭṭhārasa pubbantakappike dassetuṃ santi, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha atītakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ pubbantaṃ kappetvā vikappetvā gaṇhantīti pubbantakappikā. Pubbantakappo [M 4.0015] vā etesaṃ atthīti pubbantakappikā. Evaṃ sesampi pubbe vuttappakāraṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sassato attā ca loko cāti rūpādīsu aññataraṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gahetvā sassato amaro nicco dhuvoti abhivadanti. Yathāha “rūpaṃ attā ceva loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti vitthāro. Asassatādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca paṭhamavādena cattāro sassatavādā vuttā, dutiyavādena satta ucchedavādā.

27. Thus, having shown the forty-four views of those who speculate about the future end, now, in order to show the eighteen views of those who speculate about the past beginning, he spoke the words beginning with 'Santi, bhikkhave' (There are, O bhikkhus...). Herein, they are called 'pubbantakappikā' (speculators about the past beginning) because they conjecture and speculate about the past beginning—reckoned as the portion of past time—and grasp it as such. Or, they have speculation about the past beginning, hence they are called 'pubbantakappikā'. Similarly, the remaining terms should also be understood in the manner and way previously explained. Regarding 'The self and the world are eternal': taking one of the aggregates, such as form, to be the self and the world, they declare it to be eternal, immortal, permanent, and stable. As it is said: 'They proclaim form as the self and the world, and as eternal,' thus they proclaim the self and the world. This is the detailed explanation. The same method applies to the views beginning with 'non-eternal' and so forth. And here, by the first doctrine, four eternalist views are stated; by the second doctrine, seven annihilationist views.

Nanu cete heṭṭhā āgatā, idha kasmā puna gahitāti. Heṭṭhā tattha tattha mato tattha tattheva ucchijjatīti dassanatthaṃ āgatā. Idha pana pubbenivāsalābhī diṭṭhigatiko atītaṃ passati, na anāgataṃ, tassa evaṃ hoti “pubbantato āgato attā idheva ucchijjati, ito paraṃ na gacchatī”ti imassatthassa dassanatthaṃ gahitā. Tatiyavādena cattāro ekaccasassatavādā vuttā, catutthavādena cattāro amarāvikkhepikā vuttā. Antavāti sapariyanto paricchinno parivaṭumo. Avaḍḍhitakasiṇassa [P 4.0024] taṃ kasiṇaṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gahetvā evaṃ hoti. Dutiyavādo vaḍḍhitakasiṇassa vasena vutto, tatiyavādo tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho avaḍḍhitakasiṇassa, catutthavādo takkivasena vutto. Anantaracatukkaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Surely, have these not been addressed previously? Why are they taken up again here? Previously, they were mentioned to show this: 'Having died in this or that existence, one is annihilated right in that very existence.' Here, however, they are taken up to show this meaning for one who has gained the power of remembering past lives and holds such a view, who sees the past but not the future, for whom it occurs thus: 'The self, having come from a past beginning, is annihilated right here; it does not go beyond this.' By the third proposition, four types of partial-eternalists are spoken of. By the fourth proposition, four types of eel-wrigglers are spoken of. 'Finite' means having a boundary, limited, and rounded. For one with an undeveloped kasiṇa, this view arises from taking that kasiṇa to be the self and the world. The second proposition is spoken of on account of one with a developed kasiṇa; the third, on account of one who has developed the kasiṇa horizontally but not upwards and downwards; the fourth proposition is spoken of by means of reasoning. The subsequent tetrad is just as was explained previously.

Ekantasukhīti nirantarasukhī. Ayaṃ diṭṭhi lābhījātissaratakkīnaṃ vasena uppajjati. Lābhino hi pubbenivāsañāṇena khattiyādikule ekantasukhameva attano jātiṃ anussarantassa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati. Tathā jātissarassa paccuppannaṃ sukhamanubhavato atītāsu sattasu jātīsu tādisameva attabhāvaṃ anussarantassa. Takkissa pana idha sukhasamaṅgino “atītepāhaṃ evameva ahosi”nti takkeneva uppajjati.

'Exclusively happy' means continuously happy. This view arises on account of those who have gained higher knowledge, those who remember past births, and reasoners. For one who has gained this knowledge, when, by means of the knowledge of past lives, they recollect their own birth in a khattiya family or the like as being exclusively happy, such a view arises. Similarly, for one who remembers past births, while experiencing present happiness and recollecting a similar state of existence in seven past lives, this view arises. But for the reasoner, who is endowed with happiness here, it arises simply through reasoning: 'In the past, too, I was just like this.'

Ekantadukkhīti [V 4.0015] ayaṃ diṭṭhi lābhino nuppajjati. So hi ekanteneva idha jhānasukhena sukhī hoti. Idha dukkhena phuṭṭhassa pana jātissarassa takkisseva ca sā uppajjati. Tatiyā idha vokiṇṇasukhadukkhānaṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ uppajjati, tathā catutthā diṭṭhi. Lābhino hi idāni catutthajjhānavasena adukkhamasukhassa, pubbe catutthajjhānikameva brahmalokaṃ anussarantassa[M 4.0016]. Jātissarassāpi paccuppanne majjhattassa, anussarantassāpi majjhattabhūtaṭṭhānameva anussarantassa, takkinopi paccuppanne majjhattassa, atītepi evaṃ bhavissatīti takkeneva gaṇhantassa esā diṭṭhi uppajjati. Ettāvatā cattāro sassatavādā, cattāro ekaccasassatikā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā[P 4.0025], dve adhicca-samuppannikāti aṭṭhārasapi pubbantakappikā kathitā honti.

'Exclusively suffering': this view does not arise for one who has gained higher knowledge, for they are indeed happy here exclusively with the bliss of jhāna. But for one who remembers past births and for a reasoner who is afflicted by suffering here, that view arises. The third view arises here for all of those who experience mixed pleasure and pain; similarly the fourth view. Indeed, this view arises for one who has gained knowledge, who is now neither-suffering-nor-pleasant by virtue of the fourth jhāna, while recollecting a Brahma-world that was exclusively of the fourth jhāna in the past; also for one who remembers past births, who is neutral in the present and recollects only a place that was neutral; and also for a reasoner, who is neutral in the present and holds through reasoning alone, 'It was thus in the past too.' Thus far, the four eternalists, the four partial-eternalists, the four finitists-and-infinitists, the four eel-wrigglers, and the two holding fortuitous origination—all eighteen speculators on the past have been explained.

28. Idāni diṭṭhuddhāraṃ uddharanto tatra, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha paccattaṃyeva ñāṇanti paccakkhañāṇaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Pariyodātanti pabhassaraṃ. Sabbapadehi vipassanāñāṇaṃyeva kathitaṃ. Saddhādayo hi pañca dhammā bāhirasamayasmimpi honti, vipassanāñāṇaṃ sāsanasmiṃyeva. Tattha ñāṇabhāgamattameva pariyodapentīti mayamidaṃ jānāmāti evaṃ tattha ñāṇakoṭṭhāsaṃ otārentiyeva. Upādānamakkhāyatīti na taṃ ñāṇaṃ, micchādassanaṃ nāmetaṃ, tasmā tadapi tesaṃ bhavantānaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ akkhāyatīti attho. Athāpi taṃ jānanamattalakkhaṇattā ñāṇabhāgamattameva, tathāpi tassa dassanassa anupātivattanato upādānapaccayato ca upādānameva. Tadupātivattoti taṃ diṭṭhiṃ atikkanto. Ettāvatā cattāro sassatavādā, cattāro ekaccasassatikā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā, dve adhiccasamuppannikā, soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā, aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, satta ucchedavādā, pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti brahmajāle āgatā dvāsaṭṭhipi diṭṭhiyo kathitā honti. Brahmajāle pana kathite idaṃ suttaṃ akathitameva hoti. Kasmā? Idha tato atirekāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā āgatattā. Imasmiṃ pana kathite brahmajālaṃ kathitameva hoti.

28. Now, extracting the exposition of views, the Blessed One said, 'Therein, bhikkhus,' and so on. Therein, 'knowledge for oneself' means direct knowledge. 'Perfectly pure' means without defilement. 'Perfectly purified' means luminous. By all these terms, insight knowledge alone is spoken of. For the five qualities beginning with faith exist even in external systems, but insight knowledge exists only in the Dispensation. Therein, 'they purify only a portion of knowledge' means they introduce a part that is like knowledge, thinking, 'We know this.' 'It is called clinging' means: that is not knowledge; it is called wrong view. Therefore, for those venerable ones, that too is called the clinging of wrong view. And although it is only a portion of knowledge because its characteristic is mere knowing, still, because of not transcending that view and because it is conditioned by clinging, it is just clinging. 'One who has passed beyond that' means one who has transcended that view. Thus far, the four eternalists, the four partial-eternalists, the four finitists-and-infinitists, the four eel-wrigglers, the two holding fortuitous origination, the sixteen perceptionists, the eight non-perceptionists, the eight neither-perceptionists-nor-non-perceptionists, the seven annihilationists, and the five holding Nibbāna here-and-now—all sixty-two views that come in the Brahmajāla have been explained. However, when the Brahmajāla is explained, this sutta remains unexplained. Why? Because here, the personality view is presented in addition to those. But when this sutta is explained, the Brahmajāla is indeed explained.

30. Idāni imā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo uppajjamānā sakkāyadiṭṭhipamukheneva uppajjantīti dassetuṃ idha, bhikkhave, ekaccotiādimāha. Tattha [P 4.0026] paṭinissaggāti pariccāgena. Kāmasaṃyojanānaṃ [V 4.0016] anadhiṭṭhānāti pañcakāmaguṇataṇhānaṃ nissaṭṭhattā. Pavivekaṃ pītinti sappītikajjhānadvayapītiṃ. Nirujjhatīti jhānanirodhena nirujjhati. Samāpattito pana vuṭṭhitassa niruddhā nāma hoti. Yatheva [M 4.0017] hi “adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya nirodhā uppajjati nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ, nirāmisasukhassa nirodhā uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā”ti ettha na ayamattho hoti – catutthajjhānanirodhā tatiyajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti. Ayaṃ panettha attho – catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhāya tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjati, tatiyajjhānā vuṭṭhāya catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjatīti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Uppajjati domanassanti hīnajjhānapariyādānakadomanassaṃ. Samāpattito vuṭṭhitacittassa pana kammanīyabhāvo kathito.

30. Now, to show that when these sixty-two views arise, they arise with the personality view as their forerunner, the Blessed One said, 'Here, bhikkhus, someone,' and so on. Therein, 'paṭinissaggā' means by relinquishment. 'Anadhiṭṭhānā kāmasaṃyojanānaṃ' means non-adherence to the fetters of sensual pleasure, because of having discarded craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Pavivekaṃ pītiṃ' means the joy of the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. 'Nirujjhati' means it ceases with the cessation of the jhāna. For one who has emerged from the attainment, however, it is called 'ceased.' Just as in the passage, 'From the cessation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly bliss arises; from the cessation of unworldly bliss, neither-suffering-nor-pleasant feeling arises,' the meaning is not this: that from the cessation of the fourth jhāna, one attains and dwells in the third jhāna. This is the meaning here: emerging from the fourth jhāna, one attains the third jhāna; emerging from the third jhāna, one attains the fourth jhāna. This sequence should be understood thus. 'Domanassaṃ uppajjati' means the displeasure that takes over due to a lower jhāna. But for the mind that has emerged from the attainment, a state of workability is spoken of.

Pavivekā pītīti sā eva jhānadvayapīti. Yaṃ chāyā jahatīti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ chāyā jahati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmiṃ ṭhāne chāyā atthi, tasmiṃ ātapo natthi. Yasmiṃ ātapo atthi, tasmiṃ chāyā natthīti.

'Pavivekā pīti' (joy born of seclusion) is that very joy of the two jhānas. 'Yaṃ chāyā jahati' means the place which the shadow leaves. What is meant? In whichever place there is shadow, in that place there is no sunlight. In whichever place there is sunlight, in that place there is no shadow.

31. Nirāmisaṃ sukhanti tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ.

31. "Non-sensual pleasure" refers to the pleasure of the third jhāna.

32. Adukkhamasukhanti catutthajjhānavedanaṃ.

32. "Neither painful nor pleasant" refers to the feeling of the fourth jhāna.

33. Anupādānohamasmīti niggahaṇo ahamasmi. Nibbānasappāyanti nibbānassa sappāyaṃ upakārabhūtaṃ[P 4.0027]. Nanu ca maggadassanaṃ nāma sabbattha nikantiyā sukkhāpitāya uppajjati, kathametaṃ nibbānassa upakārapaṭipadā nāma jātanti, sabbattha anupādiyanavasena aggaṇhanavasena upakārapaṭipadā nāma jātaṃ. Abhivadatīti abhimānena upavadati. Pubbantānudiṭṭhinti aṭṭhārasavidhampi pubbantānudiṭṭhiṃ. Aparantānudiṭṭhinti catucattārīsavidhampi aparantānudiṭṭhiṃ. Upādānamakkhāyatīti ahamasmīti gahaṇassa sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyāpannattā diṭṭhupādānaṃ akkhāyati.

33. 'I am without clinging' means 'I am restrained.' 'Conducive to Nibbāna' means a practice that is suitable and beneficial for Nibbāna. Does not the vision of the path arise when craving for all things is dried up? How then has this become called 'the practice beneficial for Nibbāna'? It has become called 'the practice beneficial for Nibbāna' by way of not clinging and not grasping in regard to all things. 'He reviles' means he speaks disparagingly with conceit. 'View of the past' refers to the eighteen kinds of view of the past. 'View of the future' refers to the forty-four kinds of view of the future. 'Clinging is declared' means: because the grasping 'I am' is included in identity view, it is called clinging to views.

Santivarapadanti vūpasantakilesattā santaṃ uttamapadaṃ. Channaṃ phassāyatanānanti bhagavatā “yattha [V 4.0017] cakkhu ca nirujjhati rūpasaññā ca nirujjhati so āyatano veditabbo”ti ettha dvinnaṃ āyatanānaṃ paṭikkhepena nibbānaṃ dassitaṃ.

'The supreme state of peace' means the peaceful, supreme state, due to the pacification of defilements. Regarding 'the six bases of contact': in this context, Nibbāna was shown by the Blessed One through the rejection of two bases.

“Yattha āpo ca pathavī, tejo vāyo na gādhati;

Ato sarā nivattanti, ettha vaṭṭaṃ na vattati;

Ettha nāmañca rūpañca, asesaṃ uparujjhatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.27) –

"Where water, earth, fire, and air gain no footing; from there, cravings turn back. Here the round does not revolve. Here name and form cease without remainder."

Ettha pana saṅkhārapaṭikkhepena nibbānaṃ dassitaṃ.

Here, in this verse, Nibbāna is shown by the rejection of formations.

“Kattha [M 4.0018][P 4.0028] āpo ca pathavī, tejo vāyo na gādhati;

Kattha dīghañca rassañca, aṇuṃ thūlaṃ subhāsubhaṃ;

Kattha nāmañca rūpañca, asesaṃ uparujjhatī”ti. (dī. ni. 1.498);

"Where do water, earth, fire, and air find no footing? Where do long and short, fine and coarse, fair and foul cease? Where do name and form cease without remainder?"

Tatra veyyākaraṇaṃ bhavati –

The answer to that is:

“Viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ, anantaṃ sabbato pabha”nti –

"Consciousness, non-manifest, boundless, radiant all around."

Ettha saṅkhārapaṭikkhepena nibbānaṃ dassitaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte chaāyatanapaṭikkhepena dassitaṃ. Aññattha ca anupādāvimokkhoti nibbānameva dassitaṃ, idha pana arahattaphalasamāpatti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Here, Nibbāna is shown by the rejection of formations. In this sutta, however, it is shown by the rejection of the six sense-bases. Elsewhere, by the term 'liberation through non-clinging', Nibbāna itself is shown; here, however, it is the fruition-attainment of arahantship. The rest is clear throughout.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Pañcattayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pañcattaya Sutta is finished.

3. Kintisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Kinti Sutta

34. Evaṃ [V 4.0018] me sutanti kintisuttaṃ. Tattha pisinārāyanti evaṃnāmake maṇḍalapadese. Baliharaṇeti tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe bhūtānaṃ baliṃ āharanti, tasmā so baliharaṇanti vutto. Cīvarahetūti cīvarakāraṇā, cīvaraṃ paccāsīsamānoti attho. Itibhavābhavahetūti evaṃ imaṃ desanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthuṃ nissāya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave sukhaṃ vedissāmīti dhammaṃ desetīti kiṃ tumhākaṃ evaṃ hotīti attho.

34. Thus have I heard—this is the Kinti Sutta. Therein, `pisinārāyaṃ` means in a district of that name. `Baliharaṇe` means: in that grove they bring offerings to spirits, therefore it is called ‘Baliharaṇa’. `Cīvarahetu` means for the sake of a robe; that is, hoping for a robe.
