This is the meaning. `Itibhavābhavahetu` means: Does it occur to you that he teaches the Dhamma with the thought, “Relying on this basis for meritorious action consisting of the teaching, I will experience happiness in this or that existence”? This is the meaning.

35. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānātiādayo sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā lokiyalokuttarāva kathitā. Tatthāti [P 4.0029] tesu sattatiṃsāya dhammesu. Siyaṃsūti bhaveyyuṃ. Abhidhammeti visiṭṭhe dhamme, imesu sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammesūti attho. Tatra ceti idampi bodhipakkhiyadhammesveva bhummaṃ. Atthato ceva nānaṃ byañjanato cāti ettha “kāyova satipaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāva satipaṭṭhāna”nti vutte atthato nānaṃ hoti[M 4.0019], “satipaṭṭhānā”ti vutte pana byañjanato nānaṃ nāma hoti. Tadamināpīti taṃ tumhe imināpi kāraṇena jānāthāti atthañca byañjanañca samānetvā athassa ca aññathā gahitabhāvo byañjanassa ca micchā ropitabhāvo dassetabbo. Yo dhammo yo vinayoti ettha atthañca byañjanañca viññāpanakāraṇameva dhammo ca vinayo ca.

35. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness, are taught as being only mundane and supramundane. `Tattha` means among those thirty-seven factors. `Siyaṃsū` means 'they might be.' `Abhidhamme` means in the higher Dhamma, that is, in these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. And `tatra ce` is also a locative term referring only to the factors of enlightenment. Herein, regarding 'different in meaning and different in phrasing': when it is said, 'The body itself is an establishment of mindfulness, feeling itself is an establishment of mindfulness,' it is different in meaning. But when it is said, 'establishments of mindfulness,' it is called different in phrasing. `Tadamināpī` means: You should know this by this reason as well. Having reconciled the meaning and the phrasing, the fact that the meaning has been grasped otherwise and the fact that the phrasing has been wrongly applied should be shown. In 'Whatever the Dhamma, whatever the Discipline,' the meaning and the phrasing are simply the cause for making known; this is the Dhamma and the Vinaya.

37. Atthato hi kho sametīti satiyeva satipaṭṭhānanti gahitā. Byañjanato nānanti kevalaṃ byañjanameva satipaṭṭhānoti vā satipaṭṭhānāti vā micchā ropetha. Appamattakaṃ khoti suttantaṃ patvā byañjanaṃ appamattakaṃ nāma hoti. Parittamattaṃ dhanitaṃ katvā ropitepi hi nibbutiṃ pattuṃ sakkā hoti.

37. `Atthato hi kho sameti` means: it is taken that mindfulness itself is the establishment of mindfulness. `Byañjanato nānaṃ` means: you might wrongly apply just the phrasing as `satipaṭṭhāno` or `satipaṭṭhānāti`. `Appamattakaṃ kho` means: with regard to the Suttanta, the phrasing is called a small matter. For even when a minor point is misapplied with aspiration, it is possible to attain Nibbāna.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – vijayārāmavihāravāsī kireko khīṇāsavatthero dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ suttaṃ āharitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento – “samuddho samuddhoti, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano bhāsatī”ti dhanitaṃ katvā āha. Eko bhikkhu “samuddho nāma, bhante”ti [P 4.0030] āha. Āvuso, samuddhoti [V 4.0019] vuttepi samuddoti vuttepi mayaṃ loṇasāgarameva jānāma, tumhe pana no atthagavesakā, byañjanagavesakā, gacchatha mahāvihāre paguṇabyañjanānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike byañjanaṃ sodhāpethāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ akathetvāva uṭṭhāpesi. So aparabhāge mahāvihāre bheriṃ paharāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa catūsu maggesu pañhaṃ kathetvāva parinibbuto. Evaṃ suttantaṃ patvā byañjanaṃ appamattakaṃ nāma hoti.

Here is the story. They say a certain elder who was an Arahant, residing at the Vijayārāma monastery, while bringing a Sutta and teaching a meditation subject to two bhikkhus, said, making the consonant aspirated: '“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling says, ‘samuddho, samuddho’ (the ocean, the ocean).”' One bhikkhu said: 'Venerable sir, it is called ‘samuddo’ (with an unaspirated ‘d’).' The elder replied: 'Friend, whether one says ‘samuddho’ or ‘samuddo’, we understand it just as the salt ocean. You, however, are not seekers of meaning, but seekers of phrasing. Go! Have the phrasing purified in the presence of the bhikkhus at the Mahāvihāra who are skilled in phrasing.' And without teaching the meditation subject, he dismissed them. Later, that elder had a drum beaten at the Mahāvihāra, and after explaining a problem concerning the four paths to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he attained Parinibbāna. Thus, with regard to the Suttanta, the phrasing is called a small matter.

Vinayaṃ pana patvā no appamattakaṃ. Sāmaṇerapabbajjāpi hi ubhatosuddhito vaṭṭati, upasampadādikammānipi sithilādīnaṃ dhanitādikaraṇamatteneva kuppanti. Idha pana suttantabyañjanaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

With regard to the Vinaya, however, it is not a small matter. For even the novice ordination is valid only from purity on both sides, and acts such as higher ordination are invalidated merely by making lax consonants into aspirated ones, and so on. Here, however, this was said with reference to the phrasing of the Suttanta.

38. Atha catutthavāre vivādo kasmā? Saññāya vivādo. “Ahaṃ satimeva satipaṭṭhānaṃ vadāmi, ayaṃ ‘kāyo satipaṭṭhāna’nti vadatī”ti hi nesaṃ saññā hoti. Byañjanepi eseva nayo.

38. Then why is there a dispute in the fourth case? It is a dispute of understanding. For their understanding is: 'I say that mindfulness itself is the establishment of mindfulness, but this one says, “The body is the establishment of mindfulness.”' This same principle should be understood in the case of the phrasing as well.

39. Na [M 4.0020] codanāya taritabbanti na codanatthāya vegāyitabbaṃ. Ekacco hi puggalo “nalāṭe te sāsapamattā piḷakā”ti vutto “mayhaṃ nalāṭe sāsapamattaṃ piḷakaṃ passasi, attano nalāṭe tālapakkamattaṃ mahāgaṇḍaṃ na passasī”ti vadati. Tasmā puggalo upaparikkhitabbo. Adaḷhadiṭṭhīti anādānadiṭṭhī suṃsumāraṃ hadaye pakkhipanto viya daḷhaṃ na gaṇhāti.

39. `Na codanāya taritabbaṃ` means one should not be hasty for the sake of accusation. For a certain person, when told, “You have a mustard-seed-sized pimple on your forehead,” says, “You see a mustard-seed-sized pimple on my forehead, but you do not see a palm-fruit-sized great boil on your own forehead.” Therefore, a person should be examined. `Adaḷhadiṭṭhi` means a view not held firmly; one does not grasp it firmly, like one putting a crocodile into one's heart.

Upaghātoti caṇḍabhāvena vaṇaghaṭṭitassa viya dukkhuppatti. Suppaṭinissaggīti [P 4.0031] “kiṃ nāma ahaṃ āpanno, kadā āpanno”ti vā “tvaṃ āpanno, tava upajjhāyo āpanno”ti vā ekaṃ dve vāre vatvāpi “asukaṃ nāma asukadivase nāma, bhante, āpannattha, saṇikaṃ anussarathā”ti saritvā tāvadeva vissajjeti. Vihesāti bahuṃ atthañca kāraṇañca āharantassa kāyacittakilamatho. Sakkomīti evarūpo hi puggalo okāsaṃ kāretvā “āpattiṃ āpannattha, bhante”ti vutto “kadā kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti vatvā “asukadivase asukasmiṃ vatthusmi”nti vutte “na sarāmi, āvuso”ti vadati, tato “saṇikaṃ, bhante, sarathā”ti [V 4.0020] bahuṃ vatvā sārito saritvā vissajjeti. Tenāha “sakkomī”ti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

`Upaghāto` means the arising of suffering through harshness, like that of one whose wound is struck. `Suppaṭinissaggī` is one who, whether he asks, 'What offense did I commit? When did I commit it?' or is told once or twice, 'You committed an offense; your preceptor committed an offense,' when he is then told, 'Venerable sir, you committed such-and-such an offense on such-and-such a day; please recall it slowly,' upon recalling, he abandons it at that very moment. `Vihesā` is the physical and mental fatigue for one who brings up much meaning and reason. `Sakkomī`: such a person, when an opportunity is made and he is told, 'Venerable sir, you have committed an offense,' after saying, 'When? In what matter?' and being told, 'On such-and-such a day, in such-and-such a matter,' says, 'Friend, I do not remember.' Then, after being repeatedly told, 'Venerable sir, please recall it slowly,' and being reminded, he recalls and abandons it. Therefore, the Blessed One said, `sakkomī`. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Upekkhā nātimaññitabbāti upekkhā na atikkamitabbā, kattabbā janetabbāti attho. Yo hi evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ ṭhitakaṃyeva passāvaṃ karontaṃ disvāpi “nanu, āvuso, nisīditabba”nti vadati, so upekkhaṃ atimaññati nāma.

`Upekkhā nātimaññitabbā` means equanimity should not be transgressed; it should be practiced, it should be generated. This is the meaning. For one who, upon seeing such a person urinating while standing, says, “Friend, should you not be seated?”—such a one is called one who disdains equanimity.

40. Vacīsaṃhāroti vacanasañcāro. Imehi kathitaṃ amūsaṃ antaraṃ paveseyya, tumhe imehi idañcidañca vuttāti amūhi kathitaṃ imesaṃ antaraṃ paveseyyāti attho. Diṭṭhipaḷāsotiādīhi cittassa anārādhaniyabhāvo kathito. Taṃ jānamāno samāno garaheyyāti taṃ satthā jānamāno samāno nindeyya amheti. Etaṃ [P 4.0032] panāvuso, dhammanti etaṃ kalahabhaṇḍanadhammaṃ.

40. `Vacīsaṃhāro` means the carrying of speech back and forth. The meaning is: one might introduce what was said by these among those, and what was said by those among these, saying, 'You were told this and that by these people.' Through `diṭṭhipalāso`, etc., the state of the mind being unpleasable is taught. `Taṃ jānamāno samāno garaheyya` means: the Teacher, being aware of this, would censure us. `Etaṃ panāvuso, dhammaṃ` means this nature of quarreling and contention.

Tañceti [M 4.0021] taṃ saññattikārakaṃ bhikkhuṃ. Evaṃ byākareyyāti mayā ete suddhante patiṭṭhāpitāti avatvā yena kāraṇena saññatti katā, tadeva dassento evaṃ byākareyya. Tāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvāti ettha dhammoti sāraṇīyadhammo adhippeto. Na ceva attānantiādīsu “brahmalokappamāṇo hesa aggi uṭṭhāsi, ko etamaññatra mayā nibbāpetuṃ samattho”ti hi vadanto attānaṃ ukkaṃseti nāma. “Ettakā janā vicaranti, okāso laddhuṃ na sakkā, ekopi ettakamattaṃ nibbāpetuṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti vadamāno paraṃ vambheti nāma. Tadubhayampesa na karoti. Dhammo panettha sammāsambuddhassa byākaraṇaṃ, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saññattikaraṇaṃ anudhammo, tadeva byākaroti nāma. Na ca koci sahadhammikoti añño cassa koci sahetuko parehi vutto vādo vā anuvādo vā garahitabbabhāvaṃ āgacchanto nāma natthi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

‘As for that’ refers to that bhikkhu who causes agreement. ‘He should respond thus’ means he should respond by explaining the reason for the agreement, without saying boastfully, ‘I have established them in purity.’ ‘Having heard that Dhamma.’ Here, ‘Dhamma’ refers to the Dhamma that should be remembered. ‘Not exalting oneself,’ etc. In this context, one who says, “A fire arose as vast as the Brahma-world—who else but me could extinguish it?” is said to exalt himself. One who says, “So many people wander about, yet no opportunity can be found; not even one among them is capable of extinguishing even this much,” is said to disparage others. He does neither of these two. Here, the Dhamma is the discourse of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha; the causing of agreement among those bhikkhus is the teaching that accords with the Dhamma, and that is what he is said to declare. ‘And no one with legitimate grounds’ means there is no other accusation or subsequent accusation spoken by others with reason that would come to be considered blameworthy. The rest is clear throughout.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Kintisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Kinti Sutta is finished.

4. Sāmagāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Sāmagāma Sutta.

41. Evaṃ [V 4.0021] me sutanti sāmagāmasuttaṃ. Tattha sāmagāmeti sāmākānaṃ ussannattā evaṃladdhanāme gāme. Adhunā kālaṅkatoti sampati kālaṃ kato. Dvedhikajātāti [P 4.0033] dvejjhajātā dvebhāgajātā. Bhaṇḍanādīsu bhaṇḍanaṃ pubbabhāgakalaho, taṃ daṇḍādānādivasena paṇṇattivītikkamavasena ca vaddhitaṃ kalaho, “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsī”tiādikaṃ viruddhavacanaṃ vivādo. Vitudantāti vitujjantā. Sahitaṃ meti mama vacanaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti yaṃ tava adhiciṇṇaṃ cirakālasevanavasena paguṇaṃ, taṃ mama vādaṃ āgamma nivattaṃ. Āropito te vādoti tuyhaṃ upari mayā doso āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti bhattapuṭaṃ ādāya taṃ taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vādappamokkhatthāya uttari [M 4.0022] pariyesamāno cara. Nibbeṭhehi vāti atha mayā āropitavādato attānaṃ mocehi. Sace pahosīti sace sakkosi. Vadhoyevāti maraṇameva.

41. Thus have I heard. This is the Sāmagāma Sutta. Therein, ‘Sāmagāma’ is a village so named because of the abundance of sāmāka plants. ‘Recently passed away’ means he has recently died. ‘Divided into two factions’ means split into two, divided into two parts. Among ‘quarrels’ and so forth: a ‘quarrel’ (bhaṇḍana) is the initial stage of conflict. When that has grown by way of taking up weapons and so forth, and by way of transgressing precepts, it becomes a ‘conflict’ (kalaho). A ‘dispute’ (vivādo) is contradictory speech such as, ‘You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya.’ ‘Piercing with words’ means piercing with verbal spears. ‘My words are fitting’ means my words are beneficial. ‘Your long-practiced views have been overturned’ means what you have long practiced and become accustomed to has now been reversed on account of my argument. ‘A charge has been placed on you’ means a fault has been placed upon you by me. ‘Go forth for the sake of release from this argument’ means: taking a food-packet, approaching one place after another, and wandering further seeking a teacher for the sake of release from this argument. ‘Or free yourself’ means: then free yourself from the fault I have placed on you. ‘If you are able’ means if you are capable. ‘It is simply death’ means it is death itself, by way of killing one another.

Nāṭaputtiyesūti nāṭaputtassa antevāsikesu. Nibbinnarūpāti [P 4.0034] ukkaṇṭhitasabhāvā, abhivādanādīni na karonti. Virattarūpāti vigatapemā. Paṭivānarūpāti tesaṃ nipaccakiriyato nivattasabhāvā. Yathā tanti yathā ca durakkhātādisabhāve dhammavinaye nibbinnavirattapaṭivānarūpehi bhavitabbaṃ, tatheva jātāti attho. Durakkhāteti dukkathite. Duppavediteti duviññāpite. Anupasamasaṃvattaniketi rāgādīnaṃ upasamaṃ kātuṃ asamattho. Bhinnathūpeti bhinnapatiṭṭhe. Ettha hi nāṭaputtova nesaṃ patiṭṭhena thūpo, so pana bhinno mato. Tena vuttaṃ “bhinnathūpe”ti. Appaṭisaraṇeti tasseva abhāvena paṭisaraṇavirahite.

‘Among the followers of Nāṭaputta’ means among the disciples of Nāṭaputta. ‘Appearing disgusted’ means having a discontented nature; they do not perform acts of respect such as salutation. ‘Appearing detached’ means devoid of affection. ‘Appearing turned away’ means having a nature turned away from showing them deference. ‘Just as’ means: just as in a Dhamma and Discipline that is poorly taught, one should be disgusted, detached, and turned away, so too have they become; this is the meaning. ‘Poorly taught’ means badly spoken. ‘Poorly explained’ means poorly made known. ‘Not leading to peace’ means unable to bring about the calming of lust and so forth. ‘With a shattered monument’ means with a broken foundation. Here, Nāṭaputta himself was their foundation and thus their monument; but he is shattered, that is, he is dead. Therefore, it is said, ‘with a shattered monument.’ ‘Without refuge’ means without refuge due to his very absence.

Nanu cāyaṃ nāṭaputto nāḷandavāsiko, so kasmā pāvāyaṃ kālaṃkatoti. So kira upālinā gahapatinā paṭividdhasaccena dasahi gāthāhi bhāsite buddhaguṇe sutvā uṇhaṃ lohitaṃ chaḍḍesi. Atha naṃ aphāsukaṃ gahetvā pāvaṃ agamaṃsu, so tattha kālamakāsi. Kālaṃ kurumāno ca “mama laddhi aniyyānikā sārarahitā, mayaṃ tāva naṭṭhā, avasesajano mā apāyapūrako ahosi[V 4.0022]. Sace panāhaṃ ‘mama sāsanaṃ aniyyānika’nti vakkhāmi, na saddahissanti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dvepi jane na ekanīhārena uggaṇhāpeyyaṃ, te mamaccayena aññamaññaṃ vivadissanti. Satthā taṃ vivādaṃ paṭicca ekaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathessati, tato te sāsanassa mahantabhāvaṃ jātissantī”ti.

But was this Nāṭaputta not a resident of Nāḷandā? Why then did he die at Pāvā? It is said that after hearing the qualities of the Buddha spoken in ten stanzas by the householder Upāli, who had penetrated the truth, he vomited hot blood. Then, as he was unwell, they took him to Pāvā, and there he died. And as he was dying, he thought: ‘My doctrine does not lead to liberation and is devoid of essence. We are indeed lost; may the remaining people not become fillers of the woeful states. But if I say, “My teaching does not lead to liberation,” they will not believe me. What if I were to teach even two people not in the same way? After my passing, they will argue among themselves. The Teacher, on account of that dispute, will give a discourse on the Dhamma, and then they will understand the greatness of the teaching.’

Atha naṃ eko antevāsiko upasaṅkamitvā āha [P 4.0035] “bhante, tumhe dubbalā, mayhaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme sāraṃ ācikkhatha ācariyappamāṇa”nti. Āvuso, tvaṃ mamaccayena sassatanti gaṇheyyāsīti. Aparopi taṃ upasaṅkami, taṃ ucchedaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Evaṃ dvepi jane ekaladdhike akatvā bahū nānānīhārena uggaṇhāpetvā kālamakāsi. Te tassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā sannipatitvā aññamaññaṃ pucchiṃsu “kassāvuso, ācariyo sāramācikkhī”ti? Eko uṭṭhahitvā mayhanti āha. Kiṃ ācikkhīti? Sassatanti. Aparo taṃ paṭibāhitvā mayhaṃ sāraṃ ācikkhīti āha. Evaṃ sabbe “mayhaṃ sāraṃ ācikkhi, ahaṃ jeṭṭhako”ti aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ vaḍḍhetvā akkose [M 4.0023] ceva paribhāse ca hatthapādapahārādīni ca pavattetvā ekamaggena dve agacchantā nānādisāsu pakkamiṃsu, ekacce gihī ahesuṃ.

Then a certain disciple approached him and said, ‘Venerable sir, you are weak. Please tell me the essence of this Dhamma, the teacher’s reserved teaching.’ He replied, ‘Friend, after my passing, you should grasp the view of eternalism.’ Another also approached him, and he had him grasp the view of annihilationism. Thus, without making even two people hold the same view, he taught many disciples in various different ways and then died. After performing his funeral rites, they gathered and asked one another, ‘Friend, to whom did the teacher explain the essence?’ One stood up and said, ‘To me.’ ‘What did he explain?’ ‘Eternalism.’ Another, refuting that statement, said, ‘He explained the essence to me.’ In this way, all of them, claiming, ‘He explained the essence to me; I am the senior,’ increased their dispute, resorting to insults, abuse, blows with hands and feet, and the like. With not even two going by the same path, they departed in different directions; some even became householders.

Bhagavato pana dharamānakālepi bhikkhusaṅghe vivādo na uppajji. Satthā hi tesaṃ vivādakāraṇe uppannamatteyeva sayaṃ vā gantvā te vā bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā khanti mettā paṭisaṅkhā avihiṃsā sāraṇīyadhammesu ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathetvā vivādaṃ vūpasameti. Evaṃ dharamānopi saṅghassa patiṭṭhāva ahosi. Parinibbāyamānopi avivādakāraṇaṃ katvāva parinibbāyi. Bhagavatā hi sutte desitā cattāro mahāpadesā (a. ni. 4.180; dī. ni. 2.187) yāvajjadivasā bhikkhūnaṃ patiṭṭhā ca avassayo ca. Tathā khandhake desitā cattāro mahāpadesā (mahāva. 305) sutte vuttāni cattāri pañhabyākaraṇāni (a. ni. 4.42) ca. Tenevāha – “yo vo mayā, ānanda, dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216).

However, even during the Blessed One’s lifetime, no dispute arose in the Saṅgha. For whenever a cause for dispute arose, the Teacher himself would either go to them or summon those monks, and by explaining one of the principles among the states to be remembered—patience, loving-kindness, reflection with wisdom, and non-harming—he would resolve the dispute. Thus, even while he lived, he was the Saṅgha’s foundation. And as he was passing into Parinibbāna, he passed into Parinibbāna only after having established the cause for non-dispute. For the Four Great References taught by the Blessed One in the suttas have served as the foundation and refuge for the monks to this very day. Similarly, the Four Great References taught in the Khandhaka, and the Four Methods of Answering Questions mentioned in the suttas. Therefore, he declared, ‘Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and laid down for you shall be your teacher after my passing’.

42. Atha [P 4.0036] kho cundo samaṇuddesoti ayaṃ thero dhammasenāpatissa kaniṭṭhabhātiko. Taṃ bhikkhū anupasampannakāle cundo samaṇuddesoti samudācaritvā therakālepi tatheva samudācariṃsu. Tena [V 4.0023] vuttaṃ “cundo samaṇuddeso”ti. Upasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Nāṭaputte kira kālaṃkate jambudīpe manussā tattha tattha kathaṃ pavattayiṃsu – “nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto eko satthāti paññāyittha, tassa kālakiriyāya sāvakānaṃ evarūpo vivādo jāto, samaṇo pana gotamo jambudīpe cando viya sūriyo viya ca pākaṭoyeva, kīdiso nu kho samaṇe gotame parinibbute sāvakānaṃ vivādo bhavissatī”ti. Thero taṃ kathaṃ sutvā cintesi – “imaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā dasabalassa ārocessāmi, satthā ca etaṃ atthuppattiṃ katvā ekaṃ desanaṃ kathessatī”ti. So nikkhamitvā yena sāmagāmo, yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami. Ujumeva bhagavato santikaṃ agantvā yenassa upajjhāyo āyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkamīti attho. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “upajjhāyo me mahāpañño, so imaṃ sāsanaṃ [M 4.0024] satthu ārocessati, atha satthā tadanurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desessatī”ti. Kathāpābhatanti kathāmūlaṃ, mūlañhi pābhatanti vuccati. Yathāha –

42. ‘Then the novice Cunda’—this elder was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma. The monks, having addressed him as ‘Cunda the novice’ before his higher ordination, continued to address him in the same way even when he became an elder. Hence it is said, ‘Cunda the novice’. ‘Why did he approach?’ It is said that after the death of the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, people across Jambudīpa spread the word: ‘The Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was known as a prominent teacher, yet after his death, such a dispute arose among his disciples. But the ascetic Gotama is as renowned in Jambudīpa as the moon and the sun—what kind of dispute will arise among his disciples after the ascetic Gotama passes into Parinibbāna?’ Hearing this talk, the elder thought, ‘I will take this matter to the One of Ten Powers, and the Teacher, having made this the occasion for a teaching, will deliver a discourse.’ So he set out and went to Sāmagāma, to where the Venerable Ānanda was. The meaning is that he did not go directly to the presence of the Blessed One but approached his preceptor, the Venerable Ānanda. It is said that he thought, ‘My preceptor is greatly wise; he will report this message to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will teach a suitable Dhamma in response.’ ‘Kathāpābhata’ means the root of the talk; for the root is called ‘pābhata’. As it is said—

“Appakenapi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti. (jā. 2.1.4);

“Even with little, the wise, discerning one raises himself up, like one kindling a small fire by blowing on it.”

Dassanāyāti dassanatthāya. Kiṃ paniminā bhagavā na diṭṭhapubboti? No na diṭṭhapubbo, ayañhi āyasmā divā nava vāre rattiṃ nava vāreti ekāhaṃ [P 4.0037] aṭṭhārasa vāre upaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Divasassa pana satakkhattuṃ vā sahassakkhattuṃ vā gantukāmo samānopi na akāraṇā gacchati, ekaṃ pañhuddhāraṃ gahetvāva gacchati. So taṃdivasaṃ tena gantukāmo evamāha.

‘For seeing’ means for the sake of seeing. But is it that the Blessed One had not been seen by him before? No, it is not that he had not been seen before; indeed, he had been seen before. For this venerable one goes to attend upon him eighteen times in a single day—nine times during the day and nine times at night. However, though wishing to go a hundred or a thousand times a day, he does not go without a reason; he goes only after taking up a question to be raised. So, on that day, wishing to go with the Venerable Ānanda, he spoke thus.

Ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānanti ekasmiṃ vihāre saṅghamajjhe uppanno vivādo kathaṃ devamanussānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattati? Kosambakakkhandhake (mahāva. 451) viya hi dvīsu bhikkhūsu vivādaṃ āpannesu tasmiṃ vihāre tesaṃ antevāsikā vivadanti, tesaṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhanto bhikkhunisaṅgho vivadati, tato tesaṃ upaṭṭhākā vivadanti, atha manussānaṃ ārakkhadevatā dve koṭṭhāsā honti. Tattha dhammavādīnaṃ ārakkhadevatā dhammavādiniyo honti, adhammavādīnaṃ adhammavādiniyo honti. Tato tāsaṃ ārakkhadevatānaṃ mittā bhummadevatā bhijjanti. Evaṃ paramparāya yāva brahmalokā ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake sabbe devamanussā dve koṭṭhāsā [V 4.0024] honti. Dhammavādīhi pana adhammavādinova bahutarā honti, tato yaṃ bahūhi gahitaṃ, taṃ gaṇhanti. Dhammaṃ vissajjetvā bahutarāva adhammaṃ gaṇhanti. Te adhammaṃ pūretvā viharantā apāye nibbattanti. Evaṃ ekasmiṃ vihāre saṅghamajjhe uppanno vivādo bahūnaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya hoti.

‘For the harm and suffering of devas and humans’—how does a dispute arising in the midst of the Saṅgha in a single monastery lead to harm and suffering for devas and humans? As in the Kosambaka chapter, when two monks fall into dispute, their students in that monastery also quarrel. The Saṅgha of nuns who accept their advice also quarrels, then their lay supporters quarrel. Next, the guardian deities of humans become two factions. Therein, the guardian deities of those who advocate the Dhamma become advocates of the Dhamma, while those of the advocates of non-Dhamma become advocates of non-Dhamma. Then the friends of those guardian deities—the earth deities—become divided. In this way, in succession, all devas and humans up to the Brahmā realm—setting aside the noble disciples—become two factions. But those who advocate non-Dhamma are more numerous than those who advocate the Dhamma; therefore, they accept what is taken up by the many. Having abandoned the Dhamma, the majority take up non-Dhamma. Dwelling while fulfilling non-Dhamma, they are reborn in the lower realms. In this way, a dispute arising in the midst of the Saṅgha in a single monastery leads to the harm and suffering of many.

43. Abhiññā desitāti mahābodhimūle nisinnena paccakkhaṃ katvā paveditā. Patissayamānarūpā viharantīti upanissāya viharanti. Bhagavato [P 4.0038] accayenāti etarahi bhagavantaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā sagāravā viharanti, tumhākaṃ, bhante, uggatejatāya durāsadatāya vivādaṃ janetuṃ na [M 4.0025] sakkonti, bhagavato pana accayena vivādaṃ janeyyunti vadati. Yattha pana taṃ vivādaṃ janeyyuṃ, taṃ dassento ajjhājīve vā adhipātimokkhe vāti āha. Tattha ajjhājīveti ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā – “bhikkhu uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapati āpatti pārājikassā”tiādinā (pari. 287) nayena parivāre paññattāni cha sikkhāpadāni, tāni ṭhapetvā sesāni sabbasikkhāpadāni adhipātimokkhaṃ nāma. Appamattako so ānandāti ajjhājīvaṃ adhipātimokkhañca ārabbha uppannavivādo nāma yasmā parassa kathāyapi attano dhammatāyapi sallakkhetvā suppajaho hoti, tasmā “appamattako”ti vutto.

43. ‘Taught with higher knowledge’ means proclaimed after having been directly realized while seated at the root of the great Bodhi tree. ‘They dwell in a state of reliance’ means they dwell in dependence on it. ‘After the Blessed One’s passing’—this means: now, they dwell with reverence, making the Blessed One their chief. It is said, ‘Venerable sir, due to your sharp majesty and unapproachability, they are unable to generate a dispute. But after the Blessed One’s passing, they might generate a dispute.’ Then, showing where they might generate that dispute, he said, ‘either regarding livelihood or regarding the Adhipātimokkha.’ Therein, ‘regarding livelihood’ refers to the six training rules laid down in the Parivāra by the method beginning, ‘For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, a monk claims a superhuman state; it is an offense of defeat.’ Setting those aside, all the remaining training rules are called Adhipātimokkha. ‘That is a small matter, Ānanda’—a dispute that has arisen concerning livelihood or the Adhipātimokkha is called ‘a small matter’ because, having reflected upon another's words and upon one's own nature, it is easy to abandon.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – idhekacco “na sakkā uttarimanussadhammaṃ anullapantena kiñci laddhu”ntiādīni cintetvā ājīvahetu uttarimanussadhammaṃ vā ullapati sañcarittaṃ vā āpajjati, yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu arahātiādinā nayena sāmantajappanaṃ vā karoti, agilāno vā attano atthāya paṇītabhojanāni viññāpetvā bhuñjati, bhikkhunī vā pana tāni viññāpetvā pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpajjati, yo koci dukkaṭavatthukaṃ yaṃkiñci sūpodanaviññattimeva vā karoti, aññataraṃ vā pana paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ karonto viharati, tamenaṃ sabrahmacārī evaṃ sañjānanti – “kiṃ imassa iminā lābhena laddhena, yo sāsane pabbajitvā micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappeti, paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ karotī”ti. Attano dhammatāyapissa evaṃ hoti – “kissa mayhaṃ iminā lābhena, yvāhaṃ evaṃ [P 4.0039] svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitvā micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappemi, paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ karomī”ti sallakkhetvā [V 4.0025] tato oramati. Evaṃ parassa kathāyapi attano dhammatāyapi sallakkhetvā suppajaho hoti. Tena bhagavā “appamattako”ti āha.

Herein, this is the method: Here, a certain monk, thinking, 'It is not possible to obtain anything without speaking of a superhuman state,' and so on, for the sake of livelihood, either speaks of a superhuman state or commits the act of being a go-between. Or, by the method of saying such things as, 'The monk who lives in your monastery is an Arahant,' he makes suggestive talk. Or, though not ill, for his own sake, having requested excellent foods, he eats them. Or a bhikkhunī, having requested them, falls into a Pāṭidesanīya offense. Or whoever commits any act that is a basis for a Dukkaṭa offense, such as merely requesting curry and rice, or else dwells transgressing some other prescribed rule—his fellow monks know him thus: 'What is the use of this gain obtained by this one, who, having gone forth in the Dispensation, makes a living by wrong livelihood and transgresses the prescribed rules?' And by his own nature, it occurs to him thus: 'What is the use of this gain to me, who, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, make a living by wrong livelihood and transgress the prescribed rules?' Reflecting thus, he desists from it. In this way, by reflecting on another's words and on his own nature, it becomes easy to abandon. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'It is a small matter.'

Magge vā hi, ānanda, paṭipadāya vāti lokuttaramaggaṃ patvā vivādo nāma sabbaso vūpasammati, natthi adhigatamaggānaṃ vivādo. Pubbabhāgamaggaṃ pana pubbabhāgapaṭipadañca sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

For, Ānanda, in the path or in the practice, upon reaching the supramundane path, dispute is entirely pacified; there is no dispute for those who have attained the path. However, this was said in reference to the preliminary-part path and the preliminary-part practice.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – evaṃ bhikkhuṃ manussā lokuttaradhamme sambhāventi. So saddhivihārikādayo āgantvā vanditvā ṭhite pucchati “kiṃ āgatatthā”ti. Manasikātabbakammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchituṃ, bhanteti. Nisīdatha, khaṇeneva [M 4.0026] arahattaṃ pāpetuṃ samatthakammaṭṭhānakathaṃ ācikkhissāmīti vatvā vadati – “idha bhikkhu attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nisinno mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, tassa taṃ manasikaroto obhāso uppajjati. Ayaṃ paṭhamamaggo nāma. So dutiyaṃ obhāsañāṇaṃ nibbatteti, dutiyamaggo adhigato hoti, evaṃ tatiyañca catutthañca. Ettāvatā maggappatto ceva phalappatto ca hotī”ti. Atha te bhikkhū “akhīṇāsavo nāma evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetuṃ na sakkoti, addhāyaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti niṭṭhaṃ gacchanti.

Herein, this is the method: People praise a monk for his supramundane qualities. When his co-residents and others come, pay homage, and are standing, he asks, 'Why have you come?' 'Venerable sir, to ask about a meditation subject to be attended to.' Saying, 'Sit down, I will shortly explain a meditation subject capable of leading to Arahantship,' he speaks: 'Here, a monk, having entered his dwelling place and sat down, attends to the root meditation subject. For him, while attending to it, a light arises. This is called the first path. He generates the knowledge of the light for a second time; the second path is attained. Similarly, the third and the fourth. By this much, he has attained the path and attained the fruit.' Then those monks come to the conclusion: 'One who is not an Arahant cannot teach a meditation subject in this way. Surely, this one is an Arahant.'

So aparena samayena kālaṃ karoti. Samantā bhikkhācāragāmehi manussā āgantvā pucchanti “kenaci, bhante, thero pañhaṃ pucchito”ti. Upāsakā pubbeva therena pañho kathito amhākanti. Te pupphamaṇḍapaṃ pupphakūṭāgāraṃ sajjetvā suvaṇṇena akkhipidhānamukhapidhānādiṃ karitvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷikaṃ [P 4.0040] kīḷetvā jhāpetvā aṭṭhīni ādāya cetiyaṃ karonti. Aññe āgantukā vihāraṃ āgantvā pāde dhovitvā “mahātheraṃ passissāma, kahaṃ, āvuso, mahāthero”ti pucchanti. Parinibbuto, bhanteti. Dukkaraṃ, āvuso, therena kataṃ maggaphalāni nibbattentena, pañhaṃ pucchittha, āvusoti. Bhikkhūnaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento iminā niyāmena kathesi, bhanteti. Na eso, āvuso, maggo, vipassanupakkileso nāmesa, na tumhe jānittha, puthujjano, āvuso, theroti. Te kalahaṃ karontā uṭṭhahitvā “sakalavihāre bhikkhū ca bhikkhācāragāmesu manussā ca na jānanti, tumheyeva jānātha. Kataramaggena tumhe āgatā, kiṃ [V 4.0026] vo vihāradvāre cetiyaṃ na diṭṭha”nti. Evaṃvādīnaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ vā, hotu sahassaṃ vā, yāva taṃ laddhiṃ nappajahanti, saggopi maggopi vāritoyeva.

At a later time, he passes away. People from the surrounding alms-villages come and ask, 'Venerable sirs, was the elder asked any question by anyone?' The lay disciples say, 'The question was answered for us by the elder beforehand.' They prepare a flower pavilion and a gabled chamber of flowers, make eye-coverings and mouth-coverings with gold, and having honored him with perfumes and garlands, they celebrate joyfully for seven days. Then they cremate him, take the bones, and build a cetiya. Other visiting monks arrive at the monastery, wash their feet, and ask, 'We wish to see the great elder. Where is the great elder, friends?' 'He has attained Parinibbāna, venerable sirs.' 'Friends, a difficult thing was done by the elder in generating the paths and fruits. Did you ask him the question, friends?' 'Venerable sirs, while teaching the meditation subject to the monks, he spoke according to this method.' 'Friends, that is not the path. It is called a corruption of insight. You did not know. Friends, the elder was a worldling.' They, quarreling, get up and say, 'The monks in the whole monastery and the people in the alms-villages do not know; only you know? By which road did you come? Did you not see the cetiya at the monastery gate?' But for monks who speak thus, whether there be a hundred or a thousand, as long as they do not abandon that view, both heaven and the path are indeed obstructed for them.

Aparopi tādisova kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento evaṃ katheti – citteneva tīsu uddhanesu tīṇi kapallāni āropetvā heṭṭhā aggiṃ katvā citteneva attano dvattiṃsākāraṃ uppāṭetvā kapallesu pakkhipitvā citteneva daṇḍakena parivattetvā parivattetvā bhajjitabbaṃ, yā jhāyamāne chārikā hoti, sā mukhavātena palāsetabbā. Ettakena dhūtapāpo nāmesa samaṇo hoti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

Another of a similar kind, while teaching a meditation subject, speaks thus: 'With the mind alone, one should place three potsherds on three hearths and make a fire underneath. With the mind alone, one should extract one's own thirty-two parts and place them in the potsherds. With the mind alone, they should be roasted, turning them over and over with a stick. The ash that remains while it is burning should be blown away with the breath from the mouth. By just this much, the ascetic is called one who has shaken off evil.' The remainder should be elaborated in the same way as before.

Aparo [M 4.0027] evaṃ katheti – citteneva mahācāṭiṃ ṭhapetvā matthuṃ yojetvā citteneva attano dvattiṃsākāraṃ uppāṭetvā tattha pakkhipitvā matthuṃ otāretvā manthitabbaṃ. Mathiyamānaṃ vilīyati, vilīne upari pheṇo uggacchati. So pheṇo paribhuñjitabbo. Ettāvatā vo amataṃ paribhuttaṃ nāma bhavissati[P 4.0041]. Ito paraṃ “atha te bhikkhū”tiādi sabbaṃ purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

Another speaks thus: 'With the mind alone, having placed a great pot and attached the churning stick, and with the mind alone, having extracted one’s own thirty-two parts and placed them therein, and having lowered the churning stick, one should churn. While being churned, it dissolves, and when it has dissolved, foam rises to the top. That foam should be consumed. By this much, you will have consumed what is called the Deathless.' Beyond this, everything beginning with 'then those monks' should be elaborated in the same way as before.

44. Idāni yo evaṃ vivādo uppajjeyya, tassa mūlaṃ dassento chayimānītiādimāha. Tattha agāravoti gāravavirahito. Appatissoti appatissayo anīcavutti. Ettha pana yo bhikkhu satthari dharamāne tīsu kālesu upaṭṭhānaṃ na yāti, satthari anupāhane caṅkamante saupāhano caṅkamati, nīce caṅkame caṅkamante ucce caṅkame caṅkamati, heṭṭhā vasante upari vasati, satthu dassanaṭṭhāne ubho aṃse pārupati, chattaṃ dhāreti, upāhanaṃ dhāreti, nhānatitthe uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā karoti, parinibbute vā pana cetiyaṃ vandituṃ na gacchati, cetiyassa paññāyanaṭṭhāne satthudassanaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ sabbaṃ karoti, aññehi ca bhikkhūhi “kasmā evaṃ karosi, na idaṃ vaṭṭati, sammāsabuddhassa nāma lajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte “tūṇhī hoti, kiṃ buddho buddhoti vadasī”ti bhaṇati, ayaṃ satthari agāravo nāma.

44. Now, to show the root of such a dispute that might arise, He said, 'These six...' and so on. Therein, 'disrespectful' means devoid of respect. 'Without deference' means without submission, not of humble conduct. Herein, a certain monk, while the Teacher is living, does not go to attend upon Him at the three times; while the Teacher is walking on a walkway without footwear, he walks with footwear; while the Teacher is walking on a low walkway, he walks on a high walkway; while the Teacher is dwelling below, he dwells above; in a place where the Teacher can be seen, he covers both shoulders, holds an umbrella, and wears footwear; he passes excrement or urine at a bathing place. Or, when the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, he does not go to venerate a cetiya; and in a place where the cetiya is visible, he does all the things previously mentioned as being disrespectful in a place where the Teacher can be seen. And when told by other monks, 'Why do you do this? This is not proper. It is proper to feel shame before the Perfectly Enlightened One,' he is silent, or he says, 'Why do you say, "Buddha, Buddha"?' This is called disrespect toward the Teacher.

Yo pana dhammassavane saṅghuṭṭhe sakkaccaṃ na gacchati, sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ na suṇāti, niddāyati vā sallapento vā nisīdati, sakkaccaṃ na gaṇhāti na dhāreti, “kiṃ dhamme agāravaṃ [V 4.0027] karosī”ti vutte “tuṇhī hoti, dhammo dhammoti vadasi, kiṃ dhammo nāmā”ti vadati, ayaṃ dhamme agāravo nāma.

Furthermore, a certain monk, when a Dhamma hearing is announced, does not go attentively, does not listen to the Dhamma attentively, sits dozing or conversing, and does not grasp or retain it attentively. When told, 'Why do you show disrespect toward the Dhamma?' he is silent, or he says, 'You say, "Dhamma, Dhamma." What is this thing called Dhamma?' This is called disrespect toward the Dhamma.

Yo pana therena bhikkhunā anajjhiṭṭho dhammaṃ deseti, nisīdati pañhaṃ katheti, vuḍḍhe bhikkhū ghaṭṭento gacchati, tiṭṭhati nisīdati, dussapallatthikaṃ vā hatthapallatthikaṃ vā karoti, saṅghamajjhe ubho aṃse pārupati, chattupāhanaṃ dhāreti, “bhikkhusaṅghassa lajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttepi “tuṇhī hoti, saṅgho saṅghoti vadasi, kiṃ saṅgho, migasaṅgho ajasaṅgho”tiādīni vadati, ayaṃ saṅghe agāravo nāma. Ekabhikkhusmimpi hi agārave [P 4.0042] kate saṅghe [M 4.0028] katoyeva hoti. Tisso sikkhā pana aparipūrayamānova sikkhāya na paripūrakārī nāma.

Furthermore, a certain monk, uninvited by a senior monk, teaches the Dhamma, sits down, and answers a question; he walks, stands, or sits, jostling senior monks; he makes a 'robe-lap' or a 'hand-lap'; in the midst of the Sangha, he covers both shoulders, holds an umbrella, and wears footwear. Even when told, 'It is proper to feel shame before the community of monks,' he is silent, or he says, 'You say, "Sangha, Sangha." What is a Sangha? A herd of deer? A flock of goats?' and so on. This is called disrespect toward the Sangha. For when disrespect is shown even to a single monk, it is indeed done to the Sangha. And one who does not fulfill the three trainings is called 'one who is not a fulfiller of the training'.

Ajjhattaṃ vāti attani vā attano parisāya vā. Bāhiddhāti parasmiṃ vā parassa parisāya vā.

'Internally' means in oneself or in one's own following. 'Externally' means in another or in another's following.

46. Idāni ayaṃ cha ṭhānāni nissāya uppannavivādo vaḍḍhanto yāni adhikaraṇāni pāpuṇāti, tāni dassetuṃ cattārimānītiādimāha. Tattha vūpasamanatthāya pavattamānehi samathehi adhikātabbānīti adhikaraṇāni. Vivādova adhikaraṇaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ. Itaresupi eseva nayo.

46. Now, to show which legal issues this dispute develops into, as it arises based on the six grounds and grows, He said, 'These four...' and so on. Therein, they are called 'legal issues' (adhikaraṇāni) because they are to be dealt with (adhikātabbāni) by settlements undertaken for the purpose of resolution. A dispute itself is a legal issue, hence a 'legal issue concerning a dispute' (vivādādhikaraṇa). This same method applies to the others.

Idāni imānipi cattāri adhikaraṇāni patvā upari vaḍḍhento so vivādo yehi samathehi vūpasammati, tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ satta kho panimetiādimāha. Tattha adhikaraṇāni samenti vūpasamentīti adhikaraṇasamathā. Uppannuppannānanti uppannānaṃ uppannānaṃ. Adhikaraṇānanti etesaṃ vivādādhikaraṇādīnaṃ catunnaṃ. Samathāya vūpasamāyāti samanatthañceva vūpasamanatthañca. Sammukhāvinayo dātabbo…pe… tiṇavatthārakoti ime satta samathā dātabbā.

Now, to show by which settlements that dispute is resolved, after it has reached these four legal issues and is growing further, the Blessed One said, 'There are, furthermore, these seven...' and so on. Therein, they are called 'settlements of legal issues' (adhikaraṇasamathā) because they settle (samenti) and resolve (vūpasamenti) legal issues. 'Of those that have arisen again and again' (uppannuppannānaṃ) means of each and every one that has arisen. 'Of the legal issues' (adhikaraṇānaṃ) means of these four, beginning with legal issues concerning disputes. 'For settling, for resolving' (samathāya vūpasamāya) means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of resolving. 'The procedure in the presence of... is to be applied... (and so on)... the covering over as with grass'—these seven settlements are to be applied.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayakathā – adhikaraṇesu tāva dhammoti [P 4.0043] vā adhammoti vāti aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi vivadantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yo vivādo, idaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Sīlavipattiyā vā ācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattiyā vā anuvadantānaṃ yo anuvādo upavadanā ceva codanā ca, idaṃ [V 4.0028] anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Mātikāyaṃ āgatā pañca vibhaṅge dveti satta āpattikkhandhā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ saṅghassa apalokanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ kammānaṃ karaṇaṃ, idaṃ kiccādhikaraṇaṃ nāma.

Herein, this is the detailed explanation: Among the legal issues, firstly, whatever dispute arises among monks who are disputing over the eighteen grounds, saying 'this is Dhamma' or 'this is not-Dhamma'—this is called a legal issue concerning a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa). Whatever accusation, blaming, and admonishing arises among those who accuse another due to a failing in virtue, or failings in conduct, view, or livelihood—this is called a legal issue concerning an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa). The five groups of offenses that come in the Mātikā and the two in the Vibhaṅga—these seven groups of offenses are called a legal issue concerning an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa). Whatever performance of the four formal acts of the Sangha, beginning with announcement—this is called a legal issue concerning a duty (kiccādhikaraṇa).

Tattha vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dvīhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca. Sammukhāvinayeneva sammamānaṃ yasmiṃ vihāre uppannaṃ, tasmiṃyeva vā, aññattha vūpasametuṃ gacchantānaṃ antarāmagge vā, yattha gantvā saṅghassa niyyātitaṃ, tattha saṅghena vā gaṇena vā vūpasametuṃ asakkonte tattheva ubbāhikāya sammatapuggalehi vā vinicchitaṃ sammati. Evaṃ sammamāne pana [M 4.0029] tasmiṃ yā saṅghasammukhatā dhammasammukhatā, vinayasammukhatā, puggalasammukhatā, ayaṃ sammukhāvinayo nāma.

Therein, a legal issue concerning a dispute is settled by two settlements: by the procedure in the presence of... and by the decision of the majority. When being settled by the procedure in the presence of..., it is settled in the very monastery where it arose; or on the way for those going elsewhere to settle it; or where, having gone, it is handed over to the Sangha, and if the Sangha or a group is unable to settle it, it is settled right there by a decision of persons authorized by a formal act of arbitration. Furthermore, when it is being settled in this way, whatever presence of the Sangha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individual(s) there is—this is called the procedure in the presence of...

Tattha ca kārakasaṅghassa sāmaggivasena sammukhībhāvo saṅghasammukhatā. Sametabbassa vatthuno bhūtatā dhammasammukhatā. Yathā taṃ sametabbaṃ, tatheva samanaṃ vinayasammukhatā. Yo ca vivadati, yena ca vivadati, tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ attapaccatthikānaṃ sammukhībhāvo puggalasammukhatā. Ubbāhikāya vūpasame panettha saṅghasammukhatā parihāyati. Evaṃ tāva sammukhāvinayeneva sammati.

Herein, the being present of the acting Sangha by way of its harmony is the presence of the Sangha (saṅghasammukhatā). The factuality of the matter to be settled is the presence of the Dhamma (dhammasammukhatā). The settling of it in just the way it should be settled is the presence of the Vinaya (vinayasammukhatā). The being present of both parties, the proponent and the opponent, is the presence of the individual(s) (puggalasammukhatā). In a settlement by arbitration, however, the presence of the Sangha is absent. Thus, it is settled primarily by the procedure in the presence of...

Sace panevampi na sammati, atha naṃ [P 4.0044] ubbāhikāya sammatā bhikkhū “na mayaṃ sakkoma vūpasametu”nti saṅghasseva niyyātenti. Tato saṅgho pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ salākaggāhakaṃ sammannitvā tena guḷhakavivaṭakasakaṇṇajappakesu tīsu salākaggāhesu aññataravasena salākaṃ gāhetvā sannipatitaparisāya dhammavādīnaṃ yebhuyyatāya yathā te dhammavādino vadanti, evaṃ vūpasantaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Tattha sammukhāvinayo vuttanayo eva. Yaṃ pana yebhuyyasikāya kammassa karaṇaṃ, ayaṃ yebhuyyasikā nāma. Evaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dvīhi samathehi sammati.

Furthermore, if it is not settled even in this way, the monks authorized by a formal act of arbitration declare, 'We are unable to settle it,' and entrust it to the Sangha itself. Then the Sangha, having appointed a monk endowed with five qualities as the ballot-taker, and having had him take a ballot by one of the three methods—secret, open, or whispering in the ear—in the assembled company, settles the matter according to the majority of those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma, just as those speakers of the Dhamma declare. A legal issue settled in this way is considered settled by both the procedure in the presence of... and by the decision of the majority. Herein, the procedure in the presence of... is as has been explained. The performance of the formal act by the majority, however, is called the decision of the majority (yebhuyyasikā). In this way, a legal issue concerning a dispute is settled by two settlements.

Anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ catūhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca sativinayena ca amūḷhavinayena ca tassapāpiyasikāya ca. Sammukhāvinayeneva sammamānaṃ yo ca anuvadati, yañca [V 4.0029] anuvadati, tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, sace kāci āpatti natthi, ubho khamāpetvā, sace atthi, ayaṃ nāmettha āpattīti evaṃ vinicchitaṃ vūpasammati. Tattha sammukhāvinayalakkhaṇaṃ vuttanayameva.

A legal issue concerning an accusation is settled by four settlements: by the procedure in the presence of..., by the procedure of mindfulness, by the procedure for one who is no longer confused, and by the procedure for one who is corrupt. When being settled by the procedure in the presence of... alone, having heard the statements of both the accuser and the accused, if there is no offense whatsoever, it is settled by having both ask forgiveness of each other. If there is an offense, it is settled by the decision that 'This is the name of the offense here.' Herein, the characteristic of the procedure in the presence of... is as has been explained.

Yadā pana khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno amūlikāya sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsitassa sativinayaṃ yācamānassa saṅgho ñatticatutthena kammena sativinayaṃ deti, tadā sammukhāvinayena ca sativinayena ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Dinne pana sativinaye puna tasmiṃ puggale kassaci anuvādo na ruhati.

But when the Sangha, by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements, grants the procedure of mindfulness to a taint-free monk who requests it, having been accused of a groundless breach of virtue, then it is settled by both the procedure in the presence of... and by the procedure of mindfulness. Furthermore, once the procedure of mindfulness has been granted, no accusation by anyone can arise again against that person.

Yadā ummattako bhikkhu ummādavasena kate assāmaṇake ajjhācāre “saratāyasmā evarūpiṃ āpatti”nti bhikkhūhi vuccamāno – “ummattakena me, āvuso, etaṃ kataṃ, nāhaṃ [P 4.0045] taṃ sarāmī”ti bhaṇantopi bhikkhūhi [M 4.0030] codiyamānova puna acodanatthāya amūḷhavinayaṃ yācati, saṅgho cassa ñatticatutthena kammena amūḷhavinayaṃ deti, tadā sammukhāvinayena ca amūḷhavinayena ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Dinne pana amūḷhavinaye puna tasmiṃ puggale kassaci tappaccayā anuvādo na ruhati.

When a monk who is insane, on account of his insanity, has committed an unseemly transgression not befitting a recluse, and when he is told by the monks, 'Venerable sir, do you remember such an offense?'—even while saying, 'Friends, this was done by me while I was insane; I do not remember it,' he is still being charged by the monks and requests the procedure for one who is no longer confused for the sake of not being charged again. The Sangha grants him the procedure for one who is no longer confused by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements. Then, it is settled by both the procedure in the presence of... and by the procedure for one who is no longer confused. Furthermore, once the procedure for one who is no longer confused has been granted, no accusation by anyone can arise again against that person on that account.

Yadā pana pārājikena vā pārājikasāmantena vā codiyamānassa aññenāññaṃ paṭicarato pāpussannatāya pāpiyassa puggalassa – “sacāyaṃ acchinnamūlo bhavissati, sammā vattitvā osāraṇaṃ labhissati, sace chinnamūlo, ayamevassa nāsanā bhavissatī”ti maññamāno saṅgho ñatticatutthena kammena tassapāpiyasikaṃ karoti, tadā sammukhāvinayena ca tassa pāpiyasikāya ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Evaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ catūhi samathehi sammati.

Furthermore, when a person is being accused of a pārājika offense or an offense bordering on a pārājika, and he evades by speaking of one thing and another, the Sangha, on account of his abundance of evil, thinking of that corrupt person: 'If he is not one whose root is severed, having conducted himself well, he will obtain rehabilitation; but if he is one whose root is severed, this very act will be his ruin,' performs the procedure for one who is corrupt by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements. Then the legal issue is settled by the procedure in the presence of... and by the procedure for one who is corrupt. In this way, a legal issue concerning an accusation is settled by four settlements.

Āpattādhikaraṇaṃ tīhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca. Tassa sammukhāvinayeneva vūpasamo natthi. Yadā pana ekassa vā bhikkhuno santike saṅghagaṇamajjhesu vā bhikkhu lahukaṃ āpattiṃ deseti, tadā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca vūpasammati. Tattha sammukhāvinayo tāva yo ca deseti, yassa ca deseti, tesaṃ sammukhatā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Puggalassa ca gaṇassa ca desanākāle [V 4.0030] saṅghasammukhatā parihāyati. Yaṃ panettha “ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ apanno”ti ca, āma “passāmī”ti ca paṭiññātāya [P 4.0046] “āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti karaṇaṃ, taṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ nāma. Saṅghādisese parivāsādiyācanā paṭiññā, parivāsādīnaṃ dānaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ nāma.

A legal issue arising from an offense is settled by three means of settlement: by the face-to-face procedure, by the procedure of acknowledgment, and by the procedure of covering over as with grass. There is no settlement for it by the face-to-face procedure alone. But when a monk confesses a light offense in the presence of a single monk, or in the midst of a group or the Saṅgha, then the legal issue arising from an offense is settled by the face-to-face procedure and by the procedure of acknowledgment. Herein, the face-to-face procedure is the being face-to-face of both the one who confesses and the one to whom he confesses. The rest is as has been explained. At the time of confession to an individual or a group, the presence of the Saṅgha is not required. Herein, the act, based on the acknowledgment 'I, venerable sir, have committed such-and-such an offense' and 'Yes, I see it,' of saying 'You should restrain yourself in the future,' is called the procedure of acknowledgment. In the case of a saṅghādisesa offense, the requesting of probation and so on is the acknowledgment; the giving of probation and so on is called the procedure of acknowledgment.

Dvepakkhajātā pana bhaṇḍanakārakā bhikkhū bahuṃ assāmaṇakaṃ ajjhācāraṃ caritvā puna lajjidhamme uppanne “sace mayaṃ imāhi āpattīhi aññamaññaṃ kāressāma, siyāpi taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kakkhaḷattāya saṃvatteyyā”ti aññamaññaṃ āpattiyā kārāpane dosaṃ disvā yadā tiṇavatthārakakammaṃ karonti, tadā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca sammati. Tatra hi yattakā hatthapāsupagatā “na me taṃ khamatī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhāvikammaṃ akatvā “dukkaṭaṃ kammaṃ puna kātabbaṃ kamma”nti na ukkoṭenti, niddampi [M 4.0031] okkantā honti, sabbesampi ṭhapetvā thullavajjañca gihipaṭisaṃyuttañca sabbāpattiyo vuṭṭhahanti. Evaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ tīhi samathehi sammati. Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ ekena samathena sammati sammukhāvinayeneva.

But when quarrelsome monks who have formed two factions, having committed much unseemly transgression not befitting a recluse, and with a sense of shame having later arisen, thinking, 'If we have each other dealt with for these offenses, that legal issue might lead to harshness,' and seeing the fault in having each other dealt with for an offense, perform the formal act of covering over as with grass, then the legal issue arising from an offense is settled by the face-to-face procedure and by the procedure of covering over as with grass. For in that case, all those who are within reach of the hand, without making their view apparent by saying, 'This is not agreeable to me,' do not protest, saying, 'The formal act is wrongly done; the formal act must be done again.' They have even fallen asleep. And for all of them, setting aside grave offenses and offenses connected with householders, all offenses are lifted. In this way, a legal issue arising from an offense is settled by three means of settlement. A legal issue concerning duties is settled by one means of settlement, by the face-to-face procedure alone.

Imāni cattāri adhikaraṇāni yathānurūpaṃ imehi sattahi samathehi sammanti. Tena vuttaṃ “uppannuppannānaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ samathāya vūpasamāya sammukhāvinayo dātabbo…pe… tiṇavatthārako”ti. Ayamettha vinicchayanayo, vitthāro pana samathakkhandhake (cūḷava. 185) āgatoyeva. Vinicchayopissa samantapāsādikāya vutto.

These four legal issues are settled, as is appropriate, by these seven means of settlement. Therefore it was said: 'For the settling and pacifying of legal issues as they arise, the face-to-face procedure should be applied… (and so on)... the procedure of covering over as with grass.' This here is the method of determination. The detailed account, however, is given in the Chapter on Settlements. Its adjudication is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā.

47. Yo panāyaṃ imasmiṃ sutte “idhānanda, bhikkhū vivadantī”tiādiko vitthāro vutto, so etena nayena saṅkhepatova vuttoti veditabbo. Tattha dhammotiādīsu suttantapariyāyena tāva [P 4.0047] dasa kusalakammapathā dhammo, akusalakammapathā adhammo. Tathā “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti heṭṭhā āgatā sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā, tayo satipaṭṭhānā tayo sammappadhānā tayo iddhipādā cha indriyāni cha balāni aṭṭha bojjhaṅgā navaṅgiko maggo cāti, cattāro upādānā pañca nīvaraṇānītiādayo saṅkaliṭṭhadhammā cāti ayaṃ adhammo.

47. The detailed exposition in this sutta, beginning with 'Here, Ānanda, monks dispute,' should be understood as having also been stated in brief by this method. Therein, regarding terms such as 'Dhamma,' first, according to the Suttanta method: the ten wholesome courses of action are Dhamma; the ten unwholesome courses of action are Adhamma. Similarly, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment mentioned below, beginning with 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' are Dhamma—namely, three foundations of mindfulness, three right strivings, three bases of spiritual power, six faculties, six powers, eight factors of enlightenment, and the nine-limbed path. And the defiled states, such as the four kinds of clinging and the five hindrances, are Adhamma.

Tattha [V 4.0031] yaṃkiñci ekaṃ adhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ gahetvā “imaṃ adhammaṃ dhammoti karissāma, evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyakulaṃ niyyānikaṃ bhavissati, mayañca loke pākaṭā bhavissāmā”ti taṃ adhammaṃ “dhammo aya”nti kathentā dhammoti vivadanti. Tattheva dhammakoṭṭhāsesu ekaṃ gahetvā “adhammo aya”nti kathentā adhammoti vivadanti.

Therein, taking some portion of Adhamma and thinking, 'We will make this Adhamma into Dhamma; in this way, our teachers' lineage will become liberating, and we will become famous in the world,' they proclaim that Adhamma, saying, 'This is Dhamma,' and dispute, saying, 'It is Dhamma.' In the same way, taking a portion from among the portions of Dhamma and proclaiming, 'This is Adhamma,' they dispute, saying, 'It is Adhamma.'

Vinayapariyāyena pana bhūtena vatthunā codetvā sāretvā yathāpaṭiññāya kātabbakammaṃ dhammo nāma, abhūtena pana vatthunā acodetvā asāretvā apaṭiññāya katabbakammaṃ adhammo nāma. Tesupi adhammaṃ “dhammo aya”nti kathentā dhammoti vivadanti, “adhammo aya”nti kathentā adhammoti vivadanti.

According to the Vinaya method, however, an act to be performed after accusing and reminding based on a true matter, in accordance with the admission, is called Dhamma. But an act to be performed without accusing and reminding based on an untrue matter, without an admission, is called Adhamma. In these cases too, those who proclaim Adhamma as 'This is Dhamma' dispute, saying, 'It is Dhamma'; and those who proclaim Dhamma as 'This is Adhamma' dispute, saying, 'It is Adhamma.'

Suttantapariyāyena pana rāgavinayo dosavinayo mohavinayo saṃvaro pahānaṃ paṭisaṅkhāti ayaṃ vinayo nāma, rāgādīnaṃ avinayo asaṃvaro [M 4.0032] appahānaṃ appaṭisaṅkhāti ayaṃ avinayo nāma. Vinayapariyāyena vatthusampatti ñattisampatti anusāvanasampatti sīmasampati parisasampattīti ayaṃ vinayo nāma, vatthuvipatti…pe… parisavipattīti [P 4.0048] ayaṃ avinayo nāma. Tesupi yaṃkiñci avinayaṃ “vinayo aya”nti kathentā vinayoti vivadanti, vinayaṃ avinayoti kathentā avinayoti vivadanti.

According to the Suttanta method, the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, the removal of delusion, restraint, abandonment, and reflection—this is called discipline. The non-removal of lust and so forth, non-restraint, non-abandonment, and non-reflection—this is called non-discipline. According to the Vinaya method, the perfection of the matter, the perfection of the motion, the perfection of the proclamation, the perfection of the boundary, and the perfection of the assembly—this is called discipline. The failure of the matter... the failure of the assembly—this is called non-discipline. In these cases too, those who proclaim some non-discipline as 'This is discipline' dispute, saying, 'It is discipline'; and those who proclaim discipline as 'non-discipline' dispute, saying, 'It is non-discipline.'

Dhammanetti samanumajjitabbāti dhammarajju anumajjitabbā ñāṇena ghaṃsitabbā upaparikkhitabbā. Sā panesā dhammanetti “iti kho vaccha ime dasa dhammā akusalā dasa dhammā kusalā”ti evaṃ mahāvacchagottasutte (ma. ni. 2.194) āgatāti vuttā. Sā eva vā hotu, yo vā idha dhammoti ca vinayo ca vutto. Yathā tattha sametīti yathā tāya dhammanettiyā sameti, “dhammo dhammova hoti, adhammo adhammova, vinayo vinayova hoti, avinayo avinayova”. Tathā tanti evaṃ taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Ekaccānaṃ adhikaraṇānanti idha vivādādhikaraṇameva dassitaṃ, sammukhāvinayo pana na kismiñci adhikaraṇe na labbhati.

'The guideline of the Dhamma should be scrutinized' means the measuring line of the Dhamma should be scrutinized, polished with wisdom, and investigated. Now, this guideline of the Dhamma is said to be that which is found in the Mahāvacchagottasutta: 'Thus, Vaccha, these ten things are unwholesome, these ten things are wholesome.' Or let it be that which is spoken of here as Dhamma and Vinaya. 'As it accords there' means as it accords with that guideline of the Dhamma: 'Dhamma is indeed Dhamma, Adhamma is indeed Adhamma, Vinaya is indeed Vinaya, and Avinaya is indeed Avinaya.' 'Thus that' means that legal issue should be settled in that way. By 'of some legal issues,' here only a legal issue of dispute is shown. The face-to-face procedure, however, is not unobtainable in any legal issue.

48. Taṃ panetaṃ yasmā dvīhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca, tasmā [V 4.0032] heṭṭhā mātikāya ṭhapitānukkamena idāni sativinayassa vāre pattepi taṃ avatvā vivādādhikaraṇayeva tāva dutiyasamathaṃ dassento kathañcānanda, yebhuyyasikātiādimāha. Tattha bahutarāti antamaso dvīhi tīhipi atirekatarā. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

48. Now, because this legal issue of dispute is settled by two settlements—by the procedure in the presence and by a majority decision—therefore, following the sequence previously established in the basic outline, now, even though the turn for the settlement by mindfulness has come, without speaking of it, the Blessed One first explains the second settlement only in the context of a legal issue of dispute, saying, 'And how, Ānanda, is the majority decision?' and so on. Herein, 'by the majority' means more by at least two or three. The rest here should be understood in the same way as explained previously.

49. Idāni heṭṭhā avitthāritaṃ sativinayaṃ ādiṃ katvā vitthāritāvasesasamathe [P 4.0049] paṭipāṭiyā vitthāretuṃ kathañcānanda, sativinayotiādimāha. Tattha pārājikasāmantena vāti dve sāmantāni khandhasāmantañca āpattisāmantañca. Tattha pārājikāpattikkhandho saṅghādisesāpattikkhandho thullaccaya-pācittiya-pāṭidesanīya-dukkaṭa-dubbhāsitāpattikkhandhoti evaṃ purimassa pacchimakhandhaṃ khandhasāmantaṃ nāma hoti. Paṭhamapārājikassa pana pubbabhāge dukkaṭaṃ, sesānaṃ thullaccayanti idaṃ āpattisāmantaṃ nāma. Tattha [M 4.0033] khandhasāmante pārājikasāmantaṃ garukāpatti nāma hoti. Saratāyasmāti saratu āyasmā. Ekaccānaṃ adhikaraṇānanti idha anuvādādhikaraṇameva dassitaṃ.

49. Now, in order to explain in sequence the remaining settlements, beginning with the settlement by mindfulness which was not explained in detail before, the Blessed One said, 'And how, Ānanda, is the settlement by mindfulness?' and so on. Therein, 'by adjacency to a pārājika' refers to two kinds of adjacency: adjacency of the group and adjacency of the offense. Therein, regarding the group of pārājika offenses, the group of saṅghādisesa offenses, and the group of thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita offenses—in this way, the subsequent group in relation to a preceding one is called 'adjacency of the group.' However, a dukkaṭa in the preliminary stage of the first pārājika, and a thullaccaya for the others—this is called 'adjacency of the offense.' Therein, within adjacency of the group, adjacency to a pārājika is called a grave offense. 'Saratāyasmā' is to be parsed as 'saratu āyasmā' (May the venerable one remember). By 'of some legal issues,' here only a legal issue of accusation is shown.

50. Bhāsitaparikkantanti vācāya bhāsitaṃ kāyena ca parikkantaṃ, parakkamitvā katanti attho. Ekaccānanti idhāpi anuvādādhikaraṇameva adhippetaṃ. Paṭiññātakaraṇe “ekaccāna”nti āpattādhikaraṇaṃ dassitaṃ.

50. 'Bhāsitaparikkanta' means what is spoken by speech and performed by the body; the meaning is: done by striving. By 'of some,' here too, only a legal issue of accusation is intended. In the case of the procedure for an admitted offense, 'of some' shows a legal issue of an offense.

52. Davāti sahasā. Ravāti aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmena aññaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ kho, ānanda, tassapāpiyasikā hotīti tassapuggalassa pāpussannatā pāpiyasikā hoti. Iminā kammassa vatthu dassitaṃ. Evarūpassa hi puggalassa kammaṃ kāttabbaṃ. Kammena hi adhikaraṇassa vūpasamo hoti, na puggalassa pāpussannatāya. Idhāpi ca anuvādādhikaraṇameva adhikaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

52. Dava means impetuously. Rava means something else was said by one intending to say another thing. 'Thus, Ānanda, it is a state of greater evil for him' means that for such a person, the abundance of evil is the 'state of greater evil.' By this, the basis for the formal act is shown. For it is for such a person that the formal act should be performed. Indeed, it is by the formal act that the settlement of the legal issue occurs, not by the person's abundance of evil. Here too, it should be understood that by 'legal issue,' only a legal issue of accusation is meant.

53. Kathañcānanda[P 4.0050], tiṇavatthārakoti ettha idaṃ kammaṃ tiṇavatthārakasadisattā tiṇavatthārakoti vuttaṃ. Yathā hi gūthaṃ vā muttaṃ vā ghaṭṭiyamānaṃ duggandhatāya bādhati, tiṇehi avattharitvā suppaṭicchāditassa panassa so gandho na bādhati, evameva yaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ mūlānumūlaṃ gantvā vūpasamiyamānaṃ kakkhaḷattāya vāḷattāya bhedāya saṃvattati, taṃ iminā kammena vūpasantaṃ gūthaṃ viya tiṇavatthārakena paṭicchannaṃ vūpasantaṃ hotīti idaṃ kammaṃ tiṇavatthārakasadisattā [V 4.0033] tiṇavatthārakoti vuttaṃ. Tassa idhānanda, bhikkhūnaṃ bhaṇḍanajātānantiādivacanena ākāramattameva dassitaṃ, khandhake āgatāyeva panettha kammavācā pamāṇaṃ. Ṭhapetvā thullavajjaṃ ṭhapetvā gihipaṭisaṃyuttanti. Ettha pana thullavajjanti thūllavajjaṃ pārājikañceva saṅghādisesañca. Gihipaṭisaṃyuttanti gihīnaṃ hīnena khuṃsanavambhanadhammikapaṭissavesu āpannā āpatti. Adhikaraṇānanti idha āpattādhikaraṇameva veditabbaṃ. Kiccādhikaraṇassa pana vasena idha na kiñci vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi na vuttaṃ, sammukhāvinayeneva panassa vūpasamo hotīti veditabbo.

53. And how, Ānanda, is it 'covering with grass'? Here, this formal act is called 'covering with grass' because it is similar to covering with grass. For just as excrement or urine, when stirred, is offensive due to its foul smell, but when covered over with grass and well-concealed, that smell is no longer offensive; even so, when a legal issue, if pursued to its very root while being settled, would lead to harshness, fierceness, and division, that issue is settled by this formal act. Like excrement covered with a covering of grass, it is settled. Thus, this formal act is called 'covering with grass' because it is similar to covering with grass. Of this, Ānanda, the manner alone is shown here by the words beginning, 'monks among whom a quarrel has arisen...'; the authoritative text for the formal procedure of the act is that which is found in the Khandhaka: 'Excluding a gross offense, excluding what is connected with householders.' Here, 'gross offense' means a grave offense, namely both a Pārājika and a Saṅghādisesa. 'Connected with householders' means an offense incurred in relation to householders through reviling, censuring, or a righteous admission. By 'legal issues' here, only a legal issue of an offense should be understood. However, with regard to a legal issue of duties, nothing is said here. And although nothing is said, it should be understood that its settlement is by the procedure of being in the presence.

54. Chayime[M 4.0034], ānanda, dhammā sāraṇīyāti heṭṭhā kalahavasena suttaṃ āraddhaṃ, upari sāraṇīyadhammā āgatā. Iti yathānusandhināva desanā gatā hoti. Heṭṭhā kosambiyasutte (ma. ni. 1.498-500) pana sotāpattimaggasammādiṭṭhi kathitā, imasmiṃ [P 4.0051] sutte sotāpattiphalasammādiṭṭhi vuttāti veditabbā. Aṇunti appasāvajjaṃ. Thūlanti mahāsāvajjaṃ. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

54. ‘These six, Ānanda, are principles of cordiality.’ Previously, the Sutta was begun on account of a quarrel; subsequently, the principles of cordiality are presented. Thus, the teaching proceeds according to its connection. Furthermore, previously in the Kosambiya Sutta, the right view of the path to stream-entry was discussed; in this Sutta, the right view of the fruit of stream-entry is spoken of—thus it should be understood. ‘Minor’ means of little fault. ‘Gross’ means of great fault. The rest here is clear.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,

Sāmagāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta is concluded.

5. Sunakkhattasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Sunakkhatta Sutta

55. Evaṃ [V 4.0034] me sutanti sunakkhattasuttaṃ. Tattha aññāti arahattaṃ. Byākatāti khīṇā jātītiādīhi catūhi padehi kathitā. Adhimānenāti appatte pattasaññino, anadhigate adhigatasaññino hutvā adhigataṃ amhehīti mānena byākariṃsu.

5. ‘Thus have I heard’ is the Sunakkhatta Sutta. Therein, ‘final knowledge’ is Arahantship. ‘Declared’ means it was stated with the four phrases beginning, ‘Destroyed is birth.’ ‘Through overestimation’ means that, perceiving they had attained what they had not attained, and perceiving they had realized what they had not realized, they declared out of conceit, ‘It has been realized by us.’

56. Evañcettha sunakkhatta tathāgatassa hotīti sunakkhatta ettha etesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pañhabyākaraṇe – “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ etesaṃ avibhūtaṃ andhakāraṃ, tenime anadhigate adhigatasaññino, handa nesaṃ visodhetvā pākaṭaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desemī”ti, evañca tathāgatassa hoti. Atha ca panidhekacce…pe… tassapi hoti aññathattanti bhagavā paṭipannakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Yattha pana icchācāre ṭhitā ekacce moghapurisā honti, tatra bhagavā passati – “ime imaṃ pañhaṃ uggahetvā ajānitvāva jānantā viya appatte pattasaññino hutvā gāmanigamādīsu visevamānā vicarissanti, taṃ nesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti evamassāyaṃ icchācāre [P 4.0052] ṭhitānaṃ kāraṇā paṭipannakānampi atthāya “dhammaṃ desissāmī”ti uppannassa cittassa aññathābhāvo hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

55. ‘And in this case, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata thus’: Sunakkhatta, in this case, regarding the answering of the question for these monks, it occurs to the Tathāgata: ‘This point is unclear and obscure to them; for that reason, they perceive they have realized what they have not realized. Come now, having clarified and made it plain for them, I will teach the Dhamma.’ Thus it occurs to the Tathāgata. ‘But then in a certain case here… for him, too, there is an alteration’: The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to those who are practicing. But where there are some worthless men established in base desires, there the Blessed One sees: ‘These monks, having learned this question without knowing its meaning, will act as if they know. Perceiving they have attained what they have not attained, they will wander about in villages, towns, and so on, proclaiming a special attainment. That will be for their long-term harm and suffering.’ Thus, on account of those established in base desires, the thought that had arisen, ‘I will teach the Dhamma for the benefit of those who are practicing,’ undergoes an alteration. This is what was said in reference to that.

58. Lokāmisādhimuttoti vaṭṭāmisa-kāmāmisa-lokāmisabhūtesu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu adhimutto tanninno taggaruko tappabbhāro. Tappatirūpīti [M 4.0035] kāmaguṇasabhāgā. Āneñjapaṭisaṃyuttāyāti āneñjasamāpattipaṭisaṃyuttāya. Saṃseyyāti katheyya. Āneñjasaṃyojanena hi kho visaṃyuttoti āneñjasamāpattisaṃyojanena visaṃsaṭṭho. Lokāmisādhimuttoti evarūpo hi lūkhacīvaradharo mattikāpattaṃ ādāya attano sadisehi katipayehi saddhiṃ paccantajanapadaṃ gacchati, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhakāle manussā disvā “mahāpaṃsukulikā āgatā”ti yāgubhattādīni sampādetvā sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ denti, bhattakicce niṭṭhite anumodanaṃ sutvā – “svepi, bhante, idheva piṇḍāya pavisathā”ti vadanti. Alaṃ upāsakā, ajjāpi vo bahūnaṃ dinnanti. Tena hi, bhante, antovassaṃ idha vaseyyāthāti adhivāsetvā vihāramaggaṃ pucchitvā vihāraṃ [V 4.0035] gacchanti. Tattha senāsanaṃ gahetvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmenti. Sāyaṃ eko āvāsiko te bhikkhū pucchati “kattha piṇḍāya caritthā”ti? Asukagāmeti. Bhikkhāsampannāti? Āma evarūpā nāma manussānaṃ saddhā hoti. “Ajjeva nu kho ete edisā, niccampi edisā”ti? Saddhā te manussā niccampi edisā, te nissāyeva ayaṃ vihāro vaḍḍhatīti. Tato te paṃsukulikā punappunaṃ tesaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathenti[P 4.0053], divasāvasesaṃ kathetvā rattimpi kathenti. Ettāvatā icchācāre ṭhitassa sīsaṃ nikkhantaṃ hoti udaraṃ phālitaṃ. Evaṃ lokāmisādhimutto veditabbo.

58. ‘One set on worldly bait’: One is set on, inclined towards, gives weight to, and is biased towards the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are the bait of the round of existence, the bait of sensuality, and the bait of the world. ‘In conformity with that’: This refers to speech that has the nature of sensual pleasures. ‘Connected with the imperturbable’: Connected with the attainment of the imperturbable. ‘He might speak’: He would speak. ‘For he is disjoined from the fetter of the imperturbable’: He is not associated with the fetter of the attainment of the imperturbable. As to ‘one set on worldly bait’: such a person, a shameless monk wearing rough robes and carrying an earthen bowl, goes with a few others like himself to a border district. When they enter a village for alms, people see them and say, ‘Great wearers of rag-robes have come!’ They prepare rice-gruel, rice, and so on, and give the offering respectfully. When the meal is finished, having heard the blessing, they say, ‘Venerable sirs, please enter here for alms tomorrow as well.’ The monks reply, ‘That is enough, lay supporters. Even today you have given to many.’ The lay people then say, ‘In that case, venerable sirs, may you stay here for the rains residence.’ Having accepted, they ask the way to the monastery and go to the monastery. There, having taken a lodging, they put away their bowl and robes. In the evening, a resident monk asks those monks, ‘Where did you go for alms?’ ‘In such-and-such a village.’ ‘Was the alms-food abundant?’ ‘Yes, the people have such faith.’ ‘Are they like this only today, or are they always like this?’ ‘Those people are faithful; they are always like this. It is because of them that this monastery prospers.’ Then those wearers of rag-robes repeatedly praise them, speaking of it for the rest of the day and speaking of it at night. By this much, for one established in base desires, his head goes out and his belly is split. In this way, ‘one set on worldly bait’ should be understood.

59. Idāni āneñjasamāpattilābhiṃ adhimānikaṃ dassento ṭhānaṃ kho panetantiādimāha. Āneñjādhimuttassāti kilesasiñcanavirahitāsu heṭṭhimāsu chasu samāpattīsu adhimuttassa tanninnassa taggaruno tappabbhārassa. Se pavutteti taṃ pavuttaṃ. Cha samāpattilābhino hi adhimānikassa pañcakāmaguṇāmisabandhanā patitapaṇḍupalāso viya upaṭṭhāti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

59. Now, to show the conceited person who has obtained the imperturbable attainment, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'There is, indeed, a case...' As for 'one intent on the imperturbable,' it refers to one who is intent upon, inclined towards, gives weight to, and is biased towards the six lower attainments that are free from the agitation of defilements. As for 'He is free,' it means he is free from that. Indeed, for the conceited one who has obtained the six attainments, the bond of bait that is the five strands of sensual pleasure appears like a fallen, withered leaf. Therefore, this was said.

60. Idāni ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti lābhino adhimānikassa nighaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ ṭhānaṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha dvedhā bhinnāti majjhe bhinnā. Appaṭisandhikāti khuddakā muṭṭhipāsāṇamattā jatunā vā silesena vā allīyāpetvā paṭisandhātuṃ sakkā. Mahantaṃ pana kuṭāgārappamāṇaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Se bhinneti taṃ bhinnaṃ. Upari [M 4.0036] samāpattilābhino hi heṭṭhāsamāpatti dvedhābhinnā selā viya hoti, taṃ samāpajjissāmīti cittaṃ na uppajjati. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

60. Now, to show the limit for the conceited person who has obtained the attainment of the base of nothingness, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'There is, indeed, a case...' Therein, 'split in two' means split in the middle. As for 'that cannot be rejoined': a small stone the size of a fist can be rejoined by applying lac or resin. But this was said with reference to a large stone the size of a gabled house. As for 'He is split,' it means that his connection with the lower attainments is broken. Indeed, for one who has obtained a higher attainment, the lower attainment is like a large stone split in two; the thought, 'I will enter that attainment,' does not arise. Therefore, this was said.

61. Idāni nevasaññānāsaññāyatanalābhino adhimānikassa ca nighaṃsaṃ dassento ṭhānaṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha se vanteti taṃ vantaṃ. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino [P 4.0054] hi heṭṭhāsamāpattiyo vantasadisā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, puna samāpajjissāmīti cittaṃ na uppajjati. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

61. Now, wishing to show the limit for the conceited person who has obtained the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'There is, indeed, a case...' Therein, as for 'He has vomited,' it means he has vomited that. Indeed, for one who has obtained the eight attainments, the lower attainments appear as if they have been vomited; the thought, 'I will enter them again,' does not arise. Therefore, this was said.

62. Idāni khīṇāsavassa nighaṃsaṃ dassento ṭhānaṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha se ucchinnamūleti so ucchinnamūlo. Upari samāpattilābhino hi heṭṭhāsamāpatti mūlacchinnatālo viya upaṭṭhāti, taṃ samāpajjissāmīti cittaṃ na uppajjati. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

62. Now, wishing to show the limit for one whose cankers are destroyed, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'There is, indeed, a case...' Therein, as for 'He has his root cut off,' it means he has the root of his connection with that cut off. Indeed, for one who has obtained the higher attainment, the lower attainment appears like a palm tree with its root cut off; the thought, 'I will enter that attainment,' does not arise. Therefore, this was said.

63. Ṭhānaṃ [V 4.0036] kho panāti pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhā hi samāpattilābhino adhimānikassapi khīṇāsavassapi nighaṃso kathito, sukkhavipassakassa pana adhimānikassapi khīṇāsavassapi na kathito. Tesaṃ dvinnampi nighaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Taṃ pana paṭikkhittaṃ. Samāpattilābhino hi adhimānikassa nighaṃse kathite sukkhavipassakassapi adhimānikassa kathitova hoti, samāpattilābhino ca khīṇāsavassa kathite sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavassa kathitova hoti. Etesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sappāyāsappāyaṃ kathetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

63. 'There is, indeed, a case...' is a separate connection. For previously, the limit for the conceited person who has obtained the attainments and for the one whose cankers are destroyed has been spoken of, but the limit for the conceited dry-insight practitioner and for the dry-insight practitioner whose cankers are destroyed has not been spoken of.
