This discourse was begun to show the limit for both of them. But that view is rejected. For when the limit for the conceited person who has obtained the attainments is spoken of, the limit for the conceited dry-insight practitioner is also spoken of; and when the limit for the one with attainments whose cankers are destroyed is spoken of, the limit for the dry-insight practitioner whose cankers are destroyed is also spoken of. Rather, this discourse was begun to speak about what is suitable and unsuitable for these two kinds of monks.

Tattha siyā – puthujjanassa tāva ārammaṇaṃ asappāyaṃ hotu, khīṇāsavassa kathaṃ asappāyanti. Yadaggena puthujjanassa asappāyaṃ, tadaggena khīṇāsavassāpi asappāyameva. Visaṃ nāma jānitvā khāditampi ajānitvā khāditampi visameva. Na hi khīṇāsavenapi “ahaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti asaṃvutena bhavitabbaṃ. Khīṇāsavenapi yuttapayutteneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭati.

Herein, an objection might be raised: 'Let an object be unsuitable for a worldling, but how can it be unsuitable for one whose cankers are destroyed?' In whatever way it is unsuitable for a worldling, in that same way it is unsuitable even for one whose cankers are destroyed. Poison, whether eaten knowingly or unknowingly, is still poison. For even one whose cankers are destroyed should not be unrestrained, thinking, 'I am one whose cankers are destroyed.' It is fitting for even one whose cankers are destroyed to act with due application and effort.

64. Tattha [P 4.0055] samaṇenāti buddhasamaṇena. Chandarāgabyāpādenāti so avijjāsaṅkhāto visadoso chandarāgena ca byāpādena ca ruppati kuppati. Asappāyānīti avaḍḍhikarāni ārammaṇāni. Anuddhaṃseyyāti soseyya [M 4.0037] milāpeyya. Saupādisesanti sagahaṇasesaṃ, upāditabbaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ idha upādīti vuttaṃ. Analañca te antarāyāyāti jīvitantarāyaṃ te kātuṃ asamatthaṃ. Rajosūkanti rajo ca vīhisukādi ca sūkaṃ. Asu ca visadosoti so ca visadoso. Tadubhayenāti yā sā asappāyakiriyā ca yo visadoso ca, tena ubhayena. Puthuttanti mahantabhāvaṃ.

64. Herein, 'by the recluse' means by the Buddha, the recluse. As for 'by sensual lust and ill will,' that fault of poison called ignorance is vexed and agitated by sensual lust and by ill will. 'Unsuitable' means objects that do not lead to growth. 'Should dry up' means it would cause wholesome states to dry up and wither. 'With a residue' means with a residue of what is grasped; here, that which is to be grasped is called 'upādi' (substratum). 'And is not enough for your harm' means it is unable to cause a danger to your life. 'Dust-awn' means dust and an awn, such as the awn of grain. 'And that fault of poison': this refers to that same fault of poison. 'By both' means by both of these: that unsuitable action and that fault of poison. 'Puthuttaṃ' means the state of being great.

Evameva khoti ettha saupādānasalluddhāro viya appahīno avijjāvisadoso daṭṭhabbo, asappāyakiriyāya ṭhitabhāvo viya chasu dvāresu asaṃvutakālo, tadubhayena vaṇe puthuttaṃ gate maraṇaṃ viya sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattanaṃ, maraṇamattaṃ dukkhaṃ viya aññatarāya garukāya saṃkiliṭṭhāya āpattiyā āpajjanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sukkapakkhepi imināva nayena opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Just so, herein, the unabandoned fault of the poison of ignorance should be seen like the extraction of a dart with its substratum remaining. The time of being unrestrained at the six doors should be seen like the state of persisting in unsuitable action. Reverting to the lower life after renouncing the training should be seen like death, which occurs when a wound has grown large due to both of these factors. Falling into some grave, defiled offense should be seen like suffering equivalent to death. In the bright side, too, the connection of the simile should be understood by this same method.

65. Satiyāyetaṃ [V 4.0037] adhivacananti ettha sati paññāgatikā. Lokikāya paññāya lokikā hoti, lokuttarāya lokuttarā. Ariyāyetaṃ paññāyāti parisuddhāya vipassanāpaññāya.

65. ‘This is a designation for mindfulness’—herein, mindfulness has wisdom as its resort. With mundane wisdom, it is mundane; with supramundane wisdom, it is supramundane. ‘This is by noble wisdom’ means by purified insight-wisdom.

Idāni khīṇāsavassa balaṃ dassento so vatātiādimāha. Tattha saṃvutakārīti pihitakārī. Iti [P 4.0056] viditvā nirupadhīti evaṃ jānitvā kilesupadhipahānā nirupadhi hoti, nirupādānoti attho. Upadhisaṅkhaye vimuttoti upadhīnaṃ saṅkhayabhūte nibbāne ārammaṇato vimutto. Upadhisminti kāmupadhismiṃ. Kāyaṃ upasaṃharissatīti kāyaṃ allīyāpessati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – taṇhakkhaye nibbāne ārammaṇato vimutto khīṇāsavo pañca kāmaguṇe sevituṃ, kāyaṃ vā upasaṃharissati cittaṃ vā uppādessatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Now, wishing to show the power of one whose cankers are destroyed, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'He, indeed...' Therein, 'one who acts with restraint' means one who acts with closure. 'Having known this, he is without substratum' means: having known thus, he is without substratum because of having abandoned the substratum of defilements; the meaning is 'without clinging.' 'Liberated at the destruction of substrata' means liberated by taking as object Nibbāna, which is the destruction of substrata. 'In a substratum' means in the substratum of sensual pleasures. 'He will apply his body' means he will cause his body to adhere. This is what is said: For one whose cankers are destroyed, who is liberated by taking as object Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, that he would apply his body or arouse his mind in order to indulge in the five strands of sensual pleasure—this case does not exist. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Sunakkhattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Sunakkhatta Sutta is concluded.

6. Āneñjasappāyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Āneñjasappāya Sutta

66. Evaṃ [V 4.0038][M 4.0038] me sutanti āneñjasappāyasuttaṃ. Tattha aniccāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Kāmāti vatthukāmāpi kilesakāmāpi. Tucchāti niccasāradhuvasāraattasāravirahitattā rittā, na pana natthīti gahetabbā. Na hi tucchamuṭṭhīti vutte muṭṭhi nāma natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yassa pana abbhantare kiñci natthi, so vuccati tuccho. Musāti nāsanakā. Mosadhammāti nassanasabhāvā, khettaṃ viya vatthu viya hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ca na paññāyittha, katipāheneva [P 4.0057] supinake diṭṭhā viya nassanti na paññāyanti. Tena vuttaṃ “mosadhammā”ti, māyākatametanti yathā māyāya udakaṃ maṇīti katvā dassitaṃ, badaripaṇṇaṃ kahāpaṇoti katvā dassitaṃ, aññaṃ vā pana evarūpaṃ dassanūpacāre ṭhitasseva tathā paññāyati, upacārātikkamato paṭṭhāya pākatikameva paññāyati. Evaṃ kāmāpi ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena “māyākata”nti vuttā. Yathā ca māyākāro udakādīni maṇiādīnaṃ vasena dassento vañceti, evaṃ kāmāpi aniccādīni niccādisabhāvaṃ dassentā vañcentīti vañcanakaṭṭhenapi “māyākata”nti vuttā. Bālalāpananti mayhaṃ putto, mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ hiraññaṃ mayhaṃ suvaṇṇanti evaṃ bālānaṃ lāpanato bālalāpanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammikā kāmāti mānusakā pañca kāmaguṇā. Samparāyikāti te ṭhapetvā avasesā. Diṭṭhadhammikā. Kāmasaññāti mānusake kāme ārabbha uppannasaññā. Ubhayametaṃ māradheyyanti ete kāmā ca kāmasaññā ca ubhayampi māradheyyaṃ. Yehi ubhayametaṃ gahitaṃ, tesañhi upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya “ubhayametaṃ māradheyya”nti vuttaṃ.

66. Thus have I heard—this refers to the Āneñjasappāya Sutta. Herein, 'impermanent' means impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having been. 'Sensual pleasures' refers to both sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements. 'Empty' means void, being devoid of the essence of permanence, the essence of stability, and the essence of self—but it should not be taken to mean nonexistent. For when 'an empty fist' is said, it is not meant that the fist does not exist. Rather, that which has nothing inside it is called empty. 'False' means destructive. 'Subject to vanishing' means having the nature of perishing; they are not manifest like a field, an estate, or gold and silver, but vanish after only a few days like things seen in a dream and are no longer perceived. Therefore, it is said, 'subject to vanishing.' 'Created by illusion' means that just as an illusionist shows water as a gem, a badari leaf as a coin, or anything else of that sort—it appears so only to one who remains within the range of vision, but once that range is exceeded, it is perceived as it truly is. In the same way, sensual pleasures are called 'created by illusion' because of their nature of appearing momentarily. And just as an illusionist deceives by showing water and the like as gems and so forth, sensual pleasures deceive by showing what is impermanent and so on as having the nature of permanence and so on; thus they are also called 'created by illusion' in the sense of being deceptive. 'The prattle of fools' is so called because of the prattling of fools, saying, 'My son, my daughter, my silver, my gold.' 'Sensual pleasures pertaining to this life' are the five strands of human sensual pleasure. 'Pertaining to the next life' refers to the remainder, having set those aside. 'Perception of sensual pleasure pertaining to this life' is the perception that arises in relation to human sensual pleasures. 'Both these are Māra's domain'—both these sensual pleasures and the perception of sensual pleasure are Māra's domain. For over those by whom both these are grasped, Māra exercises control. With reference to this, it is said, 'Both these are Māra's domain.'

Mārassesa visayotiādīsupi yathā coḷassa visayo coḷavisayo, paṇḍassa visayo paṇḍavisayo, saṃvarānaṃ visayo saṃvaravisayoti pavattanaṭṭhānaṃ visayoti vuccati, evaṃ yehi ete kāmā gahitā, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa visayoti vuttaṃ. Pañca pana kāmaguṇe nivāpabījaṃ viya vippakiranto [P 4.0058] māro gacchati. Yehi pana te gahitā, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa nivāpoti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca yattha hatthiādayo [V 4.0039] vasaṃ vattenti, so hatthigocaro assagocaro ajagocaroti vuccati, evaṃ [M 4.0039] yehi ete kāmā gahitā, tesu māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa gocaroti vuttaṃ.

In the phrases beginning with 'This is Māra's domain,' and so on: just as the domain of the Coḷas is called the Coḷa domain, the domain of the Paṇḍus is called the Paṇḍu domain, and the domain of the Saṃvaras is called the Saṃvara domain, so too, over those by whom these sensual pleasures are grasped, Māra exercises control. With reference to this, it is said, 'This is Māra's domain.' Furthermore, Māra goes about scattering the five strands of sensual pleasure like bait-seeds. Over those by whom they are grasped, Māra exercises control. With reference to this, it is said, 'This is Māra's bait.' And just as the place where elephants and others exercise control is called the elephant range, horse range, or goat range, so too, over those by whom these sensual pleasures are grasped, Māra exercises control. With reference to this, it is said, 'This is Māra's range.'

Etthāti etesu kāmesu. Mānasāti cittasambhūtā. Tattha siyā – duvidhe tāva kāme ārabbha abhijjhānalakkhaṇā abhijjhā, karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho ca uppajjatu, byāpādo kathaṃ uppajjatīti? Mamāyite vatthusmiṃ acchinnepi socanti, acchijjantepi socanti, acchinnasaṅkinopi socanti, yo evarūpo cittassa āghātoti evaṃ uppajjati. Teva ariyasāvakassāti te ariyasāvakassa. Vakāro āgamasandhimattaṃ hoti. Idha manusikkhatoti imasmiṃ sāsane sikkhantassa te tayopi kilesā antarāyakarā honti. Abhibhuyya lokanti kāmalokaṃ abhibhavitvā. Adhiṭṭhāya manasāti jhānārammaṇacittena adhiṭṭhahitvā. Aparittanti kāmāvacaracittaṃ parittaṃ nāma, tassa paṭikkhepena mahaggataṃ aparittaṃ nāma. Pamāṇantipi kāmāvacarameva, rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ appamāṇaṃ. Subhāvitanti pana etaṃ kāmāvacarādīnaṃ nāmaṃ na [P 4.0059] hoti, lokuttarassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā etassa vasena aparittaṃ appamāṇaṃ subhāvitanti sabbaṃ lokuttarameva vaṭṭati.

‘Herein’ refers to these sensual pleasures. ‘Mental’ means arisen from the mind. Here, there might be this question: Granted that in relation to the two kinds of sensual pleasures, covetousness—which is characterized by coveting—and aggression—which is characterized by excessive action—may arise, but how does ill will arise? Regarding a cherished object, people grieve even when it is snatched away, they grieve even when it is being destroyed, and they grieve even when they suspect it will be snatched away. Whatever resentment of the mind is of such a nature, thus it arises. ‘For the noble disciple’ (`Teva ariyasāvakassa`) means `te ariyasāvakassa` (for that noble disciple). The letter ‘v’ is merely an augment for euphonic combination. ‘Here one trains’ means that for one training in this dispensation, those three defilements are makers of obstacles. ‘Having overcome the world’ means having overcome the sensual world. ‘Having resolved with the mind’ means having resolved with a mind that has the jhāna object. ‘Unlimited’—the sense-sphere mind is called ‘limited’; in contrast to that, the exalted is called ‘unlimited.’ ‘Measured’ also refers only to the sense-sphere; the form-sphere and the formless-sphere are ‘immeasurable.’ As for ‘well-developed’—this term is not a name for the sense-sphere and so on; it is a name only for the supramundane. Therefore, by means of this term, ‘unlimited,’ ‘immeasurable,’ and ‘well-developed’ all apply only to the supramundane.

Tabbahulavihārinoti kāmapaṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āyatane cittaṃ pasīdatīti kāraṇe cittaṃ pasīdati. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ? Arahattaṃ vā, arahattassa vipassanaṃ vā, catutthajjhānaṃ vā, catutthajjhānassa upacāraṃ vā. Sampasāde satīti ettha duvidho sampasādo adhimokkhasampasādo ca paṭilābhasampasādo ca. Arahattassa hi vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā viharato mahābhūtādīsu upaṭṭhahantesu yenime nīhārena mahābhūtā upaṭṭhahanti, upādārūpā upaṭṭhahanti nāmarūpā upaṭṭhahanti, paccayā sabbathā upaṭṭhahanti, lakkhaṇārammaṇā vipassanā upaṭṭhahati, ajjeva arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmīti appaṭiladdheyeva āsā santiṭṭhati, adhimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Tatiyajjhānaṃ vā pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānatthāya kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontassa nīvaraṇavikkhambhanādīni samanupassato yenime nīhārena nīvaraṇā vikkhambhanti, kilesā sannisīdanti, sati santiṭṭhati, saṅkhāragataṃ vā vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā dibbacakkhukassa paraloko viya upaṭṭhāti[M 4.0040], cittuppādo lepapiṇḍe laggamāno viya upacārena samādhiyati, ajjeva catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattessāmīti apaṭiladdheyeva āsā santiṭṭhati, adhimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati[V 4.0040]. Ayaṃ adhimokkhasampasādo [P 4.0060] nāma. Tasmiṃ sampasāde sati. Yo pana arahattaṃ vā paṭilabhati catutthajjhānaṃ vā, tassa cittaṃ vippasannaṃ hotiyeva. Idha pana “āyatane cittaṃ pasīdatī”ti vacanato arahattavipassanāya ceva catutthajjhānūpacārassa ca paṭilābho paṭilābhasampasādoti veditabbo. Vipassanā hi paññāya adhimuccanassa kāraṇaṃ, upacāraṃ āneñjasamāpattiyā.

“Dwelling much in that” means for one who dwells frequently practicing that very path by restraining sensual desires. “The mind becomes serene in the sphere” means the mind becomes serene in the cause. What is the cause here? It is either Arahantship, or insight for Arahantship, or the fourth jhāna, or the access concentration of the fourth jhāna. In the passage “when there is serene confidence,” serene confidence is twofold: the serene confidence of conviction and the serene confidence of attainment. For one who dwells having established insight for Arahantship, when the great elements and so forth appear—in such a way that these great elements appear, the derived forms appear, name-and-form appear, conditions appear in every way, and insight with the characteristics as its object appears—even before attaining it, the hope, “Today I will attain Arahantship,” is established, and one obtains conviction. Or, for one who, having made the third jhāna a basis, performs preparatory work on the kasiṇa for the sake of the fourth jhāna, observing the suppression of hindrances and so forth—in such a way that these hindrances are suppressed, the defilements subside, mindfulness is established, or the conditioned formations become distinct and manifest, appearing like the next world to one with the divine eye—the arising of mind becomes concentrated through access concentration, as if sticking to a lump of clay. Even before attaining it, the hope, “Today I will produce the fourth jhāna,” is established, and one obtains conviction. This is called the serene confidence of conviction. When that serene confidence is present… But as for one who attains either Arahantship or the fourth jhāna, their mind is indeed especially serene. Here, however, from the statement “the mind becomes serene in the sphere,” the attainment of both insight for Arahantship and access to the fourth jhāna should be understood as the serene confidence of attainment. For insight is the cause of conviction through wisdom, and access concentration is the cause of conviction for the imperturbable attainment.

Etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Paññāya vā adhimuccatīti ettha etarahi vā paññāya adhimuccati, āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjatīti evaṃ padaparivattanaṃ katvā attho veditabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – tasmiṃ sampasāde sati etarahi vā paññāya adhimuccati, arahattaṃ sacchikarotīti attho. Taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjati, atha vā paññāya vā adhimuccatīti arahattamaggaṃ bhāveti, taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjati. Arahattamaggaṃ bhāvetuṃ asakkonto etarahi catusaccaṃ vā sacchikaroti. Taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjatīti.

Alternatively, now one enters the imperturbable attainment. In the passage “or becomes resolved through wisdom,” the meaning should be understood by rearranging the words thus: “Now one becomes resolved through wisdom, or one enters the imperturbable attainment.” For this is what is meant: when that serene confidence is present, now one becomes resolved through wisdom, meaning one realizes Arahantship. Not being able to attain that, one enters the imperturbable attainment. Alternatively, “becomes resolved through wisdom” means one develops the Arahant path. Not being able to attain that, one enters the imperturbable attainment. Unable to develop the Arahant path, now one realizes the four truths with the lower paths. Not being able to attain that, one enters the imperturbable attainment.

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – idha bhikkhu tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānassa kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti. Tassa nīvaraṇā vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So rūpārūpaṃ parigaṇhāti, paccayaṃ pariggaṇhāti, lakkhaṇārammaṇikaṃ vipassanaṃ vavatthapeti, tassa evaṃ hoti – “upacārena me jhānaṃ visesabhāgiyaṃ bhaveyya, tiṭṭhatu visesabhāgiyatā, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ naṃ karissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchikaroti. Ettakenassa kiccaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti. Arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkonto pana tato osakkitamānaso antarā na tiṭṭhati, catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjatiyeva. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā puriso “vanamahiṃsaṃ ghātessāmī”ti sattiṃ gahetvā anubandhanto [P 4.0061] sace taṃ ghāteti, sakalagāmavāsino tosessati, asakkonto pana antarāmagge sasagodhādayo khuddakamige ghātetvā kājaṃ pūretvā etiyeva.

Herein, this is the method: Here, a monk, having made the third jhāna a basis, performs the preparatory work on the kasiṇa for the fourth jhāna. For him, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is established, and the mind is concentrated through access concentration. He comprehends form and the formless, comprehends conditions, and establishes insight that has the characteristics as its object. For him, it occurs thus: “Through my access concentration, the jhāna might become partaking of distinction. Let the partaking of distinction be; I will make it partaking of penetration.” Developing insight, he realizes Arahantship. By this much, his task is considered done. But being unable to realize Arahantship, his mind, having fallen back from that, does not stop in between; he definitely enters the fourth jhāna. What is this like? It is like a man who, thinking, “I will kill a wild buffalo,” takes a spear and pursues it. If he kills it, he will please all the villagers. But being unable to do so, he kills small game like hares and monitor lizards along the way, fills his carrying pole, and just comes back.

Tattha [M 4.0041] purisassa sattiṃ gahetvā vanamahiṃsānubandhanaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānassa parikammakaraṇaṃ, vanamahiṃsaghātanaṃ viya – “nīvaraṇavikkhambhanādīni samanupassato visesabhāgiyaṃ bhaveyya, tiṭṭhatu visesabhāgiyatā, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ [V 4.0041] naṃ karissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattassa sacchikaraṇaṃ, mahiṃsaṃ ghātetuṃ asakkontassa antarāmagge sasagodhādayo khuddakamige ghātetvā kājaṃ pūretvā gamanaṃ viya arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkontassa, tato osakkitvā catutthajjhānasamāpajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Maggabhāvanā catusaccasacchikiriyāyojanāsupi eseva nayo.

Therein, this monk's making the third jhāna a basis and performing the preparatory work for the fourth jhāna should be understood to be like a man taking a spear and pursuing a wild buffalo. The realization of Arahantship by developing insight—while observing the suppression of hindrances and so on, and thinking, “It might become partaking of distinction. Let the partaking of distinction be; I will make it partaking of penetration”—should be understood to be like the killing of the wild buffalo. For one unable to realize Arahantship, the falling back from that and entering the fourth jhāna should be understood to be like a man unable to kill the buffalo who, killing small game such as hares and monitor lizards along the way, fills his carrying pole and goes on. This same method should be understood also in the applications of developing the path to Arahantship and of realizing the four truths with the lower paths.

Idāni arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkontassa nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ dassento kāyassa bhedātiādimāha. Tattha yanti yena kāraṇena taṃ saṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa āneñjūpagaṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjatīti attho. Ettha ca taṃsaṃvattanikanti tassa bhikkhuno saṃvattanikaṃ. Yena vipākaviññāṇena so bhikkhu saṃvattati nibbattati, taṃ viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjūpaganti kusalāneñjasabhāvūpagataṃ assa, tādisameva bhaveyyāti [P 4.0062] attho. Keci kusalaviññāṇaṃ vadanti. Yaṃ tassa bhikkhuno saṃvattanikaṃ upapattihetubhūtaṃ kusalaviññāṇaṃ āneñjūpagataṃ assa, vipākakālepi tannāmakameva assāti attho. So panāyamattho – “puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāroti, apuññupagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.51) iminā nayena veditabbo. Āneñjasappāyāti āneñjassa catutthajjhānassa sappāyā. Na kevalañca sā āneñjasseva, upari arahattassāpi sappāyāva upakārabhūtāyevāti veditabbā. Iti imasmiṃ paṭhamakaāneñje samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

Now, wishing to show the place of rebirth for one who is unable to realize Arahantship, the Blessed One said, “With the breakup of the body,” and so on. Therein, yanti means: the cause exists by which that consciousness conducive to rebirth would reach the imperturbable; this is the meaning. And here, taṃsaṃvattanikanti means conducive to rebirth for that monk. It is the resultant consciousness by which that monk is reborn. Āneñjūpaganti means it would have attained the nature of the wholesome imperturbable; it would be of that very kind. This is the meaning. Some say it is wholesome consciousness. The meaning is that the wholesome consciousness which is the cause of that monk's rebirth and has reached the imperturbable would have that very name even at the time of its result. This meaning, however, should be understood according to this method: “If one generates a meritorious formation, consciousness becomes based on merit. If one generates a demeritorious formation, consciousness becomes based on demerit. If one generates an imperturbable formation, consciousness becomes based on the imperturbable” (SN 12.51). Āneñjasappāyāti means suitable for the imperturbable, that is, the fourth jhāna. And it should be known that this is not only suitable for the imperturbable, but is also suitable for and helpful towards the higher attainment of Arahantship. Thus, in this first imperturbable attainment, falling back by way of concentration is spoken of.

67. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti catutthajjhānaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi bhikkhu heṭṭhimena bhikkhunā paññavantataro tassa ca bhikkhuno attano cāti dvinnampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Tabbahulavihārinoti rūpapaṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjatīti [M 4.0042] ākāsānañcāyatānāneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha visesamattameva pana vakkhāma. Iti imasmiṃ dutiyaāneñje vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā, “yaṃkiñci [P 4.0063] rūpa”nti evaṃ vipassanāmaggaṃ dassentena kathitāti attho.

67. Iti paṭisañcikkhati means: having attained the fourth jhāna, he reflects thus. For this monk is more discerning than the monk below. He comprehends the meditation subject of both—that monk and himself—having made them one. Tabbahulavihārino means: for one who dwells having frequently practiced that very path by overcoming form. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjati means: he attains the imperturbable attainment of the base of the infinity of space. The rest is just as before. And as here, so everywhere; we, however, will speak only of the difference. Thus, in this second imperturbable attainment, falling back by way of insight is spoken of. The meaning is that it is spoken of by the one showing the path of insight thus: 'Whatever form...'

Iti [V 4.0042] paṭisañcikkhatīti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā dvīhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti tiṇṇampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Ubhayametaṃ aniccanti ettha aṭṭha ekekakoṭṭhāsā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikavasena pana saṅkhipitvā ubhayanti vuttaṃ. Nālaṃ abhinanditunti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandituṃ na yuttaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tabbahulavihārinoti kāmapaṭibāhanena ca rūpapaṭibāhanena ca tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjatīti viññāṇañcāyatanāneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Imasmiṃ tatiyaāneñje vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhati means: having reached the base of the infinity of space, he reflects thus. For this one is more discerning than the two monks below. He comprehends the meditation subjects of those monks and his own, thus of all three, having made them one. Regarding Ubhayametaṃ aniccanti ('Both these are impermanent'): here there are eight individual portions, but having summarized them by way of the present life and the future life, it is said as 'both'. Nālaṃ abhinanditunti means it is not proper to delight by way of craving and wrong view. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases. Tabbahulavihārino means: for one who dwells having frequently practiced that very path by repelling sensual perceptions and by repelling form perceptions. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjati means: he attains the imperturbable attainment of the base of the infinity of consciousness. In this third imperturbable attainment, falling back by way of insight is spoken of.

68. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā tīhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti catunnampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ patvā etā heṭṭhā vuttā sabbasaññā nirujjhanti. Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti etaṃ aṅgasantatāya ārammaṇasantatāya ca santaṃ, atappakaṭṭhena paṇītaṃ. Tabbahulavihārinoti tāsaṃ saññānaṃ paṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ paṭhamākiñcaññāyatane samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

68. Iti paṭisañcikkhati means: having reached the base of the infinity of consciousness, he reflects thus. For this one is more discerning than the three monks below. He comprehends the meditation subjects of those three monks and his own, thus of all four, having made them one. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantīti means: having reached the base of nothingness, these perceptions spoken of below cease without remainder. Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti means: this is peaceful due to the peacefulness of its factors and the peacefulness of its object, and it is sublime due to its excellence. Tabbahulavihārino means: for one who dwells having frequently practiced that very path by repelling those perceptions. In this first attainment of the base of nothingness, falling back by way of concentration is spoken of.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanameva patvā evaṃ [P 4.0064] paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā catūhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti pañcannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Attena vā attaniyena vāti ahaṃ mamāti gahetabbena suññaṃ tucchaṃ rittaṃ. Evamettha dvikoṭikā suññatā dassitā. Tabbahulavihārinoti heṭṭhā vuttapaṭipadañca imañca suññatapaṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ dutiyākiñcaññāyatane vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhati means: having reached the base of the infinity of consciousness itself, he reflects thus. For this one is more discerning than the four monks below, and he comprehends the meditation subjects of those monks and his own, thus of all five, having made them one. Attena vā attaniyena vāti means: empty, void, and devoid of anything that can be grasped as 'I' or 'mine'. Thus, the two-ended emptiness is shown here. Tabbahulavihārino means: for one who dwells having frequently practiced both the path spoken of below and this path of emptiness. In this second attainment of the base of nothingness, falling back by way of insight is spoken of.

70. Iti [M 4.0043] paṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanameva patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā pañcahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti channampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Nāhaṃ kvacani kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ, na ca mama kvacani kismiñci [V 4.0043] kiñcanaṃ natthīti ettha pana catukoṭikā suññatā kathitā. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi nāhaṃ kvacanīti kvaci attānaṃ na passati, kassaci kiñcanatasminti attano attānaṃ kassaci parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ na passati, attano bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāraṃ maññitvā upagantvā upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama – saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā na ca kvacani parassa ca attānaṃ kvaci na passatīti ayamattho. Idāni mama – saddaṃ āharitvā mama kismiñci kiñcanaṃ natthīti so parassa attā mama kismiñci kiñcanabhāve atthīti na passati. Attano bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāranti kismiñci ṭhāne parassa attānaṃ iminā kiñcanabhāvena upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Evamayaṃ yasmā neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve [P 4.0065] upanetabbaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, tasmā ayaṃ suññatā catukoṭikāti veditabbā. Tabbahulavihārinoti heṭṭhā vuttappaṭipadaṃ imaṃ catukoṭisuññatañca bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ tatiyākiñcaññāyatanepi vipassanāvaseneva osakkanā kathitā.

70. “Thus he reflects” means: having attained the sphere of consciousness, he reflects in this way. Indeed, this one is more intelligent than the five monks below. He considers the meditation subject of those monks and his own, thus combining the meditation subjects of all six. In the phrase, “I am not a 'something' of anyone anywhere, nor is there for me a 'something' in anything anywhere,” a four-limbed emptiness is taught. How so? “I am not anywhere” means he does not see a self anywhere. “Of anyone a 'something'” means he does not see his own self as something to be brought forward on account of being a concern for any other person; the meaning is that he does not see it as something to be brought forward, having considered a brother in the place of a brother, a companion in the place of a companion, or an attendant in the place of an attendant, and having approached them. In “Nor for me anywhere,” first setting aside the word “mama” (for me), the meaning is that he does not see the self of another anywhere. Now, bringing in the word “mama,” “for me in anything there is no 'something'” means he does not see that the self of another exists in the state of being a concern for him in any way. The meaning is that he does not see the self of another in any place as something to be brought forward on account of this state of being a concern, whether as a brother in the place of a brother, a companion in the place of a companion, or an attendant in the place of an attendant. Thus, because he neither sees a self anywhere, nor sees that self as something to be brought forward on account of being a concern for another, nor sees the self of another, nor sees the self of another as something to be brought forward on account of being a concern for himself, therefore, this emptiness should be known as four-limbed. “For one who dwells much in that” means for one who dwells having frequently practiced both the path spoken of below and this four-limbed emptiness. In this third sphere of nothingness, too, a falling away by the power of insight is taught.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā chahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti sattannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ patvā ettha etā heṭṭhā vuttā sabbasaññā nirujjhanti. Tabbahulavihārinoti tāsaṃ saññānaṃ paṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatane samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

“Thus he reflects” means: having reached the sphere of nothingness, he reflects in this way. Indeed, this one is more intelligent than the six monks below. He considers the meditation subject of those monks and his own, thus combining the meditation subjects of all seven. “Where these cease without remainder” means: having reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there all these perceptions spoken of below cease. “For one who dwells much in that” means: for one who dwells having frequently practiced that very path by means of warding off those perceptions. In this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a falling away by the power of concentration is taught.

71. No cassa no ca me siyāti sace mayhaṃ pubbe pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ na āyūhitaṃ assa, yaṃ me idaṃ etarahi evaṃ pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ etaṃ me na [M 4.0044] siyā nappavatteyyāti attho. Na bhavissatīti sace etarahi pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ āyūhitaṃ na bhavissati. Na me bhavissatīti tasmiṃ asati anāgate me pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ na bhavissati. Yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ [V 4.0044] taṃ pajahāmīti yaṃ atthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ etarahi khandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ pajahāmi. Evaṃ [P 4.0066] upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatīti so bhikkhu evaṃ vipassanupekkhaṃ labhatīti attho.

71. “If it had not been, it would not be for me” means: if in the past the fivefold round of kamma had not been accumulated by me, then this fivefold round of result that is now for me would not be; it would not occur. This is the meaning. “It will not be” means: if now the fivefold round of kamma will not be accumulated. “It will not be for me” means: when that is not, in the future the fivefold round of result will not be for me. “What exists, what has come to be, that I abandon” means: what exists, what has come to be now—the five aggregates—that I abandon. “Thus he attains equanimity” means: that monk thus attains the equanimity of insight. This is the meaning.

Parinibbāyeyya nu kho so, bhante, bhikkhu na vā parinibbāyeyyāti kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati, tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa arahattampi osakkanāpi paṭipadāpi paṭisandhipi kathitā, tathā catutthajjhānādīni pādakāni katvā ṭhitānaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa na kiñci kathitaṃ, taṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Apetthāti api ettha. So taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandatīti so taṃ vipassanupekkhaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiabhinandanāhi abhinandati. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇanti viññāṇaṃ vipassanānissitaṃ hoti. Tadupādānanti yaṃ nikantiviññāṇaṃ, taṃ tassa upādānaṃ nāma gahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Saupādānoti sagahaṇo. Na parinibbāyatīti vipassanāya sālayo bhikkhu mama sāsane na parinibbāyati. Yo pana vihārapariveṇaupaṭṭhākādīsu sālayo, tasmiṃ vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. Kahaṃ panāti? Kattha pana? Upādiyamāno [P 4.0067] upādiyatīti paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhamāno gaṇhāti. Upādānaseṭṭhaṃ kira so, bhanteti, bhante, so kira bhikkhu gahetabbaṭṭhānaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ bhavaṃ upādiyati, seṭṭhabhave paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhātīti attho. Iminā tassa bhikkhuno paṭisandhi kathitā. Idānissa arahattaṃ kathetuṃ idhānandātiādimāha.

“Venerable sir, would that monk attain final Nibbāna, or would he not?” means: he asks, explaining the premise of his question: For a monk established having made the third jhāna his basis, arahantship, falling away, the path, and rebirth-linking have been taught; likewise for those established having made the fourth jhāna and so on their basis. But for a monk established having made the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception his basis, nothing has been taught. He asks, “I am asking about that monk.” “Apettha” means “api ettha.” “He delights in that equanimity” means: he greatly delights in that equanimity of insight with the delighting of craving and wrong view. In the remaining two phrases, this is the same method. “Consciousness is dependent on that” means: consciousness becomes dependent on insight. “That is its clinging” means: whatever consciousness of delight there is, that is called its clinging, called its grasping. “With clinging” means: with grasping. “He does not attain final Nibbāna” means: a monk with attachment to insight does not attain final Nibbāna in my dispensation. He shows that as for one who has attachment to monasteries, grounds, supporters, and so on, there is nothing more to be said. “But where?” means: in what place? “Clinging, he clings” means: taking rebirth-linking, he takes it. “Venerable sir, it seems he clings to the supreme object of clinging” means: Venerable sir, that monk, it seems, clings to the best place to be grasped, the supreme existence; he takes rebirth-linking in the best existence. This is the meaning. By this, the rebirth-linking of that monk is taught. Now, to teach his arahantship, the Blessed One said, “Here, Ānanda,” and so on.

73. Nissāya nissāyāti taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ nissāya. Oghassa nittharaṇā akkhātāti oghataraṇaṃ kathitaṃ, tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitabhikkhuno oghanittharaṇā kathitā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitabhikkhuno oghanittharaṇā kathitāti vadati.

73. “Depending, depending” means: depending on this and that attainment. “The crossing of the flood is declared” means: the crossing of the flood is taught. For a monk established having made the third jhāna his basis, the crossing of the flood is taught… For a monk established having made the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception his basis, the crossing of the flood is taught—thus he says.

Katamo pana, bhante, ariyo vimokkhoti idha kiṃ pucchati? Samāpattiṃ tāva padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhanto bhikkhu nāvaṃ vā uḷumpādīni vā nissāya mahoghaṃ taritvā pāraṃ gacchanto viya [M 4.0045] na kilamati. Sukkhavipassako pana pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ gaṇhanto bāhubalena sotaṃ chinditvā pāraṃ gacchanto viya kilamati. Iti imassa sukkhavipassakassa arahattaṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Ariyasāvakoti sukkhavipassako ariyasāvako. Ayañhi heṭṭhā aṭṭhahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ [V 4.0045] attano cāti navannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Esa sakkāyo yāvatā sakkāyoti yattako tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhāto sakkāyo nāma atthi, sabbopi so esa sakkāyo, na ito paraṃ sakkāyo atthīti paṭisañcikkhati.

Herein, what is asked by the phrase, 'Venerable sir, what is the noble liberation?' First, a bhikkhu who, having made attainment a basis and developed insight, attains the fruit of Arahantship is not fatigued, like one who crosses a great flood and reaches the other shore by relying on a boat or a raft. A dry-insight practitioner, however, who contemplates the miscellaneous formations and attains the fruit of Arahantship, is fatigued, like one who cuts through the stream by the strength of his arms and reaches the other shore. Thus, he asks, 'I ask about the fruit of Arahantship of this dry-insight practitioner.' 'A noble disciple' means a noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner. Indeed, this one is wiser than the eight bhikkhus mentioned previously. And he contemplates the meditation subjects of all nine—those of the eight bhikkhus and his own—having combined them into one. As for 'This is identity, as far as identity extends,' he reflects thus: 'Whatever identity, known as the round of the three planes, exists, all of that is this identity; beyond this, there is no other identity.'

Etaṃ [P 4.0068] amataṃ yadidaṃ anupādā cittassa vimokkhoti yo panesa cittassa anupādāvimokkho nāma, etaṃ amataṃ etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti paṭisañcikkhati. Aññattha ca “anupādā cittassa vimokkho”ti nibbānaṃ vuccati. Imasmiṃ pana sutte sukkhavipassakassa arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

As for 'This is the Deathless, that is, the liberation of the mind without clinging,' one reflects thus: 'Whatever is called this liberation of the mind without clinging, this is the Deathless, this is peaceful, this is sublime.' And elsewhere, 'the liberation of the mind without clinging' is said to be Nibbāna. In this sutta, however, the fruit of Arahantship of a dry-insight practitioner is taught. The remainder is clear in all respects.

Kevalaṃ pana imasmiṃ sutte sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanā kathitā, aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu paṭisandhi, navasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ tāva pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa bhikkhuno osakkanā kathitā, paṭisandhi kathitā, arahattaṃ kathitaṃ, tathā catutthajjhānaṃ, tathā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ pana padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā ṭhitānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ osakkanā kathitā, paṭisandhi kathitā, arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Tathā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa bhikkhuno. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa pana osakkanā natthi, paṭisandhi pana arahattañca kathitaṃ. Sukkhavipassakassa arahattameva kathitanti. Evaṃ sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanā kathitā, aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu paṭisandhi, navasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Imañca pana sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanaṃ aṭṭhasu paṭisandhiṃ navasu arahattaṃ samodhānetvā kathentena imaṃ āneñjasappāyasuttaṃ sukathitaṃ nāma hotīti.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in this sutta, falling away is taught in seven cases, rebirth-linking in eight cases, and the fruit of Arahantship in nine cases. How so? For a bhikkhu established with the third jhāna as a foundation, falling away is taught, rebirth-linking is taught, and the fruit of Arahantship is taught. Similarly for the fourth jhāna, and similarly for the base of the infinitude of space. For a bhikkhu established with the base of the infinitude of consciousness as a foundation, falling away is taught, rebirth-linking is taught, and the fruit of Arahantship is taught. Similarly for the bhikkhu established with the base of nothingness as a foundation. For one established with the base of neither perception nor non-perception as a foundation, however, there is no falling away, but rebirth-linking and the fruit of Arahantship are taught. For the dry-insight practitioner, only the fruit of Arahantship is taught. Thus, it should be understood that falling away is taught in seven cases, rebirth-linking in eight cases, and the fruit of Arahantship in nine cases. And when one teaches by combining this falling away in seven cases, this rebirth-linking in eight, and this fruit of Arahantship in nine, this Āneñjasappāya Sutta comes to be well-taught.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Āneñjasappāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āneñjasappāya Sutta is concluded.

7. Gaṇakamoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta

74. Evaṃ [V 4.0046][P 4.0069][M 4.0046] me sutanti gaṇakamoggallānasuttaṃ. Tattha yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāti yāva paṭhamasopānaphalakā ekadivaseneva sattabhūmiko pāsādo na sakkā kātuṃ, vatthuṃ sodhetvā thambhussāpanato paṭṭhāya pana yāva cittakammakaraṇā anupubbakiriyā cettha paññāyatīti dasseti. Yadidaṃ ajjheneti tayopi vedā na sakkā ekadivaseneva adhīyituṃ, etesaṃ ajjhenepi pana anupubbakiriyāva paññāyatīti dasseti. Issattheti āvudhavijjāyapi ekadivaseneva vālavedhi nāma na sakkā kātuṃ, ṭhānasampādanamuṭṭhikaraṇādīhi pana etthāpi anupubbakiriyā paññāyatīti dasseti. Saṅkhāneti gaṇanāya. Tattha anupubbakiriyaṃ attanāva dassento evaṃ gaṇāpemātiādimāha.

74. Thus have I heard—this is the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta. Therein, the phrase 'up to the last timber of the staircase' means 'up to the first plank of the staircase'. A seven-storied palace cannot be built in a single day; rather, starting from clearing the site and erecting the pillars up to the point of doing the painting, a gradual process is apparent here—thus it shows. Regarding 'that which is this learning', the three Vedas cannot be learned in a single day; rather, in the study of these also, a gradual process is apparent—thus it shows. Regarding 'in archery', in the art of weapons also, the skill called 'hair-splitting' cannot be achieved in a single day; rather, through accomplishing the stance, making the fist, and so on, here too a gradual process is apparent—thus it shows. 'In calculation' means by counting. Therein, wishing to show the gradual process himself, he said, 'Thus we make them calculate,' and so on.

75. Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇāti idha bhagavā yasmā bāhirasamaye yathā yathā sippaṃ uggaṇhanti, tathā tathā kerāṭikā honti, tasmā attano sāsanaṃ bāhirasamayena anupametvā bhadraassājānīyena upamento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Bhadro hi assājānīyo yasmiṃ kāraṇe damito hoti, taṃ jīvitahetupi nātikkamati. Evameva sāsane sammāpaṭipanno kulaputto sīlavelaṃ nātikkamati. Mukhādhāneti mukhaṭṭhapane.

75. Just as, brahmin—here, the Blessed One, because in external doctrines, the more they learn a craft, the more deceitful they become, therefore, not comparing His own Sāsana with an external doctrine, but wishing to make a comparison with a fine thoroughbred horse, spoke the words beginning with 'Just as...'. For a fine thoroughbred horse, in whatever matter it has been tamed, it does not transgress that, even for the sake of its life. In the very same way, a clansman who is practicing rightly in the Sāsana does not transgress the boundary of virtue. 'In the placing of the bit' (mukhādhāne) means in the placing in the mouth.

76. Satisampajaññāya cāti satisampajaññāhi samaṅgibhāvatthāya[P 4.0070]. Dve hi khīṇāsavā satatavihārī ca nosatatavihārī ca. Tattha satatavihārī yaṃkiñci kammaṃ katvāpi phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ sakkoti, no satatavihārī pana appamattakepi kicce kiccappasuto hutvā phalasamāpattiṃ appetuṃ na sakkoti.

76. 'And with mindfulness and clear comprehension' (satisampajaññāya ca) means for the purpose of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. For there are two kinds of Arahants: one who dwells constantly and one who does not dwell constantly. Among them, one who dwells constantly can enter fruition attainment even after doing any work, but one who does not dwell constantly, being absorbed in a task even if it is a minor one, is not able to enter fruition attainment.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira khīṇāsavatthero khīṇāsavasāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā araññavāsaṃ gato, tattha mahātherassa senāsanaṃ pattaṃ, sāmaṇerassa na pāpuṇāti, taṃ vitakkento thero ekadivasampi phalasamāpattiṃ appetuṃ nāsakkhi. Sāmaṇero pana temāsaṃ phalasamāpattiratiyā vītināmetvā “sappāyo[V 4.0047], bhante, araññavāso jāto”ti [M 4.0047] theraṃ pucchi. Thero “na jāto, āvuso”ti āha. Iti yo evarūpo khīṇāsavo, so ime dhamme ādito paṭṭhāya āvajjitvāva samāpajjituṃ sakkhissatīti dassento “satisampajaññāya cā”ti āha.

Here is the story: A certain elder who was an Arahant, taking a novice who was an Arahant, went to a forest dwelling, it is said. There, a lodging was obtained for the great elder, but one did not reach the novice. While thinking about this, the elder could not enter fruition attainment even for a single day. The novice, however, after spending the three months delighting in fruition attainment, asked the elder, 'Venerable sir, has the forest dwelling become suitable?' The elder replied, 'No, friend.' Thus, showing that an Arahant of this kind will be able to enter attainment only after adverting to these dhammas from the very beginning, the Blessed One said, 'and with mindfulness and clear comprehension'.

78. Yeme, bho gotamāti tathāgate kira kathayanteva brāhmaṇassa “ime puggalā na ārādhenti, ime ārādhentī”ti nayo udapādi, taṃ dassento evaṃ vattumāraddho.

78. 'Those, Master Gotama'—while the Tathāgata was speaking, it is said, this line of reasoning arose in the brahmin: 'These persons, it seems, do not succeed; these persons, it seems, do succeed.' Showing this, he began to speak thus.

Paramajjadhammesūti ajjadhammā nāma chasatthāradhammā, tesu gotamavādova, paramo uttamoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'In the highest of today's doctrines' means: 'today's doctrines' are the doctrines of the six teachers. Among them, the doctrine of Gotama alone is the highest, the supreme—this is the meaning. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Gaṇakamoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta is concluded.

8. Gopakamoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Gopaka Moggallāna Sutta.

79. Evaṃ [V 4.0048] me sutanti gopakamoggallānasuttaṃ. Tattha aciraparinibbute bhagavatīti bhagavati aciraparinibbute, dhātubhājanīyaṃ katvā dhammasaṅgītiṃ kātuṃ rājagahaṃ āgatakāle[P 4.0071]. Rañño pajjotassa āsaṅkamānoti caṇḍapajjoto nāmesa rājā bimbisāramahārājassa sahāyo ahosi, jīvakaṃ pesetvā bhesajjakāritakālato paṭṭhāya pana daḷhamittova jāto, so “ajātasattunā devadattassa vacanaṃ gahetvā pitā ghātito”ti sutvā “mama piyamittaṃ ghātetvā esa rajjaṃ karissāmīti maññati, mayhaṃ sahāyassa sahāyānaṃ atthikabhāvaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti parisati vācaṃ abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā tassa āsaṅkā uppannā. Tena vuttaṃ “rañño pajjotassa āsaṅkamāno”ti. Kammantoti bahinagare nagarapaṭisaṅkhārāpanatthāya kammantaṭṭhānaṃ.

79. Thus have I heard: the Gopaka Moggallāna Sutta. Therein, 'when the Blessed One had not long passed into Parinibbāna' refers to the time shortly after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, after having distributed the relics and having come to Rājagaha to hold the Dhamma recitation. 'Fearing King Pajjota' means: King Caṇḍapajjota was a friend of the great king Bimbisāra. Moreover, from the time he sent Jīvaka to have medicine administered, he became a firm friend. Having heard that 'Ajātasattu, taking Devadatta's word, had his father killed,' he (Caṇḍapajjota) spoke these words in his assembly: 'Having killed my dear friend, this one thinks, "I will rule the kingdom." I will make him know that my friend has friends.' Hearing that, fear arose in him (Ajātasattu). Therefore it is said, 'fearing King Pajjota.' 'Work' means a place of work outside the city for the purpose of having the city repaired.

Upasaṅkamīti mayaṃ dhammavinayasaṅgītiṃ kāressāmāti vicarāma, ayañca mahesakkho rājavallabho saṅgahe kate veḷuvanassa ārakkhaṃ kareyyāti maññamāno upasaṅkami. Tehi dhammehīti tehi sabbaññutaññāṇadhammehi. Sabbena sabbanti sabbākārena sabbaṃ. Sabbathā sabbanti sabbakoṭṭhāsehi [M 4.0048] sabbaṃ. Kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati? Cha hi satthāro paṭhamataraṃ appaññātakulehi nikkhamitvā pabbajitā, te tathāgate dharamāneyeva kālaṃkatā, sāvakāpi nesaṃ appaññātakuleheva pabbajitā. Te tesaṃ accayena mahāvivādaṃ akaṃsu. Samaṇo pana gotamo mahākulā pabbajito, tassa accayena sāvakānaṃ mahāvivādo bhavissatīti ayaṃ kathā sakalajambudīpaṃ pattharamānā udapādi. Sammāsambuddhe ca dharante bhikkhūnaṃ vivādo nāhosi. Yopi ahosi, sopi tattheva vūpasamito. Parinibbutakāle panassa – “aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedhaṃ [P 4.0072] sineruṃ apavāhituṃ samatthassa vātassa purato purāṇapaṇṇaṃ kiṃ ṭhassati, dasa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pattassa satthu alajjamāno maccurājā kassa lajjissatī”ti mahāsaṃvegaṃ janetvā bhiyyosomattāya bhikkhū samaggā jātā ativiya upasantupasantā, kiṃ nu kho etanti idaṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Anusaññāyamānoti anusañjāyamāno, katākataṃ janantoti attho. Anuvicaramāno vā.

'He approached' means: We are wandering about, thinking, 'We will hold the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.' And thinking, 'This brahmin is powerful and a favorite of the king; if I show him favor, he might provide protection for the Veḷuvana monastery,' he (Ānanda) approached. 'By those dhammas' means by those qualities of omniscient knowledge. 'In every way' means completely in all aspects. 'In every respect' means completely in all parts. Thinking, 'What shall I ask?' he asks. For the six teachers, having first gone forth from unknown families, became wanderers. They passed away while the Tathāgata was still living. Their disciples, too, had gone forth from unknown families. After the passing of their teachers, they engaged in great disputes. But the ascetic Gotama went forth from a great family. 'After his passing, there will be a great dispute among his disciples'—this talk, spreading, arose throughout all of Jambudīpa. And while the Sammāsambuddha was living, there was no dispute among the bhikkhus. Whatever dispute did arise was settled right there. But at the time of his Parinibbāna, arousing great spiritual urgency by thinking, 'Before a wind capable of unsettling Mount Sineru, one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas in height, how can an old leaf stand? The King of Death is not ashamed before the Teacher who attained omniscient knowledge after fulfilling the ten perfections; before whom would he be ashamed?'—the bhikkhus became harmonious beyond measure, exceedingly peaceful and calm. 'What is the reason for this?'—he asks this, meaning, 'I ask this cause.' `Anusaññāyamāno` means repeatedly knowing, knowing what has been done and what has not been done; that is the meaning. Or, investigating.

80. Atthi [V 4.0049] nu khoti ayampi heṭṭhimapucchameva pucchati. Appaṭisaraṇeti appaṭisaraṇe dhammavinaye. Ko hetu sāmaggiyāti tumhākaṃ samaggabhāvassa ko hetu ko paccayo. Dhammappaṭisaraṇāti dhammo amhākaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, dhammo avassayoti dīpeti.

80. By the phrase 'Is there indeed?', this one too asks the same question as the former one. `Appaṭisaraṇe` means in the Dhamma and Vinaya without a refuge. 'What is the cause of harmony?' means: what is the cause, what is the condition, for your state of harmony? 'Having the Dhamma as refuge' means the Dhamma is our refuge; it indicates that the Dhamma is our support.

81. Pavattatīti paguṇaṃ hutvā āgacchati. Āpatti hoti vītikkamoti ubhayametaṃ buddhassa āṇātikkamanameva. Yathādhammaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ kāremāti yathā dhammo ca anusiṭṭhi ca ṭhitā, evaṃ kāremāti attho.

81. `Pavattati` means it becomes well-practiced. 'There is an offense, a transgression' means both of these are simply a transgression of the Buddha's command. 'We act according to the Dhamma, according to the instruction' means: in whatever way the Dhamma and the instruction are established, so do we act. This is the meaning.

Na kira no bhavanto kārenti dhammo no kāretīti padadvayepi no kāro nipātamattaṃ. Evaṃ sante na kira bhavanto kārenti, dhammova kāretīti ayamettha attho.

Regarding the phrase 'Na kira no bhavanto kārenti, dhammo no kāreti': in both parts, the word 'no' is merely a particle. This being so, the meaning here is this: 'It is not, indeed, that you, venerable sirs, cause it; the Dhamma alone causes it'.

83. Tagghāti [P 4.0073] ekaṃse nipāto. Kahaṃ pana bhavaṃ ānandoti kiṃ therassa veḷuvane vasanabhāvaṃ na jānātīti? Jānāti. Veḷuvanassa pana [M 4.0049] anena ārakkhā dinnā, tasmā attānaṃ ukkaṃsāpetukāmo pucchati. Kasmā pana tena tattha ārakkhā dinnā? So kira ekadivasaṃ mahākaccāyanattheraṃ gijjhakūṭā otarantaṃ disvā – “makkaṭo viya eso”ti āha. Bhagavā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā – “sace khamāpeti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce khamāpeti, imasmiṃ veḷuvane gonaṅgalamakkaṭo bhavissatī”ti āha. So taṃ kathaṃ sutvā – “samaṇassa gotamassa kathāya dvedhābhāvo nāma natthi, pacchā me makkaṭabhūtakāle gocaraṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti veḷuvane nānāvidhe rukkhe ropetvā ārakkhaṃ adāsi. Aparabhāge kālaṃ katvā makkaṭo hutvā nibbatti. “Vassakārā”ti vutte āgantvā samīpe aṭṭhāsi. Tagghāti sabbavāresu ekaṃsavacaneyeva nipāto. Taggha, bho ānandāti evaṃ therena parisamajjhe attano ukkaṃsitabhāvaṃ ñatvā ahampi theraṃ ukkaṃsissāmīti evamāha.

83. `Taggha` is a particle in the sense of 'certainly.' 'But where is the Venerable Ānanda?' Does he not know that the Elder is dwelling in the Veḷuvana? He knows. But since he (Vassakāra) had provided protection for the Veḷuvana, he asks, wishing to have himself praised. Why did he provide protection there? It is said that one day, seeing the Elder Mahākaccāyana descending from Gijjhakūṭa, he said, 'This one is like a monkey.' The Blessed One, hearing those words, said: 'If he asks for forgiveness, that is good. If he does not ask for forgiveness, he will become a monkey with a tail like a cow's in this Veḷuvana.' Hearing those words, he thought: 'There is no such thing as the word of the ascetic Gotama being twofold.' Thinking, 'Later, when I have become a monkey, this will be my feeding ground,' he had various kinds of trees planted in the Veḷuvana and gave it protection. In a later time, after dying, he was reborn as a monkey there. When called, 'Vassakāra!', it would come and stand nearby. Regarding 'Indeed, Venerable Ānanda': having realized that he himself had been praised by the Elder in the midst of the assembly, he spoke thus, thinking, 'I too shall praise the Elder'.

84. Na ca kho, brāhmaṇāti thero kira cintesi “sammāsambuddhena vaṇṇitajjhānampi atthi, avaṇṇitajjhānampi atthi, ayaṃ pana brāhmaṇo sabbameva vaṇṇetīti pañhaṃ visaṃvādeti, na kho pana sakkā imassa mukhaṃ ulloketuṃ na piṇḍapātaṃ rakkhituṃ, pañhaṃ ujuṃ katvā kathessāmī”ti [V 4.0050] idaṃ vattuṃ āraddhaṃ. Antaraṃ karitvāti abbhantaraṃ karitvā. Evarūpaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, so bhagavā jhānaṃ vaṇṇesīti idha sabbasaṅgāhakajjhānaṃ nāma kathitaṃ.

84. 'Not so, brahmin': It is said the Elder thought: 'There is jhāna praised by the Sammāsambuddha and jhāna not praised, but this brahmin praises all of it, thus he distorts the question. Indeed, it is not possible to look at this one's face, nor to guard one's alms-food. I will make the question straight and then I will speak.' Having thought thus, he began to speak this. `Antaraṃ karitvā` means having made an internal distinction. By the phrase 'Such, brahmin, is the jhāna that the Blessed One praised,' here what is called 'all-encompassing jhāna' is spoken of.

Yaṃ [P 4.0074] no mayanti ayaṃ kira brāhmaṇo vassakārabrāhmaṇaṃ usūyati, tena pucchitapañhassa akathanaṃ paccāsīsamāno kathitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “vassakārena pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ punappunaṃ tassa nāmaṃ gaṇhanto vitthāretvā kathesi, mayā pucchitapañhaṃ pana yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷento viya ekadesameva kathesī”ti anattamano ahosi, tasmā evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Regarding the phrase 'Yaṃ no mayaṃ': It seems this brahmin envies the brahmin Vassakāra. Because of that, expecting that the question he asked would not be answered, yet having learned that it was answered, he became displeased, thinking: 'He answered the question asked by Vassakāra in detail, repeatedly mentioning his name, but he answered only a part of the question I asked, as if pressing it down with the tip of a staff.' Therefore, he spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,

Gopakamoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Gopaka Moggallāna Sutta is completed.

9. Mahāpuṇṇamasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta

85. Evaṃ [V 4.0051][M 4.0050] me sutanti mahāpuṇṇamasuttaṃ. Tattha tadahūti tasmiṃ ahu, tasmiṃ divaseti attho. Upavasanti etthāti uposatho. Upavasantīti sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha atthuddhāro – “āyāma, āvuso, kappina, uposathaṃ gamissāmā”tiādīsu hi pātimokkhuddeso uposatho. “Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho visākhe uposatho upavuttho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.53) sīlaṃ. “Suddhassa ve sadā phaggu, suddhassuposatho sadā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.79) upavāso. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246) paññatti. “Na, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe sabhikkhukā āvāsā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 181) upavasitabbadivaso. Idhāpi soyeva adhippeto[P 4.0075]. So panesa aṭṭhamīcātuddasīpannarasībhedena tividho. Tasmā sesadvayanivāraṇatthaṃ pannaraseti vuttaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “upavasanti etthāti uposatho”ti. Māsapuṇṇatāya puṇṇā saṃpuṇṇāti puṇṇā. Mā-iti cando vuccati, so ettha puṇṇoti puṇṇamā. Evaṃ puṇṇāya puṇṇamāyāti imasmiṃ padadvaye attho veditabbo.

85. The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta. Therein, 'tadahu' means 'on that day'; this is the meaning. 'Uposatha' is so called because 'they observe' (upavasanti) 'therein' (ettha). 'They observe' means they dwell endowed with virtue or with fasting; this is the meaning. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: in passages such as, 'Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha,' 'uposatha' is the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In passages such as, 'Visākha, the Uposatha observed with eight factors is indeed well-observed,' it is virtue. In passages such as, 'For the pure one, it is always an auspicious day; for the pure one, it is always an Uposatha,' it is fasting. In passages such as, 'Uposatha is the name of a nāga king,' it is a designation. In passages such as, 'Monks, on that Uposatha day, a monastery should not be without monks,' it is the day of observance. Here too, that very meaning is intended. Now, this day is threefold: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. Therefore, to exclude the other two, 'on the fifteenth' (pannarase) is stated. Because of the fullness of the month, it is 'puṇṇā' (full), completely full. By 'mā', the moon is meant; herein it is full (puṇṇo), thus it is 'puṇṇamā' (full moon). Thus, in this pair of words, 'puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya', the meaning should be understood.

Desanti kāraṇaṃ. Tena hi tvaṃ bhikkhu sake āsane nisīditvā pucchāti kasmā bhagavā ṭhitassa akathetvā nisīdāpesīti. Ayaṃ kira bhikkhu saṭṭhimattānaṃ padhāniyabhikkhūnaṃ saṅghatthero saṭṭhi bhikkhū gahetvā araññe vasati, te tassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ghaṭenti vāyamanti. Mahābhūtāni pariggaṇhanti upādārūpāni, nāmarūpapaccayalakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanaṃ pariggaṇhanti. Atha ne ācariyupaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinne thero mahābhūtapariggahādīni pucchati. Te sabbaṃ kathenti, maggaphalapañhaṃ pucchitā pana kathetuṃ na sakkonti. Atha thero cintesi – “mama santike etesaṃ ovādassa parihāni natthi, ime ca āraddhavīriyā viharanti. Kukkuṭassa pānīyapivanakālamattampi nesaṃ pamādakiriyā natthi. Evaṃ santepi maggaphalāni nibbattetuṃ na sakkonti. Ahaṃ imesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ na jānāmi, buddhaveneyyā ete bhavissanti[V 4.0052], gahetvā ne satthu santikaṃ gacchāmi, atha nesaṃ satthā cariyavasena dhammaṃ desessatī”ti, te bhikkhū gahetvā [P 4.0076] satthu santikaṃ āgato.

The reason is explained. Regarding the words, 'Therefore, you, monk, sit down on your own seat and ask,' why did the Blessed One not speak to the monk while he was standing, but had him sit down? It seems this monk was the Saṅghatthera of about sixty striving monks. Taking sixty monks, he lived in the forest. They took a meditation subject from him and strove and exerted themselves. They comprehended the great elements. Then, when they came to attend on their teacher, paid homage, and were seated, the elder asked them about the comprehension of the great elements and so on. They explained everything, but when asked the question about the path and fruition, they were unable to explain. Then the elder thought: 'There is no deficiency in my instruction to them, and they dwell with aroused energy. For them, there is not even a careless action for the time it takes a chicken to drink water. Even so, they are unable to bring forth the path and fruition. I do not know their inclination; they must be ones to be trained by a Buddha. I will take them and go to the Teacher's presence, and then the Teacher will teach them the Dhamma according to their disposition.' Taking those monks, he came to the Teacher's presence.

Satthāpi [M 4.0051] sāyanhasamaye ānandattherena upanītaṃ udakaṃ ādāya sarīraṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpetvā migāramātupāsādapariveṇe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi, bhikkhusaṅghopi naṃ parivāretvā nisīdi.

The Teacher too, in the evening time, having taken the water brought by the Venerable Ānanda and having caused his body to be warmed, sat down on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat in the precincts of the palace of Migāra's mother. The community of monks also, having surrounded him, sat down.

Tasmiṃ samaye sūriyo atthaṅgameti, cando uggacchati, majjhaṭṭhāne ca bhagavā nisinno. Candassa pabhā natthi, sūriyassa pabhā natthi, candimasūriyānaṃ pabhaṃ makkhetvā chabbaṇṇā yamakabuddharasmiyo vijjotamānā puñjā puñjā hutvā disāvidisāsu dhāvantīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena vitthāretabbaṃ. Vaṇṇabhūmi nāmesā, dhammakathikassevettha thāmo pamāṇaṃ, yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Dukkathitanti na vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ sannisinnāya parisāya thero uṭṭhahitvā satthāraṃ pañhassa okāsaṃ kāresi. Tato bhagavā – “sace imasmiṃ ṭhitake pucchante ‘ācariyo no uṭṭhito’ti sesabhikkhū uṭṭhahissanti, evaṃ tathāgate agāravo kato bhavissati. Atha nisinnāva pucchissanti, ācariye agāravo kato bhavissati, ekaggā hutvā dhammadesanaṃ paṭicchituṃ na sakkuṇissanti. Ācariye pana nisinne tepi nisīdissanti. Tato ekaggā dhammadesanaṃ paṭicchituṃ sakkuṇissantī”ti iminā kāraṇena bhagavā ṭhitassa akathetvā nisīdāpetīti.

At that time, the sun was setting and the moon was rising, and the Blessed One was seated in the middle. There was no radiance of the moon, no radiance of the sun; having eclipsed the radiance of the moon and sun, the six-colored twin Buddha-rays shone brilliantly, becoming cluster upon cluster and running in the cardinal and intermediate directions—all this should be elaborated according to the method stated previously. This is called the 'ground of praise'; herein, the strength of the Dhamma-preacher is the measure. As much as one is able, that much should be spoken. It should not be said, 'It was poorly spoken.' While the assembly was thus seated together, the elder stood up and requested an opportunity from the Teacher to ask a question. Then the Blessed One thought: 'If, while this elder is standing and asking, the other monks should also stand up, thinking, "Our teacher has stood up," thus disrespect would be shown to the Tathāgata. And if they, while seated, were to ask questions of their standing teacher, disrespect would be shown to the teacher, and they would not be able to receive the Dhamma teaching with one-pointed minds. But when the teacher is seated, they too will sit. Then, being one-pointed, they will be able to receive the Dhamma teaching.' For this reason, the Blessed One, not speaking to the elder while he was standing, had him sit down.

Ime nu kho, bhanteti vimatipucchā viya kathitā. Thero pana pañcakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ pariggaṇhitvā arahattaṃ [P 4.0077] patto mahākhīṇāsavo, natthi etassa vimati. Jānantenapi pana ajānantena viya hutvā pucchituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace hi jānanto viya pucchati, “jānāti aya”nti tassa tassa vissajjento ekadesameva katheti. Ajānantena viya pucchite pana kathento ito ca etto ca kāraṇaṃ āharitvā pākaṭaṃ katvā katheti. Koci pana ajānantopi jānanto viya pucchati. Thero evarūpaṃ vacanaṃ kiṃ karissati, jānantoyeva pana ajānanto viya pucchatīti veditabbo.

Regarding the words 'Ime nu kho, bhante,' this was spoken as if it were a question of uncertainty. But the Elder, having comprehended the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, had attained Arahantship and was a great one whose cankers were destroyed; for him there is no uncertainty. However, it is proper for one who knows to ask as if not knowing. For if one asks as if knowing, the one answering, thinking 'This one knows,' speaks only in part on each point. But when asked by one as if not knowing, the one speaking brings reasons from here and there, makes it clear, and speaks. Some, however, not knowing, ask as if knowing. What would the elder do with such a speech? It should be understood that, knowing, he asks as if not knowing.

Chandamūlakāti [V 4.0053] taṇhāmūlakā. Evaṃrūpo siyanti sace odāto hotukāmo, haritālavaṇṇo vā manosilāvaṇṇo vā siyanti pattheti[M 4.0052]. Sace kāḷo hotukāmo, nīluppalavaṇṇo vā añjanavaṇṇo vā atasīpupphavaṇṇo vā siyanti pattheti. Evaṃvedanoti kusalavedano vā sukhavedano vā siyanti pattheti. Saññādīsupi eseva nayo. Yasmā pana atīte patthanā nāma natthi, patthentenāpi ca na sakkā taṃ laddhuṃ, paccuppannepi na hoti, na hi odāto kāḷabhāvaṃ patthetvā paccuppanne kāḷo hoti, na kāḷo vā odāto, dīgho vā rasso, rasso vā dīgho, dānaṃ pana datvā sīlaṃ vā samādiyitvā “anāgate khattiyo vā homi brāhmaṇo vā”ti patthentassa patthanā samijjhati. Tasmā anāgatameva gahitaṃ.

Rooted in desire means rooted in craving. 'May I be of such a form': if one wishes to be fair-skinned, one aspires, 'May I be the color of orpiment or red arsenic.' If one wishes to be dark-skinned, one aspires, 'May I be the color of a blue water lily, collyrium, or a flax flower.' 'May I have such a feeling': one aspires, 'May I have a wholesome feeling or a pleasant feeling.' This same method applies to perception and the other aggregates. For in the past, there is no such thing as aspiration, and even by aspiring, it is not possible to obtain it. Nor does it occur in the present; for a fair-skinned person, having aspired for a dark complexion, does not become dark in the present, nor does a dark-skinned person become fair, a tall person short, or a short person tall. However, the aspiration of one who, having given a gift or undertaken moral precepts, aspires, 'In the future, may I be a noble or a brahmin,' succeeds. Therefore, only the future was taken up.

Khandhādhivacananti khandhānaṃ khandhapaṇṇatti kittakena hotīti pucchati.

The designation of the aggregates: he asks, 'By how much does the conceptual designation of the aggregates come to be?'

Mahābhūtā hetūti “tayo kusalahetū”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1441) hi hetuhetu vutto. Avijjā puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ sādhāraṇattā sādhāraṇahetu. Kusalākusalaṃ attano attano vipākadāne uttamahetu. Idha paccayahetu adhippeto. Tattha pathavīdhātu mahābhūtaṃ itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhūtānaṃ upādārūpassa ca [P 4.0078] paññāpanāya dassanatthāya hetu ceva paccayo ca. Evaṃ sesesupi yojanā veditabbā.

The great elements are a cause: In passages such as 'the three wholesome roots,' `hetu` is spoken of as a root-cause. Ignorance is a common cause for meritorious formations and so on, due to its commonality. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is the supreme cause in giving its own respective result. Here, a condition-cause is intended. In this context, the earth-element, a great element, is both a cause and a condition for the conceptual designation and for the seeing of the other three great elements and of derived matter. Thus, the application should be understood in the remaining cases as well.

Phassoti “phuṭṭho, bhikkhave, vedeti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti, phuṭṭho cetetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.93) vacanato phasso tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ paññāpanāya hetu ceva paccayo ca. Viññāṇakkhandhassāti ettha paṭisandhiviññāṇena tāva saddhiṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ uparimaparicchedena samatiṃsa rūpāni sampayuttā ca tayo khandhā uppajjanti, taṃ nāmarūpaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paññāpanāya hetu ceva paccayo ca. Cakkhudvāre cakkhupasādo ceva rūpārammaṇañca rūpaṃ, sampayuttā tayo khandhā nāmaṃ. Taṃ nāmarūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa paññāpanāya hetu ceva paccayo ca. Eseva nayo sesaviññāṇesu.

Contact: Because of the teaching, 'Having been contacted, O bhikkhus, one feels; having been contacted, one perceives; having been contacted, one intends,' contact is both a cause and a condition for the conceptual designation of the three aggregates. Regarding the consciousness aggregate: Here, firstly, together with rebirth-linking consciousness, for those lying in the womb, thirty material phenomena with an upper limit and the three associated aggregates arise. That name-and-form is both a cause and a condition for the conceptual designation of rebirth-linking consciousness. At the eye-door, the eye-sensitivity and the visible object are form; the three associated aggregates are name. That name-and-form is both a cause and a condition for the conceptual designation of eye-consciousness. This same method applies to the remaining consciousnesses.

87. Kathaṃ pana, bhanteti idaṃ kittakena nu khoti vaṭṭaṃ pucchanto evamāha. Sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotīti idaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ pucchanto evamāha.

87. 'But how, venerable sir?': asking this about the round of existence—'To what extent does it come to be?'—he spoke thus. '...identity view does not come to be': asking this about what is not the round of existence, he spoke thus.

88. Ayaṃ [V 4.0054][M 4.0053] rūpe assādoti iminā pariññāpaṭivedho ceva dukkhasaccañca kathitaṃ. Ayaṃ rūpe ādīnavoti iminā pahānapaṭivedho ceva samudayasaccañca. Idaṃ rūpe nissaraṇanti iminā sacchikiriyāpaṭivedho ceva nirodhasaccañca. Ye imesu tīsu ṭhānesu sammādiṭṭhiādayo dhammā, ayaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedho maggasaccaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

88. 'This is the gratification in form'—by this, the penetration of full understanding and the truth of suffering are stated. 'This is the danger in form'—by this, the penetration of abandoning and the truth of the origin are stated. 'This is the escape from form'—by this, the penetration of realization and the truth of cessation are stated. As for the qualities such as right view and so forth in these three instances, this is the penetration of development, the truth of the path. The same method applies to the remaining passages as well.

89. Bahiddhāti parassa saviññāṇake kāye. Sabbanimittesūti iminā pana anindriyabaddhampi saṅgaṇhāti. “Saviññāṇake kāye”ti vacanena vā attano ca parassa ca kāyo gahitova, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittaggahaṇena anindriyabaddhaṃ gaṇhāti.

89. 'External' means in the conscious body of another. By 'in all signs,' moreover, even that which is not bound by the faculties is included. Or, by the phrase 'in the conscious body,' one's own body and that of another are indeed included; and by the grasping of all external signs, that which is not bound by the faculties is included.

90. Anattakatānīti [P 4.0079] anattani ṭhatvā katāni. Kamattānaṃ phusissantīti katarasmiṃ attani ṭhatvā vipākaṃ dassentīti sassatadassanaṃ okkamanto evamāha. Taṇhādhipateyyenāti taṇhājeṭṭhakena. Tatra tatrāti tesu tesu dhammesu. Saṭṭhimattānanti ime bhikkhū pakatikammaṭṭhānaṃ jahitvā aññaṃ navakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasantā pallaṅkaṃ abhinditvā tasmiṃyeva āsane arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

90. 'Done by non-self' means done while established in what is not self. 'Which self will they touch?' means, 'Established in which self will they give their result?'—he spoke thus, descending into the view of eternalism. 'Through the dominance of craving' means with craving as the chief. 'In this and that' means in these and those teachings. 'About sixty': these bhikkhus, having abandoned their regular meditation subject and contemplating a new one, without breaking their cross-legged posture, attained Arahantship on that very seat. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāpuṇṇamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta is concluded.

10. Cūḷapuṇṇamasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta

91. Evaṃ [V 4.0055] me sutanti cūḷapuṇṇamasuttaṃ. Tattha tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ anuviloketi, tattha tattha tuṇhībhūtameva. Anuviloketvāti pañcapasādapaṭimaṇḍitāni akkhīni ummīletvā tato tato viloketvā antamaso hatthakukkuccapādakukkuccānampi abhāvaṃ disvā. Asappurisoti pāpapuriso. No hetaṃ, bhanteti yasmā andho andhaṃ viya so taṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā evamāhaṃsu. Eteneva nayena ito paresupi vāresu attho veditabbo. Assaddhasamannāgatoti pāpadhammasamannāgato. Asappurisabhattīti asappurisasevano. Asappurisacintīti [M 4.0054][P 4.0080] asappurisacintāya cintako. Asappurisamantīti asappurisamantanaṃ mantetā. Asappurisavācoti asappurisavācaṃ bhāsitā. Asappurisakammantoti asappurisakammānaṃ kattā. Asappurisadiṭṭhīti asappurisadiṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Asappurisadānanti asappurisehi dātabbaṃ dānaṃ. Tyāssa mittāti te assa mittā. Attabyābādhāyapi cetetīti pāṇaṃ hanissāmi, adinnaṃ ādiyissāmi, micchā carissāmi, dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattissāmīti evaṃ attano dukkhatthāya cinteti. Parabyābādhāyāti yathā asuko asukaṃ pāṇaṃ hanti, asukassa santakaṃ adinnaṃ ādiyati, dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattati, evaṃ naṃ āṇāpessāmīti evaṃ parassa dukkhatthāya cinteti. Ubhayabyābādhāyāti ahaṃ asukañca asukañca gahetvā dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattissāmīti evaṃ ubhayadukkhatthāya cintetīti.

91. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta. Therein, “silent” (tuṇhībhūtaṃ) means that whichever direction he looks, in that very direction, it is only silent. “Having looked around” (anuviloketvā) means having opened his eyes, which are adorned with the five sensitive parts, and having looked here and there, seeing the absence of even the fidgeting of hands and feet. “An unvirtuous person” (asappuriso) means an evil person. “It is not so, venerable sir” (no hetaṃ, bhante)—because just as a blind person is not able to know another blind person, so that unvirtuous person is not able to know that other unvirtuous person, therefore the monks spoke thus. In this same way, the meaning should be understood in the subsequent phrases. “Endowed with evil qualities” (asaddhammasamannāgato) means endowed with evil qualities. “Having the devotion of an unvirtuous person” (asappurisabhattī) means one who associates with unvirtuous people. “Thinking like an unvirtuous person” (asappurisacintī) means one who thinks the thoughts of an unvirtuous person. “Consulting like an unvirtuous person” (asappurisamantī) means one who deliberates the counsel of unvirtuous people. “Speaking like an unvirtuous person” (asappurisavāco) means one who speaks the speech of an unvirtuous person. “Acting like an unvirtuous person” (asappurisakammanto) means one who is a doer of the deeds of unvirtuous people. “Holding the views of an unvirtuous person” (asappurisadiṭṭhī) means one who is endowed with the views of an unvirtuous person. “The gift of an unvirtuous person” (asappurisadānaṃ) means a gift to be given by unvirtuous people. “Tyāssa mittā” means “te assa mittā” (they are his friends). “He thinks for his own affliction” (attabyābādhāyapi ceteti) means he thinks for his own suffering thus: “I will kill a living being, I will take what is not given, I will engage in sexual misconduct, I will undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action.” “For the affliction of others” (parabyābādhāya) means he thinks for the suffering of others thus: “I will command that person to kill such and such a living being, to take what is not given belonging to so-and-so, and to undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action.” “For the affliction of both” (ubhayabyābādhāya) means he thinks for the suffering of both thus: “I, having taken this person and that person, will undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action.”

Attabyābādhāyapi mantetītiādīsu ahaṃ dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattissāmīti mantento attabyābādhāya manteti nāma.
