Asukaṃ dasa akusalakammapathe samādapessāmīti mantento parabyābādhāya manteti nāma. Aññena saddhiṃ – “mayaṃ ubhopi ekato hutvā dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattissāmā”ti mantento ubhayabyābādhāya manteti nāma.

In phrases such as “he consults for his own affliction” (attabyābādhāyapi manteti), one who consults, “I will undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action,” is said to consult for his own affliction. One who consults, “I will cause such and such a person to undertake the ten unwholesome courses of action,” is said to consult for the affliction of others. One who consults together with another, “Both of us, having come together, will undertake and practice the ten unwholesome courses of action,” is said to consult for the affliction of both.

Asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ detīti deyyadhammampi puggalampi [P 4.0081] na sakkaroti. Deyyadhammaṃ na sakkaroti [V 4.0056] nāma uttaṇḍulādidosasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ deti, na pasannaṃ karoti. Puggalaṃ na sakkaroti nāma nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ asammajjitvā yattha vā tattha vā nisīdāpetvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā ādhārakaṃ ṭhapetvā dānaṃ deti. Asahatthāti attano hatthena, na deti, dāsakammakārādīhi dāpeti. Acittikatvāti heṭṭhā vuttanayena deyyadhammepi puggalepi na cittīkāraṃ katvā deti. Apaviddhanti chaḍḍetukāmo hutvā vammike uragaṃ pakkhipanto viya deti. Anāgamanadiṭṭhikoti no phalapāṭikaṅkhī hutvā deti.

“He gives a gift disrespectfully” (asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ deti) means he does not respect either the gift or the recipient. Not respecting the gift means he gives food endowed with flaws such as unhusked rice, and does not make it appealing. Not respecting the recipient means he gives the gift without sweeping the sitting place, making them sit just anywhere, and placing any old bowl-stand. “Not with his own hand” (asahatthā) means he does not give with his own hand, but has it given by servants, workers, and so forth. “Without showing respect” (acittikatvā) means he gives without showing respect to either the gift or the recipient, in the manner stated previously. “As if discarding it” (apaviddhaṃ) means, wishing to throw it away, he gives it like one casting a snake into an anthill. “One with the view that there is no future result” (anāgamanadiṭṭhiko) means he gives without expecting any fruit.

Tattha [M 4.0055] upapajjatīti na dānaṃ datvā niraye upapajjati. Yaṃ pana tena pāpaladdhikāya micchādassanaṃ gahitaṃ, tāya micchādiṭṭhiyā niraye upapajjati. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo. Devamahattatāti chakāmāvacaradevā. Manussamahattatāti tiṇṇaṃ kulānaṃ sampatti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ suddhavaṭṭavaseneva kathitanti.

“Is reborn there” (tattha upapajjati) does not mean that one is reborn in hell because of having given a gift. Rather, it is because of that wrong view, which was grasped by that person due to his evil doctrine, that he is reborn in hell. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. “Divine greatness” (devamahattatā) is the destination of the six kāma-sphere devas. “Human greatness” (manussamahattatā) is the destination of the accomplishment of the three families. The remainder is clear everywhere. This sutta, moreover, was taught purely by way of the round of existence.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cūḷapuṇṇamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Anupadavaggo

2. The Chapter on Step-by-Step

1. Anupadasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Anupada Sutta

93. Evaṃ [V 4.0057][P 4.0082][M 4.0056] me sutanti anupadasuttaṃ. Tattha etadavocāti etaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.4) “paṇḍito”tiādinā nayena dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa guṇakathaṃ avoca. Kasmā? Avasesattheresu hi mahāmoggallānattherassa iddhimāti guṇo pākaṭo, mahākassapassa dhutavādoti, anuruddhattherassa dibbacakkhukoti, upālittherassa vinayadharoti, revatattherassa jhāyī jhānābhiratoti, ānandattherassa bahussutoti. Evaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ therānaṃ te te guṇā pākaṭā, sāriputtattherassa pana apākaṭā. Kasmā? Paññavato hi guṇā na sakkā akathitā jānituṃ. Iti bhagavā “sāriputtassa guṇe kathessāmī”ti sabhāgaparisāya sannipātaṃ āgamesi. Visabhāgapuggalānañhi santike vaṇṇaṃ kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati, te vaṇṇe kathiyamāne avaṇṇameva kathenti. Imasmiṃ pana divase therassa sabhāgaparisā sannipati, tassā sannipatitabhāvaṃ disvā satthā vaṇṇaṃ kathento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

93. The Anupada Sutta is the one that begins with 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, the Blessed One spoke the discourse on the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, by the method beginning with 'paṇḍito' (wise). Why did he speak? Because, among the remaining elders, the virtue of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was manifest as 'possessing psychic power'; for Mahākassapa, as 'an exponent of the ascetic practices'; for the Elder Anuruddha, as 'possessing the divine eye'; for the Elder Upāli, as 'an upholder of the Vinaya'; for the Elder Revata, as 'one who is a meditator, one who delights in meditation'; and for the Elder Ānanda, as 'one of great learning.' Thus, for those elders, those virtues were manifest. But the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta were not manifest. Why? Because the virtues of a wise person cannot be known if they are not spoken of. Therefore, the Blessed One, having reflected, 'I will declare the virtues of Sāriputta,' awaited the gathering of a suitable assembly. Indeed, it is not fitting to speak praise in the presence of unsuitable individuals, for when praise is spoken, they speak only dispraise. On this day, however, a suitable assembly for the Elder gathered. Seeing that they had gathered, the Teacher, wishing to speak his praise, began this discourse.

Tattha paṇḍitoti dhātukusalatā āyatanakusalatā paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalatāti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi paṇḍito. Mahāpaññotiādīsu mahāpaññādīhi samannāgatoti [P 4.0083] attho.

Therein, one is called 'wise' (paṇḍita) for these four reasons: skillfulness in the elements, skillfulness in the sense bases, skillfulness in dependent origination, and skillfulness in what is a possible cause and what is not a possible cause. In 'great in wisdom' and so on, the meaning is 'endowed with great wisdom and so forth'.

Tatridaṃ mahāpaññādīnaṃ nānattaṃ – tattha katamā mahāpaññā? Mahante sīlakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā, mahante samādhikkhandhe, paññākkhandhe, vimuttikkhandhe, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā, mahantāni ṭhānāṭṭhānāni, mahantā vihārasamāpattiyo[V 4.0058], mahantāni ariyasaccāni, mahante satipaṭṭhāne, sammappadhāne, iddhipāde, mahantāni indriyāni, balāni, bojjhaṅgāni, mahante ariyamagge, mahantāni sāmaññaphalāni, mahantā abhiññāyo, mahantaṃ paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā.

Herein, this is the distinction of 'great wisdom' and so forth. Therein, what is great wisdom? It comprehends the great aggregates of virtue; therefore, it is called great wisdom. It comprehends the great aggregates of concentration, the great aggregates of wisdom, the great aggregates of liberation, and the great aggregates of the knowledge and vision of liberation; therefore, it is called great wisdom. It comprehends the great possible and impossible causes, the great attainments of abiding, the great Noble Truths, the great foundations of mindfulness, the great right strivings, the great bases of spiritual power, the great faculties, the great powers, the great factors of enlightenment, the great noble paths, the great fruits of the contemplative life, the great direct knowledges, and the supreme ultimate reality, Nibbāna; therefore, it is called great wisdom.

Katamā [M 4.0057] puthupaññā, puthu nānākhandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā. Puthu nānādhātūsu, puthu nānāāyatanesu, puthu nānāatthesu, puthu nānāpaṭiccasamuppādesu, puthu nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesu, puthu nānāatthesu, dhammesu, niruttīsu, paṭibhānesu, puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesu, puthu nānāsamādhi-paññā-vimutti-vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhesu, puthu nānāṭhānāṭṭhānesu, puthu nānāvihārasamāpattīsu, puthu nānāariyasaccesu, puthu nānāsatipaṭṭhānesu, sammappadhānesu, iddhipādesu, indriyesu, balesu, bojjhaṅgesu, puthu nānāariyamaggesu, sāmaññaphalesu, abhiññāsu, puthu nānājanasādhāraṇe dhamme samatikkamma paramatthe nibbāne ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā.

What is extensive wisdom? Knowledge that functions with respect to various different aggregates; therefore, it is called extensive wisdom. Knowledge that functions with respect to various different elements; various different sense bases; various different meanings; various different dependent originations; various different states of emptiness and unapprehendability; various different analytical knowledges of meaning, phenomena, language, and ready speech; with respect to various different aggregates of virtue; various different aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; with respect to various different possible and impossible causes; various different attainments of abiding; various different Noble Truths; various different foundations of mindfulness, right strivings, bases of spiritual power, faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment; various different noble paths, fruits of the contemplative life, and direct knowledges; having transcended the various dhammas common to ordinary people, knowledge functions with respect to the supreme reality, Nibbāna; therefore, it is called extensive wisdom.

Katamā [P 4.0084] hāsapaññā, idhekacco hāsabahulo vedabahulo tuṭṭhibahulo pāmojjabahulo sīlaṃ paripūreti, indriyasaṃvaraṃ paripūreti, bhojane mattaññutaṃ, jāgariyānuyogaṃ, sīlakkhandhaṃ, samādhikkhandhaṃ, paññākkhandhaṃ, vimuttikkhandhaṃ, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhaṃ paripūretīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo pāmojjabahulo ṭhānāṭṭhānaṃ paṭivijjhati, hāsabahulo vihārasamāpattiyo paripūretīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati. Satipaṭṭhāne, sammappadhāne, iddhipāde, indriyāni, balāni, bojjhaṅgāni, ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo sāmaññaphalāni sacchikaroti, abhiññāyo paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo vedatuṭṭhipāmojjabahulo paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotīti hāsapaññā.

What is joyful wisdom? Here, a certain person, being one with much joy, much enthusiasm, much satisfaction, and much happiness, fulfills virtue, fulfills restraint of the senses, fulfills moderation in eating, fulfills the practice of wakefulness, fulfills the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; therefore, it is called joyful wisdom. Being one with much joy and happiness, one penetrates what is a possible cause and what is not; being one with much joy, one fulfills the attainments of abiding; therefore, it is called joyful wisdom. Being one with much joy, one penetrates the Noble Truths. One develops the foundations of mindfulness, the right strivings, the bases of spiritual power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble path; therefore, it is called joyful wisdom. Being one with much joy, one realizes the fruits of the contemplative life and penetrates the direct knowledges; therefore, it is called joyful wisdom. Being one with much joy, enthusiasm, satisfaction, and happiness, one realizes the supreme reality, Nibbāna; therefore, it is called joyful wisdom.

Katamā javanapaññā, yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Dukkhato khippaṃ… anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccato dukkhato [V 4.0059] anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena, anattā asārakaṭṭhenāti tulayitvā tīrayitvā vibhāvayitvā vibhūtaṃ katvā rūpanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ [P 4.0085] javatīti javanapaññā. Vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇaṃ[M 4.0058], cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena…pe… vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ. Cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammanti tulayitvā tīrayitvā vibhāvayitvā vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā.

What is swift wisdom? Whatever form—past, future, or present, whether far or near—one swiftly penetrates all form as impermanent; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. One swiftly penetrates it as suffering and as not-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Whatever feeling… whatever consciousness—past, future, or present—one swiftly penetrates all consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. The eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—one swiftly penetrates as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of perishing, suffering in the sense of being fearful, and not-self in the sense of being without substance. Having weighed, judged, clarified, and made it manifest, one swiftly penetrates to Nibbāna, the cessation of form; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Feeling, perception, formations, consciousness, the eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—are impermanent in the sense of perishing… Having made it manifest, one swiftly penetrates to Nibbāna, the cessation of aging-and-death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Form—past, future, or present… consciousness; the eye… aging-and-death—past, future, or present—are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Having weighed, judged, clarified, and made them manifest, one swiftly penetrates to Nibbāna, the cessation of aging-and-death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom.

Katamā tikkhapaññā, khippaṃ kilese chindatīti tikkhapaññā. Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti, uppannaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ, uppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ, uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme, uppannaṃ rāgaṃ, dosaṃ, mohaṃ, kodhaṃ, upanāhaṃ, makkhaṃ, paḷāsaṃ, issaṃ, macchariyaṃ, māyaṃ, sāṭheyyaṃ, thambhaṃ, sārambhaṃ, mānaṃ, atimānaṃ, madaṃ, pamādaṃ, sabbe kilese, sabbe duccarite, sabbe abhisaṅkhāre, sabbe bhavagāmikamme nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gametīti tikkhapaññā. Ekasmiṃ āsane cattāro ariyamaggā, cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, catasso paṭisambhidāyo, cha ca abhiññāyo adhigatā honti sacchikatā passitā paññāyāti tikkhapaññā.

What is sharp wisdom? Because it quickly cuts off defilements, it is called sharp wisdom. It does not allow arisen sensual thought to persist, nor arisen thought of ill will, nor arisen thought of harming, nor any arisen evil, unwholesome states, nor arisen greed, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, denigration, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, stubbornness, contention, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence, nor any defilements, any misconduct, any volitional formations, or any actions leading to renewed existence. It abandons, dispels, makes them absent, and brings them to non-existence—thus it is sharp wisdom. In a single sitting, the four noble paths, the four fruits of the contemplative life, the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges are attained, realized, and seen by wisdom—thus it is sharp wisdom.

Katamā nibbedhikapaññā, idhekacco sabbasaṅkhāresu ubbegabahulo hoti uttāsabahulo ukkaṇṭhanabahulo aratibahulo [P 4.0086] anabhiratibahulo bahimukho na ramati sabbasaṅkhāresu, anibbiddhapubbaṃ appadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā. Anibbiddhapubbaṃ appadālitapubbaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ, mohakkhandhaṃ, kodhaṃ, upanāhaṃ…pe… sabbe bhavagāmikamme nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā.

What is penetrating wisdom? Here, a certain person is often full of dread regarding all formations, often full of terror, often full of aversion, often full of discontent, often full of extreme discontent; being outwardly turned, they do not delight in any formations. Previously unpierced, previously unsplit, they pierce and split apart the aggregate of greed—thus it is penetrating wisdom. Previously unpierced, previously unsplit, they pierce and split apart the aggregate of hatred, the aggregate of delusion, anger, enmity… and all actions leading to renewed existence—thus it is penetrating wisdom.

Anupadadhammavipassananti samāpattivasena vā jhānaṅgavasena vā anupaṭipāṭiyā dhammavipassanaṃ vipassati, evaṃ vipassanto addhamāsena arahattaṃ patto. Mahāmoggallānatthero pana [V 4.0060] sattahi divasehi. Evaṃ santepi sāriputtatthero mahāpaññavantataro. Mahāmoggallānatthero hi sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāraṃ yaṭṭhikoṭiyā uppīḷento viya ekadesameva sammasanto satta divase vāyamitvā arahattaṃ patto. Sāriputtatthero ṭhapetvā buddhānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca sammasanacāraṃ sāvakānaṃ sammasanacāraṃ nippadesaṃ sammasi. Evaṃ sammasanto addhamāsaṃ vāyami. Arahattañca kira patvā aññāsi – “ṭhapetvā buddhe ca paccekabuddhe ca añño sāvako nāma paññāya [M 4.0059] mayā pattabbaṃ pattuṃ samattho nāma na bhavissatī”ti. Yathā hi puriso veḷuyaṭṭhiṃ gaṇhissāmīti mahājaṭaṃ veḷuṃ disvā jaṭaṃ chindantassa papañco bhavissatīti antarena hatthaṃ pavesetvā sampattameva yaṭṭhiṃ mūle ca agge ca chinditvā ādāya pakkameyya, so kiñcāpi paṭhamataraṃ gacchati, yaṭṭhiṃ pana sāraṃ vā ujuṃ vā na labhati. Aparo ca tathārūpameva veṇuṃ disvā “sace sampattaṃ yaṭṭhiṃ gaṇhissāmi, sāraṃ vā ujuṃ vā na labhissāmī”ti kacchaṃ bandhitvā [P 4.0087] mahantena satthena veṇujaṭaṃ chinditvā sārā ceva ujū ca yaṭṭhiyo uccinitvā ādāya pakkameyya. Ayaṃ kiñcāpi pacchā gacchati, yaṭṭhiyo pana sārā ceva ujū ca labhati. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ therānaṃ padhānaṃ.

‘Successive insight into phenomena’ means that one contemplates insight into phenomena in sequence, either by way of meditative attainments or by way of the jhāna factors. Contemplating thus, he attained Arahantship in half a month. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, however, attained it in seven days. Even so, the Venerable Sāriputta was more greatly endowed with wisdom. For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having contemplated only a portion of the disciples' range of comprehension—as if pressing with the tip of a staff—and having striven for seven days, attained Arahantship. The Venerable Sāriputta, setting aside the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, comprehended the disciples' range of comprehension without remainder. Contemplating thus, he strove for half a month. And it is said that upon attaining Arahantship, he knew: “Setting aside the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, no other disciple will be able to attain what I have attained through wisdom.” For it is as if a man, wishing to get a bamboo staff, sees a large, tangled bamboo grove and thinks, “It will be a complication for me to cut through the tangle.” So he inserts his hand in between, and taking the very staff he comes upon, cuts it at the base and at the tip, and departs with it. Although he leaves sooner, he does not get a staff that is strong or straight. But another man, seeing a similar bamboo grove, thinks, “If I take the staff I happen upon, I will not get one that is strong or straight.” So, girding his waist-cloth, he cuts through the bamboo tangle with a large knife, and having selected staffs that are both strong and straight, he departs with them. Although this man leaves later, he gets staffs that are both strong and straight. The accomplishment of the striving of these two elders should be understood in this way.

Evaṃ pana addhamāsaṃ vāyamitvā dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero sūkarakhataleṇadvāre bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanāpariggahasuttante desiyamāne dasabalaṃ bījayamāno ṭhito desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā pabbajitadivasato pannarasame divase sāvakapāramiñāṇassa matthakaṃ patvā sattasaṭṭhi ñāṇāni paṭivijjhitvā soḷasavidhaṃ paññaṃ anuppatto.

Thus, having striven for half a month, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, was standing at the entrance of the Boar’s Lair Cave, fanning the One with Ten Powers while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being taught to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha. Sending forth his knowledge in accordance with the teaching, on the fifteenth day from the day he went forth, he reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, penetrated sixty-seven knowledges, and attained the sixteen-fold wisdom.

Tatridaṃ, bhikkhave, sāriputtassa anupadadhammavipassanāyāti yā anupadadhammavipassanaṃ vipassatīti anupadadhammavipassanā vuttā, tatra anupadadhammavipassanāya sāriputtassa idaṃ hoti. Idāni vattabbaṃ taṃ taṃ vipassanākoṭṭhāsaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Herein, monks, regarding Sāriputta's successive insight into phenomena: that which was taught is the 'successive insight into phenomena' wherein one contemplates phenomena in sequence. Therein, in that successive insight into phenomena, this pertains to Sāriputta. This was said in reference to those respective sections of insight which are now to be spoken of.

94. Paṭhame jhāneti ye paṭhame jhāne antosamāpattiyaṃ dhammā. Tyāssāti te assa. Anupadavavatthitā hontīti anupaṭipāṭiyā vavatthitā paricchinnā ñātā viditā honti. Kathaṃ? Thero hi te dhamme olokento abhiniropanalakkhaṇo vitakko vattatīti jānāti. Tathā anumajjanalakkhaṇo vicāro, pharaṇalakkhaṇā pīti, sātalakkhaṇaṃ sukhaṃ, avikkhepalakkhaṇā [V 4.0061] cittekaggatā, phusanalakkhaṇo phasso vedayitalakkhaṇā vedanā, sañjānanalakkhaṇā saññā, cetayitalakkhaṇā cetanā, vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ [P 4.0088] viññāṇaṃ, kattukamyatālakkhaṇo chando, adhimokkhalakkhaṇo adhimokkho, paggāhalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyaṃ [M 4.0060] upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sati, majjhattalakkhaṇā upekkhā, anunayamanasikāralakkhaṇo manasikāro vattatīti jānāti. Evaṃ jānaṃ abhiniropanaṭṭhena vitakkaṃ sabhāvato vavatthapeti…pe… anunayamanasikāraṇaṭṭhena manasikāraṃ sabhāvabhāvato vavatthapeti. Tena vuttaṃ “tyāssa dhammā anupadavavatthitā hontī”ti.

94. ‘In the first jhāna’ means: those factors that are in the first jhāna, within the attainment. ‘These factors for him’ means they belong to him. ‘They are established in sequence’ means they are established in order, defined, known, and made clear. How? The elder, while observing these factors, knows: ‘Applied thought, with the characteristic of directing, is occurring.’ Likewise, he knows: ‘Sustained thought, with the characteristic of examining, is occurring; rapture, with the characteristic of pervading, is occurring; happiness, with the characteristic of satisfaction, is occurring; unification of mind, with the characteristic of non-distraction, is occurring; contact, with the characteristic of touching, is occurring; feeling, with the characteristic of experiencing, is occurring; perception, with the characteristic of perceiving, is occurring; volition, with the characteristic of intending, is occurring; consciousness, with the characteristic of cognizing, is occurring; desire, with the characteristic of wishing to act, is occurring; resolution, with the characteristic of deciding, is occurring; energy, with the characteristic of exertion, is occurring; mindfulness, with the characteristic of establishing, is occurring; equanimity, with the characteristic of neutrality, is occurring; attention, with the characteristic of adverting, is occurring.’ Knowing thus, he defines applied thought by its intrinsic nature as having the function of directing… and so on… he defines attention by its intrinsic nature as having the function of adverting. Therefore, it was said: “These factors for him are established in sequence.”

Viditā uppajjantīti uppajjamānā viditā pākaṭāva hutvā uppajjanti. Viditā upaṭṭhahantīti tiṭṭhamānāpi viditā pākaṭāva hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchantīti nirujjhamānāpi viditā pākaṭāva hutvā nirujjhanti. Ettha pana taṃñāṇatā ceva ñāṇabahutā ca mocetabbā. Yathā hi teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ na sakkā phusituṃ, evameva teneva cittena tassa cittassa uppādo vā ṭhiti vā bhaṅgo vā na sakkā jānitunti. Evaṃ tāva taṃñāṇatā mocetabbā. Yadi pana dve cittāni ekato uppajjeyyuṃ, ekena cittena ekassa uppādo vā ṭhiti vā bhaṅgo vā sakkā bhaveyya jānituṃ. Dve pana phassā vā vedanā vā saññā vā cetanā vā cittāni vā ekato uppajjanakāni nāma natthi, ekekameva uppajjati. Evaṃ ñāṇabahutā mocetabbā. Evaṃ sante kathaṃ? Mahātherassa antosamāpattiyaṃ soḷasa dhammā viditā pākaṭā hontīti. Vatthārammaṇānaṃ pariggahitatāya. Therena hi vatthu ceva ārammaṇañca pariggahitaṃ, tenassa tesaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādaṃ āvajjantassa uppādo pākaṭo hoti, ṭhānaṃ āvajjantassa ṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, bhedaṃ āvajjantassa [P 4.0089] bhedo pākaṭo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “viditā uppajjanti viditā upaṭṭhahanti viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti. Ahutvā sambhontīti iminā udayaṃ passati. Hutvā paṭiventīti iminā vayaṃ passati.

“Known, they arise” means that as they are arising, they arise having become known and manifest. “Known, they are present” means that even while they are persisting, they persist having become known and manifest. “Known, they pass away” means that even while they are ceasing, they cease having become known and manifest. Here, however, the notions that the knowledge is the same as the thing known and that there is a multiplicity of knowledges should be dismissed. For just as it is not possible to touch a fingertip with that same fingertip, so too it is not possible for a mind to know its own arising, persistence, or cessation with that same mind. Thus, the notion that the knowledge is the same as the thing known should be dismissed. If, however, two minds were to arise simultaneously, it would be possible for one mind to know the arising, persistence, or cessation of the other. But two instances of contact, feeling, perception, volition, or mind do not arise simultaneously; only one arises at a time. Thus, the notion of a multiplicity of knowledges should be dismissed. This being so, how is it that for the great elder, within his meditative attainment, the sixteen phenomena are known and manifest? It is because of the full comprehension of the base and the object. For the elder has fully comprehended both the base and the object. Therefore, for him, when adverting to the arising of those phenomena, the arising is manifest; when adverting to their persistence, the persistence is manifest; when adverting to their dissolution, the dissolution is manifest. Therefore it is said: “Known, they arise; known, they are present; known, they pass away.” By “not having been, they come to be,” he sees arising. By “having been, they pass away,” he sees cessation.

Anupāyoti rāgavasena anupagamano hutvā. Anapāyoti paṭighavasena anapagato. Anissitoti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayehi anissito. Appaṭibaddhoti chandarāgena abaddho. Vippamuttoti kāmarāgato vippamutto. Visaṃyuttoti catūhi yogehi sabbakilesehi vā visaṃyutto. Vimariyādīkatenāti nimmariyādīkatena. Cetasāti evaṃvidhena cittena viharati.

‘Not approaching’ means not drawing near on account of lust. ‘Not departing’ means not moving away on account of aversion. ‘Unsupported’ means not dependent on the supports of craving and views. ‘Unbound’ means not bound by desire and lust. ‘Released’ means released from sensual lust. ‘Disjoined’ means disjoined from the four yokes or from all defilements. ‘With a mind made limitless’ means with a mind that has no limits. With a mind of this kind, he dwells.

Tattha [V 4.0062][M 4.0061] dve mariyādā kilesamariyādā ca ārammaṇamariyādā ca. Sace hissa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavatte soḷasa dhamme ārabbha rāgādayo uppajjeyyuṃ, kilesamariyādā tena katā bhaveyya, tesu panassa ekopi na uppannoti kilesamariyādā natthi. Sace panassa antosamāpattiyaṃ pavatte soḷasa dhamme āvajjantassa ekacce āpāthaṃ nāgaccheyyuṃ. Evamassa ārammaṇamariyādā bhaveyyuṃ. Te panassa soḷasa dhamme āvajjantassa āpāthaṃ anāgatadhammo nāma natthīti ārammaṇamariyādāpi natthi.

Herein, there are two limits: the limit of defilements and the limit of the object. If, for him, in regard to the sixteen phenomena occurring within the attainment, defilements such as lust were to arise, a limit of defilements would have been made by him. But since not even one such defilement arose for him in regard to them, there is no limit of defilements. If, for him, while adverting to the sixteen phenomena occurring within the attainment, some did not come into range, there would be a limit of the object for him. But for him, while adverting to the sixteen phenomena, there is no phenomenon that does not come into range; therefore, there is also no limit of the object.

Aparāpi dve mariyādā vikkhambhanamariyādā ca samucchedamariyādā ca. Tāsu samucchedamariyādā upari āgamissati, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne vikkhambhanamariyādā adhippetā. Tassa vikkhambhitapaccanīkattā natthīti vimariyādikatena cetasā viharati.

There are also another two limits: the limit of suppression and the limit of eradication. Among these, the limit of eradication will come later, but in this place, the limit of suppression is intended. Because for him the opposing factors have been suppressed, they are absent; thus he dwells with a mind made limitless.

Uttari [P 4.0090] nissaraṇanti ito uttari nissaraṇaṃ. Aññesu ca suttesu “uttari nissaraṇa”nti nibbānaṃ vuttaṃ, idha pana anantaro viseso adhippetoti veditabbo. Tabbahulīkārāti tassa pajānanassa bahulīkaraṇena. Atthitvevassa hotīti tassa therassa atthītiyeva daḷhataraṃ hoti. Iminā nayena sesavāresupi attho veditabbo.

‘A further escape’ means an escape beyond this. In other suttas, ‘a further escape’ refers to Nibbāna, but here it should be understood that the immediately superior state is intended. ‘By making that abundant’ means by the repeated cultivation of that understanding. ‘It truly exists for him’ means that for the elder, the understanding ‘it exists’ becomes even firmer. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the remaining sections as well.

Dutiyavāre pana sampasādanaṭṭhena sampasādo. Sabhāvato vavatthapeti.

In the second section, ‘confidence’ (sampasāda) is in the sense of ‘clarifying’ (sampasādana). It establishes its inherent nature.

Catutthavāre upekkhāti sukhaṭṭhāne vedanupekkhāva. Passaddhattā cetaso anābhogoti yo so “yadeva tattha sukha”nti cetaso ābhogo, etenetaṃ oḷārikamakkhāyatīti evaṃ passaddhattā cetaso anābhogo vutto, tassa abhāvāti attho. Satipārisuddhīti parisuddhāsatiyeva. Upekkhāpi pārisuddhiupekkhā.

In the fourth section, ‘equanimity’ (upekkhā) in the context of pleasure is simply the equanimity of feeling. As for ‘non-adverting of the mind due to tranquility’ (passaddhattā cetaso anābhogo), that mental adverting which is ‘whatever pleasure is there’ is described as gross. Thus, ‘non-adverting of the mind due to tranquility’ is stated, meaning the absence of that adverting. ‘Purity of mindfulness’ (satipārisuddhi) is simply purified mindfulness. Equanimity, too, is purified equanimity.

95. Sato vuṭṭhahatīti satiyā samannāgato ñāṇena sampajāno hutvā vuṭṭhāti. Te dhamme samanupassatīti yasmā nevasaññānāsaññāyatane buddhānaṃyeva anupadadhammavipassanā hoti, na sāvakānaṃ, tasmā ettha kalāpavipassanaṃ dassento evamāha.

95. ‘He emerges mindful’ (sato vuṭṭhahati) means he emerges endowed with mindfulness, clearly comprehending with knowledge. ‘He contemplates those phenomena’ (te dhamme samanupassati) is said because in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, only Buddhas have insight into phenomena one by one (anupadadhammavipassanā), not disciples. Therefore, here, showing insight into groups (kalāpavipassanā), He said thus.

Paññāya [V 4.0063][M 4.0062] cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti maggapaññāya cattāri saccāni disvā cattāro āsavā khīṇā honti. Sāriputtattherassa samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ āharitvā [P 4.0091] arahattaṃ pattavāropi atthi, nirodhasamāpattisamāpannavāropi. Arahattaṃ pattavāro idha gahito, nirodhaṃ pana ciṇṇavasitāya aparāparaṃ samāpajjissatīti vadanti.

‘And having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed’ (paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti) means that by the wisdom of the path, having seen the four truths, the four taints are destroyed. For the Elder Sāriputta, there is the section on attaining Arahantship by bringing forth serenity and insight yoked together, and there is also the section on entering the attainment of cessation. Here, the section on attaining Arahantship is taken, but they say that he will enter cessation again and again because of his mastery from practice.

Tatthassa yasmiṃ kāle nirodhasamāpatti sīsaṃ hoti, nirodhassa vāro āgacchati, phalasamāpatti gūḷhā hoti. Yasmiṃ kāle phalasamāpatti sīsaṃ hoti, phalasamāpattiyā vāro āgacchati, nirodhasamāpatti gūḷhā hoti. Jambudīpavāsino therā pana vadanti “sāriputtatthero samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ āharitvā anāgāmiphalaṃ sacchikatvā nirodhaṃ samāpajji, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto”ti. Te dhammeti antosamāpattiyaṃ pavatte tisamuṭṭhānikarūpadhamme, heṭṭhā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ pavattadhamme vā. Tepi hi imasmiṃ vāre vipassitabbadhammāva, tasmā te vā vipassatīti dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Among these, at whatever time the attainment of cessation is prominent, the turn for cessation arrives, and the fruition attainment is hidden. At whatever time the fruition attainment is prominent, the turn for the fruition attainment arrives, and the attainment of cessation is hidden. The elders residing in Jambudīpa, however, say: 'The Elder Sāriputta, having brought serenity and insight into union, realized the fruit of non-returning and entered cessation. Having arisen from cessation, he attained arahantship.' 'Those phenomena' (te dhamme) refers to the phenomena such as contact that occur within the attainment, or the phenomena that occur in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception below. For these too, in this section, are indeed phenomena to be contemplated with insight. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said to show that he also contemplates those phenomena with insight.

97. Vasippatoti ciṇṇavasitaṃ patto. Pāramippattoti nipphattiṃ patto. Orasotiādīsu thero bhagavato ure nibbattasaddaṃ sutvā jātoti oraso, mukhena pabhāvitaṃ saddaṃ sutvā jātoti mukhato jāto, dhammena pana jātattā nimmitattā dhammajo dhammanimmito, dhammadāyassa ādiyanato dhammadāyādo, āmisadāyassa anādiyanato no āmisadāyādoti veditabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

97. ‘Vasippatto’ means one who has attained mastery. ‘Pāramippatto’ means one who has attained completion. In the cases of ‘oraso’ and so forth, it should be understood thus: the Elder, because he was born having heard the sound that arose in the Blessed One’s breast, is called ‘oraso’ (born from the breast); because he was born having heard the sound produced from the mouth, he is called ‘mukhato jāto’ (born from the mouth); furthermore, because of being born of the Dhamma and created by it, he is ‘dhammajo’ (born of Dhamma) and ‘dhammanimmito’ (created by Dhamma); because of taking up the inheritance of the Dhamma, he is ‘dhammadāyādo’ (heir of Dhamma); because of not taking up the material inheritance, he is ‘no āmisadāyādo’ (not an heir of material things). The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Anupadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anupada Sutta is concluded.

2. Chabbisodhanasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Chabbisodhana Sutta

98. Evaṃ [V 4.0064][P 4.0092] me sutanti chabbisodhanasuttaṃ. Tattha khīṇā jātītiādīsu ekenāpi padena aññā byākatāva hoti, dvīhipi. Idha pana catūhi padehi aññabyākaraṇaṃ āgataṃ. Diṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditātiādīsu yāya [M 4.0063] cetanāya diṭṭhe diṭṭhaṃ meti vadati, sā diṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā nāma. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ayamanudhammoti ayaṃ sabhāvo. Abhinanditabbanti na kevalaṃ abhinanditabbaṃ, parinibbutassa panassa sabbopi khīṇāsavassa sakkāro kātabbo. Uttariṃ pañhoti sace panassa veyyākaraṇena asantuṭṭhā hotha, uttarimpi ayaṃ pañho pucchitabboti dasseti. Ito paresupi tīsu vāresu ayameva nayo.

98. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Chabbisodhana Sutta. Therein, regarding “birth is destroyed,” etc., final knowledge is declared even with a single phrase, and also with two. Here, however, the declaration of final knowledge comes with four phrases. Regarding “in the seen, speaking of the seen,” etc., the volition by which one says, “In what is seen, it is seen by me,” is called “in the seen, speaking of the seen.” This same method applies to the remaining phrases. “This is in accordance with the Dhamma” means this is its nature. “It should be rejoiced in” means not only should it be rejoiced in, but every honor should be paid to that one who has attained final Nibbāna, that one whose taints are destroyed. “A further question” shows that if you are not satisfied with his explanation, this further question should be asked. This same method applies in the three subsequent sections.

99. Abalanti dubbalaṃ. Virāgunanti vigacchanasabhāvaṃ. Anassāsikanti assāsavirahitaṃ. Upāyūpādānāti taṇhādiṭṭhīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṇhādiṭṭhiyo hi tebhūmakadhamme upentīti upāyā, upādiyantīti upādānā. Cetaso adiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayātipi tāsaṃyeva nāmaṃ. Cittañhi taṇhādiṭṭhīhi sakkāyadhammesu tiṭṭhati adhitiṭṭhatīti taṇhādiṭṭhiyo cetaso adhiṭṭhānā, tāhi taṃ abhinivisatīti abhinivesā, tāhiyeva taṃ anusetīti anusayāti vuccanti. Khayā [P 4.0093] virāgātiādīsu khayena virāgenāti attho. Sabbāni cetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva.

99. “Powerless” (abalaṃ) means weak. “Without passion” (virāguṇaṃ) means having a nature of departing. “Without solace” (anassāsikaṃ) means devoid of comfort. “Approaches and appropriations” (upāyūpādānā) is a designation for craving and views. For craving and views approach (upenti) the phenomena of the three realms, thus they are “approaches” (upāyā); they appropriate (upādiyanti), thus they are “appropriations” (upādānā). “The mind’s establishments, adherences, and underlying tendencies” (cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayā) is also a name for them. For the mind, through craving and views, stands (tiṭṭhati) or establishes itself (adhitiṭṭhati) in the phenomena of the personal continuity; thus craving and views are called the mind’s “establishments” (adhiṭṭhānā). Through them, it adheres (abhinivisati), thus they are called “adherences” (abhinivesā); and through them, it lies latent (anuseti), thus they are called “underlying tendencies” (anusayā). In “from destruction, from dispassion” (khayā virāgā), etc., the meaning is “through destruction, through dispassion.” And all of these are but synonyms for one another.

100. Pathavīdhātūti patiṭṭhānadhātu. Āpodhātūti ābandhanadhātu. Tejodhātūti paripācanadhātu. Vāyodhātūti vitthambhanadhātu. Ākāsadhātūti asamphuṭṭhadhātu. Viññāṇadhātūti vijānanadhātu. Na anattato upagacchinti ahaṃ attāti attakoṭṭhāsena na upagamiṃ. Na ca pathavīdhātunissitanti pathavīdhātunissitā sesadhātuyo ca upādārūpañca arūpakkhandhā ca. Tepi hi nissitavatthurūpānaṃ pathavīdhātunissitattā ekena pariyāyena pathavīdhātunissitāva. Tasmā “na ca pathavīdhātunissita”nti vadanto sesarūpārūpadhammepi attato na upagacchinti vadati. Ākāsadhātunissitapade pana avinibbhogavasena sabbampi bhūtupādārūpaṃ ākāsadhātunissitaṃ nāma[V 4.0065], tathā taṃnissitarūpavatthukā arūpakkhandhā. Evaṃ idhāpi rūpārūpaṃ gahitameva hoti. Viññāṇadhātunissitapade pana sahajātā tayo khandhā cittasamuṭṭhānarūpañca viññāṇadhātunissitanti rūpārūpaṃ gahitameva hoti.

100. “Earth element” is the foundation element. “Water element” is the binding element. “Fire element” is the maturing element. “Wind element” is the supporting element. “Space element” is the untouched element. “Consciousness element” is the cognizing element. “Did not approach it from the standpoint of self” means: I did not approach it with the notion “I am self” or as a constituent part of a self. “And not dependent on the earth element” means: dependent on the earth element are the remaining elements, derived matter, and the formless aggregates. Since the material phenomena that are their support are dependent on the earth element, they too are, in a sense, dependent on the earth element. Therefore, one who says, “and not dependent on the earth element,” is saying that they did not approach the remaining material and immaterial phenomena from the standpoint of self either. In the phrase “dependent on the space element,” however, by way of inseparability, all primary and derived matter is called “dependent on the space element,” and likewise the formless aggregates that have that matter dependent on space as their support. Thus, here too, material and immaterial phenomena are included. In the phrase “dependent on the consciousness element,” the three co-arisen aggregates and mind-originated matter are dependent on the consciousness element, and thus material and immaterial phenomena are included.

101. Rūpe cakkhuviññāṇe cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbesu dhammesūti ettha yaṃ atīte cakkhudvārassa āpāthaṃ āgantvā niruddhaṃ, yañca anāgate āpāthaṃ [M 4.0064] āgantvā nirujjhissati, yampi etarahi āgantvā niruddhaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana atītepi āpāthaṃ anāgantvā niruddhaṃ, anāgatepi anāgantvā nirujjhissati, etarahipi anāgantvā niruddhaṃ, taṃ cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbadhammesu saṅgahitanti vutte tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero [P 4.0094] āha – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne dvidhā karotha, upari chandovāre kinti karissatha, nayidaṃ labbhatī”ti. Tasmā tīsu kālesu āpāthaṃ āgataṃ vā anāgataṃ vā sabbampi taṃ rūpameva, cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttā pana tayo khandhā cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbadhammāti veditabbā. Ayañhettha attho “cakkhuviññāṇena saddhiṃ viññātabbesu dhammesū”ti. Chandoti taṇhāchando. Rāgoti sveva rajjanavasena rāgo. Nandīti sveva abhinandanavasena nandī. Taṇhāti sveva taṇhāyanavasena taṇhā. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo.

101. Regarding “in forms, in eye-consciousness, in phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness”: Herein, whatever form in the past came into the range of the eye-door and ceased, whatever in the future will come into range and will cease, and whatever at present comes into range and ceases—all of that is called “form.” But whatever in the past ceased without coming into range, whatever in the future will cease without coming into range, and whatever at present ceases without coming into range—that is included in “phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness.” When this was said, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: “In this place, you make it twofold. Further on, in the section on desire, what will you do? This is not tenable.” Therefore, all form in the three periods of time, whether it has come into range or not, is just “form.” The three aggregates associated with eye-consciousness, however, are to be understood as “phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness.” For this is the meaning here: “in the phenomena to be cognized together with eye-consciousness.” “Desire” (chando) is craving-desire. “Lust” (rāgo) is that very thing in the sense of infatuation. “Delight” (nandī) is that very thing in the sense of rejoicing. “Craving” (taṇhā) is that very thing in the sense of thirsting. This same method applies to the remaining sense-doors.

102. Ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayāti ettha ahaṅkāro māno, mamaṅkāro taṇhā, sveva mānānusayo. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti idaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ dibbacakkhuñca avatvā kasmā vuttaṃ? Bhikkhū lokiyadhammaṃ na pucchanti, lokuttarameva pucchanti, tasmā pucchitapañhaṃyeva kathento evamāha. Ekavissajjitasuttaṃ nāmetaṃ, chabbisodhanantipissa nāmaṃ. Ettha hi cattāro vohārā pañca khandhā cha dhātuyo cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni attano saviññāṇakakāyo paresaṃ saviññāṇakakāyoti ime cha koṭṭhāsā visuddhā, tasmā “chabbisodhaniya”nti vuttaṃ. Parasamuddavāsittherā pana attano ca parassa ca viññāṇakakāyaṃ ekameva katvā catūhi [P 4.0095] āhārehi saddhinti cha koṭṭhāse vadanti.

102. Herein, 'I-making' (ahaṅkāra) is conceit (māna), 'mine-making' (mamaṅkāra) is craving (taṇhā), and that very conceit is the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya). Regarding the phrase 'for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints,' why was this stated without having mentioned the recollection of past lives and the divine eye? Monks do not ask about worldly phenomena; they ask only about the supramundane. Therefore, in explaining only the question that was asked, he spoke thus. This is called the Ekavissajjita Sutta, and its name is also Chabbisodhaniya. Herein, the four expressions, the five aggregates, the six elements, the six internal and external sense bases, one’s own conscious body, and others' conscious bodies—these six parts are purified. Therefore, it is called the Chabbisodhaniya. However, the elders dwelling across the ocean, having made one's own and another's conscious body into just one part, speak of six parts together with the four nutriments.

Ime pana cha koṭṭhāsā “kiṃ te adhigataṃ, kinti te adhigataṃ, kadā te adhigataṃ, kattha [V 4.0066] te adhigataṃ, katame te kilesā pahīnā, katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti (pārā. 198) evaṃ vinayaniddesapariyāyena sodhetabbā.

Now, these six parts should be purified according to the method of the Vinaya exposition: 'What have you attained? How have you attained it? When did you attain it? Where did you attain it? Which defilements of yours have been abandoned? Of which dhammas are you a gainer?'

Ettha hi kiṃ te adhigatanti adhigamapucchā, jhānavimokkhādīsu sotāpattimaggādīsu vā kiṃ tayā adhigataṃ. Kinti te adhigatanti upāyapucchā. Ayañhi etthādhippāyo – kiṃ tayā aniccalakkhaṇaṃ dhuraṃ katvā adhigataṃ, dukkhānattalakkhaṇesu aññataraṃ vā, kiṃ vā samādhivasena abhinivisitvā[M 4.0065], udāhu vipassanāvasena, tathā kiṃ rūpe abhinivisitvā, udāhu arūpe, kiṃ vā ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā, udāhu bahiddhāti. Kadā te adhigatanti kālapucchā, pubbaṇhamajjhanhikādīsu katarasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, 'What have you attained?' is a question about attainment: among the jhānas, liberations, etc., or the paths of stream-entry, etc., what have you attained? 'How have you attained it?' is a question about the means. For this is the intended meaning here: Did you attain it by making the characteristic of impermanence foremost, or one of the characteristics of suffering or non-self? Or did you attain it by focusing by means of concentration, or by means of insight? Likewise, did you focus on form, or on the formless? Or did you focus internally, or externally? 'When did you attain it?' is a question about time, which means: 'At which time among the morning, midday, and so on?'

Kattha te adhigatanti okāsapucchā, kismiṃ okāse, kiṃ rattiṭṭhāne divāṭṭhāne rukkhamūle maṇḍape katarasmiṃ vā vihāreti vuttaṃ hoti. Katame te kilesā pahīnāti pahīnakilese pucchati, kataramaggavajjhā tava kilesā pahīnāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Where did you attain it?' is a question about place, which means: 'In what place? At a place for the night, a place for the day, at the root of a tree, in a pavilion, or in which monastery?' 'Which defilements of yours have been abandoned?' asks about the abandoned defilements, which means: 'Which defilements, to be destroyed by which path, have been abandoned by you?'

Katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhīti paṭiladdhadhammapucchā, paṭhamamaggādīsu katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Of which dhammas are you a gainer?' is a question about the attained dhamma. It means: 'Among the first path and so on, of which dhammas are you a gainer?'

Tasmā idāni cepi koci bhikkhu uttarimanussadhammādhigamaṃ byākareyya, na so ettāvatāva sakkātabbo. Imesu pana chasu ṭhānesu sodhanatthaṃ vattabbo “kiṃ te adhigataṃ, kiṃ jhānaṃ udāhu vimokkhādīsu aññatara”nti? Yo hi yena adhigato dhammo, so tassa pākaṭo hoti. Sace “idaṃ nāma me adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kinti te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo. Aniccalakkhaṇādīsu kiṃ dhuraṃ katvā, aṭṭhatiṃsāya vā ārammaṇesu [P 4.0096] rūpārūpaajjhattabahiddhādibhedesu vā dhammesu kena mukhena abhinivisitvāti? Yo hi yassābhiniveso, so tassa pākaṭo hoti.

Therefore, if any monk should now declare the attainment of a superior human state, he is not to be honored on that account alone. Rather, for the purpose of investigation, he should be questioned in these six instances: 'What have you attained? Is it a jhāna, or one among the liberations and so forth?' For whatever Dhamma has been attained by someone, that is manifest to him. If he says, 'I have attained such-and-such,' then he should be asked, 'How did you attain it?' That is: 'Among the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, what did you make foremost? Or among the thirty-eight objects, or among the dhammas with their divisions of form and formless, internal and external, and so forth, by what approach did you direct your mind?' For whatever one's focus is, that is manifest to him.

Sace pana “ayaṃ nāma me abhiniveso, evaṃ mayā adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kadā te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ pubbaṇhe, udāhu majjhanhikādīsu aññatarasmiṃ kāle”ti[V 4.0067]? Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatakālo pākaṭo hoti. Sace “amukasmiṃ nāma me kāle adhigata”nti vadati, tato “kattha te adhigata”nti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ divāṭṭhāne, udāhu rattiṭṭhānādīsu aññatarasmiṃ okāse”ti? Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatokāso pākaṭo hoti. Sace “amukasmiṃ nāma me okāse adhigata”nti vadati, tato “katame te kilesā pahīnā”ti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ paṭhamamaggavajjhā, udāhu dutiyādimaggavajjhā”ti? Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatamaggena pahīnakilesā pākaṭā honti.

If he says, 'This is my focus; in this way it was attained by me,' then he should be asked, 'When did you attain it? Was it in the forenoon, or at midday or some other time?' For to everyone, the time of their own attainment is manifest. If he says, 'I attained it at such-and-such a time,' then he should be asked, 'Where did you attain it? Was it in a daytime lodging, or in a nighttime lodging, or some other place?' For to everyone, the place of their own attainment is manifest. If he says, 'I attained it in such-and-such a place,' then he should be asked, 'Which of your defilements have been abandoned? Were they those to be eliminated by the first path, or by the second path and so forth?' For to everyone, the defilements abandoned by the path they have attained are manifest.

Sace [M 4.0066] “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti vadati, tato “katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti pucchitabbo, “kiṃ sotāpattimaggassa, udāhu sakadāgāmimaggādīsu aññatarassā”ti? Sabbesañhi attanā adhigatadhammo pākaṭo hoti. Sace “imesaṃ nāmāhaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī”ti vadati, ettāvatāpissa vacanaṃ na saddhātabbaṃ. Bahussutā hi uggahaparipucchākusalā bhikkhū imāni cha ṭhānāni sodhetuṃ sakkonti. Imassa bhikkhuno āgamanapaṭipadā sodhetabbā, yadi āgamanapaṭipadā na sujjhati, “imāya paṭipadāya lokuttaradhammā nāma na labbhantī”ti apanetabbo.

If he says, 'These defilements have been abandoned by me,' then he should be asked, 'Of which dhammas are you a recipient? Is it of the path of stream-entry, or of one of the others, such as the path of the once-returner?' For the Dhamma attained by oneself is manifest to everyone. If he says, 'I am a recipient of these dhammas,' even with that, his statement is not to be believed. For monks who are learned and skilled in study and inquiry are able to investigate these six points. This monk's practice leading to the path should be investigated. If his practice leading to the path is not pure, he should be dismissed with the words, 'Supramundane dhammas are not attained by this practice.'

Yadi panassa āgamanapaṭipadā sujjhati, “dīgharattaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu appamatto jāgariyamanuyutto catūsu paccayesu alaggo ākāse pāṇisamena cetasā viharatī”ti paññāyati, tassa bhikkhuno byākaraṇaṃ paṭipadāya [P 4.0097] saddhiṃ saṃsandati sameti. “Seyyathāpi nāma gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena saddhiṃ saṃsandati sameti, evameva supaññattā tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati sameti nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.296) vuttasadisaṃ hoti.

But if his practice leading to the path is pure, and it is apparent that 'for a long time he has been diligent in the three trainings, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like a hand in open space,' then that monk’s declaration accords with and matches his practice. It is like what was said: 'Just as the water of the Ganges accords with and matches the water of the Yamunā, even so the well-proclaimed practice leading to Nibbāna for the disciples by that Blessed One accords with and matches—both Nibbāna and the practice' (DN 2.296).

Apica kho ettakenāpi sakkāro na kātabbo. Kasmā? Ekaccassa hi puthujjanassāpi sato khīṇāsavapaṭipattisadisā paṭipadā hoti. Tasmā so bhikkhu tehi tehi upāyehi uttāsetabbo. Khīṇāsavassa nāma asaniyāpi matthake patamānāya bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā na hoti, puthujjanassa appamattakenāpi hoti.

Moreover, honor should not be given on account of this alone. Why? Because for a certain ordinary person, there can be a practice similar to that of one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, that monk should be frightened by various means. For one whose taints are destroyed, even if a thunderbolt were to fall on his head, no fear, stiffness, or horripilation arises; but for an ordinary person, it arises even from a trifle.

Tatrimāni [V 4.0068] vatthūni – dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero kira ekaṃ piṇḍapātikaṃ pariggahetuṃ asakkonto daharassa saññaṃ adāsi. So taṃ nhāyamānaṃ kalyāṇīnadīmukhadvāre nimujjitvā pāde aggahesi. Piṇḍapātiko kumbhīloti saññāya mahāsaddamakāsi, tadā naṃ puthujjanoti sañjāniṃsu. Candamukhatissarājakāle pana mahāvihāre saṅghatthero khīṇāsavo dubbalacakkhuko vihāreyeva acchi. Rājā theraṃ pariggaṇhissāmīti bhikkhūsu bhikkhācāraṃ gatesu appasaddo upasaṅkamitvā sappo viya pāde aggahesi. Thero silāthambho viya niccalo hutvā ko etthāti āha[M 4.0067]? Ahaṃ, bhante, tissoti. Sugandhaṃ vāyasi no tissāti? Evaṃ khīṇāsavassa bhayaṃ nāma natthīti.

In this regard, these are the illustrative stories. It is said that the Elder Abhaya, the Dīgha-reciter, being unable to test a certain alms-goer, gave a sign to a young monk. While that alms-goer was bathing at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River, the young monk dived under and grabbed his feet. The alms-goer, perceiving 'It is a crocodile!', cried out loudly. Then they knew him to be an ordinary person. Again, in the time of King Candamukha Tissa, the Saṅghatthera in the Mahāvihāra was one whose taints are destroyed and who had weak eyes; he stayed only in the monastery. The king, thinking, 'I will test the Elder,' approached without a sound when the monks had gone on their alms-round and grabbed his feet like a snake. The Elder, being as motionless as a stone pillar, said, 'Who is here?' 'Venerable sir, I am Tissa.' 'Tissa, does a sweet fragrance waft, or not?' Thus, for one whose taints are destroyed, there is no fear.

Ekacco pana puthujjanopi atisūro hoti nibbhayo. So rañjanīyena ārammaṇena pariggaṇhitabbo. Vasabharājāpi hi ekaṃ theraṃ pariggaṇhamāno ghare nisīdāpetvā tassa [P 4.0098] santike badarasāḷavaṃ maddamāno nisīdi. Mahātherassa kheḷo cali, tato therassa puthujjanabhāvo āvibhūto. Khīṇāsavassa hi rasataṇhā nāma suppahīnā, dibbesupi rasesu nikanti nāma na hoti. Tasmā imehi upāyehi pariggahetvā sacassa bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā rasataṇhā vā uppajjati, na tvaṃ arahāti apanetabbo. Sace pana abhīrū acchambhī anutrāsī hutvā sīho viya nisīdati, dibbārammaṇepi nikantiṃ na janeti. Ayaṃ bhikkhu sampannaveyyākaraṇo samantā rājarājamahāmattādīhi pesitaṃ sakkāraṃ arahatīti.

However, a certain ordinary person may be exceedingly brave and fearless. He should be tested with an enticing object. Indeed, King Vasabha, while testing a certain elder, had him sit in the palace and sat near him, kneading a jujube confection. The great elder's saliva stirred, and thereupon his status as an ordinary person became manifest. For one whose taints are destroyed, craving for tastes is well abandoned; even for divine tastes, delight does not arise. Therefore, having tested him by these means, if fear, stiffness, horripilation, or craving for tastes should arise in him, he should be dismissed with the words, 'You are not an Arahant.' But if, being fearless, unshaken, and untroubled, he sits like a lion and does not generate delight even in a divine object, then this monk, being accomplished in answering questions, is worthy of the honor sent from all around by kings, royal ministers, and others.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Chabbisodhanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Chabbisodhanasutta is concluded.

3. Sappurisadhammasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Qualities of a Superior Person.

105. Evaṃ [V 4.0069] me sutanti sappurisadhammasuttaṃ. Tattha sappurisadhammanti sappurisānaṃ dhammaṃ. Asappurisadhammanti pāpapurisānaṃ dhammaṃ. Evaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvāpi puna yathā nāma maggakusalo puriso vāmaṃ muñcitvā dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhāti. Paṭhamaṃ muñcitabbaṃ katheti, evaṃ pahātabbaṃ dhammaṃ paṭhamaṃ desento katamo ca, bhikkhave, asappurisadhammotiādimāha. Tattha uccākulāti khattiyakulā vā brāhmaṇakulā vā. Etadeva hi kuladvayaṃ “uccākula”nti vuccati. So tattha pujjoti so bhikkhu tesu bhikkhūsu pūjāraho. Antaraṃ karitvāti abbhantaraṃ katvā.

105. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Discourse on the Qualities of a True Person. Therein, 'the qualities of a true person' means the qualities of true persons. 'The qualities of an untrue person' means the qualities of evil persons. Having thus established the matrix, it is as when a man skilled in the path, abandoning the left path to take the right, first speaks of the path to be abandoned. So too, the Blessed One, first teaching the qualities that are to be abandoned, said: 'And what, bhikkhus, are the qualities of an untrue person?' and so on. Therein, 'from a high family' means from a khattiya family or a brahmin family. Indeed, this pair of families alone is called a 'high family.' 'He is venerable there' means that bhikkhu is worthy of veneration among those bhikkhus. 'Having made an interval' means having made it internal.

Mahākulāti khattiyakulā vā brāhmaṇakulā vā vessakulā [P 4.0099] vā. Idameva hi kulattayaṃ “mahākula”nti vuccati. Mahābhogakulāti mahantehi [M 4.0068] bhogehi samannāgatā kulā. Uḷārabhogakulāti uḷārehi paṇītehi bhogehi sampannakulā. Imasmiṃ padadvaye cattāripi kulāni labbhanti. Yattha katthaci kule jāto hi puññabalehi mahābhogopi uḷārabhogopi hotiyeva.

'From a great family' means from a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a vessa family. Indeed, this triad of families alone is called a 'great family.' 'From a family of great wealth' means from families endowed with great wealth. 'From a family of lavish wealth' means from families endowed with extensive and excellent wealth. In this pair of terms, all four families may be found. For one born into any family whatsoever, through the power of merit, can indeed become one of great wealth or of lavish wealth.

106. Yasassīti parivārasampanno. Appaññātāti rattiṃ khittasarā viya saṅghamajjhādīsu na paññāyanti. Appesakkhāti appaparivārā.

106. 'Renowned' means endowed with a retinue. 'Unknown' means they are not apparent in the midst of the Saṅgha and so on, like arrows shot at night. 'Of little influence' means having a small retinue.

107. Āraññikoti samādinnaāraññikadhutaṅgo. Sesadhutaṅgesupi eseva nayo. Imasmiñca sutte pāḷiyaṃ naveva dhutaṅgāni āgatāni, vitthārena panetāni terasa honti. Tesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge dhutaṅganiddese vuttameva.

107. 'A forest-dweller' means one who has undertaken the forest-dweller's ascetic practice. This same method applies to the remaining ascetic practices. And in this sutta, in the Pāḷi, only nine ascetic practices are mentioned, but in detail they are thirteen. Regarding them, whatever is to be said has all been said in every way in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of the Ascetic Practices.

108. Atammayatāti tammayatā vuccati taṇhā, nittaṇhāti attho. Atammayataññeva antaraṃ karitvāti nittaṇhataṃyeva kāraṇaṃ katvā abbhantaraṃ vā katvā, citte uppādetvāti attho.

108. Regarding 'non-identification': 'identification' is a term for craving; 'without craving' is the meaning. 'Having made non-identification the interval' means having made the state of being without craving the cause, or having made it internal, having caused it to arise in the mind—this is the meaning.

Nirodhavāre [V 4.0070] yasmā anāgāmikhīṇāsavāva taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjanti, puthujjanassa sā natthi, tasmā asappurisavāro parihīno. Na kañci maññatīti kañci puggalaṃ tīhi maññanāhi na maññati. Na [P 4.0100] kuhiñci maññatīti kismiñci okāse na maññati. Na kenaci maññatīti kenaci vatthunāpi taṃ puggalaṃ na maññati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the section on cessation, because only non-returners and arahants enter that attainment, and it does not exist for a worldling, the section on the untrue person is therefore omitted. 'He does not conceive anything' means he does not conceive of any person with the three kinds of conceiving. 'He does not conceive anywhere' means he does not conceive in any location. 'He does not conceive by means of anything' means he does not conceive of that person by means of any thing whatsoever. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Sappurisadhammasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Qualities of a True Person is concluded.

4. Sevitabbāsevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated

109. Evaṃ [V 4.0071] me sutanti sevitabbāsevitabbasuttaṃ. Tattha tañca aññamaññaṃ kāyasamācāranti aññaṃ sevitabbaṃ kāyasamācāraṃ, aññaṃ asevitabbaṃ vadāmi, sevitabbameva kenaci pariyāyena asevitabbanti, asevitabbaṃ vā sevitabbanti ca na vadāmīti attho. Vacīsamācārādīsu eseva nayo. Iti [M 4.0069] bhagavā sattahi padehi mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārato avibhajitvāva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Kasmā? Sāriputtattherassa okāsakaraṇatthaṃ.

109. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Discourse on What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated. Therein, regarding 'the one and the other bodily conduct,' the meaning is this: I say that one kind of bodily conduct should be cultivated, and another should not be cultivated. I do not say that what should be cultivated should in some way not be cultivated, or that what should not be cultivated should be cultivated. The same method applies to verbal conduct and so forth. Thus, the Blessed One established the framework with seven phrases and concluded the teaching without elaborating. Why? To create an opportunity for the Venerable Sāriputta.

113. Manosamācāre micchādiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhiyo diṭṭhipaṭilābhavasena visuṃ aṅgaṃ hutvā ṭhitāti na gahitā.

113. In mental conduct, wrong view and right view are not included, as they stand as distinct factors by way of the acquisition of views.

114. Cittuppāde akammapathappattā abhijjhādayo veditabbā.

114. In the arising of thought, covetousness and the like that have not reached the state of a course of action should be understood.

115. Saññāpaṭilābhavāre abhijjhāsahagatāya saññāyātiādīni kāmasaññādīnaṃ dassanatthaṃ vuttāni.

115. In the section on the acquisition of perception, phrases such as 'perception accompanied by covetousness' are stated to illustrate perceptions of sensual desire and so forth.

117. Sabyābajjhanti sadukkhaṃ. Apariniṭṭhitabhāvāyāti bhavānaṃ apariniṭṭhitabhāvāya. Ettha ca sabyābajjhattabhāvā nāma cattāro honti. Puthujjanopi hi yo tenattabhāvena bhavaṃ pariniṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkoti, tassa paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya akusalā dhammā vaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā ca parihāyanti, sadukkhameva [P 4.0101] attabhāvaṃ abhinibbatteti nāma. Tathā sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino. Puthujjanādayo tāva hontu, anāgāmī kathaṃ sabyābajjhaṃ attabhāvaṃ abhinibbatteti, kathañcassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantīti. Anāgāmīpi hi suddhāvāse nibbatto uyyānavimānakapparukkhe oloketvā “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udāneti, anāgāmino bhavalobho bhavataṇhā appahīnāva honti, tassa appahīnataṇhatāya akusalā vaḍḍhanti nāma, kusalā parihāyanti nāma, sadukkhameva attabhāvaṃ abhinibbatteti, apariniṭṭhitabhavoyeva hotīti veditabbo.

117. 'Accompanied by distress' means accompanied by suffering. 'Because of the state of being unfinished' means because of the unfinished state of existences. Here, there are four kinds of selfhood accompanied by distress. For even an ordinary person who is unable to bring existence to an end with that selfhood, from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, unwholesome qualities increase, and wholesome qualities decline, and they are said to produce a selfhood that is indeed accompanied by suffering. The same applies to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. Let the ordinary persons and so on be, but how does a non-returner produce a selfhood accompanied by distress? And how do unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline for them? For even a non-returner, reborn in the Pure Abodes, looking upon the pleasure gardens, celestial mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees, exclaims an inspired utterance, 'Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!' For a non-returner, greed for existence and craving for becoming are not yet abandoned. Due to this unabandoned craving, it is said that unwholesome qualities increase, wholesome qualities decline, they produce a selfhood that is indeed accompanied by suffering, and it should be understood that existence is indeed unfinished.

Abyābajjhanti [V 4.0072] adukkhaṃ. Ayampi catunnaṃ janānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Yo hi puthujjanopi tenattabhāvena bhavaṃ pariniṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkoti, puna paṭisandhiṃ na gaṇhāti, tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya akusalā parihāyanti, kusalāyeva vaḍḍhanti, adukkhameva attabhāvaṃ nibbatteti, pariniṭṭhitabhavoyeva nāma hoti. Tathā sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino. Sotāpannādayo tāva hontu, puthujjano kathaṃ abyābajjhaattabhāvaṃ nibbatteti, kathañcassa akusalaparihāniādīni hontīti. Puthujjanopi pacchimabhaviko tenattabhāvena bhavaṃ pariniṭṭhāpetuṃ samattho hoti. Tassa [M 4.0070] aṅgulimālassa viya ekenūnapāṇasahassaṃ ghātentassāpi attabhāvo abyābajjhoyeva nāma, bhavaṃ pariniṭṭhāpetiyeva nāma. Akusalameva hāyati, vipassanameva gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpeti nāma.

'Abyābajjha' means without suffering. This too should be understood by way of four kinds of persons. For an ordinary person who is able to bring existence to an end with that selfhood and does not take rebirth again, from the taking of rebirth-linking onwards, their unwholesome qualities decline, and wholesome qualities alone increase. They produce a selfhood that is indeed free from suffering, and are said to be one whose existence is completed. The same applies to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. Let the stream-enterers and so forth be, but how does an ordinary person produce a selfhood free from suffering, and how do the decline of unwholesome qualities and so forth occur for them? Even an ordinary person in their final existence is capable of bringing existence to an end with that selfhood. For such a one, like Aṅgulimāla, even having killed a thousand beings less one, their selfhood is indeed without suffering, and they indeed bring existence to an end. Unwholesomeness alone declines, and it is said that insight alone brings about conception.

119. Cakkhuviññeyyantiādīsu yasmā ekaccassa tasmiṃyeva rūpe rāgādayo uppajjanti, abhinandati assādeti, abhinandanto [P 4.0102] assādento anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti, ekaccassa nuppajjanti, nibbindati virajjati, nibbindanto virajjanto nibbutiṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā “tañca aññamañña”nti na vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

119. In the case of 'visible forms cognizable by the eye' and so forth, because for one person lust and other defilements arise regarding that very form—they delight in it and savor it. Delighting in it and savoring it, they meet with calamity and ruin. For another person, they do not arise—they become disenchanted and dispassionate. Becoming disenchanted and dispassionate, they attain Nibbāna. Therefore, it was not said, 'the one and the other.' This method applies everywhere.

Evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyunti ettha ke bhagavato imassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti, ke na ājānantīti? Ye tāva imassa suttassa pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca uggaṇhitvā takkarā na honti, yathāvuttaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ na paṭipajjanti, te na ājānanti nāma. Ye pana takkarā honti, yathāvuttaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanti, te ājānanti nāma. Evaṃ santepi sapaṭisandhikānaṃ tāva dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hotu, appaṭisandhikānaṃ kathaṃ hotīti. Appaṭisandhikā anupādānā viya jātavedā parinibbāyanti, kappasatasahassānampi accayena tesaṃ puna dukkhaṃ nāma natthi. Iti ekaṃsena tesaṃyeva dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Thus, 'one should understand the meaning in detail'—here, who understands the meaning of this statement of the Blessed One, and who does not? Those who, having learned the Pāḷi of this discourse and its commentary, are not practitioners of it and do not follow the corresponding practice as described—they are said not to understand. But those who are practitioners of it and follow the corresponding practice as described—they are said to understand. Even so, let it be for the long-term welfare and happiness of those who are subject to rebirth; but how is it for those who are not subject to rebirth? Those who are not subject to rebirth are fully extinguished like a fire without fuel. Even after hundreds of thousands of aeons, there is no suffering for them again. Thus, it is certainly for their long-term welfare and happiness alone. The rest is clear throughout.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Sevitabbāsevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated is concluded.

5. Bahudhātukasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Many Elements

124. Evaṃ [V 4.0073] me sutanti bahudhātukasuttaṃ. Tattha bhayānītiādīsu bhayanti cittutrāso. Upaddavoti anekaggatākāro. Upasaggoti upasaṭṭhākāro tattha tattha lagganākāro. Tesaṃ evaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ – pabbatādivisamanissitā corā janapadavāsīnaṃ pesenti “mayaṃ asukadivase nāma tumhākaṃ gāmaṃ paharissāmā”ti. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutakālato [M 4.0071][P 4.0103] paṭṭhāya bhayaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjanti. Ayaṃ cittutrāso nāma. “Idha no corā kupitā anatthampi āvaheyyu”nti hatthasāraṃ gahetvā dvipadacatuppadehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha tattha bhūmiyaṃ nipajjanti, ḍaṃsamakasādīhi khajjamānā gumbantarāni pavisanti, khāṇukaṇṭake maddanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ vicarantānaṃ vikkhittabhāvo anekaggatākāro nāma. Tato coresu yathāvutte divase anāgacchantesu “tucchakasāsanaṃ taṃ bhavissati, gāmaṃ pavisissāmā”ti saparikkhārā gāmaṃ pavisanti, atha tesaṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā gāmaṃ parivāretvā dvāre aggiṃ datvā manusse ghātetvā corā sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ vilumpetvā gacchanti. Tesu ghātitāvasesā aggiṃ nibbāpetvā koṭṭhacchāyabhitticchāyādīsu tattha tattha laggitvā nisīdanti naṭṭhaṃ anusocamānā. Ayaṃ upasaṭṭhākāro lagganākāro nāma.

124. Thus have I heard—the Discourse on the Many Elements. Herein, regarding 'fears' and so on, 'fear' is mental terror. 'Danger' is the state of distraction. 'Affliction' is the state of being assailed, the state of clinging here and there. Their diversity should be understood thus: Bandits, relying on mountains and other uneven places, send word to the villagers, saying, "On such and such a day, we will attack your village." From the moment they hear that news, they fall into fear and terror. This is called mental terror. Thinking, "Here, the angry bandits might bring us harm," they take their valuables and, together with their biped and quadruped animals, enter the forest, lying down here and there on the ground. Being bitten by gnats and mosquitoes, they enter thickets and trample on stumps and thorns. As they wander thus, their scattered state, the state of distraction, is called 'danger'. Then, when the bandits do not arrive on the day mentioned, they think, "That message must have been empty," and enter the village with their belongings. But knowing they have entered, the bandits surround the village, set fire to the gates, kill the people, and plunder all their wealth before leaving. The survivors of the slaughter, having extinguished the fires, sit clinging here and there in the shade of granaries and walls, lamenting what was lost. This is called the state of being assailed, the state of clinging.

Naḷāgārāti naḷehi paricchannā agārā, sesasambhārā panettha rukkhamayā honti. Tiṇāgārepi eseva nayo. Bālato uppajjantīti bālameva nissāya uppajjanti. Bālo hi apaṇḍitapuriso rajjaṃ vā uparajjaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ patthento katipaye attanā sadise vidhavāputte mahādhutte gahetvā “etha ahaṃ tumhe issare karissāmī”ti pabbatagahanādīni nissāya antante gāme paharanto dāmarikabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā anupubbena nigamepi janapadepi paharati, manussā gehāni chaḍḍetvā khemantaṭṭhānaṃ patthayamānā pakkamanti, te nissāya vasantā bhikkhūpi bhikkhuniyopi attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni pahāya pakkamanti. Gatagataṭṭhāne bhikkhāpi senāsanampi [P 4.0104] dullabhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hoti. Pabbajitesupi dve bālā bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ paṭṭhapetvā codanaṃ ārabhanti[V 4.0074]. Iti kosambivāsikānaṃ viya mahākalaho uppajjati, catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hotīti evaṃ yāni kānici bhayāni uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjantīti veditabbāni.

Reed houses are houses covered with reeds, while the remaining materials here are made of wood. The same method applies to grass houses. They arise from fools—meaning they arise dependent on fools. For a fool, an unwise person, desiring kingship, viceroyship, or some other high position, takes along a few great scoundrels, sons of widows, who are like himself, and says, "Come, I will make you lords." Relying on mountain thickets and such, he plunders border villages, making his banditry known. Gradually, he plunders towns and districts as well. People abandon their homes and flee, seeking a safe place. Monks and nuns who live dependent on them also leave their respective dwellings. In every place they go, alms and lodging become hard to find. Thus, danger certainly befalls the fourfold assembly. Even among the renunciates, two foolish monks may start a dispute, initiating accusations against each other. Thus, a great quarrel arises, like that among the residents of Kosambi, and danger certainly befalls the fourfold assembly. Therefore, whatever dangers arise, they should all be understood as arising from fools.

Etadavocāti bhagavatā dhammadesanā matthakaṃ apāpetvāva niṭṭhāpitā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dasabalaṃ pucchitvā sabbaññutaññāṇenevassa desanāya pāripūriṃ kareyyanti [M 4.0072] cintetvā etaṃ “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Regarding the phrase 'He said this': the Blessed One had concluded the teaching without bringing it to its culmination. Thinking, 'What if I were to ask the Ten-Powered One and bring his teaching to its full completion through his very knowledge of omniscience?' he spoke the words beginning with, 'To what extent, venerable sir...'

125. Aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggaho, aḍḍhaṭṭhamakadhātuyo arūpapariggahoti rūpārūpapariggahova kathito. Sabbāpi khandhavasena pañcakkhandhā honti. Pañcapi khandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ samuṭṭhāpikā taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Iti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetā dhātuyo visuddhimagge kathitāva. Jānāti passatīti saha vipassanāya maggo vutto.

125. Among the eighteen elements, ten and a half elements are included by way of matter, and seven and a half elements are included by way of non-matter; thus it is taught as the inclusion by way of matter and non-matter. All of them, in terms of aggregates, are the five aggregates. The five aggregates are the truth of suffering; the craving that gives rise to them is the truth of the origin; the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; the practice for understanding cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, the meditation subject of the four noble truths is taught, having been brought to its conclusion and culmination for a single monk. This is the summary here; but these elements have been explained in detail by me in the Visuddhimagga. By 'knows and sees,' the path together with insight is spoken of.

Pathavīdhātuādayo saviññāṇakakāyaṃ suññato nissattato dassetuṃ vuttā. Tāpi purimāhi aṭṭhārasahi dhātūhi pūretabbā. Pūrentena viññāṇadhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Viññāṇadhātu hesā cakkhuviññāṇādivasena chabbidhā hoti. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā pariggahitāya tassā vatthu cakkhudhātu, ārammaṇaṃ rūpadhātūti dve dhātuyo pariggahitāva [P 4.0105] honti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Manoviññāṇadhātuyā pana pariggahitāya tassā purimapacchimavasena manodhātu, ārammaṇavasena dhammadhātūti dve dhātuyo pariggahitāva honti. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

The earth element and others are spoken of to show the body with consciousness as empty and devoid of a being. These too should be completed with the aforementioned eighteen elements. When completing them, one should complete them by extracting from the consciousness element. For that consciousness element is sixfold, as eye-consciousness and so on. Here, when the eye-consciousness element is comprehended, its base, the eye element, and its object, the form element, are also comprehended—thus two elements are comprehended. This method applies everywhere. But when the mind-consciousness element is comprehended, its base, the mind element, in terms of preceding and succeeding, and its object, the mental-object element, are also comprehended—thus two elements are comprehended. Thus, among these eighteen elements, ten and a half elements are included by way of matter. In the same way as before, this too is taught, having been brought to its conclusion and culmination for a single monk.

Sukhadhātūtiādīsu sukhañca taṃ nissattasuññataṭṭhena dhātu cāti sukhadhātu. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ettha ca purimā catasso dhātuyo sappaṭipakkhavasena gahitā, pacchimā dve sarikkhakavasena. Avibhūtabhāvena hi upekkhādhātu avijjādhātuyā sarikkhā. Ettha ca sukhadukkhadhātūsu [V 4.0075] pariggahitāsu kāyaviññāṇadhātu pariggahitāva hoti, sesāsu pariggahitāsu manoviññāṇadhātu pariggahitāva hoti. Imāpi cha dhātuyo heṭṭhā aṭṭhārasahiyeva pūretabbā. Pūrentena upekkhādhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti [M 4.0073] purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

In 'pleasure element' and so on: it is pleasure, and that which is an element in the sense of being non-sentient and void of a self; thus, it is the 'pleasure element.' This method applies everywhere. And here, the first four elements are taken by way of opposition, while the last two are taken by way of similarity. Indeed, due to its unmanifested nature, the equanimity element is similar to the ignorance element. And here, when the pleasure and pain elements are comprehended, the body-consciousness element is indeed comprehended; when the remaining elements are comprehended, the mind-consciousness element is indeed comprehended. These six elements should also be completed by means of the eighteen below. One who is completing them should do so by extracting from the equanimity element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, ten and a half elements are the comprehension of matter.
