Satthā pavattā sarabhaṅgo lomahaṃso uccaṅgamāyoti ime pañca janā. Asito anāsavo manomayoti imepi tayo janā. Mānacchido ca bandhumāti bandhumā nāma eko, mānassa pana chinnattā mānacchidoti vutto. Tadādhimuttotipi nāmameva.

Satthā, Pavattā, Sarabhaṅga, Lomahaṃsa, and Uccaṅgamāya—these are five persons. Asito, Anāsavo, and Manomaya—these also are three persons. As for 'Mānacchido and Bandhumā': one is named Bandhumā, but because he had cut off conceit, he is called 'Mānacchido'. 'Tadādhimutto' is also just a name.

Ketumbharāgo ca mātaṅgo ariyoti ime tayo janā. Athaccutoti atha accuto. Accutagāmabyāmaṅkoti ime dve janā. Khemābhirato ca soratoti ime dveyeva.

Ketumbharāga, Mātaṅga, and Ariya—these are three persons. Athaccuta and Accutagāmabyāmaṅka—these are two persons. Khemābhirata and Sorata—these are just two.

Sayho anomanikkamoti sayho nāma so buddho, anomavīriyattā pana anomanikkamoti [V 4.0093] vutto. Ānando nando upanando dvādasāti cattāro ānandā, cattāro nandā cattāro upanandāti evaṃ dvādasa. Bhāradvājo [P 4.0130] antimadehadhārīti bhāradvājo nāma so buddho. Antimadehadhārīti thuti.

As for 'Sayha of unequalled exertion': Sayha is the name of that Buddha, but because of his unequalled energy, he is called 'Anomanikkama.' 'Ānanda, Nanda, Upananda, twelve' means four Ānandas, four Nandas, and four Upanandas, thus twelve. As for 'Bhāradvāja, bearer of the final body': Bhāradvāja is the name of that Buddha. 'Bearer of the final body' is praise.

Taṇhacchidoti sikharissāyaṃ thuti. Vītarāgoti maṅgalassa thuti. Usabhacchidā jāliniṃ dukkhamūlanti usabho nāma so buddho dukkhamūlabhūtaṃ jāliniṃ acchidāti attho. Santaṃ padaṃ ajjhagamopanītoti upanīto nāma so buddho santaṃ padaṃ ajjhagamā. Vītarāgotipi ekassa nāmameva. Suvimuttacittoti ayaṃ kaṇhassa thuti.

'Taṇhacchido' (the cutter of craving) is praise for Sikhari. 'Vītarāgo' (free from lust) is praise for Maṅgala. As for 'Usabha cut the net, the root of suffering': Usabha is the name of that Buddha, and the meaning is that he cut the net of craving, which is the root of suffering. As for 'Upanīta attained the peaceful state': Upanīta is the name of that Buddha; he attained the peaceful state. 'Vītarāgo' is also the name of one. 'Suvimuttacitto' (one whose mind is well-liberated) is praise for Kaṇha.

Ete ca aññe cāti ete pāḷiyaṃ āgatā ca pāḷiyaṃ anāgatā aññe ca etesaṃ ekanāmakāyeva. Imesu hi pañcasu paccekabuddhasatesu dvepi tayopi dasapi dvādasapi ānandādayo viya ekanāmakā ahesuṃ. Iti pāḷiyaṃ āgatanāmeheva sabbesaṃ nāmāni vuttāni [M 4.0092] hontīti ito paraṃ visuṃ visuṃ avatvā “ete ca aññe cā”ti āha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'These and others' means: these whose names appear in the Pāḷi text, and others whose names do not, who have the same names as them. For among these five hundred Paccekabuddhas, there were those with the same name—two, three, ten, or twelve of them—like Ānanda and the others. Thus, so that the names of all would be stated by means of only the names appearing in the Pāḷi, he did not state them individually hereafter but said, 'these and others.' The rest is clear in every case.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Isigilisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Isigili Sutta is concluded.

7. Mahācattārīsakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Great Forty Discourse

136. Evaṃ [V 4.0094] me sutanti mahācattārīsakasuttaṃ. Tattha ariyanti niddosaṃ lokuttaraṃ, niddosañhi “ariya”nti vuccati. Sammāsamādhinti maggasamādhiṃ. Saupanisanti sapaccayaṃ. Saparikkhāranti saparivāraṃ.

136. Thus have I heard: the Great Forty Discourse. Herein, 'noble' (ariya) means faultless, supramundane; for what is faultless is called 'noble'. Right concentration (sammāsamādhi) means the concentration of the path. With its support (saupanisa) means with its conditions. With its accessories (saparikkhāra) means with its retinue.

Parikkhatāti parivāritā. Sammādiṭṭhi [P 4.0131] pubbaṅgamā hotīti dvidhā sammādiṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti purecārikā vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi ca maggasammādiṭṭhi ca. Vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi tebhūmakasaṅkhāre aniccādivasena parivīmaṃsati; maggasammādiṭṭhi pana parivīmaṃsanapariyosāne bhūmiladdhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ samugghāṭayamānā vūpasamayamānā sītudakaghaṭasahassaṃ matthake āsiñcamānā viya uppajjati. Yathā hi khettaṃ kurumāno kassako paṭhamaṃ araññe rukkhe chindati, pacchā aggiṃ deti, so aggi paṭhamaṃ chinne rukkhe anavasese jhāpeti, evameva vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi paṭhamaṃ aniccādivasena saṅkhāre vīmaṃsati, maggasammādiṭṭhi tāya vīmaṃsanatthaṃ saṅkhāre puna appavattivasena samugghāṭayamānā uppajjati, sā duvidhāpi idha adhippetā.

'Encompassed' (parikkhata) means surrounded. 'Right view is foremost' (sammādiṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti): Right view is twofold and serves as the forerunner, namely, the right view of insight and the right view of the path. The right view of insight (vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi) examines the formations of the three realms (tebhūmaka-saṅkhāra) as impermanent and so forth. The right view of the path (maggasammādiṭṭhi), however, arises at the culmination of that examination, uprooting and pacifying the round (vaṭṭa) pertaining to that plane of attainment—as if pouring a thousand pots of cool water over one's head. Just as a farmer preparing a field first cuts down the trees in the forest and later sets them on fire, and that fire burns all the cut trees without remainder, so too the right view of insight first examines formations as impermanent and so forth, while the right view of the path arises, uprooting those formations so that they do not recur. Both types are intended here.

Micchādiṭṭhīti pajānātīti micchādiṭṭhiṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena ārammaṇato pajānāti, sammādiṭṭhiṃ kiccato asammohato pajānāti. Sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhīti sā evaṃ pajānanā assa sammādiṭṭhi nāma hoti.

'He understands wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajānāti): He understands wrong view as impermanent, suffering, and not-self by penetrating its characteristics, taking it as an object. He understands right view by its function and as non-delusion. 'This becomes his right view' (sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi): That very understanding of his is called right view.

Dvāyaṃ vadāmīti dvayaṃ vadāmi, duvidhakoṭṭhāsaṃ vadāmīti attho. Puññabhāgiyāti puññakoṭṭhāsabhūtā. Upadhivepakkāti upadhisaṅkhātassa vipākassa dāyikā.

'I say twofold' (dvayaṃ vadāmi): I say twofold, meaning I declare a division into two parts. 'Partaking of merit' (puññabhāgiya) means that which forms the portion of merit. 'Ripening in the substrata of existence' (upadhivepakka) means being the giver of the result termed the substratum.

Paññā paññindriyantiādīsu vibhajitvā vibhajitvā amatadvāraṃ paññapeti dassetīti paññā. Tasmiṃ atthe indattaṃ karotīti paññindriyaṃ. Avijjāya na [M 4.0093] kampatīti paññābalaṃ. Bojjhaṅgappattā [P 4.0132] hutvā catusaccadhamme vicinātīti dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo. Maggasampattiyā pasaṭṭhā sobhanā [V 4.0095] diṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhi. Ariyamaggassa aṅganti maggaṅgaṃ. Soti so bhikkhu. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthāya. Upasampadāyāti paṭilābhatthāya. Sammāvāyāmoti niyyāniko kusalavāyāmo. Satoti satiyā samannāgato hutvā. Anuparidhāvanti anuparivattantīti sahajātā ca purejātā ca hutvā parivārenti. Ettha hi sammāvāyāmo ca sammāsati ca lokuttarasammādiṭṭhiṃ sahajātā parivārenti rājānaṃ viya ekarathe ṭhitā asiggāhachattaggāhā. Vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi pana purejātā hutvā parivāreti rathassa purato pattikādayo viya. Dutiyapabbato paṭṭhāya pana sammāsaṅkappādīnaṃ tayopi sahajātaparivārāva hontīti veditabbā.

'Wisdom' (paññā) is so called because, having analyzed again and again, it makes known the door to the Deathless. It exercises sovereignty in that meaning; thus it is the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). It is unshaken by ignorance; thus it is the power of wisdom (paññābala). Having reached the state of an enlightenment factor, it investigates the Four Noble Truths; thus it is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga). By means of attainment of the path, it is a praised and beautiful view; thus it is right view (sammādiṭṭhi). It is a factor of the noble path; thus it is a path factor (maggaṅga). 'He' (so) refers to that monk. 'For abandoning' (pahānāya) means for the purpose of abandoning. 'For attainment' (upasampadāya) means for the purpose of obtaining. 'Right effort' (sammāvāyāma) is the liberating wholesome effort. 'Mindful' (sato) means being endowed with mindfulness. 'They run along with, they revolve around' (anuparidhāvanti anuparivattanti) means they surround it, being both co-nascent and pre-nascent. Herein, right effort and right mindfulness surround supramundane right view as co-nascent attendants, like a sword-bearer and a parasol-bearer standing with a king in a single chariot. The right view of insight, however, surrounds it as a pre-nascent attendant, like foot-soldiers and others in front of a chariot. But from the second section onward, it should be understood that for right thought and the others, all three—right view, right effort, and right mindfulness—are only co-nascent attendants.

137. Micchāsaṅkappoti pajānātīti micchāsaṅkappaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena ārammaṇato pajānāti sammāsaṅkappaṃ kiccato asammohato pajānāti. Ito aparesu sammāvācādīsupi evameva yojanā veditabbā. Kāmasaṅkappādayo dvedhāvitakkasutte (ma. ni. 1.206) vuttāyeva.

137. 'He understands wrong thought' (micchāsaṅkappaṃ pajānāti): He understands wrong thought as impermanent, suffering, and not-self by penetrating its characteristics, taking it as an object; he understands right thought by its function and as non-delusion. The same method of application should be understood for the others that follow, such as right speech. Sensual thought and the like have already been explained in the Discourse on Two Sorts of Thinking (MN 19).

Takkotiādīsu takkanavasena takko. Sveva ca upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vitakkoti vutto, sveva saṅkappanavasena saṅkappo. Ekaggo hutvā ārammaṇe appetīti appanā[P 4.0133]. Upasaggena pana padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā byappanāti vuttaṃ. Cetaso abhiniropanāti cittassa abhiniropanā. Vitakkasmiñhi sati vitakko ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti vitakke pana asati attanoyeva dhammatāya cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ abhiruhati jātisampanno abhiññātapuriso viya rājagehaṃ. Anabhiññātassa hi paṭihārena vā dovārikena vā attho hoti, abhiññātaṃ jātisampannaṃ sabbe rājarājamahāmattā jānantīti attanova dhammatāya nikkhamati ceva pavisati ca, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vācaṃ saṅkharotīti vacīsaṅkhāro. Ettha ca lokiyavitakko vācaṃ saṅkharoti, na lokuttaro. Kiñcāpi na saṅkharoti, vacīsaṅkhārotveva ca panassa nāmaṃ hoti. Sammāsaṅkappaṃ anuparidhāvantīti lokuttarasammāsaṅkappaṃ parivārenti. Ettha ca tayopi nekkhammasaṅkappādayo [M 4.0094] pubbabhāge nānācittesu labbhanti, maggakkhaṇe pana tiṇṇampi kāmasaṅkappādīnañca padacchedaṃ samugghātaṃ karonto maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova sammāsaṅkappo uppajjitvā nekkhammasaṅkappādivasena tīṇi nāmāni labhati. Parato sammāvācādīsupi eseva nayo.

In such terms as 'reasoning' (takka), it is 'reasoning' by way of reasoning. That same term, when augmented with a prefix, is called 'initial application' (vitakka); that same term, by way of intending, is 'thought' (saṅkappa). Being one-pointed, it applies to the object; thus it is 'absorption' (appanā). When augmented with a prefix, it is called 'application' (byappanā). 'Directing of the mind' (cetaso abhiniropanā) is the directing of the mind. For when there is initial application, initial application directs the mind to the object. But when there is no initial application, the mind by its own nature ascends to the object, like a well-born, recognized person entering the king’s palace. An unrecognized person needs a doorkeeper or gatekeeper, but a recognized, well-born person is known by all the king's great ministers, and so by his own nature he goes out and comes in. This analogy should be understood. 'It conditions speech' (vācaṃ saṅkharoti); thus it is 'verbal conditioner' (vacīsaṅkhāra). Herein, mundane initial application conditions speech, not the supramundane. Although it does not condition speech, its name is nevertheless 'verbal conditioner'. 'They run along with right thought' (sammāsaṅkappaṃ anuparidhāvanti) means they surround supramundane right thought. Herein, the three—thought of renunciation and so on—are found in various minds in the preliminary stage. But at the moment of the path, while cutting the basis of and uprooting the three—sensual thought and so on—and fulfilling the path factor, a single right thought arises and obtains three names by way of thought of renunciation and so on. This same method applies to right speech and the others that follow.

138. Musāvādā [V 4.0096] veramaṇītiādīsu viratipi cetanāpi vaṭṭati. Āratītiādīsu vacīduccaritehi ārakā ramatīti ārati. Vinā tehi ramatīti virati. Tato tato paṭinivattāva hutvā tehi vinā ramatīti paṭivirati. Upasaggavasena vā padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, sabbamidaṃ oramanabhāvasseva adhivacanaṃ. Veraṃ maṇati vināsetīti veramaṇi. Idampi oramanasseva vevacanaṃ.

138. In such terms as 'abstinence from false speech' (musāvādā veramaṇī), both abstinence (virati) and volition (cetanā) are applicable. In such terms as 'abstention' (ārati), it means one delights in being far (ārakā) from verbal misconduct; thus it is 'abstention' (ārati). 'Abstinence' (virati) means one delights without (vinā) them. 'Refraining' (paṭivirati) means having turned back (paṭinivattā) from this and that, one delights without them. Or, the word is augmented by way of a prefix. All this is a designation for the state of abstaining. 'It destroys enmity' (veraṃ maṇati); thus it is 'abstinence' (veramaṇī). This too is a synonym for abstaining.

139. Pāṇātipātā veramaṇītiādīsupi cetanā viratīti ubhayampi vaṭṭatiyeva.

139. In such terms as 'abstinence from the destruction of life' (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), both volition (cetanā) and abstinence (virati) are indeed applicable.

140. Kuhanātiādīsu [P 4.0134] tividhena kuhanavatthunā lokaṃ etāya kuhayanti vimhāpayantīti kuhanā. Lābhasakkāratthikā hutvā etāya lapantīti lapanā. Nimittaṃ sīlametesanti nemittikā, tesaṃ bhāvo nemittikatā. Nippeso sīlametesanti nippesikā, tesaṃ bhāvo nippesikatā. Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanti magganti pariyesantīti lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā, tesaṃ bhāvo lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena panetā kuhanādikā visuddhimagge sīlaniddeseyeva pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca āharitvā pakāsitā. Micchāājīvassa pahānāyāti ettha na kevalaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatova micchāājīvo, ājīvahetu pana pavattitā pāṇātipātādayo sattakammapathacetanāpi micchāājīvova. Tāsaṃyeva sattannaṃ cetanānaṃ padapacchedaṃ samugghātaṃ kurumānaṃ maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā uppannā virati sammāājīvo nāma.

140. In such terms as 'deceit' (kuhanā): by this, with the threefold basis of deceit, they cause wonder and bewilderment in the world; therefore, it is called 'deceit' (kuhanā). Desiring gain and honor, they speak by means of this; therefore, it is called 'chattering' (lapanā). The practice of making signs is theirs, thus they are 'those who make signs' (nemittikā); their state is 'the making of signs' (nemittikatā). The practice of pressuring is theirs, thus they are 'those who pressure' (nippesikā); their state is 'pressuring' (nippesikatā). With gain they seek gain, meaning they search for it; thus, this is 'seeking gain with gain' (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā); their state is 'the state of seeking gain with gain' (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā). This is the summary here. But in detail, these things beginning with deceit have been explained by me in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on virtue, by citing both the Pāḷi and the commentary. Regarding the phrase 'for the abandoning of wrong livelihood,' here it is not only the wrong livelihood that has come in the Pāḷi that is meant. Indeed, the seven volitions of the courses of action, beginning with the destruction of life, which are undertaken for the sake of livelihood, are also wrong livelihood. The abstinence that arises while fulfilling the path factor, bringing about the cutting off of the basis and complete uprooting of those very seven volitions, is called right livelihood.

141. Sammādiṭṭhissāti maggasammādiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa puggalassa. Sammāsaṅkappo pahotīti maggasammāsaṅkappo pahoti, phalasammādiṭṭhissapi phalasammāsaṅkappo pahotīti evaṃ sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Sammāñāṇassa [M 4.0095] sammāvimuttīti ettha pana maggasammāsamādhimhi ṭhitassa maggapaccavekkhaṇaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ pahoti, phalasammāsamādhimhi ṭhitassa phalapaccavekkhaṇaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ pahoti. Maggapaccavekkhaṇasammāñāṇe ca ṭhitassa maggasammāvimutti pahoti, phalapaccavekkhaṇasammāñāṇe [P 4.0135] ṭhitassa phalasammāvimutti pahotīti attho. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā aṭṭha phalaṅgāni sammāñāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ katvā sammāvimuttiṃ phalaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ.

141. Regarding 'for one with right view' (sammādiṭṭhissa): this means for a person established in right view associated with the path. Regarding 'right intention arises' (sammāsaṅkappo pahoti): right intention associated with the path arises. For one with right view associated with the fruit, right intention associated with the fruit also arises. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Now, regarding 'for right knowledge, right liberation' (sammāñāṇassa sammāvimutti): for one established in right concentration of the path, the right knowledge that is the reviewing of the path arises. For one established in right concentration of the fruit, the right knowledge that is the reviewing of the fruit arises. And for one established in the right knowledge that is the reviewing of the path, right liberation of the path arises. For one established in the right knowledge that is the reviewing of the fruit, right liberation of the fruit arises. This is the meaning. And here it is said that, having set aside the eight fruit-factors, it is proper to take the reviewing knowledge as right knowledge, and to take the fruit as right liberation.

142. Sammādiṭṭhissa[V 4.0097], bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hotītiādīsu avasesanikāyabhāṇakā phalaṃ kathitanti vadanti, majjhimabhāṇakā pana dasannaṃ nijjaravatthūnaṃ āgataṭṭhāne maggo kathitoti vadanti. Tattha dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi veditabbā, viditakaraṇaṭṭhena sammāñāṇaṃ, tadadhimuttaṭṭhena sammāvimutti.

142. In such passages as, 'For one with right view, bhikkhus, wrong view is worn out,' the reciters of the Nikāyas other than the Majjhima Nikāya say that the fruit of the contemplative life was taught. But the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say that the path was taught in the context where the ten items of wearing out are mentioned. Therein, right view should be known in the sense of seeing; right knowledge should be known in the sense of making known what has been seen; and right liberation should be known in the sense of being resolved on that.

Vīsati kusalapakkhāti sammādiṭṭhiādayo dasa, “sammādiṭṭhipaccayā ca aneke kusalā dhammā”tiādinā nayena vuttā dasāti evaṃ vīsati kusalapakkhā honti. Vīsati akusalapakkhāti “micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hotī”tiādinā nayena vuttā micchādiṭṭhiādayo dasa, “ye ca micchādiṭṭhipaccayā aneke pāpakā”tiādinā vuttā dasa cāti evaṃ vīsati akusalapakkhā veditabbā. Mahācattārīsakoti mahāvipākadānena mahantānaṃ kusalapakkhikānañceva akusalapakkhikānañca cattārīsāya dhammānaṃ pakāsitattā mahācattārīsakoti.

'Twenty wholesome factors' means the ten states beginning with right view, and the ten taught in the manner of 'And conditioned by right view are many wholesome states'; thus there are twenty factors on the wholesome side. 'Twenty unwholesome factors' means the ten states beginning with wrong view, taught in the manner of 'Wrong view is worn out,' and the ten taught in the manner of 'And those many evil states conditioned by wrong view'; thus the twenty factors on the unwholesome side should be known. It is called the 'Mahācattārīsaka' (The Great Forty) because it explains the forty states—those belonging to the great wholesome side and those belonging to the great unwholesome side—which give great results.

Imasmiñca pana sutte pañca sammādiṭṭhiyo kathitā vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi kammassakatāsammādiṭṭhi maggasammādiṭṭhi phalasammādiṭṭhi paccavekkhaṇāsammādiṭṭhīti. Tattha “micchādiṭṭhiṃ micchādiṭṭhīti pajānātī”tiādinā nayena vuttā vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi nāma. “Atthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena vuttā kammassakatāsammādiṭṭhi nāma. “Sammādiṭṭhissa, bhikkhave, sammāsaṅkappo pahotī”ti ettha pana maggasammādiṭṭhi phalasammādiṭṭhīti dvepi kathitā. “Sammāñāṇaṃ pahotī”ti. Ettha pana paccavekkhaṇāsammādiṭṭhi kathitāti veditabbā.

Furthermore, in this discourse, five kinds of right view were taught by the Blessed One: insight right view, right view of ownership of kamma, path right view, fruit right view, and reviewing right view. Therein, the right view taught in the manner of 'one understands wrong view as wrong view,' and so on, is called insight right view. The right view taught in the manner of 'there is what is given,' and so on, is called right view of ownership of kamma. But in the passage, 'For one with right view, bhikkhus, right intention arises,' both path right view and fruit right view were taught. In the passage, 'Right knowledge arises,' it should be known that reviewing right view was taught.

143. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ [M 4.0096][P 4.0136] ce bhavaṃ garahatīti micchādiṭṭhi nāmāyaṃ sobhanāti vadantopi sammādiṭṭhi nāmāyaṃ na sobhanāti vadantopi sammādiṭṭhiṃ garahati nāma. Okkalāti okkalajanapadavāsino. Vassabhaññāti vasso ca bhañño cāti dve janā. Ahetuvādāti natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti evamādivādino. Akiriyavādāti karoto na karīyati pāpanti evaṃ kiriyapaṭikkhepavādino. Natthikavādāti natthi dinnantiādivādino. Te imesu tīsupi dassanesu okkantaniyāmā ahesuṃ. Kathaṃ panetesu niyāmo hotīti. Yo hi evarūpaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinno sajjhāyati vīmaṃsati, tassa “natthi hetu [V 4.0098] natthi paccayo karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ, natthi dinnaṃ, kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”ti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe micchāsati santiṭṭhati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, javanāni javanti. Paṭhamajavane satekiccho hoti, tathā dutiyādīsu. Sattame buddhānampi atekiccho anivattī ariṭṭhakaṇḍakasadiso hoti.

143. Regarding 'If you, sir, disparage right view': one who says, 'This so-called wrong view is excellent,' or one who says, 'This so-called right view is not excellent,' is said to disparage right view. 'Okkalā' refers to the inhabitants of the Okkala country. 'Vassa and Bhañña' refers to two persons, Vassa and Bhañña. 'Those who hold the doctrine of no-cause' are those who hold such views as, 'There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings.' 'Those who hold the doctrine of inaction' are those who hold the view that denies action, such as, 'For one who does an evil deed, it is not done.' 'Those who hold the doctrine of nihilism' are those who hold such views as, 'There is no fruit of giving.' They had entered the fixed course of wrongness in these three views. But how does this fixed course come to be in them? When someone, having adopted such a belief, sits in a place for day or night and recites and examines it, then, with respect to that object of thought—'There is no cause, no condition; for one who does an evil deed, it is not done; there is no fruit of giving; at the breakup of the body, one is annihilated'—wrong mindfulness becomes established, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the javanas run their course. At the first javana, it is remediable; likewise at the second and so on. At the seventh, it is irremediable even for the Buddhas, irreversible, like the novice Ariṭṭha Kaṇḍaka.

Tattha koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamati, koci dve, koci tīṇipi, niyatamicchādiṭṭhikova hoti, patto saggamaggāvaraṇañceva mokkhamaggāvaraṇañca. Abhabbo tassa attabhāvassa anantaraṃ saggampi gantuṃ, pageva mokkhaṃ, vaṭṭakhāṇu nāmesa satto pathavīgopako, yebhuyyena [P 4.0137] evarūpassa bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ natthi. Vassabhaññāpi edisā ahesuṃ. Nindābyārosaupārambhabhayāti attano nindābhayena ghaṭṭanabhayena upavādabhayena cāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Therein, someone enters into one view, someone into two, and someone even into all three; he becomes one with fixed wrong view, having reached the obstruction to the path to heaven and the obstruction to the path to liberation. Immediately after that existence, he is incapable of going even to heaven, to say nothing of liberation. Such a being is called a 'stump in the round of existence,' a 'guardian of the earth.' For the most part, for such a one, there is no rising up from existence. Vassa and Bhañña were also of such a nature. 'Through fear of blame, friction, and accusation' means through fear of one's own blame, through fear of friction, and through fear of accusation. The rest is clear in every way.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Mahācattārīsakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta is concluded.

8. Ānāpānassatisuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Ānāpānassati Sutta

144. Evaṃ [V 4.0099] me sutanti ānāpānassatisuttaṃ. Tattha aññehi cāti ṭhapetvā pāḷiyaṃ āgate dasa there aññehipi abhiññātehi bahūhi [M 4.0097] sāvakehi saddhiṃ. Tadā kira mahā bhikkhusaṅgho ahosi aparicchinnagaṇano.

144. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Ānāpānassati Sutta. Therein, as for 'and with others,' it means: having set aside the ten elders who are mentioned in the Pāli, it was also with many other well-known disciples. At that time, it is said, the assembly of bhikkhus was great, of an unreckonable number.

Ovadanti anusāsantīti āmisasaṅgahena dhammasaṅgahena cāti dvīhi saṅgahehi saṅgaṇhitvā kammaṭṭhānovādānusāsanīhi ovadanti ca anusāsanti ca. Te cāti cakāro āgamasandhimattaṃ. Uḷāraṃ pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ jānantīti sīlaparipūraṇādito pubbavisesato uḷārataraṃ aparaṃ kasiṇaparikammādivisesaṃ jānantīti attho.

As for 'they advise and instruct,' it means: having supported them with the two kinds of support, namely material support and Dhamma support, they advise with the giving of meditation subjects and admonition, and they instruct repeatedly. As for 'and they' (te ca), the 'ca' is merely a euphonic conjunction. As for 'they know a sublime, subsequent distinction from a previous one,' the meaning is: they know a more sublime, subsequent distinction, such as the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, than the previous distinction which begins with the fulfillment of virtue.

145. Āraddhoti tuṭṭho. Appattassa pattiyāti appattassa arahattassa pāpuṇanatthaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi ayameva attho. Komudiṃ cātumāsininti pacchimakattikacātumāsapuṇṇamaṃ. Sā hi kumudānaṃ atthitāya komudī, catunnaṃ vassikānaṃ māsānaṃ pariyosānattā cātumāsinīti vuccati. Āgamessāmīti udikkhissāmi, ajja apavāretvā yāva sā āgacchati, tāva katthaci agantvā idheva vasissāmīti attho. Iti bhikkhūnaṃ pavāraṇasaṅgahaṃ anujānanto evamāha.

145. As for 'delighted,' it means pleased. As for 'for the attainment of the unattained,' it means for the purpose of attaining the unattained Arahantship. This very meaning should be understood for the remaining two phrases as well. As for 'the Komudī Cātumāsinī,' it is the full moon of the last Kattika, the four-month period. Indeed, it is called 'Komudī' because of the existence of kumuda lotuses, and it is called 'Cātumāsinī' because it is the end of the four rainy-season months. As for 'I will await,' it means 'I will look forward to.' The meaning is: 'Having postponed the Pavāraṇā today, I will dwell right here without going anywhere until that day arrives.' Thus, wishing to permit the Pavāraṇā-support for the bhikkhus, he spoke thus.

Pavāraṇasaṅgaho nāma ñattidutiyena kammena diyyati kassa [P 4.0138] panesa diyyati, kassa na diyyatīti. Akārakassa tāva bālaputhujjanassa na diyyati, tathā āraddhavipassakassa ceva ariyasāvakassa ca. Yassa pana samatho vā taruṇo hoti vipassanā vā, tassa diyyati. Bhagavāpi tadā bhikkhūnaṃ cittācāraṃ parivīmaṃsanto samathavipassanānaṃ taruṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā – “mayi ajja pavārente disāsu vassaṃvuṭṭhā bhikkhū idha osarissanti. Tato ime bhikkhū vuḍḍhatarehi bhikkhūhi senāsane gahite visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Sacepi cārikaṃ pakkamissāmi, imesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dullabhameva bhavissati. Mayi pana apavārente bhikkhūpi imaṃ [V 4.0100] sāvatthiṃ na osarissanti, ahampi cārikaṃ na pakkamissāmi, evaṃ imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ apalibuddhaṃ bhavissati. Te attano attano vasanaṭṭhāne phāsu viharantā samathavipassanā thāmajātā katvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkhissantī”ti so taṃdivasaṃ apavāretvā kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ pavāressāmīti bhikkhūnaṃ pavāraṇasaṅgahaṃ [M 4.0098] anujāni. Pavāraṇasaṅgahasmiñhi laddhe yassa nissayapaṭipannassa ācariyupajjhāyā pakkamanti, sopi “sace patirūpo nissayadāyako āgamissati, tassa santike nissayaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti yāva gimhānaṃ pacchimamāsā vasituṃ labhati. Sacepi saṭṭhivassā bhikkhū āgacchanti, tassa senāsanaṃ gahetuṃ na labhanti. Ayañca pana pavāraṇasaṅgaho ekassa dinnopi sabbesaṃ dinnoyeva hoti.

That which is called the Pavāraṇā-support is given by an act with a motion as its second part. To whom, then, is it given, and to whom is it not given? Firstly, it is not given to a foolish worldling who is not a practitioner, nor likewise to one who has undertaken insight meditation, nor to a noble disciple. But it is given to one whose serenity or insight is still developing. The Blessed One, too, at that time, while examining the conduct of the bhikkhus' minds and knowing the developing state of their serenity and insight, thought: 'If I hold the Pavāraṇā today, the bhikkhus who have completed the rains-residence in the various regions will converge here. Then, when the lodgings have been taken by the more senior bhikkhus, these bhikkhus will not be able to bring about a special attainment. And if I were to set out on a journey, a place to stay would be difficult for them to find. But if I do not hold the Pavāraṇā, the bhikkhus will not converge on this Sāvatthī, and I too will not set out on a journey. In this way, the dwelling place of these bhikkhus will be unhindered. Dwelling at ease in their respective dwelling places, having made their serenity and insight powerful, they will be able to bring about a special attainment.' Thinking, 'Therefore, not holding the Pavāraṇā on that day, I will hold it on the full moon of Kattika,' he permitted the Pavāraṇā-support for the bhikkhus. For when the Pavāraṇā-support has been received, a dependent bhikkhu whose teachers and preceptors depart is also able to stay until the last month of the hot season, thinking, 'If a suitable support-giver arrives, I will take dependence from him.' Even if bhikkhus of sixty vassas arrive, they are not able to take his lodging. Moreover, this Pavāraṇā-support, though given to one, is indeed given to all.

Sāvatthiṃ osarantīti bhagavatā pavāraṇasaṅgaho dinnoti sutasutaṭṭhāneyeva yathāsabhāvena ekaṃ māsaṃ vasitvā kattikapuṇṇamāya uposathaṃ katvā osarante sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Pubbenāparanti idha taruṇasamathavipassanāsu kammaṃ [P 4.0139] katvā samathavipassanā thāmajātā akaṃsu, ayaṃ pubbe viseso nāma. Tato samāhitena cittena saṅkhāre sammasitvā keci sotāpattiphalaṃ…pe… keci arahattaṃ sacchikariṃsu. Ayaṃ aparo uḷāro viseso nāma.

As for 'they were converging on Sāvatthī,' this was said in reference to them converging after having heard, right where they were, 'The Pavāraṇā-support has been given by the Blessed One,' and then having stayed for one month according to their conditions and performed the Uposatha on the full moon day of Kattika. As for 'a subsequent from a previous,' here, having done the work on their developing serenity and insight, they made their serenity and insight powerful; this is called the previous distinction. Thereafter, with a concentrated mind, having contemplated the formations, some realized the fruit of stream-entry... and some realized Arahantship. This is called the subsequent, sublime distinction.

146. Alanti yuttaṃ. Yojanagaṇanānīti ekaṃ yojanaṃ yojanameva, dasapi yojanāni yojanāneva, tato uddhaṃ yojanagaṇanānīti vuccanti. Idha pana yojanasatampi yojanasahassampi adhippetaṃ. Puṭosenāpīti puṭosaṃ vuccati pātheyyaṃ. taṃ pātheyyaṃ gahetvāpi upasaṅkamituṃ yuttamevāti attho. “Puṭaṃsenā”tipi pāṭho, tassattho – puṭo aṃse assāti puṭaṃso, tena puṭaṃsena, aṃse pātheyyapuṭaṃ vahantenāpīti vuttaṃ hoti.

146. As for 'alaṃ,' it means it is fitting. As for 'multiples of yojanas' (yojanagaṇanāni), one yojana is just a yojana, and ten yojanas are just yojanas; beyond that is called 'multiples of yojanas.' Here, however, a hundred yojanas or even a thousand yojanas are intended. As for 'even with provisions' (puṭosenāpi), provisions are called 'puṭosa.' The meaning is: it is indeed fitting to approach even while carrying those provisions. There is also the reading 'puṭaṃsena,' the meaning of which is: 'puṭaṃso' is one who has a bundle (puṭo) on their shoulder (aṃse). By that 'puṭaṃsena,' it is meant 'even by one carrying a bundle of provisions on the shoulder.'

147. Idāni evarūpehi caraṇehi samannāgatā ettha bhikkhū atthīti dassetuṃ santi, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānantiādīni tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abhiniviṭṭhakammaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Tattha sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā lokiyalokuttarā kathitā. Tatra hi ye bhikkhū tasmiṃ khaṇe maggaṃ bhāventi, tesaṃ lokuttarā honti. Āraddhavipassakānaṃ lokiyā. Aniccasaññābhāvanānuyoganti ettha saññāsīsena vipassanā kathitā[V 4.0101]. Yasmā panettha ānāpānakammaṭṭhānavasena abhiniviṭṭhāva [M 4.0099] bahū bhikkhū, tasmā sesakammaṭṭhānāni saṅkhepena kathetvā ānāpānakammaṭṭhānaṃ vitthārena kathento ānāpānassati, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Idaṃ pana ānāpānakammaṭṭhānaṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge vitthāritaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayenevassa pāḷittho ca bhāvanānayo ca veditabbo.

147. Now, to show that 'There are bhikkhus here, endowed with such conduct,' the Blessed One said, 'There are, O bhikkhus,' and so on. Therein, 'of the four establishments of mindfulness,' etc., were spoken to show the meditation subjects to which those bhikkhus were devoted. Therein, the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment are taught as both mundane and supramundane. For, among them, for those bhikkhus who are developing the path at that moment, these are supramundane. For those who have undertaken insight, they are mundane. In the phrase 'devotion to the development of the perception of impermanence,' insight is taught with perception as the heading. Because many bhikkhus here were devoted by way of the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, therefore, after teaching the remaining meditation subjects in brief, while teaching the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing in detail, he said, 'Mindfulness of breathing, O bhikkhus,' and so on. This meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, however, has been explained in detail in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, its Pāḷi meaning and the method of development should be understood in the very way stated there.

149. Kāyaññataranti [P 4.0140] pathavīkāyādīsu catūsu kāyesu aññataraṃ vadāmi, vāyo kāyaṃ vadāmīti attho. Atha vā rūpāyatanaṃ…pe… kabaḷīkāro āhāroti pañcavīsati rūpakoṭṭhāsā rūpakāyo nāma. Tesu ānāpānaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatane saṅgahitattā kāyaññataraṃ hoti, tasmāpi evamāha. Tasmātihāti yasmā catūsu kāyesu aññataraṃ vāyokāyaṃ, pañcavīsatirūpakoṭṭhāse vā rūpakāye aññataraṃ ānāpānaṃ anupassati, tasmā kāye kāyānupassīti attho. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Vedanāññataranti tīsu vedanāsu aññataraṃ, sukhavedanaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sādhukaṃ manasikāranti pītipaṭisaṃveditādivasena uppannaṃ sundaramanasikāraṃ. Kiṃ pana manasikāro sukhavedanā hotīti. Na hoti, desanāsīsaṃ panetaṃ. Yatheva hi “aniccasaññābhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā”ti ettha saññānāmena paññā vuttā, evamidhāpi manasikāranāmena vedanā vuttāti veditabbā. Etasmiṃ catukke paṭhamapade pītisīsena vedanā vuttā, dutiyapade sukhanti sarūpeneva vuttā. Cittasaṅkhārapadadvaye “saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā, ete dhammā cittapaṭibaddhā cittasaṅkhārā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.174) vacanato “vitakkavicāre ṭhapetvā sabbepi cittasampayuttakā dhammā cittasaṅkhāre saṅgahitā”ti vacanato cittasaṅkhāranāmena vedanā vuttā. Taṃ sabbaṃ manasikāranāmena saṅgahetvā idha “sādhukaṃ manasikāra”nti āha.

149. ‘One among the bodies’ means: I speak of one among the four bodies beginning with the earth-body; I speak of the wind-body. This is the meaning. Or alternatively, the form sense-base… up to… solid food—these twenty-five constituents of form are called the form-body. Among them, since in-and-out-breathing is included in the tangible sense-base, it is one among the bodies. Therefore, He also spoke thus. As to ‘Therefore’: because one contemplates the wind-body, which is one among the four bodies, or contemplates in-and-out-breathing, which is one among the twenty-five constituents of form in the form-body, therefore the meaning is ‘contemplating the body in the bodies.’ Thus, the meaning should be understood everywhere. ‘One among the feelings’ means one among the three feelings; this was said referring to pleasant feeling. ‘Thorough attention’ means the excellent attention that has arisen by way of experiencing joy, etc. But is attention pleasant feeling? It is not. This, however, is a heading of the discourse. For just as in the phrase ‘devoted to the development and practice of the perception of impermanence,’ wisdom is spoken of by the name ‘perception,’ so too here, it should be understood that feeling is spoken of by the name ‘attention.’ In this tetrad, in the first phrase, feeling is spoken of with joy as its head; in the second phrase, it is spoken of as ‘pleasant’ by its own nature. In the two phrases on mental formations, because it is said, ‘Perception and feeling are mental; these phenomena are bound up with the mind, hence mental formations’ (Paṭi. Ma. 1.174), and because it is said, ‘Excluding initial and sustained thought, all phenomena associated with the mind are included in mental formations,’ feeling is spoken of by the name ‘mental formations.’ Having encompassed all that by the name ‘attention,’ here He said, ‘thorough attention.’

Evaṃ santepi yasmā esā vedanā ārammaṇaṃ na hoti, tasmā vedanānupassanā na yujjatīti. No na yujjati, satipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanāyampi hi “taṃtaṃsukhādīnaṃ [P 4.0141] vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayati, taṃ pana vedanāpavattiṃ upādāya ‘ahaṃ vedayāmī’ti vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ[M 4.0100]. Apica pītipaṭisaṃvedītiādīnaṃ atthavaṇṇanāyametassa parihāro vuttoyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ visuddhimagge –

Even so, it is objected: ‘Since this feeling is not an object, the contemplation of feelings is not suitable.’ It is not that it is unsuitable; it is indeed suitable. For in the commentary on the Foundations of Mindfulness, it is also said: ‘One indeed experiences feeling by taking as object the basis of this or that pleasure, etc.; but based on the occurrence of that feeling, “I feel” is merely a conventional expression.’ Moreover, the resolution to this has already been stated by me in the explanation of the meaning of ‘experiencing joy,’ etc. For this has been said in the Visuddhimagga:

“Dvīhākārehi [V 4.0102] pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇato ca asammohato ca. Kathaṃ ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati, tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattā. Kathaṃ asammohato (pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti)? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttaṃ pītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati, tassa vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇapaṭivedhā asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ ‘dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, tāya satiyā, tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī’ti. Eteneva nayena avasesapadānipi atthato veditabbānī”ti.

‘Joy is clearly known in two ways: with regard to its object and with regard to non-delusion. How is joy clearly known with regard to its object? One attains the two jhānas accompanied by joy. For such a one, at the moment of attainment, through the attainment of jhāna, joy is clearly known with regard to its object because its object is clearly known. How is joy clearly known with regard to non-delusion? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by joy and having emerged, one contemplates the joy associated with the jhāna as perishing and vanishing. For such a one, at the moment of insight, through the penetration of its characteristics, joy is clearly known with regard to non-delusion. And this has been said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “For one who knows the unification and non-distraction of the mind by way of a long out-breath, mindfulness is established. By that mindfulness, by that knowledge, that joy is clearly known.” In this very way, the remaining phrases should also be understood according to their meaning.’

Iti yatheva jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pītisukhacittasaṅkhārā paṭisaṃviditā honti, evaṃ imināpi jhānasampayuttena vedanāsaṅkhātamanasikārapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato vedanā paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Tasmā suvuttametaṃ hoti “vedanāsu vedanānupassī tasmiṃ samaye bhikkhu viharatī”ti.

Thus, just as through the attainment of jhāna, joy, pleasure, and mental formations are clearly known with regard to their object, so too, through the attainment of this attention associated with jhāna, which is designated as ‘feeling,’ feeling is clearly known with regard to its object. Therefore, it is well said: ‘A bhikkhu at that time dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.’

Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassāti ettha ayamadhippāyo – yasmā cittapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmītiādinā nayena pavatto bhikkhu kiñcāpi assāsapassāsanimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tassa pana cittassa ārammaṇe satiñca sampajaññañca upaṭṭhapetvā pavattanato citte cittānupassīyeva nāmesa hoti. Na hi muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassa [P 4.0142] ānāpānassatibhāvanā atthi. Tasmā ārammaṇato cittapaṭisaṃviditādivasena citte cittānupassī tasmiṃ samaye bhikkhu viharatīti. So yaṃ taṃ abhijjhādomanassānaṃ pahānaṃ, taṃ paññāya disvā sādhukaṃ ajjhupekkhitā hotīti ettha abhijjhāya kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, domanassavasena byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ [M 4.0101] dassitaṃ. Idañhi catukkaṃ vipassanāvaseneva vuttaṃ, dhammānupassanā ca nīvaraṇapabbādivasena chabbidhā hoti, tassā nīvaraṇapabbaṃ ādi, tassapi idaṃ nīvaraṇadvayaṃ ādi, iti dhammānupassanāya ādiṃ dassetuṃ “abhijjhādomanassāna”nti āha. Pahānanti aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatīti evaṃ pahānakarañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃ paññāya disvāti taṃ aniccavirāganirodhapaṭinissaggāñāṇasaṅkhātaṃ pahānañāṇaṃ [V 4.0103] aparāya vipassanāpaññāya, tampi aparāyāti evaṃ vipassanāparamparaṃ dasseti. Ajjhupekkhitā hotīti yañca samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca ekato upaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhatīti dvidhā ajjhupekkhati nāma. Tattha sahajātānampi ajjhupekkhanā hoti ārammaṇassapi ajjhupekkhanā, idha ārammaṇaajjhupekkhanā adhippetā. Tasmātiha, bhikkhaveti yasmā aniccānupassī assasissāmītiādinā nayena pavatto na kevalaṃ nīvaraṇādidhamme, abhijjhādomanassasīsena pana vuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānañāṇampi paññāya disvā ajjhupekkhitā hoti, tasmā “dhammesu dhammānupassī tasmiṃ samaye bhikkhu viharatī”ti veditabbo.

“Monks, I do not say this of one with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension”—here, this is the intended meaning: Because a bhikkhu who proceeds in the manner of “I will breathe in, experiencing the mind,” and so on, although he makes the counterpart sign of in-and-out breathing his object, is indeed called one who contemplates mind in mind, since he proceeds having established mindfulness and wisdom concerning the object of that mind. For there is no development of mindfulness of breathing for one with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension. Therefore, by way of the object, through the power of making the mind manifest, and so on, the statement “at that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in mind” is well-spoken. As for the passage, “He, having seen with wisdom that abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, looks on with thorough equanimity”: here, by covetousness, the hindrance of sensual desire is shown; by the power of displeasure, the hindrance of ill will is shown. Indeed, this tetrad was taught solely by way of insight. And the contemplation of phenomena is sixfold, by way of the hindrances section and so on. Of that, the hindrances section is the beginning; and of that section too, this pair of hindrances is the beginning. Thus, to show the beginning of the contemplation of phenomena, he said, “of covetousness and displeasure.” By “abandoning” is intended the insight-knowledge that is the cause for accomplishing abandonment, as in the statement, “one abandons the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence.” By the phrase “having seen with wisdom,” it shows a succession of insight: that knowledge of abandonment—which is called the knowledge of impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment—is seen by a subsequent insight-wisdom, and that too is seen by a further one. By “looks on with equanimity” is meant equanimity in two ways: one looks on with equanimity at the continuity of jhāna-mind that proceeds by way of serenity, and one looks on with equanimity at the jhāna-mind that appears as remote from the opposing hindrances. Therein, there is equanimity towards co-arisen states and equanimity towards the object; here, equanimity towards the object is intended. Therefore, it should be understood thus: because a bhikkhu who proceeds in the manner of “I will breathe in, contemplating impermanence,” and so on, is one who looks on with equanimity, having seen with wisdom not only the hindrances and other phenomena, but also the knowledge that is the cause for abandoning the phenomena spoken of under the heading of covetousness and displeasure; therefore, “at that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.”

150. Pavicinatīti aniccādivasena pavicinati. Itaraṃ padadvayaṃ etasseva vevacanaṃ. Nirāmisāti [P 4.0143] nikkilesā. Passambhatīti kāyikacetasikadarathapaṭippassaddhiyā kāyopi cittampi passambhati. Samādhiyatīti sammā ṭhapiyati, appanāpattaṃ viya hoti. Ajjhupekkhitā hotīti sahajātaajjhupekkhanāya ajjhupekkhitā hoti.

150. “He investigates” means he investigates by way of impermanence and so on. The other two terms are synonyms of this very word. “Unworldly” means without defilements. “It becomes tranquil” means: due to the calming of physical and mental distress, both the physical body and the mind become tranquil. “It becomes concentrated” means it is well placed on the object; it becomes steady as if it had reached absorption. “He is one who looks on with equanimity” means he looks on with equanimity by means of equanimity towards co-arisen states.

Evaṃ cuddasavidhena kāyapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno tasmiṃ kāye sati satisambojjhaṅgo, satiyā sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, taṃsampayuttameva kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pīti, passaddhi, cittekaggatā samādhisambojjhaṅgo, imesaṃ channaṃ sambojjhaṅgānaṃ anosakkanaanativattanasaṅkhāto majjhattākāro upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo. Yatheva hi samappavattesu assesu sārathino “ayaṃ olīyatī”ti tudanaṃ vā, “ayaṃ atidhāvatī”ti ākaḍḍhanaṃ vā natthi, kevalaṃ evaṃ passamānassa ṭhitākārova hoti, evameva imesaṃ channaṃ sambojjhaṅgānaṃ anosakkanaanativattanasaṅkhāto majjhattākāro upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo nāma hoti. Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Ekacittakkhaṇikā nānārasalakkhaṇā vipassanāsambojjhaṅgā nāma kathitā.

Thus, for a bhikkhu who comprehends the body of breaths in these fourteen ways, the mindfulness regarding that body is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. The knowledge associated with that mindfulness is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. The physical and mental energy associated with that very mindfulness is the enlightenment factor of energy. Joy is the enlightenment factor of joy. Tranquility is the enlightenment factor of tranquility. Unification of mind is the enlightenment factor of concentration. The state of balance with regard to these six enlightenment factors, described as neither falling short nor over-exerting, is the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For just as with evenly-moving horses, a charioteer neither prods one, thinking, “This one is lagging,” nor pulls on the reins of another, thinking, “This one is running too fast,” but for one who is merely observing, there is only a state of stability; even so, the state of balance with regard to these six enlightenment factors, described as neither falling short nor over-exerting, is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity. By this much, what has been taught? It has been taught that insight, which occurs in a single moment of consciousness and has diverse functions and characteristics, is called the enlightenment factors.

152. Vivekanissitantiādīni [M 4.0102] vuttatthāneva. Ettha pana ānāpānapariggāhikā sati lokiyā hoti, lokiyā ānāpānā lokiyasatipaṭṭhānaṃ paripūrenti, lokiyā satipaṭṭhānā lokuttarabojjhaṅge paripūrenti, lokuttarā bojjhaṅgā vijjāvimuttiphalanibbānaṃ [P 4.0144] paripūrenti. Iti lokiyassa [V 4.0104] āgataṭṭhāne lokiyaṃ kathitaṃ, lokuttarassa āgataṭṭhāne lokuttaraṃ kathitanti. Thero panāha “aññattha evaṃ hoti, imasmiṃ pana sutte lokuttaraṃ upari āgataṃ, lokiyā ānāpānā lokiyasatipaṭṭhāne paripūrenti, lokiyā satipaṭṭhānā lokiye bojjhaṅge paripūrenti, lokiyā bojjhaṅgā lokuttaraṃ vijjāvimuttiphalanibbānaṃ paripūrenti, vijjāvimuttipadena hi idha vijjāvimuttiphalanibbānaṃ adhippeta”nti.

152. “Dependent on seclusion” and so forth have the same meaning as previously explained. Here, however, the mindfulness that comprehends the in-and-out breathing is mundane. Mundane in-and-out breaths fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness. The mundane foundations of mindfulness fulfill the supramundane enlightenment factors. The supramundane enlightenment factors fulfill Nibbāna as the fruit of knowledge-and-liberation. Thus, it should be known that where the mundane is discussed, the mundane was taught, and where the supramundane is discussed, the supramundane was taught. The Elder, however, says: “Elsewhere it is so, but in this sutta, the supramundane comes later. Mundane in-and-out breaths fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness. The mundane foundations of mindfulness fulfill the mundane enlightenment factors. The mundane enlightenment factors fulfill the supramundane Nibbāna as the fruit of knowledge-and-liberation. For here, by the term ‘knowledge-and-liberation,’ Nibbāna as the fruit of knowledge-and-liberation is intended.”

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Ānāpānassatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānāpānassati Sutta is completed.

9. Kāyagatāsatisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Kāyagatāsati Sutta

153-4. Evaṃ [V 4.0105] me sutanti kāyagatāsatisuttaṃ. Tattha gehasitāti pañcakāmaguṇanissitā. Sarasaṅkappāti dhāvanasaṅkappā. Sarantīti hi sarā, dhāvantīti attho. Ajjhattamevāti gocarajjhattasmiṃyeva. Kāyagatāsatinti kāyapariggāhikampi kāyārammaṇampi satiṃ. Kāyapariggāhikanti vutte samatho kathito hoti, kāyārammaṇanti vutte vipassanā. Ubhayena samathavipassanā kathitā honti.

“Thus have I heard”: this is the Kāyagatāsati Sutta. Therein, “based on the household life” means dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. “Thoughts that wander” means thoughts that run. For “they wander” (saranti) means they run (dhāvanti); this is the meaning. “Internally” means only within the internal sphere of the meditation object. “Mindfulness directed to the body” means mindfulness that both comprehends the body and has the body as its object. When “comprehending the body” is said, serenity is spoken of; when “having the body as its object” is said, insight is spoken of. By both, serenity and insight are spoken of.

Puna caparaṃ…pe… evampi, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyagatāsatiṃ bhāvetīti satipaṭṭhāne cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanā kathitā.

“Furthermore… and so on… In this way, monks, a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body”—thus, in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the contemplation of the body was taught in fourteen ways.

156. Antogadhāvāssāti tassa bhikkhuno bhāvanāya abbhantaragatāva honti. Vijjābhāgiyāti ettha sampayogavasena vijjaṃ bhajantīti [P 4.0145] vijjābhāgiyā. Vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vattantītipi vijjābhāgiyā. Tattha [M 4.0103] vipassanāñāṇaṃ, manomayiddhi, cha abhiññāti aṭṭha vijjā. Purimena atthena tāhi sampayuttadhammāpi vijjābhāgiyā. Pacchimena atthena tāsu yā kāci ekā vijjā vijjā, sesā vijjābhāgiyāti evaṃ vijjāpi vijjāya sampayuttā dhammāpi vijjābhāgiyāteva veditabbā. Cetasā phuṭoti ettha duvidhaṃ pharaṇaṃ āpopharaṇañca, dibbacakkhupharaṇañca, tattha āpokasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā āpena pharaṇaṃ āpopharaṇaṃ nāma. Evaṃ phuṭepi mahāsamudde sabbā samuddaṅgamā kunnadiyo antogadhāva honti, ālokaṃ pana vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā sakalasamuddassa dassanaṃ dibbacakkhupharaṇaṃ nāma. Evaṃ pharaṇepi mahāsamudde sabbā samuddaṅgamā kunnadiyo antogadhāva honti.

156. 'They are included within' means that for that monk, they become internal to his development. 'Partaking of knowledge': here, because they partake of knowledge by way of association, they are called 'partaking of knowledge.' Or, because they occur in the portion of knowledge, in the category of knowledge, they are called 'partaking of knowledge.' Therein, there are eight kinds of knowledge: insight-knowledge, the power of the mind-made body, and the six direct knowledges. According to the first meaning, the states associated with these are also 'partaking of knowledge.' According to the latter meaning, among them, any one is 'knowledge,' and the rest are 'partaking of knowledge.' Thus, both knowledge itself and the states associated with knowledge should be understood as 'partaking of knowledge.' 'Pervaded by the mind': here, pervading is twofold: pervading with water and pervading with the divine eye. Therein, having attained the water kasiṇa, pervading with water is called 'pervading with water.' When one has thus pervaded, all the small rivers that flow into the great ocean are included within it. Alternatively, having developed the light, seeing the entire ocean with the divine eye is called 'pervading with the divine eye.' When one has thus pervaded, all the small rivers that flow into the great ocean are included within it.

Otāranti vivaraṃ chiddaṃ. Ārammaṇanti kilesuppattipaccayaṃ. Labhetha otāranti labheyya pavesanaṃ, vinivijjhitvā yāva pariyosānā gaccheyyāti attho. Nikkhepananti nikkhipanaṭṭhānaṃ.

'An opportunity' means an opening, a fissure. 'A support' means a condition for the arising of defilements. 'Might find an opportunity' means: might it find entry? Having penetrated, might it go all the way to the end? This is the meaning. 'A place to set it down' means a place to deposit it.

157. Evaṃ [V 4.0106] abhāvitakāyagatāsatiṃ puggalaṃ allamattikapuñjādīhi upametvā idāni bhāvitakāyagatāsatiṃ sāraphalakādīhi upametuṃ seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha aggaḷaphalakanti kavāṭaṃ.

157. Thus, having compared the person with undeveloped mindfulness of the body to a lump of wet clay and so on, now, to compare the person with developed mindfulness of the body to a plank of heartwood and so on, the Blessed One said the words beginning with 'Just as...'. Therein, 'aggaḷaphalakaṃ' means a door-panel.

158. Kākapeyyoti mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ nisīditvā kākena gīvaṃ anāmetvāva pātabbo. Abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassāti abhiññāya sacchikātabbassa. Sakkhibhabbataṃ [P 4.0146] pāpuṇātīti paccakkhabhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Sati sati āyataneti satisati kāraṇe. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇanti? Abhiññāva kāraṇaṃ. Āḷibandhāti mariyādabaddhā.

158. 'Crow-drinkable' means water that can be drunk by a crow sitting on the rim of a vessel without bending its neck. 'Of that which is to be realized through direct knowledge' means of that which is to be realized by direct knowledge. 'It becomes realizable' means it attains a state of being directly experienced. 'When there is a basis' means when there is a cause. What is the cause here? Direct knowledge itself is the cause. 'With banks built up' means with its boundaries constructed.

Yānīkatāyāti yuttayānaṃ viya katāya. Vatthukatāyāti patiṭṭhākatāya. Anuṭṭhitāyāti anuppavattitāya. Paricitāyāti paricayakatāya. Susamāraddhāyāti suṭṭhu samāraddhāya susampaggahitāya. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Made into a vehicle' means made like a yoked vehicle. 'Made a foundation' means made a basis of establishment. 'Pursued' means repeatedly practiced. 'Familiarized' means made a habit. 'Well undertaken' means thoroughly undertaken and well grasped. The rest is clear in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Kāyagatāsatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body is concluded.

10. Saṅkhārupapattisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Arising of Formations

160. Evaṃ [V 4.0107][M 4.0104] me sutanti saṅkhārupapattisuttaṃ. Tattha saṅkhārupapattinti saṅkhārānaṃyeva upapattiṃ, na sattassa, na posassa, puññābhisaṅkhārena vā bhavūpagakkhandhānaṃ upapattiṃ.

160. “Thus have I heard.” This is the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta. Therein, “the arising of formations” means the arising of the formations themselves, not of a being, not of a person; or, it means the arising of the aggregates that have gone to a state of becoming due to meritorious formations.

161. Saddhāya samannāgatoti saddhādayo pañca dhammā lokikā vaṭṭanti. Dahatīti ṭhapeti. Adhiṭṭhātīti patiṭṭhāpeti. Saṅkhārā ca vihārā cāti saha patthanāya saddhādayova pañca dhammā. Tatrupapattiyāti tasmiṃ ṭhāne nibbattanatthāya. Ayaṃ maggo ayaṃ paṭipadāti saha patthanāya pañca [P 4.0147] dhammāva. Yassa hi pañca dhammā atthi, na patthanā, tassa gati anibaddhā. Yassa patthanā atthi, na pañca dhammā, tassapi anibaddhā. Yesaṃ ubhayaṃ atthi, tesaṃ gati nibaddhā. Yathā hi ākāse khittadaṇḍo aggena vā majjhena vā mūlena vā nipatissatīti niyamo natthi, evaṃ sattānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ aniyataṃ. Tasmā kusalaṃ kammaṃ katvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne patthanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

161. “Endowed with faith” means that the five qualities beginning with faith, being worldly, proceed. “He places” means he establishes. “He determines” means he causes to be established. “Formations and abidings” means the five qualities beginning with faith, together with aspiration. “For rebirth there” means for the purpose of being reborn in that place. “This is the path, this is the practice” means the five qualities together with aspiration. For one who has the five qualities but not the aspiration, their destination is not fixed. For one who has the aspiration but not the five qualities, their destination is also not fixed. For those who have both, their destination is fixed. For just as there is no certainty that a stick thrown into the air will fall on its tip, its middle, or its base, so the taking of rebirth-linking for beings is not certain. Therefore, having done a wholesome deed, it is proper to make an aspiration for a particular place.

165. Āmaṇḍanti āmalakaṃ. Yathā taṃ parisuddhacakkhussa purisassa sabbasova pākaṭaṃ hoti, evaṃ tassa brahmuno saddhiṃ tattha nibbattasattehi sahassī lokadhātu. Esa nayo sabbattha.

165. “Āmaṇḍa” means the āmalaka fruit. Just as that is entirely manifest to a person with purified vision, so to that Brahmā is the thousandfold world-system manifest, together with the beings reborn there. This is the method in all cases.

167. Subhoti sundaro. Jātimāti ākarasampanno. Suparikammakatoti dhovanādīhi suṭṭhukataparikammo. Paṇḍukambale nikkhittoti rattakambale ṭhapito.

167. “Beautiful” means lovely. “Of good stock” means endowed with fine features. “Well-wrought” means well-prepared by washing and other means. “Placed on a paṇḍu-blanket” means placed on a red blanket.

168. Satasahassoti lokadhātusatasahassamhi ālokapharaṇabrahmā. Nikkhanti nikkhena kataṃ piḷandhanaṃ, nikkhaṃ nāma pañcasuvaṇṇaṃ, ūnakanikkhena kataṃ pasādhanañhi ghaṭṭanamajjanakkhamaṃ na hoti, atirekena kataṃ ghaṭṭanamajjanaṃ khamati, vaṇṇavantaṃ pana na hoti, pharusadhātukaṃ khāyati. Nikkhena kataṃ ghaṭṭanamajjanañceva khamati, vaṇṇavantañca hoti. Jambonadanti jambunadiyaṃ nibbattaṃ. Mahājamburukkhassa hi ekekā sākhā paṇṇāsa paṇṇāsa yojanāni [V 4.0108] vaḍḍhitā, tāsu mahantā nadiyo sandanti, tāsaṃ nadīnaṃ [P 4.0148] ubhayatīresu jambupakkānaṃ patitaṭṭhāne suvaṇṇaṅkurā uṭṭhahanti, te nadījalena vuyhamānā [M 4.0105] anupubbena mahāsamuddaṃ pavisanti. Taṃ sandhāya jambonadanti vuttaṃ. Dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhanti dakkhena sukusalena kammāraputtena ukkāmukhe pacitvā sampahaṭṭhaṃ. Ukkāmukheti uddhane. Sampahaṭṭhanti dhotaghaṭṭitamajjitaṃ. Vatthopame (ma. ni. 1.75-76) ca dhātuvibhaṅge (ma. ni. 3.357-360) ca piṇḍasodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte katabhaṇḍasodhanaṃ vuttaṃ.

168. “A hundred thousand” refers to the Brahmā who pervades a hundred-thousandfold world-system with light. “Nikkha” means an ornament made with a nikkha’s weight of gold. A nikkha is five suvaṇṇas. An adornment made with less than a nikkha is not fit for rubbing and polishing. One made with more is fit for rubbing and polishing, but it is not beautiful; it appears as a rough substance. One made with a nikkha’s weight is fit for rubbing and polishing, and it is also beautiful. “Jambonada” means produced in the Jambu river. For each branch of the great Jambu tree extends for fifty yojanas, and in them great rivers flow. On both banks of those rivers, in the places where the ripe Jambu fruits have fallen, golden sprouts arise. Being carried along by the river water, they gradually enter the great ocean. In reference to this, it is called 'jambonada.' “Well-struck by a skilled goldsmith’s son in the mouth of a furnace” means struck after being heated in the mouth of a furnace by a skilled, expert goldsmith’s son. “In the mouth of a furnace” means in a hearth. “Well-struck” means washed, rubbed, and polished. In the Vatthūpama Sutta and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the cleansing of a lump of raw material is spoken of. In this sutta, the cleansing of a finished article is spoken of.

Yaṃ pana sabbavāresu pharitvā adhimuccitvāti vuttaṃ, tattha pañcavidhaṃ pharaṇaṃ cetopharaṇaṃ kasiṇapharaṇaṃ dibbacakkhupharaṇaṃ ālokapharaṇaṃ sarīrapharaṇanti. Tattha cetopharaṇaṃ nāma lokadhātusahasse sattānaṃ cittajānanaṃ. Kasiṇapharaṇaṃ nāma lokadhātusahasse kasiṇapattharaṇaṃ. Dibbacakkhupharaṇaṃ nāma ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā sahassalokadhātudassanaṃ. Ālokapharaṇampi etadeva. Sarīrapharaṇaṃ nāma lokadhātusahasse sarīrapabhāya pattharaṇaṃ. Sabbattha imāni pañca pharaṇāni avināsentena kathetabbanti.

Regarding what is said in all instances as “having pervaded and being resolved,” therein pervasion is of five kinds: mental pervasion, kasiṇa pervasion, divine-eye pervasion, light pervasion, and bodily pervasion. Therein, mental pervasion is the knowing of the minds of beings in a thousandfold world-system. Kasiṇa pervasion is the spreading of the kasiṇa in a thousandfold world-system. Divine-eye pervasion is, having augmented the light, the seeing of a thousandfold world-system with the divine eye. Light pervasion is just this. Bodily pervasion is the spreading of the body’s radiance in a thousandfold world-system. In all cases, these five pervasions should be explained without omitting any.

Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero panāha – “maṇiopamme kasiṇapharaṇaṃ viya nikkhopamme sarīrapharaṇaṃ viya dissatī”ti. Tassa vādaṃ viya aṭṭhakathā nāma natthīti paṭikkhitvā sarīrapharaṇaṃ na sabbakālikaṃ, cattārimāni [P 4.0149] pharaṇāni avināsetvāva kathetabbanti vuttaṃ. Adhimuccatīti padaṃ pharaṇapadasseva vevacanaṃ, atha vā pharatīti pattharati. Adhimuccatīti jānāti.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, however, said: “In the simile of the jewel, it appears like kasiṇa pervasion; in the simile of the nikkha, it appears like bodily pervasion.” Rejecting his view as if to say, “There is no such commentary,” it was said that bodily pervasion is not constant, and that these four pervasions should be explained without being set aside. The word “adhimuccati” (is resolved) is a synonym for the word “pharana” (pervasion). Alternatively, “pharati” (pervades) means “spreads,” and “adhimuccati” (is resolved) means “knows.”

169. Ābhātiādīsu ābhādayo nāma pāṭiyekkā devā natthi, tayo parittābhādayo devā ābhā nāma, parittāsubhādayo ca. Subhakiṇhādayo ca subhā nāma. Vehapphalādivārā pākaṭāyeva.

169. In “Ābhā, etc.,” there are no individual devas called by such names. Rather, the three types of devas beginning with the Parittābhā are called “Ābhā”; and those beginning with the Parittasubhā and those beginning with the Subhakiṇha are called “Subhā.” The sections concerning the Vehapphala and so on are self-evident.

Ime tāva pañca dhamme bhāvetvā kāmāvacaresu nibbattatu. Brahmaloke nibbattaṃ pana āsavakkhayañca kathaṃ pāpuṇātīti? Ime pañca dhammā sīlaṃ, so imasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhāya kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā tā tā samāpattiyo bhāvetvā rūpībrahmaloke nibbattati, arūpajjhānāni [V 4.0109] nibbattetvā [M 4.0106] arūpībrahmaloke, samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anāgāmiphalaṃ sacchikatvā pañcasu suddhāvāsesu nibbattati. Uparimaggaṃ bhāvetvā āsavakkhayaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

First, having developed these five qualities, let one be reborn in the sense-sphere realms. But how does one attain rebirth in the Brahma-world and also the destruction of the taints? These five qualities are virtue. Established in this virtue, having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas and developed those various attainments, one is reborn in the fine-material Brahma-world. Having brought forth the formless jhānas, one is reborn in the formless Brahma-world. Having developed insight which has the attainments as its proximate cause, and having realized the fruit of non-returning, one is reborn in the five Pure Abodes. By developing the higher path, one attains the destruction of the taints.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Saṅkhārupapattisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta is finished.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.

3. Suññatavaggo

3. The Chapter on Emptiness

1. Cūḷasuññatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Cūḷasuññata Sutta

176. Evaṃ [V 4.0110][M 4.0107] me sutanti cūḷasuññatasuttaṃ. Tattha ekamidanti thero kira bhagavato vattaṃ katvā attano divāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā kālaparicchedaṃ katvā nibbānārammaṇaṃ suññatāphalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisinno yathāparicchedena vuṭṭhāsi. Athassa saṅkhārā suññato upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So suññatākathaṃ sotukāmo jāto. Athassa etadahosi [P 4.0150] – “na kho pana sakkā dhurena dhuraṃ paharantena viya gantvā ‘suññatākathaṃ me, bhante, kathethā’ti bhagavantaṃ vattuṃ, handāhaṃ yaṃ me bhagavā nagarakaṃ upanissāya viharanto ekaṃ kathaṃ kathesi, taṃ sāremi, evaṃ me bhagavā suññatākathaṃ kathessatī”ti dasabalaṃ sārento ekamidantiādimāha.

176. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Cūḷasuññata Sutta. Therein, regarding 'ekamidaṃ': It is said that the Elder, having performed his duties for the Blessed One, went to his own daytime resting place. Having made a determination of time, he entered and sat in the attainment of the fruit of emptiness which has Nibbāna as its object, and arose according to the determined time. Then formations appeared to him as empty. He became desirous of hearing a discourse on emptiness. Then this thought occurred to him: “Indeed, it is not possible to go and say directly to the Blessed One, ‘Venerable sir, please give me a discourse on emptiness,’ as if striking one yoke-end with another. Well now, let me remind the Blessed One of a certain discourse he gave while dwelling depending on Nagaraka. In this way, the Blessed One will give me a discourse on emptiness.” Thus, intending to remind the One of Ten Powers, he spoke the words beginning with 'ekamidaṃ'.

Tattha idanti nipātamattameva. Kaccimetaṃ, bhanteti thero ekapade ṭhatvā saṭṭhipadasahassāni uggahetvā dhāretuṃ samattho, kiṃ so “suññatāvihārenā”ti ekaṃ padaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkhissati, sotukāmena pana jānantena viya pucchituṃ na vaṭṭati, pākaṭaṃ katvā vitthāriyamānaṃ suññatākathaṃ sotukāmo ajānanto viya evamāha. Eko ajānantopi jānanto viya hoti, thero evarūpaṃ kohaññaṃ kiṃ karissati, attano jānanaṭṭhānepi bhagavato apacitiṃ dassetvā “kaccimeta”ntiādimāha.

Therein, 'idaṃ' is merely a particle. Regarding 'Kacci me taṃ, bhante': the Elder, while standing on one word, was capable of learning and retaining sixty thousand words. Why would he not be able to retain the single phrase 'suññatāvihārena'? However, it is not proper for one who desires to listen to ask as if knowing. Desiring to hear the discourse on emptiness being made clear and explained in detail, he spoke thus as if not knowing. Someone who does not know may act as if he knows, but why would the Elder engage in such cunning? Even in a matter he knows, showing reverence to the Blessed One, he spoke the words beginning with 'kacci me taṃ'.

Pubbepīti paṭhamabodhiyaṃ nagarakaṃ upanissāya viharaṇakālepi. Etarahipīti idānipi. Evaṃ pana vatvā cintesi – “ānando suññatākathaṃ sotukāmo, eko pana sotuṃ sakkoti, na uggahetuṃ, eko sotumpi uggahetumpi sakkoti, na kathetuṃ, ānando pana sotumpi sakkoti [V 4.0111] uggahetumpi kathetumpi, (kathemissa) suññatākatha”nti. Iti taṃ kathento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha suñño hatthigavāssavaḷavenāti tattha kaṭṭharūpapotthakarūpacittarūpavasena katā hatthiādayo atthi, vessavaṇamandhātādīnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne cittakammavasena katampi, ratanaparikkhatānaṃ vātapānadvārabandhamañcapīṭhādīnaṃ vasena saṇṭhitampi, jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇatthaṃ [M 4.0108] ṭhapitampi jātarūparajataṃ atthi, kaṭṭharūpādivasena katā dhammasavanapañhapucchanādivasena āgacchantā [P 4.0151] ca itthipurisāpi atthi, tasmā na so tehi suñño. Indriyabaddhānaṃ saviññāṇakānaṃ hatthiādīnaṃ, icchiticchitakkhaṇe paribhuñjitabbassa jātarūparajatassa, nibaddhavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ itthipurisānañca abhāvaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'pubbepi' (even in the past): also at the time of dwelling depending on Nagaraka at the time of the first awakening. Regarding 'etarahi' (even now): also now. Having spoken thus, he reflected: 'Ānanda is desirous of hearing the discourse on emptiness. One person is able to listen but not to learn it. Another is able to listen and learn it, but not to speak of it. Ānanda, however, is able to listen, to learn it, and to speak of it. I will give the discourse on emptiness.' Thus, explaining it, he spoke the words beginning with 'seyyathāpi' (just as). Therein, regarding 'suñño hatthigavāssavaḷavena' (empty of elephants, cattle, horses, and mares): in that place, there are elephants and so on, made by way of wooden figures, clay figures, and painted figures. In the places where figures of Vessavaṇa, Mandhāta, and others stand, there are also things made by way of painted work. There is also gold and silver established by way of jewel-adorned windows, door-frames, beds, seats, and so on, and also placed there for repairing what is worn out. There are also men and women made by way of wooden figures and so on, and those who come for purposes such as listening to the Dhamma and asking questions. Therefore, it is not empty of these. This was said referring to the absence of sentient elephants and so on, endowed with sense faculties; of gold and silver to be used at any desired moment; and of men and women who live there as permanent residents.

Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṭiccāti bhikkhūsu hi piṇḍāya paviṭṭhesupi vihārabhattaṃ sādiyantehi bhikkhūhi ceva gilānagilānupaṭṭhākauddesacīvarakammapasutādīhi ca bhikkhūhi so asuññova hoti, iti niccampi bhikkhūnaṃ atthitāya evamāha. Ekattanti ekabhāvaṃ, ekaṃ asuññataṃ atthīti attho. Eko asuññabhāvo atthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Amanasikaritvāti citte akatvā anāvajjitvā apaccavekkhitvā. Gāmasaññanti gāmoti pavattavasena vā kilesavasena vā uppannaṃ gāmasaññaṃ. Manussasaññāyapi eseva nayo. Araññasaññaṃ paṭicca manasi karoti ekattanti idaṃ araññaṃ, ayaṃ rukkho, ayaṃ pabbato, ayaṃ nīlobhāso vanasaṇḍoti evaṃ ekaṃ araññaṃyeva paṭicca araññasaññaṃ manasi karoti. Pakkhandatīti otarati. Adhimuccatīti evanti adhimuccati. Ye assu darathāti ye ca pavattadarathā vā kilesadarathā vā gāmasaññaṃ paṭicca bhaveyyuṃ, te idha araññasaññāya na santi. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Atthi cevāyanti ayaṃ pana ekaṃ araññasaññaṃ paṭicca uppajjamānā pavattadarathamattā atthi.

Regarding 'dependent on the Bhikkhu Saṅgha': for even when the bhikkhus have gone for alms-food, that place is not empty because of the bhikkhus who consent to the monastery meal, and also because of bhikkhus who are sick, attending the sick, reciting, engaged in robe-making, and so on. Thus, because of the constant presence of bhikkhus, he spoke thus. 'Oneness' (ekattaṃ) means the state of being one; the meaning is 'there is one non-emptiness.' It is said, 'there is one state of non-emptiness.' 'Not attending to' (amanasikaritvā) means not placing in the mind, not adverting to, not reflecting upon. 'Perception of a village' (gāmasaññaṃ) means the perception of 'village' that has arisen either by way of existence or by way of defilement. This same method should be understood for 'perception of people' as well. Regarding 'he attends to oneness based on the perception of the forest' (araññasaññaṃ paṭicca manasi karoti ekattaṃ): 'This is a forest, this is a tree, this is a mountain, this is a dark green forest grove'—thus, based on the one forest alone, he attends to the perception of the forest. 'He enters' (pakkhandati) means he descends into it. 'He is resolved' (adhimuccati) means he is resolved thus. Regarding 'whatever disturbances there might be' (ye assu darathā): whatever disturbances of existence or disturbances of defilement might arise dependent on the perception of a village, they are not present here with the perception of the forest. This same method should be understood for the second phrase as well. Regarding 'and yet there is this' (atthi cevāyaṃ): however, there is just this measure of disturbance of existence that arises dependent on the one perception of the forest.

Yañhi [P 4.0152] kho tattha na hotīti yaṃ migāramātupāsāde hatthiādayo viya imissā araññasaññāya gāmasaññāmanussasaññāvasena uppajjamānaṃ pavattadarathakilesadarathajātaṃ, taṃ na hoti. Yaṃ pana tattha avasiṭṭhanti yaṃ migāramātupāsāde bhikkhusaṅgho viya tattha araññasaññāya pavattadarathamattaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti. Taṃ santamidaṃ atthīti pajānātīti taṃ vijjamānameva “atthi ida”nti pajānāti, suññatāvakkantīti suññatānibbatti.

Regarding 'For what is not there' (yaṃ hi kho tattha na hoti): just as there are no elephants and so on in the mansion of Migāra's mother, so too in this perception of the forest, that mass of disturbances of existence and disturbances of defilement that arises by way of the perception of a village and the perception of people is not present. Regarding 'But what remains there' (yaṃ pana tattha avasiṭṭhaṃ): just as the Bhikkhu Saṅgha remains in the mansion of Migāra's mother, so too there remains just that measure of disturbance of existence connected with the perception of the forest. Regarding 'He knows of that which is present: "This is present"' (taṃ santamidaṃ atthīti pajānāti): he knows of that which actually exists, 'This exists.' 'Entry into emptiness' (suññatāvakkanti) means the arising of emptiness.

177. Amanasikaritvā [V 4.0112] manussasaññanti idha gāmasaññaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “manussasaññāya gāmasaññaṃ nivattetvā, araññasaññāya manussasaññaṃ, pathavīsaññāya araññasaññaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāya pathavīsaññaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāya ākiñcaññāyatanasaññaṃ[M 4.0109], vipassanāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññaṃ, maggena vipassanaṃ nivattetvā anupubbena accantasuññataṃ nāma dassessāmī”ti. Tasmā evaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha pathavīsaññanti kasmā araññasaññaṃ pahāya pathavīsaññaṃ manasi karoti? Araññasaññāya visesānadhigamanato. Yathā hi purisassa ramaṇīyaṃ khettaṭṭhānaṃ disvā – “idha vuttā sāliādayo suṭṭhu sampajjissanti, mahālābhaṃ labhissāmī”ti sattakkhattumpi khettaṭṭhānaṃ olokentassa sāliādayo na sampajjanteva, sace pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ vihatakhāṇukakaṇṭakaṃ katvā kasitvā vapati, evaṃ sante sampajjanti, evameva – “idaṃ araññaṃ, ayaṃ rukkho, ayaṃ pabbato, ayaṃ nīlobhāso vanasaṇḍo”ti sacepi sattakkhattuṃ araññasaññaṃ manasi karoti, nevūpacāraṃ na samādhiṃ pāpuṇāti, pathavīsaññāya panassa dhuvasevanaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ parikammaṃ katvā jhānāni nibbattetvā [P 4.0153] jhānapadaṭṭhānampi vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sakkā arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Tasmā araññasaññaṃ pahāya pathavīsaññaṃ manasi karoti. Paṭiccāti paṭicca sambhūtaṃ.

177. Regarding 'not attending to the perception of humans': here, in this second section, one does not take up the perception of a village. Why? Because it is said that this thought occurred to him: 'Having averted the perception of a village by means of the perception of humans, the perception of humans by means of the perception of the forest, the perception of the forest by means of the perception of earth, the perception of earth by means of the perception of the base of infinite space… and so on… the perception of the base of nothingness by means of the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of insight, and having averted insight by means of the path, I shall gradually show what is called ultimate emptiness—that is, the fruit of Arahantship.' Therefore, he began the teaching in this way. Therein, regarding 'the perception of earth': why does one attend to the perception of earth after abandoning the perception of the forest? Because of not attaining a special state through the perception of the forest. For it is like a man who, upon seeing a pleasant field, thinks, 'Rice and other crops sown here will thrive well; I will get a great gain.' Even if he looks at the field seven times, the rice and other crops do not thrive. But if, having cleared that place of stumps and thorns, he plows and sows it, then they thrive. In the very same way, even if one attends to the perception of the forest seven times, thinking, 'This is the forest, this is a tree, this is a mountain, this is the blue hue of the woodland,' one attains neither access concentration nor absorption concentration. But by means of the perception of earth, having undertaken the preliminary work for the earth kasiṇa, which is a constantly frequented meditation subject, having produced the jhānas, and having developed insight which has jhāna as its proximate cause, it is possible to attain Arahantship. Therefore, one abandons the perception of the forest and attends to the perception of earth. 'Dependent' means arisen in dependence.

Idāni yasmiṃ pathavīkasiṇe so pathavīsaññī hoti, tassa opammadassanatthaṃ seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha usabhassa etanti āsabhaṃ. Aññesaṃ pana gunnaṃ gaṇḍāpi honti pahārāpi. Tesañhi cammaṃ pasāriyamānaṃ nibbalikaṃ na hoti, usabhassa lakkhaṇasampannatāya te dosā natthi. Tasmā tassa cammaṃ gahitaṃ. Saṅkusatenāti khilasatena. Suvihatanti pasāretvā suṭṭhu vihataṃ. Ūnakasatasaṅkuvihatañhi nibbalikaṃ na hoti, saṅkusatena vihataṃ bheritalaṃ viya nibbalikaṃ hoti. Tasmā evamāha. Ukkūlavikkūlanti uccanīcaṃ thalaṭṭhānaṃ ninnaṭṭhānaṃ. Nadīvidugganti nadiyo ceva duggamaṭṭhānañca. Pathavīsaññaṃ paṭicca manasi karoti ekattanti kasiṇapathaviyaṃyeva paṭicca sambhūtaṃ ekaṃ saññaṃ manasi karoti. Darathamattāti ito paṭṭhāya sabbavāresu pavattadarathavasena darathamattā veditabbā.

Now, regarding the earth kasiṇa in which that monk is one with the perception of earth, to show a simile for it, the Blessed One said, 'Just as a bull's hide,' and so on. Therein, 'of a bull' (`usabhassa etaṃ`) means it is called a bull's hide (`āsabhaṃ`). Other cattle, however, have swellings and marks from being struck.
