When their hides are stretched, they are not without wrinkles; but because a bull is endowed with excellent characteristics, those faults are not present. Therefore, its hide was taken as a simile. 'With a hundred pegs' (`saṅkusatena`) means with a hundred stakes. 'Well-pegged' (`suvihataṃ`) means, having been stretched out, it is well secured with pegs. A hide secured with fewer than a hundred pegs is not without wrinkles, but one secured with a hundred pegs becomes without wrinkles, like the surface of a drum. Therefore, he spoke thus. 'Uneven' (`ukkūlavikkūlaṃ`) means high and low, upland and lowland. 'Rivers and rugged terrain' (`nadīviduggaṃ`) means rivers and places difficult to traverse. 'He attends to oneness dependent on the perception of earth' (`pathavīsaññaṃ paṭicca manasi karoti ekattaṃ`) means he attends to a single perception that has arisen in dependence on the earth kasiṇa itself. 'A measure of disturbance' (`darathamattā`): from this point forward, in all sections, a measure of disturbance should be understood in the sense of the disturbance of existence.

182. Animittaṃ cetosamādhinti vipassanācittasamādhiṃ. So hi niccanimittādivirahito [V 4.0113] animittoti vuccati. Imameva kāyanti vipassanāya vatthuṃ dasseti. Tattha imamevāti imaṃ eva catumahābhūtikaṃ. Saḷāyatanikanti [M 4.0110][P 4.0154] saḷāyatanapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Jīvitapaccayāti yāva jīvitindriyānaṃ pavatti, tāva jīvitapaccayā pavattadarathamattā atthīti vuttaṃ hoti.

182. 'The signless concentration of mind' (`animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ`) means the concentration of the insight-mind. Indeed, it is called 'signless' because it is devoid of the sign of permanence and so on. By 'this very body' (`imameva kāyaṃ`), he indicates the object of insight. Therein, 'this very' (`imameva`) means this very body composed of the four great elements. 'Pertaining to the six sense bases' (`saḷāyatanikaṃ`) means connected with the six sense bases. 'Conditioned by life' (`jīvitapaccayā`): it is said that for as long as the life faculty persists, there is a measure of the disturbance of existence conditioned by life.

183. Puna animittanti vipassanāya paṭivipassanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmāsavaṃ paṭiccāti kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca uppajjanapavattadarathā idha na santi, ariyamagge ceva ariyaphale ca natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Imameva kāyanti imaṃ upādisesadarathadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Iti manussasaññāya gāmasaññaṃ nivattetvā…pe… maggena vipassanaṃ nivattetvā anupubbena accantasuññatā nāma dassitā hoti.

183. Again, 'signless' (`animittaṃ`) is said in order to show the reviewing of insight. 'Dependent on the taint of sensual desire' (`kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca`) means that the agitations that would arise and occur dependent on the taint of sensual desire are not present here; that is, they are not present in the noble path and the noble fruit. This is the meaning. 'This very body' (`imameva kāyaṃ`) was said in order to show the agitation related to the remaining aggregates with residue. Thus, having averted the perception of a village by means of the perception of humans… and so on… having averted insight by means of the path, what is called ultimate emptiness—that is, the fruit of Arahantship—is shown sequentially.

184. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Anuttaranti uttaravirahitaṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ. Suññatanti suññataphalasamāpattiṃ. Tasmāti yasmā atītepi, buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakasaṅkhātā samaṇabrāhmaṇā. Anāgatepi, etarahipi buddhabuddhasāvakasaṅkhātā samaṇabrāhmaṇā imaṃyeva parisuddhaṃ paramaṃ anuttaraṃ suññataṃ upasampajja vihariṃsu viharissanti viharanti ca, tasmā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

184. 'Perfectly pure' (`parisuddhaṃ`) means without defilement. 'Unsurpassed' (`anuttaraṃ`) means devoid of a superior, the highest of all. 'Emptiness' (`suññataṃ`) means the attainment of the fruition of emptiness. 'Therefore' (`tasmā`) is used because in the past, ascetics and brahmins known as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of Buddhas, and also in the future and at present, ascetics and brahmins known as Buddhas and disciples of Buddhas, having entered and abided in this same perfectly pure, supreme, unsurpassed emptiness, they dwelt thus, will dwell thus, and are dwelling thus. Therefore... The rest is clear in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cūḷasuññatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Cūḷasuññata Sutta is concluded.

2. Mahāsuññatasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Mahāsuññata Sutta

185. Evaṃ [V 4.0114][P 4.0155] me sutanti mahāsuññatasuttaṃ. Tattha kāḷakhemakassāti chavivaṇṇena so kāḷo, khemakoti panassa nāmaṃ. Vihāroti tasmiṃyeva nigrodhārāme ekasmiṃ padese pākārena parikkhipitvā dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ māpetvā haṃsavaṭṭakādisenāsanāni ceva maṇḍalamāḷabhojanasālādīni ca patiṭṭhapetvā kato vihāro. Sambahulāni senāsanānīti mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisibimbohanaṃ taṭṭikā cammakhaṇḍo tiṇasanthāro paṇṇasanthāro palālasanthārotiādīni paññattāni honti, mañcena mañcaṃ…pe… palālasanthāreneva palālasanthāraṃ āhacca ṭhapitāni, gaṇabhikkhūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānasadisaṃ ahosi.

The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Mahāsuññata Sutta. Therein, as for Kāḷakhemaka: by his skin color, he was dark (kāḷa), and Khemaka was his name. As for 'vihāra': it is a monastery constructed in that very Nigrodhārāma, in a certain area, having enclosed it with a wall, having created a gateway, and having established lodgings with roofing in the shape of a goose's wing and so on, as well as circular pavilions, dining halls, and the like. As for 'many lodgings': beds, chairs, mattresses, cushions, mats, pieces of hide, grass spreads, leaf spreads, straw spreads, and so on, were prepared. The lodgings were placed touching, a bed with a bed... a straw spread with a straw spread; it was like the dwelling place of monks living as a group.

Sambahulā [M 4.0111] nu khoti bhagavato bodhipallaṅkeyeva sabbakilesānaṃ samugghāṭitattā saṃsayo nāma natthi, vitakkapubbabhāgā pucchā, vitakkapubbabhāge cāyaṃ nukāro nipātamatto. Pāṭimatthakaṃ gacchante avinicchito nāma na hoti. Ito kira pubbe bhagavatā dasa dvādasa bhikkhū ekaṭṭhāne vasantā na diṭṭhapubbā.

2. As for 'Sambahulā nu kho': for the Blessed One, because of having completely uprooted all defilements at the very seat of enlightenment, there is no such thing as doubt. It is a question that has thought as its preceding part, and this letter 'nu' is merely a particle that indicates a preceding thought. For the Blessed One, who goes to the very pinnacle of the teaching, there is nothing that is undecided. It is said that before this, the Blessed One had not previously seen ten or twelve monks dwelling in one place.

Athassa etadahosi – gaṇavāso nāmāyaṃ vaṭṭe āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo nadīotiṇṇaudakasadiso, nirayatiracchānayonipettivisayāsurakāyesupi, manussaloka-devalokabrahmalokesupi gaṇavāsova āciṇṇo. Dasayojanasahasso hi nirayo tipucuṇṇabharitā nāḷi viya [P 4.0156] sattehi nirantaro, pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇakaraṇaṭṭhāne sattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ vā paricchedo vā natthi, tathā vāsīhi tacchanādiṭhānesu, iti gaṇabhūtāva paccanti. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ ekasmiṃ vammike upasikānaṃ pamāṇaṃ vā paricchedo vā natthi, tathā ekekabilādīsupi kipillikādīnaṃ. Tiracchānayoniyampi gaṇavāsova. Petanagarāni ca gāvutikāni aḍḍhayojanikānipi petabharitāni honti. Evaṃ pettivisayepi gaṇavāsova. Asurabhavanaṃ dasayojanasahassaṃ kaṇṇe pakkhittasūciyā kaṇṇabilaṃ viya hoti. Iti asurakāyepi gaṇavāsova. Manussaloke sāvatthiyaṃ sattapaṇṇāsa kulasatasahassāni, rājagahe anto [V 4.0115] ca bahi ca aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo vasiṃsu. Evaṃ aññesupi ṭhānesūti manussalokepi gaṇavāsova. Bhummadevatā ādiṃ katvā devalokabrahmalokesupi gaṇavāsova. Ekekassa hi devaputtassa aḍḍhatiyā nāṭakakoṭiyo honti, navapi koṭiyo honti, ekaṭṭhāne dasasahassāpi brahmāno vasanti.

185. Then this thought arose in him: 'This living in a group is a practice constantly cultivated by beings in the round of rebirth, like water that has descended into a river. In the realms of hell, animals, ghosts, and asuras, and in the human, deva, and brahma worlds, living in a group is the practiced custom. For the hell realm, ten thousand yojanas in extent, is filled with beings without any interval, like a tube filled with lead powder. In the place of the five kinds of binding and torture, there is no measure or limit to the beings. In the animal realm, in a single anthill, there is no measure or limit to the termites; likewise, in each and every hole and so on, there is no measure or limit to ants and the like. In the animal realm, too, living in a group is the practiced custom. And the cities of the petas, a gāvuta or half a yojana in size, are filled with petas. Thus, in the peta-realm, too, living in a group is the practiced custom. The asura abode, ten thousand yojanas in extent, is like an ear-hole filled by a needle inserted into it. Thus, in the asura-realm, too, living in a group is the practiced custom. In the human world, in Sāvatthī, fifty-seven hundred thousand families dwell; in Rājagaha, inside and outside, eighteen koṭis of people dwelt. Thus in other places, too; so in the human world, living in a group is the practiced custom. Beginning with the earth-devas, in the deva and brahma worlds, too, living in a group is the practiced custom. For each single devaputta, there are two and a half koṭis of female dancers, or there are nine koṭis. In one place, even ten thousand brahmās dwell.

Tato cintesi – “mayā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni gaṇavāsaviddhaṃsanatthaṃ dasa pāramiyo pūritā, ime ca bhikkhū ito paṭṭhāyeva gaṇaṃ bandhitvā gaṇābhiratā jātā ananucchavikaṃ karontī”ti. So dhammasaṃvegaṃ uppādetvā puna cintesi – “sace ‘ekaṭṭhāne dvīhi bhikkhūhi na vasitabba’nti sakkā bhaveyya sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetuṃ, sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpeyyaṃ, na kho panetaṃ sakkā. Handāhaṃ mahāsuññatāpaṭipattiṃ nāma suttantaṃ [M 4.0112] desemi, yaṃ sikkhākāmānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sikkhāpadapaññatti viya nagaradvāre [P 4.0157] nikkhittasabbakāyikaādāso viya ca bhavissati. Tato yathā nāmekasmiṃ ādāse khattiyādayo attano vajjaṃ disvā taṃ pahāya anavajjā honti, evamevaṃ mayi parinibbutepi pañcavassasahassāni imaṃ suttaṃ āvajjitvā gaṇaṃ vinodetvā ekībhāvābhiratā kulaputtā vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ karissantī”ti. Bhagavato ca manorathaṃ pūrentā viya imaṃ suttaṃ āvajjitvā gaṇaṃ vinodetvā vaṭṭadukkhaṃ khepetvā parinibbutā kulaputtā gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Vālikapiṭṭhivihārepi hi ābhidhammikaabhayatthero nāma vassūpanāyikasamaye sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ imaṃ suttaṃ sañjhāyitvā “sammāsambuddho evaṃ kāreti, mayaṃ kiṃ karomā”ti āha. Te sabbepi antovasse gaṇaṃ vinodetvā ekībhāvābhiratā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Gaṇabhedanaṃ nāma idaṃ suttanti.

Then he reflected: 'By me, for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kappas more, the ten perfections were fulfilled for the sake of destroying living in a group. And these monks, starting from now, forming a group and delighting in the group, are doing what is unsuitable.' Having aroused a sense of urgency regarding the Dhamma, he further reflected: 'If it were possible to lay down a training rule stating, "Two monks should not dwell in one place," I would establish such a rule. But this is not feasible. Well now, I shall teach the discourse named the Practice of Great Emptiness, which, for clansmen who desire the training, will be like the laying down of a training rule and like a full-length mirror placed at the city gate. Just as, for instance, Khattiyas and others, seeing their own fault in a mirror, abandon that fault and become faultless, so too, even when I have attained Parinibbāna, for five thousand years, clansmen, by reflecting on this sutta, will dispel the group, delight in being alone, and make an end of the suffering of the round.' And as if fulfilling the heart's wish of the Blessed One, the clansmen who reflected on this sutta, dispelled the group, exhausted the suffering of the round, and attained Parinibbāna have surpassed all reckoning. For even in the Vālikapiṭṭhi monastery, the elder named Ābhidhammika Abhaya, at the time of the rains-residence, having recited this sutta together with many monks, said: 'The Sammāsambuddha enjoins thus; what should we do?' All of them, within the rains-residence, having dispelled the group and come to delight in being alone, attained Arahantship. This sutta is named 'The Dispeller of the Group'.

186. Ghaṭāyāti evaṃnāmakassa sakkassa. Vihāreti ayampi vihāro nigrodhārāmasseva ekadese kāḷakhemakassa vihāro viya katoti veditabbo. Cīvarakammanti jiṇṇamalinānaṃ aggaḷaṭṭhānuppādanadhovanādīhi kataparibhaṇḍampi, cīvaratthāya uppannavatthānaṃ vicāraṇasibbanādīhi akataṃ saṃvidhānampi vaṭṭati, idha pana akataṃ saṃvidhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Manussā hi ānandattherassa cīvarasāṭake adaṃsu. Tasmā thero sambahule bhikkhū gahetvā tattha cīvarakammaṃ akāsi. Tepi bhikkhū pātova sūcipāsakassa paññāyanakālato paṭṭhāya nisinnā apaññāyanakāle uṭṭhahanti. Sūcikamme [V 4.0116] niṭṭhiteyeva senāsanāni saṃvidahissāmāti na saṃvidahiṃsu. Cīvarakārasamayo noti thero kira cintesi – “addhā etehi bhikkhūhi na paṭisāmitāni senāsanāni, bhagavatā ca diṭṭhāni bhavissanti. Iti anattamano satthā suṭṭhu niggahetukāmo, imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upatthambho bhavissāmī”ti; tasmā evamāha. Ayaṃ panettha [P 4.0158] adhippāyo – “na, bhante, ime bhikkhū kammārāmā eva, cīvarakiccavasena pana evaṃ vasantī”ti.

186. ‘Ghaṭāya’ refers to the Sakyan of that name. Regarding ‘in the dwelling’: this dwelling, too, should be understood as having been built in a certain part of the Nigrodhārāma, just like the dwelling of the Sakyan named Kāḷakhemaka. Regarding ‘robe-work’: this can refer to the mending of worn-out and soiled robes by means of patching, washing, and so on; it can also refer to the preparation of cloth that has arisen for the purpose of robes, which has not yet been worked on, by means of inspecting, sewing, and so on. Here, however, the preparation of that which is not yet done is intended. For people had given robe-cloths to the Elder Ānanda. Therefore, the Elder, taking many bhikkhus, did the robe-work there. And those bhikkhus, having sat down starting from the time early in the morning when the eye of the needle is visible, rise at the time when the eye of the needle is not visible. Thinking, ‘Only when the needlework is finished will we arrange our lodgings,’ they did not arrange them. Regarding ‘It is our time for robe-making,’ the Elder, it is said, thought: ‘Surely, these bhikkhus have not put away their lodgings, and they will be seen by the Blessed One.’ Thus displeased, he thought, ‘The Teacher will desire to reprove these bhikkhus severely; I will become a support for them.’ Therefore, he spoke thus. The intention here is this: ‘Venerable sir, it is not that these bhikkhus delight in work; rather, it is on account of the business of the robes that they are living thus.’

Na kho, ānandāti, ānanda, kammasamayo vā hotu akammasamayo vā, cīvarakārasamayo vā hotu acīvarakārasamayo vā, atha kho saṅgaṇikārāmo bhikkhu na sobhatiyeva. Mā tvaṃ anupatthambhaṭṭhāne upatthambho ahosīti. Tattha saṅgaṇikāti sakaparisasamodhānaṃ. Gaṇoti nānājanasamodhānaṃ. Iti saṅgaṇikārāmo vā hotu gaṇārāmo [M 4.0113] vā, sabbathāpi gaṇabāhullābhirato gaṇabandhanabaddho bhikkhu na sobhati. Pacchābhatte pana divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā sudhotahatthapādo mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ekārāmatamanuyutto bhikkhu buddhasāsane sobhati. Nekkhammasukhanti kāmato nikkhantassa sukhaṃ. Pavivekasukhampi kāmapavivekasukhameva. Rāgādīnaṃ pana vūpasamatthāya saṃvattatīti upasamasukhaṃ. Maggasambodhatthāya saṃvattatīti sambodhisukhaṃ. Nikāmalābhīti kāmalābhī icchitalābhī. Akicchalābhīti adukkhalābhī. Akasiralābhīti vipulalābhī.

‘Not so, Ānanda,’ [the Blessed One said]. ‘Ānanda, whether it is a time for work or not a time for work, whether it is a time for robe-making or not a time for robe-making, indeed, a bhikkhu who delights in company does not shine at all. You should not be a support in a matter where one should not give support.’ Therein, ‘company’ (saṅgaṇikā) is association with one’s own assembly. ‘Group’ (gaṇa) is association with various people. Thus, whether one delights in one's own assembly or delights in various people, in every way a bhikkhu who is fond of the multiplicity of groups, bound by the bond of forming groups, does not shine. However, after the meal, having swept the day-resting place, with hands and feet well-washed, having taken up the root meditation subject, a bhikkhu devoted to delighting in solitude shines in the Buddha’s Dispensation. ‘The happiness of renunciation’ (nekkhammasukha) is the happiness of one who has departed from sensual pleasures. ‘The happiness of seclusion’ (pavivekasukha) is indeed the happiness of seclusion from sensual pleasures. Furthermore, because it leads to the calming of passion and so on, it is called ‘the happiness of peace’ (upasamasukha). Because it leads to awakening to the path, it is called ‘the happiness of enlightenment’ (sambodhisukha). ‘One who obtains at will’ (nikāmalābhī) is one who obtains what is desired. ‘One who obtains without trouble’ (akicchalābhī) is one who obtains without difficulty. ‘One who obtains without hardship’ (akasiralābhī) is one who obtains abundantly.

Sāmāyikanti appitappitasamaye kilesehi vimuttaṃ. Kantanti manāpaṃ. Cetovimuttinti rūpārūpāvacaracittavimuttiṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “cattāri ca jhānāni catasso ca arūpasamāpattiyo, ayaṃ sāmāyiko vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.213). Asāmāyikanti [P 4.0159] na samayavasena kilesehi vimuttaṃ, atha kho accantavimuttaṃ lokuttaraṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “cattāro ca ariyamaggā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, ayaṃ asāmāyiko vimokkho”ti. Akuppanti kilesehi akopetabbaṃ.

‘Temporary’ (sāmāyikaṃ) refers to being freed from defilements at the very time of entering absorption. ‘Pleasing’ (kantaṃ) means delightful. ‘Liberation of mind’ (cetovimuttiṃ) refers to the liberation of mind that is the consciousness of the form and formless spheres. And this was stated: ‘The four jhānas and the four formless attainments—this is the temporary liberation.’ ‘Non-temporary’ (asāmāyikaṃ) does not mean being freed from defilements by means of a specific time; rather, the supramundane, which is completely freed from defilements, is meant. And this was stated: ‘The four noble paths and the four fruits of recluseship—this is the non-temporary liberation.’ ‘Unshakable’ (akuppaṃ) means that which is not to be shaken by defilements.

Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Saṅgaṇikārāmo bhikkhu gaṇabandhanabaddho neva lokiyaguṇaṃ, na ca lokuttaraguṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti, gaṇaṃ vinodetvā pana ekābhirato sakkoti. Tathā hi vipassī bodhisatto caturāsītiyā pabbajitasahassehi parivuto satta vassāni vicaranto sabbaññuguṇaṃ [V 4.0117] nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi, gaṇaṃ vinodetvā sattadivase ekībhāvābhirato bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha sabbaññuguṇaṃ nibbattesi. Amhākaṃ bodhisatto pañcavaggiyehi saddhiṃ chabbassāni vicaranto sabbaññuguṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi, tesu pakkantesu ekībhāvābhirato bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha sabbaññuguṇaṃ nibbattesi.

By this much, what has been stated? A bhikkhu who delights in company, bound by the bond of a group, is able neither to produce the worldly quality nor the supramundane quality. However, one who has dispelled the group and delights in solitude is able to do so. For so it is: the Bodhisatta Vipassī, though surrounded by eighty-four thousand renunciates and wandering for seven years, was not able to produce the quality of omniscience. Having dispelled the group and delighting in being alone, within seven days he ascended to the seat of enlightenment and produced the quality of omniscience. Our Bodhisatta, wandering together with the group of five ascetics for six years, was not able to produce the quality of omniscience. When they had departed, delighting in being alone, he ascended to the seat of enlightenment and produced the quality of omniscience.

Evaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmassa guṇādhigamābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni dosuppattiṃ dassento nāhaṃ ānandātiādimāha. Tattha rūpanti sarīraṃ. Yattha rattassāti yasmiṃ rūpe rāgavasena rattassa. Na uppajjeyyunti yasmiṃ rūpe rattassa na uppajjeyyuṃ, taṃ rūpaṃ na samanupassāmi, atha kho sāriputtamoggallānānaṃ dasabalasāvakattupagamanasaṅkhātena aññathābhāvena sañcayassa [M 4.0114] viya, upāligahapatino aññathābhāvena nāṭaputtassa viya, piyajātikasutte seṭṭhiādīnaṃ viya ca uppajjantiyeva.

Having thus shown the non-attainment of special qualities for one who delights in company, now, wishing to show the arising of faults, he said, ‘I do not, Ānanda…’ and so on. Therein, ‘form’ (rūpaṃ) is the body. ‘For one attached to which’ (yattha rattassa) means for one who is attached by way of lust to that form. ‘Would not arise’ (na uppajjeyyuṃ) means: I do not see that form for which, in one attached to it, sorrow and so on would not arise. Indeed, just as for Sañjaya, on account of the change designated as Sāriputta and Moggallāna going over to the discipleship of the Ten-Powered One, sorrow and so on arose; and just as for Nāṭaputta, on account of the change in Upāli the householder, sorrow and so on arose; and just as in the Piyajātika Sutta, for the wealthy man and others, sorrow and so on arose—so they do indeed arise.

187. Ayaṃ [P 4.0160] kho panānandāti ko anusandhi? Sace hi koci dubbuddhī navapabbajito vadeyya – “sammāsambuddho khettaṃ paviṭṭhā gāviyo viya amheyeva gaṇato nīharati, ekībhāve niyojeti, sayaṃ pana rājarājamahāmattādīhi parivuto viharatī”ti, tassa vacanokāsupacchedanatthaṃ – “cakkavāḷapariyantāya parisāya majjhe nisinnopi tathāgato ekakovā”ti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha sabbanimittānanti rūpādīnaṃ saṅkhanimittānaṃ. Ajjhattanti visayajjhattaṃ. Suññatanti suññataphalasamāpattiṃ. Tatra ceti upayogatthe bhummaṃ, taṃ ceti vuttaṃ hoti. Puna tatrāti tasmiṃ parisamajjhe ṭhito. Vivekaninnenāti nibbānaninnena. Byantībhūtenāti āsavaṭṭhānīyadhammehi vigatantena nissaṭena visaṃyuttena. Uyyojanikapaṭisaṃyuttanti gacchatha tumheti evaṃ uyyojanikena vacanena paṭisaṃyuttaṃ.

187. Regarding the phrase ‘Now, this, Ānanda…,’ what is the connection? For if some newly ordained one of little wisdom were to say, ‘Just as one drives out cows that have entered a field, the Perfectly Enlightened One drives only us out from the group and enjoins us to solitude, while he himself dwells surrounded by kings, great ministers of kings, and so on’—in order to cut off the opportunity for such speech, and to show that ‘Even when seated in the midst of an assembly extending to the limits of the universe, the Tathāgata is indeed alone,’ this discourse was begun. Therein, ‘not attending to all signs’ refers to not attending to the conditioned signs of form and so on. ‘Internally’ (ajjhattaṃ) means internally with respect to the object. ‘Emptiness’ (suññataṃ) means the emptiness fruition attainment. The phrase ‘tatra ce’ is a locative used in the sense of the accusative; it means ‘if they were to approach him.’ Again, ‘there’ (tatra) means standing in the midst of that assembly. ‘With a mind inclined to seclusion’ (vivekaninnena) means with a mind inclined to Nibbāna. ‘Aloof’ (byantībhūtena) means with a mind that is aloof from, released from, and disjoined from things that are a basis for the taints. ‘Connected with dismissal’ (uyyojanikapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ) means connected with a word of dismissal, such as, ‘You may go.’

Kāya pana velāya bhagavā evaṃ katheti? Pacchābhattakiccavelāya, vā purimayāmakiccavelāya vā. Bhagavā hi pacchābhatte gandhakuṭiyaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā vuṭṭhāya phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdati. Tasmiṃ samaye dhammassavanatthāya parisā sannipatanti. Atha bhagavā kālaṃ viditvā gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā buddhāsanavaragato dhammaṃ desetvā bhesajjatelapākaṃ gaṇhanto viya kālaṃ anatikkamitvā vivekaninnena cittena parisaṃ uyyojeti[V 4.0118]. Purimayāmepi “abhikkantā kho vāseṭṭhā ratti, yassa dāni kālaṃ maññathā”ti (dī. ni. 3.299) evaṃ uyyojeti[P 4.0161]. Buddhānañhi bodhipattito paṭṭhāya dve pañcaviññāṇānipi nibbānaninnāneva. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā suññatāvihāro santo paṇīto, tasmā.

Now, at what time does the Blessed One speak thus? At the time for post-meal duties, or at the time for duties of the first watch. For after the meal, the Blessed One, having arranged his lion’s resting place in the fragrant chamber, having arisen, and having entered into fruition attainment, sits. At that time, the assembly gathers to hear the Dhamma. Then, knowing the time, the Blessed One emerges from the fragrant chamber, and having gone to the excellent Buddha seat, teaches the Dhamma. Like one taking up the cooking of medicinal oil, not letting the time pass, with a mind inclined to Nibbāna, he dismisses the assembly. In the first watch too, he dismisses them thus, ‘Vāseṭṭha, the night is far advanced; it is now time for that which you deem fit’ (Dī. ni. 3.299). For indeed, from the attainment of Bodhi onward, even the two sets of five consciousnesses of the Buddhas are inclined only towards Nibbāna. Therefore, Ānanda: because the dwelling in emptiness is peaceful and sublime, therefore...

188. Ajjhattamevāti gocarajjhattameva. Ajjhattaṃ suññatanti idha niyakajjhattaṃ, attano pañcasu khandhesu nissitanti attho. Sampajāno hotīti kammaṭṭhānassa asampajjanabhāvajānanena sampajāno. Bahiddhāti parassa pañcasu khandhesu. Ajjhattabahiddhāti kālena ajjhattaṃ kālena bahiddhā[M 4.0115]. Āneñjanti ubhatobhāgavimutto bhavissāmāti āneñjaṃ arūpasamāpattiṃ manasi karoti.

188. ‘Internally only’ means the internal sphere of the object only. ‘Internal emptiness’: here, this means one's own internal sphere; the meaning is that it is dependent on one's own five aggregates. ‘Is fully aware’ means one is possessed of discernment by knowing the state of non-completion of the meditation subject. ‘Externally’ means in the five aggregates of another. ‘Internally and externally’ means at one time internally, at another time externally. ‘The imperturbable’ means, having attended with the thought, ‘I will be one liberated in both ways,’ one attends to the imperturbable, the formless attainment.

Tasmiṃyeva purimasminti pādakajjhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Apaguṇapādakajjhānato vuṭṭhitassa hi ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ manasikaroto tattha cittaṃ na pakkhandati. Tato “parassa santāne nu kho katha”nti bahiddhā manasi karoti, tatthapi na pakkhandati. Tato – “kālena attano santāne, kālena parassa santāne nu kho katha”nti ajjhattabahiddhā manasi karoti, tatthapi na pakkhandati. Tato ubhatobhāgavimutto hotukāmo “arūpasamāpattiyaṃ nu kho katha”nti āneñjaṃ manasi karoti, tatthapi na pakkhandati. Idāni – “na me cittaṃ pakkhandatīti vissaṭṭhavīriyena upaṭṭhākādīnaṃ pacchato na caritabbaṃ, pādakajjhānameva pana sādhukaṃ punappunaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Evamassa rukkhe chindato pharasumhi avahante puna nisitaṃ kāretvā [P 4.0162] chindantassa chijjesu pharasu viya kammaṭṭhāne manasikāro vahatī”ti dassetuṃ tasmiṃyevātiādimāha. Idānissa evaṃ paṭipannassa yaṃ yaṃ manasi karoti, tattha tattha manasikāro sampajjatīti dassento pakkhandatīti āha.

‘In that very former [state]’: this was spoken in reference to the foundational jhāna. For one who has arisen from an unpracticed foundational jhāna, when attending to internal emptiness, the mind does not enter into it. Then, thinking, ‘How might it be in another's continuum?’, he attends externally, but even there the mind does not enter. Then, thinking, ‘How might it be at times in one's own continuum, and at times in another's continuum?’, he attends internally and externally, but even there the mind does not enter. Then, desiring to be one liberated in both ways, thinking, ‘How might it be in the formless attainment?’, he attends to the imperturbable, but even there the mind does not enter. Now, to show that one should not follow after attendants and others with slackened effort, thinking, ‘My mind does not enter,’ but that one should attend well and repeatedly only to the foundational jhāna, which is the basis of insight—just as for one cutting a tree, when the axe is not effective, he has it sharpened again, and upon cutting, the axe becomes effective in its cutting; in the same way, the attention to the meditation subject becomes effective, bringing forth path and fruition—to show this meaning, the Blessed One said, ‘in that very [state],’ and so on. Now, to show that for one practicing thus, whatever he attends to, in every case the attention succeeds, he said, ‘it enters.’

189. Iminā vihārenāti iminā samathavipassanāvihārena. Itiha tattha sampajānoti iti caṅkamantopi tasmiṃ kammaṭṭhāne sampajjamāne “sampajjati me kammaṭṭhāna”nti jānanena sampajāno hoti. Sayatīti nipajjati. Ettha kañci kālaṃ caṅkamitvā – “idāni ettakaṃ kālaṃ caṅkamituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti ñatvā iriyāpathaṃ ahāpetvā ṭhātabbaṃ. Esa nayo sabbavāresu[V 4.0119]. Na kathessāmīti, itiha tatthāti evaṃ na kathessāmīti jānanena tattha sampajānakārī hoti.

189. ‘By this dwelling’ means by this dwelling in serenity and insight. ‘Thus, one is fully aware there’: thus, even while walking, one is fully aware by knowing, ‘My meditation subject is succeeding’ in that meditation subject. ‘Lies down’ means he lies down. Here, having walked for some time, knowing, ‘Now I will not be able to walk for this long,’ one should stand without letting the posture decline. This method should be understood in all instances. ‘I will not speak’: thus, by knowing, ‘Thus I will not speak animal talk,’ one acts with full awareness in that matter.

Puna dutiyavāre evarūpiṃ kathaṃ kathessāmīti jānanena sampajānakārī hoti, imassa bhikkhuno samathavipassanā taruṇāva, tāsaṃ anurakkhaṇatthaṃ –

Again, in the second instance, by knowing, ‘I will speak such a talk that causes defilements to wither, such as talk on contentment,’ he acts with full awareness. For this monk, serenity and insight are still tender; for their preservation—

“Āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ, puggalo atha bhojanaṃ;

Utu iriyāpatho ceva, sappāyo sevitabbako”ti.

‘An agreeable residence, alms-round, speech, person, and also food, climate, and posture should be associated with.’

Satta sappāyāni icchitabbāni. Tesaṃ dassanatthamidaṃ vuttaṃ. Vitakkavāresu avitakkanassa ca vitakkanassa ca jānanena sampajānatā veditabbā.

The seven agreeable things that have been mentioned should be desired. This was said to show them. In the instances of thought, full awareness should be understood as the knowing of what is not to be thought and what is to be thought.

190. Iti [M 4.0116] vitakkapahānena dve magge kathetvā idāni tatiyamaggassa vipassanaṃ ācikkhanto pañca kho ime, ānanda, kāmaguṇātiādimāha. Āyataneti tesuyeva kāmaguṇesu kismiñcideva kilesuppattikāraṇe. Samudācāroti samudācaraṇato appahīnakileso. Evaṃ [P 4.0163] santanti evaṃ vijjamānameva. Sampajānoti kammaṭṭhānassa asampattijānanena sampajāno. Dutiyavāre evaṃ santametanti evaṃ sante etaṃ. Sampajānoti kammaṭṭhānasampattijānanena sampajāno. Ayañhi “pahīno nu kho me pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgo no”ti paccavekkhamāno apahīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā vīriyaṃ paggahetvā taṃ anāgāmimaggena samugghāṭeti, tato maggānantaraṃ phalaṃ, phalato vuṭṭhāya paccavekkhamāno pahīnabhāvaṃ jānāti, tassa jānanena “sampajāno hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

190. Thus, having taught the two paths—the path of stream-entry and the path of once-returning—by means of the abandoning of thought, now, explaining the insight for the third path, the path of non-returning, the Blessed One said, ‘Ānanda, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure,’ and so on. ‘Base’ (āyatane): in the cause for the arising of defilements, which is any one of those very strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Activity’ (samudācāro): from its activity, the unabandoned defilement arises. ‘Thus existing’ (evaṃ santaṃ): the defilement that is actually present. ‘Is fully aware’ (sampajāno): one is fully aware by knowing the non-completion of the meditation subject. In the second instance, ‘this thus existing’ (evaṃ santam etaṃ): this being so, this abandoning of desire and lust. ‘Is fully aware’ (sampajāno): one is fully aware by knowing the completion of the meditation subject. For this monk, reflecting, ‘Has my desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned or not?’ and knowing its state of non-abandonment, rouses his effort and uproots it with the path of non-returning. Then, immediately after the path comes the fruit. Arising from the fruit and reflecting, he knows its state of abandonment. By means of that knowing, it is said, ‘one is fully aware.’

191. Idāni arahattamaggassa vipassanaṃ ācikkhanto pañca kho ime, ānanda, upādānakkhandhātiādimāha. Tattha so pahīyatīti rūpe asmīti māno asmīti chando asmīti anusayo pahīyati. Tathā vedanādīsu sampajānatā vuttanāyeneva veditabbā.

191. Now, explaining the insight for the path of Arahantship, the Blessed One said, ‘Ānanda, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging,’ and so on. Therein, ‘it is abandoned’ means that with regard to form, the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ and the underlying tendency ‘I am’—that is, the underlying tendencies of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance—are abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Likewise with regard to feeling and so on. The state of being fully aware should be understood in the same way as was stated before.

Ime kho te, ānanda, dhammāti heṭṭhā kathite samathavipassanāmaggaphaladhamme sandhāyāha. Kusalāyatikāti [V 4.0120] kusalato āgatā. Kusalā hi kusalāpi honti kusalāyatikāpi, seyyathidaṃ, paṭhamajjhānaṃ kusalaṃ, dutiyajjhānaṃ kusalañceva kusalāyatikañca…pe… ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ kusalaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ kusalañceva kusalāyatikañca, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ kusalaṃ, sotāpattimaggo kusalo ceva kusalāyatiko ca…pe… anāgāmimaggo kusalo, arahattamaggo kusalo ceva kusalāyatiko ca. Tathā paṭhamajjhānaṃ kusalaṃ, taṃsampayuttakā dhammā kusalā ceva kusalāyatikā ca…pe… arahattamaggo kusalo, taṃsampayuttakā dhammā kusalā ceva kusalāyatikā ca.

"These, Ānanda, are the dhammas": The Blessed One said this referring to the dhammas of serenity, insight, path, and fruit spoken of below. "Coming from the skillful" means coming from what is skillful. For skillful things are both skillful and also coming from the skillful. For instance: the first jhāna is skillful, the second jhāna is both skillful and coming from the skillful... (and so on)... the base of nothingness is skillful, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is both skillful and coming from the skillful. The stream-entry path is both skillful and coming from the skillful... (and so on)... the non-returner path is skillful, the Arahant path is both skillful and coming from the skillful. Likewise, the first jhāna is skillful, and the dhammas associated with it are both skillful and coming from the skillful... (and so on)... the Arahant path is skillful, and the dhammas associated with it are both skillful and coming from the skillful.

Ariyāti nikkilesā visuddhā. Lokuttarāti loke uttarā visiṭṭhā. Anavakkantā [P 4.0164] pāpimatāti pāpimantena mārena anokkantā. Vipassanāpādakā [M 4.0117] aṭṭha samāpattiyo appetvā nisinnassa hi bhikkhuno cittaṃ māro na passati, “idaṃ nāma ārammaṇaṃ nissāya saṃvattatī”ti jātituṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā “anavakkantā”ti vuttaṃ.

"Noble" means without defilements, especially pure. "Supramundane" means surpassing, distinguished in the world. "Not trodden upon by the Evil One" means not trodden upon by the evil Māra. Indeed, Māra does not see the mind of a bhikkhu sitting having entered the eight attainments which are the basis for insight; he is unable to know, "Relying on this object, it arises." Therefore, it was said as "not trodden upon".

Taṃ kiṃ maññasīti idaṃ kasmā āha? Gaṇepi eko ānisaṃso atthi, taṃ dassetuṃ idamāha. Anubandhitunti anugacchituṃ paricarituṃ.

Why did the Blessed One say this, beginning with "What do you think?" There is one benefit even in a group; the Blessed One said this to show that benefit. "To follow" means to follow after, to attend to.

Na kho, ānandāti ettha kiñcāpi bhagavatā – “sutāvudho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 7.67) bahussuto pañcāvudhasampanno yodho viya kato. Yasmā pana so sutapariyattiṃ uggahetvāpi tadanucchavikaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ na paṭipajjati, na tassa taṃ āvudhaṃ hoti. Yo paṭipajjati, tasseva hoti. Tasmā etadatthaṃ anubandhituṃ nārahatīti dassento na kho, ānandāti āha.

Regarding "Not so, Ānanda": Although the Blessed One has made the learned one like a warrior endowed with five weapons, saying, "Bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple with the weapon of learning abandons the unskillful, develops the skillful, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity," yet, because a certain person, even having learned the scriptural teaching, does not practice the conduct that is suitable and conformable to it, for him that teaching is not a weapon. Only for the one who practices is it a weapon. Therefore, showing that for this reason, such a person is not worthy to be followed, He said, "Not so, Ānanda."

Idāni yadatthaṃ anubandhitabbo, taṃ dassetuṃ yā ca khotiādimāha. Iti imasmiṃ sutte tīsu ṭhānesu dasa kathāvatthūni āgatāni. “Iti evarūpaṃ kathaṃ kathessāmī”ti sappāyāsappāyavasena āgatāni, “yadidaṃ suttaṃ geyya”nti ettha sutapariyattivasena āgatāni, imasmiṃ [V 4.0121] ṭhāne paripūraṇavasena āgatāni. Tasmā imasmiṃ sutte dasa kathāvatthūni kathentena imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhatvā kathetabbāni.

Now, to show for what purpose one should be followed, the Blessed One said that which begins with "And whatever...". Thus, in this Sutta, the ten topics of discussion are found in three places. In the passage, "Thus, 'I will give such a talk,'" they are presented by way of suitability and unsuitability. In the passage, "that is, sutta, geyya," they are presented by way of the learned teaching. In this place, they are presented by way of completion. Therefore, in this Sutta, one who discusses the ten topics of discussion should speak being established in this point.

Idāni yasmā ekaccassa ekakassa viharatopi attho na sampajjati, tasmā taṃ sandhāya ekībhāve ādīnavaṃ dassento evaṃ sante kho, ānandātiādimāha. Tattha [P 4.0165] evaṃ santeti evaṃ ekībhāve sante.

Now, because for a certain person, even while dwelling alone, the goal is not accomplished, therefore, with reference to him, and showing the danger in solitude, the Blessed One said that which begins with: "This being so, Ānanda..." Therein, "this being so" means: when there is such a state of solitude.

193. Satthāti bāhirako titthakarasatthā. Anvāvattantīti anuāvattanti upasaṅkamanti. Mucchaṃ kāmayatīti mucchanataṇhaṃ pattheti, pavattetīti attho. Ācariyūpaddavenāti abbhantare uppannena kilesūpaddavena ācariyassupaddavo. Sesupaddavesupi eseva nayo. Avadhiṃsu nanti mārayiṃsu naṃ. Etena hi guṇamaraṇaṃ kathitaṃ.

193. "Teacher" means an external, sectarian teacher. "They revolve around" means they repeatedly approach, they attend upon. "He desires questioning" means he desires and gives rise to the craving for questioning; this is the meaning. "By the teacher's affliction" means the teacher's affliction is due to the affliction of defilements that has arisen within oneself. For the other afflictions as well, this same method should be understood. "They killed him" is a gloss for "they slew him." Indeed, by this, the death of virtue was taught.

Vinipātāyāti [M 4.0118] suṭṭhu nipatanāya. Kasmā pana brahmacārupaddavova – “dukkhavipākataro ca kaṭukavipākataro ca vinipātāya ca saṃvattatī”ti vuttoti. Bāhirapabbajjā hi appalābhā, tattha mahanto nibbattetabbaguṇo natthi, aṭṭhasamāpattipañcābhiññāmattakameva hoti. Iti yathā gadrabhapiṭṭhito patitassa mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ na hoti, sarīrassa paṃsumakkhanamattameva hoti, evaṃ bāhirasamaye lokiyaguṇamattatova parihāyati, tena purimaṃ upaddavadvayaṃ na evaṃ vuttaṃ. Sāsane pana pabbajjā mahālābhā, tattha cattāro maggā cattāri phalāni nibbānanti mahantā adhigantabbaguṇā. Iti yathā ubhato sujāto khattiyakumāro hatthikkhandhavaragato nagaraṃ anusañcaranto hatthikkhandhato patito mahādukkhaṃ nigacchati, evaṃ sāsanato parihāyamāno navahi lokuttaraguṇehi parihāyati. Tenāyaṃ brahmacārupaddavo evaṃ vutto.

"For downfall" means for falling completely. But why is only the affliction of the holy life said to "lead to a more painful result, a more bitter result, and to downfall"? Because the external going-forth is of little gain; therein, there is no great quality to be produced; there are only the eight attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. Thus, just as for one who has fallen from a donkey's back there is no great suffering, there is only the smearing of dust on the body, so too in an external system, one declines only from worldly qualities. Therefore, the former two afflictions were not spoken of in this way. But in the Dispensation, the going-forth is of great gain. Therein, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna are great qualities to be realized. Thus, just as a well-born khattiya prince, mounted on a fine elephant and touring the city, meets with great suffering if he falls from the elephant's back, so too one who is declining from the Dispensation falls away from the nine supramundane qualities. For that reason, this affliction of the holy life is spoken of in this way.

196. Tasmāti yasmā sesupaddavehi brahmacārupaddavo dukkhavipākataro, yasmā vā sapattapaṭipattiṃ vītikkamanto dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya [P 4.0166] saṃvattati, mittapaṭipatti hitāya, tasmā. Evaṃ uparimenapi heṭṭhimenapi atthena yojetabbaṃ. Mittavatāyāti mittapaṭipattiyā. Sapattavatāyāti verapaṭipattiyā.

196. "Therefore": because, compared to the other afflictions, the affliction of the holy life has a more painful result; or because one who transgresses conduct like an enemy's leads for a long time to non-benefit and suffering, while conduct like a friend's is for one's benefit; therefore one should act accordingly. Thus, the upper and lower meanings should be connected. "As a friend" means with the conduct of a friend. "As an enemy" means with hostile conduct.

Vokkamma [V 4.0122] ca satthusāsanāti dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattampi hi sañcicca vītikkamanto vokkamma vattati nāma. Tadeva avītikkamanto na vokkamma vattati nāma.

Regarding "having transgressed the Teacher's Dispensation": Indeed, one who intentionally transgresses even a mere offense of wrong-doing or wrong speech is said to be one who acts having transgressed. One who does not transgress just that is said to be one who does not act having transgressed.

Na vo ahaṃ, ānanda, tathā parakkamissāmīti ahaṃ tumhesu tathā na paṭipajjissāmi. Āmaketi apakke. Āmakamatteti āmake nātisukkhe bhājane. Kumbhakāro hi āmakaṃ nātisukkhaṃ apakkaṃ ubhohi hatthehi saṇhikaṃ gaṇhāti “mā bhijjatū”ti. Iti yathā kumbhakāro tattha paṭipajjati, nāhaṃ tumhesu tathā paṭipajjissāmi. Niggayha niggayhāti sakiṃ ovaditvā tuṇhī na bhavissāmi, niggaṇhitvā niggaṇhitvā punappunaṃ ovadissāmi anusāsissāmi. Pavayha pavayhāti dose pavāhetvā pavāhetvā. Yathā pakkabhājanesu kumbhakāro bhinnachinnajajjarāni pavāhetvā [M 4.0119] ekato katvā supakkāneva ākoṭetvā ākoṭetvā gaṇhāti, evameva ahampi pavāhetvā pavāhetvā punappunaṃ ovadissāmi anusāsissāmi. Yo [P 4.0167] sāro so ṭhassatīti evaṃ vo mayā ovadiyamānānaṃ yo maggaphalasāro, so ṭhassati. Apica lokiyaguṇāpi idha sārotveva adhippetā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

‘I will not strive in that way towards you, Ānanda,’ means: ‘I will not act towards you in that way.’ ‘Raw’ means unbaked. ‘A mere raw thing’ means in a raw, not-too-dry vessel. For a potter takes a raw, not-too-dry, unbaked pot gently with both hands, thinking, ‘May it not break.’ Just as the potter acts towards it, so I will not act towards you. ‘Having rebuked, having rebuked’ means: having admonished once, I will not be silent; having rebuked and rebuked, I will admonish and instruct again and again. ‘Having discarded, having discarded’ means having discarded the faults again and again. Just as a potter, with baked vessels, discards the broken, pierced, and decrepit ones, and takes only the well-baked ones after repeatedly tapping them, so too will I, after repeatedly discarding, admonish and instruct again and again. ‘Whatever is the essence, that will remain’ means: thus, while being admonished by me, the essence of the path and fruit that is in you will remain. Moreover, worldly qualities are also intended here as essence. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses, Papañcasūdanī.

Mahāsuññatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Great Discourse on Emptiness is concluded.

3. Acchariyaabbhutasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Amazing and Wonderful.

197. Evaṃ [V 4.0123] me sutanti acchariyaabbhutasuttaṃ. Tattha yatra hi nāmāti acchariyatthe nipāto. Yo nāma tathāgatoti attho. Chinnapapañceti ettha papañcā nāma taṇhā māno diṭṭhīti ime tayo kilesā. Chinnavaṭumeti ettha vaṭumanti kusalākusalakammavaṭṭaṃ vuccati. Pariyādinnavaṭṭeti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbadukkhavītivatteti sabbaṃ vipākavaṭṭasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ vītivatte. Anussarissatīti idaṃ yatrāti nipātavasena anāgatavacanaṃ, attho panettha atītavasena veditabbo. Bhagavā hi te buddhe anussari, na idāni anussarissati. Evaṃjaccāti vipassīādayo khattiyajaccā, kakusandhādayo brāhmaṇajaccāti. Evaṃgottāti vipassīādayo koṇḍaññagottā, kakusandhādayo kassapagottāti. Evaṃsīlāti lokiyalokuttarasīlena evaṃsīlā. Evaṃdhammāti ettha samādhipakkhā dhammā adhippetā[P 4.0168]. Lokiyalokuttarena samādhinā evaṃsamādhinoti attho. Evaṃpaññāti lokiyalokuttarapaññāya evaṃpaññā. Evaṃvihārīti ettha pana heṭṭhā samādhipakkhānaṃ dhammānaṃ gahitattā vihāro gahitova, puna kasmā gahitameva gaṇhātīti ce, na idaṃ gahitameva. Idañhi nirodhasamāpattidīpanatthaṃ, tasmā evaṃnirodhasamāpattivihārīti ayamettha attho.

197. ‘Thus have I heard’ begins the Discourse on the Amazing and Wonderful. Therein, ‘yatra hi nāma’ is a particle in the sense of wonder. The meaning is, ‘The one who is the Tathāgata.’ In ‘one whose proliferations are cut off,’ ‘proliferations’ refers to these three defilements: craving, conceit, and wrong view. In ‘one whose cycle is cut off,’ ‘cycle’ refers to the cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. ‘One whose cycle is mastered’ is a synonym for the same. ‘One who has overcome all suffering’ means those who have overcome all suffering, known as the cycle of results. ‘He will recollect’ is a future tense word due to the particle ‘yatra,’ but the meaning here should be understood in the past tense. For the Blessed One did recollect those Buddhas; he will not recollect them now. ‘Of such a birth’ means that Vipassī and others were of the khattiya birth, while Kakusandha and others were of the brahmin birth. ‘Of such a clan’ means that Vipassī and others were of the Koṇḍañña clan, while Kakusandha and others were of the Kassapa clan. ‘Of such virtue’ means of such virtue through mundane and supramundane virtue. In ‘of such a nature,’ the qualities associated with concentration are intended. The meaning is, ‘of such concentration’ through mundane and supramundane concentration. ‘Of such wisdom’ means of such wisdom through mundane and supramundane wisdom. As for ‘dwelling in such a way,’ since the qualities associated with concentration have already been mentioned above, the ‘dwelling’ has already been covered. If it is asked why what has already been covered is mentioned again, it is not a mere repetition. This is for the purpose of indicating the attainment of cessation. Therefore, the meaning here is, ‘one who dwells in such an attainment of cessation.’

Evaṃvimuttāti [M 4.0120] ettha vikkhambhanavimutti tadaṅgavimutti samucchedavimutti paṭippassaddhivimutti nissaraṇavimuttīti pañcavidhā vimuttiyo. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo sayaṃ vikkhambhitehi nīvaraṇādīhi vimuttattā vikkhambhanavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Aniccānupassanādikā satta anupassanā sayaṃ tassa tassa paccanīkaṅgavasena paricattāhi niccasaññādīhi vimuttattā tadaṅgavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Cattāro ariyamaggā sayaṃ samucchinnehi kilesehi vimuttattā samucchedavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Cattāri sāmaññaphalāni maggānubhāvena kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhante uppannattā paṭippassaddhivimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Nibbānaṃ sabbakilesehi nissaṭattā apagatattā dūre ṭhitattā nissaraṇavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Iti imāsaṃ pañcannaṃ vimuttīnaṃ vasena evaṃvimuttāti evamettha attho veditabbo.

In ‘thus liberated,’ there are five kinds of liberation: liberation by suppression, liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by cutting off, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape. Therein, the eight attainments are called ‘liberation by suppression’ because they are liberated from the hindrances and so forth which have been suppressed by them. The seven contemplations, such as the contemplation of impermanence, are called ‘liberation by substitution of opposites’ because they are liberated from the perceptions of permanence and so forth, which have been abandoned by way of the opposing factor for each. The four noble paths are called ‘liberation by cutting off’ because they are liberated from the defilements which have been cut off by them. The four fruits of recluseship are called ‘liberation by tranquillization’ because they arise at the end of the tranquillization of the defilements through the power of the path. Nibbāna is called ‘liberation by escape’ because it has escaped from all defilements, has departed from them, and stands afar. Thus, the meaning here of ‘thus liberated’ should be understood according to these five kinds of liberation.

199. Tasmātihāti [V 4.0124] yasmā tvaṃ “tathāgatā acchariyā”ti vadasi, tasmā taṃ bhiyyoso mattāya paṭibhantu tathāgatassa acchariyā abbhutadhammāti. Sato sampajānoti ettha dvesampajaññāni manussaloke devaloke ca. Tattha vessantarajātake brāhmaṇassa [P 4.0169] dve putte datvā punadivase sakkassa deviṃ datvā sakkena pasīditvā dinne aṭṭha vare gaṇhanto –

199. ‘Therefore’ means: since you say, ‘The Tathāgatas are wonderful,’ therefore may the wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata appear to you even more. ‘Mindful and clearly comprehending’ means there are two kinds of clear comprehension: in the human world and in the divine world. There is the instance in the Vessantara Jātaka, when, after giving his two children to the brahmin and, on the following day, giving his wife to Sakka, he received eight boons from Sakka who was pleased:

“Ito vimuccamānāhaṃ, saggagāmī visesagū;

Anivattī tato assaṃ, aṭṭhametaṃ varaṃ vare”ti. (jā. 2.22.2300) –

“Being freed from here, I shall go to heaven, attaining excellence; may I not return from there. This eighth boon I choose.”

Evaṃ tusitabhavane me paṭisandhi hotūti varaṃ aggahesi, tato paṭṭhāya tusitabhavane uppajjissāmīti jānāti, idaṃ manussaloke sampajaññaṃ. Vessantarattabhāvato pana cuto puna tusitabhavane nibbattitvā nibbattosmīti aññāsi, idaṃ devaloke sampajaññaṃ.

Thus he took the boon, “May my rebirth be in the Tusita abode.” From then on, he knows, “I will be reborn in the Tusita abode.” This is clear comprehension in the human world. But having passed away from the Vessantara existence and having been reborn in the Tusita abode, he knew, “I have been reborn.” This is clear comprehension in the divine world.

Kiṃ pana sesadevatā na jānantīti? No na jānanti. Tā pana uyyānavimānakapparukkhe oloketvā devanāṭakehi tūriyasaddena pabodhitā “mārisa ayaṃ devaloko tumhe idha nibbattā”ti sāritā jānanti. Bodhisatto paṭhamajavanavāre na jānāti, dutiyajavanato paṭṭhāya jānāti. Iccassa aññehi asādhāraṇajānanaṃ hoti.

But do other deities not know? It is not that they do not know; they do indeed know. However, they know only after looking at the parks, celestial mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees, and being awakened by the sound of celestial music from divine performers, and being reminded, “Friend, this is the divine world; you have been reborn here.” The Bodhisatta does not know in the first moment of impulsion, but knows from the second moment of impulsion onward. Thus, his is a knowing not shared with others.

Aṭṭhāsīti [M 4.0121] ettha kiñcāpi aññepi devā tattha ṭhitā ṭhitamhāti jānanti, te pana chasu dvāresu balavatā iṭṭhārammaṇena abhibhuyyamānā satiṃ vissajjetvā attano bhuttapītabhāvampi ajānantā āhārūpacchedena kālaṃ karonti. Bodhisattassa kiṃ tathārūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ natthīti? No natthi. So hi sesadeve dasahi ṭhānehi adhiggaṇhāti, ārammaṇena pana attānaṃ maddituṃ na deti, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ abhibhavitvā tiṭṭhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sato sampajāno, ānanda, bodhisatto tusite kāye aṭṭhāsī”ti.

Here, regarding 'he remained' (aṭṭhāsīti), although other devas dwelling there know, 'We are dwelling here,' they, however, being overpowered at the six sense doors by a powerful, desirable object, relinquish mindfulness and, not even knowing their own state of having eaten and drunk, die from the cutting off of nourishment. Is there no such object for the Bodhisatta? It is not that there is no such object. For he surpasses the other devas in ten respects; however, he does not allow himself to be crushed by an object, but overcomes that object and remains. Therefore it was said: 'Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta remained in the Tusita realm.'

200. Yāvatāyukanti sesattabhāvesu kiṃ yāvatāyukaṃ na tiṭṭhattīti? Āma na tiṭṭhati. Aññadā hi dīghāyukadevaloke nibbatto tattha pāramiyo na sakkā pūretunti akkhīni nimīletvā adhimuttikālaṃkiriyaṃ nāma katvā manussaloke nibbattati[P 4.0170]. Ayaṃ kālaṅkiriyā [V 4.0125] aññesaṃ na hoti. Tadā pana adinnadānaṃ nāma natthi, arakkhitasīlaṃ nāma natthi, sabbapāramīnaṃ pūritattā yāvatāyukaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

200. Regarding 'for the full extent of his lifespan' (yāvatāyukaṃ), does he not remain for his full lifespan in other states of existence? Indeed, he does not remain. For at another time, when reborn in a long-lived deva world, thinking, 'It is not possible to fulfill the perfections there,' he closes his eyes, performs what is called 'death by determination,' and is reborn in the human world. This kind of passing away does not happen for others. But at that time, there was no such thing as a gift not yet given, no such thing as morality not yet guarded. Because all the perfections had been fulfilled, he remained for the full extent of his lifespan.

Sato sampajāno tusitā kāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkamatīti evaṃ tāva sabbapāramiyo pūretvā tadā bodhisatto yāvatāyukaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Devatānaṃ pana – “manussagaṇanāvasena idāni sattahi divasehi cuti bhavissatī”ti pañca pubbanimittāni uppajjanti – mālā milāyanti, vatthāni kilissanti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, kāye dubbaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, devo devāsane na saṇṭhāti.

Regarding the passage, 'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he passes away from the Tusita realm and enters his mother’s womb': Thus, having first fulfilled all the perfections, the Bodhisatta at that time remained for the full extent of his lifespan. However, for devas, when it is said, 'According to human reckoning, passing away will now occur in seven days,' five portents arise: the garlands wither, the garments become soiled, sweat is released from the armpits, unattractiveness descends upon the body, and the deva cannot remain steady in his divine seat.

Tattha mālāti paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase piḷandhanamālā. Tā kira saṭṭhisatasahassādhikā sattapaṇṇāsa-vassakoṭiyo amilāyitvā tadā milāyanti. Vatthesupi eseva nayo. Ettakaṃ pana kālaṃ devānaṃ neva sītaṃ na uṇhaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ kāle sarīrato bindubinduvasena sedā muccanti. Ettakañca kālaṃ tesaṃ sarīre khaṇḍiccapāliccādivasena vivaṇṇatā na paññāyati, devadhītā soḷasavassuddesikā viya, devaputtā vīsativassuddesikā viya khāyanti. Maraṇakāle pana nesaṃ kilantarūpo attabhāvo hoti. Ettakañca nesaṃ kālaṃ devaloke ukkaṇṭhitā [M 4.0122] nāma natthi, maraṇakāle pana nissasanti vijambhanti, sake āsane nābhiramanti.

Herein, 'garlands' refers to the garlands worn on the day of taking rebirth-linking. It is said that these garlands, not having withered for fifty-seven crores and six million years, then wither. The same principle applies to the garments. For such a length of time, there is neither cold nor heat for the devas, but at that time, sweat is released from their bodies drop by drop. And for such a length of time, no unattractiveness by way of broken teeth, grey hair, and so on, is apparent on their bodies; the devadhītās appear as if sixteen years of age, and the devaputtas as if twenty years of age. At the time of death, however, their physical existence becomes exhausted. And for such a length of time, there is no such thing as discontent for them in the deva world; but at the time of death, they sigh and yawn, and do not delight in their own seats.

Imāni pana pubbanimittāni, yathā loke mahāpuññānaṃ rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃyeva ukkāpātabhūmicālacandaggāhādīni [P 4.0171] nimittāni paññāyanti, na sabbesaṃ, evameva mahesakkhānaṃ devatānaṃyeva paññāyanti, na sabbesaṃ. Yathā ca manussesu pubbanimittāni nakkhattapāṭhakādayova jānanti, na sabbe, evameva tānipi sabbe devā na jānanti, paṇḍitā eva pana jānanti. Tattha ye ca mandena kusalakammena nibbattā devaputtā, te tesu uppannesu – “idāni ko jānāti, kuhiṃ nibbattissāmā”ti bhāyanti. Ye mahāpuññā, te – “amhehi dinnaṃ dānaṃ rakkhitaṃ sīlaṃ bhāvitaṃ bhāvanaṃ āgamma uparidevalokesu sampattiṃ anubhavissāmā”ti na bhāyanti. Bodhisattopi tāni pubbanimittāni disvā “idāni anantare attabhāve buddho bhavissāmī”ti na bhāyi. Athassa tesu nimittesu pātubhūtesu dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatitvā – “mārisa tumhehi dasa pāramiyo pūrentehi na sakkasampattiṃ na mārabrahmacakkavattisampattiṃ [V 4.0126] patthentehi pūritā, lokanittharaṇatthāya pana buddhattaṃ patthayamānehi pūritā. So vo idāni kālo mārisa buddhattāya, samayo mārisa buddhattāyā”ti yācanti.

These portents, however, just as in the world signs such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses appear only for those of great merit—kings, ministers of kings, and the like—and not for everyone, so too do they appear only for devas of great power, and not for all. And just as among humans, only those skilled in astrology and the like know the portents, not everyone, so too among devas, not all know them; only the wise do. Among them, those devaputtas born from weak wholesome kamma, when these portents arise, become fearful, thinking, 'Who knows now where we will be reborn?' But those of great merit do not fear, thinking, 'Relying on the gifts we have given, the morality we have guarded, and the meditation we have developed, we will experience prosperity in higher deva worlds.' The Bodhisatta, too, seeing these portents, did not fear, thinking, 'Now, in my very next existence, I will become a Buddha.' Then, when these signs had appeared to him, the devas of the ten thousand world-systems assembled and entreated him, saying: 'Venerable Sir, when you were fulfilling the ten perfections, you did so not aspiring for the splendor of Sakka, nor for the splendor of Māra, Brahmā, or a universal monarch, but aspiring to Buddhahood for the sake of liberation from the world. Now, Venerable Sir, is the time for your Buddhahood; now, Venerable Sir, is the occasion for your Buddhahood.'

Atha mahāsatto devatānaṃ paṭiññaṃ adatvāva kāladīpadesakulajanettiāyuparicchedavasena pañcamahāvilokanaṃ nāma vilokesi. Tattha “kālo nu kho, na kālo”ti paṭhamaṃ kālaṃ vilokesi. Tattha vassasatasahassato uddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaāyukālo kālo nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā hi sattānaṃ jātijarāmaraṇāni na paññāyanti, buddhānañca dhammadesanā nāma tilakkhaṇamuttā natthi, tesaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti kathentānaṃ “kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathentī”ti neva sotuṃ na saddhātuṃ [P 4.0172] maññanti, tato abhisamayo na hoti, tasmiṃ asati aniyyānikaṃ sāsanaṃ hoti. Tasmā so akālo. Vassasatato ūnaāyukālopi kālo nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā hi sattā ussannakilesā honti, ussannakilesānañca dinnovādo ovādaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati. Udake daṇḍarāji viya khippaṃ vigacchati. Tasmā sopi akālo. Satasahassato [M 4.0123] pana paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā vassasatato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ āyukālo kālo nāma. Tadā ca vassasatakālo hoti. Atha mahāsatto “nibbattitabbakālo”ti kālaṃ passi.

Then the Great Being, without giving his pledge to the devas, made the survey known as the five great considerations: time, continent, country, clan, and the mother's lifespan. Therein, he first surveyed the time, thinking, 'Is it the right time or not?' In this regard, a time when the lifespan is more than one hundred thousand years is not called the right time. Why? Because at that time, birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings, and there is no Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas that is apart from the three characteristics. When the Buddhas preach of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, beings think, 'What is this they are saying?' and are not inclined to listen or to have faith. Consequently, there is no realization, and in its absence, the teaching does not lead out of saṃsāra. Therefore, that is an inappropriate time. A time when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not called the right time. Why? Because at that time, beings have abundant defilements, and for those with abundant defilements, the advice given does not remain in its place. Like a line drawn on water, it quickly vanishes. Therefore, that too is an inappropriate time. However, a lifespan from one hundred thousand years downwards and from one hundred years upwards is called the right time. And at that time, the lifespan was one hundred years. Then the Great Being saw, 'It is the time to be born.'

Tato dīpaṃ vilokento saparivāre cattāro dīpe oloketvā – “tīsu dīpesu buddhā na nibbattanti, jambudīpeyeva nibbattantī”ti dīpaṃ passi.

Then, surveying the continent, he looked at the four continents together with their surrounding islands and, seeing that 'Buddhas do not arise in the three continents; they arise only in Jambudīpa,' he saw the continent.

Tato – “jambudīpo nāma mahā, dasayojanasahassaparimāṇo, katarasmiṃ nu kho padese buddhā nibbattantī”ti desaṃ vilokento majjhimadesaṃ passi. Majjhimadeso nāma “puratthimāya disāya gajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo”tiādinā nayena vinaye (mahāva. 259) vuttova. So pana āyāmato tīṇi yojanasatāni. Vitthārato aḍḍhatiyāni, parikkhepato navayojanasatānīti. Etasmiñhi padese cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyāni, kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambuddhā uppajjanti. Dve asaṅkhyeyyāni, kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā paccekabuddhā uppajjanti, ekaṃ [P 4.0173] asaṅkhyeyyaṃ, kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūretvā sāriputtamoggallānādayo mahāsāvakā uppajjanti, catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ dvisahassānaṃ parittadīpānañca issariyādhipaccakārakacakkavattirājāno uppajjanti, aññe ca mahesakkhā khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatimahāsālā [V 4.0127] uppajjanti. Idañcettha kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ, tattha mayā nibbattitabbanti niṭṭhamagamāsi.

Then, surveying the region, thinking: 'The great Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent. In which region, I wonder, do Buddhas arise?' he saw the Middle Country. The Middle Country is indeed that which was spoken of in the Vinaya by the method beginning with: 'In the eastern direction is the market town named Gajaṅgala.' Now, it is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in breadth, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. For in this region, having fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas arise. Having fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons, Paccekabuddhas arise. Having fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand aeons, great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna arise. Wheel-turning monarchs who exercise sovereignty and dominion over the four great continents and the two thousand minor islands arise. And other powerful ones—great personages of the warrior, brahmin, and householder classes—arise. And here is this city named Kapilavatthu; there I must be born.' Thus he came to a conclusion.

Tato kulaṃ vilokento – “buddhā nāma lokasammate kule nibbattanti, idāni ca khattiyakulaṃ lokasammataṃ, tattha nibbattissāmi, suddhodano nāma rājā me pitā bhavissatī”ti kulaṃ passi.

Then, surveying the family, he reflected: 'Buddhas are born in a family esteemed by the world, and now the warrior family is esteemed by the world. I shall be born there. The king named Suddhodana will be my father.' Thus he saw the family.

Tato mātaraṃ vilokento – “buddhamātā nāma lolā surādhuttā na hoti, kappasatasahassaṃ pūritapāramī jātito paṭṭhāya akhaṇḍapañcasīlā hoti, ayañca mahāmāyā nāma devī edisā. Ayaṃ me mātā bhavissati. Kittakaṃ panassā āyū”ti āvajjanto – “dasannaṃ māsānaṃ upari satta divasānī”ti passi.

Then, surveying the mother, he reflected: 'The mother of a Buddha is not frivolous or a drunkard. Having fulfilled the perfections for one hundred thousand aeons, from birth onwards she possesses the unbroken five precepts. And this queen named Mahāmāyā is of such a nature. This one will be my mother. Now, what will be her lifespan?' Adverting to this, he saw: 'Seven days over and above ten months.'

Iti [M 4.0124] imaṃ pañcamahāvilokanaṃ viloketvā – “kālo me mārisā buddhabhāvāyā”ti devatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karonto paṭiññaṃ datvā “gacchatha tumhe”ti tā devatā uyyojetvā tusitadevatāhi parivuto tusitapure nandanavanaṃ pāvisi. Sabbadevalokesu hi nandanavanaṃ atthiyeva. Tattha naṃ devatā – “ito cuto sugatiṃ gaccha, ito cuto sugatiṃ gacchā”ti pubbekatakusalakammokāsaṃ sārayamānā vicaranti. So evaṃ devatāhi kusalaṃ sārayamānāhi parivuto tattha vicarantova cavi.

Thus, having made these five great surveyings, showing favour to the devas who were requesting, 'Sirs, it is time for my Buddhahood,' he gave his consent. Saying, 'You may go,' he dismissed those devas and, surrounded by the Tusita devas, entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita celestial realm. Indeed, in all deva worlds there is a Nandana Grove. There, the devas wander about, causing him to recollect the opportunity of wholesome kamma done in the past, saying: 'Having passed away from here, go to a good destination! Having passed away from here, go to a good destination!' Thus, surrounded by devas who were causing him to recollect what is wholesome, he passed away while wandering there.

Evaṃ cuto cavāmīti pajānāti, cuticittaṃ na [P 4.0174] jānāti. Paṭisandhiṃ gahetvāpi paṭisandhicittaṃ na jānāti, imasmiṃ me ṭhāne paṭisandhi gahitāti evaṃ pana jānāti. Keci pana therā “āvajjanapariyāyo nāma laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, dutiyatatiyacittavāreyeva jānissatī”ti vadanti. Tipiṭakamahāsīvatthero panāha – “mahāsattānaṃ paṭisandhi na aññesaṃ paṭisandhisadisā, koṭippattaṃ tesaṃ satisampajaññaṃ. Yasmā pana teneva cittena taṃ cittaṃ ñātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā cuticittaṃ na jānāti. Cutikkhaṇepi cavāmīti pajānāti, paṭisandhiṃ gahetvāpi paṭisandhicittaṃ na jānāti, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne paṭisandhi gahitāti pajānāti, tasmiṃ kāle dasasahassī kampatī”ti. Evaṃ sato sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamanto pana ekūnavīsatiyā paṭisandhicittesu [V 4.0128] mettāpubbabhāgassa somanassa-sahagata-ñāṇasampayutta-asaṅkhārika-kusalacittassa sadisamahāvipākacittena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Mahāsīvatthero pana “upekkhāsahagatenā”ti āha.

Thus, when passing away, he knows, 'I am passing away,' but he does not know the death-consciousness. Even after taking rebirth-linking, he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness. However, he knows thus: 'By me, rebirth-linking has been taken in this place.' But some elders say: 'It is fitting that a mode of adverting is obtained; he will know it only in the second or third mind-moment.' The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva, however, said: 'The rebirth-linking of great beings is not like the rebirth-linking of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension have reached the pinnacle. However, because it is not possible to know that consciousness with that very same consciousness, therefore he does not know the death-consciousness. Even at the moment of death, he knows, "I am passing away." Even after taking rebirth-linking, he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness. He knows, "Rebirth-linking has been taken in such-and-such a place," and at that time the ten-thousandfold world-system trembles.' Now, entering the mother’s womb mindful and clearly comprehending, among the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness, he took rebirth-linking with a great resultant consciousness that is similar to an unprompted wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge, accompanied by joy, and preceded by loving-kindness. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, said it was with one accompanied by equanimity.

Paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanto pana āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāyaṃ uttarāsāḷhanakkhattena aggahesi. Tadā kira mahāmāyā pure puṇṇamāya sattamadivasato paṭṭhāya vigatasurāpānaṃ mālāgandhavibhūsanasampannaṃ nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānā sattame divase pāto vuṭṭhāya gandhodakena nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā varabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya sirīgabbhaṃ [P 4.0175] pavisitvā sirīsayane nipannā niddaṃ okkamamānā idaṃ supinaṃ addasa – “cattāro kira naṃ mahārājāno sayaneneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā anotattadahaṃ netvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ deviyo āgantvā manussamalaharaṇatthaṃ nhāpetvā dibbavatthaṃ nivāsetvā gandhehi vilimpetvā dibbapupphāni piḷandhitvā tato avidūre rajatapabbato, tassa anto kanakavimānaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ pācīnato [M 4.0125] sīsaṃ katvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Atha bodhisatto setavaravāraṇo hutvā tato avidūre eko suvaṇṇapabbato, tattha caritvā tato oruyha rajatapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā uttaradisato āgamma kanakavimānaṃ pavisitvā mātaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ phāletvā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso ahosi.

Now, taking rebirth-linking, he did so on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation. At that time, it is said, Queen Mahāmāyā, for seven days prior to the full moon, had been abstaining from intoxicants and enjoying the constellation festival, adorned with garlands and perfumes. On the seventh day, rising early in the morning, she bathed with scented water, adorned herself with all her ornaments, partook of excellent food, and undertook the Uposatha precepts. Entering the royal chamber and lying down on the royal couch, as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: The four great kings, it is said, lifted her up together with her couch, took her to Lake Anotatta, and set her down in a secluded place. Then their queens came and, to remove human stains, bathed her, dressed her in divine clothes, anointed her with divine perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there is a silver mountain, and within it, a golden mansion. There they laid her down with her head to the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a splendid white elephant, was roaming on a golden mountain not far from there. Descending from it and ascending the silver mountain, he approached from the north, entered the golden mansion, circumambulated his mother to the right, and it was as if he entered her womb by splitting her right side.

Atha pabuddhā devī taṃ supinaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā pabhātāya rattiyā catusaṭṭhimatte brāhmaṇapāmokkhe pakkosāpetvā haritūpalittāya lājādīhi katamaṅgalasakkārāya bhūmiyā mahārahāni āsanāni paññāpetvā tattha nisinnānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ sappimadhusakkarābhisaṅkhārassa varapāyāsassa suvaṇṇarajatapātiyo pūretvā suvaṇṇarajatapātītiheva paṭikujjitvā adāsi, aññehi ca ahatavatthakapilagāvīdānādīhi te santappesi. Atha nesaṃ sabbakāmasantappitānaṃ supinaṃ ārocāpetvā – “kiṃ bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā āhaṃsu – “mā cintayi mahārāja, deviyā te kucchimhi gabbho patiṭṭhito, so ca kho purisagabbho, na itthigabbho, putto te bhavissati. So sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasissati, rājā bhavissati cakkavattī. Sace agārā nikkhamma pabbajissati, buddho bhavissati [P 4.0176] loke vivaṭṭacchado”ti. Evaṃ sato sampajāno bodhisatto tusitakāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkamati.

Then the queen, having awakened, related that dream to the king. When the night had dawned, the king had sixty-four leading brahmins summoned. On ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and where auspicious offerings of puffed rice and other things had been made, he had seats worthy of great personages prepared. To the brahmins seated there, he filled golden and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, and covering them with golden and silver bowls, he presented them. Moreover, he gratified them with other things such as new cloth and tawny cows. Then, when they were well gratified with all desired things, he had the dream related and asked, “What will be the result?” The brahmins replied, “Do not worry, great king. A conception has been established in the queen’s womb, and it is a male conception, not a female conception. You will have a son. If he dwells in the household, he will become a wheel-turning monarch. If he goes forth from the household and becomes a renunciant, he will become a Buddha in the world, one who has rolled back the veil.” Thus, mindful and fully aware, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the host of Tusita devas, descends into his mother’s womb.

Tattha [V 4.0129] sato sampajānoti iminā catutthāya gabbhāvakkantiyā okkamatīti dasseti. Catasso hi gabbhāvakkantiyo.

Herein, by the phrase “mindful and fully aware,” it is shown that he descends by the fourth mode of conception in the womb. For there are four modes of conception in the womb.

“Catasso imā, bhante, gabbhāvakkantiyo. Idha, bhante, ekacco asampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ paṭhamā gabbhāvakkanti.

“Venerable sir, there are these four modes of conception in the womb. Here, venerable sir, a certain person descends into the mother’s womb not fully aware, remains in the mother's womb not fully aware, and emerges from the mother's womb not fully aware. This is the first mode of conception in the womb.

Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ dutiyā gabbhāvakkanti.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb fully aware, remains in the mother's womb not fully aware, and emerges from the mother's womb not fully aware. This is the second mode of conception in the womb.

Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ tatiyā gabbhāvakkanti.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb fully aware, remains in the mother's womb fully aware, but emerges from the mother's womb not fully aware. This is the third mode of conception in the womb.

Puna [M 4.0126] caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, sampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ catutthā gabbhāvakkantī”ti (dī. ni. 3.147).

Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb fully aware, remains in the mother's womb fully aware, and emerges from the mother's womb fully aware. This is the fourth mode of conception in the womb.”

Etāsu paṭhamā lokiyamanussānaṃ hoti, dutiyā asītimahāsāvakānaṃ, tatiyā dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ paccekabodhisattānañca. Te kira kammajavātehi uddhaṃpādā adhosirā anekasataporise papāte viya yonimukhe tāḷacchiggalena hatthī viya ativiya sambādhena yonimukhena nikkhamamānā anantaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti. Tena nesaṃ “mayaṃ nikkhamāmā”ti sampajānatā na hoti. Catutthā sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ. Te hi mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantāpi jānanti, tattha vasantāpi jānanti. Nikkhamanakālepi [P 4.0177] nesaṃ kammajavātā uddhaṃpāde adhosire katvā khipituṃ na sakkonti, dve hatthe pasāretvā akkhīni ummīletvā ṭhitakāva nikkhamanti.

Among these, the first is for worldly human beings, the second for the eighty great disciples, and the third for the two chief disciples and the Paccekabodhisattas. It is said that they, by the karmic winds, are turned with feet up and head down at the opening of the womb, like one falling into a precipice of more than a hundred men's height. Emerging through the extremely constricted opening of the womb, like an elephant through a keyhole, they experience endless suffering. Therefore, for them, there is no full awareness of “we are emerging.” The fourth is for the all-knowing Bodhisattas. For they know even when taking rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, and they know while dwelling there. Even at the time of emerging, the karmic winds are not able to cast them down with feet up and head down; stretching out both hands and opening their eyes, they emerge while standing.

201. Mātukucchiṃ okkamatīti ettha mātukucchiṃ okkanto hotīti attho. Okkante [V 4.0130] hi tasmiṃ evaṃ hoti, na okkamamāne. Appamāṇoti buddhappamāṇo, vipuloti attho. Uḷāroti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Devānubhāvanti ettha devānaṃ ayamānubhāvo – nivatthavatthassa pabhā dvādasa yojanāni pharati, tathā sarīrassa, tathā alaṅkārassa, tathā vimānassa, taṃ atikkamitvāti attho.

201. In the phrase “He descends into the mother's womb,” the meaning is “he has descended into the mother's womb.” For this is so of one who has descended, not of one who is in the process of descending. “Immeasurable” means of the measure of a Buddha; the meaning is “vast.” “Sublime” is a synonym for that very word. In the phrase “surpassing the divine power,” this is the power of the devas: the radiance of a worn garment spreads for twelve yojanas, likewise that of the body, likewise that of the ornaments. The meaning is “having surpassed that.”

Lokantarikāti tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ antarā ekeko lokantarikā hoti, tiṇṇaṃ sakaṭacakkānaṃ pattānaṃ vā aññamaññaṃ āhacca ṭhapitānaṃ majjhe okāso viya. So pana lokantarikanirayo parimāṇato aṭṭhayojanasahasso hoti. Aghāti niccavivaṭā. Asaṃvutāti heṭṭhāpi appatiṭṭhā. Andhakārāti tamabhūtā. Andhakāratimisāti cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇato andhabhāvakaraṇatimisena samannāgatā. Tattha kira cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na jāyati. Evaṃmahiddhikāti candimasūriyā kira ekappahāreneva tīsu dīpesu paññāyanti, evaṃmahiddhikā. Ekekāya disāya navanavayojanasatasahassāni andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokaṃ dassenti, evaṃ mahānubhāvā. Ābhāya [P 4.0178] nānubhontīti attano [M 4.0127] pabhāya nappahonti. Te kira cakkavāḷapabbatassa vemajjhena caranti, cakkavāḷapabbatañca atikkamma lokantarikanirayo, tasmā te tattha ābhāya nappahonti.

Lokantarikā means that between every three world-systems, there is one Lokantarika hell, like the space in the middle of three cart-wheels or bowls placed touching one another. That Lokantarika hell measures eight thousand yojanas in extent. Agha means always open. Asaṃvutā means having no foundation below. Andhakārā means being utter darkness. Andhakāratimisā means endowed with a darkness that causes blindness by preventing the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there. Evaṃmahiddhikā (of such great power): it is said the moon and sun appear in three continents at the very same instant; thus they are of great power. In each direction, they dispel darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas and show light; thus they are of great might. Ābhāya nānubhonti (they are not able with their radiance) means they are not sufficient with their own radiance. It is said they travel through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and the Lokantarika hell is situated beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain range; therefore, they are not sufficient with their radiance there.

Yepi tattha sattāti yepi tasmiṃ lokantaramahāniraye sattā upapannā. Kiṃ pana kammaṃ katvā te tattha uppajjantīti? Bhāriyaṃ dāruṇaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānañca upari aparādhaṃ aññañca divase divase pāṇavadhādisāhasikakammaṃ katvā uppajjanti tambapaṇṇidīpe abhayacoranāgacorādayo viya. Tesaṃ attabhāvo tigāvutiko hoti, vaggulīnaṃ viya dīghanakhā honti. Te rukkhe vagguliyo viya nakhehi cakkavāḷapāde lagganti. Yadā pana saṃsappantā aññamaññassa hatthapāsaṃ gatā honti, atha “bhakkho no laddho”ti maññamānā tattha vāvaṭā viparivattitvā lokasandhārakaudake patanti. Vāte paharante madhukaphalāni viya chijjitvā udake patanti. Patitamattā ca accantakhāre udake piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya vilīyanti.
