“Those beings there” refers to those beings born in that great Lokantarika hell. What deeds lead them to be reborn there? By committing grave and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous ascetics and brahmins, and by daily committing other violent acts such as killing living beings, they are reborn there, like the thieves Abhayacora and Nāgacora on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their bodies are three gāvutas in height, and they have long nails like bats. They cling to the foot of the Cakkavāḷa mountain with their nails, just as bats cling to trees. When, crawling, they come within arm’s reach of one another, thinking, “We have found food,” they strive to seize them, but turning over, they fall into the world-sustaining water. As if struck by the wind, they are severed like madhuca fruits and fall into the water. The moment they fall, they dissolve like lumps of flour in the extremely caustic water.

Aññepi kira bho santi sattāti – “yathā mayaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavāma, evaṃ aññepi kira sattā idaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantā idhūpapannā”ti taṃ divasaṃ passanti. Ayaṃ pana obhāso ekayāgupānamattampi [V 4.0131] na tiṭṭhati, yāvatā niddāyitvā pabuddho ārammaṇaṃ vibhāveti, tattakaṃ kālaṃ hoti. Dīghabhāṇakā pana “accharāsaṅghāṭamattameva vijjubhāso viya niccharitvā kiṃ idanti bhaṇantānaṃyeva antaradhāyatī”ti vadanti. Saṅkampatīti [P 4.0179] samantato kampati. Itaradvayaṃ purimapasseva vevacanaṃ. Puna appamāṇo cātiādi nigamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Sirs, it seems there are other beings”—thinking, “Just as we experience great suffering, so too, it seems, other beings experiencing this suffering are reborn here,” they see one another on that day. This radiance, however, does not last even for the time it takes to drink a single portion of gruel; it lasts only as long as it takes for one who has slept to awaken and discern an object. The reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya, however, say, “It flashes out for only the duration of a finger-snap, like lightning, and vanishes even as they are saying, ‘What is this?’” “It trembles” means it trembles all around. The other two terms are synonyms of the preceding one. Again, the passage beginning “immeasurable” is stated for the purpose of conclusion.

202. Cattāro devaputtā catuddisaṃ ārakkhāya upagacchantīti ettha cattāroti catunnaṃ mahārājūnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, dasasahassacakkavāḷe pana cattāro cattāro katvā cattālīsadasasahassā honti. Tattha imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe mahārājāno khaggahatthā āgantvā bodhisattassa ārakkhaṇatthāya upagantvā sirīgabbhaṃ paviṭṭhā, itare gabbhadvārato paṭṭhāya avaruddhapaṃsupisācakādiyakkhagaṇe [M 4.0128] paṭikkamāpetvā yāva cakkavāḷā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu.

202. In the passage, “Four devaputtas came from the four directions to provide protection,” the word “four” is stated with reference to the four Great Kings. However, in the ten-thousand-fold world-system, taking them four by four, there are forty thousand. Among them, the Great Kings of this world-system, with swords in hand, came to guard the Bodhisatta and entered the auspicious chamber. The others, starting from the chamber door, drove back the unpleasant hordes of yakkhas, such as the paṃsupisācakas, and established a guard as far as the edge of the world-system.

Kimatthaṃ panāyaṃ rakkhā āgatā? Nanu paṭisandhikkhaṇe kalalakālato paṭṭhāya sacepi koṭisatasahassā mārā koṭisatasahassaṃ sineruṃ ukkhipitvā bodhisattassa vā bodhisattamātuyā vā antarāyakaraṇatthaṃ āgaccheyyuṃ, sabbe antarāva antaradhāyeyyuṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā ruhiruppādavatthusmiṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ parūpakkamena tathāgataṃ jīvitā voropeyya. Anupakkamena, bhikkhave, tathāgatā parinibbāyanti. Gacchatha tumhe, bhikkhave, yathāvihāraṃ, arakkhiyā, bhikkhave, tathāgatā”ti (cūḷava. 341). Evametaṃ, na parūpakkamena tesaṃ jīvitantarāyo atthi. Santi kho pana amanussā virūpā duddasikā, bheravarupā pakkhino, yesaṃ rūpaṃ disvā saddaṃ vā sutvā bodhisattamātu bhayaṃ vā santāso vā uppajjeyya, tesaṃ nivāraṇatthāya [P 4.0180] rakkhaṃ aggahesuṃ. Apica kho bodhisattassa puññatejena sañjātagāravā attano gāravacoditāpi te evamakaṃsu.

For what purpose, then, has this protection come? Is it not the case that from the moment of conception, from the kalala stage onwards, even if a hundred thousand koṭis of Māras were to lift a hundred thousand koṭis of Mount Sinerus and come to harm the Bodhisatta or his mother, they would all vanish midway? Indeed, this was stated by the Blessed One in the account of the shedding of his blood: “It is impossible, monks, it cannot be, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life by an attack. Tathāgatas, monks, attain final Nibbāna without being attacked. Go, monks, to your dwellings; Tathāgatas do not need to be guarded.” That is true; there is no danger to their lives from an external attack. However, there are non-human beings, deformed and unpleasant to see, and birds of terrifying form, seeing whose appearance or hearing whose sounds might cause fear or terror to arise in the Bodhisatta’s mother. To prevent this, they undertook the guard. Moreover, with reverence born from the Bodhisatta’s power of merit, and also impelled by their own reverence, they acted thus.

Kiṃ pana te antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā ṭhitā cattāro mahārājāno bodhisattamātuyā attānaṃ dassenti na dassentīti? Nahānamaṇḍanabhojanādisarīrakiccakāle na dassenti, sirīgabbhaṃ pavisitvā varasayane nipannakāle pana dassenti. Tattha kiñcāpi amanussadassanaṃ nāma manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ hoti, bodhisattamātā pana attano ceva puttassa ca puññānubhāvena te disvā na bhāyati, pakatiantepurapālakesu viya assā tesu cittaṃ uppajjati.

Now, do those four Great Kings who have entered and are standing in the inner chamber show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not? During bodily activities such as bathing, adorning herself, and eating, they do not show themselves. However, when she has entered the auspicious chamber and is lying on her excellent bed, they do show themselves. In this case, although the sight of non-human beings is frightening to humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother, by the power of her own and her son’s merit, feels no fear upon seeing them. Her thought towards them arises just as it would towards the ordinary palace guards.

203. Pakatiyā [V 4.0132] sīlavatīti sabhāveneva sīlasampannā. Anuppanne kira buddhe manussā tāpasaparibbājakānaṃ santike vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā sīlaṃ gaṇhanti, bodhisattamātāpi kāladevilassa isino santike gaṇhāti. Bodhisatte pana kucchigate aññassa pādamūle nisīdituṃ nāma na sakkā, samāsane nisīditvā gahitasīlampi avaññā kāraṇamattaṃ hoti. Tasmā sayameva sīlaṃ aggahesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

203. “Naturally virtuous” means that she was endowed with virtue by her very nature. It is said that when a Buddha has not yet arisen, people go to ascetics and wanderers, pay homage, sit in the squatting posture, and undertake the precepts. The Bodhisatta’s mother, too, used to undertake the precepts in the presence of the sage Kāladevila. However, once the Bodhisatta was in her womb, it was not possible for her to sit at the feet of another; even to undertake the precepts while sitting on an equal seat would have been a cause for disrespect. Therefore, it is said that she undertook the precepts by herself.

Purisesūti [M 4.0129] bodhisattassa pitaraṃ ādiṃ katvā kesuci manussesu purisādhippāyacittaṃ nuppajjati. Tañca kho bodhisatte gāravena, na pahīnakilesatāya. Bodhisattamātu rūpaṃ pana sukusalāpi sippikā potthakammādīsupi kātuṃ na sakkonti, taṃ disvā purisassa rāgo nuppajjatīti na sakkā vattuṃ. Sace pana taṃ rattacitto upasaṅkamitukāmo hoti, pādā na vahanti, dibbasaṅkhalikā viya bajjhanti. Tasmā “anatikkamanīyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Toward men” means that a mind with lustful intent toward any man, beginning with the Bodhisatta's father, did not arise in her. This was out of reverence for the Bodhisatta, not because her defilements were eradicated. As for the Bodhisatta's mother’s beauty, even highly skilled artisans could not reproduce it in clay work or other media. It cannot be said that lust would not arise in a man upon seeing her. But if a man with a lustful mind wished to approach her, his feet would not carry him; they would be bound as if by divine fetters. Therefore, it was said that she was “unapproachable,” and so on.

Pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānanti pubbe “kāmaguṇūpasaṃhita”nti [P 4.0181] purisādhippāyavasena vatthupaṭikkhepo kathito, idha ārammaṇappaṭilābho dassito. Tadā kira “deviyā evarūpo putto kucchismiṃ uppanno”ti, sutvā samantato rājāno mahagghaābharaṇatūriyādivasena pañcadvārārammaṇavatthubhūtaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesenti, bodhisattassa ca bodhisattamātuyā ca katakammassa ussannattā lābhasakkārassa pamāṇaparicchedo nāma natthi.

Regarding 'of the five strands of sensual pleasure': previously, in the phrase 'associated with the strands of sensual pleasure,' the rejection of the object was spoken of by way of a man's intention. Here, the acquisition of the sense-object is shown. At that time, it is said, upon hearing, “A son of such a nature has arisen in the queen’s womb,” kings from all around sent gifts—which are the objects for the five sense-doors—by way of very valuable ornaments, musical instruments, and so forth. And due to the abundance of the meritorious kamma performed by the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta's mother, there was no measure or limit to the gain and honor.

204. Akilantakāyāti yathā aññā itthiyo gabbhabhārena kilamanti, hatthapādā uddhumātakādīni pāpuṇanti, na evaṃ tassā koci kilamatho ahosi. Tirokucchigatanti antokucchigataṃ. Kalalādikālaṃ atikkamitvā sañjātaaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ ahīnindriyabhāvaṃ upagataṃyeva passati. Kimatthaṃ passati? Sukhavāsatthaṃ. Yatheva hi mātā puttena saddhiṃ nisinnā vā nipannā vā “hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā olambantaṃ ukkhipitvā saṇṭhapessāmī”ti sukhavāsatthaṃ puttaṃ oloketi, evaṃ bodhisattamātāpi yaṃ taṃ mātu uṭṭhānagamanaparivattananisajjādīsu uṇhasītaloṇikatittakakaṭukāhāraajjhoharaṇakālesu ca gabbhassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati, atthi nu kho me taṃ puttassāti sukhavāsatthaṃ bodhisattaṃ olokayamānā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnaṃ bodhisattaṃ passati. Yathā hi aññe antokucchigatā pakkāsayaṃ ajjhottharitvā āmāsayaṃ ukkhipitvā [V 4.0133] udarapaṭalaṃ piṭṭhito katvā piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ nissāya ukkuṭikā dvīsu muṭṭhīsu hanukaṃ ṭhapetvā deve vassante rukkhasusire makkaṭā viya nisīdanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto. Bodhisatto pana piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ piṭṭhito katvā dhammāsane dhammakathiko viya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā puratthābhimukho nisīdati. Pubbe katakammaṃ panassā vatthuṃ sodheti, suddhe vatthumhi sukhumacchavilakkhaṇaṃ nibbattati[M 4.0130]. Atha naṃ kucchigataṃ taco paṭicchādetuṃ na sakkoti, olokentiyā bahi ṭhito viya paññāyati. Tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Bodhisatto pana antokucchigato mātaraṃ na passati. Na hi antokucchiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjati.

204. Regarding 'Akilantakāyā': just as other women become weary from the burden of pregnancy, their hands and feet swelling and so forth, for her no such fatigue arose. Regarding 'Tirokucchigataṃ': gone inside the womb. Having passed beyond the stage of the kalala and so forth, she sees him having attained a state of well-formed major and minor limbs and unimpaired faculties. For what purpose does she see him? For the sake of a comfortable abiding. For just as a mother, sitting or lying with her child, looks at her child for his comfortable abiding, thinking, “I will lift and adjust his hanging hand or foot,” so too the Bodhisatta’s mother, for the sake of his comfortable abiding, considers, “Does any suffering that arises for a fetus during the mother's rising, walking, turning, sitting, or consuming hot, cold, salty, bitter, or pungent food, exist for my son?” and observing the Bodhisatta, she sees him seated with his legs crossed. For whereas other beings inside the womb—covering the receptacle for digested food, lifting the receptacle for undigested food, with the abdominal wall behind them, relying on the backbone, squatting, and placing their chin on their two fists—sit like monkeys in a hollow tree when it is raining, the Bodhisatta is not so. Rather, the Bodhisatta, with the backbone behind him, sits with his legs crossed facing eastward, like a Dhamma-preacher on the Dhamma-seat. Moreover, her past kamma purifies the womb, and when the womb is pure, a characteristic of very subtle skin appears. Then the skin is unable to conceal him within the womb, and to her who is looking, he appears as if standing outside. To illustrate this meaning with a simile, he said, “Just as...” and so on. The Bodhisatta, however, being inside the womb, does not see his mother, for eye-consciousness does not arise inside the womb.

205. Kālaṃ [P 4.0182] karotīti na vijātabhāvapaccayā, āyuparikkhayeneva. Bodhisattena vasitaṭṭhānañhi cetiyakuṭisadisaṃ hoti aññesaṃ aparibhogaṃ, na ca sakkā bodhisattamātaraṃ apanetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetunti tattakaṃyeva bodhisattamātu āyuppamāṇaṃ hoti, tasmā tadā kālaṃ karoti. Katarasmiṃ pana vaye kālaṃ karotīti? Majjhimavaye. Paṭhamavayasmiñhi sattānaṃ attabhāve chandarāgo balavā hoti, tena tadā sañjātagabbhā itthī taṃ gabbhaṃ anurakkhituṃ na sakkonti, gabbho bahvābādho hoti. Majjhimavayassa pana dve koṭṭhāse atikkamma tatiyakoṭṭhāse vatthuṃ visadaṃ hoti, visade vatthumhi nibbattā dārakā arogā honti. Tasmā bodhisattamātāpi paṭhamavaye sampattiṃ anubhavitvā majjhimavayassa tatiyakoṭṭhāse vijāyitvā kālaṃ karoti.

205. Regarding 'kālaṃ karoti': she passes away not on account of having given birth, but solely due to the exhaustion of her lifespan. For the place inhabited by the Bodhisatta is like a cetiya-chamber, not for the use of others. And it is not possible to remove the Bodhisatta's mother and place another in the position of chief queen; thus, the lifespan of the Bodhisatta's mother is just that much. Therefore, she passes away at that time. In which age, then, does she pass away? In the middle age. For in the first age, beings' sensual passion for their own existence is strong; therefore, a woman who conceives at that time is not able to protect the fetus, and the fetus has many afflictions. But after passing two parts of the middle age, in the third part, the womb is pure. Children born in a pure womb are without illness. Therefore, the Bodhisatta's mother, too, having experienced prosperity in the first age, gives birth in the third part of the middle age and passes away.

Nava vā dasa vāti ettha vā-saddena vikappanavasena satta vā aṭṭha vā ekādasa vā dvādasa vāti evamādīnampi saṅgaho veditabbo. Tattha sattamāsajāto jīvati, sītuṇhakkhamo pana na hoti. Aṭṭhamāsajāto na jīvati, sesā jīvanti.

In 'nine or ten,' by the word 'or,' by way of alternation, the inclusion of such as 'seven or eight or eleven or twelve' should be understood. Among them, one born at seven months lives, but is not able to endure cold and heat. One born at eight months does not live. The rest live.

Ṭhitāvāti ṭhitāva hutvā. Mahāmāyāpi devī upavijaññā ñātikulagharaṃ gamissāmīti rañño ārocesi. Rājā kapilavatthuto devadahanagaragāmimaggaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā deviṃ suvaṇṇasivikāya nisīdāpesi. Sakalanagaravāsino sakyā parivāretvā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā deviṃ gahetvā pāyiṃsu. Sā devadahanagarassa avidūre lumbinisālavanuyyānaṃ disvā uyyānavicaraṇatthāya cittaṃ uppādetvā rañño saññaṃ adāsi. Rājā uyyānaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā ārakkhaṃ [V 4.0134] saṃvidahāpesi. Deviyā uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhamattāya kāyadubbalyaṃ [P 4.0183] ahosi, athassā maṅgalasālamūle sirīsayanaṃ paññāpetvā sāṇiyā parikkhipiṃsu. Sā [M 4.0131] antosāṇiṃ pavisitvā sālasākhaṃ hatthena gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā tāvadeva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi.

Regarding 'ṭhitāva': it means 'while standing.' Queen Mahāmāyā, as her delivery was approaching, informed the king, saying, “I will go to my relatives' home.” The king had the road from Kapilavatthu to the city of Devadaha adorned and had the queen seated in a golden palanquin. The Sakyans, residents of the entire city, surrounded her, and honoring her with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, they took the queen and proceeded. Seeing the Lumbinī sāl-tree grove not far from the city of Devadaha, she conceived a desire to stroll in the park and gave a sign to the king. The king had the park prepared and arranged for its protection. As soon as the queen entered the park, a bodily weakness arose. Then, at the foot of an auspicious sāl tree, they prepared a royal couch for her and surrounded it with a curtain. She entered inside the curtain, grasped a branch of the sāl tree with her hand, and stood. At that very moment, the emergence from the womb occurred.

Devā naṃ paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhantīti khīṇāsavā suddhāvāsabrahmāno paṭiggaṇhanti. Kathaṃ? Sūtivesaṃ gaṇhitvāti eke. Taṃ pana paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – tadā bodhisattamātā suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā macchakkhisadisaṃ dukūlapaṭaṃ yāva pādantāva pārupitvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā sallahukaṃ gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi dhammakaraṇato udakanikkhamanasadisaṃ. Atha te pakatibrahmaveseneva upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggahesuṃ. Tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “devā naṃ paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti pacchā manussā”ti.

Regarding 'Devā naṃ paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti': the Pure Abode Brahmās, who are destroyers of the taints, receive him. How? Some say, “Having taken the guise of a midwife.” But rejecting that, this is said: At that time, the Bodhisatta's mother, having worn a cloth embroidered with gold, stood wrapped down to her feet in a fine muslin cloth like a fish's eye. Then for her, the emergence from the womb was very light, like water flowing from a water-pot. Then they, having approached in their natural Brahmā appearance, first received him with a golden net. From their hands, humans received him with a roll of fine muslin. Therefore it was said: “The devas first receive him, afterwards humans.”

206. Cattāro naṃ devaputtāti cattāro mahārājāno. Paṭiggahetvāti ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahetvā. Mahesakkhoti mahātejo mahāyaso lakkhaṇasampannoti attho.

206. `Cattāro naṃ devaputtā` means the four great kings. `Paṭiggahetvā` means having received him in a covering made of black antelope skin. `Mahesakkho` means of great power, of great renown, endowed with the characteristics—this is the meaning.

Visadova nikkhamatīti yathā aññe sattā yonimagge laggantā bhaggavibhaggā nikkhamanti, na evaṃ nikkhamati, alaggo hutvā nikkhamatīti attho. Udenāti udakena. Kenaci asucināti yathā aññe sattā kammajavātehi uddhaṃpādā adhosirā yonimagge pakkhittā sataporisanarakapapātaṃ patantā viya tāḷacchiddena nikkaḍḍhiyamānā hatthī viya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantā nānāasucimakkhitāva [P 4.0184] nikkhamanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto. Bodhisattañhi kammajavātā uddhaṃpādaṃ adhosiraṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti. So dhammāsanato otaranto dhammakathiko viya nisseṇito otaranto puriso viya ca dve hatthe ca pāde ca pasāretvā ṭhitakova mātukucchisambhavena kenaci asucinā amakkhitova nikkhamati.

`Visadova nikkhamati` means that unlike other beings who emerge from the birth canal stuck, broken, and disordered, he does not emerge in such a way; he emerges unstuck—this is the meaning. `Udena` means 'with water.' `Kenaci asucinā` means that unlike other beings who, driven by karmic winds, are thrown into the birth canal headfirst with feet up, falling as if from a cliff a hundred men high, experiencing great suffering like an elephant being dragged through a keyhole, and emerging smeared with various impurities—the Bodhisatta does not emerge in such a way. Indeed, the karmic winds cannot make the Bodhisatta go headfirst with feet up. Instead, like a Dhamma-preacher descending from the Dhamma-seat or a man coming down a staircase, he emerges with both hands and feet extended, standing, unsmeared by any impurity from his mother’s womb.

Udakassa dhārāti udakavaṭṭiyo. Tāsu sītā suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patati, uṇhā rajatakaṭāhe. Idañca pathavītale kenaci asucinā asammissaṃ tesaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīyaudakañceva aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ [V 4.0135] kīḷanaudakañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Aññassa pana suvaṇṇarajataghaṭehi āhariyamānaudakassa ceva haṃsavaṭṭakādipokkharaṇigatassa ca udakassa paricchedo natthi.

`Udakassa dhārā` means streams of water. Among them, the cool stream falls into a golden basin, and the warm stream into a silver one. This was said to show that on the earth's surface, their drinking and bathing water, as well as their special water for play, was unmixed with any impurity and not shared with others. As for other water, however, such as that brought in golden and silver pots or that in ponds like Haṃsavaṭṭaka and so on, there is no limit.

207. Sampatijātoti [M 4.0132] muhuttajāto. Pāḷiyaṃ pana mātukucchito nikkhantamatto viya dassito, na pana evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nikkhantamattañhi taṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno maṅgalasammatāya sukhasamphassāya ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena, manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito.

207. `Sampatijāta` means 'just born.' In the Pāli, however, he is shown as if he had just emerged from his mother's womb, but it should not be understood in this way. For, as soon as he emerged, he was first received by the Brahmas in a golden net. From their hands, the Four Great Kings received him in a covering of black antelope skin, which is considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch. From their hands, humans received him in a roll of fine cloth. Released from the hands of humans, he stood established on the earth.

Setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāneti dibbasetacchatte anudhāriyamāne. Ettha ca chattassa parivārāni khaggādīni [P 4.0185] pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍānipi āgatāneva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana rājagamane rājā viya chattameva vuttaṃ. Tesu chattameva paññāyati, na chattaggāhakā. Tathā khagga-tālavaṇṭa-morahatthaka-vāḷabījani-uṇhīsamattāyeva paññāyanti, na tesaṃ gāhakā. Sabbāni kira tāni adissamānarūpā devatā gaṇhiṃsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

`Setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne` means while a divine white parasol was being held up. And here, the retinue of the parasol, the five royal regalia such as the sword, also arrived. In the Pāli, however, just as in the case of a king's procession only the king is mentioned, so only the parasol is mentioned. Among them, only the parasol is visible, not the parasol-bearers. Similarly, only the sword, palm-leaf fan, peacock-feather fan, yak-tail whisk, and turban are visible, not their bearers. Indeed, all of them were held by deities with invisible forms. And this was also stated:

“Anekasākhañca sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā”ti. (su. ni. 693);

A many-ribbed parasol with a thousand circles, the gods held in the sky; golden-handled chowries waved to and fro, but the bearers of the chowries and parasol were not seen.

Sabbā ca disāti idaṃ sattapadavītihārūpari ṭhitassa viya sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ vuttaṃ, na kho panevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā puratthimadisaṃ olokesi, anekacakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni ahesuṃ. Tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā – “mahāpurisa idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā, heṭṭhā, uparīti dasapi disā anuviloketvā attanā sadisaṃ adisvā ayaṃ uttarā disāti sattapadavītihārena agamāsīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti [V 4.0136] guṇehi sabbapaṭhamo. Itarāni dve padāni etasseva vevacanāni. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti padadvayena imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

`Sabbā ca disā`: This is said as if it were a surveying of all directions by one standing after taking seven steps, but it should not be understood in this way. For the Great Being, having been released from the hands of humans, looked toward the eastern direction, and many thousands of world-systems became a single open space. There, gods and humans, honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, said: 'Great Being, here there is no one equal to you, so whence could there be one more excellent?' In this way, he surveyed the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—all ten directions. Not seeing anyone equal to himself, and thinking, 'This is the northern direction,' he went forward with a seven-step stride. Thus should the meaning here be understood. `Āsabhaṃ` means 'supreme.' `Aggo` means 'foremost of all in virtues.' The other two terms are synonyms of this one. With the two phrases, 'This is my last birth' and 'Now there is no more renewed existence,' he declared the Arahantship to be attained in this very existence.

Ettha [M 4.0133] ca samehi pādehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhānaṃ catuiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, uttarābhimukhabhāvo mahājanaṃ ajjhottharitvā abhibhavitvā gamanassa pubbanimittaṃ[P 4.0186], sattapadagamanaṃ sattabojjhaṅgaratanapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, dibbasetacchattadhāraṇaṃ vimutticchattapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, pañcarājakakudhabhaṇḍāni pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuccanassa pubbanimittaṃ, disānuvilokanaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, āsabhīvācābhāsanaṃ appaṭivattiyadhammacakkappavattanassa pubbanimittaṃ. “Ayamantimā jātī”ti sīhanādo anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānassa pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ. Ime vārā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, sambahulavāro pana āgato, āharitvā dīpetabbo.

And here, standing on the earth with even feet is a foretoken of attaining the four bases of spiritual power. Facing north is a foretoken of going forth, having surpassed and overcome the great populace. The seven-step stride is a foretoken of attaining the seven enlightenment-factor gems. The holding of the divine white parasol is a foretoken of attaining the parasol of liberation. The five royal regalia are a foretoken of being liberated by the five kinds of liberation. Surveying the directions is a foretoken of attaining unobstructed knowledge. Uttering the supreme speech is a foretoken of setting in motion the irreversible Wheel of the Dhamma. The lion’s roar, 'This is my last birth,' is a foretoken of the final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without remainder—thus it should be understood. These sections are found in the Pāli. The section on many things, however, is not found here; it should be brought from elsewhere and explained.

Mahāpurisassa hi jātadivase dasasahassilokadhātu kampi. Dasasahassilokadhātumhi devatā ekacakkavāḷe sannipatiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ devā paṭiggahiṃsu, pacchā manussā. Tantibaddhā vīṇā cammabaddhā bheriyo ca kenaci avāditā sayameva vajjiṃsu, manussānaṃ andubandhanādīni khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ bhijjiṃsu. Sabbarogā ambilena dhotatambamalaṃ viya vigacchiṃsu, jaccandhā rūpāni passiṃsu. Jaccabadhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu, pīṭhasappī javanasampannā ahesuṃ, jātijaḷānampi eḷamūgānaṃ sati patiṭṭhāsi, videse pakkhandanāvā supaṭṭanaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, ākāsaṭṭhakabhūmaṭṭhakaratanāni sakatejobhāsitāni ahesuṃ, verino mettacittaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, avīcimhi aggi nibbāyi. Lokantare āloko udapādi, nadīsu jalaṃ na pavatti, mahāsamuddesu madhurasadisaṃ udakaṃ ahosi, vāto na vāyi, ākāsapabbatarukkhagatā sakuṇā bhassitvā pathavīgatā [P 4.0187] ahesuṃ, cando atiroci, sūriyo na uṇho na sītalo nimmalo utusampanno ahosi, devatā attano attano vimānadvāre ṭhatvā apphoṭanaseḷanacelukkhepādīhi mahākīḷaṃ kīḷiṃsu, cātuddīpikamahāmegho vassi, mahājanaṃ neva khudā na pipāsā pīḷesi, dvārakavāṭāni sayameva vivariṃsu, pupphūpagaphalūpagā rukkhā pupphaphalāni gaṇhiṃsu, dasasahassilokadhātu ekaddhajamālā ahosīti.

On the day the Great Being was born, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. In the ten-thousandfold world-system, deities gathered in a single world-sphere. First, the deities received him, and afterward, humans. Stringed lutes and skin-covered drums, though untouched by anyone, sounded by themselves. The bonds and fetters of humans, and so forth, shattered into pieces. All diseases vanished like copper stains washed away with sour liquid. Those blind from birth saw forms. Those deaf from birth heard sounds. The cripples became endowed with swiftness. Even for the congenitally dull and mute, mindfulness was established. Ships bound for foreign lands reached safe harbors. Jewels in the sky and on earth shone with their own splendor. Enemies developed thoughts of loving-kindness. The fire in Avīci was extinguished. Light arose in the inter-world spaces. Water in the rivers did not flow. The water in the great oceans became like sweet water. The wind did not blow. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the ground. The moon shone exceedingly. The sun was neither hot nor cold, stainless, and seasonable. Deities, standing at the doors of their respective mansions, engaged in great sport with clapping, whistling, tossing of garments, and so forth. A great cloud rained over the four continents. The great multitude was afflicted neither by hunger nor by thirst. Doors and gates opened by themselves. Flowering and fruit-bearing trees bore their flowers and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world-system became a single garland of banners.

Tatrāpissa [V 4.0137] dasasahassilokadhātukampo sabbaññutañāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, devatānaṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipāto dhammacakkappavattanakāle ekappahārena sannipatitvā dhammapaṭiggaṇhanassa pubbanimittaṃ, paṭhamaṃ devatānaṃ [M 4.0134] paṭiggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pacchā manussānaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, tantibaddhavīṇānaṃ sayaṃ vajjanaṃ anupubbavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, cammabaddhabherīnaṃ vajjanaṃ mahatiyā dhammabheriyā anussāvanassa pubbanimittaṃ, andubandhanādīnaṃ chedo asmimānasamucchedassa pubbanimittaṃ, sabbarogavigamo sabbakilesavigamassa pubbanimittaṃ, jaccandhānaṃ rūpadassanaṃ dibbacakkhupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, jaccabadhirānaṃ saddassavanaṃ dibbasotadhātupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ[P 4.0188], pīṭhasappīnaṃ javanasampadā catuiddhipādādhigamassa pubbanimittaṃ, jaḷānaṃ satipatiṭṭhānaṃ catusatipaṭṭhānapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, videsapakkhandanāvānaṃ supaṭṭanasampāpuṇanaṃ catupaṭisambhidādhigamassa pubbanimittaṃ, ratanānaṃ sakatejobhāsitattaṃ yaṃ lokassa dhammobhāsaṃ dassessati tassa pubbanimittaṃ.

Herein, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system is a foretoken of the attainment of omniscient knowledge. The gathering of deities in a single world-sphere is a foretoken of their gathering together at one stroke at the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma and receiving the Dhamma. The deities' initial reception is a foretoken of the attainment of the four form-realm jhānas. The subsequent reception by humans is a foretoken of the attainment of the four formless jhānas. The self-sounding of stringed lutes is a foretoken of the attainment of the sequential abodes. The sounding of skin-covered drums is a foretoken of the proclamation with the great drum of the Dhamma. The severing of bonds and fetters, and so forth, is a foretoken of the complete eradication of the conceit 'I am.' The vanishing of all diseases is a foretoken of the vanishing of all defilements. The seeing of forms by those born blind is a foretoken of the attainment of the divine eye. The hearing of sounds by those born deaf is a foretoken of the attainment of the divine ear element. The cripples' endowment with swiftness is a foretoken of the acquisition of the four bases of psychic power. The establishment of mindfulness in the dull-witted is a foretoken of the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness. The reaching of safe harbors by ships bound for foreign lands is a foretoken of the acquisition of the four analytical knowledges. The shining of jewels with their own splendor is a foretoken of the light of the Dhamma that he will show to the world.

Verīnaṃ mettacittapaṭilābho catubrahmavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, avīcimhi agginibbānaṃ ekādasaagginibbānassa pubbanimittaṃ, lokantarāloko avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ñāṇālokadassanassa pubbanimittaṃ, mahāsamuddassa madhuratā nibbānarasena ekarasabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ, vātassa avāyanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatabhindanassa pubbanimittaṃ, sakuṇānaṃ pathavīgamanaṃ mahājanassa ovādaṃ sutvā pāṇehi saraṇagamanassa pubbanimittaṃ, candassa ativirocanaṃ bahujanakantatāya pubbanimittaṃ, sūriyassa uṇhasītavivajjanautusukhatā kāyikacetasikasukhuppattiyā pubbanimittaṃ, devatānaṃ vimānadvāresu apphoṭanādīhi kīḷanaṃ buddhabhāvaṃ patvā udānaṃ udānassa pubbanimittaṃ, cātuddīpikamahāmeghavassanaṃ mahato dhammameghavassanassa pubbanimittaṃ, khudāpīḷanassa abhāvo kāyagatāsatiamatapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, pipāsāpīḷanassa abhāvo vimuttisukhena sukhitabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ, dvārakavāṭānaṃ sayameva vivaraṇaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggadvāravivaraṇassa pubbanimittaṃ, rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalagahaṇaṃ vimuttipupphehi pupphitassa ca sāmaññaphalabhārabharitabhāvassa ca pubbanimittaṃ, dasasahassilokadhātuyā [P 4.0189] ekaddhajamālatā ariyaddhajamālāmālitāya pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ sambahulavāro nāma.

The enemies' attainment of a mind of loving-kindness is a foretoken of the attainment of the four divine abodes. The extinguishing of fire in Avīci is a foretoken of the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The light in the inter-world spaces dispelling the darkness of ignorance is a foretoken of the vision of the light of knowledge. The sweetness of the great ocean is a foretoken of the state of having a single taste, the flavor of Nibbāna. The ceasing of the wind is a foretoken of the shattering of the sixty-two wrong views. The birds' descent to the ground is a foretoken of the great multitude, after hearing the teaching, going for refuge with their very lives. The surpassing radiance of the moon is a foretoken of being beloved by many people. The sun's pleasant seasonableness, being devoid of heat and cold, is a foretoken of the arising of bodily and mental happiness. The deities' playing with clapping, and so forth, at the doors of their mansions is a foretoken of his uttering an inspired utterance upon having attained Buddhahood. The great cloud raining over the four continents is a foretoken of the raining of the great Dhamma cloud. The absence of affliction by hunger is a foretoken of the attainment of the deathless through mindfulness directed to the body. The absence of affliction by thirst is a foretoken of the state of being gladdened by the bliss of liberation. The doors and gates opening by themselves is a foretoken of the opening of the door of the Noble Eightfold Path. The trees' bearing of flowers and fruits is a foretoken of being blossomed with the flowers of liberation and being heavily laden with the fruits of recluseship. The ten-thousandfold world-system being a single garland of banners is a foretoken of being adorned with the garland of the Noble Banner. Thus it should be understood. This is called the section on numerous foretokens.

Ettha [V 4.0138] pañhe pucchanti – “yadā mahāpuriso pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho gantvā āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tadā kiṃ pathaviyā gato[M 4.0135], udāhu ākāsena? Dissamāno gato, udāhu adissamāno? Acelako gato, udāhu alaṅkatappaṭiyatto? Daharo hutvā gato, udāhu mahallako? Pacchāpi kiṃ tādisova ahosi, udāhu puna bāladārako”ti? Ayaṃ pana pañho heṭṭhā lohapāsāde saṅghasannipāte tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherena vissajjitova. Thero kirettha niyati pubbekatakamma-issaranimmānavādavasena taṃ taṃ bahuṃ vatvā avasāne evaṃ byākāsi – “mahāpuriso pathaviyaṃ gato, mahājanassa pana ākāse gacchanto viya ahosi. Dissamāno gato, mahājanassa pana adissamāno viya ahosi. Acelako gato, mahājanassa pana alaṅkatappaṭiyattova upaṭṭhāsi. Daharova gato, mahājanassa pana soḷasavassuddesiko viya ahosi. Pacchā pana bāladārakova ahosi, na tādiso”ti. Evaṃ vutte parisā cassa “buddhena viya hutvā bho therena pañho kathito”ti attamanā ahosi. Lokantarikavāro vuttanayo eva.

Here, questions are asked: "When the Great Being, having stood on the earth, faces north and utters the bull-like speech, does he go on the earth or through the sky? Does he go visibly or invisibly? Does he go unclothed or adorned and prepared? Does he go as a youth or as an elder? Afterwards, was he still the same, or did he become a young child again?" This question was previously answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya in the assembly of the Sangha at the Lohapāsāda. The elder, it is said, having spoken at length on the topics of destiny, past karma, and divine creation, concluded thus: "The Great Being went on the earth, but to the great multitude, it was as though he went through the sky. He went visibly, but to the great multitude, it was as though he went invisibly. He went unclothed, but to the great multitude, he appeared adorned and prepared. He went as a youth, but to the great multitude, he seemed like one of sixteen years of age. Afterwards, he became a young child again; he was not the same." When this was said, the assembly was delighted, saying, "The elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself." The section concerning the interspace of worlds is to be understood in the manner already stated.

Viditāti pākaṭā hutvā. Yathā hi sāvakā nahānamukhadhovanakhādanapivanādikāle anokāsagate atītasaṅkhāre [P 4.0190] nippadese sammasituṃ na sakkonti, okāsapattayeva sammasanti, na evaṃ buddhā. Buddhā hi sattadivasabbhantare vavatthitasaṅkhāre ādito paṭṭhāya sammasitvā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvāva vissajjenti, tesaṃ avipassitadhammo nāma natthi, tasmā “viditā”ti āha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

"Known" means having become manifest. For just as disciples, at a time that is not an opportunity—such as during bathing, washing the face, eating, or drinking—cannot contemplate past formations without remainder, and contemplate them only when an opportunity is attained, it is not so for the Buddhas. For the Buddhas, from the beginning, contemplate the formations that have occurred within seven days, apply the three characteristics, and then elucidate them. For them, there is no phenomenon that has not been investigated. Therefore, it is said, "known." The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Acchariyaabbhutasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta is concluded.

4. Bākulasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bākula Sutta

209. Evaṃ [V 4.0139] me sutanti bākulasuttaṃ. Tattha bākuloti yathā dvāvīsati dvattiṃsātiādimhi vattabbe bāvīsati bāttiṃsātiādīni vuccanti, evameva dvikuloti vattabbe bākuloti vuttaṃ. Tassa hi therassa dve kulāni ahesuṃ. So kira devaloko cavitvā kosambinagare nāma [M 4.0136] mahāseṭṭhikule nibbatto, tamenaṃ pañcame divase sīsaṃ nhāpetvā gaṅgākīḷaṃ akaṃsu. Dhātiyā dārakaṃ udake nimujjanummujjanavasena kīḷāpentiyā eko maccho dārakaṃ disvā “bhakkho me aya”nti maññamāno mukhaṃ vivaritvā upagato. Dhātī dārakaṃ [P 4.0191] chaḍḍetvā palātā. Maccho taṃ gili. Puññavā satto dukkhaṃ na pāpuṇi, sayanagabbhaṃ pavisitvā nipanno viya ahosi. Maccho dārakassa tejena tattakapallaṃ gilitvā dayhamāno viya vegena tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ gantvā bārāṇasinagaravāsino macchabandhassa jālaṃ pāvisi, mahāmacchā nāma jālabaddhā pahariyamānā maranti. Ayaṃ pana dārakassa tejena jālato nīhaṭamattova mato. Macchabandhā ca mahantaṃ macchaṃ labhitvā phāletvā vikkiṇanti. Taṃ pana dārakassa ānubhāvena aphāletvā sakalameva kājena haritvā sahassena demāti vadantā nagare vicariṃsu. Koci na gaṇhāti.

209. Thus have I heard—this is the Bākula Sutta. Therein, concerning the word 'Bākula,' just as one might say 'bāvīsati' or 'bāttiṃsā' when 'dvāvīsati' (twenty-two) or 'dvattiṃsā' (thirty-two) should be said, in the same way 'Bākula' is said when 'Dvikula' (of two families) should be said. For that elder had two families. It is said that after passing away from the deva realm, he was reborn in the city of Kosambī, in the family of a great merchant. On the fifth day, they bathed his head and had him play in the Ganges. While a nurse was playing with the child, dipping him in and out of the water, a fish saw the child and, thinking, 'This is my food,' opened its mouth and approached. The nurse abandoned the child and fled. The fish swallowed him. The meritorious being, however, did not come to harm; it was as if he had entered a sleeping chamber and lay down. The fish, due to the child's power, felt as if it had swallowed a hot pan and was burning. It swiftly traveled a distance of thirty yojanas and entered the net of a fisherman who lived in Bārāṇasī. Large fish, when caught in a net, die when they are struck. This one, however, due to the child's power, died the very moment it was taken from the net. Fishermen, having caught a large fish, would split it to sell it. But this one, due to the child's influence, they did not split. Carrying it whole on a carrying-pole, they went around the city saying, 'We will give it for a thousand!' Yet no one would take it.

Tasmiṃ pana nagare aputtakaṃ asītikoṭivibhavaṃ seṭṭhikulaṃ atthi, tassa dvāramūlaṃ patvā “kiṃ gahetvā dethā”ti vuttā kahāpaṇanti āhaṃsu. Tehi kahāpaṇaṃ datvā gahito. Seṭṭhibhariyāpi aññesu divasesu macche na kelāyati, taṃ divasaṃ pana macchaṃ phalake ṭhapetvā sayameva phālesi. Macchañca nāma kucchito phālenti, sā pana piṭṭhito phālentī macchakucchiyaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ dārakaṃ disvā – “macchakucchiyaṃ me putto laddho”ti nādaṃ naditvā dārakaṃ ādāya sāmikassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Seṭṭhi tāvadeva bheriṃ carāpetvā dārakaṃ ādāya rañño santikaṃ gantvā – “macchakucchiyaṃ me deva dārako laddho, kiṃ karomī”ti āha. Puññavā esa, yo macchakucchiyaṃ arogo vasi, posehi nanti.

In that city, however, there was a childless merchant family with a fortune of eighty crores. When the fishermen arrived at their door and were asked, "What will you take for it?", they replied, "A kahāpaṇa." Having given a kahāpaṇa, the family took the fish. The merchant's wife, who on other days was not fond of fish, on that day placed the fish on a board and cut it open herself. Now, fish are normally cut open from the belly, but she, cutting it from the back, saw a golden-hued child in the fish's belly. She cried out, "I have found a son in the fish's belly!" and, taking the child, went to her husband. The merchant at that very moment had a drum beaten and, taking the child, went to the king and said, "Your Majesty, I have found a child in a fish's belly. What should I do?" The king replied, "He is a meritorious one, who lived unharmed in a fish's belly. You should raise him."

Assosi [V 4.0140] kho itaraṃ kulaṃ – “bārāṇasiyaṃ kira ekaṃ seṭṭhikulaṃ macchakucchiyaṃ dārakaṃ labhatī”ti, te tattha agamaṃsu. Athassa mātā dārakaṃ alaṅkaritvā kīḷāpiyamānaṃ disvāva “manāpo vatāyaṃ [P 4.0192] dārako”ti gantvā pavatiṃ ācikkhi. Itarā mayhaṃ puttotiādimāha. Kahaṃ te laddhoti? Macchakucchiyanti. No tuyhaṃ putto, mayhaṃ puttoti. Kahaṃ te laddhoti? Mayā dasamāse kucchiyā dhārito, atha naṃ nadiyā kīḷāpiyamānaṃ [M 4.0137] maccho gilīti. Tuyhaṃ putto aññena macchena gilito bhavissati, ayaṃ pana mayā macchakucchiyaṃ laddhoti, ubhopi rājakulaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā āha – “ayaṃ dasa māse kucchiyā dhāritattā amātā kātuṃ na sakkā, macchaṃ gaṇhantāpi vakkayakanādīni bahi katvā gaṇhantā nāma natthīti macchakucchiyaṃ laddhattā ayampi amātā kātuṃ na sakkā, dārako ubhinnampi kulānaṃ dāyādo hotu, ubhopi naṃ jaggathā”ti ubhopi jaggiṃsu.

Now, the other family heard the news: "It is said that a certain merchant family in Bārāṇasī has found a child in the belly of a fish," so they went there. Then his mother, upon seeing the child adorned and being played with, exclaimed, "What a lovely child this is!" and went and related her story. The other woman said, "He is my son." When asked, "Where did you find him?" she replied, "In the belly of a fish." The first mother said, "He is not your son, he is my son." When she in turn was asked, "Where did you get him?" she replied, "I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then, while he was being played with in the river, a fish swallowed him." The other retorted, "Your son must have been swallowed by another fish; this one, however, I found in the belly of a fish." Both went to the royal court. The king declared: "This woman, because she carried him in her womb for ten months, cannot be made not a mother. And this other woman, because she found him in the belly of a fish, also cannot be made not a mother. Let the child be the heir of both families. Both of you are to raise him." And so, both of them raised him.

Viññutaṃ pattassa dvīsupi nagaresu pāsādaṃ kāretvā nāṭakāni paccupaṭṭhāpesuṃ. Ekekasmiṃ nagare cattāro cattāro māse vasati, ekasmiṃ nagare cattāro māse vuṭṭhassa saṅghāṭanāvāya maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā tattha naṃ saddhiṃ nāṭakāhi āropenti. So sampattiṃ anubhavamāno itaraṃ nagaraṃ gacchati. Taṃnagaravāsino nāṭakāni upaḍḍhamaggaṃ agamaṃsu. Te paccuggantvā taṃ parivāretvā attano pāsādaṃ nayanti. Itarāni nāṭakāni nivattitvā attano nagarameva gacchanti. Tattha cattāro māse vasitvā teneva niyāmena puna itaraṃ nagaraṃ gacchati. Evamassa sampattiṃ anubhavantassa asīti vassāni paripuṇṇāni.

For him who had reached discernment, they had mansions built in both cities and provided theatrical performers. He would live for four months in each city. After he had lived for four months in one city, they would have a pavilion built on a joined boat and place him on board it together with the theatrical performers. He, experiencing such prosperity, would go to the other city. The theatrical performers resident in that city would come halfway to meet him. Having gone out to meet him, they would surround him and lead him to their own mansion. The other theatrical performers would turn back and go to their own city. Having lived there for four months, he would again go to the other city by that same arrangement. Thus, for him experiencing such prosperity, eighty years were completed.

Atha bhagavā cārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasiṃ patto. So bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajito. Pabbajitvā sattāhameva puthujjano ahosi, aṭṭhame pana so [P 4.0193] saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti evamassa dve kulāni ahesuṃ. Tasmā bākuloti saṅkhaṃ agamāsīti.

Then the Blessed One, while wandering on tour, arrived at Bārāṇasī. He, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, gained faith and went forth. Having gone forth, he was a worldling for only seven days; but on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus, he came to have two families. Therefore, he came to be known as Bākula.

Purāṇagihisahāyoti pubbe gihikāle sahāyo. Ayampi dīghāyukova theraṃ pabbajitaṃ passituṃ gacchanto asītime vasse gato. Methuno dhammoti bālo naggasamaṇako bālapucchaṃ pucchati, na sāsanavacanaṃ, idāni therena dinnanaye ṭhito imehi pana teti pucchi.

‘Former householder companion’ means a companion in a former time, when he was a householder. This one too, being long-lived, went to see the Elder who had gone forth; he went in his eightieth year. With the phrase ‘the act of sexual intercourse,’ the foolish naked ascetic asks the Elder a foolish question, not a word concerning the Teaching. Now, standing in the method given by the Elder, he asked, ‘But with these…?’

210. Yaṃpāyasmātiādīni [V 4.0141] padāni sabbavāresu dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi niyametvā ṭhapitāni. Tattha saññā uppannamattāva, vitakko kammapathabhedakoti[M 4.0138]. Thero panāha – “kasmā visuṃ karotha, ubhayampetaṃ kammapathabhedakamevā”ti.

210. The words beginning with ‘Venerable sir…’ were determined and established in all sections by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma. Therein, perception is mere arising, while thought is what distinguishes the course of action. But the Elder said: ‘Why do you make them separate? Both of these are indeed what distinguishes the course of action.’

211. Gahapaticīvaranti vassāvāsikaṃ cīvaraṃ. Satthenāti pipphalakena. Sūciyāti sūciṃ gahetvā sibbitabhāvaṃ na sarāmīti attho. Kathine cīvaranti kathinacīvaraṃ, kathinacīvarampi hi vassāvāsikagatikameva. Tasmā tattha “sibbitā nābhijānāmī”ti āha.

211. ‘A householder’s robe’ means a robe for the rains-residence. ‘With a knife’ means with a small blade. ‘With a needle’—the meaning is: taking a needle, ‘I do not recall the state of having sewn.’ A robe offered during the Kaṭhina period is a Kaṭhina robe; for indeed, a Kaṭhina robe is also of the nature of a rains-residence robe. Therefore, in that context, he said, ‘I do not recall sewing.’

Ettakaṃ panassa kālaṃ gahapaticīvaraṃ asādiyantassa chindanasibbanādīni akarontassa kuto cīvaraṃ uppajjatīti. Dvīhi nagarehi. Thero hi mahāyasassī, tassa puttadhītaro nattapanattakā sukhumasāṭakehi cīvarāni kāretvā rajāpetvā samugge pakkhipitvā pahiṇanti. Therassa nhānakāle nhānakoṭṭhake ṭhapenti. Thero tāni nivāseti ceva pārupati ca, purāṇacīvarāni [P 4.0194] sampattapabbajitānaṃ deti. Thero tāni nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca navakammaṃ na karoti, kiñci āyūhanakammaṃ natthi. Phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā appetvā nisīdati. Catūsu māsesu pattesu lomakiliṭṭhāni honti, athassa puna teneva niyāmena pahiṇitvā denti. Aḍḍhamāse aḍḍhamāse parivattatītipi vadantiyeva.

But for him who for such a long time did not delight in a householder’s robe and did not do things such as cutting and sewing, from where does a robe arise? From the two cities. For the Elder is of great renown; his sons, daughters, grandsons, and great-grandsons have robes made from fine cloths, have them dyed, place them in chests, and send them. At the time of the Elder’s bath, they place them in the bathing chamber. The Elder wears them as an under-robe and drapes them as an upper-robe, and he gives the old robes to monastics who have arrived. The Elder, having worn and draped himself in them, does no new work; there is no work of striving whatsoever. Having repeatedly entered the attainment of fruition, he sits. When four months have passed, they become soiled with body hair. Then they again have robes sent and given to him in that same manner. Some even say that he changes them every half-month.

Anacchariyañcetaṃ therassa mahāpuññassa mahābhiññassa satasahassakappe pūritapāramissa, asokadhammarañño kulūpako nigrodhatthero divasassa nikkhattuṃ cīvaraṃ parivattesi. Tassa hi ticīvaraṃ hatthikkhandhe ṭhapetvā pañcahi ca gandhasamuggasatehi pañcahi ca mālāsamuggasatehi saddhiṃ pātova āhariyittha, tathā divā ceva sāyañca. Rājā kira divasassa nikkhattuṃ sāṭake parivattento “therassa cīvaraṃ nīta”nti pucchitvā “āma nīta”nti sutvāva parivattesi. Theropi na bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapesi, sampattasabrahmacārīnaṃ adāsi. Tadā kira jambudīpe bhikkhusaṅghassa yebhuyyena nigrodhasseva santakaṃ cīvaraṃ ahosi.

And this is no wonder for an Elder of great merit, of great direct knowledge, who had fulfilled the perfections over a hundred thousand aeons. The Elder Nigrodha, a frequent visitor to the court of King Asokadhammarāja, changed his robe three times a day. For his three robes, placed on an elephant’s back, were brought early in the morning together with five hundred caskets of perfumes and five hundred caskets of garlands; and likewise during the day and in the evening. The king, it is said, while changing his own garments three times a day, would ask, ‘Has the robe been brought for the Elder?’ and only upon hearing, ‘Yes, it has been brought,’ would he change his own. The Elder, too, did not tie them in a bundle and store them away; he gave them to his companions in the holy life who had arrived. At that time, it is said, in Jambudīpa, the robes of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus were for the most part the property of Nigrodha.

Aho vata maṃ koci nimanteyyāti kiṃ pana cittassa anuppādanaṃ bhāriyaṃ, uppannassa pahānanti. Cittaṃ nāma lahukaparivattaṃ, tasmā anuppādanaṃ bhāriyaṃ[M 4.0139], uppannassa pahānampi bhāriyameva[V 4.0142]. Antaraghareti mahāsakuludāyisutte (ma. ni. 2.237) indakhīlato paṭṭhāya [P 4.0195] antaragharaṃ nāma idha nimbodakapatanaṭṭhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Kuto panassa bhikkhā uppajjitthāti. Thero dvīsu nagaresu abhiññāto, gehadvāraṃ āgatassevassa pattaṃ gahetvā nānārasabhojanassa pūretvā denti. So laddhaṭṭhānato nivattati, bhattakiccakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ panassa nibaddhameva ahosi. Anubyañjanasoti therena kira rūpe nimittaṃ gahetvā mātugāmo na olokitapubbo. Mātugāmassa dhammanti mātugāmassa chappañcavācāhi dhammaṃ desetuṃ vaṭṭati, pañhaṃ puṭṭhena gāthāsahassampi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Thero pana kappiyameva na akāsi. Yebhuyyena hi kulūpakatherānametaṃ kammaṃ hoti. Bhikkhunupassayanti bhikkhuniupassayaṃ. Taṃ pana gilānapucchakena gantuṃ vaṭṭati, thero pana kappiyameva na akāsi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Cuṇṇenāti kosambacuṇṇādinā. Gattaparikammeti sarīrasambāhanakamme. Vicāritāti payojayitā. Gaddūhanamattanti gāviṃ thane gahetvā ekaṃ khīrabinduṃ dūhanakālamattampi.

Regarding the thought, ‘Oh, that someone might invite me!’: what is more burdensome, the non-arising of the thought, or the abandoning of it once arisen? The mind, indeed, is quick to change; therefore, its non-arising is burdensome, and the abandoning of it once arisen is also burdensome indeed. ‘Within the village’: in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta, ‘within the village’ is from the threshold post onwards; here it is intended as the place where water drips from the eaves. But from where did alms-food arise for him? The Elder was well-known in the two cities; as soon as he arrived at the door of a house, they would take his bowl, fill it with food of various flavors, and give it to him. He would return from the place where he received it, but his place for the business of eating was always fixed. ‘By way of the minor characteristics’: it is said that the Elder had never before looked at a woman by apprehending the sign in her form. ‘Dhamma for a woman’: it is allowable to teach the Dhamma to a woman with five or six words; if asked a question, one is allowed to speak even a thousand verses. But the Elder did not do even what was allowable. For the most part, this is the work of elders who are frequent visitors to families. ‘To a nun’s dwelling’: to the dwelling of a nun. It is allowable for one inquiring about the sick to go there, but the Elder did not do even what was allowable. This is the method to be understood in all cases. ‘With powder’: with powder of the kosamba seed, and so on. ‘Body care’: in the act of massaging the body. ‘Attended to’: employed. ‘For as long as the milking of a cow’: for as long as it takes to take a cow by the udder and squeeze out a single drop of milk.

Kena pana kāraṇena thero nirābādho ahosi. Padumuttare kira bhagavati satasahassabhikkhuparivāre [P 4.0196] cārikaṃ caramāne himavati visarukkhā pupphiṃsu. Bhikkhusatasahassānampi tiṇapupphakarogo uppajjati. Thero tasmiṃ samaye iddhimā tāpaso hoti, so ākāsena gacchanto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā otaritvā rogaṃ pucchitvā himavantato osadhaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Upasiṅghanamatteneva rogo vūpasami. Kassapasammāsambuddhakālepi paṭhamavappadivase vappaṃ ṭhapetvā bhikkhusaṅghassa paribhogaṃ aggisālañceva vaccakuṭiñca kāretvā bhikkhusaṅghassa bhesajjavattaṃ nibandhi, iminā kammena nirābādho ahosi. Ukkaṭṭhanesajjiko panesa ukkaṭṭhāraññako ca tasmā “nābhijānāmi apassenakaṃ apassayitā”tiādimāha.

For what reason was the Elder free from illness? It is said that when the Blessed One Padumuttara, surrounded by one hundred thousand monks, was wandering on tour, poisonous trees bloomed in the Himālaya. A disease named Tiṇapupphaka arose among the one hundred thousand monks. At that time, the Elder was an ascetic possessing psychic power. While traveling through the sky, he saw the community of monks, descended, and asked about the illness. He then brought medicine from the Himālaya and gave it. It is said the illness subsided merely by smelling it. Also, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, on the first day of sowing, having set aside the work of sowing, he had a fire-hall and a latrine built for the use of the community of monks and, it is said, gave a constant supply of medicine to the community of monks. Through this kamma, he was free from illness. Furthermore, this Elder is one who undertakes the strict sitter's practice and the strict forest-dweller's practice. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning, 'I do not recall leaning on a support...'

Saraṇoti sakileso. Aññā udapādīti anupasampannassa aññaṃ byākātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Thero kasmā byākāsi? Na thero ahaṃ arahāti āha, aññā udapādīti panāha. Apica thero arahāti pākaṭo, tasmā evamāha.

`Saraṇo` means with defilements. Regarding 'Final knowledge has arisen': It is not proper for one who is not fully ordained to declare final knowledge. Why then did the Elder declare it? The Elder did not say, 'I am an Arahant,' but rather he said, 'Final knowledge has arisen.' Furthermore, the Elder was well-known as an Arahant; therefore, he spoke thus.

212. Pabbajjanti [M 4.0140] thero sayaṃ neva pabbājesi, na upasampādesi aññehi pana bhikkhūhi evaṃ kārāpesi. Avāpuraṇaṃ ādāyāti kuñcikaṃ gahetvā.

212. Regarding `pabbajantaṃ` (the one going forth): The Elder himself neither gave the going forth nor the higher ordination, but rather had other monks do so. `Apāpuraṇaṃ ādāya` means taking the key.

Nisinnakova [V 4.0143] parinibbāyīti ahaṃ dharamānopi na aññassa bhikkhussa bhāro ahosiṃ, parinibbutassāpi me sarīraṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa palibodho mā ahosīti tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā parinibbāyi. Sarīrato jālā uṭṭhahi, chavimaṃsalohitaṃ sappi viya jhāyamānaṃ parikkhayaṃ gataṃ, sumanamakulasadisā [P 4.0197] dhātuyova avasesiṃsu. Sesaṃ sabbattha pākaṭameva. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ dutiyasaṅgahe saṅgītanti.

`Nisinnakova parinibbāyī` (He attained parinibbāna while seated): Reflecting, 'Even while living I was not a burden to any other monk; may my body not be a trouble for the community of monks even after I have attained parinibbāna,' he entered the fire element and attained parinibbāna. A flame arose from his body. His skin, flesh, and blood, burning like ghee, were consumed. Only relics resembling jasmine buds remained. The rest is clear everywhere. This sutta was recited at the Second Council.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Bākulasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bākula Sutta is concluded.

5. Dantabhūmisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Dantabhūmi Sutta

213. Evaṃ [V 4.0144] me sutanti dantabhūmisuttaṃ. Tattha araññakuṭikāyanti tasseva veḷuvanassa ekasmiṃ vivittaṭṭhāne padhānakammikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya katasenāsane. Rājakumāroti bimbisārassa putto orasako.

213. The sutta beginning with `Evaṃ me sutaṃ` is the Dantabhūmi Sutta. Therein, `araññakuṭikāyaṃ` means: in a dwelling made in a secluded place of that very Veḷuvana for the sake of monks engaged in the practice of meditation. `Rājakumāra` means the legitimate son of King Bimbisāra.

Phuseyyāti labheyya. Ekaggatanti evaṃ paṭipanno samāpattiṃ nāma labhati, jhānaṃ nāma labhatīti idaṃ mayā sutanti vadati. Kilamathoti kāyakilamatho. Vihesāti sveva kilamatho vutto. Yathāsake tiṭṭheyyāsīti attano ajānanakoṭṭhāseyeva tiṭṭheyyāsīti.

`Phuseyya` means one might obtain. `Ekaggataṃ`: He says, 'I have heard this saying: one who practices thus obtains what is called attainment, obtains what is called jhāna.' By `kilamatho`, bodily fatigue is meant. By `vihesā`, that very same fatigue is meant. `Yathāsake tiṭṭheyyāsi` means: you should remain only in the sphere of your own not-knowing.

214. Desesīti cittekaggataṃ nāma evaṃ labhati, samāpattiṃ evaṃ nibbattetīti appanāupacāraṃ pāpetvā ekakasiṇaparikammaṃ kathesi. Pavedetvāti pakāsetvā.

214. `Desesi`: The novice taught the preliminary kasina practice, having brought it to access and absorption concentration, saying, 'Thus one obtains what is called one-pointedness of mind; thus one produces attainment.' `Pavedetvā` means having explained.

Nekkhammena ñātabbanti kāmato nissaṭaguṇena ñātabbaṃ. Kāmato nissaṭaguṇe ṭhitena puggalena ekaggaṃ nāma jānitabbanti adhippāyenetaṃ vuttaṃ[M 4.0141]. Sesāni tasseva vevacanāni. Kāme [P 4.0198] paribhuñjantoti duvidhepi kāme bhuñjamāno.

`Nekkhammena ñātabbaṃ` means it is to be known by the quality of being free from sensual pleasures (of objects and defilements). This was said by the Blessed One with the intention that what is called one-pointedness is to be known by a person established in the quality of being free from sensual pleasures. The remaining terms are synonyms for that. `Kāme paribhuñjanto` means one who enjoys both kinds of sensual pleasures.

215. Hatthidammā vā assadammā vā godammā vāti ettha adantahatthidammādayo viya cittekaggarahitā puggalā daṭṭhabbā. Dantahatthiādayo viya cittekaggasampannā. Yathā adantahatthidammādayo kūṭākāraṃ akatvā dhuraṃ achaḍḍetvā dantagamanaṃ vā gantuṃ, dantehi vā pattabbaṃ bhūmiṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkonti, evameva cittekaggarahitā sampannacittekaggehi nibbattitaguṇaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ pattabhūmiṃ vā pāpuṇituṃ na sakkonti.

215. Regarding `hatthidammā vā assadammā vā godammā vā`: Herein, persons devoid of one-pointedness of mind should be seen as like untamed elephants and so on. Persons endowed with one-pointedness of mind should be seen as like tamed elephants and so on. Just as untamed elephants and the like, without acting crookedly and without throwing off the yoke, are unable to go the way of the tamed or to reach the ground that is to be reached by the tamed, just so, persons devoid of one-pointedness of mind are unable to produce the quality produced by those with accomplished one-pointedness of mind or to reach the attainable state.

216. Hatthavilaṅghakenāti hatthena hatthaṃ gahetvā.

216. `Hatthavilaṅghakena` means by taking one person's hand with another's hand.

Daṭṭheyyanti [V 4.0145] passitabbayuttakaṃ. Āvutoti āvarito. Nivutoti nivārito. Ophuṭoti onaddho.

`Diṭṭheyyaṃ` means what is fit to be seen. `Āvuṭo` means covered. `Nivuṭo` means hindered. `Ophuṭo` means overspread.

217. Nāgavanikanti hatthipadopame (ma. ni. 1.288 ādayo) nāgavanacarako puriso “nāgavaniko”ti vutto, idha hatthisikkhāya kusalo hatthiṃ gahetuṃ samattho. Atipassitvāti disvā. Etthagedhāti etasmiṃ pavattagedhā. Sarasaṅkappānanti dhāvanasaṅkappānaṃ. Manussakantesu sīlesu samādapanāyāti ettha yadā nāgo itthipurisehi kumārakumārikāhi soṇḍādīsu [P 4.0199] gahetvā upakeḷayamāno vikāraṃ na karoti sukhāyati, tadānena manussakantāni sīlāni samādinnāni nāma honti.

217. `Nāgavanikaṃ`: In the Hatthipadopama Sutta, a man who roams in an elephant forest is called a `nāgavanika`; here, a man skilled in elephant-lore and able to capture an elephant is called a `nāgavanika`. `Atipassitvā` means having observed. `Etthagedhā` means greed that has arisen in this. `Sarasaṅkappānaṃ` means thoughts of harming. Regarding `manussakantesu sīlesu samādapanāya`: Here, when an elephant, being played with by men and women, boys and girls, who grab its trunk and so on, shows no adverse reaction and is at ease, then it is said that it has undertaken conduct that is pleasing to humans.

Pemanīyāti tāta rājā te pasanno maṅgalahatthiṭṭhāneva ṭhapessati, rājārahāni bhojanādīni labhissasīti evarūpī nāgehi piyāpitabbā kathā. Sussūsatīti taṃ pemanīyakathaṃ sotukāmo hoti. Tiṇaghāsodakanti tiṇaghāsañceva udakañca, tiṇaghāsanti ghāsitabbaṃ tiṇaṃ, khāditabbanti attho.

`Pemanīyā`: This is speech that is to be endeared to elephants, such as: 'My dear, the king is pleased with you. He will place you in the position of the state elephant. You will receive food and so on fit for a king.' `Sussūsati` means he becomes desirous of hearing that endearing speech. `Tiṇaghāsodakaṃ` means grass-fodder and water. `Tiṇaghāsaṃ`: the meaning is grass to be eaten and grass to be chewed.

Paṇavoti ḍiṇḍimo. Sabbavaṅkadosanihitaninnītakasāvoti nihitasabbavaṅkadoso ceva apanītakasāvo ca. Aṅganteva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti aṅgasamo hoti.

`Paṇavo` means a ḍiṇḍima drum. `Sabbavaṅkadosanihitaninnītakasāvo` means one who has laid down all faults of crookedness and has removed the astringent stain. `Aṅganteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati` means he becomes like a limb.

219. Gehasitasīlānanti [M 4.0142] pañcakāmaguṇanissitasīlānaṃ. Ñāyassāti aṭṭhaṅgikamaggassa.

219. `Gehasitasīlānaṃ` means of virtues dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. `Ñāyassa` means for the attainment of the Eightfold Path.

222. Adantamaraṇaṃ mahallako rañño nāgo kālaṅkatoti rañño mahallako nāgo adantamaraṇaṃ mato kālaṃ kato hoti, adantamaraṇaṃ kālaṃkiriyaṃ nāma kariyatīti ayamettha attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti.

222. `Adantaṃ maraṇaṃ mahallako rañño nāgo kālaṅkato`: The king's old elephant died an untamed death. This is the meaning here: it is called 'dying an untamed death'. This method should be understood everywhere. The rest is clear.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Dantabhūmisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dantabhūmi Sutta is concluded.

6. Bhūmijasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta

223. Evaṃ [V 4.0146] me sutanti bhūmijasuttaṃ. Tattha bhūmijoti ayaṃ thero jayasenarājakumārassa mātulo. Āsañca anāsañcāti kālena āsaṃ kālena anāsaṃ. Sakena [P 4.0200] thālipākenāti pakatipavattāya bhikkhāya attano niṭṭhitabhattatopi bhattena parivisi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

223. Thus have I heard—this is the Bhūmija Sutta. Therein, as to 'Bhūmija': this elder was the maternal uncle of Prince Jayasena. As to 'hope and no hope': at times there is hope, at times there is no hope. As to 'with his own pot of cooked rice': he served with rice from that which was prepared for his own benefit. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bhūmijasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta is concluded.

7. Anuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta.

230. Evaṃ [V 4.0147] me sutanti anuruddhasuttaṃ. Tattha evamāhaṃsūti tassa upāsakassa aphāsukakālo ahosi, tadā upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu. Apaṇṇakanti avirādhitaṃ. Ekatthāti appamāṇāti vā mahaggatāti vā jhānameva cittekaggatāyeva evaṃ vuccatīti imaṃ sandhāya evamāha.

230. Thus have I heard—this is the Anuruddha Sutta. Therein, as to 'thus they spoke': when that lay follower was unwell, the monks approached and spoke thus. As to 'incontrovertible': it means not incorrect. As to 'of one meaning': it is said thus, meaning either 'immeasurable' or 'exalted,' referring to jhāna itself or unification of mind itself. Having this in mind, he spoke thus.

231. Yāvatā [M 4.0143] ekaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ mahaggatanti pharitvā adhimuccitvā viharatīti ekarukkhamūlapamāṇaṭṭhānaṃ kasiṇanimittena ottharitvā tasmiṃ kasiṇanimitte mahaggatajjhānaṃ pharitvā adhimuccitvā viharati. Mahaggatanti panassa ābhogo natthi, kevalaṃ mahaggatajjhānapavattivasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Iminā kho etaṃ gahapati pariyāyenāti iminā kāraṇena. Ettha hi appamāṇāti vuttānaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ nimittaṃ na vaḍḍhati, ugghāṭanaṃ na jāyati, tāni jhānāni abhiññānaṃ vā nirodhassa vā pādakāni na honti, vipassanāpādakāni pana vaṭṭapādakāni bhavokkamanāni ca honti. “Mahaggatā”ti vuttānaṃ pana kasiṇajjhānānaṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhati, ugghāṭanaṃ jāyati, samatikkamā honti, abhiññāpādakāni [P 4.0201] nirodhapādakāni vaṭṭapādakāni bhavokkamanāni ca honti. Evamime dhammā nānatthā, appamāṇā mahaggatāti evaṃ nānābyañjanā ca.

231. As to 'he dwells having pervaded and resolved upon it as exalted as far as a single tree-root': this means that having covered a place the size of a single tree-root with the kasiṇa sign, he dwells having pervaded that kasiṇa sign with the exalted jhāna and having resolved upon it. But as to 'exalted,' there is no reflection of this for him; it is said merely on account of the occurrence of the exalted jhāna. This is the method in all cases. As to 'By this method, householder': it means by this reason. For herein, of the divine abidings called 'immeasurable,' the sign does not expand, removal does not arise, and those jhānas are not a basis for the direct knowledges or for cessation. However, they are a basis for insight, a basis for the round of existence, and a means of entry into existence. But of the kasiṇa-jhānas called 'exalted,' the sign expands, removal arises, there are transcendences, and they are a basis for the direct knowledges, a basis for cessation, a basis for the round of existence, and a means of entry into existence. In this way, these states are of different meanings, and as 'immeasurable' and 'exalted,' they are also of different phrasing.

232. Idāni mahaggatasamāpattito nīharitvā bhavūpapattikāraṇaṃ dassento catasso kho imātiādimāha. Parittābhāti pharitvā jānantassa ayamābhogo atthi, parittābhesu pana devesu nibbattikāraṇaṃ jhānaṃ bhāvento evaṃ vutto. Esa nayo sabbattha. Parittābhā siyā saṃkiliṭṭhābhā honti siyā parisuddhābhā, appamāṇābhā siyā saṃkiliṭṭhābhā honti siyā parisuddhābhā. Kathaṃ? Suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ nibbattetvā pañcahākārehi āciṇṇavasibhāvo paccanīkadhammānaṃ suṭṭhu aparisodhitattā dubbalameva samāpattiṃ vaḷañjitvā appaguṇajjhāne ṭhito kālaṃ katvā parittābhesu nibbattati, vaṇṇo panassa paritto ceva hoti saṃkiliṭṭho ca. Pañcahi panākārehi āciṇṇavasibhāvo paccanīkadhammānaṃ suṭṭhu parisodhitattā suvisuddhaṃ samāpattiṃ vaḷañjitvā paguṇajjhāne ṭhito kālaṃ katvā parittābhesu nibbattati, vaṇṇo [V 4.0148] panassa paritto ceva hoti parisuddho ca. Evaṃ parittābhā siyā saṃkiliṭṭhābhā honti siyā parisuddhābhā. Kasiṇe pana vipulaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ nibbattetvā pañcahākārehi āciṇṇavasibhāvoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ appamāṇābhā siyā saṃkiliṭṭhābhā honti siyā parisuddhābhāti.

232. Now, leading out from the exalted attainment and showing the cause for arising in existence, he said, 'There are these four…' and so on. As to 'of limited radiance': for one who knows by pervading, this reflection exists. But one who develops the jhāna that is the cause for rebirth among the devas of limited radiance is spoken of thus. This is the method in all cases. Those of limited radiance may be of defiled radiance, or they may be of pure radiance. Those of immeasurable radiance may be of defiled radiance, or they may be of pure radiance. How so? Having done the preliminary work on a kasiṇa the size of a tray or a bowl and produced the attainment, one who has not practiced mastery in the five aspects, because the opposing states have not been well purified, having used a weak attainment and being established in a jhāna of little quality, after making an end, is reborn among the devas of limited radiance. And his complexion is both limited and defiled. But one who has practiced mastery in the five aspects, because the opposing states have been well purified, having used a very pure attainment and being established in a proficient jhāna, after making an end, is reborn among the devas of limited radiance. And his complexion is both limited and pure. In this way, those of limited radiance may be of defiled radiance, or they may be of pure radiance. But having done extensive preliminary work on the kasiṇa and produced the attainment, one who has practiced mastery in the five aspects… all this should be understood as being similar to the preceding. In this way, those of immeasurable radiance may be of defiled radiance, or they may be of pure radiance.

Vaṇṇanānattanti [M 4.0144] sarīravaṇṇassa nānattaṃ. No ca ābhānānattanti āloke nānattaṃ na paññāyati. Accinānattanti [P 4.0202] dīgharassaaṇuthūlavasena acciyā nānattaṃ.

As to 'diversity of complexion': it is the diversity of the body's complexion. But as to 'no diversity of radiance': diversity in light is not apparent. As to 'diversity of flame': it is the diversity of the flame by way of long, short, fine, and coarse.

Yattha yatthāti uyyānavimānakapparukkhanadītīrapokkharaṇītīresu yattha yattha. Abhinivisantīti vasanti. Abhiramantīti ramanti na ukkaṇṭhanti. Kājenāti yāgubhattatelaphāṇitamacchamaṃsakājesu yena kenaci kājena. “Kācenāti”pi pāṭho, ayameva attho. Piṭakenāti pacchiyā. Tattha tatthevāti sappimadhuphāṇitādīnaṃ sulabhaṭṭhānato loṇapūtimacchādīnaṃ ussannaṭṭhānaṃ nītā “pubbe amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ phāsukaṃ, tattha sukhaṃ vasimhā, idha loṇaṃ vā no bādhati pūtimacchagandho vā sīsarogaṃ uppādetī”ti evaṃ cittaṃ anuppādetvā tattha tattheva ramanti.

As to 'wherever, wherever': in parks, mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, on river banks, on pond banks, wherever. As to 'they settle down': they dwell. As to 'they delight': they take pleasure, they are not dissatisfied. As to 'with a carrying pole': with any kind of carrying pole, such as for rice-gruel, cooked rice, oil, molasses, fish, or meat. There is also the reading 'kācena,' which has the same meaning. As to 'with a basket': by means of a basket. As to 'right there': flies taken from a place where ghee, honey, molasses, and so on are easy to get, to a place where salt, rotten fish, and so on are abundant, do not give rise to the thought, 'Previously, our dwelling place was pleasant; we dwelt there happily. Here, the salt afflicts us, or the smell of rotten fish causes a headache.' Instead, they delight right there.

234. Ābhāti ābhāsampannā. Tadaṅgenāti tassā bhavūpapattiyā aṅgena, bhavūpapattikāraṇenāti attho. Idāni taṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchanto ko nu kho, bhantetiādimāha.

234. As to 'radiant': it means endowed with radiance. As to 'by that factor': by a factor for that arising in existence; the meaning is 'by the cause for arising in existence.' Now, asking about that cause, he said, 'What now, venerable sir?' and so on.

Kāyaduṭṭhullanti kāyālasiyabhāvo. Jhāyatoti jalato.

As to 'bodily grossness': it is the state of bodily laziness. As to 'of one meditating': it means of one burning.

235. Dīgharattaṃ kho meti thero kira pāramiyo pūrento isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā samāpattiṃ nibbattetvā nirantaraṃ tīṇi attabhāvasatāni brahmaloke paṭilabhi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ āha. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

235. As to 'For a long time for me': it is said that the elder, while fulfilling the perfections, having gone forth with the going-forth of a sage and produced the meditative attainments, uninterruptedly obtained three hundred states of existence in the Brahma world. Having this in mind, he said this. And this too was said:

“Avokiṇṇaṃ [V 4.0149] tīṇi sataṃ, yaṃ pabbajiṃ isipabbajjaṃ;

Asaṅkhataṃ gavesanto, pubbe sañcaritaṃ mama”nti.

Unmixed for three hundred existences, I went forth with the going-forth of a sage; seeking the unconditioned, this was my practice in the past.

Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Anuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta is concluded.

8. Upakkilesasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta

236. Evaṃ [V 4.0150][P 4.0203] me sutanti upakkilesasuttaṃ. Tattha etadavocāti neva bhedādhippāyena na piyakamyatāya, atha khvāssa etadahosi – “ime bhikkhū [M 4.0145] mama vacanaṃ gahetvā na oramissanti, buddhā ca nāma hitānukampakā, addhā nesaṃ bhagavā ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathessati, taṃ sutvā ete oramissanti, tato tesaṃ phāsuvihāro bhavissatī”ti. Tasmā etaṃ “idha, bhante”tiādivacanamavoca. Mā bhaṇḍanantiādīsu “akatthā”ti pāṭhasesaṃ gahetvā “mā bhaṇḍanaṃ akatthā”ti evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Aññataroti so kira bhikkhu bhagavato atthakāmo, ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – “ime bhikkhū kodhābhibhūtā satthu vacanaṃ na gaṇhanti, mā bhagavā ete ovadanto kilamī”ti, tasmā evamāha.

236. Thus have I heard—the Upakkilesa Sutta. Therein, 'he spoke thus' means he spoke not with the intention of causing division, nor out of a desire to be dear, but rather this thought occurred to him: 'These monks, having taken my words, will not desist. Buddhas, however, are compassionate for the welfare of beings. Surely, the Blessed One will state a reason to them. Having heard it, they will desist, and then they will have a comfortable abiding.' Therefore, he spoke the words beginning, 'Here, venerable sir.' In the passage beginning 'Do not quarrel,' by supplying the elided text 'akattha,' the meaning should be understood as 'Do not quarrel.' 'A certain one' means that that monk, it seems, desired the Blessed One's welfare. This, it seems, was his intention: 'These monks, overcome by anger, do not accept the Teacher's word. May the Blessed One not become weary admonishing them.' Therefore, he spoke thus.

Piṇḍāya pāvisīti na kevalaṃ pāvisi, yenapi janena na diṭṭho, so maṃ passatūtipi adhiṭṭhāsi. Kimatthaṃ adhiṭṭhāsīti? Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ damanatthaṃ. Bhagavā hi tadā piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto “puthusaddo samajano”tiādigāthā bhāsitvā kosambito bālakaloṇakāragāmaṃ gato. Tato pācīnavaṃsadāyaṃ, tato pālileyyakavanasaṇḍaṃ gantvā pālileyyahatthināgena upaṭṭhahiyamāno temāsaṃ vasi. Nagaravāsinopi – “satthā vihāraṃ gato, gacchāma dhammassavanāyā”ti gandhapupphahatthā vihāraṃ gantvā “kahaṃ, bhante, satthā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Kahaṃ tumhe satthāraṃ dakkhatha, satthā ‘ime bhikkhū samagge [P 4.0204] karissāmī’ti āgato, samagge kātuṃ asakkonto nikkhamitvā gato”ti. “Mayaṃ satampi sahassampi datvā satthāraṃ ānetuṃ na sakkoma, so no ayācito sayameva āgato, mayaṃ ime bhikkhū nissāya satthu sammukhā dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ na labhimhā. Ime satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajitā, tasmimpi sāmaggiṃ karonte samaggā na jātā, kassāññassa vacanaṃ karissanti. Alaṃ na imesaṃ bhikkhā dātabbā”ti sakalanagare daṇḍaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Te punadivase sakalanagaraṃ piṇḍāya caritvā kaṭacchumattampi bhikkhaṃ alabhitvā vihāraṃ āgamaṃsu. Upāsakāpi te puna āhaṃsu – “yāva satthāraṃ na khamāpetha, tāva vo tameva daṇḍakamma”nti. Te “satthāraṃ khamāpessāmā”ti bhagavati sāvatthiyaṃ anuppatte [V 4.0151] tattha agamaṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni desesīti ayamettha pāḷimuttakakathā.

'He entered for alms-food' means he did not merely enter, but he also made the resolution: 'Let that person by whom I have not been seen, see me.' Why did he make this resolution? For the purpose of subduing those monks. For at that time, the Blessed One, having returned from his alms-round, spoke the verses beginning, 'Great was the noise of the assembly,' and then went from Kosambī to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra. From there he went to the Pācīnavaṃsa grove, and from there he went to the Pālileyyaka forest tract, where he dwelt for the three months of the rains retreat, being attended upon by the elephant king Pālileyyaka. The city-dwellers, thinking, 'The Teacher has gone to the monastery; let us go to hear the Dhamma,' went to the monastery with perfumes and flowers in hand and asked, 'Venerable sirs, where is the Teacher?' The monks replied, 'Where would you see the Teacher? The Teacher came thinking, "I will bring these monks to concord," but being unable to bring them to concord, he departed and went away.' The lay followers said, 'We cannot bring the Teacher here even by giving a hundred or a thousand. He came to us uninvited, of his own accord, yet on account of these monks, we did not get to hear a Dhamma talk in the Teacher’s presence. These monks went forth for the sake of the Teacher, but when he himself was creating harmony, they did not become harmonious. Whose word will they now follow? Enough! Alms should not be given to them.' And they imposed a penalty throughout the entire city. The next day, after wandering through the whole city for alms-food and not receiving even a ladle-full, they returned to the monastery. The lay followers told them again, 'As long as you do not gain the Teacher's forgiveness, that same penalty will apply to you.' Thinking, 'We will gain the Teacher's forgiveness,' they went to Sāvatthī when the Blessed One arrived there. The Teacher then taught them the eighteen grounds for causing schism. This here is the extra-canonical account.

237. Idāni puthusaddotiādigāthāsu puthu mahāsaddo assāti puthusaddo. Samajanoti samāno ekasadiso jano, sabbovāyaṃ bhaṇḍanakārakajano [M 4.0146] samantato saddaniccharaṇena puthusaddo ceva sadiso cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na bālo koci maññathāti tatra koci ekopi ahaṃ bāloti na maññati, sabbepi paṇḍitamāninoyeva. Nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññarunti koci ekopi ahaṃ bāloti na ca maññi, bhiyyo ca saṅghasmiṃ bhijjamāne aññampi ekaṃ “mayhaṃ kāraṇā saṅgho bhijjatī”ti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ na maññīti attho.
