237. Now, in the verses beginning 'puthusaddo': 'puthusaddo' means 'it has a great noise.' 'Samajano' means a group of people who are the same, of one kind. It is said that this entire group of quarrel-makers, by emitting sounds all around, is both of 'great noise' and 'of one kind.' Regarding 'No one thought himself a fool': there, not even one thinks, 'I am a fool'; all are conceited of their own wisdom. Regarding 'Nor did they think anything further': not even one thought, 'I am a fool,' and furthermore, as the Sangha was splitting, they did not consider this other single reason: 'The Sangha is splitting because of me.' This is the meaning.

Parimuṭṭhāti muṭṭhassatino. Vācāgocarabhāṇinoti rākārassa rassādeso kato; vācāgocarāva[P 4.0205], na satipaṭṭhānagocarā, bhāṇino ca, kathaṃ bhāṇino? Yāvicchanti mukhāyāmaṃ, yāva mukhaṃ pasāretuṃ icchanti, tāva pasāretvā bhāṇino, ekopi saṅghagāravena mukhasaṅkocanaṃ na karotīti attho. Yena nītāti yena kalahena imaṃ nillajjabhāvaṃ nītā. Na taṃ vidū na taṃ jānanti “evaṃ sādīnavo aya”nti.

'They are bewildered' means they are of lost mindfulness. In 'speakers whose domain is speech,' the short vowel is substituted for the long one; their domain is only speech, not the domain of the establishments of mindfulness. And they are speakers. How are they speakers? 'To the extent they wish, they stretch their mouths' means they speak, stretching their mouths as much as they wish to stretch them. The meaning is that not even one contracts their mouth out of respect for the Sangha. 'By which they are led' means by which quarrel they have been led to this state of shamelessness. 'They do not know it' means they do not know, 'This has such a disadvantage.'

Ye ca taṃ upanayhantīti taṃ akkocchi mantiādikaṃ ākāraṃ ye upanayhanti. Sanantanoti porāṇo.

'And those who bind it to themselves' means those who bind that attitude of 'He abused me,' and so on. 'Sanantano' means ancient.

Pareti paṇḍite ṭhapetvā tato aññe bhaṇḍanakārakā pare nāma. Te ettha saṅghamajjhe kalahaṃ karontā “mayaṃ yamāmase upayamāma nassāma satataṃ samitaṃ maccusantikaṃ gacchāmā”ti na jānanti. Ye ca tattha vijānantīti ye ca tattha paṇḍitā “mayaṃ maccuno samīpaṃ gacchāmā”ti vijānanti. Tato sammanti medhagāti evañhi te jānantā yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetvā medhagānaṃ kalahānaṃ vūpasamāya paṭipajjanti.

'Others' refers to the quarrel-makers who are other than the wise, setting the wise aside. While making quarrels in the midst of the Sangha, they do not know: 'We are perishing, we are coming to ruin, we are constantly and perpetually going to the presence of death.' 'And those who understand there' means those wise ones there who understand: 'We are going to the vicinity of death.' 'Thence quarrels are allayed' means that because they, knowing thus, generate wise attention and practice for the appeasement of quarrels, the quarrels are therefore allayed.

Aṭṭhicchinnāti ayaṃ gāthā jātake (jā. 1.9.16) āgatā, brahmadattañca dīghāvukumārañca sandhāya [V 4.0152] vuttā. Ayañhettha attho – tesampi tathā pavattaverānaṃ hoti saṅgati, kasmā [P 4.0206] tumhākaṃ na hoti, yesaṃ vo neva mātāpitūnaṃ aṭṭhīni chinnāni, na pāṇā haṭā na gavāssadhanāni haṭānīti.

This verse beginning 'Bones were broken' comes from the Jātaka and was spoken in reference to Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu. And this is the meaning here: even for them, whose enmity had proceeded in such a way, there was reconciliation. Why should there not be for you, for whom neither were the bones of your parents broken, nor lives taken, nor cattle, horses, and wealth carried away?

Sace [M 4.0147] labhethātiādigāthā paṇḍitasahāyassa ca bālasahāyassa ca vaṇṇāvaṇṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttā. Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayānīti pākaṭaparissaye ca paṭicchannaparissaye ca abhibhavitvā tena saddhiṃ attamano satimā careyyāti.

The verses beginning 'If one should find' were spoken to illuminate the good and bad qualities of a wise companion and a foolish companion. 'Having overcome all dangers' means that having overcome both manifest dangers and concealed dangers, one should wander with him, glad-minded and mindful.

Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitanti yathā attano vijitaraṭṭhaṃ mahājanakarājā ca arindamamahārājā ca pahāya ekakā vicariṃsu, evaṃ vicareyyāti attho. Mātaṅgaraññeva nāgoti mātaṅgo araññe nāgova. Mātaṅgoti hatthi vuccati. Nāgoti mahantādhivacanametaṃ. Yathā hi mātuposako mātaṅganāgo araññe eko cari, na ca pāpāni akāsi, yathā ca pālileyyako, evaṃ eko care, na ca pāpāni kayirāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'As a king a conquered kingdom': just as King Mahājanaka and King Arindama, having abandoned their own conquered kingdom, wandered alone, so should one wander; this is the meaning. 'Like a great elephant in the forest': like a great elephant (mātaṅga) in the forest. By 'mātaṅga' an elephant is meant. 'Nāga' is a term for 'great'. Just as the great elephant who supported his mother wandered alone in the forest and did no evil, and just as Pālileyyaka did, so should one wander alone and not do evil; this is what is meant.

238. Bālakaloṇakāragāmoti upāligahapatissa bhogagāmo. Tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Gaṇe kirassa ādīnavaṃ disvā ekavihāriṃ bhikkhuṃ passitukāmatā udapādi, tasmā sītādīhi pīḷito uṇhādīni patthayamāno viya upasaṅkami. Dhammiyā kathāyāti ekībhāve ānisaṃsappaṭisaṃyuttāya. Yena [P 4.0207] pācīnavaṃsadāyo, tattha kasmā upasaṅkami? Kalahakārake kirassa diṭṭhādīnavattā samaggavāsino bhikkhū passitukāmatā udapādi, tasmā sītādīhi pīḷito uṇhādīni patthayamāno viya tattha upasaṅkami. Āyasmā ca anuruddhotiādi vuttanayameva.

238. 'The village of Bālakaloṇakāra' was the estate village of the householder Upāli. Why did he approach? It is said that, having seen the disadvantage in a group, the desire arose in him to see a monk who lives alone; therefore, like one afflicted by cold and so on desiring warmth and so on, he approached. 'With Dhamma talk' means with talk connected with the advantages of being alone. Why did he go to the Pācīnavaṃsa grove? It is said that, because he had seen the disadvantage in the quarrelsome ones, the desire arose in him to see the monks who live in harmony; therefore, like one afflicted by cold and so on desiring warmth and so on, he approached there. 'The Venerable Anuruddha' and so on is in the manner already explained.

241. Atthi pana voti pacchimapucchāya lokuttaradhammaṃ puccheyya. So pana therānaṃ natthi, tasmā taṃ pucchituṃ na yuttanti parikammobhāsaṃ pucchati. Obhāsañceva sañjānāmāti parikammobhāsaṃ sañjānāma. Dassanañca rūpānanti dibbacakkhunā rūpadassanañca sañjānāma. Tañca nimittaṃ nappaṭivijjhāmāti tañca kāraṇaṃ na jānāma, yena no obhāso ca rūpadassanañca antaradhāyati.

241. With the final question, 'But is there for you...?', he would be asking about the supramundane Dhamma. That, however, the elders did not possess; therefore, thinking, 'It is not proper to ask that,' he asks about the preliminary light. 'We perceive light' means: we perceive the preliminary light. 'And the seeing of forms' means: we also perceive the seeing of forms with the divine eye. 'But we do not penetrate that sign' means: we do not know that cause by which the light and the seeing of forms disappear for us.

Taṃ kho pana vo anuruddhā nimittaṃ paṭivijjhitabbanti taṃ vo kāraṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Ahampi sudanti anuruddhā tumhe kiṃ na āḷulessanti, ahampi imehi ekādasahi upakkilesehi [V 4.0153] āḷulitapubboti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ [M 4.0148] ārabhi. Vicikicchā kho metiādīsu mahāsattassa ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā nānāvidhāni rūpāni disvā “idaṃ kho ki”nti vicikicchā udapādi. Samādhi cavīti parikammasamādhi cavi. Obhāsoti parikammobhāsopi antaradhāyi, dibbacakkhunāpi rūpaṃ na passi. Amanasikāroti rūpāni passato vicikicchā uppajjati, idāni kiñci na manasikarissāmīti amanasikāro udapādi.

'But that sign, Anuruddhas, should be penetrated by you' means: that cause should be known by you. He began this discourse to show the following meaning: 'I too, you see, Anuruddhas... How could you not be troubled? I too was formerly troubled by these eleven defilements.' Regarding 'Doubt arose in me,' and so on: for the Great Being, having increased the light and seen various forms with the divine eye, the doubt 'What is this?' arose. 'The concentration shifted' means: the preliminary concentration shifted. 'The light' means: the preliminary light also disappeared, and he did not see the form with the divine eye. 'Inattention' means: for him who was seeing forms, doubt arose; then the inattention, 'Now I will not attend to anything,' arose.

Thinamiddhanti [P 4.0208] kiñci amanasikarontassa thinamiddhaṃ udapādi.

'Sloth and torpor' means: for him who was not attending to anything, sloth and torpor arose.

Chambhitattanti himavantābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dānavarakkhasaajagarādayo addasa, athassa chambhitattaṃ udapādi.

'Being terror-struck' means: having increased the light towards the Himālaya, he saw dānavas, rakkhasas, pythons, and so on; then, being terror-struck arose in him.

Uppilanti “mayā diṭṭhabhayaṃ pakatiyā olokiyamānaṃ natthi. Adiṭṭhe kiṃ nāma bhaya”nti cintayato uppilāvitattaṃ udapādi. Sakidevāti ekapayogeneva pañca nidhikumbhiyopi passeyya.

'Elation' means: for him who was thinking, 'The fear seen by me is not something naturally observed. In what has not been seen before, what fear could there be?', a state of elation arose. 'Just once' means: with a single effort, one might see even five jars of treasure.

Duṭṭhullanti mayā vīriyaṃ gāḷhaṃ paggahitaṃ, tena me uppilaṃ uppannanti vīriyaṃ sithilamakāsi, tato kāyadaratho kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ kāyālasiyaṃ udapādi.

'Bodily coarseness' means: thinking, 'I exerted effort strongly, and because of that, elation arose in me,' he slackened his effort. From that, bodily discomfort, bodily coarseness, and bodily laziness arose.

Accāraddhavīriyanti mama vīriyaṃ sithilaṃ karoto duṭṭhullaṃ uppannanti puna vīriyaṃ paggaṇhato accāraddhavīriyaṃ udapādi. Patameyyāti mareyya.

'Excessive effort' means: for him who, thinking, 'When I slackened my effort, coarseness arose,' exerted effort again, excessive effort arose. 'Might fall' means: might die.

Atilīnavīriyanti mama vīriyaṃ paggaṇhato evaṃ jātanti puna vīriyaṃ sithilaṃ karoto atilīnavīriyaṃ udapādi.

'Excessively slack effort' means: for him who, thinking, 'For me, while exerting effort, it became thus (i.e., excessive),' slackened his effort again, excessively slack effort arose.

Abhijappāti devalokābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā devasaṅghaṃ passato taṇhā udapādi.

'Longing' means: for him who, having increased the light towards the deva-world, was seeing the assembly of devas, craving arose.

Nānattasaññāti mayhaṃ ekajātikaṃ rūpaṃ manasikarontassa abhijappā uppannā, nānāvidharūpaṃ [V 4.0154] manasi karissāmīti kālena devalokābhimukhaṃ kālena manussalokābhimukhaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nānāvidhāni rūpāni manasikaroto nānattasaññā udapādi.

'Perception of diversity' means: for him who, thinking, 'For me, while attending to a single kind of form, longing arose; I will attend to various kinds of forms,' at times increased the light towards the deva-world and at times towards the human world, and was attending to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose.

Atinijjhāyitattanti mayhaṃ nānāvidhāni rūpāni manasikarontassa nānattasaññā udapādi, iṭṭhaṃ vā aniṭṭhaṃ [P 4.0209] vā ekajātikameva manasi karissāmīti tathā manasikaroto atinijjhāyitattaṃ rūpānaṃ udapādi.

'The state of overly meditating on forms' means: for him who, thinking, 'For me, while attending to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose; I will attend to only one kind, whether desirable or undesirable,' attended in that way, the state of overly meditating on forms arose.

243. Obhāsanimittaṃ [M 4.0149] manasi karomīti parikammobhāsameva manasi karomi. Na ca rūpāni passāmīti dibbacakkhunā rūpāni na passāmi. Rūpanimittaṃ manasi karomīti dibbacakkhunā visayarūpameva manasi karomi.

243. 'I attend to the sign of light' means: I attend only to the preliminary light. 'And I do not see forms' means: I do not see forms with the divine eye. 'I attend to the sign of form' means: I attend only to the object-form with the divine eye.

Parittañceva obhāsanti parittakaṭṭhāne obhāsaṃ. Parittāni ca rūpānīti parittakaṭṭhāne rūpāni. Vipariyāyena dutiyavāro veditabbo. Paritto samādhīti parittako parikammobhāso, obhāsaparittatañhi sandhāya idha parikammasamādhi “paritto”ti vutto. Parittaṃ me tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ samaye dibbacakkhupi parittakaṃ hoti. Appamāṇavārepi eseva nayo.

'And the light is limited' means: the light in a limited place. 'And the forms are limited' means: the forms in a limited place. The second case should be understood in the opposite way. 'The concentration is limited' means: the preliminary light is limited; for with reference to the limitedness of the light, the preliminary concentration is here called 'limited'. 'My... was limited at that time' means: at that time the divine eye is also limited. In the case of the immeasurable, this same method should be understood.

245. Avitakkampi vicāramattanti pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānasamādhiṃ. Avitakkampi avicāranti catukkanayepi pañcakanayepi jhānattayasamādhiṃ. Sappītikanti dukatikajjhānasamādhiṃ. Nippītikanti dukajjhānasamādhiṃ. Sātasahagatanti tikacatukkajjhānasamādhiṃ. Upekkhāsahagatanti catukkanaye catutthajjhānasamādhiṃ pañcakanaye pañcamajjhānasamādhiṃ.

245. 'Without initial application but with sustained application' refers to the concentration of the second jhāna in the fivefold system. 'Without initial application and without sustained application' refers to the concentration of the jhānas from the second (in the fourfold system) or third (in the fivefold system) onwards. 'With rapture' refers to the concentration of the first two jhānas in the fourfold system or the first three jhānas in the fivefold system. 'Without rapture' refers to the concentration of the third and fourth jhānas in the fourfold system or the fourth and fifth jhānas in the fivefold system. 'Accompanied by pleasure' refers to the concentration of the first three jhānas in the fourfold system or the first four jhānas in the fivefold system. 'Accompanied by equanimity' refers to the concentration of the fourth jhāna in the fourfold system and the fifth jhāna in the fivefold system.

Kadā pana bhagavā imaṃ tividhaṃ samādhiṃ bhāveti? Mahābodhimūle nisinno pacchimayāme. Bhagavato hi paṭhamamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko ahosi, dutiyādayo dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānikā[P 4.0210]. Pañcakanaye pañcamajjhānassa maggo natthīti so lokiyo ahosīti lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

When, now, does the Blessed One develop this threefold concentration? While seated at the foot of the Great Bodhi Tree during the last watch of the night. For the Blessed One, the first path was associated with the first jhāna, and the subsequent paths were associated with the second, third, and fourth jhānas. In the fivefold method, there is no path for the fifth jhāna; thus it was mundane. This was stated with reference to the mixture of the mundane and supramundane. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Upakkilesasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta is concluded.

9. Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta

246. Evaṃ [V 4.0155] me sutanti bālapaṇḍitasuttaṃ. Tattha bālalakkhaṇānīti bālo ayanti etehi lakkhiyati ñāyatīti bālalakkhaṇāni. Tāneva tassa sañjānanakāraṇānīti bālanimittāni. Bālassa apadānānīti bālāpadānāni[M 4.0150]. Duccintitacintīti cintayanto abhijjhābyāpādamicchādassanavasena duccintitameva cinteti. Dubbhāsitabhāsīti bhāsamānopi musāvādādibhedaṃ dubbhāsitameva bhāsati. Dukkaṭakammakārīti karontopi pāṇātipātādivasena dukkaṭakammameva karoti. Tatra ceti yattha nisinno, tassaṃ parisati. Tajjaṃ tassāruppanti tajjātikaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ, pañcannaṃ verānaṃ diṭṭhadhammakasamparāyikaādīnavappaṭisaṃyuttanti adhippāyo. Tatrāti [P 4.0211] tāya kathāya kacchamānāya. Bālantiādīni sāmiatthe upayogavacanaṃ.

246. ‘Thus have I heard’—this is the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta. Therein, ‘the characteristics of a fool’ (bālalakkhaṇāni) means that by these one is marked and known as ‘this is a fool’; hence they are the characteristics of a fool. Those very things are the causes for recognizing him; hence they are ‘the signs of a fool’ (bālanimittāni). ‘The grounds of a fool’ (bālāpadānāni) means the causes of a fool. ‘He thinks evil thoughts’ (duccintitacintī) means that when thinking, by way of covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, he thinks only evil thoughts. ‘He speaks evil words’ (dubbhāsitabhāsī) means that when speaking, he speaks only evil words of the kind of false speech and so on. ‘He does evil deeds’ (dukkaṭakammakārī) means that when acting, by way of killing living beings and so on, he does only evil deeds. ‘And there’ (tatra ca) means in whatever assembly he is seated. ‘Befitting him, suitable for him’ (tajjaṃ tassāruppaṃ) means of his kind, suitable for him; the meaning is that he discusses matters connected with the danger in this life and the next of the five kinds of enmity. ‘There’ (tatrāti) means while that talk is being spoken. ‘The fool’ (bālaṃ) and so on is a term in the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive.

248. Olambantīti upaṭṭhahanti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ, olambanādiākārena hi tāni upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Pathaviyā olambantīti pathavitale pattharanti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pattharaṇākāroyeva hesa. Tatra, bhikkhave, bālassāti tasmiṃ upaṭṭhānākāre āpāthagate bālassa evaṃ hoti.

248. ‘Olambanti’ means they present themselves. The remaining two terms are synonyms for that very word, for they present themselves in the manner of hanging down and so on; therefore, it is said thus. ‘Pathaviyā olambanti’ means they spread out on the surface of the earth. The remaining two terms are synonyms for that very word. For it has the very manner of spreading. ‘Therein, monks, for the fool’ (tatra, bhikkhave, bālassa) means that when that manner of presentation comes into range, it occurs thus to the fool.

249. Etadavocāti anusandhikusalo bhikkhu “nirayassa upamā kātuṃ na sakkā”ti na bhagavā vadati, “na sukarā”ti pana vadati, na sukaraṃ pana sakkā hoti kātuṃ, handāhaṃ dasabalaṃ upamaṃ kārāpemīti cintetvā etaṃ “sakkā, bhante”ti vacanaṃ avoca. Haneyyunti vinivijjhitvā gamanavasena yathā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne dve pahārā nipatanti, evaṃ haneyyuṃ. Tenassa dve vaṇamukhasatāni honti. Ito uttaripi eseva nayo.

249. ‘He said this’ (etadavoca) means a monk skilled in making connections thought, ‘The Blessed One does not say, “It is not possible to make a simile for hell,” but he says, “It is not easy.” However, what is not easy is possible to do. Come now, I will have the One of Ten Powers make a simile.’ Thinking thus, he spoke this statement: ‘It is possible, venerable sir.’ ‘They would strike’ (haneyyuṃ) means they would strike in such a way that, by piercing through and through, two blows fall in one place. By that, he has two hundred wound-openings. From here on, the method is the same.

250. Pāṇimattanti antomuṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapanamattaṃ. Saṅkhampi na upetīti gaṇanamattampi na gacchati. Kalabhāgampīti satimaṃ kalaṃ sahassimaṃ kalaṃ satasahassimaṃ vā kalaṃ upagacchatītipi vattabbataṃ na upeti. Upanidhampīti upanikkhepanamattampi na upeti, olokentassa olokitamattampi [V 4.0156] natthi. Tattaṃ [P 4.0212] ayokhilanti tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ sampajjalitāya lohapathaviyā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā tassa dakkhiṇahatthe tālappamāṇaṃ ayasūlaṃ pavesenti, tathā vāmahatthādīsu. Yathā ca uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā, evaṃ urenapi dakkhiṇapassenapi vāmapassenapi nipajjāpetvā taṃ kammakāraṇaṃ karontiyeva. Saṃvesetvāti sampajjalitāya lohapathaviyā tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ nipajjāpetvā. Kuṭhārīhīti mahatīhi gehassa ekapakkhachadanamattāhi kuṭhārīhi tacchanti. Lohitaṃ nadī hutvā sandati, lohapathavito jālā uṭṭhahitvā tacchitaṭṭhānaṃ gaṇhanti. Mahādukkhaṃ uppajjati, tacchantā [M 4.0151] pana suttāhataṃ karitvā dārū viya aṭṭhaṃsampi chaḷaṃsampi karonti. Vāsīhīti mahāsuppapamāṇāhi vāsīhi. Tāhi tacchantā tacato yāva aṭṭhīni saṇikaṃ tacchanti, tacchitaṃ tacchitaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ hoti. Rathe yojetvāti saddhiṃ yugayottapañcaracakkakubbarapācanehi sabbato sampajjalite rathe yojetvā. Mahantanti mahākūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ. Āropentīti sampajjalitehi ayamuggarehi pothentā āropenti. Sakimpi [P 4.0213] uddhanti supakkuthitāya ukkhaliyā pakkhittataṇḍulā viya uddhaṃ adho tiriyañca gacchati.

250. ‘The size of a hand’ (pāṇimattaṃ) means the measure of what can be placed inside a closed fist. ‘It does not approach comparison’ (saṅkhampi na upeti) means it does not reach even the measure of counting. ‘Even a fraction’ (kalabhāgampi) means it does not reach a state where it could be said that it approaches a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousandth part. ‘Even a likeness’ (upanidhampi) means it does not even reach the measure of being placed nearby; for one looking, there is not even the measure of a glance. ‘A heated iron stake’ (tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ) means having made his body, three gāvutas in size, lie face-up on a blazing iron ground, they drive an iron stake the size of a palm tree trunk into his right hand, and similarly into his left hand and other parts. And just as they make him lie face-up, so too they make him lie on his chest, on his right side, and on his left side, and perform that same act of torture. ‘Having laid him down’ (saṃvesetvā) means having made his body, three gāvutas in size, lie on the blazing iron ground. ‘With axes’ (kuṭhārīhi) means they chop him with great axes, each the size of one side of a large house’s roof. Blood flows, becoming a river. From the iron ground, flames rise up and seize the chopped place. Great suffering arises. And as they chop, they make the wood, as it were, into eight-sided or six-sided pieces after marking it with a string. ‘With adzes’ (vāsīhīti) means with adzes the size of a large winnowing basket. Chopping with these, they slowly slice from the skin down to the bone. Each place that is sliced becomes whole again. ‘Having yoked him to a chariot’ (rathe yojetvā) means having yoked him to a chariot that is blazing on all sides, together with its yoke, straps, frame, wheels, axle, and goad. ‘Great’ (mahantaṃ) means the size of a great gabled mansion. ‘They make him ascend’ (āropenti) means they make him ascend it, striking him with blazing iron hammers. ‘Tossed up’ (sakimpi uddhaṃ) means he is cooked, going upwards, downwards, and across, like rice grains thrown into a very boiling pot.

Bhāgaso mitoti bhāge ṭhapetvā ṭhapetvā vibhatto. Pariyantoti parikkhitto. Ayasāti upari ayapaṭṭena chādito.

‘Measured out by portions’ (bhāgaso mito) means divided, having been set out in portions. ‘With a boundary’ (pariyanto) means enclosed all around. ‘Of iron’ (ayasā) means covered above with an iron plate.

Samantā yojanasataṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, yathā samantā yojanasate ṭhāne ṭhatvā olokentassa akkhīni yamakagoḷakā viya nikkhamanti.

‘It stands pervading a hundred yojanas all around’ (samantā yojanasataṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati) means it stands pervading in such a way that, for one standing in a place a hundred yojanas all around and looking, the eyes pop out like a pair of playing balls.

Na sukarā akkhānena pāpuṇitunti nirayo nāma evampi dukkho evampi dukkhoti vassasataṃ vassasahassaṃ kathentenāpi matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathetuṃ na sukarāti attho.

‘It is not easy to reach the end by description’ (na sukarā akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ) means that it is not easy to speak to the very end, even for one speaking for a hundred years or a thousand years, saying, ‘Hell is painful in this way, and painful in that way.’ This is the meaning.

251. Dantullehakanti dantehi ullehitvā, luñcitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rasādoti rasagedhena paribhuttaraso.

251. ‘Licking with the teeth’ (dantullehakaṃ) means licking with the teeth, plucking out; thus it is said. ‘A taster of flavors’ (rasādo) means one who has consumed flavors with greed for taste.

252. Aññamaññakhādikāti aññamaññakhādanaṃ.

252. ‘Eating one another’ (aññamaññakhādikā) means the eating of one another.

Dubbaṇṇoti [V 4.0157] durūpo. Duddasikoti dārakānaṃ bhayāpanatthaṃ katayakkho viya duddaso. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako paviṭṭhagīvo mahodaro. Kāṇoti ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā. Kuṇīti ekahatthakuṇī vā ubhayahatthakuṇī vā. Pakkhahatoti pīṭhasappī. So [P 4.0214] kāyenāti idamassa dukkhānupabandhadassanatthaṃ āraddhaṃ.

‘Of bad complexion’ (dubbaṇṇo) means ugly. ‘Ugly to see’ (duddasiko) means hard to look at, like a yakkha created to frighten children. ‘Deformed’ (okoṭimako) means a dwarf, with a sunken-in neck and a large belly. ‘Blind’ (kāṇo) means blind in one eye or blind in both eyes. ‘Crippled’ (kuṇī) means crippled in one hand or crippled in both hands. ‘Paralyzed’ (pakkhahato) means a cripple who moves by dragging himself. ‘He, with his body’ (so kāyena) — this was stated by the Blessed One to show his continuous connection with suffering.

Kaliggahenāti parājayena. Adhibandhaṃ nigaccheyyāti yasmā bahuṃ jito sabbasāpateyyampissa nappahoti, tasmā attanāpi bandhaṃ nigaccheyya. Kevalā paripūrā bālabhūmīti bālo tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā [M 4.0152] niraye nibbattati, tattha pakkāvasesena manussattaṃ āgato pañcasu nīcakulesu nibbattitvā puna tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā niraye nibbattatīti ayaṃ sakalā paripuṇṇā bālabhūmi.

'By being overcome in gambling' means by defeat. 'He would fall into bondage' means: because for one who has lost much, all his wealth is not sufficient, therefore he himself would fall into bondage. 'The entire, complete ground of a fool' means: the fool, having fulfilled the three kinds of misconduct, is born in hell; there, by the remainder of ripened karma, having returned to the human state, he is born into one of the five low families, and again, having fulfilled the three kinds of misconduct, he is born in hell. This is the entire, complete ground of a fool.

253. Paṇḍitalakkhaṇānītiādi vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Sucintitacintītiādīni cettha manosucaritādīnaṃ vasena yojetabbāni.

253. 'The characteristics of the wise,' and so forth, should be understood just in accordance with what has been stated. And here, 'thinking well-thought thoughts,' and so forth, should be connected by way of mental good conduct and so forth.

Cakkaratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Wheel-Gem

256. Sīsaṃ nhātassāti sīsena saddhiṃ gandhodakena nhātassa. Uposathikassāti samādinnauposathaṅgassa. Uparipāsādavaragatassāti pāsādavarassa upari gatassa subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā pāsādavarassa upari mahātale sirīgabbhaṃ pavisitvā sīlāni āvajjantassa. Tadā kira rājā pātova satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ datvā punapi soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi sīsaṃ nhāyitvā katapātarāso suddhaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekaṃsaṃ katvā uparipāsādassa sirīsayane pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno attano dānamayapuññasamudayaṃ āvajjetvā nisīdati, ayaṃ sabbacakkavattīnaṃ dhammatā[P 4.0215].

256. 'Of one who has bathed his head' means of one who has bathed, including his head, with fragrant water. 'Of one on Uposatha' means of one who has undertaken the Uposatha factors. 'Of one who has gone up to the excellent palace' means of one who, having ascended to the top of the excellent palace, having eaten a fine meal, having entered the auspicious chamber on the great upper terrace of the excellent palace, is reflecting on his virtues. At that time, it is said, the king, having early in the morning given away a hundred thousand and made a great donation, then bathed his head again with sixteen pots of fragrant water, and having had his morning meal, draped a clean upper robe over one shoulder, and sat cross-legged on the splendid couch in the upper palace, reflecting on the accumulation of merit born of his generosity. This is the nature of all universal monarchs.

Tesaṃ taṃ āvajjantānaṃyeva vuttappakārapuññakammapaccayaṃ utusamuṭṭhānaṃ nīlamaṇisaṅghāṭasadisaṃ pācīnasamuddajalatalaṃ chindamānaṃ viya ākāsaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ viya dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Tayidaṃ dibbānubhāvayuttattā dibbanti vuttaṃ. Sahassaṃ assa arānanti sahassāraṃ. Saha [V 4.0158] nemiyā saha nābhiyā cāti sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ. Sabbehi ākārehi paripūranti sabbākāraparipūraṃ.

For them, while they were thus reflecting, conditioned by their meritorious deeds of the kind described and produced by the physical environment, a divine wheel-gem appeared, like a mass of blue gems, as if splitting the surface of the eastern ocean, as if adorning the sky. And this is called 'divine' because it is endowed with divine power. 'It has a thousand spokes' (sahassaṃ assa arānanti), thus it is 'thousand-spoked' (sahassāraṃ). 'With a rim and with a hub' (saha nemiyā saha nābhiyā cāti), thus it is 'with-rim' (sanemikaṃ) and 'with-hub' (sanābhikaṃ). 'Complete in all aspects' (sabbehi ākārehi paripūranti), thus it is 'all-aspects-complete' (sabbākāraparipūraṃ).

Tattha cakkañca taṃ ratijananaṭṭhena ratanañcāti cakkaratanaṃ. Yāya pana taṃ nābhiyā “sanābhika”nti vuttaṃ, sā indanīlamaṇimayā hoti. Majjhe panassā rajatamayā panāḷi, yāya suddhasiniddhadantapantiyā hasamānaṃ viya virocati. Majjhe chiddena viya candamaṇḍalena ubhosupi bāhirantesu rajatapaṭṭena kataparikkhepo hoti. Tesu panassā nābhipanāḷi parikkhepapaṭṭesu yuttaṭṭhāne paricchedalekhā suvibhattāva hutvā paññāyanti. Ayaṃ tāvassa nābhiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

Therein, it is a wheel (cakka) and it is a gem (ratana) in the sense that it generates delight; hence, it is a wheel-gem (cakkaratana). Now, the hub, on account of which it is called 'with a hub,' is made of sapphire. And in its middle is a silver tube, by which it shines as if smiling with a row of pure, smooth teeth. Like a moon-disc pierced in the middle, it is encircled on both outer edges with a silver band. And on its hub, tube, and encircling bands, the demarcation lines in the appropriate places appear clearly divided. This, firstly, is the all-around completeness of its hub.

Yehi [M 4.0153] pana taṃ arehi “sahassāra”nti vuttaṃ, te sattaratanamayā sūriyarasmiyo viya pabhāsampannā honti. Tesampi ghaṭamaṇikaparicchedalekhādīni suvibhattāneva paññāyanti. Ayamassa arānaṃ sabbākāraparipūratā.

Now, the spokes, on account of which it is called 'thousand-spoked,' are made of the seven kinds of gems and are endowed with radiance like the rays of the sun. Of these too, the settings, gems, demarcation lines, and so on, appear clearly divided. This is the all-around completeness of its spokes.

Yāya pana taṃ nemiyā saha “sanemika”nti vuttaṃ, sā bālasūriyarasmikalāpasiriṃ [P 4.0216] avahasamānā viya surattasuddhasiniddhapavāḷamayā hoti. Sandhīsu panassā sañjhārāgasassirikarattajambonadapaṭṭā vaṭṭaparicchedalekhā ca suvibhattā paññāyanti. Ayamassa nemiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

Now, the rim, on account of which it is called 'with a rim,' is made of bright red, pure, and smooth coral, as if mocking the splendor of a cluster of rays from the morning sun. And at its joints, plates of red Jambu-river gold possessing the splendor of the color of twilight, and circular demarcation lines, appear clearly divided. This is the all-around completeness of its rim.

Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyaṃ panassa dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānamantare dhamanavaṃso viya antosusiro chiddamaṇḍalacitto vātagāhī pavāḷadaṇḍo hoti, yassa vātena paharitassa sukusalasamannāhatassa pañcaṅgikatūriyassa viya saddo vaggu ca rajanīyo ca kamanīyo ca hoti. Tassa kho pana pavāḷadaṇḍassa upari setacchattaṃ, ubhosu passesu samosaritakusumadāmapantiyoti evaṃ samosaritakusumadāmapantisatadvayaparivārena setacchattasatadhārinā pavāḷadaṇḍasatena samupasobhitanemiparikkhepassa dvinnampi nābhipanāḷīnaṃ anto dve sīhamukhāni honti, yehi tālakkhandhappamāṇā puṇṇacandakiraṇakalāpasassirikā taruṇaravisamānarattakambalageṇḍukapariyantā ākāsagaṅgāgatisobhaṃ abhibhavamānā viya dve muttakalāpā olambanti, yehi cakkaratanena saddhiṃ [V 4.0159] ākāse samparivattamānehi tīṇi cakkāni ekato parivattantāni viya khāyanti. Ayamassa sabbaso sabbākāraparipūratā.

Furthermore, on the surface of the rim-circle, between every ten spokes, there is a coral rod that catches the wind, is hollow inside like a flute, and is variegated with a circle of holes. When struck by the wind, its sound is lovely, enchanting, and captivating, like that of a five-part orchestra skillfully played. Above that coral rod is a white parasol, with rows of hanging flower garlands on both sides. Thus, from within the two hub-tubes of the rim-circumference—which is magnificently adorned by a hundred coral rods bearing a hundred white parasols and surrounded by two hundred rows of hanging flower garlands—hang two clusters of pearls. These are the size of palm-trunks, splendid with a cluster of rays from the full moon, bordered by woolen balls as red as the morning sun, and seem to surpass the beauty of the celestial Ganges' flow. As they revolve in the sky together with the wheel-gem, it appears as if three wheels are revolving together. This is its all-around completeness in every way.

Taṃ panetaṃ evaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ pakatiyā sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā attano attano gharadvāre paññattāsanesu [P 4.0217] nisīditvā pavattakathāsallāpesu manussesu vīthicatukkādīsu kīḷamāne dārakajane nātiuccena nātinīcena vanasaṇḍamatthakāsannena ākāsappadesena upasobhayamānaṃ viya rukkhasākhaggāni, dvādasayojanato paṭṭhāya suyyamānena madhurassarena sattānaṃ sotāni odhāpayamānaṃ yojanato paṭṭhāya nānappabhāsamudayasamujjalena vaṇṇena nayanāni samākaḍḍhantaṃ [M 4.0154] rañño cakkavattissa puññānubhāvaṃ ugghosayantaṃ viya rājadhāniabhimukhaṃ āgacchati.

Now this wheel-gem, thus complete in every aspect, approaches the royal capital as if proclaiming the power of merit of the wheel-turning king. It comes while people, having eaten their usual evening meal, are sitting on seats prepared at their own house doors engaged in conversation, and while children are playing in the streets, at crossroads, and so on. It travels through a region of the sky that is not too high and not too low, near the tops of the forest groves, as if beautifying the tips of the tree branches. From twelve yojanas away, it causes the ears of beings to attend with its sweet sound, which can be heard from that distance. From one yojana away, it strongly attracts their eyes with its color, resplendent with the arising of various radiances.

Atha tassa cakkaratanassa saddassavaneneva “kuto nu kho, kassa nu kho ayaṃ saddo”ti āvajjitahadayānaṃ puratthimadisaṃ olokayamānānaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ aññataro aññataraṃ evamāha – “passa bho acchariyaṃ, ayaṃ puṇṇacando pubbe eko uggacchati, ajja pana attadutiyo uggato, etañhi rājahaṃsamithunaṃ viya puṇṇacandamithunaṃ pubbāpariyena gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghatī”ti. Tamañño āha – “kiṃ kathesi samma kahaṃ nāma tayā dve puṇṇacandā ekato uggacchantā diṭṭhapubbā, nanu esa tapanīyaraṃsidhāro piñcharakiraṇo divākaro uggato”ti. Tamañño sitaṃ katvā evamāha – “kiṃ ummattosi, nanu kho idānimeva divākaro atthaṅgato, so kathaṃ imaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ anubandhamāno uggacchissati, addhā panetaṃ anekaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ ekassa puññavato vimānaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Te sabbepi apasādayantā aññe evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ bahuṃ vippalapatha, nevesa puṇṇacando, na sūriyo na devavimānaṃ. Na hetesaṃ evarūpā [P 4.0218] sirisampatti atthi, cakkaratanena panetena bhavitabba”nti.

Then, just by hearing the sound of that wheel-gem, those people, their hearts reflecting, 'From where, indeed, does this sound come? Whose sound is it, indeed?', looked toward the eastern direction. Among them, one man said to another, 'Look, friend, what a marvel! Previously, this full moon rises alone, but today it has risen with itself as a second. Indeed, like a pair of royal haṃsa birds, this pair of full moons rises into the expanse of the sky, one after the other!' Another said to him, 'What are you saying, friend? Where, indeed, have you ever before seen two full moons rising together? Surely, this is the day-maker that has risen, the orb bearing heat-giving rays, with rays like a peacock's tail feather!' Another, smiling, said to him, 'Are you mad? Has not the day-maker just now set? How then could it rise following this full moon? Surely, this must be the celestial mansion of some meritorious being, resplendent with the light of many jewels.' Then others, dismissing all of them, said, 'Why do you babble so much? This is not the full moon, nor the sun, nor a celestial mansion. For these do not possess such a perfection of sound. It must be the wheel-gem.'

Evaṃ pavattasallāpasseva tassa janassa candamaṇḍalaṃ ohāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti. Tato tehi “kassa nu kho idaṃ nibbatta”nti vutte bhavanti vattāro – “na kassaci aññassa, nanu amhākaṃ rājā pūritacakkavattivatto, tassetaṃ nibbatta”nti. Atha so ca mahājano, yo ca añño passati, sabbo cakkaratanameva anugacchati. Tampi cakkaratanaṃ raññoyeva atthāya attano āgatabhāvaṃ ñāpetukāmaṃ viya sattakkhattuṃ pākāramatthakeneva nagaraṃ anusaṃyāyitvā [V 4.0160] rañño antepuraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā antepurassa uttarasīhapañjaraāsanne ṭhāne yathā gandhapupphādīhi sukhena sakkā hoti pūjetuṃ, evaṃ akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati.

While that populace was thus engaged in conversation, leaving behind the moon's orb, that wheel-gem came to face the king's palace. Then, when it was said by them, 'For whose sake, indeed, has this arisen?', there were those who spoke: 'For no one else. Is not our king one who has fulfilled the practice of wheel-turning monarchs? For his sake this has arisen.' Then that great multitude, and whoever else saw it, all followed the wheel-gem. And that wheel-gem, as if wishing to make known the fact of its own arrival for the king's sake, circled the city seven times along the top of the ramparts. Then, having circumambulated the king's inner palace to the right, it stood in a place near the northern lion-window of the inner palace, in such a way that it could be easily honored with perfumes, flowers, and the like, standing as if fixed by an axle.

Evaṃ ṭhitassa panassa vātapānacchiddādīhi pavisitvā nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ anto pāsādaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ pabhāsamūhaṃ disvā dassanatthāya sañjātābhilāso rājā hoti. Parijanopissa piyavacanapābhatena āgantvā tamatthaṃ nivedeti. Atha rājā balavapītipāmojjaphuṭasarīro pallaṅkaṃ [M 4.0155] mocetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā sīhapañjarasamīpaṃ gantvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ disvā “sutaṃ kho pana meta”ntiādikaṃ cintanaṃ cintesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “disvāna rañño khattiyassa…pe… assaṃ nu kho ahaṃ rājā cakkavattī”ti. Tattha so hoti rājā cakkavattīti kittāvatā cakkavattī hoti? Ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi cakkaratane ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte.

Now, upon seeing the mass of light from this gem that stood thus—a light resplendent with the splendor of various and diverse jewels—entering through window openings and the like and adorning the interior of the palace, the king conceived a desire to see it. His retinue also, having approached with the gift of pleasing words, informed him of that matter. Then the king, his body suffused with strong joy and delight, released his cross-legged posture, rose from his seat, went near the lion-window, and upon seeing the wheel-gem, thought the thought beginning with, 'I have indeed heard of this...' Therefore it was said by the Blessed One: 'Having seen, of the Khattiya king... (etc.)... Might I, indeed, be a wheel-turning king?' Therein, regarding 'he is a wheel-turning king': to what extent is one a wheel-turning monarch? When the wheel-gem, having ascended into the sky by even the measure of one or two finger-breadths, turns.

Idāni tassa pavattāpanatthaṃ yaṃ kātabbaṃ taṃ dassento atha kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha [P 4.0219] uṭṭhāyāsanāti nisinnāsanato uṭṭhahitvā cakkaratanasamīpaṃ āgantvā. Bhiṅkāraṃ gahetvāti hatthisoṇḍasadisapanāḷiṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ ukkhipitvā vāmahatthena udakaṃ gahetvā. Pavattatu bhavaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratananti. Anvadeva rājā cakkavattī saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyāti sabbacakkavattīnañhi udakena abhisiñcitvā “abhivijānātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti vacanasamanantarameva vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā cakkaratanaṃ pavattati, yassa pavattisamakālameva so rājā cakkavattī nāma hoti.

Now, showing what must be done to cause it to turn, He said the words beginning with, 'Then, O monks...' Therein, 'rising from his seat' means having risen from the seat where he was sitting and having approached the wheel-gem. 'Having taken the water pot' means having lifted up the golden water pot, which has a spout like an elephant's trunk, with the left hand, and having taken the water with the right hand, he sprinkles it, saying: 'May the venerable wheel-gem turn! May the venerable wheel-gem conquer completely!' In the passage, 'The wheel-turning king follows with his fourfold army': for all wheel-turning monarchs, immediately after sprinkling with water and saying, 'May the venerable wheel-gem conquer completely!', the wheel-gem, having ascended into the sky, turns. At the very same time of its turning, that king becomes one named 'wheel-turning monarch'.

Pavatte pana cakkaratane taṃ anubandhamānova rājā cakkavattī yānavaraṃ āruyha vehāsaṃ abbhuggacchati, athassa chattacāmarādihattho parijano ceva antepurajano ca. Tato nānappakārakañcukakavacādisannāhavibhūsitena vividhāharaṇappabhāsamujjalitena samussitaddhajapaṭākapaṭimaṇḍitena attano attano balakāyena saddhiṃ uparājasenāpati pabhūtayopi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivārenti. Rājayuttā pana janasaṅgahatthaṃ nagaravīthīsu bheriyo carāpenti “tātā amhākaṃ rañño cakkaratanaṃ [P 4.0220] nibbattaṃ, attano attano vibhavānurūpena maṇḍitappasādhitā sannipatathā”ti. Mahājano pana pakatiyā cakkaratanasaddeneva sabbakiccāni [V 4.0161] pahāya gandhapupphādīni ādāya sannipatitova, sopi sabbo vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivāreti. Yassa yassa hi raññā saddhiṃ gantukāmatā uppajjati, so so ākāsagatova hoti. Evaṃ dvādasayojanāyāmavitthārā parisā hoti. Tattha ekapurisopi chinnabhinnasarīro vā kiliṭṭhavattho vā natthi. Suciparivāro hi rājā cakkavattī. Cakkavattiparisā nāma vijjādharaparisā viya ākāse gacchamānā indanīlamaṇitale [M 4.0156] vippakiṇṇaratanasadisā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “anvadeva rājā cakkavattī saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā”ti.

When the wheel-gem turns, the wheel-turning king, following it, mounts an excellent vehicle and ascends into the sky. Then his retinue holding parasols, whisks, and so on, and the people of the inner palace also follow. Then the viceroy, the commander-in-chief, and other prominent figures, together with their own forces—adorned with various kinds of tunics, armor, and other gear, resplendent with the light of diverse weapons, and decorated with uplifted banners and flags—also ascend into the sky and surround the king. The king's ministers, in order to rally the people, cause great drums to be sounded in the city streets, proclaiming: 'Dears, our king's wheel-gem has arisen! Having decorated and adorned yourselves according to your own means, assemble!' The great populace, by nature, just by the sound of the wheel-gem, abandons all duties, and taking perfumes, flowers, and the like, they assemble. All of them also ascend into the sky and surround the king. For whoever the desire to go with the king arises, that very person is one who has gone into the sky. Thus the assembly is twelve yojanas in length and breadth. Therein, there is not even one man with a cut or broken body, or with soiled clothes. For the wheel-turning king has a pure retinue. The assembly of a wheel-turning monarch, moving through the sky like an assembly of knowledge-holders, is like scattered jewels on a surface of sapphire. Therefore it was said: 'The wheel-turning king follows with his fourfold army.'

Tampi cakkaratanaṃ rukkhaggānaṃ uparūpari nātiuccena gaganapadesena pavattati, yathā rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalapallavehi atthikā tāni sukhena gahetuṃ sakkonti, bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitā “esa rājā, esa uparājā, esa senāpatī”ti sallakkhetuṃ sakkonti. Ṭhānādīsupi iriyāpathesu yo yena icchati, so teneva gacchati. Cittakammādisippapasutā cettha attano attano kiccaṃ karontāyeva gacchanti. Yatheva hi bhūmiyaṃ, tathā nesaṃ sabbakiccāni ākāse ijjhanti. Evaṃ cakkavattiparisaṃ gahetvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ vāmapassena sineruṃ pahāya samuddassa uparibhāgena aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ pubbavidehaṃ gacchati.

That wheel-treasure also revolves and travels through a region of the sky not too high, above the treetops, in such a way that those who desire the flowers, fruits, and shoots of the trees are able to take them with ease. Those standing on the ground are able to recognize, 'This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief.' Also, in the postures beginning with standing, whoever desires a particular posture, they travel in that very posture. And among this retinue, those engaged in crafts such as painting travel while performing their own respective tasks. Indeed, just as on the ground, so are all their tasks accomplished in the sky. Thus, taking the retinue of the wheel-turning monarch, that wheel-treasure, leaving Mount Sineru on its left side, travels over the upper part of the ocean to Pubbavideha, which has an extent of eighty thousand yojanas.

Tattha yo vinibbedhena dvādasayojanāya parikkhepato chattiṃsayojanaparisāya sannivesakkhamo sulabhāhārūpakaraṇo chāyūdakasampanno sucisamatalo ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo, tassa uparibhāge taṃ cakkaratanaṃ ākāse akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Atha tena saññāṇena so mahājano otaritvā yathāruci nhānabhojanādīni sabbakiccāni karonto vāsaṃ kappeti, tena vuttaṃ “yasmiṃ [P 4.0221] kho pana, bhikkhave, padese taṃ cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāti, tattha rājā cakkavattī vāsaṃ upeti saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā”ti.

There, there is a delightful region of the earth—suitable for the encampment of the retinue which is twelve yojanas in breadth and thirty-six yojanas in circumference, having facilities that make provisions easy to obtain, endowed with shade and water, and with a clean and level surface. In the sky above that region, the wheel-treasure stands still, as if struck by an axle. Then, by that sign, that great populace descends and, according to their wish, performs all tasks beginning with bathing and eating, and establishes their residence. Therefore, it was said: 'Monks, in whatever region that wheel-treasure comes to rest, there the wheel-turning monarch takes up residence together with his fourfold army.'

Evaṃ vāsaṃ upagate cakkavattimhi ye tattha rājāno, te “paracakkaṃ āgata”nti sutvāpi na balakāyaṃ sannipātetvā yuddhasajjā honti. Cakkaratanassa uppattisamanantarameva natthi so satto nāma, yo paccatthikasaññāya rājānaṃ ārabbha āvudhaṃ ukkhipituṃ visaheyya. Ayamanubhāvo cakkaratanassa.

When the wheel-turning monarch has thus taken up residence, the kings who are there, even upon hearing the words, 'A foreign power has arrived,' do not assemble their host of forces and prepare for battle. Immediately after the arising of the wheel-treasure, there is no being whatsoever who would dare, with the perception of being an enemy, to raise a weapon against the king. This is the power of the wheel-treasure.

Cakkānubhāvena [V 4.0162] hi tassa rañño,

Arī asesā damathaṃ upenti;

Arindamaṃ nāma narādhipassa,

Teneva taṃ vuccati tassa cakkaṃ.

Indeed, by the power of the wheel, all enemies of that king attain the state of being subdued. The lord of men is named Arindama, 'Subduer of Enemies'; for that very reason, that wheel of his is called a 'cakka'.

Tasmā [M 4.0157] sabbepi te rājāno attano attano rajjasirivibhavānurūpaṃ pābhataṃ gahetvā taṃ rājānaṃ upagamma onatasirā attano moḷiyamaṇippabhābhisekenassa pādapūjaṃ karonto “ehi kho mahārājā”tiādīhi vacanehi tassa kiṅkārappaṭissāvitaṃ āpajjanti. Tena vuttaṃ ye kho pana, bhikkhave, puratthimāya…pe… anusāsa mahārājāti.

Therefore, all those kings, taking gifts befitting their own royal splendor and wealth, approach that king. With bowed heads, performing the worship of his feet with the anointment of the radiance of the jewels on their own crowns, they arrive at the state of proclaiming their readiness to serve with words such as, 'Come, O great king!' Therefore, it was said: 'And those, O monks, who are in the east... instruct, O great king.'

Tattha svāgatanti suāgamanaṃ. Ekasmiñhi āgate socanti, gate nandanti. Ekasmiṃ āgate nandanti, gate socanti. Tādiso tvaṃ āgatanandano gamanasocano, tasmā tava āgamanaṃ suāgamananti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ [P 4.0222] vutte pana cakkavattī nāpi “ettakaṃ nāma me anuvassaṃ baliṃ upakappethā”ti vadati, nāpi aññassa bhogaṃ acchinditvā aññassa deti. Attano pana dhammarājabhāvassa anurūpāya paññāya pāṇātipātādīni upaparikkhitvā pemanīyena mañjunā sarena “passatha tātā, pāṇātipāto nāmesa āsevito bhāvito bahulīkato nirayasaṃvattaniko hotī”tiādinā nayena dhammaṃ desetvā “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādikaṃ ovādaṃ deti. Tena vuttaṃ rājā cakkavattī evamāha pāṇo na hantabbo…pe… yathābhuttañca bhuñjathāti.

Therein, 'svāgataṃ' means a good coming. Indeed, when a certain person comes, people grieve, and when they go, they rejoice. When another person comes, people rejoice, and when they go, they grieve. You, being of such a nature, are one who causes rejoicing upon arrival and causes grieving upon departure. Therefore, it is meant that your coming is a good coming. But when this is said, the wheel-turning monarch neither says, 'Prepare for me this much tribute annually,' nor does he, having seized the wealth of another, give it to another. Rather, with wisdom befitting his own state as a Dhamma-king, having examined the taking of life and other such things, he teaches the Dhamma with a lovable and pleasant voice, by the method beginning with: 'See, my dears, this taking of life, when practiced, developed, and made much of, is conducive to hell.' He then gives advice beginning with, 'Life should not be taken.' Therefore, it was said that the wheel-turning monarch speaks thus: 'Life should not be taken... and consume what has been rightfully obtained.'

Kiṃ pana sabbepi rañño imaṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhantīti. Buddhassapi tāva sabbe na gaṇhanti, rañño kiṃ gaṇhissanti. Tasmā ye paṇḍitā vibhāvino, te gaṇhanti. Sabbe pana anuyantā bhavanti. Tasmā “ye kho pana, bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

But do all kings accept this advice of the king? Even the Buddha's advice is not accepted by all; how then will they accept the king's? Therefore, those who are wise and discerning accept it. But all become followers. Therefore, the Blessed One said the passage beginning with, 'And those, O monks...'

Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ evaṃ pubbavidehavāsīnaṃ ovāde dinne katapātarāse cakkavattībalena vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhati. Yathā yathā ca taṃ ajjhogāhati, tathā tathā agadagandhaṃ ghāyitvā saṃkhittaphaṇo nāgarājā viya saṃkhittaūmivipphāraṃ hutvā ogacchamānaṃ [V 4.0163] mahāsamuddasalilaṃ yojanamattaṃ ogantvā antosamudde veḷuriyabhitti viya tiṭṭhati. Taṅkhaṇaññeva ca tassa rañño puññasiriṃ daṭṭhukāmāni viya mahāsamuddatale vippakiṇṇāni nānāratanāni tato tato āgantvā taṃ padesaṃ pūrayanti. Atha sā rājaparisā taṃ nānāratanaparipūraṃ mahāsamuddatalaṃ disvā yathāruci ucchaṅgādīhi ādiyati, yathāruci ādinnaratanāya [M 4.0158] pana parisāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ paṭinivattati. Paṭinivattamāne ca tasmiṃ parisā aggato hoti, majjhe rājā, ante cakkaratanaṃ. Tampi jalanidhijalaṃ palobhiyamānamiva [P 4.0223] cakkaratanasiriyā, asahamānamiva ca tena viyogaṃ, nemimaṇḍalapariyantaṃ abhihanantaṃ nirantarameva upagacchati.

Then, when the advice had thus been given to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha and the morning meal had been eaten, that wheel-treasure, by the power of its turning, rose up into the sky and plunged into the eastern ocean. And as it plunged, the water of the great ocean, as if smelling the scent of an antidote, receded for a yojana, its wave-surge contracted like a Nāga king with its hood drawn in, and stood like a wall of beryl within the ocean. At that very moment, as if desiring to see the meritorious glory of that king, various jewels scattered on the floor of the great ocean came from here and there and filled that region. Then that royal retinue, seeing the great ocean floor filled with various jewels, took them as they wished. When the retinue had taken the jewels according to their wish, that wheel-treasure turned back. And as it was turning back, the retinue was in front, the king in the middle, and the wheel-treasure at the rear. That ocean water also, as if being enticed by the glory of the wheel-treasure and as if unable to bear separation from it, followed closely without any gap, striking up to the edge of the rim.

257. Evaṃ rājā cakkavattī puratthimasamuddapariyantaṃ pubbavidehaṃ abhivijinitvā dakkhiṇasamuddapariyantaṃ jambudīpaṃ vijetukāmo cakkaratanadesitena maggena dakkhiṇasamuddābhimukho gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavattatīti. Evaṃ pavattamānassa pana tassa pavattanavidhānaṃ senāsanniveso paṭirājagamanaṃ tesaṃ anusāsanippadānaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhanaṃ samuddasalilassa ogacchanaṃ ratanādānanti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

257. Thus, the wheel-turning king, having conquered Pubbavideha up to the eastern ocean, and being desirous of conquering Jambudīpa up to the southern ocean, proceeds towards the southern ocean by the path indicated by the wheel-treasure. Therefore, it was said: 'Then, O monks, the wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and re-emerged, proceeds towards the southern direction.' Now, as for this proceeding wheel-treasure, the manner of its proceeding, the assembling of the army, the coming of rival kings, the giving of instruction to them, the plunging into the southern ocean, the receding of the ocean's water, and the taking of the treasures—all this should be understood in the very same way as before.

Vijinitvā pana taṃ dasasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ jambudīpaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā sattayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ aparagoyānaṃ vijetuṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijinitvā pacchimasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ uttarakuruṃ vijetuṃ tatheva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijiya uttarasamuddatopi paccuttarati.

Then, having conquered that Jambudīpa, which measures ten thousand yojanas, and having re-emerged from the southern ocean, he went to conquer Aparagoyāna, measuring seven thousand yojanas, in the very same way as was said before. Having conquered that too up to the ocean's boundary in the very same way, and having re-emerged from the western ocean, he went to conquer Uttarakuru, measuring eight thousand yojanas, in the very same way. Having conquered that too up to the ocean's boundary in the very same way, he re-emerges from the northern ocean.

Ettāvatā raññā cakkavattinā cāturantāya pathaviyā ādhipaccaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. So evaṃ vijitavijayo attano rajjasirisampattidassanatthaṃ sapariso uddhaṃ gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghitvā suvikasitapadumuppalapuṇḍarīkavanavicitte cattāro jātassare viya pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāre cattāro mahādīpe oloketvā cakkaratanadesiteneva maggena yathānukkamaṃ attano rājadhānimeva paccāgacchati. Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ [P 4.0224] antepuradvāraṃ sobhayamānaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati.

By this much, the wheel-turning king has obtained sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans. Thus victorious, for the sake of beholding the glorious accomplishment of his own kingdom, he ascends with his retinue to the vault of the sky. He looks upon the four great continents—each surrounded by five hundred small islands and variegated with groves of well-blossomed paduma lotuses, uppala water lilies, and puṇḍarīka lotuses—as if looking upon the four Jātassara lakes. Then, by the very path indicated by the wheel-treasure, he returns in due order to his own royal capital. Then, that wheel-treasure stands as if adorning the gate of the inner palace.

Evaṃ [V 4.0164] patiṭṭhite pana tasmiṃ cakkaratane rājantepure ukkāhi vā dīpikāhi vā kiñci karaṇīyaṃ na hoti, cakkaratanobhāsoyeva rattiṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamati. Ye ca pana rattiṃ andhakāratthikā honti, tesaṃ andhakārameva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā…pe… evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

Now, when the wheel-treasure is thus established, in the royal inner palace there is no need for torches or lamps, for the radiance of the wheel-treasure alone dispels the darkness at night. And for those who desire darkness at night, for them it is dark. Therefore, it is said: 'Having plunged into the southern ocean... (etc.)... such a wheel-treasure appears.'

Hatthiratanavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Elephant Treasure

258. Evaṃ [M 4.0159] pātubhūtacakkaratanassa panassa cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ sucibhūmibhāgaṃ kāretvā haricandanādīhi surabhigandhehi upalimpāpetvā heṭṭhā vicittavaṇṇasurabhikusumasamākiṇṇaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakānaṃ antarantarā samosaritamanuñña-kusumadāmappaṭimaṇḍitavitānaṃ devavimānaṃ viya abhisaṅkharitvā “evarūpassa nāma deva hatthiratanassa āgamanaṃ cintethā”ti vadanti. So pubbe vuttanayeneva mahādānaṃ datvā sīlāni samādāya taṃ puññasampattiṃ āvajjanto nisīdati, athassa puññānubhāvacodito chaddantakulā vā uposathakulā vā taṃ sakkāravisesaṃ anubhavitukāmo taruṇaravimaṇḍalābhirattacaraṇa-gīvamukhappaṭimaṇḍitavisuddhasetasarīro sattappatiṭṭho susaṇṭhitaṅgapaccaṅgasanniveso vikasitaratta-padumacārupokkharo iddhimā yogī viya vehāsaṃ gamanasamattho manosilācuṇṇarañjitapariyanto viya rajatapabbato hatthiseṭṭho tasmiṃ padese patiṭṭhāti. So chaddantakulā āgacchanto sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchati, uposathakulā sabbajeṭṭho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “uposatho nāgarājā” icceva āgacchati. Svāyaṃ [P 4.0225] pūritacakkavattivattānaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ sutte vuttanayeneva cintayantānaṃ āgacchati, na itaresaṃ. Sayameva pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā maṅgalahatthiṃ apanetvā tattha tiṭṭhati. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… nāgarājāti.

258. Furthermore, when the Wheel Treasure had thus appeared for the Wheel-Turning Monarch, his ministers prepared the customary place for the auspicious elephant. They made a portion of the ground clean, had it smeared with fragrant substances like golden sandalwood, strewed it below with flowers of variegated color and good fragrance, and above fashioned a canopy adorned with delightful hanging flower garlands interspersed among golden stars, like a celestial mansion. They then said, “O Deva, may you contemplate the arrival of such an elephant treasure.” As previously described, that monarch, having given great alms and undertaken the precepts, sits reflecting on that accumulation of merit. Then, impelled by the power of his merit, from either the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage, desiring to enjoy that special honor, a supreme elephant appears. It has a completely pure white body, adorned with feet, neck, and face that are crimson like the newly risen sun's orb; it is firmly established on seven points; it has well-proportioned major and minor limbs; it has a beautiful mouth like a blooming red lotus; it is powerful, capable of traversing the sky like a yogī; and it is like a silver mountain whose edges are colored with realgar powder. This supreme elephant becomes established in that place. If it comes from the Chaddanta lineage, it is the very youngest of all elephants that comes; if from the Uposatha lineage, it is the very eldest. In the Pāḷi Canon, however, it is stated simply as, 'Uposatha, the Nāga king.' This elephant king comes to Wheel-Turning Monarchs who have fulfilled the duties of a Wheel-Turner and are contemplating in the manner described in the Sutta; it does not come to others. Of its own accord, it comes to the customary place for the auspicious elephant, displaces the existing auspicious elephant, and stands there. Therefore, it was said: “Furthermore, O monks… the Nāga king.”

Evaṃ pātubhūtaṃ pana taṃ hatthiratanaṃ disvā hatthigopakādayo haṭṭhatuṭṭhā vegena gantvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā turitaturitaṃ āgantvā taṃ disvā pasannacitto “bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā”ti cintayanto hatthaṃ pasāreti. Atha so gharadhenuvacchako viya kaṇṇe olambetvā sūratabhāvaṃ dassento rājānaṃ upasaṅkamati, rājā taṃ abhiruhitukāmo hoti. Athassa [V 4.0165] parijanā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā taṃ hatthiratanaṃ sovaṇṇaddhajaṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkāraṃ hemajālapaṭicchannaṃ katvā upanenti. Rājā taṃ anisīdāpetvāva sattaratanamayāya nisseṇiyā abhiruyha ākāsaṃ gamananinnacitto hoti. Tassa saha cittuppādeneva so hatthirājā rājahaṃso viya indanīlamaṇippabhājālanīlagaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghati, tato cakkacārikāya vuttanayeneva [M 4.0160] sakalarājaparisā. Iti sapariso rājā antopātarāseyeva sakalapathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati, evaṃ mahiddhikaṃ cakkavattino hatthiratanaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ disvāna rañño cakkavattissa…pe… evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

Furthermore, seeing that elephant treasure that had thus appeared, the elephant keepers and others, being joyful and delighted, went quickly and informed the king. The king came in great haste, and seeing it, his mind became serene. Thinking, “Sirs, this elephant vehicle is indeed excellent! If only it would attain a state of being trained,” he extended his hand. Then, that elephant king, like a calf of a domestic cow, lowered its ears, and displaying its tameness, approached the king. The king desired to mount it. Then his attendants, knowing his intention, adorned the elephant treasure with golden banners and golden ornaments, covered it with a golden net, and brought it to him. The king, without making it kneel, mounted it by a ladder made of the seven treasures, his mind inclined to travel through the sky. Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, the elephant king, like a royal swan, soared up to the dark blue sky-expanse, radiant with a net of sapphire-like lustre. Thereafter, in the same manner as was described for the journey of the wheel, the entire royal retinue followed. Thus, the king with his retinue, having journeyed around the entire earth within the time of a morning meal, returned to the royal capital. So greatly powerful is the elephant treasure of a Wheel-Turning Monarch. Therefore, it was said: “Having seen, for the Wheel-Turning Monarch… such an elephant treasure appears.”

Assaratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Horse Treasure

Evaṃ pātubhūtahatthiratanassa pana cakkavattino parisā pakatimaṅgalaassaṭṭhānaṃ sucisamatalaṃ kāretvā alaṅkaritvā ca purimanayeneva rañño tassa āgamanacintanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ janenti. So purimanayeneva katadānasakkāro [P 4.0226] samādinnasīlova pāsādatale nisinno puññasampattiṃ samanussarati, athassa puññānubhāvacodito sindhavakulato vijjullatāvinaddhasaradakālasetavalāhakarāsisassiriko rattapādo rattatuṇḍo candappabhāpuñjasadisasuddhasiniddhaghanasaṅghātasarīro kākagīvā viya indanīlamaṇi viya ca kāḷavaṇṇena sīsena samannāgatattā kāḷasīso suṭṭhu kappetvā ṭhapitehi viya muñjasadisehi saṇhavaṭṭaujugatigatehi kesehi samannāgatattā muñjakeso vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhāti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ hatthiratane vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ sandhāya bhagavā puna caparantiādimāha.

Furthermore, for the Wheel-Turning Monarch for whom the elephant treasure had thus appeared, his retinue of ministers, having caused the customary place for the auspicious horse to be made clean and level, and having adorned it, in the same way as before, generated enthusiasm in the king for contemplating its arrival. That king, in the same way as before, having given alms and made offerings, having undertaken the precepts, sits on the palace terrace and repeatedly recollects his accumulation of merit. Then, impelled by the power of his merit, from the lineage of Sindhu thoroughbreds, the king of horses named Valāhaka, who can travel through the sky, comes and becomes established in that place. He has a splendor like a mass of white clouds in the autumn season, entwined with vines of lightning; he is red-footed and red-muzzled; his body is a pure, smooth, solid mass like a heap of moonlight; he is ‘black-headed’ because he is endowed with a head of a dark color like a crow's neck or a sapphire; and he is ‘muñja-maned’ because he is endowed with a mane like muñja grass, as if well-arranged, with fine, round, and straight strands. The remainder should all be understood in the same way as was explained for the elephant treasure. With reference to such a horse treasure, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, “Furthermore…”

Maṇiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Jewel Treasure

Evaṃ pātubhūtaassaratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa catuhatthāyāmaṃ sakaṭanābhisamappamāṇaṃ ubhosu antesu kaṇṇikapariyantato viniggatasuparisuddhamuttākalāpehi dvīhi kañcanapadumehi alaṅkataṃ caturāsītimaṇisahassaparivāraṃ tārāgaṇaparivutassa puṇṇacandassa siriṃ paṭippharamānaṃ viya vepullapabbatato maṇiratanaṃ āgacchati. Tassevaṃ āgatassa muttājālake [V 4.0166] ṭhapetvā veḷuparamparāya saṭṭhihatthappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ āropitassa rattibhāge samantā yojanappamāṇaṃ okāsaṃ ābhā pharati, yāya sabbo so okāso aruṇuggamanavelā viya sañjātāloko hoti. Tato kassakā kasikammaṃ, vāṇijā āpaṇugghāṭanaṃ[M 4.0161], te [P 4.0227] te ca sippino taṃ taṃ kammantaṃ payojenti divāti maññamānā. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… maṇiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

Furthermore, to the wheel-turning monarch for whom the horse treasure had thus appeared, there comes from Mount Vepulla the jewel treasure. It is four cubits in length, the size of a cart's nave, adorned at both ends with two golden lotuses and with clusters of exquisitely pure pearls emerging from the rim of the hub, having a retinue of eighty-four thousand jewels, and as if diffusing the splendor of the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When it had thus arrived, it was placed in a net of pearls and raised sixty cubits into the sky by a succession of bamboos. In the nighttime, its radiance spreads over an area of a yojana all around, by which that entire area becomes illuminated as if it were the time of sunrise. Because of this, farmers engage in their farming, merchants open their shops, and those various artisans apply themselves to their respective crafts, thinking it is day. Therefore, it was said: 'Furthermore, monks… the jewel treasure appears.'

Itthiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Woman Treasure

Evaṃ pātubhūtamaṇiratanassa pana cakkavattissa visayasukhavisesakāraṇaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Maddarājakulato vā hissa aggamahesiṃ ānenti, uttarakuruto vā puññānubhāvena sayaṃ āgacchati. Avasesā panassā sampatti “puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati abhirūpā dassanīyā”tiādinā nayena pāḷiyaṃyeva āgatā.

Furthermore, to the wheel-turning monarch for whom the jewel treasure had thus appeared, the woman treasure appears, a cause for the special pleasure of the senses. Indeed, they either bring the chief queen for him from the Madda royal family, or she comes by herself from Uttarakuru through the power of his merit. Her remaining accomplishments are given in the Pāḷi itself by the method beginning with: 'Furthermore, monks, to the wheel-turning monarch, the woman treasure appears—beautiful, lovely to behold...' and so on.

Tattha saṇṭhānapāripūriyā adhikaṃ rūpaṃ assāti abhirūpā. Dissamānā ca cakkhūni pīṇayati, tasmā aññaṃ kiccavikkhepaṃ hitvāpi daṭṭhabbāti dassanīyā. Dissamānā ca somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Paramāyāti evaṃ pasādāvahattā uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasundaratāya. Samannāgatāti upetā. Abhirūpā vā yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā dassanīyā yasmā nātikisā nātithūlā, pāsādikā yasmā nātikāḷikā naccodātā. Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā yasmā atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Manussānañhi vaṇṇābhā bahi na niccharati, devānaṃ atidūraṃ niccharati, tassā pana dvādasahatthappamāṇaṃ padesaṃ sarīrābhā obhāseti.

Herein, she is 'beautiful' (abhirūpā) because she has a surpassing form due to the perfection of her features. And when seen, she gratifies the eyes; therefore, she is to be looked at even having abandoned other distracting tasks, thus she is 'lovely to behold' (dassanīyā). And when seen, she gladdens the mind with joy, thus she is 'charming' (pāsādikā). 'Supreme' (paramāya) means supreme because she is thus one who brings delight. 'Excellence of complexion' (vaṇṇapokkharatāya) means beauty of complexion. 'Endowed' (samannāgatā) means possessed of. Alternatively, she is 'beautiful' because she is neither too tall nor too short; 'lovely to behold' because she is neither too thin nor too stout; 'charming' because she is neither too dark nor too fair. She is 'endowed with supreme excellence of complexion' because she surpasses human complexion but has not reached divine complexion. Indeed, the radiance of a human's complexion does not extend outwards, while that of devas extends very far. Her bodily radiance, however, illuminates an area of twelve cubits.

Nātidīghādīsu cassā paṭhamayugaḷena ārohasampatti, dutiyayugaḷena pariṇāhasampatti, tatiyayugaḷena vaṇṇasampatti vuttā. Chahi vāpi etehi kāyavipattiyā abhāvo, atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇanti iminā kāyasampatti vuttā.

In the phrases 'neither too tall' and so on, by the first pair her perfection of stature is stated; by the second pair, her perfection of proportion; and by the third pair, her perfection of complexion. Alternatively, by these six terms the absence of bodily defect is stated, and by 'surpassing human complexion,' the perfection of her body is stated.

Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vāti sappimaṇḍe pakkhipitvā [P 4.0228] ṭhapitassa satavihatassa tūlapicuno [V 4.0167] vā satavihatassa kappāsapicuno vā kāyasamphasso hoti. Sīteti rañño sītakāle. Uṇheti rañño uṇhakāle. Candanagandhoti niccakālameva supisitassa abhinavassa catujjātisamāyojitassa haricandanassa gandho kāyato vāyati. Uppalagandhoti hasitakathitakālesu mukhato nikkhanto taṅkhaṇaṃ vikasitasseva nīluppalassa atisurabhigandho vāyati.

The touch of her body is like that of a tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton wool that has been carded a hundred times and placed in the cream of ghee. Her touch is warm in the king's cold season and cool in his hot season. As for the fragrance of sandalwood, the scent of golden sandalwood—well-ground, fresh, and compounded with four kinds of perfumes—always wafts from her body. As for the fragrance of a blue lotus, at times of laughing and speaking, a very fragrant scent like that of a freshly blossomed blue lotus wafts from her mouth.

Evaṃ [M 4.0162] rūpasamphassagandhasampattiyuttāya panassā sarīrasampattiyā anurūpaṃ ācāraṃ dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rājānaṃ disvā nisinnāsanato aggidaḍḍhā viya paṭhamameva uṭṭhātīti pubbuṭṭhāyinī. Tasmiṃ nisinne tassa rañño tālavaṇṭena bījanādikiccaṃ katvā pacchā nipatati nisīdatīti pacchānipātinī. Kiṃ karomi devāti tassa kiṃkāraṃ paṭissāvetīti kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī. Rañño manāpameva carati karotīti manāpacārinī. Yaṃ rañño piyaṃ, tadeva vadatīti piyavādinī.

Furthermore, to show conduct appropriate to her bodily perfection, endowed as she was with such perfection of form, touch, and fragrance, the passage beginning 'And so...' was spoken. Therein, seeing the king, she rises from her seat before all else, as if burned by fire; therefore, she is called 'one who rises first' (pubbuṭṭhāyinī). When he is seated, after performing duties for the king such as fanning him with a palm-leaf fan, she sits down after him; therefore, she is called 'one who sits down after' (pacchānipātinī). She reports for duty, saying, 'What shall I do, lord?'; therefore, she is called 'one who is responsive to commands' (kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī). She acts and does only what is pleasing to the king; therefore, she is called 'one of pleasing conduct' (manāpacārinī). She speaks only what is dear to the king; therefore, she is called 'one who speaks pleasingly' (piyavādinī).

Idāni svāssā ācāro bhāvasuddhiyā eva, na sāṭheyyenāti dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha no aticaratīti na atikkamitvā carati, aññaṃ purisaṃ cittenapi na patthetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha ye tassā ādimhi “abhirūpā”tiādayo ante “pubbuṭṭhāyinī”tiādayo guṇā vuttā, te pakatiguṇā eva “atikkantā [P 4.0229] mānusaṃ vaṇṇa”ntiādayo pana cakkavattino puññaṃ upanissāya cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya purimakammānubhāvena nibbattantīti veditabbā. Abhirūpatādikāpi vā cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sabbākārapāripūrā jātā. Tenāha evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

Now, to show that her conduct is only out of purity of nature and not out of deceit, he spoke the passage beginning 'And so...'. Therein, 'she does not transgress' means she does not act transgressively; it means that she does not desire another man even in her mind. Therein, the qualities of hers that were stated—at the beginning, those such as 'beautiful,' and at the end, those such as 'one who rises first'—are her natural qualities. But the qualities such as 'surpassing human complexion' should be understood as arising dependent on the merit of the wheel-turning monarch, from the time of the wheel-treasure's appearance, through the power of the monarch's past kamma. Alternatively, her qualities such as beauty also become perfected in all aspects from the time of the wheel-treasure's appearance. Therefore, he said, 'Such a woman treasure appears.'

Gahapatiratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Householder Jewel.

Evaṃ pātubhūtaitthiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa dhanakaraṇīyānaṃ kiccānaṃ yathāsukhappavattanatthaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavati. So pakatiyāva mahābhogo mahābhogakule jāto rañño dhanarāsivaḍḍhako seṭṭhi gahapati hoti, cakkaratanānubhāvasahitaṃ panassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pātubhavati, yena antopathaviyaṃ yojanabbhantare nidhiṃ passati. So taṃ sampattiṃ disvā [V 4.0168] tuṭṭhahadayo gantvā rājānaṃ dhanena pavāretvā sabbāni dhanakaraṇīyāni sampādeti. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

When the woman jewel has thus appeared, then for the sake of the unimpeded carrying out of duties to be done with wealth for the wheel-turning monarch, the householder jewel appears. He is by nature of great wealth, born into a family of great wealth, and becomes a treasurer-householder who increases the king's store of wealth. And for him, a divine eye, born of the result of kamma and accompanied by the power of the wheel jewel, appears, with which he sees treasure within the earth, within the distance of a yojana. Seeing this attainment, with a joyful heart, he goes to the king, invites him with wealth, and accomplishes all duties to be done with wealth. Therefore, it was said: 'Furthermore, bhikkhus... such a householder jewel appears.'

Pariṇāyakaratanavaṇṇanā

Description of the Advisor Jewel.

Evaṃ pātubhūtagahapatiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa sabbakiccasaṃvidhānasamatthaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati. So rañño jeṭṭhaputtova hoti[M 4.0163]. Pakatiyā eva paṇḍito byatto medhāvī, rañño puññānubhāvaṃ nissāya panassa attano kammānubhāvena paracittañāṇaṃ uppajjati. Yena dvādasayojanāya rājaparisāya cittācāraṃ ñatvā rañño ahite hite ca vavatthapetuṃ samattho hoti. Sopi taṃ attano ānubhāvaṃ disvā tuṭṭhahadayo rājānaṃ sabbakiccānusāsanena pavāreti. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ…pe… pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavatīti. Tattha [P 4.0230] ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetunti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetuṃ.

When the householder jewel has thus appeared, then the advisor jewel, capable of managing all his affairs, appears for the wheel-turning king. He is indeed the king’s eldest son. By nature, he is wise, skilled, and intelligent. Relying on the power of the king’s merit, through the power of his own kamma, the knowledge of others’ minds arises in him. With this, having known the mental states of the royal assembly within twelve yojanas, he is able to determine for the king what is unbeneficial and what is beneficial. He also, seeing this power of his own, with a joyful heart, invites the king with instruction on all affairs. Therefore, it was said: 'Furthermore... the advisor jewel appears.' Therein, 'what should be established is to be established' means to establish what should be established in each respective high position.

259. Samavepākiniyātiādi heṭṭhā vuttameva.

259. The passage beginning with `Samavepākiniyā` has already been explained above.

260. Kaṭaggahenāti jayaggāhena. Mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhanti ekappahāreneva dve vā tīṇi vā satasahassāni. Kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmīti paṇḍito tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati, tato manussalokaṃ āgacchanto kularūpabhogasampattiyaṃ nibbattati, tattha ṭhito tīṇi ca sucaritāni pūretvā puna sagge nibbattatīti ayaṃ sakalā paripuṇṇā paṇḍitabhūmi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

260. `Kaṭaggahena` means by seizing victory. `Mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ` means two or three hundred thousand in a single stroke. `Kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmi` means: a wise person, having fulfilled the three kinds of good conduct, is reborn in heaven; from there, returning to the human world, they are reborn with accomplishment in family, appearance, and wealth; established there, they again fulfill the three kinds of good conduct and are reborn once more in heaven—this is the entire, complete stage of the wise. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta is concluded.

10. Devadūtasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Devadūta Sutta

261. Evaṃ [V 4.0169] me sutanti devadūtasuttaṃ. Tattha dve agārātiādi assapurasutte vitthāritameva.

261. The Devadūta Sutta is the one that begins 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, the passage beginning with 'two houses' has been explained in detail in the Assapura Sutta.

262. Nirayaṃ upapannāti bhagavā katthaci nirayato paṭṭhāya desanaṃ devalokena osāpeti, katthaci devalokato paṭṭhāya nirayena osāpeti. Sace saggasampattiṃ vitthāretvā kathetukāmo hoti, nirayadukkhaṃ ekadesato katheti, tiracchānayonidukkhaṃ pettivisayadukkhaṃ manussalokasampattiṃ ekadesato katheti, saggasampattimeva vitthāreti. Sace nirayadukkhaṃ vitthāretvā kathetukāmo hoti, devalokamanussalokesu [M 4.0164] sampattiṃ tiracchānayonipettivisayesu ca dukkhaṃ ekadesato katheti, nirayadukkhameva vitthāreti. So imasmiṃ sutte nirayadukkhaṃ vitthāretukāmo, tasmā devalokato [P 4.0231] paṭṭhāya desanaṃ nirayena osāpeti. Devalokamanussalokasampattiyo tiracchānayonipettivisayadukkhāni ca ekadesato kathetvā nirayadukkhameva vitthārena kathetuṃ tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālātiādimāha.

262. Regarding 'He is reborn in hell': The Blessed One sometimes begins a teaching from hell and concludes it with the celestial world, and sometimes begins from the celestial world and concludes with hell. If he wishes to elaborate on celestial attainment, he speaks briefly of the suffering of hell, the suffering of the animal realm, the suffering of the ghost realm, and the attainment of the human world, and elaborates only on celestial attainment. If he wishes to elaborate on the suffering of hell, he speaks briefly of the attainment in the celestial and human worlds and the suffering in the animal and ghost realms, and elaborates only on the suffering of hell. In this sutta, He wishes to elaborate on the suffering of hell; therefore, beginning from the celestial world, He concludes the teaching with hell. Having spoken in part of the attainments of the celestial and human worlds and the sufferings of the animal and ghost realms, in order to teach in detail only about the suffering of hell, He spoke the passage beginning with, 'O bhikkhus, those hell-guardians...'

Tattha ekacce therā “nirayapālā nāma natthi, yantarūpaṃ viya kammameva kāraṇaṃ kāretī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ taṃ “atthi niraye nirayapālāti, āmantā, atthi ca kāraṇikā”tiādinā nayena abhidhamme (kathā. 866) paṭisedhitameva. Yathā hi manussaloke kammakāraṇakārakā atthi, evameva niraye nirayapālā atthīti. Yamassa raññoti yamarājā nāma vemānikapetarājā, ekasmiṃ kāle dibbavimāne dibbakapparukkhadibbauyyānadibbanāṭakādisampattiṃ anubhavati, ekasmiṃ kāle kammavipākaṃ, dhammiko rājā.
