Na cesa ekova hoti, catūsu pana dvāresu cattāro janā honti. Nāddasanti attano santike pesitassa kassaci devadūtassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vadati. Atha naṃ yamo “nāyaṃ bhāsitassa atthaṃ sallakkhetī”ti ñatvā sallakkhāpetukāmo ambhotiādimāha.

Therein, some elders say, 'There are no such beings as hell-guardians; kamma itself, like an automaton, causes the punishment.' That statement of theirs is refuted in the Abhidhamma (Kathāvatthu 866) by the method beginning with, 'Are there hell-guardians in hell? Yes. And are there tormentors?' For just as in the human world there are those who carry out punishments, so too in hell there are hell-guardians. Regarding 'of King Yama': King Yama is a king of the vemānika petas. At one time he experiences the attainments of a celestial mansion, celestial wish-fulfilling trees, celestial parks, celestial dancers, and so on; at another time he experiences the result of his kamma. He is a righteous king. And he is not the only one; rather, at the four gates there are four such beings. Regarding 'I did not see': he says this referring to the absence of any divine messenger sent to his presence. Then Yama, knowing, 'This one does not mark the meaning of what was said,' and wishing to make him mark it, spoke the words beginning with, 'O man...'

Jātidhammoti [V 4.0170] jātisabhāvo, aparimutto jātiyā, jāti nāma mayhaṃ abbhantareyeva atthīti. Parato jarādhammotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

‘Subject to birth’ means having the nature of birth, not being freed from birth; the meaning is, ‘Birth is indeed within me.’ For the subsequent terms, ‘subject to aging’ and so on, this same method applies.

263. Paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvāti ettha daharakumāro atthato evaṃ vadati nāma “passatha, bho, mayhampi tumhākaṃ viya hatthapādā atthi, sake panamhi muttakarīse palipanno, attano dhammatāya uṭṭhahitvā nhāyituṃ [P 4.0232] na sakkomi, ahaṃ kiliṭṭhagattomhi, nhāpetha manti vattumpi na sakkomi, jātitomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi jātito aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi jāti āgamissati, iti tassā pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto, vacanattho pana maghadevasutte vuttova.

263. Regarding 'having questioned him about the first divine messenger': Here, a young child, by implication, is said to speak thus: 'See, sirs, I too have hands and feet like you, but I am wallowing in my own urine and feces. By my own nature, I cannot get up and bathe. I have a filthy body. I cannot even say, "Bathe me." Because I am not freed from birth, I have come to be in this state. Indeed, it is not only I; you too are not freed from birth. For just as birth comes to me, so will birth come to you. Therefore, before it comes, do what is good.' For that reason, he has become what is called a divine messenger. The meaning of the term, however, has been stated in the Maghadeva Sutta.

Dutiyaṃ [M 4.0165] devadūtanti etthāpi jarājiṇṇasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya taruṇo ahosiṃ ūrubalabāhubalajavanasampanno, tassa me tā balajavanasampattiyo antarahitā, vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, jarāyamhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi jarāya aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi jarā āgamissati, iti tassā pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto.

Regarding 'the second divine messenger': Here too, an aged, decrepit being, by implication, is said to speak thus: 'See, sirs, I too was once young like you, endowed with strength of thigh, strength of arm, and swiftness. For me, those attainments of strength and swiftness have vanished. Though my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the functions of hands and feet. Because I am not freed from aging, I have come to be in this state. Indeed, it is not only I; you too are not freed from aging. For just as aging comes to me, so will aging come to you. Therefore, before it comes, do what is good.' For that reason, he has become what is called a divine messenger.

Tatiyaṃ devadūtanti etthāpi gilānasatto atthato eva vadati nāma – “passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya nirogo ahosiṃ, somhi etarahi byādhinā abhihato sake muttakarīse palipanno, uṭṭhātumpi na sakkomi, vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, byādhitomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi byādhito aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākaṃ byādhi āgamissati, iti tassa pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto.

Regarding 'the third divine messenger': Here too, a sick being, by implication, is said to speak thus: 'See, sirs, I too was once healthy like you. Now I am afflicted by sickness, wallowing in my own urine and feces. I cannot even get up. Though my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the functions of hands and feet. Because I am not freed from sickness, I have come to be in this state. Indeed, it is not only I; you too are not freed from sickness. For just as sickness comes to me, so will sickness come to you. Therefore, before it comes, do what is good.' For that reason, he has become what is called a divine messenger.

265. Catutthaṃ devadūtanti ettha pana kammakāraṇā vā [P 4.0233] devadūtāti kātabbā kammakāraṇikā vā. Tattha pana kammakāraṇapakkhe bāttiṃsa tāva kammakāraṇā atthato evaṃ vadanti [V 4.0171] nāma – “mayaṃ nibbattamānā na rukkhe vā pāsāṇe vā nibbattāma, tumhādisānaṃ sarīre nibbattāma, iti amhākaṃ pure nibbattitova kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenete devadūtā nāma jātā. Kammakāraṇikāpi atthato evaṃ vadanti nāma – “mayaṃ dvattiṃsa kammakāraṇā karontā na rukkhādīsu karoma, tumhādisesu sattesuyeva karoma, iti amhākaṃ tumhesu pure kammakāraṇākaraṇatova kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenetepi devadūtā nāma jātā.

265. Regarding 'the fourth divine messenger': Here, either the acts of punishment or the inflictors of punishment should be understood as 'divine messengers.' In this context, on the side of the acts of punishment, the thirty-two acts of punishment, by implication, are said to speak thus: 'When we arise, we do not arise in a tree or a stone; we arise in the bodies of those like you. Therefore, before we arise, do what is good.' For that reason, they have become what are called divine messengers. The inflictors of punishment also, by implication, are said to speak thus: 'We, in performing the thirty-two acts of punishment, do not perform them on trees and so on; we perform them only on beings like you. Therefore, before we perform these acts of punishment on you, do what is good.' For that reason, they too have become what are called divine messengers.

266. Pañcamaṃ devadūtanti ettha matakasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “passatha bho maṃ āmakasusāne chaḍḍitaṃ uddhumātakādibhāvaṃ pattaṃ, maraṇatomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi [M 4.0166] maraṇato aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi maraṇaṃ āgamissati, iti tassa pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto.

266. Regarding 'the fifth divine messenger': Here, a dead being, by implication, is said to speak thus: 'Behold, sirs, I am cast away in a charnel ground, having reached the state of being bloated and so forth. Because I am not freed from death, I have become like this. Indeed, it is not I alone who am not freed from death; you too are not free from death. Just as death has come to me, so too will death come to you. Therefore, before its arrival, do what is good.' For that reason, this one has become what is called a divine messenger.

Imaṃ pana devadūtānuyogaṃ ko labhati, ko na labhatīti? Yena tāva bahuṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ, so gantvā niraye nibbattatiyeva. Yena pana parittaṃ pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, so labhati. Yathā hi sabhaṇḍaṃ coraṃ gahetvā kattabbameva karonti, na vinicchinanti. Anuvijjitvā gahitaṃ pana vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ nayanti, so vinicchayaṃ labhati. Evaṃsampadametaṃ. Parittapāpakammā [P 4.0234] hi attano dhammatāyapi saranti, sāriyamānāpi saranti.

Now, who receives this inquiry by the divine messengers, and who does not? One who has done much evil, having gone there, is certainly reborn in hell. But one who has done little evil kamma receives it. It is just as when they catch a thief with the stolen goods, they only do what must be done and do not hold a trial. But one who is caught after investigation, they lead to the place of judgment, and that person receives a judgment. This simile is to be understood in this way. For those with little evil kamma remember by their own nature, and they also remember when reminded.

Tattha dīghajayantadamiḷo nāma attano dhammatāya sari. So kira damiḷo sumanagirivihāre ākāsacetiyaṃ rattapaṭena pūjesi. Atha niraye ussadasāmante nibbatto aggijālasaddaṃ sutvāva attano pūjitapaṭaṃ anussari, so gantvā sagge nibbatto. Aparopi puttassa daharabhikkhuno khalisāṭakaṃ dento pādamūle ṭhapesi, maraṇakālamhi paṭapaṭāti sadde nimittaṃ gaṇhi, sopi ussadasāmante nibbatto jālasaddena taṃ sāṭakaṃ anussaritvā sagge nibbatto. Evaṃ tāva attano dhammatāya kusalaṃ kammaṃ saritvā sagge nibbattatīti.

Among them, a Tamil named Dīghajayanta remembered by his own nature. It is said that this Tamil worshipped the Ākāsacetiya at Sumanagiri monastery with a red cloth. Then, having been reborn near an Ussada hell, upon hearing the sound of the flames of fire, he remembered the cloth he had offered. Having gone from there, he was reborn in a celestial realm. Another person, while giving a coarse cloth to his son who was a young monk, placed it at his feet. At the time of death, he took as his sign the sound 'paṭapaṭā.' He too was reborn near an Ussada hell, and by the sound of the flames, he remembered that cloth and was reborn in a celestial realm. Thus, it should be understood that, firstly, by remembering a wholesome kamma by one's own nature, one is reborn in a celestial realm.

Attano dhammatāya asarante pana pañca devadūte pucchati. Tattha koci paṭhamena devadūtena sarati, koci dutiyādīhi. Yo pana pañcahipi na sarati, taṃ yamo rājā sayaṃ sāreti. Eko [V 4.0172] kira amacco sumanapupphakumbhena mahācetiyaṃ pūjetvā yamassa pattiṃ adāsi, taṃ akusalakammena niraye nibbattaṃ yamassa santikaṃ nayiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pañcahipi devadūtehi kusale asarante yamo sayaṃ olokento disvā – “nanu tvaṃ mahācetiyaṃ sumanapupphakumbhena pūjetvā mayhaṃ pattiṃ adāsī”ti sāresi, so tasmiṃ kāle saritvā devalokaṃ gato. Yamo pana sayaṃ oloketvāpi apassanto – “mahādukkhaṃ nāma anubhavissati ayaṃ satto”ti tuṇhī hoti.

But for those who do not remember by their own nature, he asks about the five divine messengers. Therein, some remember by the first divine messenger, some by the second and so on. But for one who does not remember even by all five, King Yama himself causes him to remember. It is said that a certain minister, having worshipped the Mahācetiya with a pot of jasmine flowers, gave a share of the merit to Yama. Due to unwholesome kamma, he was reborn in hell and was led into Yama's presence. When he did not remember the wholesome deed even with the five divine messengers, Yama, looking himself, saw it and caused him to remember, saying: 'Did you not worship the Mahācetiya with a pot of jasmine flowers and give me a share of the merit?' At that time, he remembered and went to the deva world. But Yama, even looking himself and not seeing, thinks, 'This being will experience great suffering,' and becomes silent.

267. Mahānirayeti avīcimahānirayamhi. Kiṃ panassa pamāṇaṃ? Abbhantaraṃ āyāmena ca vitthārena ca yojanasataṃ hoti. Lohapathavī lohachadanaṃ ekekā ca bhitti [P 4.0235] navanavayojanikā hoti. Puratthimāya bhittiyā [M 4.0167] acci uṭṭhitā pacchimaṃ bhittiṃ gahetvā taṃ vinivijjhitvā parato yojanasataṃ gacchati. Sesadisāsupi eseva nayo. Iti jālapariyantavasena āyāmavitthārato aṭṭhārasayojanādhikāni tīṇi yojanasatāni, parikkhepato pana navayojanasatāni catupaṇṇāsayojanāni, samantā pana ussadehi saddhiṃ dasayojanasahassaṃ hoti.

267. 'In the great hell' means in the great hell of Avīci. Now, what is its measure? The interior is one hundred yojanas in length and in width. The ground is of iron and the roof is of iron, and each wall is nine yojanas thick. A flame, having arisen from the eastern wall, reaches the western wall, pierces through it, and goes one hundred yojanas beyond. This same method applies to the other directions as well. Thus, by way of the extent of the flames, it is three hundred and eighteen yojanas in length and width. In circumference, however, it is nine hundred and fifty-four yojanas. But all around, together with the Ussada hells, it is ten thousand yojanas.

268. Ubbhataṃ tādisameva hotīti ettha akkantapadaṃ yāva aṭṭhito daḷhaṃ uddharitumeva na sakkā. Ayaṃ panettha attho – heṭṭhato paṭṭhāya ḍayhati, uparito paṭṭhāya jhāyati, iti akkamanakāle ḍayhamānaṃ paññāyati, uddharaṇakāle tādisameva, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Bahusampattoti bahūni vassasatavassasahassāni sampatto.

268. Regarding 'When lifted, it is just the same': Here, a foot that has stepped, being burned up to the bone, cannot be lifted. This is the meaning here: it burns starting from below, it is consumed by fire starting from above. Thus, at the time of stepping on it, it is perceived as burning; at the time of lifting it, it is just the same. Therefore, it was said thus. 'Having reached a multitude' means having reached many hundreds and thousands of years.

Kasmā panesa narako avīcīti saṅkhaṃ gatoti. Vīci nāma antaraṃ vuccati, tattha ca aggijālānaṃ vā sattānaṃ vā dukkhassa vā antaraṃ natthi. Tasmā so avīcīti saṅkhaṃ gatoti. Tassa hi puratthimabhittito jālā uṭṭhitā saṃsibbamānā yojanasataṃ gantvā pacchimabhittiṃ vinivijjhitvā parato yojanasataṃ gacchati. Sesadisāsupi eseva nayo.

Now, why has this hell come to be called Avīci? 'Vīci' is said to mean an interval, and there, there is no interval for the flames of fire, or for the beings, or for the suffering. Therefore, it has come to be called Avīci. For from its eastern wall, a continuous flame arises, goes one hundred yojanas, pierces the western wall, and goes one hundred yojanas beyond. This same method applies to the other directions as well.

Imesaṃ channaṃ jālānaṃ majjhe nibbatto devadatto, tassa yojanasatappamāṇo attabhāvo, dve pādā yāva gopphakā lohapathaviṃ paviṭṭhā, dve hatthā yāva maṇibandhā lohabhittiyo paviṭṭhā, sīsaṃ yāva bhamukaṭṭhito lohachadane paviṭṭhaṃ, adhobhāgena ekaṃ lohasūlaṃ pavisitvā kāyaṃ vinivijjhantaṃ [V 4.0173] chadane paviṭṭhaṃ, pācīnabhittito nikkhantasūlaṃ hadayaṃ vinivijjhitvā pacchimabhittiṃ paviṭṭhaṃ[P 4.0236], uttarabhittito nikkhantasūlaṃ phāsukā vinivijjhitvā dakkhiṇabhittiṃ paviṭṭhaṃ. Niccale tathāgatamhi aparaddhattā niccalova hutvā paccatīti kammasarikkhatāya ediso jāto. Evaṃ jālānaṃ nirantaratāya avīci nāma.

In the middle of these six flames, Devadatta was reborn. His bodily existence is one hundred yojanas in measure. Both feet have entered the iron ground up to the ankles; both hands have entered the iron walls up to the wrists; his head has entered the iron roof up to the brow-bone. From below, one iron spike, having entered and pierced through his body, has entered the roof. A spike coming out from the eastern wall, having pierced his heart, has entered the western wall. A spike coming out from the northern wall, having pierced his ribs, has entered the southern wall. Because he had offended against the Immovable Tathāgata, he is tormented while being immovable. This has occurred due to the similarity with his kamma. Thus, because of the uninterruptedness of the flames, it is called Avīci.

Abbhantare panassa yojanasatike ṭhāne nāḷiyaṃ koṭṭetvā pūritapiṭṭhaṃ viya sattā nirantarā, “imasmiṃ ṭhāne satto atthi, imasmiṃ natthī”ti na vattabbaṃ, gacchantānaṃ ṭhitānaṃ nisinnānaṃ nipannānaṃ anto natthi, gacchante vā ṭhite vā nisinne vā nipanne vā aññamaññaṃ na bādhanti. Evaṃ sattānaṃ nirantaratāya avīci.

Furthermore, in its interior space of one hundred yojanas, beings are uninterrupted, like flour pounded and filled into a bamboo tube. It cannot be said, 'In this place there is a being, in this place there is not.' There is no end to those who are going, standing, sitting, or lying down. Whether going, standing, sitting, or lying down, they do not obstruct one another. Thus, because of the uninterruptedness of the beings, it is called Avīci.

Kāyadvāre [M 4.0168] pana cha upekkhāsahagatāni cittāni uppajjanti, ekaṃ dukkhasahagataṃ. Evaṃ santepi yathā jivhagge cha madhubindūni ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ tambalohabindumhi ṭhapite anudahanabalavatāya tadeva paññāyati, itarāni abbohārikāni honti, evaṃ anudahanabalavatāya dukkhamevettha nirantaraṃ, itarāni abbohārikānīti. Evaṃ dukkhassa nirantaratāya avīci.

Through the body-door, six consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity arise, and one accompanied by pain. Even so, just as when six drops of honey are placed on the tip of the tongue and one drop of molten copper is placed there, due to the power of its burning, only that one is perceived while the others become insignificant; so too, due to the power of the burning, only suffering is uninterrupted here, while the others are insignificant. Thus, because of the uninterruptedness of suffering, it is called Avīci.

269. Mahantoti yojanasatiko. So tattha patatīti eko pādo mahāniraye hoti, eko gūthaniraye nipatati. Sūcimukhāti sūcisadisamukhā, te hatthigīvappamāṇā ekadoṇikanāvāppamāṇā vā honti.

269. 'Great' means one hundred yojanas in size. 'He falls there' means one foot is in the great hell, and one foot falls into the Excrement Hell. 'Needle-mouthed' means having mouths like needles; they are the size of an elephant's neck or a single-log boat.

Kukkulanirayoti yojanasatappamāṇova anto kūṭāgāramattavitaccitaaṅgārapuṇṇo ādittachārikanirayo, yattha [P 4.0237] patitapatitā kudrūsakarāsimhi khittaphālavāsisilādīni viya heṭṭhimatalameva gaṇhanti.

The Kukkula hell is one hundred yojanas in size, and its interior is filled with a quantity of flameless embers the size of a gabled house; it is a hell of glowing hot ash. Therein, those who fall sink to the very bottom, like ploughshares, adzes, stones, and so on, thrown into a heap of millet.

Āropentīti ayadaṇḍehi pothentā āropenti. Tesaṃ ārohanakāle te kaṇṭakā adhomukhā honti, orohanakāle uddhaṃmukhā.

'They make them ascend' means that the hell-wardens, striking them with iron rods, make them ascend. At the time of their ascent, those thorns are downward-facing; at the time of their descent, they are upward-facing.

Vāteritānīti [V 4.0174] kammamayena vātena calitāni. Hatthampi chindantīti phalake maṃsaṃ viya koṭṭayamānāni chindanti. Sace uṭṭhāya palāyati, ayopākāro samuṭṭhahitvā parikkhipati, heṭṭhā khuradhārā samuṭṭhāti.

'Stirred by the wind' means moved by a wind born of kamma. 'They cut even a hand' means they cut it after mincing it like meat on a board. If one rises and flees, an iron wall springs up and encircles them, and a razor-edge arises from below.

Khārodakā nadīti vetaraṇī nāma tambalohanadī. Tattha ayomayāni kharavālika-pokkharapattāni, heṭṭhā khuradhārā ubhosu tīresu vettalatā ca kusatiṇāni ca. So tattha dukkhā tibbā kharāti so tattha uddhañca adho ca vuyhamāno pokkharapattesu chijjati. Siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānāya kharavālikāya kaṇṭakehi vijjhiyati, khuradhārāhi phāliyati, ubhosu tīresu kusatiṇehi vilekhati, vettalatāhi ākaḍḍhiyati, tikkhasattīhi phāliyati.

The River of Caustic Water is the river of molten copper named Vetaraṇī. Therein are iron lotus leaves and rough sand; below are razor-edges; and on both banks are cane creepers and kusa grass. As to 'There, suffering is intense and harsh': that being, carried up and down therein, is cut by the lotus leaves, pierced by thorns on the rough sand shaped like a crossroads, split by the razor-edges, scraped by the kusa grass on both banks, dragged by the cane creepers, and split by sharp spears.

270. Tattena [M 4.0169] ayosaṅkunāti tena jigacchitomhīti [P 4.0238] vutte mahantaṃ lohapacchiṃ lohaguḷānaṃ pūretvā taṃ upagacchanti, so lohaguḷabhāvaṃ ñatvā dante samphuseti, athassa te tattena ayosaṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaranti, tambalohadhārehi mahantena lohakaṭāhena tambalohaṃ upanetvā evamevaṃ karonti. Puna mahānirayeti evaṃ pañcavidhabandhanato paṭṭhāya yāva tambalohapānā tambalohapānato paṭṭhāya puna pañcavidhabandhanādīni kāretvā mahāniraye pakkhipanti. Tattha koci pañcavidhabandhaneneva muccati, koci dutiyena, koci tatiyena, koci tambalohapānena muccati, kamme pana aparikkhīṇe puna mahāniraye pakkhipanti.

270. With a heated iron hook: When that being says, 'I am hungry,' they fill a large iron basket with iron balls and approach him. He, knowing them to be iron balls, clamps his teeth shut. Then they force open his mouth with a heated iron hook. They bring molten copper in a large iron cauldron and pour it in as a stream, doing just so. Again, in the Great Hell: Thus, from the fivefold binding up to the drinking of molten copper, and from the drinking of molten copper onwards, having again inflicted the fivefold binding and so on, they cast them into the Great Hell. There, some are released by the fivefold binding itself, some by the second, some by the third, some at the drinking of molten copper. But if their kamma is not exhausted, they are again cast into the Great Hell.

Idaṃ pana suttaṃ gaṇhanto eko daharabhikkhu, – “bhante, ettakaṃ dukkhamanubhavitasattaṃ punapi mahāniraye pakkhipantī”ti āha. Āma, āvuso, kamme aparikkhīṇe punappunaṃ evaṃ karontīti. Tiṭṭhatu, bhante, uddeso, kammaṭṭhānameva kathethāti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā sotāpanno hutvā āgamma uddesaṃ aggahesi. Aññesampi imasmiṃ padese uddesaṃ ṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pattānaṃ gaṇanā natthi. Sabbabuddhānañcetaṃ suttaṃ avijahitameva hoti.

Now, a certain young monk, while learning this sutta, said: 'Venerable sir, must so much suffering be experienced, and are they cast again into the Great Hell?' 'Yes, friend, when their kamma is not exhausted, they do so again and again.' 'Let the recitation stand, venerable sir; just explain the meditation subject.' Having had the meditation subject explained, he became a stream-enterer, and then returned and took up the recitation. There is no counting of others in this region who, having set aside the recitation, attained arahantship. And this sutta is never abandoned by any of the Buddhas.

271. Hīnakāyūpagāti hīnakāyaṃ upagatā hutvā. Upādāneti taṇhādiṭṭhigahaṇe. Jātimaraṇasambhaveti jātiyā ca maraṇassa ca kāraṇabhūte. Anupādāti catūhi upādānehi anupādiyitvā. Jātimaraṇasaṅkhayeti jātimaraṇasaṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne vimuccanti.

271. Hīnakāyūpagā: Having associated with an inferior group. Upādāne: In the grasping of craving and views. Jātimaraṇasambhave: In that which is the cause of birth and death. Anupādā: Not clinging with the four kinds of clinging. Jātimaraṇasaṅkhaye: They are liberated in Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of birth and death.

Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutāti [V 4.0175][P 4.0239] diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve sabbakilesanibbānena nibbutā. Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccagunti sabbadukkhātikkantā nāma honti.

Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā: They are extinguished in this very existence by the extinguishing of all defilements. Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccagu: They are called those who have transcended all suffering.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Devadūtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Devadūta Sutta is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Third Chapter is concluded.

4. Vibhaṅgavaggo

4. The Vibhaṅga Chapter

1. Bhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Bhaddekaratta Sutta

272. Evaṃ [V 4.0176][P 5.0001][M 4.0170] me sutanti bhaddekarattasuttaṃ. Tattha bhaddekarattassāti vipassanānuyogasamannāgatattā bhaddakassa ekarattassa. Uddesanti mātikaṃ. Vibhaṅganti vitthārabhājanīyaṃ.

272. The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, 'bhaddekarattassa' means: of an auspicious person of a single night, because of being endowed with the practice of insight meditation. 'Uddesaṃ' means the matrix. 'Vibhaṅgaṃ' means the detailed analysis.

Atītanti atīte pañcakkhandhe. Nānvāgameyyāti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nānugaccheyya. Nappaṭikaṅkheti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi na pattheyya. Yadatītanti idamettha kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā yaṃ atītaṃ, taṃ pahīnaṃ niruddhaṃ atthaṅgataṃ, tasmā taṃ puna nānugaccheyya. Yasmā ca yaṃ anāgataṃ, taṃ appattaṃ ajātaṃ anibbattaṃ, tasmā tampi na pattheyya.

'Atītaṃ' means the five aggregates of the past. 'Nānvāgameyya' means one should not pursue them with craving and wrong view. 'Nappaṭikaṅkhe' means one should not long for them with craving and wrong view. The phrase 'Yadatītaṃ' is here a statement of reason. Because whatever is past has been abandoned, has ceased, and has disappeared, therefore one should not pursue it again. And because whatever is future has not been attained, has not been born, and has not arisen, therefore one should not long for it either.

Tattha tatthāti paccuppannampi dhammaṃ yattha yattheva uppanno, tattha tattheva ca naṃ aniccānupassanādīhi sattahi anupassanāhi yo vipassati araññādīsu vā tattha tattheva vipassati. Asaṃhīraṃ [P 5.0002] asaṃkuppanti idaṃ vipassanāpaṭivipassanādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipassanā hi rāgādīhi na saṃhīrati na saṃkuppatīti asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ, taṃ anubrūhaye vaḍḍheyya, paṭivipasseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā nibbānaṃ rāgādīhi na saṃhīrati na saṃkuppatīti asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ. Taṃ vidvā paṇḍito bhikkhu anubrūhaye, punappunaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ taṃ taṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appento vaḍḍheyyāti attho.

'Tattha tattha' means: wherever a present phenomenon has arisen, right there and then, one who sees with insight sees it with the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence; or in whatever place, such as a forest, right there and then one sees with insight. This phrase 'Asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ' is said to show the seeing of a preceding insight with a subsequent insight. For insight is not drawn back or destroyed by lust and the like; thus it is 'unwavering' and 'unshakeable'. It is said that one should augment, develop, and see it again with insight. Alternatively, Nibbāna is not drawn back or destroyed by lust and the like, thus it is called 'unwavering' and 'unshakeable'. A wise, learned bhikkhu should augment it; he should develop it by repeatedly entering into that particular fruition attainment which has Nibbāna as its object. This is the meaning.

Tassa pana anubrūhantassa atthāya – ajjeva kiccamātappanti kilesānaṃ ātāpanaparitāpanena ātappanti laddhanāmaṃ vīriyaṃ ajjeva kātabbaṃ. Ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suveti [V 4.0177] sve jīvitaṃ vā maraṇaṃ vā ko jānāti. Ajjeva dānaṃ vā dassāmi, sīlaṃ vā rakkhissāmi, aññataraṃ vā pana kusalaṃ karissāmīti hi “ajja tāva papañco atthi, sve vā punadivase vā karissāmī”ti cittaṃ anuppādetvā ajjeva karissāmīti evaṃ vīriyaṃ kātabbanti dasseti. Mahāsenenāti aggivisasatthādīni anekāni maraṇakāraṇāni tassa senā, tāya mahatiyā senāya vasena mahāsenena evarūpena maccunā saddhiṃ “katipāhaṃ tāva āgamehi yāvāhaṃ buddhapūjādiṃ attano avassayakammaṃ karomī”ti[M 4.0171]. Evaṃ mittasanthavākārasaṅkhāto vā, “idaṃ sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā gahetvā katipāhaṃ āgamehī”ti evaṃ lañjānuppadānasaṅkhāto vā, “imināhaṃ balarāsinā paṭibāhissāmī”ti evaṃ balarāsisaṅkhāto vā saṅgaro natthi. Saṅgaroti hi mittasanthavākāralañjānuppadānabalarāsīnaṃ [P 5.0003] nāmaṃ, tasmā ayamattho vutto.

For the benefit of one who is augmenting it: 'Today itself the task must be done with diligence' means: the energy, named 'diligence' from its heating and tormenting of the defilements, must be exerted today itself. 'Who would know of death tomorrow?' means: who knows whether there will be life or death tomorrow? This shows that one should make the effort today, thinking, 'Today I will give alms, or I will keep the precepts, or I will do some other wholesome deed,' without giving rise to the thought, 'For today there are still distractions; I will do it tomorrow or the day after.' 'By one with a great army' means: the many causes of death, such as fire, poison, and weapons, are the army of Death. With such a Death, who has a great army, there is no compact. There is no compact in the form of making friendship, saying, 'Wait for a few days, while I perform my essential duties such as paying homage to the Buddha.' There is no compact in the form of giving a bribe, saying, 'Take this hundred or this thousand and wait for a few days.' And there is no compact in the form of amassing forces, thinking, 'I will fend you off with this host of forces.' For 'saṅgaro' is the name for making friendship, giving a bribe, and amassing forces. Therefore, this meaning is stated.

Atanditanti analasaṃ uṭṭhāhakaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipannattā bhaddo ekaratto assāti bhaddekaratto. Iti taṃ evaṃ paṭipannapuggalaṃ “bhaddekaratto aya”nti. Rāgādīnaṃ santatāya santo buddhamuni ācikkhati.

Atanditaṃ: Not indolent, but energetic and striving. Because one practices thus, 'a blessed single night is for him'—therefore, he is called bhaddekaratta. Thus, the Buddha, the sage who is at peace due to the appeasement of lust and so forth, describes such a practicing individual as, 'This is one for whom a single night is blessed.'

273. Evaṃrūpotiādīsu kāḷopi samāno indanīlamaṇivaṇṇo ahosinti evaṃ manuññarūpavaseneva evaṃrūpo ahosiṃ. Kusalasukhasomanassavedanāvaseneva evaṃvedano. Taṃsampayuttānaṃyeva saññādīnaṃ vasena evaṃsañño evaṃsaṅkhāro evaṃviññāṇo ahosiṃ atītamaddhānanti.

273. In phrases such as 'evaṃrūpo': For example, 'Though I was of dark complexion, I became the color of a sapphire gem.' Thus, it is only by way of a pleasing form-aggregate that one thinks, 'I was of such form.' It is only by way of wholesome, pleasant, and mentally joyous feelings that one thinks, 'I was of such feeling.' By way of perception and other factors associated only with those feelings, one thinks, 'I was of such perception,' 'I was of such formations,' 'I was of such consciousness' in the past.

Tattha nandiṃ samanvānetīti tesu rūpādīsu taṇhaṃ samanvāneti anupavatteti. Hīnarūpādivasena pana evaṃrūpo ahosiṃ…pe… evaṃviññāṇo ahosinti na maññati.

Therein, nandiṃ samanvāneti means he pursues and gives rise to craving for those forms, etc. However, by way of inferior forms, etc., he does not conceive: 'I was of such a form... I was of such a consciousness.'

Nandiṃ na samanvānetīti taṇhaṃ vā taṇhāsampayuttadiṭṭhiṃ vā nānupavattayati.

Nandiṃ na samanvāneti means: one does not give rise to craving or to views associated with craving.

274. Evaṃrūpo siyantiādīsupi taṃmanuññarūpādivaseneva taṇhādiṭṭhipavattasaṅkhātā nandisamanvānayanāva veditabbā.

274. Likewise, in such phrases as evaṃrūpo siyāṃ, the pursuing of delight—which is defined as the occurrence of craving and wrong view—should be understood as arising solely by way of sublime and pleasing forms, and so on.

275. Kathañca[V 4.0178], bhikkhave, paccuppannesu dhammesu saṃhīratīti idaṃ “paccuppannañca yo dhammaṃ, tattha tattha vipassati. Asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppa”nti uddesassa niddesatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmañcettha “kathañca, bhikkhave, paccuppannaṃ dhammaṃ [P 5.0004] na vipassatī”tiādi vattabbaṃ siyā, yasmā pana asaṃhīrāti ca asaṃkuppāti ca vipassanā vuttā, tasmā tassā eva abhāvañca bhāvañca dassetuṃ saṃhīratīti mātikaṃ uddharitvā vitthāro vutto. Tattha saṃhīratīti vipassanāya abhāvato taṇhādiṭṭhīhi [M 4.0172] ākaḍḍhiyati. Na saṃhīratīti vipassanāya bhāvena taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nākaḍḍhiyati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

275. 'And how, bhikkhus, is one drawn away by present phenomena?' This is said to provide the detailed explanation for the summary statement: 'And whatever phenomenon is present, one sees it right there; not drawn away, unshaken.' Although it would have been appropriate here to say, 'And how, bhikkhus, does one not see the present phenomenon with insight?' and so on, because insight has been called 'not drawn away' and 'unshaken', the detailed explanation is given after extracting the matrix heading saṃhīrati in order to show both the absence and the presence of that insight. Therein, saṃhīrati means that due to the absence of insight, one is dragged away by craving and wrong views. Na saṃhīrati means that due to the cultivation of insight, one is not dragged away by craving and wrong views. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Bhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhaddekaratta Sutta is concluded.

2. Ānandabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta

276. Evaṃ [V 4.0179] me sutanti ānandabhaddekarattasuttaṃ. Tattha paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhito. Ko nu kho, bhikkhaveti jānantova kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchi.

276. 'Thus have I heard': this is the Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, emerged from seclusion means emerged from the attainment of fruition. 'Who now, bhikkhus?': though knowing, he asked in order to initiate the discussion.

278. Sādhu sādhūti therassa sādhukāramadāsi. Sādhu kho tvanti parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi parisuddhehi kathitattā desanaṃ pasaṃsanto āha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

278. 'Good, good': he gave his approval to the elder. Praising the teaching because it was spoken with well-rounded and pure words and syllables, he said, 'Good indeed are you.' The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Ānandabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānandabhaddekaratta Sutta is concluded.

3. Mahākaccānabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Mahākaccāna Bhaddekaratta Sutta

279. Evaṃ [V 4.0180] me sutanti mahākaccānabhaddekarattasuttaṃ. Tattha tapodārāmeti tattodakassa rahadassa vasena evaṃladdhanāme ārāme. Vebhārapabbatassa [P 5.0005] kira heṭṭhā bhūmaṭṭhakanāgānaṃ pañcayojanasatikaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ devalokasadisaṃ maṇimayena talena ārāmauyyānehi ca samannāgataṃ, tattha nāgānaṃ kīḷanaṭṭhāne mahāudakarahado, tato tapodā nāma nadī sandati kuthitā uṇhodakā. Kasmā panesā edisā jātā? Rājagahaṃ kira parivāretvā mahā petaloko, tattha dvinnaṃ mahālohakumbhinirayānaṃ antarena ayaṃ tapodā āgacchati, tasmā sā kuthitā sandati. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “yatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā sandati, so daho acchodako sītodako sātodako setodako suppatittho ramaṇīyo pahūtamacchakacchapo, cakkamattāni ca padumāni pupphanti[M 4.0173]. Apicāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchati, tenāyaṃ tapodā kuthitā sandatī”ti (pārā. 231). Imassa pana ārāmassa abhisammukhaṭṭhāne tato mahāudakarahado jāto, tassa nāmavasenāyaṃ vihāro tapodārāmoti vuccati.

279. 'Thus have I heard': this is the Mahākaccāna Bhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, Tapodārāma refers to a monastery so named on account of a lake of hot water. It is said that below Mount Vebhāra there is a five-hundred-yojana abode of the earth-dwelling nāgas, which resembles a deva world and is complete with a jeweled floor and with parks and groves. There, in the nāgas' pleasure ground, is a great lake, from which flows the river named Tapodā, with boiling hot water. But why has it become so? It is said that a great peta-world surrounds Rājagaha, and this Tapodā flows between two great iron cauldron hells; that is why it flows boiling. And this has also been said: 'Bhikkhus, the lake from which this Tapodā flows has clear water, cool water, sweet water, white water, good fords, and is delightful, abounding in fish and turtles, and lotuses the size of chariot wheels bloom there. Moreover, bhikkhus, this Tapodā comes from the interval between two great hells; that is why this Tapodā flows boiling.' Now, in front of this monastery, a great lake has formed from that river; on account of its name, this monastery is called Tapodārāma.

280. Samiddhīti tassa kira therassa attabhāvo samiddho abhirūpo pāsādiko, tasmā samiddhitveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Ādibrahmacariyakoti maggabrahmacariyassa ādi pubbabhāgappaṭipattibhūto. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato uṭṭhāyāsanāti madhupiṇḍikasutte (ma. ni. 1.199 ādayo) vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

280. Samiddhi: It is said that the elder's individual existence was prosperous, very handsome, and inspiring confidence; therefore he came to be known as Samiddhi. Ādibrahmacariyaka means being the initial, preliminary practice of the path of the holy life. 'Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat…'—this should be elaborated in detail in the same way as described in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta.

282. Iti me cakkhunti imasmiṃ kira sutte bhagavā dvādasāyatanavaseneva mātikaṃ ṭhapesi. Theropi “bhagavatā heṭṭhā [P 5.0006] dvīsu, upari catutthe cāti imesu tīsu suttesu pañcakkhandhavasena mātikā ca vibhaṅgo ca kato, idha pana dvādasāyatanavaseneva vibhajanatthaṃ mātikā ṭhapitā”ti nayaṃ paṭilabhitvā evamāha. Imaṃ pana nayaṃ labhantena therena bhāriyaṃ kataṃ, apade padaṃ dassitaṃ, ākāse padaṃ kataṃ, tena naṃ bhagavā imameva suttaṃ sandhāya – “etadaggaṃ[V 4.0181], bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākaccāno”ti (a. ni. 1.197) etadagge ṭhapesi. Ettha pana cakkhūti cakkhupasādo. Rūpāti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpā. Iminā nayena sesāyatanānipi veditabbāni. Viññāṇanti nikantiviññāṇaṃ. Tadabhinandatīti taṃ cakkhuñceva rūpañca taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandati. Anvāgametīti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi anugacchati.

282. 'Thus, my eye...': It is said that in this sutta the Blessed One established the matrix only by way of the twelve sense bases. The elder, too, having grasped the method—'In the two preceding suttas and in the fourth one to come, the Blessed One has formulated the matrix and the analysis by way of the five aggregates, but here the matrix was established for the purpose of analysis by way of the twelve sense bases'—spoke accordingly. By grasping this method, the elder accomplished a difficult task; he showed a footprint where there was no track, he made a footprint in the sky. Therefore, the Blessed One, with reference to this very sutta, placed him in the foremost position, saying: 'Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who analyze in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief, the foremost is this Mahākaccāna.' Herein, eye is the eye-sensitivity. Forms are forms originating from the four causes. In this way, the remaining sense bases should also be understood. Consciousness is consciousness connected with craving. Delights in it means one delights in that eye and form by way of craving and wrong view. Follows after it means one pursues them with craving and wrong view.

Iti me mano ahosi atītamaddhānaṃ iti dhammāti ettha pana manoti bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Dhammāti tebhūmakadhammārammaṇaṃ.

In the phrase, 'Thus was my mind in the past, thus were the mental objects,' mind refers to the life-continuum consciousness. Mental objects refers to the mental objects of the three planes of existence.

283. Paṇidahatīti patthanāvasena ṭhapesi. Paṇidhānapaccayāti patthanāṭṭhapanakāraṇā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

283. He directs it means he established it by way of aspiration. Because of that directing means for the reason of aspiring and establishing. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahākaccānabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahākaccāna Bhaddekaratta Sutta is concluded.

4. Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddekaratta Sutta

286. Evaṃ [V 4.0182][M 4.0174] me sutanti lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekarattasuttaṃ. Tattha lomasakaṅgiyoti aṅgathero kira nāmesa, kāyassa pana īsakalomasākāratāya lomasakaṅgiyoti pākaṭo jāto. Candano [P 5.0007] devaputtoti kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kiresa candano nāma upāsako aḍḍho mahaddhano tīṇi ratanāni catūhi paccayehi pūjetvā devaloke nibbatto, purimanāmena candano devaputtotveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Paṇḍukambalasilāyanti rattakambalasilāyaṃ. Tassā kira rattakambalasseva jayasumanapuppharāsi viya vaṇṇo, tasmā “paṇḍukambalasilā”ti vuccati.

286. Thus have I heard. This is the Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddekaratta Sutta. Therein, regarding 'Lomasakaṅgiya': it is said this elder's name was Aṅga, but because his body was somewhat hairy, he became known as Lomasakaṅgiya. Regarding 'Candana the devaputta': it is said that during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One, this lay follower named Candana, who was affluent and of great wealth, having worshipped the Three Jewels with the four requisites, was reborn in the deva world. He came to be known by his former name, as Candana the devaputta. Regarding 'on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab': it means on the red-blanket stone slab. It is said that its color, that of the red blanket, was like a heap of jayasumana flowers; therefore, it is called the 'Paṇḍukambala stone slab'.

Kadā pana tattha bhagavā vihāsīti? Bodhipattito sattame saṃvacchare sāvatthiyaṃ āsāḷhīmāsapuṇṇamāya dvādasayojanāya parisāya majjhe yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā oruyha kaṇḍambamūle paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā dhammadesanāya mahājanaṃ mahāviduggato uddharitvā buddhā nāma yasmā pāṭihāriyaṃ katvā manussapathe na vasanti, tasmā passamānasseva tassa janassa padavīkkamaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ vassaṃ upagato, tasmiṃ samaye vihāsi.

When did the Blessed One reside there? In the seventh year from attaining enlightenment, on the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷhī in Sāvatthī, having performed the Twin Miracle in the midst of an assembly twelve leagues wide, and having descended, he sat on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree. Having lifted up the great populace from the great, hard-to-cross saṃsāra by means of the Dhamma teaching, and because Buddhas, after performing a miracle, do not dwell on the human path, therefore, while that populace was still watching, he took a few steps and went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. There, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab, he entered upon the rains-residence. It was at that time that he resided there.

Tatra bhagavāti tatra viharanto bhagavā yebhuyyena dasahi cakkavāḷasahassehi sannipatitāhi devatāhi parivuto mātaraṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ kathento gambhīraṃ nipuṇaṃ tilakkhaṇāhataṃ rūpārūpaparicchedakathaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ asakkontānaṃ devānaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ antarantarā bhaddekarattassa uddesañca vibhaṅgañca abhāsi. Tatrāyaṃ devaputto uggaṇhanto imā gāthā saddhiṃ vibhaṅgena uggaṇhi, devattassa pana pamādādhiṭṭhānattā dibbehi ārammaṇehi nippīḷiyamāno anupubbena suttaṃ sammuṭṭho gāthāmattameva dhāresi. Tenāha [P 5.0008] “evaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhu dhāremi bhaddekarattiyo gāthā”ti.

Regarding 'There, the Blessed One': The Blessed One, dwelling there, was surrounded mostly by deities assembled from ten thousand world-systems. Making his mother the principal witness, while teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—a discourse that distinguishes material and immaterial phenomena, which is profound, subtle, and stamped with the three characteristics—for the purpose of generating spiritual urgency in the devas who were unable to penetrate it, he taught, in the intervals, the summary and the analysis of the Bhaddekaratta. Therein, this devaputta, while learning, learned these verses together with the analysis. However, because the divine existence is a basis for heedlessness, being oppressed by divine sense-objects, he gradually forgot the discourse and remembered only the verses. Therefore, he said: 'Thus, O bhikkhu, do I remember the Bhaddekaratta verses'.

Uggaṇhāhi [V 4.0183][M 4.0175] tvantiādīsu tuṇhībhūto nisīditvā suṇanto uggaṇhāti nāma, vācāya sajjhāyaṃ karonto pariyāpuṇāti nāma, aññesaṃ vācento dhāreti nāma. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

In the text beginning with 'Uggaṇhāhi tvaṃ': one who, having become silent and sat down, listens, is said to 'learn' (uggaṇhāti); one who makes a recitation with the voice is said to 'master' (pariyāpuṇāti); one who teaches others is said to 'bear in mind' (dhāreti). The rest here is of clear meaning.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekarattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddekaratta Sutta is concluded.

5. Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Subha Sutta

289. Evaṃ [V 4.0184] me sutanti cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha subhoti so kira dassanīyo ahosi pāsādiko, tenassa aṅgasubhatāya subhotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Māṇavoti pana taṃ taruṇakāle vohariṃsu, so mahallakakālepi teneva vohārena vohariyati. Todeyyaputtoti todeyyassa nāma pasenadirañño purohitabrāhmaṇassa putto. So kira sāvatthiyā avidūre tudigāmo nāma atthi, tassa adhipatittā todeyyoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Mahādhano pana hoti sattāsītikoṭivibhavo paramamaccharī, “dadato bhogānaṃ aparikkhayo nāma natthī”ti cintetvā kassaci kiñci na deti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

5. Thus have I heard. This is the Subha Sutta. Therein, it is said that Subha was handsome and inspiring. Because of the beauty of his limbs, they gave him the name Subha. Furthermore, they addressed him as 'Māṇava' in his youth, and he was addressed by that very designation even when he was old. As for 'Todeyya's son,' he was the son of the chaplain brahmin of King Pasenadi named Todeyya. It is said that not far from Sāvatthī there was a village named Tudigāma, and because of his lordship over it, he came to be known as Todeyya. He was very wealthy, possessing a fortune of eighty-seven crores, and was extremely miserly. Thinking, 'For one who gives, wealth is not inexhaustible,' he gave nothing whatsoever to anyone. And this was said:

“Añjanānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, vammikānañca sañcayaṃ;

Madhūnañca samāhāraṃ, paṇḍito gharamāvase”ti.

289. “Seeing the exhaustion of collyrium, and the accumulation of anthills, and the gathering of honey, a wise person should dwell in the household life.”

Evaṃ adānameva sikkhāpesi. Dhuravihāre vasato sammāsambuddhassa yāguuḷuṅgamattaṃ vā bhattakaṭacchumattaṃ vā adatvā dhanalobhena kālaṃ katvā tasmiṃyeva ghare sunakho hutvā nibbatto. Subho taṃ sunakhaṃ ativiya piyāyati[P 5.0009], attano bhuñjanakabhattaṃyeva bhojeti, ukkhipitvā varasayane sayāpeti. Atha bhagavā ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento taṃ sunakhaṃ disvā – “todeyyabrāhmaṇo dhanalobhena attanova ghare sunakho hutvā nibbatto, ajja mayi subhassa gharaṃ gate maṃ disvā sunakho bhukkāraṃ karissati, athassāhaṃ ekaṃ vacanaṃ vakkhāmi, so ‘jānāti maṃ samaṇo gotamo’ti gantvā uddhanaṭṭhāne [M 4.0176] nipajjissati. Tatonidānaṃ subhassa mayā saddhiṃ eko kathāsallāpo bhavissati, so dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhahissati, sunakho pana kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbattissatī”ti imaṃ māṇavassa saraṇesu patiṭṭhānabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhagavā taṃ divasaṃ sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā ekakova gāmaṃ pavisitvā nikkhante māṇave taṃ gharaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Thus he taught only non-giving. Not having given even a mouthful of gruel or a ladleful of rice to the Perfectly Enlightened One, who was dwelling at the chief monastery, due to greed for wealth, he died and was reborn as a dog in that very house. Subha loved that dog exceedingly; he fed it the very rice he himself ate, and lifting it up, had it sleep on a fine bed. Then, one day at dawn, the Blessed One, while surveying the world, saw that dog and thought: 'The brahmin Todeyya, due to greed for wealth, has been reborn as a dog in his own house. Today, when I go to Subha's house, the dog will bark upon seeing me. Then I will say one word to it, and it, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama knows me," will go and lie down in the hearth. From that cause, a conversation will arise between Subha and me. Having heard the Dhamma, he will be established in the refuges. The dog, however, after dying, will be reborn in hell.' Knowing this fact of the young man's establishment in the refuges, the Blessed One on that day, having attended to his body, entered the village all alone, and when the young man had gone out, he entered that house for alms.

Sunakho [V 4.0185] bhagavantaṃ disvā bhukkāraṃ karonto bhagavato samīpaṃ gato. Tato naṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “todeyya tvaṃ pubbepi maṃ bho bhoti paribhavitvā sunakho jāto, idānipi bhukkāraṃ katvā avīciṃ gamissasī”ti. Sunakho taṃ sutvā – “jānāti maṃ samaṇo gotamo”ti vippaṭisārī hutvā gīvaṃ onāmetvā uddhanantare chārikāyaṃ nipanno. Manussā ukkhipitvā sayane sayāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Subho āgantvā – “kenāyaṃ sunakho sayanā oropito”ti āha. Manussā na kenacīti vatvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Māṇavo sutvā – “mama pitā brahmaloke nibbatto, todeyyo nāma sunakho natthi. Samaṇo pana gotamo pitaraṃ sunakhaṃ karoti, yaṃkiñci esa mukhāruḷhaṃ bhāsatī”ti kujjhitvā bhagavantaṃ musāvādena niggahetukāmo vihāraṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ pucchi.

The dog, seeing the Blessed One, approached him, barking. Then the Blessed One said this to it: 'Todeyya, in a previous life too you scorned me by addressing me as "bho, bho," and were reborn as a dog. Now too, having barked, you will go to Avīci.' Hearing this, the dog became remorseful, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama knows me,' and lowering its neck, it lay down in the ashes within the hearth. The people were unable to lift it up and make it sleep on the bed. Subha arrived and asked, 'Who has taken this dog down from the bed?' The people said, 'No one,' and related the incident. Hearing this, the young man became angry and said, 'My father has been reborn in the Brahma-world; there is no dog named Todeyya. But the ascetic Gotama makes my father out to be a dog. He says whatever comes to his mouth!' Wishing to censure the Blessed One for false speech, he went to the monastery and questioned him about the incident.

Bhagavāpi tassa tatheva vatvā avisaṃvādanatthaṃ āha – “atthi pana te māṇava pitarā anakkhātaṃ dhana”nti[P 5.0010]. Atthi, bho gotama, satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇamālā satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇapādukā satasahassagghanikā suvaṇṇapāti satasahassañca kahāpaṇanti. Gaccha taṃ sunakhaṃ appodakapāyāsaṃ bhojāpetvā sayane āropetvā īsakaṃ niddaṃ okkantakāle puccha, sabbaṃ te ācikkhissati. Atha naṃ jāneyyāsi “pitā me eso”ti. Māṇavo – “sace saccaṃ bhavissati, dhanaṃ lacchāmi, no ce, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ musāvādena niggaṇhissāmī”ti dvīhipi kāraṇehi tuṭṭho gantvā tathā akāsi. Sunakho – “ñātomhi iminā”ti roditvā huṃ hunti karonto dhananidhānaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā pādena pathaviṃ khaṇitvā saññaṃ adāsi, māṇavo dhanaṃ gahetvā – “bhavapaṭicchannaṃ nāma evaṃ sukhumaṃ paṭisandhiantaraṃ pākaṭaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa, addhā esa sabbaññū”ti bhagavati pasannacitto cuddasa pañhe abhisaṅkhari. Aṅgavijjāpāṭhako kiresa, tenassa [M 4.0177] etadahosi – “idaṃ dhammapaṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pañhe pucchissāmī”ti dutiyagamanena yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, tena puṭṭhapañhe pana bhagavā ekappahāreneva vissajjento kammassakātiādimāha.

The Blessed One, also speaking to him in the same way, said, in order to demonstrate the truth of his statement: 'Young man, is there any wealth left undisclosed by your father?' 'There is, venerable Gotama: a golden garland worth a hundred thousand, golden sandals worth a hundred thousand, a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, and a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas.' 'Go, have that dog eat some thick rice-gruel, place it on a bed, and when it has fallen into a light sleep, ask. It will tell you everything. Then you will know, "This is my father."' The young man, thinking, 'If this is true, I will get the wealth; if not, I will censure the ascetic Gotama for false speech,' pleased for both reasons, went and did so. The dog, thinking, 'I am known by this one,' wept, and making a 'huṃ huṃ' sound, went to the place where the treasure was hidden, scratched the earth with its paw, and gave a sign. The young man took the wealth and, with a mind confident in the Blessed One, thought: 'So subtle a thing, the interval between rebirths, concealed by existence, is manifest to the ascetic Gotama! Surely, he is all-knowing!' He then formulated fourteen questions. It is said he was a reader of the science of divination, and so this occurred to him: 'Taking this as a gift of Dhamma, I will ask the ascetic Gotama questions.' On his second visit, he approached the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One, answering the questions asked by him in a single stroke, spoke on 'Beings are owners of their kamma,' and so on.

Tattha kammaṃ etesaṃ sakaṃ attano bhaṇḍakanti kammassakā. Kammassa dāyādāti kammadāyādā, kammaṃ etesaṃ dāyajjaṃ bhaṇḍakanti attho. Kammaṃ etesaṃ yoni kāraṇanti kammayonī. Kammaṃ etesaṃ bandhūti kammabandhū, kammañātakāti attho. Kammaṃ etesaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ patiṭṭhāti [V 4.0186] kammapaṭisaraṇā. Yadidaṃ [P 5.0011] hīnappaṇītatāyāti yaṃ idaṃ “tvaṃ hīno bhava, tvaṃ paṇīto, tvaṃ appāyuko, tvaṃ dīghāyuko…pe… tvaṃ duppañño bhava, tvaṃ paññavā”ti evaṃ hīnappaṇītatāya vibhajanaṃ, taṃ na añño koci karoti, kammameva evaṃ satte vibhajatīti attho. Na māṇavo kathitassa atthaṃ sañjānāsi, ghanadussapaṭṭenassa mukhaṃ bandhitvā madhuraṃ purato ṭhapitaṃ viya ahosi. Mānanissito kiresa paṇḍitamānī, attanā samaṃ na passati. Athassa “kiṃ samaṇo gotamo katheti, yamahaṃ jānāmi, tadeva kathetīti ayaṃ māno mā ahosī”ti mānabhañjanatthaṃ bhagavā “āditova duppaṭivijjhaṃ katvā kathessāmi, tato ‘nāhaṃ bho gotama jānāmi, vitthārena me pākaṭaṃ katvā kathethā’ti maṃ yācissati, athassāhaṃ yācitakāle kathessāmi, evañcassa sātthakaṃ bhavissatī”ti duppaṭivijjhaṃ katvā kathesi.

Herein, the analysis should be understood thus: Kamma is their own property, hence they are `kammassakā` (owners of their kamma). They are heirs of kamma, hence they are `kammadāyādā`; the meaning is that kamma is their inherited property. Kamma is their origin and cause, hence they are `kammayonī`. Kamma is their relative, hence they are `kammabandhū`; the meaning is that kamma is their kin. Kamma is their refuge and support, hence they are `kammapaṭisaraṇā`. As for the phrase 'by way of inferiority and superiority,' the meaning is this: whatever division there is into inferior and superior, such as, 'You be inferior, you be superior; you be short-lived, you be long-lived… you be unwise, you be wise'—that division is not made by anyone else; kamma alone divides beings in this way. The young man did not understand the meaning of what was said; it was as if his face had been bound with a thick cloth and something sweet was placed before him. It seems this one, reliant on conceit and considering himself wise, does not see anyone equal to himself. Then, to break his conceit, so that this conceit—'What will the recluse Gotama say? He will say only that which I already know'—might not arise, the Blessed One thought: 'I will speak from the very beginning, making it difficult to penetrate. Then he will request me, saying, "Venerable Gotama, I do not understand. Please explain it to me clearly and in detail." Then, when he has requested, I will speak to him, and in this way, it will be beneficial for him.' Having considered this, he spoke, making it difficult to penetrate.

Idāni so attano appaṭividdhabhāvaṃ pakāsento na kho ahantiādimāha.

Now, wishing to reveal his own state of not having penetrated the meaning, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Indeed, I do not...'

290. Samattenāti paripuṇṇena. Samādinnenāti gahitena parāmaṭṭhena. Appāyukasaṃvattanikā esā, māṇava, paṭipadā yadidaṃ pāṇātipātīti yaṃ idaṃ pāṇātipātakammaṃ, esā appāyukasaṃvattanikā paṭipadāti.

290. By `samattena` is meant 'completely.' By `samādinnena` is meant 'taken up' or 'wrongly grasped.' As for the passage, 'This, young man, is the practice conducive to a short life, that is, the destruction of life,' the meaning is this: whatever kamma of destroying life there is, that practice is conducive to a short life.

Kathaṃ panesā appāyukataṃ karoti? Cattāri hi kammāni upapīḷakaṃ upacchedakaṃ janakaṃ upatthambhakanti. Balavakammena hi nibbattaṃ pavatte upapīḷakaṃ āgantvā [M 4.0178] atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “sacāhaṃ paṭhamataraṃ jāneyyaṃ, na te idha nibbattituṃ dadeyyaṃ, catūsuyeva taṃ apāyesu nibbattāpeyyaṃ. Hotu, tvaṃ yattha [P 5.0012] katthaci nibbatta, ahaṃ upapīḷakakammaṃ nāma taṃ pīḷetvā nirojaṃ niyūsaṃ kasaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ tādisaṃ karoti. Kiṃ karoti? Parissayaṃ upaneti, bhoge vināseti.

But how does this practice cause one to be short-lived? Indeed, there are four kinds of kamma: oppressive, cutting-off, generative, and supportive. For one who has been reborn through a powerful wholesome kamma, in the course of life, the oppressive kamma comes and, in effect, speaks thus: 'If I had known earlier, I would not have let you be reborn here; I would have caused you to be reborn only in the four states of woe. So be it. Wherever you may be reborn, I, called oppressive kamma, having oppressed you, will render you without vitality, without sap, and without substance.' From then on, it makes that being so. What does it do? It brings danger and destroys wealth.

Tattha dārakassa mātukucchiyaṃ nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya mātu assādo vā sukhaṃ vā na hoti, mātāpitūnaṃ pīḷāva uppajjati. Evaṃ parissayaṃ upaneti. Dārakassa pana mātukucchimhi nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya gehe bhogā udakaṃ patvā loṇaṃ viya rājādīnaṃ vasena nassanti, kumbhadohanadhenuyo khīraṃ na denti, sūratā goṇā caṇḍā honti, kāṇā honti, khujjā [V 4.0187] honti, gomaṇḍale rogo patati, dāsādayo vacanaṃ na karonti, vāpitaṃ sassaṃ na jāyati, gehagataṃ gehe, araññagataṃ araññe nassati, anupubbena ghāsacchādanamattaṃ dullabhaṃ hoti, gabbhaparihāro na hoti, vijātakāle mātuthaññaṃ chijjati, dārako parihāraṃ alabhanto pīḷito nirojo niyūso kasaṭo hoti, idaṃ upapīḷakakammaṃ nāma.

Therein, from the time the child is established in the mother's womb, the mother has no pleasure or happiness; only affliction arises for the parents. Thus it brings danger. Furthermore, from the time the child is established in the mother's womb, the wealth in the house is destroyed by the power of kings and so on, like salt that has reached water. Cows that give a potful of milk do not give milk; well-behaved bulls become fierce, one-eyed, or hunchbacked; disease falls upon the herd of cattle; servants and others do not obey orders; sown crops do not grow; what is in the house is destroyed in the house, and what is in the forest is destroyed in the forest. Gradually, even mere food and clothing become difficult to obtain. There is no proper care of the pregnancy, and at the time of birth, the mother's milk is cut off. The child, not receiving care, becomes afflicted, without vitality, without sap, and without substance. This is called oppressive kamma.

Dīghāyukakammena pana nibbattassa upacchedakakammaṃ āgantvā āyuṃ chindati. Yathā hi puriso aṭṭhusabhagamanaṃ katvā saraṃ khipeyya tamañño dhanuto vimuttamattaṃ muggarena paharitvā tattheva pāteyya, evaṃ dīghāyukakammena nibbattassa upacchedakakammaṃ āyuṃ chindati. Kiṃ karoti? Corānaṃ aṭaviṃ paveseti, vāḷamacchodakaṃ otāreti, aññataraṃ vā pana saparissayaṭṭhānaṃ upaneti, idaṃ upacchedakakammaṃ nāma, “upaghātaka”ntipi etasseva nāmaṃ.

But for one who is reborn through kamma for a long life, the cutting-off kamma comes and cuts off the life-span. Just as a man might shoot an arrow that would travel a distance of eight usabhas, but another man, striking it with a club just as it is released from the bow, might make it fall right there; in the same way, for one who is reborn through kamma for a long life, the cutting-off kamma cuts off the life-span. What does it do? It causes one to enter a forest of thieves, makes one go down into water with fierce sea-creatures, or brings one to some other place of danger. This is called cutting-off kamma; 'destructive kamma' is also a name for this very thing.

Paṭisandhinibbattakaṃ pana kammaṃ janakakammaṃ nāma. Appabhogakulādīsu nibbattassa bhogasampadādikaraṇena upatthambhakakammaṃ upatthambhakakammaṃ [P 5.0013] nāma.

The kamma that produces rebirth-linking is called generative kamma. For one reborn in a family with little wealth and so on, the kamma that provides support by bringing about the accomplishment of wealth and the like is called supportive kamma.

Imesu catūsu purimāni dve akusalāneva, janakaṃ kusalampi akusalampi, upatthambhakaṃ kusalameva. Tattha pāṇātipātakammaṃ upacchedakakammena appāyukasaṃvattanikaṃ hoti. Pāṇātipātinā vā kataṃ kusalakammaṃ [M 4.0179] uḷāraṃ na hoti, dīghāyukapaṭisandhiṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti. Evaṃ pāṇātipāto appāyukasaṃvattaniko hoti. Paṭisandhimeva vā niyāmetvā appāyukaṃ karoti, sanniṭṭhānacetanāya vā niraye nibbattati, pubbāparacetanāhi vuttanayena appāyuko hoti.

Among these four kammas, the first two are only unwholesome. Generative kamma is both wholesome and unwholesome. Supportive kamma is only wholesome. Therein, the kamma of destroying life, through cutting-off kamma, is conducive to a short life. Or, the wholesome kamma performed by one who destroys life is not great; it is not able to generate a rebirth-linking with a long life. In this way too, the destruction of life is conducive to a short life. Or, having determined the rebirth-linking itself, it makes one short-lived. Or, by the decisive volition, one is reborn in hell, and by the prior and subsequent volitions, in the way that has been explained, one becomes short-lived.

Dīghāyukasaṃvattanikā esā māṇava paṭipadāti ettha parittakammenapi nibbattaṃ pavatte etaṃ pāṇātipātā viratikammaṃ āgantvā atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “sacāhaṃ paṭhamataraṃ jāneyyaṃ, na te idha nibbattituṃ dadeyyaṃ, devalokeyeva taṃ nibbattāpeyyaṃ. Hotu, tvaṃ yattha katthaci nibbatti, ahaṃ upatthambhakakammaṃ nāma thambhaṃ te karissāmī”ti upatthambhaṃ karoti. Kiṃ karoti? Parissayaṃ nāseti, bhoge uppādeti.

In the passage, 'This, young man, is the practice conducive to a long life,' even for one who is reborn through a minor kamma, in the course of life, this kamma of abstaining from destroying life comes and, in effect, speaks thus: 'If I had known earlier, I would not have let you be reborn here; I would have caused you to be reborn only in the deva world. So be it. Wherever you were reborn, I, called supportive kamma, will provide support for you.' As if speaking thus, it provides support. What does it do? It destroys danger and produces wealth.

Tattha [V 4.0188] dārakassa mātukucchiyaṃ nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya mātāpitūnaṃ sukhameva sātameva hoti. Yepi pakatiyā manussāmanussaparissayā honti, te sabbe apagacchanti. Evaṃ parissayaṃ nāseti. Dārakassa pana mātukucchimhi nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya gehe bhogānaṃ pamāṇaṃ na hoti, nidhikumbhiyo puratopi pacchatopi gehaṃ pavaṭṭamānā pavisanti. Mātāpitaro parehi ṭhapitadhanassāpi sammukhībhāvaṃ gacchanti. Dhenuyo bahukhīrā honti, goṇā sukhasīlā honti, vappaṭṭhāne sassāni sampajjanti. Vaḍḍhiyā vā sampayuttaṃ, tāvakālikaṃ vā dinnaṃ dhanaṃ acoditā sayameva āharitvā denti, dāsādayo suvacā honti, kammantā na parihāyanti. Dārako [P 5.0014] gabbhato paṭṭhāya parihāraṃ labhati, komārikavejjā sannihitāva honti. Gahapatikule jāto seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, amaccakulādīsu jāto senāpatiṭṭhānādīni labhati. Evaṃ bhoge uppādeti. So aparissayo sabhogo ciraṃ jīvatīti. Evaṃ apāṇātipātakammaṃ dīghāyukasaṃvattanikaṃ hoti.

In that family, from the time a child is established in the mother’s womb, there is only happiness and pleasure for the mother and father. Whatever dangers from humans and non-humans that naturally exist, they all disappear. Thus, it eliminates danger. Furthermore, from the time the child is established in the mother's womb, there is no measure of wealth in the house; treasure pots roll into the house from the front and the back. The mother and father come into possession of wealth deposited by others. Cows have abundant milk, oxen have a pleasant disposition, and crops are abundant in the fields. Wealth given out for interest or lent for a temporary period is brought and given back of its own accord, without being asked for. Servants and the like are obedient, and work does not decline. The child receives care from the womb onwards, and physicians specializing in children are always at hand. Born into a householder's family, one obtains the position of a great merchant; born into the families of ministers and the like, one obtains the positions of a general and so on. Thus, it generates wealth. That person, being without danger and possessing wealth, lives long. In this way, the kamma of abstaining from killing is conducive to a long life.

Apāṇātipātinā vā kataṃ aññampi kusalaṃ uḷāraṃ hoti, dīghāyukapaṭisandhiṃ janetuṃ sakkoti, evampi dīghāyukasaṃvattanikaṃ hoti. Paṭisandhimeva vā niyāmetvā dīghāyukaṃ karoti. Sanniṭṭhānacetanāya vā devaloke nibbattati, pubbāparacetanāhi vuttanayena dīghāyuko hoti. Iminā nayena sabbapañhavissajjanesu attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, other wholesome kamma done by one who abstains from killing is also great; it is able to generate a rebirth-linking with a long lifespan. In this way too, it is conducive to long life. Or, having determined the rebirth-linking itself, it makes one long-lived. Or, by the decisive volition, one is reborn in the deva world; by the prior and subsequent volitions, in the manner already stated, one becomes long-lived. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all the answers to the questions.

Viheṭhanakammādīnipi [M 4.0180] hi pavatte āgantvā atthato tatheva vadamānāni viya upapīḷanena nibbhogataṃ āpādetvā paṭijagganaṃ alabhantassa roguppādanādīhi vā, viheṭhakādīhi katassa kusalassa anuḷāratāya vā, āditova paṭisandhiniyāmanena vā, vuttanayeneva pubbāparacetanāvasena vā bahvābādhatādīni karonti, apāṇātipāto viya ca aviheṭhanādīnipi appābādhatādīnīti.

Indeed, kamma of harming and the like, occurring in the course of existence, act in the same way in principle: having caused a state of being without wealth through oppression, they bring about many illnesses and so on for one who does not receive care, either through the arising of disease, or through the lack of greatness of wholesome kamma done by the harmer, or by the determination of rebirth-linking from the very beginning, or by the power of prior and subsequent volitions in the manner already stated. And, like abstaining from killing, abstaining from harming and the like also cause few illnesses and so on.

293. Ettha pana issāmanakoti issāsampayuttacitto. Upadussatīti issāvaseneva upakkosanto dussati. Issaṃ bandhatīti yavakalāpaṃ bandhanto viya yathā na nassati evaṃ bandhitvā viya ṭhapeti. Appesakkhoti appaparivāro, rattiṃ khitto viya saro na paññāyati, ucchiṭṭhahattho nisīditvā udakadāyakampi na labhati.

293. Here, 'issāmanako' means one whose mind is associated with envy. 'Upadussati' means that by the power of envy, while reviling, he corrupts. 'Issaṃ bandhati' means he establishes it as if binding it, just as one tying a sheaf of barley so that when it is placed it is not lost. 'Appesakkho' means having little retinue; he is not conspicuous, like an arrow shot at night that is not seen; having sat down with an unwashed hand, he cannot find even someone to give him water.

294. Na [V 4.0189] dātā hotīti macchariyavasena na dātā hoti. Tena kammenāti tena macchariyakammena.

294. "He is not a giver" means he is not a giver by the power of stinginess. "By that kamma" means by that kamma of stinginess.

295. Abhivādetabbanti [P 5.0015] abhivādanārahaṃ buddhaṃ vā paccekabuddhaṃ vā ariyasāvakaṃ vā. Paccuṭṭhātabbādīsupi eseva nayo. Imasmiṃ pana pañhavissajjane upapīḷakaupatthambhakakammāni na gahetabbāni. Na hi pavatte nīcakulinaṃ vā uccākulinaṃ vā sakkā kātuṃ, paṭisandhimeva pana niyāmetvā nīcakuliyaṃ kammaṃ nīcakule nibbatteti, uccākuliyaṃ kammaṃ uccākule.

295. 'One should pay respects' means one worthy of veneration: the Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a noble disciple. This is the same method for 'one for whom one should stand up' and so on. However, in this answer to the question, oppressive and supportive kamma should not be taken into account. For it is not possible to make one of low or high birth in the course of existence; rather, having determined the rebirth-linking itself, kamma that leads to a low family causes rebirth in a low family, and kamma that leads to a high family causes rebirth in a high family.

296. Na paripucchitā hotīti ettha pana aparipucchanena niraye na nibbattati. Aparipucchako pana “idaṃ kātabbaṃ, idaṃ na kātabba”nti na jānāti, ajānanto kātabbaṃ na karoti, akātabbaṃ karoti. Tena niraye nibbattati, itaro sagge. Iti kho, māṇava…pe… yadidaṃ hīnappaṇītatāyāti satthā desanaṃ yathānusandhiṃ pāpesi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

296. Here, regarding 'is not one who asks questions': one is not reborn in hell merely by not asking questions. However, one who does not ask questions does not know, 'This should be done; this should not be done.' Not knowing, one does not do what should be done and does what should not be done. For that reason, one is reborn in hell; the other is reborn in heaven. 'Thus, O young man... that is to say, because of inferiority and superiority,' the Teacher brought the discourse to its conclusion in accordance with its connection. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta is concluded.

Subhasuttantipi vuccati.

It is also called the Subha Sutta.

6. Mahākammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Great Analysis of Kamma Sutta

298. Evaṃ [V 4.0190][M 4.0181] me sutanti mahākammavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha moghanti tucchaṃ aphalaṃ. Saccanti tathaṃ bhūtaṃ. Idañca etena na sammukhā sutaṃ, upālisutte (ma. ni. 2.56) pana – “manokammaṃ mahāsāvajjataraṃ paññapemi pāpassa kammassa kiriyāya pāpassa kammassa [P 5.0016] pavattiyā, no tathā kāyakammaṃ no tathā vacīkamma”nti bhagavatā vuttaṃ atthi, sā kathā titthiyānaṃ antare pākaṭā jātā, taṃ gahetvā esa vadati. Atthi ca sā samāpattīti idaṃ – “kathaṃ nu kho, bho, abhisaññānirodho hotī”ti poṭṭhapādasutte (dī. ni. 1.406 ādayo) uppannaṃ abhisaññānirodhakathaṃ sandhāya vadati. Na kiñci vediyatīti ekavedanampi na vediyati. Atthi ca khoti thero nirodhasamāpattiṃ sandhāya anujānāti. Parirakkhitabbanti garahato mocanena rakkhitabbaṃ. Sañcetanā assa atthīti sañcetanikaṃ, sābhisandhikaṃ sañcetanikakammaṃ katvāti attho. Dukkhaṃ soti thero “akusalameva sandhāya paribbājako pucchatī”ti saññāya evaṃ vadati.

298. “Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, ‘moghaṃ’ means empty, fruitless. ‘Saccaṃ’ means true, real. And this was not heard by him in person; but in the Upāli Sutta, the Blessed One has said: “I declare mind-kamma to be more blameworthy for the doing of evil kamma, for the continuation of evil kamma, not so bodily kamma, not so verbal kamma.” That saying became well-known among the sectarians, and taking that up, he speaks. As for “And there is that attainment,” he says this with reference to the discussion on the cessation of perception that arose in the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. “He feels nothing” means he does not feel even a single feeling. As for “And indeed there is,” the Elder approves with reference to the attainment of cessation. “Should be guarded” means it should be guarded by being freed from blame. “There is intention for it, thus it is intentional”; the meaning is, having done intentional kamma that is with purpose. As for “It is suffering,” the Elder, with the perception that “the wanderer is asking with reference only to the unwholesome,” speaks thus.

Dassanampi kho ahanti bhagavā caturaṅgepi andhakāre samantā yojanaṭṭhāne tilamattampi saṅkhāraṃ maṃsacakkhunāva passati, ayañca paribbājako na dūre gāvutamattabbhantare vasati, kasmā bhagavā evamāhāti? Samāgamadassanaṃ sandhāyevamāha.

As for “Even seeing,” the Blessed One sees, even in a darkness of four factors, a formation the size of a sesame seed in a place of one yojana all around with the physical eye alone. And this wanderer lives not far, within about a gāvuta. Why did the Blessed One speak thus? This is the question. He spoke thus with reference to seeing in an assembly.

299. Udāyīti lāludāyī. Taṃ dukkhasminti sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhameva. Iti imaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ kilesadukkhaṃ saṅkhāradukkhaṃ sandhāya “sace bhāsitaṃ bhaveyya bhagavā”ti pucchati.

299. ‘Udāyī’ is Lāḷudāyī. As for ‘in that suffering,’ all that is only suffering. Thus, with reference to this suffering of the round, the suffering of defilements, and the suffering of formations, he [Lāḷudāyī] speaks [the words beginning], 'If it had been spoken, Blessed One...'

300. Ummaṅganti pañhāummaṅgaṃ. Ummujjamānoti sīsaṃ nīharamāno. Ayoniso ummujjissatīti anupāyena sīsaṃ nīharissati. Idañca pana bhagavā jānanto neva dibbacakkhunā na cetopariyañāṇena na sabbaññutañāṇena jāni, adhippāyeneva [P 5.0017] pana aññāsi. Kathentassa hi adhippāyo nāma suvijāno hoti, kathetukāmo gīvaṃ paggaṇhāti, hanukaṃ [V 4.0191] cāleti, mukhamassa phandati, sannisīdituṃ na sakkoti. Bhagavā tassa taṃ ākāraṃ [M 4.0182] disvā “ayaṃ udāyī sannisīdituṃ na sakkoti, yaṃ abhūtaṃ, tadeva kathessatī”ti oloketvāva aññāsi. Ādiṃ yevātiādimhiyeva. Tisso vedanāti “kiṃ so vediyatī”ti? Pucchantena “tisso vedanā pucchāmī”ti evaṃ vavatthapetvāva tisso vedanā pucchitā. Sukhavedaniyanti sukhavedanāya paccayabhūtaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

300. ‘Ummaṅgaṃ’ refers to the tunnel of wisdom. ‘Emerging’ means raising his head. ‘He will emerge improperly’ means he will raise his head by an improper means. And the Blessed One, knowing this, knew it not by the divine eye, nor by the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, nor by omniscient knowledge, but he knew it only by observing his disposition. For the intention of one who is about to speak is easy to know: one who wishes to speak stretches his neck, moves his jaw, his mouth twitches, and he cannot sit still. The Blessed One, seeing that manner of his, knew just by observing, thinking: ‘This Udāyī cannot sit still; he will speak of what is not real.’ ‘Just the beginning’ means at the very beginning. As for ‘three feelings’: when asking ‘What does he feel?’, the questioner asked about the three feelings only after having determined, ‘I am asking about the three feelings.’ ‘To be felt as pleasant’ means that which has become a condition for pleasant feeling. This same method applies to the remaining terms.

Ettha ca kāmāvacarakusalato somanassasahagatacittasampayuttā catasso cetanā, heṭṭhā tikajjhānacetanāti evaṃ paṭisandhipavattesu sukhavedanāya jananato sukhavedaniyaṃ kammaṃ nāma. Kāmāvacarañcettha paṭisandhiyaṃyeva ekantena sukhaṃ janeti, pavatte iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇe adukkhamasukhampi.

And here, the four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by joy arising from wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, and the volitions of the three lower jhānas—thus, because they generate pleasant feeling at the time of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, they are called kamma to be felt as pleasant. And here, the sense-sphere kamma generates pleasant feeling exclusively only at the time of rebirth-linking; in the course of existence, regarding a desirable-neutral object, it also generates neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Akusalacetanā paṭisandhipavattesu dukkhasseva jananato dukkhavedaniyaṃ kammaṃ nāma. Kāyadvāre pavatteyeva cetaṃ ekantena dukkhaṃ janeti, aññattha adukkhamasukhampi, sā pana vedanā aniṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattesuyeva ārammaṇesu uppajjanato dukkhātveva saṅkhaṃ gatā.

Unwholesome volition, because it generates only painful feeling at the time of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, is called kamma to be felt as painful. At the body-door, only in the course of existence, it exclusively generates painful feeling; elsewhere, it also generates neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. But that feeling, since it arises only in relation to undesirable and undesirable-neutral objects, is reckoned only as suffering.

Kāmāvacarakusalato pana upekkhāsahagatacittasampayuttā catasso cetanā, rūpāvacarakusalato catutthajjhānacetanāti evaṃ paṭisandhipavattesu tatiyavedanāya jananato adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ kammaṃ nāma. Ettha ca kāmāvacaraṃ paṭisandhiyaṃyeva ekantena adukkhamasukhaṃ janeti, pavatte iṭṭhārammaṇe sukhampi. Apica sukhavedaniyakammaṃ paṭisandhipavattivasena vaṭṭati, tathā adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ, [P 5.0018] dukkhavedaniyaṃ pavattivaseneva vaṭṭati. Etassa pana vasena sabbaṃ pavattivaseneva vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, from wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, the four volitions associated with consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and from wholesome fine-material-sphere consciousness, the volition of the fourth jhāṇa—thus, because they generate the third feeling at the time of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, they are called kamma to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. And here, the sense-sphere kamma generates neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling exclusively only at the time of rebirth-linking; in the course of existence, regarding a desirable object, it also generates pleasant feeling. Moreover, another method is stated: kamma to be felt as pleasant is applicable by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence; likewise for kamma to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Kamma to be felt as painful is applicable only by way of the course of existence. However, by the power of this latter one, all kamma is applicable only by way of the course of existence.

Etassa bhagavāti thero tathāgatena mahākammavibhaṅgakathanatthaṃ ālayo dassito, tathāgataṃ yācitvā mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa pākaṭaṃ karissāmīti cintetvā anusandhikusalatāya evamāha. Tattha mahākammavibhaṅganti mahākammavibhajanaṃ. Katame cattāro…pe… idhānanda, ekacco puggalo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjatīti idaṃ na mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇabhājanaṃ, mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇabhājanatthāya pana mātikāṭṭhapanaṃ.

Regarding the phrase 'For this, Blessed One': The Elder, seeing that the Tathāgata had shown an inclination to teach the Great Analysis of Kamma, requested the Tathāgata, and thinking, 'I will make the knowledge of the great analysis of kamma clear to the community of bhikkhus,' spoke thus due to his skill in making connections. Therein, ‘the great analysis of kamma’ means the great division of kamma. The passage ‘What are the four… here, Ānanda, a certain person… is reborn in hell’ is not the exposition of the knowledge of the great analysis of kamma; rather, it is the laying down of the matrix for the purpose of the exposition of the knowledge of the great analysis of kamma.

301. Idhānanda[V 4.0192][M 4.0183], ekacco samaṇo vāti pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Idañhi bhagavā – “dibbacakkhukā samaṇabrāhmaṇā idaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā imaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā idaṃ dassanaṃ gaṇhantī”ti pakāsanatthaṃ ārabhi. Tattha ātappantiādīni pañcapi vīriyasseva nāmāni. Cetosamādhinti dibbacakkhusamādhiṃ. Passatīti “so satto kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti olokento passati. Ye aññathāti ye “dasannaṃ kusalānaṃ kammapathānaṃ pūritattā nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti jānanti, micchā tesaṃ ñāṇanti vadati. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Viditanti pākaṭaṃ. Thāmasāti diṭṭhithāmena. Parāmāsāti diṭṭhiparāmāsena. Abhinivissa voharatīti adhiṭṭhahitvā ādiyitvā voharati.

301. The phrase 'Here, Ānanda, a certain ascetic or...' is a separate connection. For the Blessed One began this to show: 'Ascetics and brahmins with the divine eye, making this their object and obtaining this condition, grasp this view.' Therein, the five terms beginning with 'ardent' are all names for energy. 'Mental concentration' means the concentration for the divine eye. 'He sees' means that he sees while observing, 'Where has that being been reborn?' 'Those who otherwise' means those who know, 'Because of fulfilling the ten wholesome courses of kamma, one is reborn in hell'; he (the Buddha) states that their knowledge is wrong. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all cases. 'Understood' means clear. 'By strength' means by the strength of a view. 'By grasping' means by the grasping of a view. 'Having adhered to it, he declares' means having resolved upon it and grasped it firmly, he declares.

302. Tatrānandāti [P 5.0019] idampi na mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇassa bhājanaṃ, atha khvāssa mātikāṭṭhapanameva.
