Ettha pana etesaṃ dibbacakkhukānaṃ vacane ettakā anuññātā, ettakā ananuññātāti idaṃ dassitaṃ. Tattha tatrāti tesu catūsu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu. Idamassāti idaṃ vacanaṃ assa. Aññathāti aññenākārena. Iti imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vāde dvīsu ṭhānesu anuññātā, tīsu ananuññātāti evaṃ sabbattha anuññā nānuññā veditabbā.

302. The phrase 'Therein, Ānanda' is also not the exposition of the knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma, but rather merely the establishing of the matrix for it. Here, however, in the speech of those with the divine eye, this is shown: 'this much is permitted, this much is not permitted.' Therein, 'therein' refers to those four ascetics and brahmins. 'This of his' means this statement of his. 'Otherwise' means in another manner. Thus, in the doctrine of these ascetics and brahmins, in two instances it is permitted and in three it is not permitted; in this way, what is permitted and not permitted should be understood in all cases.

303. Evaṃ dibbacakkhukānaṃ vacane anuññā ca ananuññā ca dassetvā idāni mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ vibhajanto tatrānanda, yvāyaṃ puggalotiādimāha.

303. Thus, having shown what is permitted and what is not permitted in the speech of those with the divine eye, now, while analyzing the knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma, he said, 'Therein, Ānanda, this person...' and so on.

Pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hotīti yaṃ iminā dibbacakkhukena kammaṃ karonto diṭṭho, tato pubbe kataṃ. Pubbe katenapi hi niraye nibbattati, pacchā katenapi nibbattati, maraṇakāle vā pana – “khando seṭṭho sivo seṭṭho, pitāmaho seṭṭho, issarādīhi vā loko visaṭṭho”tiādinā micchādassanenapi nibbattateva. Diṭṭheva dhammeti yaṃ tattha diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ hoti, tassa diṭṭheva dhamme, yaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ, tassa upapajjitvā, yaṃ aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ, tassa aparasmiṃ pariyāye vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti.

Regarding 'Or that deed was done by him previously': it was done prior to the kamma that he was seen performing by this one with the divine eye. For one is reborn in hell due to a deed done previously, and one is reborn due to a deed done subsequently, or at the time of death, one is indeed reborn due to wrong view such as, 'Khanda is supreme, Siva is supreme, the Great Father is supreme,' or 'The world was created by lords,' and so on. Regarding 'in this very life': of the kamma therein that is to be experienced in this very life, one experiences its result in this very life; of that which is to be experienced upon rebirth, one experiences its result after having been reborn; of that which is to be experienced in a subsequent life, one experiences its result in a subsequent life.

Iti [M 4.0184] ayaṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ekaṃ kammarāsiṃ ekañca vipākarāsiṃ addasa, sammāsambuddho iminā adiṭṭhe tayo kammarāsī, dve ca vipākarāsī addasa. Iminā pana diṭṭhe [V 4.0193] adiṭṭhe ca cattāro kammarāsī tayo ca vipākarāsī addasa. Imāni satta ṭhānāni jānanañāṇaṃ tathāgatassa mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ nāma. Dutiyavāre dibbacakkhukena kiñci na diṭṭhaṃ[P 5.0020], tathāgatena pana tayo kammarāsī, dve ca vipākarāsī diṭṭhāti. Imānipi pañca paccattaṭṭhānāni jānanañāṇaṃ tathāgatassa mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ nāma. Sesavāradvayepi eseva nayo.

Thus, this ascetic or brahmin saw one heap of kamma and one heap of result. The Perfectly Enlightened One saw three heaps of kamma and two heaps of result that were unseen by this one. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, saw four heaps of kamma and three heaps of result, comprising both what was seen and what was unseen by this one. The knowledge that knows these seven instances is called the Tathāgata's knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma. In the second case, nothing was seen by the one with the divine eye, but the Tathāgata saw three heaps of kamma and two heaps of result. The knowledge that knows these five individual instances is also called the Tathāgata's knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma. In the remaining two cases as well, this is the method.

Abhabbanti bhūtavirahitaṃ akusalaṃ. Abhabbābhāsanti abhabbaṃ ābhāsati abhibhavati paṭibāhatīti attho. Bahukasmiñhi akusalakamme āyūhite balavakammaṃ dubbalakammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti idaṃ abhabbañceva abhabbābhāsañca. Kusalaṃ pana āyūhitvā āsanne akusalaṃ kataṃ hoti, taṃ kusalassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti, idaṃ abhabbaṃ bhabbābhāsaṃ. Bahumhi kusale āyūhitepi balavakammaṃ dubbalakammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti, idaṃ bhabbañceva bhabbābhāsañca. Akusalaṃ pana āyūhitvā āsanne kusalaṃ kataṃ hoti, taṃ akusalassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti, idaṃ bhabbaṃ abhabbābhāsaṃ.

'Incapable' means unwholesome, being devoid of a true state. 'Appearing incapable' means it appears as, overpowers, and obstructs other incapable kamma; this is the meaning. For when much unwholesome kamma has been accumulated, a strong kamma, having obstructed the result of a weak kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result; this is both incapable and appearing incapable. But when wholesome kamma has been accumulated and unwholesome kamma has been done near the time of death, that unwholesome kamma, having obstructed the result of the wholesome kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result; this is incapable but appearing capable. When much wholesome kamma has been accumulated, a strong kamma, having obstructed the result of a weak kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result; this is both capable and appearing capable. But when unwholesome kamma has been accumulated and wholesome kamma has been done near the time of death, that wholesome kamma, having obstructed the result of the unwholesome kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result; this is capable but appearing incapable.

Apica upaṭṭhānākārenapettha attho veditabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti, abhabbato ābhāsati upaṭṭhātīti abhabbābhāsaṃ. Tattha “yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātī”tiādinā nayena cattāro puggalā vuttā, tesu paṭhamassa kammaṃ abhabbaṃ abhabbābhāsaṃ, tañhi akusalattā abhabbaṃ, tassa ca niraye nibbattattā tattha nibbattikāraṇabhūtaṃ akusalaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Dutiyassa kammaṃ abhabbaṃ bhabbābhāsaṃ, tañhi akusalattā abhabbaṃ. Tassa pana sagge nibbattattā [P 5.0021] aññatitthiyānaṃ sagge nibbattikāraṇabhūtaṃ [M 4.0185] kusalaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Itarasmimpi kammadvaye eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood in the manner of manifestation. For this is what is said: because it appears or manifests from the incapable, it is 'appearing incapable.' Therein, four persons are mentioned in the way beginning, 'This person here is one who destroys life...' Among them, the kamma of the first is incapable and appearing incapable. For, because it is unwholesome, it is incapable; and because he is reborn in hell, it manifests as the unwholesome kamma that is the cause for rebirth there. The kamma of the second is incapable but appearing capable. For, because it is unwholesome, it is incapable. But because he is reborn in heaven, it manifests to the adherents of other teachings as the wholesome kamma that is the cause for rebirth in heaven. In the other two types of kamma as well, this is the method. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahākammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

7. Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases

304. Evaṃ [V 4.0194] me sutanti saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha veditabbānīti sahavipassanena maggena jānitabbāni. Manopavicārāti vitakkavicārā. Vitakkuppādakañhi mano idha manoti adhippetaṃ, manassa upavicārāti manopavicārā. Sattapadāti vaṭṭavivaṭṭanissitānaṃ sattānaṃ padā. Ettha hi aṭṭhārasa vaṭṭapadā nāma, aṭṭhārasa vivaṭṭapadā nāma, tepi sahavipassanena maggeneva veditabbā. Yoggācariyānanti hatthiyoggādiācārasikkhāpakānaṃ, dametabbadamakānanti attho. Sesaṃ vibhaṅgeyeva āvibhavissati. Ayamuddesoti idaṃ mātikāṭṭhapanaṃ.

304. Thus have I heard—the Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases. Herein, things to be known are to be understood by the path accompanied by insight. 'Mental excursions' are initial application and sustained application. For here, 'mind' is intended as that which produces initial application; 'mental excursions' are the investigations of the mind. 'Stations of beings' refers to the stations of beings dependent on the round of existence and the escape from it. Herein, there are eighteen stations of the round and eighteen stations of the escape, and these too should be understood by the path accompanied by insight. 'Trainers of the method' refers to those who instruct in the training of elephants and the like; the meaning is 'those who tame the tamable.' The rest will become clear in the analysis itself. This is the outline—this is the setting out of the matrix.

305. Cakkhāyatanādīni visuddhimagge vitthāritāni. Cakkhuviññāṇanti kusalākusalavipākato dve cakkhuviññāṇāni. Sesapasādaviññāṇesupi eseva nayo. Imāni pana dasa ṭhapetvā sesaṃ idha manoviññāṇaṃ nāma.

305. The eye base and other such topics are explained in detail in the Path of Purification. 'Eye-consciousness' refers to the two eye-consciousnesses that are the results of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. The same method applies to the remaining consciousnesses based on the sense faculties. However, setting aside these ten, the remaining consciousness is here called 'mind-consciousness.'

Cakkhusamphassoti cakkhumhi samphasso. Cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttasamphassassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

'Eye-contact' means contact at the eye. This is a designation for contact associated with eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the rest.

Cakkhunā [P 5.0022] rūpaṃ disvāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Somanassaṭṭhāniyanti somanassassa ārammaṇavasena kāraṇabhūtaṃ. Upavicaratīti tattha vicārapavattanena upavicarati, vitakko taṃsampayutto cāti iminā nayena aṭṭhārasa vitakkavicārasaṅkhātā manopavicārā veditabbā. Cha somanassūpavicārāti ettha pana somanassena saddhiṃ upavicarantīti somanassūpavicārā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

'Having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with eye-consciousness. The same method applies everywhere. 'A basis for joy' means that which serves as a cause for joy by way of being an object. 'Investigates' means it investigates by the occurrence of sustained application there, and initial application is also associated with it. By this method, the eighteen mental excursions, reckoned as initial application and sustained application, should be understood. 'Six investigations connected with joy' here means they investigate together with joy; hence, they are called 'investigations connected with joy.' The same method applies to the remaining two sets of terms.

306. Gehasitānīti [M 4.0186] kāmaguṇanissitāni. Nekkhammasitānīti vipassanānissitāni. Iṭṭhānanti pariyesitānaṃ. Kantānanti kāmitānaṃ. Manoramānanti mano etesu ramatīti manoramāni, tesaṃ manoramānaṃ. Lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānanti taṇhāpaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ. Atītanti paṭiladdhaṃ[V 4.0195]. Paccuppannaṃ tāva ārabbha somanassaṃ uppajjatu, atīte kathaṃ uppajjatīti. Atītepi – “yathāhaṃ etarahi iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ anubhavāmi, evaṃ pubbepi anubhavi”nti anussarantassa balavasomanassaṃ uppajjati.

306. 'Household-based' means dependent on sensual pleasures. 'Renunciation-based' means dependent on insight. 'Desirable' means sought after. 'Lovely' means desired. 'Charming' means the mind delights in them; thus, they are called 'charming,' of those charming things. 'Connected with worldly acquisitions' means connected with craving. 'Past' means obtained. Let joy arise regarding the present. How does it arise regarding the past? Regarding the past too—'Just as I now experience a desirable object, so I experienced it in the past'—when one recollects thus, strong joy arises.

Aniccatanti aniccākāraṃ. Vipariṇāmavirāganirodhanti pakativijahanena vipariṇāmaṃ, vigacchanena virāgaṃ, nirujjhanena nirodhaṃ. Sammapaññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya. Idaṃ vuccati nekkhammasitaṃ somanassanti idaṃ rañño viya attano sirisampattiṃ olokentassa vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nisinnassa saṅkhārānaṃ bhedaṃ passato saṅkhāragatamhi [P 5.0023] tikkhe sūre vipassanāñāṇe vahante uppannasomanassaṃ “nekkhammasitaṃ somanassa”nti vuccati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Impermanence' means the aspect of impermanence. 'Change, fading away, cessation' means change by abandoning its natural state, fading away by disappearing, cessation by ceasing. 'With wisdom' means with insight wisdom. This is called 'renunciation-based joy'—this joy arises in one who, having established insight and being seated, sees the dissolution of formations, when sharp and courageous insight knowledge proceeds regarding formations, like a king beholding his own glorious wealth. And this is said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī ratī hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

'For a monk who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a superhuman delight when he rightly sees the Dhamma with insight.

Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amatantaṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 373-374);

Whenever he comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, he obtains rapture and joy; that is the deathless for those who know.'

Imānīti imāni chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nisinnassa uppannāni cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni.

'These' refers to these six kinds of renunciation-based joy that arise in one who is seated, having established insight into desirable objects that have come into range at the six doors, by way of impermanence and other such characteristics.

307. Atītanti paccuppannaṃ tāva patthetvā alabhantassa domanassaṃ uppajjatu, atīte kathaṃ uppajjatīti. Atītepi “yathāhaṃ etarahi iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ patthetvā na labhāmi, evaṃ pubbepi patthetvā na labhi”nti anussarantassa balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati.

307. 'Past': Let sorrow arise for one who longs for a present object and does not obtain it. How does it arise regarding the past? Regarding the past too—'Just as I now long for a desirable object and do not obtain it, so too in the past I longed and did not obtain it'—when one recollects thus, strong sorrow arises.

Anuttaresu vimokkhesūti anuttaravimokkho nāma arahattaṃ, arahatte patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentassāti attho. Āyatananti arahattāyatanaṃ. Pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayatoti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa. Taṃ panetaṃ patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa [M 4.0187] uppajjati, iti patthanāmūlakattā “pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato”ti vuttaṃ. Imāni cha nekkhammasitāni domanassānīti imāni evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate arahatte pihaṃ paṭṭhapetvā [V 4.0196] tadadhigamāya aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ussukkāpetuṃ asakkontassa – “imampi pakkhaṃ imampi māsaṃ imampi saṃvaccharaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ nāsakkhi”nti anusocato gāmantapabbhāravāsimahāsīvattherassa viya assudhārāpavattanavasena uppannadomanassāni [P 5.0024] cha nekkhammasitadomanassānīti veditabbāni. Vatthu pana sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya sakkapañhavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.361) vitthāritaṃ, icchantena tato gahetabbaṃ.

'Among the unsurpassed liberations': the unsurpassed liberation means Arahantship. The meaning is: for one who is setting up the aspiration for Arahantship. 'The sphere' refers to the sphere of Arahantship. 'One who arouses longing' means one who is setting up aspiration. Now, this sorrow arises for one who is setting up the aspiration; therefore, because it is rooted in aspiration, it is said, 'one who arouses longing.' 'These six sorrows based on renunciation': thus, when a desirable object appears through the six sense doors, for one who, having set up longing for Arahantship, is unable to strive for its attainment through insight into impermanence and other such characteristics, and laments, 'I was not able to attain Arahantship even this fortnight, this month, or this year'—the sorrows that arise like a flowing stream of tears, as in the case of the elder Mahāsīva dwelling in a mountain valley near a village, are to be understood as the six sorrows based on renunciation. The story, however, is elaborated in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, in the explanation of the Sakkapañha Sutta. One who wishes may take it from there.

308. Uppajjati upekkhāti ettha upekkhā nāma aññāṇupekhā. Anodhijinassāti kilesodhiṃ jinitvā ṭhitattā khīṇāsavo odhijino nāma, tasmā akhīṇāsavassāti attho. Avipākajinassāti etthapi āyatiṃ vipākaṃ jinitvā ṭhitattā khīṇāsavova vipākajino nāma, tasmā akhīṇāsavassevāti attho. Anādīnavadassāvinotiādīnavato upaddavato apassantassa. Imā cha gehasitā upekkhāti imā evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate guḷapiṇḍake nilīnamakkhikā viya rūpādīni anativattamānā tattha laggā laggitā hutvā uppannā upekkhā cha gehasitā upekkhāti veditabbā.

308. “Equanimity arises”—here, equanimity means equanimity accompanied by ignorance. “For one who has not conquered the boundary”: because of having conquered the boundary of defilements and being established, one whose cankers are destroyed is called “one who has conquered the boundary.” Therefore, the meaning is: for one whose cankers are not destroyed. “For one who has not conquered the result”: here too, because of having conquered the future result and being established, one whose cankers are destroyed is called “one who has conquered the result.” Therefore, the meaning is: for one whose cankers are not destroyed. “For one who does not see the danger”: for one who does not see it as a danger or peril. “These six kinds of equanimity are based on the household life”: thus, when a desirable object comes into range at the six doors, like flies alighting on a lump of molasses, these equanimities arise, unable to overcome forms and so on, becoming stuck and attached there. They are to be understood as the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.

Rūpaṃ sā ativattatīti rūpaṃ sā anatikkamati, tattha nikantivasena na tiṭṭhati. Imā cha nekkhammasitā upekkhāti imā evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhādiārammaṇe āpāthagate iṭṭhe arajjantassa, aniṭṭhe adussantassa, asamapekkhane asammuyhantassa, uppannavipassanā-ñāṇasampayuttā cha nekkhammasitā upekkhāti veditabbā.

“It does not overcome form”: that equanimity does not transcend form; it does not stand there by way of attachment. “These six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation”: thus, when a desirable or other object comes into range at the six doors, for one who is not attached to the desirable, not resentful towards the undesirable, and not deluded in regard to indifferent seeing, these arisen equanimities associated with insight-knowledge are to be known as the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.

309. Tatra idaṃ nissāya idaṃ pajahathāti tesu chattiṃsasattapadesu aṭṭhārasa nissāya aṭṭhārasa pajahathāti attho. Teneva [P 5.0025] – “tatra, bhikkhave, yāni cha nekkhammasitānī”tiādimāha. Nissāya āgammāti pavattanavasena nissāya ceva āgamma ca. Evametesaṃ samatikkamo [M 4.0188] hotīti evaṃ nekkhammasitānaṃ pavattanena gehasitāni atikkantāni nāma honti.

309. “Therein, relying on this, abandon that”: among those thirty-six positions of beings, the meaning is: relying on eighteen, abandon eighteen. For that reason, the Blessed One said: “Therein, O bhikkhus, those six that are based on renunciation…” and so on. “Relying on, depending on”: by way of occurrence, both relying on and depending on. “Thus there is the overcoming of these”: thus, through the occurrence of the states based on renunciation, the states based on the household life are indeed overcome.

Evaṃ sarikkhakeneva sarikkhakaṃ jahāpetvā idāni balavatā dubbalaṃ jahāpento – “tatra, bhikkhave, yāni cha nekkhammasitāni somanassānī”tiādimāha. Evaṃ nekkhammasitasomanassehi nekkhammasitadomanassāni[V 4.0197], nekkhammasitaupekkhāhi ca nekkhammasitasomanassāni jahāpentena balavatā dubbalappahānaṃ kathitaṃ.

Thus, having caused the similar to be abandoned by the similar, now, in order to cause the weak to be abandoned by the strong, the Blessed One said: “Therein, O bhikkhus, those six joys based on renunciation…” and so on. Thus, by the Blessed One causing the displeasures based on renunciation to be abandoned by the joys based on renunciation, and the joys based on renunciation by the equanimities based on renunciation, the abandoning of the weak by the strong has been taught.

Ettha pana ṭhatvā upekkhākathā veditabbā – aṭṭhasu hi samāpattīsu paṭhamādīni ca tīṇi jhānāni, suddhasaṅkhāre ca pādake katvā vipassanaṃ āraddhānaṃ catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatā vā hoti upekkhāsahagatā vā, vuṭṭhānagāminī pana somanassasahagatāva. Catutthajjhānādīni pādakāni katvā vipassanaṃ āraddhānaṃ pañcannaṃ pubbabhāgavipassanā purimasadisāva. Vuṭṭhānagāminī pana upekkhāsahagatā hoti. Idaṃ sandhāya – “yā cha nekkhammasitā upekkhā, tā nissāya tā āgamma, yāni cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni, tāni pajahathā”ti vuttaṃ. Na kevalañca evaṃpaṭipannassa bhikkhuno ayaṃ vipassanāya vedanāvisesova hoti, ariyamaggepi pana jhānaṅgabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgānampi viseso hoti.

Here, however, pausing, the discourse on equanimity should be understood: For the four bhikkhus who, among the eight attainments, have made the first three jhānas and pure formations their basis and have undertaken insight, the preliminary-part insight is accompanied either by joy or by equanimity; but the insight leading to emergence is only accompanied by joy. For the five bhikkhus who have made the fourth jhāna and so on their basis and have undertaken insight, the preliminary-part insight is just like the former; but the insight leading to emergence is accompanied by equanimity. With reference to this, it was said: “Relying on and depending on the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, abandon the six kinds of joy based on renunciation.” And not only is there this distinction of feeling in insight for a bhikkhu practicing thus, but on the noble path too, there is a distinction of jhāna-factors, enlightenment-factors, and path-factors.

Ko panetaṃ visesaṃ niyameti? Keci tāva therā vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ niyametīti vadanti, keci vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentīti vadanti, keci puggalajjhāsayo niyametīti vadanti. Tesampi vāde ayameva pubbabhāge vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā niyametīti veditabbā. Vinicchayakathā [P 5.0026] panettha visuddhimagge saṅkhārupekkhāniddese vuttāva.

Now, what determines this distinction? Some elders say that the jhāna which is the basis for insight determines it. Some elders say that the aggregates which have become the object of insight determine it. Some elders say that the individual's inclination determines it. In their views too, it should be understood that in the preliminary part, this very insight leading to emergence determines it. The decisive explanation on this point has been stated by me in the Visuddhimagga, in the exposition of equanimity towards formations.

310. Nānattāti nānā bahū anekappakārā. Nānattasitāti nānārammaṇanissitā. Ekattāti ekā. Ekattasitāti ekārammaṇanissitā. Katamā panāyaṃ upekkhāti? Heṭṭhā tāva aññāṇupekkhā vuttā, upari chaḷaṅgupekkhā vakkhati, idha samathaupekkhā, vipassanupekkhāti dve upekkhā gahitā.

310. “Diversity”: diverse, many, of various kinds. “Based on diversity”: reliant on various objects. “Unity”: one. “Based on unity”: reliant on a single object. What, then, is this equanimity? Previously, equanimity accompanied by ignorance was spoken of; later, six-factored equanimity will be spoken of. Here, two equanimities are taken: serenity-equanimity and insight-equanimity.

Tattha yasmā aññāva rūpesu upekkhā, aññāva saddādīsu, na hi yā rūpe upekkhā, sā saddādīsu hoti. Rūpe upekkhā ca rūpameva ārammaṇaṃ karoti[M 4.0189], na saddādayo. Rūpe upekkhābhāvañca aññā samathaupekkhā pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati, aññā āpokasiṇādīni. Tasmā nānattaṃ nānattasitaṃ vibhajanto atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhā rūpesūtiādimāha[V 4.0198]. Yasmā pana dve vā tīṇi vā ākāsānañcāyatanāni vā viññāṇañcāyatanādīni vā natthi, tasmā ekattaṃ ekattasitaṃ vibhajanto atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhā ākāsānañcāyatananissitātiādimāha.

Therein, because the equanimity regarding forms is one thing, and that regarding sounds and so on is another; for indeed, the equanimity that occurs regarding form does not occur regarding sounds and so on. And equanimity regarding form takes only form as its object, not sounds and so on. Furthermore, as for the state of equanimity in regard to form: one serenity-equanimity arises taking the earth-kasiṇa as its object, another arises taking the water-kasiṇa and so on. Therefore, analyzing diversity and that which is based on diversity, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there is equanimity towards forms,” and so on. But because there are not two or three bases of infinite space, or bases of infinite consciousness, and so on, therefore, analyzing unity and that which is based on unity, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there is equanimity dependent on the base of infinite space,” and so on.

Tattha ākāsānañcāyatanaupekkhā sampayuttavasena ākāsānañcāyatananissitā, ākāsānañcāyatanakhandhe vipassantassa vipassanupekkhā ārammaṇavasena ākāsānañcāyatananissitā. Sesāsupi eseva nayo.

Therein, the equanimity of the base of infinite space is, by way of association, dependent on the base of infinite space. For one contemplating with insight the aggregates of the base of infinite space, the insight-equanimity is, by way of its object, dependent on the base of infinite space. This same method should be understood in the remaining cases as well.

Taṃ pajahathāti ettha arūpāvacarasamāpattiupekkhāya rūpāvacarasamāpattiupekkhaṃ pajahāpeti, arūpāvacaravipassanupekkhāya rūpāvacaravipassanupekkhaṃ.

“Abandon that”: Here, by means of the equanimity of the formless sphere attainment, one causes the equanimity of the form sphere attainment to be abandoned; and by means of the insight-equanimity concerning the formless sphere, the insight-equanimity concerning the form sphere.

Atammayatanti [P 5.0027] ettha tammayatā nāma taṇhā, tassā pariyādānato vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā atammayatāti vuccati. Taṃ pajahathāti idha vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanāya arūpāvacarasamāpattiupekkhañca vipassanupekkhañca pajahāpeti.

“Non-identification”: Here, ‘identification’ means craving. Because of the exhaustion of that craving, the insight leading to emergence is called ‘non-identification’. “Abandon that”: Here, by means of the insight leading to emergence, one causes the abandonment of both the equanimity of the formless sphere attainment and the insight-equanimity.

311. Yadariyoti ye satipaṭṭhāne ariyo sammāsambuddho sevati. Tattha tīsu ṭhānesu satiṃ paṭṭhapento satipaṭṭhāne sevatīti veditabbo. Na sussūsantīti saddahitvā sotuṃ na icchanti. Na aññāti jānanatthāya cittaṃ na upaṭṭhapenti. Vokkammāti atikkamitvā. Satthu sāsanāti satthu ovādaṃ gahetabbaṃ pūretabbaṃ na maññantīti attho. Na ca attamanoti na sakamano. Ettha ca gehasitadomanassavasena appatīto hotīti na evamattho daṭṭhabbo, appaṭipannakesu pana attamanatākāraṇassa abhāvenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Anavassutoti paṭighaavassavena anavassuto. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ca ñāṇena ca samannāgato[M 4.0190]. Upekkhakoti chaḷaṅgupekkhāya upekkhako. Attamanoti idhāpi gehasitasomanassavasena uppilāvitoti na evamattho daṭṭhabbo, paṭipannakesu pana anattamanatākāraṇassa abhāvenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Anavassutoti rāgāvassavena anavassuto.

311. 'Yadariyo' means: the foundations of mindfulness that the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, frequents. Therein, it should be understood thus: establishing mindfulness in three instances, he frequents the foundations of mindfulness. 'Na sussūsanti' means: they do not wish to listen with faith. 'Na aññā' means: they do not apply their minds for the purpose of knowing. 'Vokkamma' means: having transgressed. 'Satthu sāsana' means: they do not consider that the Teacher's instruction should be accepted or fulfilled; this is the meaning. 'Na ca anattamano' means: not displeased. And here, the meaning should not be understood thus: that he is displeased by way of sorrow connected with the household life; rather, this was said because of the absence of a reason for displeasure towards those who do not practice well. 'Anavassuto' means: not inundated by the influx of aversion. 'Sato sampajāno' means: endowed with mindfulness and with knowledge. 'Upekkhako' means: equanimous with the six-factored equanimity. 'Attamano': here too, the meaning should not be understood thus: that he is elated by way of joy connected with the household life; rather, this was said because of the absence of a reason for displeasure towards those who practice well. 'Anavassuto' means: not inundated by the influx of lust.

312. Sāritoti [V 4.0199] damito. Ekameva disaṃ dhāvatīti anivattitvā dhāvanto ekaṃyeva disaṃ dhāvati, nivattitvā pana aparaṃ dhāvituṃ sakkoti. Aṭṭha [P 5.0028] disā vidhāvatīti ekapallaṅkena nisinno kāyena anivattitvāva vimokkhavasena ekappahāreneva aṭṭha disā vidhāvati, puratthābhimukho vā dakkhiṇādīsu aññataradisābhimukho vā nisīditvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo samāpajjatiyevāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

312. 'Sārito' means: tamed. 'Ekameva disaṃ dhāvati' means: running without turning back, one runs in one direction only; however, having turned back, one is able to run in another. 'Aṭṭha disā vidhāvati' means: one sitting in a single cross-legged posture, without turning the body, by the power of the liberations, traverses the eight directions in a single impulse. Having sat facing east, or facing any other direction among the south and so on, one is indeed able to enter the eight attainments; this is the meaning. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

8. Uddesavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta

313. Evaṃ [V 4.0200] me sutanti uddesavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha uddesavibhaṅganti uddesañca vibhaṅgañca, mātikañca vibhajanañcāti attho. Upaparikkheyyāti tuleyya tīreyya pariggaṇheyya paricchindeyya. Bahiddhāti bahiddhāārammaṇesu. Avikkhittaṃ avisaṭanti nikantivasena ārammaṇe tiṭṭhamānaṃ vikkhittaṃ visaṭaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ paṭisedhento evamāha. Ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitanti gocarajjhatte nikantivasena asaṇṭhitaṃ. Anupādāya na paritasseyyāti anupādiyitvā aggahetvā taṃ viññāṇaṃ na paritasseyya. Yathā viññāṇaṃ bahiddhā avikkhittaṃ avisaṭaṃ, ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ anupādāya na paritasseyya, evaṃ bhikkhu upaparikkheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jātijarāmaraṇadukkhasamudayasambhavoti jātijarāmaraṇassa ceva avasesassa ca dukkhassa nibbatti na hotīti attho.

313. 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, 'uddesavibhaṅga' means both the exposition and the analysis, the matrix and the classification; this is the meaning. 'Upaparikkheyya' means: one should weigh, one should judge, one should investigate, one should define. 'Bahiddhā' means: in external objects. 'Avikkhittaṃ avisaṭaṃ' means: remaining on an object by way of desire is called 'scattered' and 'dispersed'; rejecting that, he spoke thus. 'Ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ' means: unestablished by way of desire in an internal object. 'Anupādāya na paritasseyya' means: without clinging, without grasping that consciousness, one would not be agitated. It is said thus: 'A bhikkhu should investigate in such a way that consciousness is externally undistracted and undispersed, internally unestablished, and without clinging, one would not be agitated.' 'Jātijarāmaraṇadukkhasamudayasambhavo' means: the arising of birth, aging, and death, and of the remaining suffering, does not occur; this is the meaning.

316. Rūpanimittānusārīti [M 4.0191] rūpanimittaṃ anussarati anudhāvatīti rūpanimittānusārī.

316. 'Rūpanimittānusārī' means: one who follows and runs after the sign of form is a 'rūpanimittānusārī'.

318. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitanti nikantivasena [P 5.0029] asaṇṭhitaṃ. Nikantivasena hi atiṭṭhamānaṃ hānabhāgiyaṃ na hoti, visesabhāgiyameva hoti.

318. Thus, friend, 'ajjhattaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ' means unestablished by way of desire. For that which is not established by way of desire does not partake of decline, but only of distinction.

320. Anupādā paritassanāti satthārā khandhiyavagge “upādāparitassanañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi anupādāaparitassanañcā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.7) evaṃ gahetvā paritassanā, aggahetvāva aparitassanā ca kathitā, taṃ mahāthero upādāparitassanameva anupādāparitassananti katvā dassento evamāha. Kathaṃ panesā anupādāparitassanā hotīti. Upādātabbassa abhāvato. Yadi hi koci saṅkhāro nicco vā dhuvo vā attā vā attaniyo vāti gahetabbayuttako abhavissa, ayaṃ paritassanā upādāparitassanāva assa. Yasmā pana evaṃ upādātabbo saṅkhāro nāma natthi, tasmā rūpaṃ attātiādinā nayena rūpādayo [V 4.0201] upādinnāpi anupādinnāva honti. Evamesā diṭṭhivasena upādāparitassanāpi samānā atthato anupādāparitassanāyeva nāma hotīti veditabbā.

320. 'Anupādā paritassanā': In the Khandha Vagga, the Teacher took up the topic thus: 'I shall teach you, bhikkhus, agitation through clinging and non-agitation through non-clinging' (SN 22.7). Here, only non-agitation is taught, without taking up agitation. The Great Elder, showing that this very agitation through clinging is in fact non-agitation through non-clinging, spoke thus. But how does this become non-agitation through non-clinging? Because of the absence of anything that can be clung to. For if any conditioned thing were fit to be grasped as permanent, stable, a self, or belonging to a self, this agitation would indeed be agitation through clinging. But since there is no conditioned thing to be clung to in this way, therefore forms and so on, even when clung to in the manner 'form is self,' etc., are in fact not clung to. Thus it should be understood that this, while being agitation through clinging by way of wrong view, is in reality named only non-agitation through non-clinging.

Aññathā hotīti parivattati pakatijahanena nassati, rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattīti “mama rūpaṃ vipariṇata”nti vā, “yaṃ ahu, taṃ vata me natthī”ti vā ādinā (ma. ni. 1.242) nayena kammaviññāṇaṃ rūpassa bhedānuparivatti hoti. Vipariṇāmānuparivattajāti vipariṇāmassa anuparivattanato vipariṇāmārammaṇacittato jātā. Paritassanā dhammasamuppādāti taṇhāparitassanā ca akusaladhammasamuppādā ca. Cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti kusalacittaṃ pariyādiyitvā gahetvā khepetvā tiṭṭhanti. Uttāsavāti bhayatāsenapi sauttāso taṇhātāsenapi sauttāso. Vighātavāti [P 5.0030] savighāto sadukkho. Apekkhavāti sālayo sasineho. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, anupādā paritassanā hotīti evaṃ maṇikaraṇḍakasaññāya tucchakaraṇḍakaṃ gahetvā tasmiṃ naṭṭhe pacchā vighātaṃ āpajjantassa viya pacchā aggahetvā paritassanā hoti.

'Aññathā hoti' means: it changes, it perishes by abandoning its natural state. 'Rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattī' means: kamma-consciousness follows after the breakup of form in the manner of 'My form has changed,' or 'What was mine, that indeed is no more,' and so on. 'Vipariṇāmānuparivattajā' means: born from following after the transformation, born from a mind that has transformation as its object. 'Paritassanā dhammasamuppādā' means: both craving-agitation and the arising of unwholesome states. 'Cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti' means: having exhausted, seized, and depleted the wholesome mind, they remain. 'Uttāsavā' means: anxious with the terror of fear, and anxious with the terror of craving. 'Vighātavā' means: with vexation, with suffering. 'Apekkhavā' means: with attachment, with affection. Thus, friend, agitation without clinging occurs, just as for one who, with the perception of a jewel-casket, takes an empty casket and then, when it is lost, afterwards falls into vexation.

321. Na [M 4.0192] ca rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattīti khīṇāsavassa kammaviññāṇameva natthi, tasmā rūpabhedānuparivatti na hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

321. 'Na ca rūpavipariṇāmānuparivattī' means: for one whose taints are destroyed, there is no kamma-consciousness at all; therefore, it does not follow after the breakup of form. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Uddesavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

9. Araṇavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta

323. Evaṃ [V 4.0202] me sutanti araṇavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha nevussādeyya na apasādeyyāti gehasitavasena kañci puggalaṃ neva ukkhipeyya na avakkhipeyya. Dhammameva deseyyāti sabhāvameva katheyya. Sukhavinicchayanti vinicchitasukhaṃ. Raho vādanti parammukhā avaṇṇaṃ, pisuṇavācanti attho. Sammukhā na khīṇanti sammukhāpi khīṇaṃ ākiṇṇaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vācaṃ na bhaṇeyya. Nābhiniveseyyāti na adhiṭṭhahitvā ādāya vohareyya. Samaññanti lokasamaññaṃ lokapaṇṇattiṃ. Nātidhāveyyāti nātikkameyya.

323. ‘Thus have I heard’—this is the Discourse on the Analysis of Non-Conflict. Therein, ‘one should neither exalt nor disparage’ means one should neither elevate nor demean any person based on worldly attachment. ‘One should teach only the Dhamma’ means one should speak only of the true nature. ‘Ascertained happiness’ means happiness that has been decided upon. ‘Speaking in private’ means speaking dispraise behind someone's back; the meaning is slanderous speech. ‘Not harshly face to face’ means one should not utter harsh, confused, or defiled speech even when face to face. ‘One should not insist’ means one should not speak after having determinedly taken a position. ‘Conventional terms’ refers to worldly conventions and worldly designations. ‘One should not overstep’ means one should not transgress.

324. Kāmapaṭisandhisukhinoti [P 5.0031] kāmapaṭisandhinā kāmūpasaṃhitena sukhena sukhitassa. Sadukkhoti vipākadukkhena saṃkilesadukkhenapi sadukkho. Saupaghātoti vipākūpaghātakilesūpaghāteheva saupaghāto. Tathā sapariḷāho. Micchāpaṭipadāti ayāthāvapaṭipadā akusalapaṭipadā.

324. ‘Happy through connection with sensual pleasure’ means: of one made happy by happiness connected with and conjoined with sensual pleasure. ‘With suffering’ means: with the suffering of result and also with the suffering of defilements. ‘With distress’ means: with the distress of result and the distress of defilements. Similarly, ‘with torment’. ‘Wrong practice’ means the un-genuine practice, the unwholesome practice.

326. Ittheke apasādetīti evaṃ gehasitavasena ekacce puggale apasādeti. Ussādanepi eseva nayo. Bhavasaṃyojananti bhavabandhanaṃ, taṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.

326. ‘Herein he disparages some’ means: thus he disparages certain individuals based on worldly attachment. In exalting, too, this is the method. ‘The fetter of existence’ means the bond of existence; this is a name for craving.

Subhūtitthero kira imaṃ catukkaṃ nissāya etadagge ṭhapito. Bhagavato hi dhammaṃ desentassa puggalānaṃ ussādanāapasādanā paññāyanti, tathā sāriputtattherādīnaṃ. Subhūtittherassa pana dhammadesanāya “ayaṃ puggalo appaṭipannako anārādhako”ti vā, “ayaṃ sīlavā guṇavā lajjipesalo ācārasampanno”ti vā natthi, dhammadesanāya panassa “ayaṃ micchāpaṭipadā, ayaṃ [M 4.0193] sammāpaṭipadā”tveva paññāyati. Tasmā bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ araṇavihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ subhūtī”ti āha.

The Elder Subhūti, it is said, having relied on this tetrad, was established as foremost. For when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, the exalting and disparaging of individuals were apparent, as with the Elder Sāriputta and others. But in the Elder Subhūti's teaching of the Dhamma, there was no such thing as, ‘This person is not practicing, is displeasing,’ or, ‘This person is virtuous, has good qualities, is conscientious, amiable, and accomplished in conduct.’ Instead, in his teaching of the Dhamma, only ‘This is wrong practice, this is right practice’ was apparent. Therefore, the Blessed One said, ‘Monks, among my monk disciples who are dwellers in non-conflict, the foremost is this one, that is, Subhūti.’

329. Kālaññū [V 4.0203] assāti asampatte ca atikkante ca kāle akathetvā “idāni vuccamānaṃ mahājano gaṇhissatī”ti yuttapattakālaṃ ñatvāva parammukhā avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya. Khīṇavādepi eseva nayo.

329. ‘He would be one who knows the time’ means: not having spoken when the time has not yet come or has passed, but having known the suitable and appropriate time, thinking, ‘Now, the great assembly will grasp what is being said,’ he should speak dispraise behind the other's back. In the case of harsh speech, too, this is the method.

330. Upahaññatīti ghātiyati. Saropi upahaññatīti saddopi bhijjati. Āturīyatīti āturo hoti gelaññappatto sābādho. Avissaṭṭhanti vissaṭṭhaṃ apalibuddhaṃ na hoti.

330. ‘Is harmed’ means is struck down. ‘Even his voice is harmed’ means his voice also breaks. ‘He becomes afflicted’ means he becomes sick, reaches a state of illness, is afflicted with disease. ‘Not clear’ means it is not clear, not unobstructed.

331. Tadevāti [P 5.0032] taṃyeva bhājanaṃ. Abhinivissa voharatīti pattanti sañjānanajanapadaṃ gantvā “pattaṃ āharatha dhovathā”ti sutvā “andhabālaputhujjano, nayidaṃ pattaṃ, pāti namesā, evaṃ vadāhī”ti abhinivissa voharati. Evaṃ sabbapadehi yojetabbaṃ. Atisāroti atidhāvanaṃ.

331. ‘That very thing’ means that very vessel. ‘He insists on using the term’ means: going to a region where they recognize it as a ‘bowl’ (patta), and hearing them say, ‘Bring the bowl, wash the bowl,’ he insists on using his term, saying, ‘You blind, foolish worldling, this is not a bowl, this is called a “pāti”; speak thus!’ Thus it should be applied to all terms. ‘Transgression’ means over-running.

332. Tathā tathā voharati aparāmasanti amhākaṃ janapade bhājanaṃ pātīti vuccati, ime pana naṃ pattanti vadantīti tato paṭṭhāya janapadavohāraṃ muñcitvā pattaṃ pattanteva aparāmasanto voharati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

332. ‘He speaks thus and thus without misapprehension’ means: thinking, ‘In our region, a vessel is called a “pāti”, but these people call it a “bowl”,’ from then on, having given up the regional usage, he speaks without misapprehension, using ‘bowl’ just as ‘bowl’. In the remaining terms, too, this is the method.

333. Idāni mariyādabhājanīyaṃ karonto tatra, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha saraṇoti sarajo sakileso. Araṇoti arajo nikkileso. Subhūti ca pana, bhikkhaveti ayaṃ thero dvīsu ṭhānesu etadaggaṃ āruḷho “araṇavihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ subhūti, dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ yadidaṃ subhūtī”ti (a. ni. 1.202).

333. Now, making a division of the boundaries, he said, ‘There, O monks,’ and so on. Therein, ‘with conflict’ means with dust, with defilements. ‘Without conflict’ means without dust, without defilements. And this Elder Subhūti, monks, was elevated to the foremost position in two respects: ‘Among dwellers in non-conflict, that is Subhūti; among those worthy of offerings, that is Subhūti’ (AN 1.24).

Dhammasenāpati kira vatthuṃ sodheti, subhūtitthero dakkhiṇaṃ sodheti. Tathā hi dhammasenāpati piṇḍāya caranto gehadvāre ṭhito yāva bhikkhaṃ āharanti, tāva pubbabhāge paricchinditvā nirodhaṃ samāpajjati, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya deyyadhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Subhūtitthero ca tatheva mettājhānaṃ samāpajjati, mettājhānā vuṭṭhāya deyyadhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Evaṃ pana kātuṃ sakkāti. Āma sakkā, neva acchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ [M 4.0194] mahābhiññappattā sāvakā evaṃ kareyyuṃ. Imasmimpi [P 5.0033] hi tambapaṇṇidīpe [V 4.0204] porāṇakarājakāle piṅgalabuddharakkhitatthero nāma uttaragāmaṃ nissāya vihāsi. Tattha satta kulasatāni honti, ekampi taṃ kuladvāraṃ natthi, yattha thero samāpattiṃ na samāpajji. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

The General of the Dhamma, it is said, purifies the basis of the offering, while the Elder Subhūti purifies the offering itself. For the General of the Dhamma, while wandering for almsfood, stands at a house door, and for the time it takes for them to bring the almsfood, having demarcated that prior portion of time, he enters the attainment of cessation. Rising from cessation, he accepts the gift. And the Elder Subhūti, in the same way, enters the absorption of loving-kindness. Rising from the absorption of loving-kindness, he accepts the gift. But is it possible to do so? Yes, it is possible. It is not at all wonderful that disciples who have attained great supernormal knowledge would do so. For even on this island of Tambapaṇṇi, in the time of the ancient kings, an elder named Piṅgala Buddharakkhita lived depending on the village of Uttara. There were seven hundred families there, and there was not a single household door where the elder did not enter an attainment. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Araṇavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Analysis of Non-Conflict is concluded.

10. Dhātuvibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements

342. Evaṃ [V 4.0205] me sutanti dhātuvibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha cārikanti turitagamanacārikaṃ. Sace te bhaggava agarūti sace tuyhaṃ bhāriyaṃ aphāsukaṃ kiñci natthi. Sace so anujānātīti bhaggavassa kira etadahosi – “pabbajitā nāma nānāajjhāsayā, eko gaṇābhirato hoti, eko ekābhirato. Sace so ekābhirato bhavissati, ‘āvuso, mā pāvisi, mayā sālā laddhā’ti vakkhati. Sace ayaṃ ekābhirato bhavissati, ‘āvuso, nikkhama, mayā sālā laddhā’ti vakkhati. Evaṃ sante ahaṃ ubhinnaṃ vivādakāretā nāma bhavissāmi, dinnaṃ nāma dinnameva vaṭṭati, kataṃ katamevā”ti. Tasmā evamāha.

342. ‘Thus have I heard’—this is the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements. Therein, ‘journeying’ means a swift journey. ‘If for you, Bhaggava, it is not inconvenient’ means: if for you, Bhaggava, there is no burden and no discomfort whatsoever. ‘If he allows it’: It seems this thought occurred to Bhaggava: ‘Renunciates have various dispositions; one delights in a group, another delights in solitude. If the first one is one who delights in solitude, he will say, “Friend, do not enter; the hall was obtained by me.” If this second one is one who delights in solitude, he will say, “Friend, depart; the hall was obtained by me.” This being so, I would become one who causes a dispute between the two. What is given is indeed given; what is done is indeed done.’ Therefore, he spoke thus.

Kulaputtoti jātikulaputtopi ācārakulaputtopi. Vāsūpagatoti vāsaṃ upagato. Kuto āgantvāti? Takkasīlanagarato.

‘Son of good family’ means a son of good family both by birth and by conduct. ‘Approached for residence’ means he has approached a dwelling. From where has he come? From the city of Takkasīlā.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – majjhimappadese kira rājagahanagare bimbisāre rajjaṃ kārente paccante takkasīlanagare pukkusāti rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Atha takkasīlato bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā vāṇijā rājagahaṃ āgatā paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ addasaṃsu. Rājā [P 5.0034] te vanditvā ṭhite “katthavāsino tumhe”ti pucchi. Takkasīlavāsino devāti. Atha ne rājā janapadassa khemasubhikkhatādīni nagarassa ca pavattiṃ pucchitvā “ko nāma tumhākaṃ rājā”ti pucchi. Pukkusāti nāma devāti. Dhammikoti? Āma deva dhammiko. Catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, lokassa mātāpitiṭṭhāne [M 4.0195] ṭhito, aṅge nipannadārakaṃ viya janaṃ tosetīti. Katarasmiṃ vaye vattatīti? Athassa vayaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Vayesupi bimbisārena samavayo jāto. Atha te rājā āha – “tātā tumhākaṃ rājā dhammiko, vayena ca me samāno, sakkuṇeyyātha tumhākaṃ rājānaṃ mama mittaṃ kātu”nti. Sakkoma devāti. Rājā tesaṃ suṅkaṃ vissajjetvā gehañca dāpetvā – “gacchatha bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā gamanakāle maṃ disvā gaccheyyāthā”ti āha. Te tathā katvā gamanakāle rājānaṃ addasaṃsu. “Gacchatha tumhākaṃ rājānaṃ [V 4.0206] mama vacanena punappunaṃ ārogyaṃ pucchitvā ‘rājā tumhehi saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ icchatī’ti vadathā”ti āha.

Here is the sequential account: It is said that while King Bimbisāra was ruling in the city of Rājagaha in the Middle Country, in the border region, King Pukkusāti ruled in the city of Takkasīlā. Then, merchants who had taken goods from Takkasīlā came to Rājagaha, and taking a gift, they saw the king. The king asked them, as they stood there having paid homage, 'Where do you reside?' 'We are residents of Takkasīlā, Your Majesty.' Then the king inquired about the country's peace and abundance and the city's affairs, and asked, 'What is your king's name?' 'His name is Pukkusāti, Your Majesty.' 'Is he righteous?' 'Yes, Your Majesty, he is righteous. He gathers the people with the four bases of sympathy, stands in the place of a mother and father to the world, and pleases the people as one would a child lying on one's lap.' 'In what age is he?' Then they told his age. It happened that he was of the same age as Bimbisāra. Then the king said to them, 'Dears, your king is righteous and of the same age as me. Would you be able to make your king my friend?' 'We are able, Your Majesty.' The king waived their tax and had a house provided for them, saying, 'Go, sell your goods, and when it is time to leave, see me before you go.' They did so, and when it was time to depart, they saw the king. He said, 'Go, and with my words, repeatedly inquire after your king’s health and say, "The king wishes to establish friendship with you."'

Te sādhūti paṭissuṇitvā gantvā bhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā bhuttapātarāsā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vandiṃsu. Rājā “kahaṃ bhaṇe tumhe ettake ime divase na dissathā”ti pucchi. Te sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā – “sādhu, tātā, tumhe nissāya mayā majjhimappadese rājā mitto laddho”ti attamano ahosi. Aparabhāge rājagahavāsinopi vāṇijā takkasīlaṃ agamaṃsu. Te paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgate pukkusāti rājā “kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchitvā “rājagahato”ti sutvā “mayhaṃ sahāyassa nagarato āgatā tumhe”ti. Āma devāti. Ārogyaṃ me sahāyassāti ārogyaṃ pucchitvā “ajja paṭṭhāya ye mayhaṃ sahāyassa nagarato jaṅghasatthena vā sakaṭasatthena vā vāṇijā āgacchanti, sabbesaṃ mama visayaṃ paviṭṭhakālato [P 5.0035] paṭṭhāya vasanagehāni, rājakoṭṭhāgārato nivāpañca dentu, suṅkaṃ vissajjentu, kiñci upaddavaṃ mā karontū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Bimbisāropi attano nagare tatheva bheriṃ carāpesi.

They assented, saying, 'Very well.' Having gone and stored their goods, and after eating their morning meal, they approached the king and paid homage. The king asked, 'Friends, where have you been? You have not been seen for all these days.' They told him the whole account. The king was pleased at heart and said, 'Excellent, dears! Through you, I have gained a royal friend in the Middle Country.' At a later time, merchants from Rājagaha also went to Takkasīlā. When they arrived with their gifts, King Pukkusāti asked, 'From where have you come?' Hearing 'From Rājagaha,' he said, 'Have you come from the city of my friend?' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' they replied. He inquired about his friend's health and then had a drum beaten to proclaim: 'From this day forward, for any merchants who come from my friend's city, whether in a caravan on foot or a caravan of carts, from the time they enter my domain, let them be given lodging and rations from the royal storehouse, let their tax be waived, and let no harm be done to them.' King Bimbisāra also had a similar proclamation beaten by drum in his own city.

Atha bimbisāro pukkusātissa paṇṇaṃ pahiṇi – “paccantadese nāma maṇimuttādīni ratanāni uppajjanti, yaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyassa rajje dassanīyaṃ vā savanīyaṃ vā ratanaṃ uppajjati, tattha me mā maccharāyatū”ti. Pukkusātipi – “majjhimadeso nāma mahājanapado, yaṃ tattha evarūpaṃ ratanaṃ uppajjati, tattha me sahāyo mā maccharāyatū”ti paṭipaṇṇaṃ pahiṇi. Evaṃ te gacchante gacchante kāle aññamaññaṃ adisvāpi daḷhamittā ahesuṃ.

Then Bimbisāra sent a letter to Pukkusāti: 'In the border country, gems such as jewels and pearls arise. Whatever gem worthy of seeing or hearing arises in my friend's kingdom, may he not be stingy towards me.' Pukkusāti also sent a return letter: 'The Middle Country is a great realm. If any such gem arises there, may my friend not be stingy towards me.' Thus, as time went on, though they had never seen each other, they became firm friends.

Evaṃ [M 4.0196] tesaṃ katikaṃ katvā vasantānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ pukkusātissa paṇṇākāro uppajji. Rājā kira aṭṭha pañcavaṇṇe anagghakambale labhi. So – “atisundarā ime kambalā, ahaṃ sahāyassa pesissāmī”ti lākhāguḷamatte aṭṭha sārakaraṇḍake likhāpetvā tesu te kambale pakkhipitvā lākhāya vaṭṭāpetvā setavatthena veṭhetvā samugge pakkhipitvā vatthena veṭhetvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā “mayhaṃ sahāyassa dethā”ti amacce pesesi. Sāsanañca adāsi – “ayaṃ paṇṇākāro nagaramajjhe amaccādiparivutena daṭṭhabbo”ti. Te gantvā bimbisārassa adaṃsu.

While they were living thus, having made this agreement, a gift arose first for Pukkusāti. It seems the king obtained eight priceless blankets of five colors. He thought, 'These blankets are exceedingly beautiful; I shall send them to my friend.' He had eight heartwood boxes, each the size of a lac-ball, turned on a lathe. He placed those blankets inside them, sealed them with lac, wrapped them in white cloth, placed them in a casket, wrapped it in cloth, and stamped it with the royal seal. Saying, 'Give these to my friend,' he dispatched his ministers. He also gave this instruction: 'This gift is to be inspected in the middle of the city, with the king surrounded by his ministers and retinue.' They went and gave them to Bimbisāra.

So [V 4.0207] sāsanaṃ sutvā amaccādayo sannipatantūti bheriṃ carāpetvā nagaramajjhe amaccādiparivuto setacchattena dhāriyamānena pallaṅkavare nisinno lañchanaṃ bhinditvā vatthaṃ apanetvā samuggaṃ vivaritvā anto bhaṇḍikaṃ muñcitvā lākhāguḷe disvā “mayhaṃ sahāyo pukkusāti ‘jutavittako me sahāyo’ti maññamāno maññe imaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pahiṇī”ti ekaṃ guḷaṃ gahetvā hatthena [P 5.0036] vaṭṭetvā tulayantova anto dussabhaṇḍikaṃ atthīti aññāsi. Atha naṃ pallaṅkapāde paharitvā tāvadeva lākhā paripati, so nakhena karaṇḍakaṃ vivaritvā anto kambalaratanaṃ disvā itarepi vivarāpesi, sabbepi kambalā ahesuṃ. Atha ne pattharāpesi, te vaṇṇasampannā phassasampannā dīghato soḷasahatthā tiriyaṃ aṭṭhahatthā ahesuṃ. Mahājano disvā aṅguliyo poṭhesi, celukkhepaṃ akāsi, – “amhākaṃ rañño adiṭṭhasahāyo pukkusāti adisvāva evarūpaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi, yuttaṃ evarūpaṃ mittaṃ kātu”nti attamano ahosi. Rājā ekamekaṃ kambalaṃ agghāpesi, sabbe anagghā ahesuṃ. Tesu cattāro sammāsambuddhassa pesesi, cattāro attano ghare akāsi. Tato cintesi – “pacchā pesentena paṭhamaṃ pesitapaṇṇākārato atirekaṃ pesetuṃ vaṭṭati, sahāyena ca me anaggho paṇṇākāro pesito, kiṃ nu kho pesemī”ti?

Having heard the message, he had the drum beaten, saying, 'Let the ministers and others assemble!' Then, in the middle of the city, surrounded by ministers and others, seated on a splendid couch with a white parasol being held over him, he broke the seal, removed the wrapping cloth, opened the casket, and untied the bundle inside. Seeing the lac balls, he thought, 'My friend Pukkusāti, thinking, "My friend is fond of playing dice," has, I suppose, sent this gift.' Taking one ball, he rolled it in his hand, and as if weighing it, he knew from its lack of weight that there was a cloth bundle inside. Then, striking it against the foot of the couch, the lac immediately fell away. He opened the small container with his fingernail and, seeing a precious blanket inside, had the others opened as well; all were blankets. Then he had them spread out. They were splendid in color and texture, sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width. Seeing this, the great crowd snapped their fingers and tossed up their garments, saying, 'Our king’s unseen friend, Pukkusāti, without ever having seen him, has sent such a gift. It is fitting to make a friend of such a person!' The great crowd was delighted. The king had each blanket appraised, and all were priceless. Of these, he sent four to the Perfectly Enlightened One and made use of four in his own palace. Then he reflected: 'One who sends a gift later ought to send something that exceeds the gift sent first. A priceless gift has been sent by my friend. What, I wonder, should I send?'

Kiṃ pana rājagahe tato adhikaṃ ratanaṃ natthīti? No natthi, mahāpuñño rājā, apica kho panassa sotāpannakālato paṭṭhāya ṭhapetvā tīṇi ratanāni aññaṃ ratanaṃ somanassaṃ janetuṃ samatthaṃ nāma natthi[M 4.0197]. So ratanaṃ vicinituṃ āraddho – ratanaṃ nāma saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha aviññāṇakaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādi, saviññāṇakaṃ indriyabaddhaṃ. Aviññāṇakaṃ saviññāṇakasseva alaṅkārādivasena paribhogaṃ hoti, iti imesu dvīsu ratanesu saviññāṇakaṃ seṭṭhaṃ. Saviññāṇakampi duvidhaṃ tiracchānaratanaṃ manussaratananti. Tattha tiracchānaratanaṃ hatthiassaratanaṃ, tampi manussānaṃ upabhogatthameva nibbattati[P 5.0037], iti imesupi dvīsu manussaratanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ. Manussaratanampi duvidhaṃ itthiratanaṃ purisaratananti. Tattha cakkavattino rañño uppannaṃ itthiratanampi purisasseva upabhogaṃ. Iti imesupi dvīsu purisaratanameva seṭṭhaṃ.

Is it then that in Rājagaha there is no jewel more excellent than that? It is not that there is none; there certainly is, for the king is of great merit. However, for him, from the time he became a stream-enterer, setting aside the Three Jewels, there was no other jewel whatsoever capable of generating mental joy. He began to select a jewel. A jewel is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. Among them, the inanimate are gold, silver, and the like; the animate are those bound by the sense faculties. The inanimate is for the use of the animate, by way of adornments and so forth. Thus, between these two jewels, the animate is superior. The animate jewel is also of two kinds: the animal-jewel and the human-jewel. Among them, the animal-jewel, such as the elephant-jewel and the horse-jewel, also arises only for the use of humans. Thus, between these two, the human-jewel is superior. The human-jewel is also of two kinds: the woman-jewel and the man-jewel. Among them, even the woman-jewel that arises for a wheel-turning king is for the use of the man. Thus, between these two, the man-jewel is indeed superior.

Purisaratanampi duvidhaṃ agāriyaratanaṃ anagāriyaratanañca. Tattha agāriyaratanesupi cakkavattirājā ajja pabbajitasāmaṇeraṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandati, iti imesupi dvīsu anagāriyaratanameva [V 4.0208] seṭṭhaṃ. Anagāriyaratanampi duvidhaṃ sekkharatanañca asekkharatanañca. Tattha satasahassampi sekkhānaṃ asekkhassa padesaṃ na pāpuṇāti, iti imesupi dvīsu asekkharatanameva seṭṭhaṃ. Tampi duvidhaṃ buddharatanaṃ sāvakaratananti. Tattha satasahassampi sāvakaratanānaṃ buddharatanassa padesaṃ na pāpuṇāti, iti imesupi dvīsū buddharatanameva seṭṭhaṃ.

The man-jewel is also of two kinds: the householder-jewel and the monastic-jewel. Among these, even a wheel-turning king, a householder-jewel, today venerates a newly ordained novice with the five-point prostration. Thus, between these two, the monastic-jewel is indeed supreme. The monastic-jewel is also of two kinds: the jewel of a trainee and the jewel of an adept. Among these, even a hundred thousand trainees do not attain a fraction of an adept. Thus, between these two, the jewel of the adept is indeed supreme. That too is of two kinds: the Buddha-jewel and the disciple-jewel. Among these, even a hundred thousand disciple-jewels do not attain a fraction of the Buddha-jewel. Thus, between these two, the Buddha-jewel is indeed supreme.

Buddharatanampi duvidhaṃ paccekabuddharatanaṃ sabbaññubuddharatananti. Tattha satasahassampi paccekabuddhānaṃ sabbaññubuddhassa padesaṃ na pāpuṇāti, iti imesupi dvīsu sabbaññubuddharatanaṃyeva seṭṭhaṃ. Sadevakasmiñhi loke buddharatanasamaṃ ratanaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā asadisameva ratanaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyassa pesessāmīti cintetvā takkasīlavāsino pucchi – “tātā tumhākaṃ janapade buddho dhammo saṅghoti imāni tīṇi ratanāni dissantī”ti. Ghosopi so mahārāja tāva tattha natthi, dassanaṃ pana kutoti.

The Buddha-jewel is also of two kinds: the Paccekabuddha-jewel and the Omniscient-Buddha-jewel. Among these, even a hundred thousand Paccekabuddhas do not attain a fraction of the Omniscient Buddha. Thus, between these two, the Omniscient-Buddha-jewel is indeed supreme. Indeed, in the world with its gods, there is no jewel whatsoever equal to the Buddha-jewel. Therefore, thinking, 'I shall send an incomparable jewel to my friend,' he asked the residents of Takkasīla, 'My dears, in your country, are these Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha—to be seen?' 'Great King, even the sound of their names does not yet exist there; whence, then, could there be the seeing of them?'

“Sundaraṃ tātā”ti rājā tuṭṭho cintesi – “sakkā bhaveyya janasaṅgahatthāya mayhaṃ sahāyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ pesetuṃ, buddhā pana [P 5.0038] paccantimesu janapadesu na aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapenti. Tasmā satthārā gantuṃ na sakkā. Sāriputtamoggallānādayo mahāsāvake pesetuṃ sakkā bhaveyya. Mayā [M 4.0198] pana ‘therā paccante vasantī’ti sutvāpi manusse pesetvā te attano samīpaṃ āṇāpetvā upaṭṭhātumeva yuttaṃ. Tasmā na therehipi sakkā gantuṃ. Yena panākārena sāsane pesite satthā ca mahāsāvakā ca gatā viya honti, tenākārena sāsanaṃ pahiṇissāmī”ti. Cintetvā caturatanāyāmaṃ vidatthimattaputhulaṃ nātitanuṃ nātibahalaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ kārāpetvā “tattha ajja akkharāni likhissāmī”ti. Pātova sīsaṃ nhāyitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya bhuttapātarāso apanītagandhamālābharaṇo suvaṇṇasarakena jātihiṅgulikaṃ ādāya heṭṭhato paṭṭhāya dvārāni pidahanto pāsādamāruyha pubbadisāmukhaṃ sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā ākāsatale nisīditvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe akkharāni likhanto – “idha tathāgato loke uppanno arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā”ti. Buddhaguṇe tāva ekadesena likhi.

“Excellent, O ministers.” Thus, the delighted king thought: “For the purpose of gathering the people, it would be possible to send the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One to my friend's dwelling place. However, Buddhas do not cause the dawn to rise in the border provinces. Therefore, it is not possible for the Teacher to go. It might be possible to send the great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna. However, even having heard that ‘the elders dwell in the borderlands,’ it would only be fitting for me to send men to summon them to my presence and attend upon them. Therefore, it is not possible for the elders to go either. I shall send a message in such a way that, when the message is sent, it will be as if the Teacher and the great disciples have gone themselves.” Having thought thus, he had a golden plaque made, four cubits in length and a hand-span in width, neither too thin nor too thick, thinking, “Today I will inscribe letters upon it.” Early in the morning, having bathed his head and undertaken the Uposatha precepts, having eaten his morning meal and removed perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, he took pure vermilion with a golden cup. Starting from the lowest one, he closed the doors, ascended the palace, opened the lion-window facing the eastern direction, and, sitting in the open space, he began inscribing letters on the golden plaque: “Here, the Tathāgata has arisen in the world, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Trainer of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.” Thus, he first wrote a portion of the Buddha's qualities.

Tato “evaṃ dasa pāramiyo pūretvā tusitabhavanato cavitvā mātukucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi[V 4.0209], evaṃ lokavivaraṇaṃ ahosi, mātukucchiyaṃ vasamāne idaṃ nāma ahosi, agāramajjhe vasamāne idaṃ nāma ahosi, evaṃ mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto evaṃ mahāpadhānaṃ padahi. Evaṃ dukkarakārikaṃ katvā mahābodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha aparājitapallaṅke nisinno sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhi, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhantassa [P 5.0039] evaṃ lokavivaraṇaṃ ahosi. Sadevake loke aññaṃ evarūpaṃ ratanaṃ nāma natthīti.

After that, he wrote: “Thus, having fulfilled the ten perfections, he passed away from the Tusita realm and took conception in his mother's womb. Thus, the unveiling of the world occurred. While dwelling in his mother's womb, this particular miracle occurred. While living in the household, this particular splendor occurred. Thus, he went forth on the great renunciation. Thus, he undertook the great striving. Thus, having performed the difficult practice, he ascended to the seat of great awakening and, seated on the unconquered throne, he penetrated the knowledge of omniscience. For him who was penetrating the knowledge of omniscience, thus the unveiling of the world occurred. In the world with its devas, there is no other such jewel.”

Yaṃkiñci vittaṃ idha vā huraṃ vā,

Saggesu vā yaṃ ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ;

Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatena,

Idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ;

Etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti. (khu. pā. 6.3; su. ni. 226) –

He wrote: “Whatever pleasing and precious jewel there is, here in the human realm or in the realms of nāgas and garuḍas, or in the celestial realms, there is none equal to the Tathāgata. This too is the excellent jewel in the Buddha. By this truth, may there be well-being!”

Evaṃ ekadesena buddhaguṇepi likhitvā dutiyaṃ dhammaratanaṃ thomento – “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo…pe… paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā…pe… ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti. “Satthārā desitadhammo nāma evarūpo ca evarūpo cā”ti sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiye ekadesena likhitvā –

Thus, having written in part about the qualities of the Buddha, while praising the second jewel, the Dhamma, he wrote: “Well-expounded by the Blessed One is the Dhamma… to be realized for oneself by the wise.” And: “The four foundations of mindfulness… the noble eightfold path.” Thus, having written in part about the thirty-seven factors of awakening, saying, “The Dhamma taught by the Teacher is of such and such a nature”—

“Yaṃ [M 4.0199] buddhaseṭṭho parivaṇṇayī suciṃ,

Samādhimānantarikaññamāhu;

Samādhinā tena samo na vijjati,

Idampi dhamme ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ;

Etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti. (khu. pā. 6.5; su. ni. 228) –

He wrote: “That pure concentration which the noblest of Buddhas praised, they call the concentration that gives immediate results. No other concentration is equal to that one. This too is the excellent jewel in the Dhamma. By this truth, may there be well-being!”

Evaṃ ekadesena dhammaguṇe likhitvā tatiyaṃ saṅgharatanaṃ thomento – “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho…pe… puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti. “Kulaputtā nāma satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā evaṃ nikkhamitvā pabbajanti, keci setacchattaṃ pahāya pabbajanti, keci uparajjaṃ, keci senāpatiṭṭhānādīni pahāya pabbajanti. Pabbajitvā ca pana imañca paṭipattiṃ pūrentī”ti cūḷasīlamajjhimasīlamahāsīlādīni [V 4.0210] ekadesena likhitvā chadvārasaṃvaraṃ satisampajaññaṃ catupaccayasantosaṃ navavidhaṃ [P 5.0040] senāsanaṃ, nīvaraṇappahānaṃ parikammaṃ jhānābhiññā aṭṭhatiṃsa kammaṭṭhānāni yāva āsavakkhayā ekadesena likhi, soḷasavidhaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ vitthāreneva likhitvā “satthu sāvakasaṅgho nāma evarūpehi ca guṇehi samannāgato.

Thus, having written in part about the qualities of the Dhamma, while praising the third jewel, the Sangha, he wrote: “The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well… an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” He continued: “Clansmen, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma talk, go forth and renounce thus: some renounce by abandoning a white parasol; some, the position of viceroy; some, positions such as army commander. And having renounced, they fulfill this practice.” Thus, he wrote in part about the minor, middle, and major precepts, restraint of the six sense doors, mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment with the four requisites, the nine kinds of lodgings, the abandoning of the hindrances, the preliminary practice, the jhānas and supernormal knowledges, and the thirty-eight meditation subjects up to the destruction of the corruptions. He wrote in detail about the sixteen-fold meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, and concluded: “The Sangha of the Teacher's disciples is endowed with such qualities.”

Ye puggalā aṭṭhasataṃ pasaṭṭhā,

Cattāri etāni yugāni honti;

Te dakkhiṇeyyā sugatassa sāvakā,

Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni;

Idampi saṅghe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ,

Etena saccena suvatthi hotū”ti. (khu. pā. 6.6; su. ni. 229) –

He wrote: “Those eight individuals who are praised by the good, they form four pairs. They are the disciples of the Sugata, worthy of offerings. Gifts given to them are of great fruit. This too is the excellent jewel in the Sangha. By this truth, may there be well-being!”

Evaṃ ekadesena saṅghaguṇe likhitvā – “bhagavato sāsanaṃ svākkhātaṃ niyyānikaṃ, sace mayhaṃ sahāyo sakkoti, nikkhamitvā pabbajatū”ti likhitvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ saṃharitvā sukhumakambalena veṭhetvā sārasamugge pakkhipitvā taṃ samuggaṃ suvaṇṇamaye, suvaṇṇamayaṃ, rajatamaye rajatamayaṃ maṇimaye, maṇimayaṃ pavāḷamaye, pavāḷamayaṃ lohitaṅkamaye, lohitaṅkamayaṃ masāragallamaye, masāragallamayaṃ phalikamaye, phalikamayaṃ dantamaye, dantamayaṃ sabbaratanamaye, sabbaratanamayaṃ kilañjamaye, kilañjamayaṃ samuggaṃ sārakaraṇḍake ṭhapesi.

Thus, having written in part about the qualities of the Sangha, he wrote: “The Blessed One's Dispensation is well-proclaimed and leads to liberation. If my friend is able, let him go forth and renounce.” Having written this, he rolled up the golden plaque, wrapped it in a fine woolen cloth, and placed it in a sandalwood casket. He then placed that casket into a golden one, the golden one into a silver one, the silver one into a jeweled one, the jeweled one into a coral one, the coral one into a ruby one, the ruby one into a cat's-eye one, the cat's-eye one into a crystal one, the crystal one into an ivory one, the ivory one into a casket of all jewels, and the casket of all jewels into a woven one. He then placed that woven casket into a casket of heartwood.

Puna [M 4.0200] sārakaraṇḍakaṃ suvaṇṇakaraṇḍaketi purimanayeneva haritvā sabbaratanamayaṃ karaṇḍakaṃ kilañjamaye karaṇḍake ṭhapesi. Tato kilañjamayaṃ karaṇḍakaṃ sāramayapeḷāyāti puna vuttanayeneva haritvā sabbaratanamayaṃ peḷaṃ kilañjamayapeḷāya ṭhapetvā bahi vatthena veṭhetvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā amacce āṇāpesi – “mama āṇāpavattiṭṭhāne maggaṃ alaṅkārāpetha maggo aṭṭhusabhavitthato hotu, catuusabhaṭṭhānaṃ sodhitamattakameva [P 5.0041] hotu, majjhe catuusabhaṃ rājānubhāvena paṭiyādethā”ti. Tato maṅgalahatthiṃ alaṅkārāpetvā tassa upari pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā nagaravīthiyo sittasammaṭṭhā samussitaddhajapaṭākā kadalipuṇṇaghaṭagandhadhūmapupphādīhi [V 4.0211] suppaṭimaṇḍitā kāretvā “attano attano visayappadese evarūpaṃ pūjaṃ kārentū”ti antarabhogikānaṃ javanadūte pesetvā sayaṃ sabbālaṅkārena alaṅkaritvā – “sabbatāḷāvacarasammissabalakāyaparivuto paṇṇākāraṃ pesemī”ti attano visayapariyantaṃ gantvā amaccassa mukhasāsanaṃ adāsi – “tāta mayhaṃ sahāyo pukkusāti imaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ paṭicchanto orodhamajjhe apaṭicchitvā pāsādaṃ āruyha paṭicchatū”ti. Evaṃ sāsanaṃ datvā paccantadesaṃ satthā gacchatīti pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā nivatti. Antarabhogikā teneva niyāmena maggaṃ paṭiyādetvā paṇṇākāraṃ nayiṃsu.

Again, following the previous method, he placed the all-jeweled casket inside a reed casket. Then he placed the reed casket inside a sandalwood chest. Again, following the method described, he placed the all-jeweled chest inside a reed chest, wrapped it on the outside with cloth, sealed it with the royal seal, and commanded the ministers: 'In the place where my authority extends, decorate the road. Let the road be eight usabhas in width. Let the four-usabha area be merely cleared. In the middle, prepare the four-usabha area by royal power.' Then, having had the state elephant adorned, having had a palanquin prepared upon it, and having had a white parasol raised, he had the city streets sprinkled and swept, and well-adorned with raised banners and flags, banana trees, full water pots, perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth. He sent swift messengers to the provincial governors, saying: 'Let them perform such worship, each in his own territory.' Having adorned himself with all his ornaments, and thinking, 'Surrounded by my entire army, complete with musicians, I am sending this gift,' he went to the border of his domain and gave an oral message to his ministers: 'Sirs, when my friend, King Pukkusāti, receives this gift, let him not receive it in the midst of the harem, but let him ascend to the palace and receive it.' Having given this message, and having reached the border region, he said, 'Go,' and after paying homage with the five-pointed prostration, he turned back. The provincial governors prepared the road according to that instruction and conveyed the gift.

Pukkusātipi attano rajjasīmato paṭṭhāya teneva niyāmena maggaṃ paṭiyādetvā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā paṇṇākārassa paccuggamanaṃ akāsi. Paṇṇākāro takkasīlaṃ pāpuṇanto uposathadivase pāpuṇi, paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā gataamaccopi rañño vuttasāsanaṃ ārocesi. Rājā taṃ sutvā paṇṇākārena saddhiṃ āgatānaṃ kattabbakiccaṃ vicāretvā paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya pāsādaṃ āruyha “mā idha koci pavisatū”ti dvāre ārakkhaṃ kāretvā sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā paṇṇākāraṃ uccāsane ṭhapetvā sayaṃ nīcāsane nisinno lañchanaṃ bhinditvā nivāsanaṃ apanetvā kilañjapeḷato paṭṭhāya anupubbena vivaranto sāramayaṃ samuggaṃ disvā cintesi – “mahāparihāro nāyaṃ aññassa ratanassa bhavissati, addhā majjhimadese sotabbayuttakaṃ ratanaṃ uppanna”nti. Atha taṃ samuggaṃ vivaritvā rājalañchanaṃ bhinditvā sukhumakambalaṃ ubhato viyūhitvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ addasa.

King Pukkusāti also, starting from the border of his own kingdom, had the road prepared in that same manner, had the city adorned, and went out to meet the gift. The gift arrived at Takkasilā on the Uposatha day. The ministers who had come with the gift also related the king's spoken message. Having heard it, the king arranged the necessary duties for those who had come with the gift. Then, taking the gift, he ascended to the palace, and having had a guard placed at the door, saying, 'Let no one enter here,' he opened the lion window, placed the gift on a high seat, and sat himself on a low seat. He broke the seal, removed the outer wrapping, and beginning from the reed chest, opening them in succession, he saw the sandalwood casket and thought: 'This great layered protection would not be for any other jewel. Surely, a jewel worthy of being heard of has arisen in the Middle Country.' Then, opening that casket, breaking the royal seal, he pushed aside the fine blanket from both sides and saw a golden plate.

So [M 4.0201] taṃ pasāretvā – “manāpāni [P 5.0042] vata akkharāni samasīsāni samapantīni caturassānī”tiādito paṭṭhāya vācetuṃ ārabhi. Tassa – “idha tathāgato loke uppanno”ti buddhaguṇe vācentassa balavasomanassaṃ uppajji, navanavutilomakūpasahassāni uddhaggalomāni ahesuṃ. Attano ṭhitabhāvaṃ vā nisinnabhāvaṃ vā na jānāti. Athassa – “kappakoṭisatasahassehipi etaṃ dullabhasāsanaṃ sahāyaṃ nissāya sotuṃ labhāmī”ti bhiyyo balavapīti udapādi. So hi upari vācetuṃ asakkonto yāva pītivegapassaddhiyā nisīditvā parato – “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”ti dhammaguṇe ārabhi. Tatrāpissa tatheva ahosi. So puna yāva pītivegapassaddhiyā nisīditvā parato “suppaṭipanno”ti saṅghaguṇe ārabhi[V 4.0212]. Tatrāpissa tatheva ahosi. Atha sabbapariyante ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ vācetvā catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattesi, so jhānasukheneva vītināmesi. Añño koci daṭṭhuṃ na labhati, ekova cūḷupaṭṭhāko pavisati. Evaṃ addhamāsamattaṃ vītināmesi.

He unrolled it and, from the beginning, began to read, thinking: 'Indeed, the letters are pleasing, of even height, in even rows, and square!' As he was reading the virtues of the Buddha—'Here, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world'—strong mental joy arose in him; the hairs of his ninety thousand pores stood on end. He did not know whether he was standing or sitting. Then, thinking, 'Even in a hundred thousand crores of aeons, this teaching is difficult to obtain, yet through my friend I get to hear it,' an even stronger rapture arose in him. Unable to read further, he sat until the surge of rapture subsided, and then he began to read the virtues of the Dhamma: 'Well-expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One.' The same thing happened to him then as well. Again, he sat until the surge of rapture subsided and then began to read the virtues of the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well.' The same thing happened to him then as well. Then, at the very end, having read the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, he brought forth the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. He passed the time solely in the bliss of jhāna. No one else was able to see him; only one young attendant would enter. In this way, he passed about half a month.

Nāgarā rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā ukkuṭṭhiṃ akaṃsu “paṇṇākāraṃ paṭicchitadivasato paṭṭhāya baladassanaṃ vā nāṭakadassanaṃ vā natthi, vinicchayadānaṃ natthi, rājā sahāyena pahitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ yassicchati tassa dassetu, rājāno nāma ekaccassa paṇṇākāravasenapi vañcetvā rajjaṃ attano kātuṃ vāyamanti. Kiṃ nāma amhākaṃ rājā karotī”ti? Rājā ukkuṭṭhisaddaṃ sutvā – “rajjaṃ nu kho dhāremi, udāhu [P 5.0043] satthāra”nti cintesi. Athassa etadahosi – “rajjakāritaattabhāvo nāma neva gaṇakena, na gaṇakamahāmattena gaṇetuṃ sakko. Satthusāsanaṃ dhāressāmī”ti sayane ṭhapitaṃ asiṃ gahetvā kese chinditvā sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā – “etaṃ gahetvā rajjaṃ kārethā”ti saddhiṃ cūḷāmaṇinā kesakalāpaṃ parisamajjhe pātesi, mahājano taṃ ukkhipitvā – “sahāyakasantikā laddhapaṇṇākārā nāma rājāno tumhādisā honti devā”ti ekappahāreneva viravi. Raññopi dvaṅgulamattaṃ kesamassu ahosi. Bodhisattassa pabbajjāsadisameva kira jātaṃ.

The citizens gathered in the royal courtyard and raised an outcry: 'From the day the gift was received, there has been no military review, no theatrical performances, and no dispensing of justice! Let the king return to his friend the gift that was sent! For some kings try to seize a kingdom for themselves by deceiving with a gift. What is our king doing?' Hearing the sound of the outcry, the king thought: 'Should I hold to the kingdom, or should I hold to the Teacher?' Then this occurred to him: 'The number of lifetimes one has ruled a kingdom cannot be counted even by an accountant or a chief accountant-minister. I will uphold the Teacher's Dispensation.' Taking the sword that was placed on his bed, he cut his hair, opened the lion window, and dropped the top-knot of hair together with the crest-jewel into the midst of the assembly, saying: 'Take this and rule the kingdom!' The great crowd lifted it up and wailed with a single voice, saying: 'O Lord, are kings who receive gifts from a friend supposed to be like you?' The king's hair and beard were about two fingers' length. It is said that his going forth was just like that of the Bodhisatta.

Tato [M 4.0202] cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ pesetvā antarāpaṇā dve kāsāyavatthāni mattikāpattañca āharāpetvā – “ye loke arahanto, te uddissa mayhaṃ pabbajjā”ti satthāraṃ uddissa ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ vāmaaṃsakūṭe katvā kattaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā – “sobhati nu kho me pabbajjā no vā”ti mahātale katipayavāre aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā – “sobhati me pabbajjā”ti dvāraṃ vivaritvā pāsādā otari. Otarantaṃ pana naṃ tīsu dvāresu ṭhitanāṭakādīni disvāpi na sañjāniṃsu. “Eko paccekabuddho amhākaṃ rañño dhammakathaṃ kathetuṃ āgato”ti kira cintayiṃsu. Uparipāsādaṃ pana āruyha rañño ṭhitanisinnaṭṭhānāni disvā rājā gatoti ñatvā samuddamajjhe osīdamānāya nāvāya jano viya ekappahāreneva viraviṃsu. Kulaputtaṃ bhūmitalaṃ otiṇṇamattaṃ aṭṭhārasaseniyo sabbe nāgarā balakāyā ca parivāretvā mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Amaccāpi taṃ etadavocuṃ – “deva majjhimadesarājāno nāma bahumāyā, sāsanaṃ pesetvā buddharatanaṃ nāma loke uppannaṃ vā no vāti ñatvā gamissatha[P 5.0044], nivattatha [V 4.0213] devā”ti. Saddahāmahaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyakassa, tassa mayā saddhiṃ dvejjhavacanaṃ nāma natthi, tiṭṭhatha tumheti. Te anugacchantiyeva.

Then, having sent a young attendant, he had two saffron-colored robes and a clay bowl brought from the bazaar.
