With the thought, ‘May my going forth be dedicated to those who are Arahants in the world,’ and dedicating it to the Teacher, he put on one saffron robe as a lower garment and draped the other over himself, slung the bowl over his left shoulder, took a staff, and thought, ‘Does my going forth look proper or not?’ After walking back and forth a few times on the great terrace, he thought, ‘My going forth looks proper.’ He then opened the door and descended from the palace. As he was descending, the dancers and others stationed at the three gates saw him but did not recognize him. It is said they thought, ‘A Paccekabuddha has come to preach the Dhamma to our king.’ But when they went up to the upper palace and saw the places where the king used to stand and sit, they knew the king was gone and cried out all at once, like people on a ship sinking in the middle of the ocean. As soon as the nobleman descended to the ground, the eighteen divisions of the army, all the citizens, and the troops surrounded him and raised a great cry. The ministers also said this to him: ‘Your Majesty, the kings of the Middle Country are very deceitful. You should first send a message to find out whether the Buddha-jewel has arisen in the world or not, and only then go. Please turn back, Your Majesty!’ He replied, ‘I trust the word of my friend. Between him and me, there is no such thing as duplicitous speech. You all stay here.’ But they continued to follow him.

Kulaputto kattaradaṇḍena lekhaṃ katvā – “idaṃ rajjaṃ kassā”ti āha? Tumhākaṃ devāti. Yo imaṃ lekhaṃ antaraṃ karoti, rājāṇāya kāretabboti. Mahājanakajātake bodhisattena katalekhaṃ sīvalidevī antaraṃ kātuṃ avisahantī vivattamānā agamāsi. Tassā gatamaggena mahājano agamāsi. Taṃ pana lekhaṃ mahājano antaraṃ kātuṃ na visahi, lekhaṃ ussīsakaṃ katvā vivattamānā viraviṃsu. Kulaputto “ayaṃ me gataṭṭhāne dantakaṭṭhaṃ vā mukhodakaṃ vā dassatī”ti antamaso ekaceṭakampi aggahetvā pakkāmi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “mama satthā ca mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā ekakova pabbajito”ti ekakova agamāsi. “Satthu lajjāmī”ti ca – “satthā kira me pabbajitvā yānaṃ nāruḷho”ti ca antamaso ekapaṭalikampi upāhanaṃ nāruhi, paṇṇacchattakampi na dhāresi. Mahājano rukkhapākāraṭṭālakādīni āruyha esa amhākaṃ rājā gacchatīti olokesi. Kulaputto – “dūraṃ gantabbaṃ, na sakkā ekena maggo nittharitu”nti ekaṃ satthavāhaṃ anubandhi. Sukhumālassa kulaputtassa kaṭhinatattāya [M 4.0203] pathaviyā gachantassa pādatalesu phoṭā uṭṭhahitvā bhijjanti, dukkhā vedanā uppajjanti. Satthavāhe khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā nisinne kulaputto maggā okkamma ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdati. Nisinnaṭṭhāne pādaparikammaṃ vā piṭṭhiparikammaṃ [P 5.0045] vā kattā nāma natthi, kulaputto ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā maggadarathakilamathapariḷāhaṃ vikkhambhetvā jhānaratiyā vītināmeti.

The nobleman drew a line with his staff and asked, ‘To whom does this kingdom belong?’ ‘To you, Your Majesty,’ they replied. ‘Whoever crosses this line is to be dealt with by royal command.’ In the Mahājanaka Jātaka, Queen Sīvalī, not daring to cross the line drawn by the Bodhisatta, turned away and departed. The great crowd followed the path she took. But the great crowd did not dare to cross that line; making the line their head-rest, they turned back and lamented. The nobleman departed without taking even a single servant boy, thinking, ‘This person here would give me a tooth-stick or water for washing my face in the places I go.’ It is said he also had this thought: ‘My Teacher, having made the Great Renunciation, went forth all alone,’ and so he went all alone. And thinking, ‘I would be ashamed before the Teacher,’ and, ‘It is said my Teacher, after going forth, never rode in a vehicle,’ he did not even wear a single-soled sandal, nor did he carry a leaf sunshade. The great crowd climbed trees, ramparts, and watchtowers and looked on, thinking, ‘There goes our king.’ The nobleman, thinking, ‘The way is long; it is not possible to cross the path alone,’ followed a caravan. As the delicate nobleman walked on the hard and heated ground, blisters arose on the soles of his feet and burst, and painful feelings arose. When the caravan leader made camp and sat down, the nobleman stepped off the path and sat at the foot of a tree. In that place, there was no one to massage his feet or his back. The nobleman entered the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing and, suppressing the travel-fatigue, weariness, and burning torment, he passed the time in the delight of jhāna.

Punadivase uṭṭhite aruṇe sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā puna satthavāhaṃ anubandhati. Pātarāsakāle kulaputtassa pattaṃ gahetvā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ patte pakkhipitvā denti. Taṃ uttaṇḍulampi hoti kilinnampi samasakkharampi aloṇātiloṇampi, kulaputto pavisanaṭṭhānaṃ paccavekkhitvā amataṃ viya paribhuñjitvā etena niyāmena aṭṭhahi ūnakāni dve yojanasatāni gato. Jetavanadvārakoṭṭhakassa pana samīpena gacchantopi – “kahaṃ satthā vasatī”ti nāpucchi. Kasmā? Satthugāravena ceva rañño pesitasāsanavasena ca. Rañño hi – “idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”ti satthāraṃ rājagahe uppannaṃ viya katvā sāsanaṃ pesitaṃ, tasmā [V 4.0214] naṃ apucchitvāva pañcacattālīsayojanamattaṃ maggaṃ atikkanto. So sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya rājagahaṃ patvā satthā kahaṃ vasatīti pucchi. Kuto nu, bhante, āgatoti? Ito uttaratoti. Satthā tuyhaṃ āgatamagge ito pañcacattālīsayojanamatte sāvatthi nāma atthi, tattha vasatīti. Kulaputto cintesi – “idāni akālo na sakkā gantuṃ, ajja idheva vasitvā sve satthu santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Tato – “vikāle sampattapabbajitā kahaṃ vasantī”ti pucchi. Imāya kumbhakārasālāya, bhanteti. Atha so taṃ kumbhakāraṃ yācitvā tattha vāsatthāya pavisitvā nisīdi.

On the following day at dawn, after attending to his bodily needs, he again followed the caravan. At the time of the morning meal, they would take the nobleman's bowl, put hard and soft food into it, and give it to him. That food was sometimes undercooked, sometimes soggy, and sometimes mixed with gravel. The nobleman, reflecting on its destination in the body, partook of it as if it were ambrosia. In this way, he traveled two hundred yojanas less eight. Even while passing near the gatehouse of Jetavana, he did not ask, ‘Where does the Teacher dwell?’ Why not? Both out of reverence for the Teacher and because of the message sent by the king. For the king had sent the message making it seem as if the Teacher had arisen in Rājagaha, saying, ‘The Tathāgata has arisen here in the world.’ Therefore, without asking, he passed beyond it by a distance of forty-five yojanas. Reaching Rājagaha at sunset, he asked, ‘Where does the Teacher dwell?’ They asked him, ‘Venerable sir, from where have you come?’ ‘From the north of here.’ They replied, ‘On the path you have come, forty-five yojanas from here, there is a city named Sāvatthī. The Teacher dwells there.’ The nobleman thought, ‘It is now the wrong time; it is not possible to go. I will stay right here today and go to the Teacher’s presence tomorrow.’ Then he asked, ‘Where do renunciants who arrive at an untimely hour stay?’ ‘In this potter’s hall, venerable sir.’ Then, having requested permission from the potter, he entered there to stay for the night and sat down.

Bhagavāpi taṃdivasaṃ paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento pukkusātiṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ kulaputto sahāyena pesitaṃ sāsanamattakaṃ [P 5.0046] vācetvā atirekatiyojanasatikaṃ mahārajjaṃ pahāya maṃ uddissa pabbajitvā aṭṭhahi ūnakāni dve yojanasatāni atikkamma rājagahaṃ pāpuṇissati, mayi agacchante pana tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni appaṭivijjhitvā ekarattivāsena anāthakālakiriyaṃ karissati, mayi pana gate [M 4.0204] tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni paṭivijjhissati. Janasaṅgahatthāyeva pana mayā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūritā, karissāmi tassa saṅgaha”nti pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā muhuttaṃ attadarathakilamathaṃ paṭipassambhetvā – “kulaputto mayi gāravena dukkaraṃ akāsi, atirekayojanasataṃ rajjaṃ pahāya antamaso mukhadhovanadāyakampi ceṭakaṃ aggahetvā ekakova nikkhanto”ti sāriputtamahāmoggallānādīsu kañci anāmantetvā sayameva attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā ekakova nikkhanto. Gacchanto ca neva ākāse uppati, na pathaviṃ saṃkhipi, – “kulaputto mama lajjamāno hatthiassarathasuvaṇṇasivikādīsu ekayānepi anisīditvā antamaso ekapaṭalikaṃ upāhanampi anāruyha paṇṇacchattakampi aggahetvā nikkhanto, mayāpi padasāva gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pana cintetvā padasāva agamāsi.

The Blessed One, too, on that day, at dawn, surveying the world, saw Pukkusāti and thought: 'This clansman, having read just a message sent by his friend, has renounced a great kingdom of over three hundred yojanas and gone forth for my sake. Having traversed one hundred and ninety-two yojanas, he will reach Rājagaha. However, if I do not go, without realizing the three lower fruits of recluseship, he will die a protectorless death in one night's stay. But if I go, he will realize the three lower fruits of recluseship. Indeed, it is for the welfare of the people that I have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kappas in addition. I will render him assistance.' Having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, surrounded by the community of monks, he went for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, he entered the Perfumed Chamber. After calming his bodily fatigue for a moment, he thought: 'The clansman, out of reverence for me, has done a difficult thing. He has renounced a kingdom of over one hundred yojanas and gone forth alone, not even taking a servant boy to give him water for washing his face.' Without informing anyone among Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and others, taking his own bowl and robe, he went forth alone by himself. And while going, he neither flew up into the sky, nor did he contract the earth. He thought further: 'The clansman, out of modesty towards me, went forth without sitting on even one vehicle among elephants, horses, chariots, golden palanquins, and so on, without even wearing a single-layered sandal, and without taking even a palm-leaf umbrella. It is proper for me too to go on foot.' Having thought thus, he went on foot.

So asīti anubyañjanāni byāmappabhā bāttiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇānīti imaṃ buddhasiriṃ paṭicchādetvā valāhakapaṭicchanno puṇṇacando viya aññatarabhikkhuvesena gacchanto ekapacchābhatteneva pañcacattālīsa yojanāni atikkamma sūriyatthaṅgamalīvelāya kulaputte paviṭṭhamatteyeva [V 4.0215] taṃ kumbhakārasālaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena, pukkusāti, nāma kulaputto bhagavantaṃ uddissa saddhāya [P 5.0047] agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so tasmiṃ kumbhakārāvesane paṭhamaṃ vāsūpagato hotī”ti.

Concealing this splendor of a Buddha—the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide radiance, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—like the full moon concealed by a cloud-bank, he went in the guise of an unknown monk. Having traversed forty-five yojanas in the time after a single meal, he reached that potter's hall at the time of sunset, just as the clansman had entered. With reference to that, it was said: 'At that time, a clansman named Pukkusāti had, out of faith, gone forth from the household life into homelessness, dedicating it to the Blessed One. He was the first to have taken up lodging in that potter's workshop.'

Evaṃ gantvāpi pana bhagavā – “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti pasayha kumbhakārasālaṃ apavisitvā dvāre ṭhitova kulaputtaṃ okāsaṃ kārento sace te bhikkhūtiādimāha. Urundanti vivittaṃ asambādhaṃ. Viharatāyasmā yathāsukhanti yena yena iriyāpathena phāsu hoti, tena tena yathāsukhaṃ āyasmā viharatūti okāsaṃ akāsi. Atirekatiyojanasatañhi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito kulaputto parassa chaḍḍitapatitaṃ [M 4.0205] kumbhakārasālaṃ kiṃ aññassa sabrahmacārino maccharāyissati. Ekacce pana moghapurisā sāsane pabbajitvā āvāsamacchariyādīhi abhibhūtā attano vasanaṭṭhāne mayhaṃ kuṭi mayhaṃ pariveṇanti aññesaṃ avāsāya parakkamanti. Nisīdīti accantasukhumālo lokanātho devavimānasadisaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pahāya tattha tattha vippakiṇṇachārikāya bhinnabhājanatiṇapalāsakukkuṭasūkaravaccādisaṃkiliṭṭhāya saṅkāraṭṭhānasadisāya kumbhakārasālāya tiṇasanthāraṃ santharitvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā devavimānasadisaṃ dibbagandhasugandhaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā nisīdanto viya nisīdi.

Having gone there, the Blessed One, without forcibly entering the potter's hall saying, 'I am the Perfectly Enlightened One,' stood at the door and, making an opportunity for the clansman, said, 'If it is not inconvenient for you, monk,' and so on. 'Spacious' (urundaṃ) means secluded, not crowded. Pukkusāti gave permission, saying, 'Dwell, venerable sir, as is comfortable,' meaning, 'May the venerable one dwell comfortably in whatever posture is agreeable.' For would the clansman, who had gone forth having renounced a kingdom of over one hundred yojanas, be stingy towards another fellow in the holy life regarding a potter's hall discarded and abandoned by another? But some worthless men, having gone forth in the Dispensation, being overcome by stinginess regarding dwellings and so on, in their own dwelling place, saying 'my hut,' 'my monastic cell,' strive to prevent others from dwelling there. As for 'He sat down': the extremely delicate Lord of the World, having left the Perfumed Chamber which was like a celestial mansion, in that potter's hall which was like a rubbish heap, with ashes scattered here and there, defiled by broken pots, grass, leaves, chicken and pig excrement, and so on, spread out a grass mat, laid out his rag-robe, and sat down as if entering his Perfumed Chamber, which was like a celestial mansion fragrant with divine scents.

Iti bhagavāpi asambhinnamahāsammatavaṃse uppanno, kulaputtopi khattiyagabbhe vaḍḍhito. Bhagavāpi abhinīhārasampanno, kulaputtopi abhinīhārasampanno. Bhagavāpi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito, kulaputtopi. Bhagavāpi [P 5.0048] suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, kulaputtopi. Bhagavāpi samāpattilābhī, kulaputtopi. Iti dvepi khattiyā dvepi abhinīhārasampannā dvepi rājapabbajitā dvepi suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dvepi samāpattilābhino kumbhakārasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinnāti tehi kumbhakārasālā ativiya sobhati, dvīhi sīhādīhi paviṭṭhaguhādīhi āharitvā dīpetabbaṃ. Tesu pana dvīsu bhagavā – “sukhumālo ahaṃ paramasukhumālo ekapacchābhattena pañcacattālīsa yojanāni āgato, muhuttaṃ tāva sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā maggadarathaṃ paṭipassambhemī”ti cittampi anuppādetvā nisīdantova phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Kulaputtopi – “dvānavutiyojanasataṃ āgatomhi, muhuttaṃ tāva nipajjitvā maggadarathaṃ vinodemī”ti cittaṃ anuppādetvā nisīdamānova [V 4.0216] ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Idaṃ sandhāya atha kho bhagavā bahudeva rattintiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One was born in the unbroken lineage of Mahāsammata, and the clansman, too, was raised in the Khattiya caste. The Blessed One was endowed with aspiration, and the clansman, too, was endowed with aspiration. The Blessed One went forth, having renounced a kingdom, and the clansman, too. The Blessed One was of golden complexion, and the clansman, too. The Blessed One was an obtainer of attainments, and the clansman, too. Thus, both being Khattiyas, both endowed with aspiration, both having gone forth from kingship, both of golden complexion, and both obtainers of attainments, entered the potter's hall and sat down. Because of them, the potter's hall shone exceedingly; this splendor should be illustrated by the example of a cave entered by two lions. Of those two, the Blessed One, without even giving rise to the thought, 'I am delicate, extremely delicate. Having come forty-five yojanas in the time after a single meal, let me for a moment assume the lion's posture and calm this travel fatigue,' just while sitting, entered into the attainment of fruition. The clansman, too, without giving rise to the thought, 'I have come one hundred and ninety-two yojanas. Let me for a moment lie down and dispel this travel fatigue,' just while sitting, entered into the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. It was with reference to this that it was said: 'Then the Blessed One, for much of the night...' and so on.

Nanu ca bhagavā kulaputtassa dhammaṃ desessāmīti āgato, kasmā na desesīti? Kulaputtassa maggadaratho appaṭipassaddho, na sakkhissati dhammadesanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ, so tāvassa paṭipassambhatūti na desesi. Apare – “rājagahaṃ nāma ākiṇṇamanussaṃ avivittaṃ dasahi saddehi, so saddo diyaḍḍhayāmamattena sannisīdati, taṃ āgamento na desesī”ti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, brahmalokappamāṇampi hi saddaṃ bhagavā attano ānubhāvena [M 4.0206] vūpasametuṃ sakkoti, maggadarathavūpasamaṃ āgamentoyeva pana na desesi.

Did not the Blessed One come with the thought, 'I will teach the Dhamma to the clansman'? Why then did he not teach? The clansman's travel-weariness was not yet allayed; he would not be able to receive the Dhamma teaching. Thinking, 'Let his travel-weariness first subside,' he did not teach. Others say: 'The city of Rājagaha is crowded with people and not secluded from the ten kinds of sounds. That sound subsides only after a period of one and a half watches. Waiting for that subsidence, he did not teach.' That is not the reason. Indeed, the Blessed One is able to silence even a sound as vast as the Brahmā world by his own power. But in fact, it was only because he was waiting for the travel-weariness to subside that he did not teach.

Tattha bahudeva rattinti diyaḍḍhayāmamattaṃ. Etadahosīti bhagavā phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya suvaṇṇavimāne maṇisīhapañjaraṃ vivaranto viya pañcapasādappaṭimaṇḍitāni akkhīni ummīletvā olokesi, athassa hatthakukkuccapādakukkuccasīsakampanavirahitaṃ sunikhātaindakhīlaṃ viya niccalaṃ avibbhantaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭimaṃ viya nisinnaṃ kulaputtaṃ disvā etaṃ – “pāsādikaṃ kho”tiādi ahosi. Tattha pāsādikanti pasādāvahaṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ [P 5.0049] panetaṃ, pāsādikena iriyāpathena iriyati. Yathā iriyato iriyāpatho pāsādiko hoti, evaṃ iriyatīti ayamettha attho. Catūsu hi iriyāpathesu tayo iriyāpathā na sobhanti. Gacchantassa hi bhikkhuno hatthā calanti, pādā calanti, sīsaṃ calati, ṭhitassa kāyo thaddho hoti, nipannassāpi iriyāpatho amanāpo hoti, pacchābhatte pana divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cammakhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā sudhotahatthapādassa catusandhikapallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nipannasseva iriyāpatho sobhati. Ayañca kulaputto pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ appetvā nisīdi. Itissa iriyāpatheneva pasanno bhagavā – “pāsādikaṃ kho”ti parivitakkesi.

Herein, 'for much of the night' means for a period of one and a half watches. As for the passage 'this occurred to him,' the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of fruition, opened his eyes—adorned with the five sensitivities, like one opening a jeweled lion-window in a golden celestial mansion—and looked. Then he saw the clansman seated, free from restlessness of the hands, restlessness of the feet, and movement of the head; immovable like a well-planted city-post; unwavering, like a golden statue. Seeing him, this thought arose: 'How pleasing!' Herein, 'pleasing' means inspiring serenity. This is a neuter noun of state, meaning 'he comports himself with a pleasing posture.' The meaning here is that he comports himself in such a way that his posture is pleasing. For among the four postures, three are not graceful: when a monk is walking, his hands move, his feet move, and his head moves; when standing, his body is stiff; and the posture of one lying down is unpleasing to those who see it. But after the meal, having swept the day-resting place, spread a piece of leather, with hands and feet well-washed, the posture of one who sits with legs folded in the four-point cross-legged posture is alone graceful. And this clansman, having folded his legs cross-wise and entered the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, was seated. Thus, the Blessed One, pleased by his posture alone, reflected, 'How pleasing!'

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ puccheyyanti kasmā pucchati? Kiṃ bhagavā attānaṃ uddissa pabbajitabhāvaṃ na jānātīti? No na jānāti, apucchite pana kathā na patiṭṭhāti, apatiṭṭhitāya kathāya kathā na sañjāyatīti kathāpatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchi.

As to 'What if I were to question him?': why does he ask? Is it that the Blessed One does not know that this man has gone forth on his account? It is not that he does not know; he surely knows. However, without a question, a conversation is not established. When a conversation is not established, the talk does not proceed. Therefore, he asked for the purpose of establishing the conversation.

Disvā [V 4.0217] ca pana jāneyyāsīti tathāgataṃ buddhasiriyā virocantaṃ ayaṃ buddhoti sabbe jānanti. Anacchariyametaṃ jānanaṃ, buddhasiriṃ pana paṭicchādetvā aññatarapiṇḍapātikavesena caranto dujjāno hoti. Iccāyasmā, pukkusāti, “na jāneyya”nti sabhāvameva katheti. Tathā hi naṃ ekakumbhakārasālāya nisinnampi na jānāti.

As for 'But having seen him, you would know': when the Tathāgata is resplendent with the glory of a Buddha, everyone knows, 'This is the Buddha.' This recognition is not remarkable. But when, having concealed his Buddha-glory, he wanders in the guise of an ordinary alms-faring monk, he is difficult to know. Therefore, the venerable Pukkusāti, in saying, 'I would not know,' speaks according to his own true state. For that very reason, he did not recognize him even when he was seated in the one potter's shed.

Etadahosīti maggadarathassa vūpasamabhāvaṃ ñatvā ahosi. Evamāvusoti kulaputto sahāyena pesitaṃ sāsanamattaṃ vācetvā rajjaṃ [M 4.0207] pahāya pabbajamāno – “dasabalassa madhuradhammadesanaṃ sotuṃ labhissāmī”ti. Pabbajito, pabbajitvā [P 5.0050] ettakaṃ addhānaṃ āgacchanto – “dhammaṃ te bhikkhu desessāmī”ti padamattassa vattāraṃ nālattha, so “dhammaṃ te bhikkhu desessāmī”ti vuttaṃ kiṃ sakkaccaṃ na suṇissati. Pipāsitasoṇḍo viya hi pipāsitahatthī viya cāyaṃ, tasmā sakkaccaṃ savanaṃ paṭijānanto “evamāvuso”ti āha.

As for 'this occurred to him,' this thought occurred after he knew that the travel-weariness had subsided. As for 'So be it, friend,' the clansman, having read merely a message sent by his friend, renounced his kingdom and went forth, thinking, 'I shall get to hear the sweet Dhamma teaching of the One with Ten Powers.' Having gone forth and having come such a long distance, he had not found anyone who would say even the mere phrase, 'Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma.' So when it was said, 'Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma,' how could he not listen respectfully? Indeed, he is like a thirsty drunkard and like a thirsty elephant. Therefore, assenting to listen respectfully, he said, 'So be it, friend.'

343. Chadhāturo ayanti bhagavā kulaputtassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ akathetvā āditova arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ accantasuññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇameva ācikkhituṃ āraddho. Yassa hi pubbabhāgapaṭipadā aparisuddhā hoti, tassa paṭhamameva sīlasaṃvaraṃ indriyesu guttadvārataṃ bhojane mattaññutaṃ jāgariyānuyogaṃ satta saddhamme cattāri jhānānīti imaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhati. Yassa panesā parisuddhā, tassa taṃ akathetvā arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vipassanameva ācikkhati. Kulaputtassa ca pubbabhāgapaṭipadā parisuddhā. Tathā hi anena sāsanaṃ vācetvā pāsādavaragateneva ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattitaṃ, yadassa dvānavutiyojanasabhaṃ āgacchantassa yānakiccaṃ sādhesi, sāmaṇerasīlampissa paripuṇṇaṃ. Tasmā pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ akathetvā arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ accantasuññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇamevassa ācikkhituṃ āraddho.

343. As for 'This person consists of six elements,' the Blessed One, without teaching the clansman the preliminary practice, from the very beginning began to point out only the characteristic of insight—which is utter emptiness and the proximate cause of Arahantship. Indeed, for one whose preliminary practice is not purified, he first teaches this preliminary practice: restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven good qualities, and the four jhānas. But for one whose practice is purified, without teaching that, he teaches only insight, which is the proximate cause of Arahantship. And the clansman's preliminary practice was purified. For that very reason, having read the message, while still on his excellent palace, he had produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. And that jhāna accomplished the function of a vehicle for him as he traveled the one hundred and ninety-two yojanas; his novice's virtue was also complete. Therefore, without teaching the preliminary practice, he began to point out to him only the characteristic of insight, which is utter emptiness and the proximate cause of Arahantship.

Tattha chadhāturoti dhātuyo vijjamānā, puriso avijjamāno. Bhagavā hi katthaci vijjamānena avijjamānaṃ dasseti, katthaci avijjamānena vijjamānaṃ, katthaci vijjamānena vijjamānaṃ, katthaci avijjamānena avijjamānanti sabbāsave vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Idha pana vijjamānena avijjamānaṃ dassento evamāha. Sace hi bhagavā [P 5.0051] purisoti paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā [V 4.0218] dhātuyo icceva vatvā cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyya, kulaputto sandehaṃ kareyya, sammohaṃ āpajjeyya, desanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Tasmā tathāgato anupubbena purisoti paṇṇattiṃ pahāya “sattoti vā purisoti vā puggaloti vā paṇṇattimattameva, paramatthato satto nāma natthi, dhātumatteyeva cittaṃ ṭhapāpetvā tīṇi phalāni paṭivijjhāpessāmī”ti [M 4.0208] anaṅgaṇasutte (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) vuttabhāsantarakusalo tāya tāya bhāsāya sippaṃ uggaṇhāpento ācariyo viya evamāha.

Herein, regarding 'a person of six elements': the elements exist in the ultimate sense, but a person does not exist in the ultimate sense. For the Blessed One sometimes teaches what does not exist by means of what exists; sometimes what exists by means of what does not exist; sometimes what exists by means of what exists; and sometimes what does not exist by means of what does not exist. This should be elaborated only in the manner stated in the Sabbāsava Sutta. Here, however, teaching what does not exist by means of what exists, he spoke thus. For if the Blessed One, having dismissed the designation 'person,' had established the mind by speaking only of 'elements,' the clansman would have become doubtful, he would have fallen into confusion, and he would not have been able to accept the teaching. Therefore the Tathāgata, thinking: 'Gradually, having him abandon the designation "person"—for "a being," or "a person," or "an individual" is merely a designation; in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a being—and having made him establish his mind only on the mere elements, I will cause him to penetrate the three lower fruits,' and being skilled in other languages as stated in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, like a teacher who instructs in an art by means of that particular language, spoke thus.

Tattha cha dhātuyo assāti chadhāturo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tvaṃ purisoti sañjānāsi, so chadhātuko, na cettha paramatthato puriso atthi, purisoti pana paṇṇattimattamevāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Caturādhiṭṭhānoti ettha adhiṭṭhānaṃ vuccati patiṭṭhā, catupatiṭṭhānoti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – svāyaṃ bhikkhu puriso chadhāturo chaphassāyatano aṭṭhārasamanopavicāro, so ettova vivaṭṭitvā uttamasiddhibhūtaṃ arahattaṃ gaṇhamāno imesu catūsu ṭhānesu patiṭṭhāya gaṇhātīti caturādhiṭṭhānoti. Yattha ṭhitanti yesu adhiṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Maññassa vā nappavattantīti maññassa vā mānassa vā nappavattanti. Muni santoti vuccatīti khīṇāsavamuni upasanto nibbutoti vuccati. Paññaṃ nappamajjeyyāti arahattaphalapaññāya paṭivijjhanatthaṃ [P 5.0052] āditova samādhivipassanāpaññaṃ nappamajjeyya. Saccamanurakkheyyāti paramatthasaccassa nibbānassa sacchikiriyatthaṃ āditova vacīsaccaṃ rakkheyya. Cāgamanubrūheyyāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesapariccāgakaraṇatthaṃ āditova kilesapariccāgaṃ brūheyya. Santimeva so sikkheyyāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesavūpasamanatthaṃ āditova kilesavūpasamanaṃ sikkheyya. Iti paññādhiṭṭhānādīnaṃ adhigamatthāya imāni samathavipassanāpaññādīni pubbabhāgādhiṭṭhānāni vuttāni.

Herein, he is a 'person of six elements' (chadhāturo) because he has six elements. This is what is meant: That which you perceive as a 'person' is one of six elements. And herein, in the ultimate sense, a person does not exist; rather, 'person' is merely a designation. This same method should be understood in the remaining terms as well. Herein, in 'one with four foundations' (caturādhiṭṭhāno), 'foundation' (adhiṭṭhāna) is called 'support' (patiṭṭhā); the meaning is 'having four supports.' This is what is meant: This monk, this person, is one of six elements, six sense-bases for contact, and eighteen mental investigations. Having turned away from this very round of existence, when taking Arahantship, which is the supreme accomplishment, he takes it established in these four places. Therefore, he is called 'one with four foundations.' 'Wherein established' means: in which foundations he is established. 'Conceit does not occur' means that neither conceit (mañña) nor pride (māna) occurs. 'The sage is peaceful, is said' means: the sage whose cankers are destroyed is called 'calmed,' 'extinguished.' 'One should not be heedless of wisdom' means: for the sake of penetrating with the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship, from the very beginning one should not be heedless of the wisdom of concentration and insight. 'One should guard truth' means: for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth, from the very beginning one should guard truth in speech. 'One should cultivate relinquishment' means: for the sake of accomplishing the abandoning of all defilements by means of the path of Arahantship, from the very beginning one should develop the abandoning of defilements. 'He should train only in peace' means: for the sake of the pacification of all defilements by means of the path of Arahantship, from the very beginning one should train in the pacification of defilements. Thus, for the sake of attaining the foundations of wisdom and so forth, these preliminary foundations—the wisdom of tranquility and insight, and so on—were taught.

345. Phassāyatananti phassassa āyatanaṃ, ākaroti attho. Paññādhiṭṭhānantiādīni pubbe vuttānaṃ arahattaphalapaññādīnaṃ vasena veditabbāni.

345. 'A sense-base for contact' (phassāyatana) means a basis for contact; the meaning is 'a source.' The words beginning with 'the foundation of wisdom' (paññādhiṭṭhāna) should be understood by way of the previously mentioned wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship and so forth.

348. Idāni nikkhittamātikāvasena “yattha ṭhitaṃ maññassa vā nappavattantī”ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, arahatte pana patte puna “paññaṃ nappamajjeyyā”tiādīhi kiccaṃ natthi. Iti [V 4.0219] bhagavā mātikaṃ uppaṭipāṭidhātukaṃ ṭhapetvāpi yathādhammavaseneva vibhaṅgaṃ vibhajanto paññaṃ nappamajjeyyātiādimāha. Tattha ko paññaṃ pamajjati, ko nappamajjati? Yo tāva imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā vejjakammādivasena ekavīsatividhāya anesanāya [M 4.0209] jīvikaṃ kappento pabbajjānurūpena cittuppādaṃ ṭhapetuṃ na sakkoti, ayaṃ paññaṃ pamajjati nāma. Yo pana sāsane pabbajitvā sīle patiṭṭhāya buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā sappāyaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ samādāya cittarucitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ nissāya kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ patvā ajjeva arahattanti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vicarati, ayaṃ paññaṃ nappamajjati nāma. Imasmiṃ pana sutte dhātukammaṭṭhānavasena esa paññāya appamādo vutto. Dhātukammaṭṭhāne panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā hatthipadopamasuttādīsu vuttameva.

348. Now, according to the established matrix, it should have been said: 'Wherein established, conceit does not occur.' But for one who has attained Arahantship, there is again no task involving instructions such as 'One should not be heedless of wisdom.' Thus the Blessed One, although having established the matrix out of its natural order, analyzing the analysis only in accordance with the nature of the Dhamma, spoke the words beginning with 'One should not be heedless of wisdom.' Therein, who is heedless of wisdom, and who is not heedless? Firstly, whoever, having gone forth in this Dispensation, makes a living by means of the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, such as medical practice, and is unable to establish a state of mind befitting the going forth—this one is called 'heedless of wisdom.' But whoever, having gone forth in the Dispensation, being established in virtue, having learned the Buddha's word, having undertaken a suitable ascetic practice, having taken up a meditation subject that is pleasing to the mind, relying on a secluded dwelling, having done the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, having attained an absorption, dwells developing insight with the thought, 'I will attain Arahantship this very day!'—this one is called 'not heedless of wisdom.' But in this sutta, this heedfulness regarding wisdom is spoken of by way of the meditation subject of the elements. Herein, whatever should be said on the meditation subject of the elements, that has already been stated below in the Hatthipadopama Sutta and others.

354. Athāparaṃ [P 5.0053] viññāṇaṃyeva avasissatīti ayampettha pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhato hi rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ, idāni arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nibbattetvā dassetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Yaṃ vā panetaṃ imassa bhikkhuno pathavīdhātuādīsu āgamaniyavipassanāvasena kammakārakaviññāṇaṃ, taṃ viññāṇadhātuvasena bhājetvā dassentopi imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha avasissatīti kimatthāya avasissati? Satthu kathanatthāya kulaputtassa ca paṭivijjhanatthāya avasissati. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Pariyodātanti pabhassaraṃ. Sukhantipi vijānātīti sukhavedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhavedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānāti. Sesapadadvayesupi eseva nayo. Sace panāyaṃ vedanākathā heṭṭhā na kathitā bhaveyya, idha ṭhatvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭeyya. Satipaṭṭhāne panesā kathitāvāti tattha kathitanayeneva veditabbā. Sukhavedaniyanti evamādi paccayavasena udayatthaṅgamanadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha sukhavedaniyanti sukhavedanāya paccayabhūtaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

354. Furthermore, 'only consciousness remains'—this too is a separate connection herein. For previously, the meditation subject of form was taught; now, this teaching was begun in order to show the meditation subject of the formless, having caused it to arise by way of feeling. Or, he also began this teaching while showing that consciousness of this monk which, by way of insight that is to be approached, performs the task in regard to the earth element and so on, having analyzed it by way of the consciousness element. Therein, 'it remains'—for what purpose does it remain? It remains for the Teacher to explain and for the clansman to penetrate. 'Purified' means without the stain of defilement. 'Exceedingly clean' means luminous. 'He also knows it as pleasant' means: when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he knows, 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.' This same method should be understood in the remaining two phrases as well. If this discourse on feeling had not been taught previously, it would be proper to stand here and teach it. But since it has been taught in the Satipaṭṭhāna, it should be understood only in the manner taught there. The words beginning with 'productive of pleasant feeling' were spoken to show the arising and passing away by way of conditions. Therein, 'productive of pleasant feeling' means the contact that has become a condition for pleasant feeling. This same method should be understood in the remaining terms as well.

360. Upekkhāyeva avasissatīti ettāvatā hi yathā nāma chekena maṇikārācariyena vajirasūciyā vijjhitvā cammakhaṇḍe pātetvā pātetvā dinnamuttaṃ antevāsiko gahetvā gahetvā suttagataṃ karonto muttolambakamuttajālādīni karoti, evameva bhagavatā kathetvā kathetvā dinnaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ayaṃ kulaputto manasikaronto manasikaronto paguṇaṃ akāsīti rūpakammaṭṭhānampissa arūpakammaṭṭhānampi paguṇaṃ [M 4.0210] jātaṃ, atha bhagavā “athāparaṃ upekkhāyeva avasissatī”ti āha.

360. Regarding the statement, 'Only equanimity will remain': By this much, it is as if a skilled master gem-cutter, having pierced the given pearls with a diamond needle and dropped them again and again onto a piece of leather, gives them to an apprentice who, taking them again and again and making them strung on a thread, fashions pearl pendants, pearl nets, and so on. In just the same way, this noble son, by reflecting again and again on the meditation subject given by the Blessed One who taught it again and again, made it proficient. Thus, for him, both the form meditation subject and the formless meditation subject became proficient. That being so, why did the Blessed One say, 'Then, only equanimity will remain'?

Kimatthaṃ [V 4.0220] pana avasissatīti? Satthu kathanatthaṃ. Kulaputtassa paṭivijjhanatthantipi vadanti[P 5.0054], taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Kulaputtena hi sahāyassa sāsanaṃ vācetvā pāsādatale ṭhiteneva ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattitaṃ, yadassa ettakaṃ maggaṃ āgacchantassa yānakiccaṃ sādheti. Satthu kathanatthaṃyeva avasissati. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne satthā kulaputtassa rūpāvacarajjhāne vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti “bhikkhu paguṇaṃ tava idaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāna”nti. Parisuddhātiādi tassāyeva upekkhāya vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ. Ukkaṃ bandheyyāti aṅgārakapallaṃ sajjeyya. Ālimpeyyāti tattha aṅgāre pakkhipitvā aggiṃ datvā nāḷikāya dhamento aggiṃ jāleyya. Ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyyāti aṅgāre viyūhitvā aṅgāramatthake vā ṭhapeyya, tattake vā pakkhipeyya. Nīhaṭanti nīhaṭadosaṃ. Ninnītakasāvanti apanītakasāvaṃ. Evameva khoti yathā taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ icchiticchitāya piḷandhanavikatiyā saṃvattati, evameva ayaṃ tāva catutthajjhānupekkhā vipassanā abhiññā nirodho bhavokkantīti imesu yaṃ icchati, tassatthāya hotīti vaṇṇaṃ kathesi.

For what purpose does it remain? For the Teacher's exposition. Some also say it is for the noble son's penetration, but that should not be accepted. Why? Because the noble son, having read his companion's message, while just standing on the palace terrace, brought forth the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, which accomplished the task of a vehicle for him while coming this great distance. It remains only for the purpose of the Teacher's exposition. For in this instance, the Teacher spoke in praise of the noble son's form-sphere jhāna. Indeed, this is what was meant: 'Monk, this form-sphere fourth jhāna of yours is proficient.' The words 'perfectly pure' and so on are a speaking of praise for that very equanimity. 'He would set up the crucible' means he would prepare a charcoal pan. 'He would light it' means having placed charcoal in it, having lit a fire, and blowing with a tube, he would make the fire blaze. 'He would place it in the mouth of the crucible' means having spread out the embers, he should place it on top of the charcoal pan, or place it in when it is hot. 'Removed' means with faults discarded. 'With dross removed' means with impurities removed. 'Just so': just as that gold serves for whatever kind of ornament is desired, in the same way, this insight which is preceded by the equanimity of the fourth jhāna—be it for higher knowledge, cessation, or entry into a good existence—whatever among these is desired, it serves that purpose. Thus he spoke in praise.

Kasmā pana bhagavā imasmiṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne nikantipariyādānatthaṃ avaṇṇaṃ akathetvā vaṇṇaṃ kathesīti. Kulaputtassa hi catutthajjhāne nikantipariyuṭṭhānaṃ balavaṃ. Sace avaṇṇaṃ katheyya, – “mayhaṃ pabbajitvā [P 5.0055] dvānavutiyojanasataṃ āgacchantassa imaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ yānakiccaṃ sādhesi, ahaṃ ettakaṃ maggaṃ āgacchanto jhānasukhena jhānaratiyā āgato, evarūpassa nāma paṇītadhammassa avaṇṇaṃ katheti, jānaṃ nu kho katheti ajāna”nti kulaputto saṃsayaṃ sammohaṃ āpajjeyya, tasmā bhagavā vaṇṇaṃ kathesi.

But why did the Blessed One, for the purpose of causing the exhaustion of attachment, speak in praise of this form-sphere fourth jhāna, instead of speaking of its drawbacks? Because the noble son's obsession with craving for the fourth jhāna was strong. If the Blessed One were to speak of its drawbacks, the noble son might fall into doubt and confusion, thinking: 'For me, who went forth and traveled a distance of one hundred and ninety-two yojanas, this fourth jhāna accomplished the task of a vehicle. I came this great distance with the bliss of jhāna, with the delight in jhāna. Yet he speaks of the drawbacks of such a sublime state. Does he speak knowing, or not knowing?' Therefore, the Blessed One spoke in praise.

361. Tadanudhammanti ettha arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ dhammo nāma, taṃ anugatattā rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ anudhammoti vuttaṃ. Vipākajjhānaṃ vā dhammo, kusalajjhānaṃ anudhammo. Tadupādānāti taggahaṇā. Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānanti vīsatikappasahassāni. Vipākavasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ito uttarimpi eseva nayo.

361. Regarding 'in accordance with that Dhamma': Here, the formless-sphere jhāna is called 'Dhamma'. Because the form-sphere jhāna follows it, it is called 'anudhamma' (in accordance with the Dhamma). Alternatively, the resultant jhāna is the 'Dhamma', and the wholesome jhāna is the 'anudhamma'. 'Because of clinging to it' means because of grasping it. 'For a long, long time' means for twenty thousand eons. Indeed, this is stated by way of the resultant jhāna. From here onwards, this same method should be understood.

362. Evaṃ [M 4.0211] catūhi vārehi arūpāvacarajjhānassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni tasseva ādīnavaṃ dassento so evaṃ pajānātītiādimāha. Tattha saṅkhatametanti kiñcāpi ettha vīsatikappasahassāni [V 4.0221] āyu atthi, etaṃ pana saṅkhataṃ pakappitaṃ āyūhitaṃ, karontena karīyati, aniccaṃ adhuvaṃ asassataṃ tāvakālikaṃ, cavanaparibhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammaṃ, jātiyā anugataṃ, jarāya anusaṭaṃ, maraṇena abbhāhataṃ, dukkhe patiṭṭhitaṃ, atāṇaṃ aleṇaṃ asaraṇaṃ asaraṇībhūtanti. Viññāṇañcāyatanādīsupi eseva nayo.

362. Having thus spoken in praise of the formless-sphere jhāna in four sections, now, wishing to show its danger, he spoke the words beginning with 'He understands thus.' Therein, regarding 'this is conditioned': Although there is a lifespan of twenty thousand eons here, this is nevertheless conditioned, fabricated, contrived, produced by a maker, impermanent, unstable, not eternal, temporary, having the nature of passing away, breaking up, and destruction, followed by birth, oppressed by aging, afflicted by death, established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, having become without refuge. The same method should be understood regarding the base of infinite consciousness and so on.

Idāni arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ gaṇhanto so neva taṃ abhisaṅkharotītiādimāha. Yathā hi cheko bhisakko visavikāraṃ disvā vamanaṃ kāretvā visaṃ ṭhānato cāvetvā upari āropetvā khandhaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā gahetuṃ adatvā visaṃ otāretvā pathaviyaṃ pāteyya, evameva bhagavā kulaputtassa [P 5.0056] arūpāvacarajjhāne vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā kulaputto rūpāvacarajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya arūpāvacarajjhāne patthanaṃ ṭhapesi.

Now, taking up the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship, he spoke the words beginning with 'He neither fabricates that.' For just as a skilled physician, seeing the adverse effects of poison, would induce vomiting, dislodge the poison from its place, raise it upwards, and without allowing it to take hold of the shoulder or head, make the poison descend and drop to the ground; in just the same way, the Blessed One spoke in praise of the formless-sphere jhāna to the noble son. Having heard that, the noble son, exhausting his delight in the form-sphere jhāna, established an aspiration for the formless-sphere jhāna.

Bhagavā taṃ ñatvā taṃ asampattassa appaṭiladdhasseva bhikkhuno “atthesā ākāsānañcāyatanādīsu sampatti nāma. Tesañhi paṭhamabrahmaloke vīsatikappasahassāni āyu, dutiye cattālīsaṃ, tatiye saṭṭhi, catutthe caturāsīti kappasahassāni āyu. Taṃ pana aniccaṃ adhuvaṃ asassataṃ tāvakālikaṃ, cavanaparibhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammaṃ, jātiyā anugataṃ, jarāya anusaṭaṃ, maraṇena abbhāhataṃ, dukkhe patiṭṭhitaṃ, atāṇaṃ aleṇaṃ asaraṇaṃ asaraṇībhūtaṃ, ettakaṃ kālaṃ tattha sampattiṃ anubhavitvāpi puthujjanakālakiriyaṃ katvā puna catūsu apāyesu patitabba”nti sabbametaṃ ādīnavaṃ ekapadeneva “saṅkhatameta”nti kathesi. Kulaputto taṃ sutvā arūpāvacarajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādiyi, bhagavā tassa rūpāvacarārūpāvacaresu nikantiyā pariyādinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā arahattanikūṭaṃ gaṇhanto “so neva taṃ abhisaṅkharotī”tiādimāha.

The Blessed One, knowing this, said to that monk who had not yet reached or obtained it: 'There is indeed this attainment in the base of infinite space and so forth. For those beings, in the first brahma world, the lifespan is twenty thousand eons; in the second, forty thousand; in the third, sixty thousand; and in the fourth, eighty-four thousand eons. But that is impermanent, unstable, not eternal, temporary, having the nature of passing away, breaking up, and destruction, followed by birth, oppressed by aging, afflicted by death, established in suffering, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, having become without refuge. Even after experiencing the attainment there for such a long time, having died the death of a worldling, one must fall again into the four states of deprivation.' Thus, he spoke of all this danger with the single phrase: 'This is conditioned.' Hearing this, the noble son exhausted his delight in the formless-sphere jhāna. The Blessed One, knowing that his delight in the form-sphere and formless-sphere jhānas had been exhausted, taking up the pinnacle with Arahantship, spoke the words beginning with 'He neither fabricates that.'

Yathā vā paneko mahāyodho ekaṃ rājānaṃ ārādhetvā satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gāmavaraṃ labheyya, puna rājā tassānubhāvaṃ saritvā – “mahānubhāvo yodho, appakaṃ tena laddha”nti – “nāyaṃ tāta gāmo [M 4.0212] tuyhaṃ anucchaviko, aññaṃ catusatasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti dadeyya so sādhu devāti taṃ vissajjetvā itaraṃ gāmaṃ gaṇheyya. Rājā asampattameva ca naṃ pakkosāpetvā – “kiṃ te tena, ahivātarogo ettha uppajjati? Asukasmiṃ pana ṭhāne mahantaṃ nagaraṃ atthi, tattha chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjaṃ kārehī”ti pahiṇeyya, so tathā kareyya.

Furthermore, it is as if a great warrior, having pleased a certain king, might receive a choice village yielding one hundred thousand. Then the king, recalling his power, might think, 'This warrior is of great power, yet what he has received is little,' and saying, 'Dear one, this village is not suitable for you. Take another yielding four hundred thousand,' he might give it. That warrior, saying, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' would relinquish that village and take the other. And even before he has taken possession of it, the king might have him summoned and say, 'What is that to you? A pestilential disease arises there. But in such-and-such a place, there is a great city. There, having raised the parasol, rule the kingdom,' and might send him off. And he would do so.

Tattha [V 4.0222] rājā viya sammāsambuddho daṭṭhabbo, mahāyodho viya pukkusāti kulaputto, paṭhamaladdhagāmo viya ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ, taṃ vissajjetvā itaraṃ gāmaṃ gaṇhāhīti vuttakālo viya ānāpānacatutthajjhāne nikantipariyādānaṃ katvā āruppakathanaṃ, taṃ gāmaṃ asampattameva [P 5.0057] pakkosāpetvā “kiṃ te tena, ahivātarogo ettha uppajjati? Asukasmiṃ ṭhāne nagaraṃ atthi, tattha chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjaṃ kārehī”ti vuttakālo viya arūpe saṅkhatametanti ādīnavakathanena appattāsuyeva tāsu samāpattīsu patthanaṃ nivatthāpetvā upari arahattanikūṭena desanāgahaṇaṃ.

Herein, the Perfectly Enlightened One should be seen as the king; the clansman Pukkusāti, as the great warrior; the fourth jhāna of mindfulness-of-breathing, as the first-obtained village. The discourse on the formless attainments, given after having brought about the exhaustion of craving for the fourth jhāna of mindfulness-of-breathing, should be seen as the time when it was said, 'Having relinquished that, take the other village.' The grasping of the teaching—crowned above with the pinnacle of Arahantship, after having turned back the aspiration for those formless attainments even before they were attained by means of the discourse on their drawbacks, stating, 'This is conditioned'—should be seen as the time when, even before he had taken possession of that village, he was summoned and told, 'What is that to you? A pestilential disease arises there. In such-and-such a place there is a city; there, having raised the parasol, rule the kingdom.'

Tattha neva abhisaṅkharotīti nāyūhati na rāsiṃ karoti. Na abhisañcetayatīti na kappeti. Bhavāya vā vibhavāya vāti vuddhiyā vā parihāniyā vā, sassatucchedavasenapi yojetabbaṃ. Na kiñci loke upādiyatīti loke rūpādīsu kiñci ekadhammampi taṇhāya na gaṇhāti, na parāmasati. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti bhagavā attano buddhavisaye ṭhatvā desanāya arahattanikūṭaṃ gaṇhi. Kulaputto pana attano yathopanissayena tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni paṭivijjhi. Yathā nāma rājā suvaṇṇabhājanena nānārasabhojanaṃ bhuñjanto attano pamāṇena piṇḍaṃ vaṭṭetvā aṅke nisinnena rājakumārena piṇḍamhi ālaye dassite taṃ piṇḍaṃ upanāmeyya, kumāro attano mukhappamāṇeneva kabaḷaṃ kareyya, sesaṃ rājā sayaṃ vā bhuñjeyya, pātiyaṃ vā pakkhipeyya, evaṃ dhammarājā tathāgato attano pamāṇena arahattanikūṭaṃ gaṇhanto desanaṃ desesi, kulaputto attano yathopanissayena tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni paṭivijjhi.

Herein, 'he neither fabricates' means he does not strive, he does not make an accumulation. 'He does not intend' means he does not arrange. 'For being or for non-being' means for increase or for decrease; it should also be connected by way of eternalism and annihilationism. 'He does not cling to anything in the world' means that in the world, regarding things such as form, he does not grasp even a single phenomenon with craving, nor does he misapprehend it. As for 'he understands: "There is no further for this state of being,"' the Blessed One, standing in his own Buddha-domain, took the pinnacle for the teaching with Arahantship. The clansman, however, in accordance with his own supporting condition, penetrated the three fruits of recluseship. It is as if a king, while eating a meal of various flavors from a golden vessel, might roll a ball of food according to his own measure, and when the prince seated on his lap shows a desire for the ball of food, he might offer it to him. The prince would then take a morsel according to the measure of his own mouth, and the king would either eat the remainder himself or place it back in the vessel. In the same way, the Tathāgata, the King of Dhamma, while taking the pinnacle of Arahantship as his own measure, delivered the teaching. The clansman, in accordance with his own supporting condition, penetrated the three fruits of recluseship.

Ito pubbe panassa khandhā dhātuyo āyatanānīti evarūpaṃ accantasuññataṃ tilakkhaṇāhataṃ kathaṃ kathentassa neva kaṅkhā, na vimati, nāpi – “evaṃ kira taṃ, evaṃ me ācariyena vutta”nti iti kira na dandhāyitattaṃ na vitthāyitattaṃ [P 5.0058] atthi[M 4.0213]. Ekaccesu ca kira ṭhānesu buddhā aññātakavesena vicaranti, sammāsambuddho nu kho esoti ahudeva saṃsayo, ahu vimati. Yato anena anāgāmiphalaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, atha ayaṃ me satthāti niṭṭhaṃ gato. Yadi evaṃ kasmā accayaṃ na desesīti. Okāsābhāvato. Bhagavā hi yathānikkhittāya mātikāya acchinnadhāraṃ katvā ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya desanaṃ desesiyeva.

But before this, for him, while the Teacher was speaking in such a way about the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as being utterly empty and struck by the three characteristics, there was no doubt, no uncertainty, nor was there any thought like, 'Is it really so? Is this what my teacher said?' It seems there was no dullness, no weariness. And it seems that in some places Buddhas wander in an unknown guise, so the doubt, 'Could this be a Perfectly Enlightened One?' certainly arose; uncertainty certainly arose. Because he penetrated the fruit of non-returning, he then came to the conclusion, 'This is my Teacher.' If so, why did he not confess his transgression? Because of the lack of opportunity. For the Blessed One was delivering the teaching just like one causing the celestial Ganges to flow down, making an unbroken stream of the matrix as it had been laid down.

363. Soti [V 4.0223] arahā. Anajjhositāti gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā gahetuṃ na yutthāti pajānāti. Anabhinanditāti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandituṃ na yuttāti pajānāti.

363. 'He' means the Arahant. 'Not settled on' means he understands: 'It is not fit to be grasped, having been swallowed and consumed.' 'Not delighted in' means he understands: 'It is not fit to be delighted in by way of craving and wrong view.'

364. Visaṃyutto naṃ vedetīti sace hissa sukhavedanaṃ ārabbha rāgānusayo, dukkhavedanaṃ ārabbha paṭighānusayo, itaraṃ ārabbha avijjānusayo uppajjeyya, saṃyutto vediyeyya nāma. Anuppajjanato pana visaṃyutto naṃ vedeti nissaṭo vippamutto. Kāyapariyantikanti kāyakoṭikaṃ. Yāva kāyapavattā uppajjitvā tato paraṃ anuppajjanavedananti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantīti dvādasasu āyatanesu kilesānaṃ visevanassa natthitāya anabhinanditāni hutvā idha dvādasasuyeva āyatanesu nirujjhissanti. Kilesā hi nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhāpi yattha natthi, tattha niruddhāti vuccanti. Svāyamattho – “etthesā taṇhā nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”ti samudayapañhena dīpetabbo. Tasmā bhagavā nibbānaṃ āgamma sītibhūtānipi idheva sītībhavissantīti āha. Nanu ca idha vedayitāni vuttāni, na kilesāti. Vedayitānipi kilesābhāveneva sītībhavanti. Itarathā nesaṃ sītibhāvo nāma natthīti suvuttametaṃ.

364. 'Disjoined, he feels it' means this: If, for him, the underlying tendency to lust were to arise in connection with a pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion in connection with a painful feeling, or the underlying tendency to ignorance in connection with a neutral feeling, then, being conjoined, he would be said to feel it. But because of their non-arising, he is disjoined; he feels it detached, liberated. 'Ending with the body' means having the body as its limit. The meaning is: feeling that arises as long as the body lasts, and after that, non-arising feeling. This same method applies to the second phrase. 'Not being delighted in, they will become cool' means that because there is no indulgence in the defilements in the twelve sense bases, not being delighted in, they will cease right here in these very twelve sense bases. For although defilements cease with Nibbāna as their object, they are said to cease where they are absent, that is, here. This meaning should be illustrated by the question on origination: 'It is here that this craving, in ceasing, ceases.' Therefore, the Blessed One said that even those things that become cool with Nibbāna as their basis will become cool right here. But were not feelings spoken of here, not defilements? Feelings, too, become cool only through the absence of defilements. Otherwise, for them, there is no such thing as becoming cool. Therefore, this statement is well-said.

365. Evameva [P 5.0059] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – yathā hi eko puriso telapadīpassa jhāyato tele khīṇe telaṃ āsiñcati, vaṭṭiyā khīṇāya vaṭṭiṃ pakkhipati, evaṃ dīpasikhāya anupacchedova hoti, evameva puthujjano ekasmiṃ bhave ṭhito kusalākusalaṃ karoti, so tena sugatiyañca apāyesu ca nibbattatiyeva, evaṃ vedanānaṃ anupacchedova [M 4.0214] hoti. Yathā paneko dīpasikhāya ukkaṇṭhito – “imaṃ purisaṃ āgamma dīpasikhā na upacchijjatī”ti nilīno tassa purisassa sīsaṃ chindeyya, evaṃ vaṭṭiyā ca telassa ca anupahārā dīpasikhā anāhārā nibbāyati, evameva vaṭṭe ukkaṇṭhito yogāvacaro arahattamaggena kusalākusalaṃ samucchindati, tassa samucchinnattā khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno kāyassa bhedā puna vedayitāni na uppajjantīti.

365. ‘Just so’—here is the application of the simile. Just as, while an oil lamp is burning, a person pours in more oil when the oil is exhausted, and puts in a new wick when the wick is spent, and in this way the lamp's flame continues without interruption; in the same way, an ordinary person, established in one existence, performs wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Through that, they are reborn in good destinations and in the planes of misery; in this way, feelings continue without interruption. But it is as if someone, being disgusted with the lamp’s flame, might think, ‘It is because of this person that the lamp's flame is not interrupted,’ and, lying in wait, might cut off that person's head. In this way, the lamp's flame, being unsupported by a wick and oil, is extinguished for lack of fuel. In the same way, a yogī who is disgusted with the round of existence, by means of the path of Arahantship, utterly cuts off wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Because that has been utterly cut off, for the monk whose taints are destroyed, after the breakup of the body, feelings to be experienced do not arise again.

Tasmāti yasmā ādimhi samādhivipassanāpaññāhi arahattaphalapaññā uttaritarā, tasmā. Evaṃ samannāgatoti iminā uttamena arahattaphalapaññādhiṭṭhānena samannāgato. Sabbadukkhakkhaye [V 4.0224] ñāṇaṃ nāma arahattamagge ñāṇaṃ, imasmiṃ pana sutte arahattaphale ñāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tenevāha tassa sā vimutti sacce ṭhitā akuppā hotīti.

‘Therefore’ means: because, from the beginning, the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship is superior to the wisdoms of concentration and insight, therefore. ‘Thus endowed’ means: endowed with this supreme foundation, which is the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. ‘Knowledge in the destruction of all suffering’ is the name for the knowledge in the path of Arahantship, but in this sutta, the knowledge in the fruit of Arahantship is intended. For that reason, he said: ‘His liberation is established in truth, unshakeable.’

366. Ettha hi vimuttīti arahattaphalavimutti, saccanti paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānaṃ. Iti akuppārammaṇakaraṇena akuppāti vuttā. Musāti vitathaṃ. Mosadhammanti nassanasabhāvaṃ. Taṃ saccanti taṃ avitathaṃ sabhāvo. Amosadhammanti anassanasabhāvaṃ.

366. Here, ‘liberation’ is the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship; ‘truth’ is the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. Thus, because it takes the unshakeable as its object, it is called ‘unshakeable.’ ‘False’ means erroneous. ‘Subject to falsehood’ means having a nature of perishing. ‘That truth’ means that which has a non-erroneous nature. ‘Not subject to falsehood’ means having a nature of not perishing.

Tasmāti yasmā ādito samathavipassanāvasena vacīsaccato dukkhasaccasamudayasaccehi ca paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānameva uttaritaraṃ, tasmā. Evaṃ samannāgatoti iminā uttamena paramatthasaccādhiṭṭhānena samannāgato.

‘Therefore’ means: because from the beginning, by means of serenity and insight, Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth, is superior to the truth of speech and to the truths of suffering and its origin, therefore. ‘Thus endowed’ means: endowed with this supreme foundation, which is the ultimate truth.

367. Pubbeti puthujjanakāle. Upadhī [P 5.0060] hontīti khandhūpadhi kilesūpadhi abhisaṅkhārūpadhi pañcakāmaguṇūpadhīti ime upadhayo honti. Samattā samādinnāti paripūrā gahitā paramaṭṭhā. Tasmāti yasmā ādito samathavipassanāvasena kilesapariccāgato, sotāpattimaggādīhi ca kilesapariccāgato arahattamaggeneva kilesapariccāgo uttaritaro, tasmā. Evaṃ samannāgatoti iminā uttamena cāgādhiṭṭhānena samannāgato.

367. ‘Formerly’ means: in the time of an ordinary person. ‘There are acquisitions’ means: there are these acquisitions: the acquisition of the aggregates, the acquisition of defilements, the acquisition of formations, and the acquisition of the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Fully undertaken’ means: completely taken up and wrongly grasped. ‘Therefore’ means: because from the beginning, the abandonment of defilements by means of the path of Arahantship alone is superior to the abandonment of defilements by means of serenity and insight, and to the abandonment of defilements by means of the path of stream-entry and so on, therefore. ‘Thus endowed’ means: endowed with this supreme foundation of relinquishment.

368. Āghātotiādīsu āghātakaraṇavasena āghāto, byāpajjanavasena byāpādo, sampadussanavasena sampadosoti tīhi padehi dosākusalamūlameva vuttaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā ādito samathavipassanāvasena [M 4.0215] kilesavūpasamato, sotāpattimaggādīhi kilesavūpasamato ca arahattamaggeneva kilesavūpasamo uttaritaro, tasmā. Evaṃ samannāgatoti iminā uttamena upasamādhiṭṭhānena samannāgato.

368. In ‘resentment,’ and so on: by way of harboring enmity, it is ‘resentment’; by way of malevolence, it is ‘ill will’; by way of complete corruption, it is ‘hostility.’ By these three terms, only the unwholesome root of aversion is stated. ‘Therefore’ means: because from the beginning, the pacification of defilements by means of the path of Arahantship alone is superior to the pacification of defilements by means of serenity and insight, and to the pacification of defilements by means of the path of stream-entry and so on, therefore. ‘Thus endowed’ means: endowed with this supreme foundation of pacification.

369. Maññitametanti taṇhāmaññitaṃ mānamaññitaṃ diṭṭhimaññitanti tividhampi vaṭṭati. Ayamahamasmīti ettha pana ayamahanti ekaṃ taṇhāmaññitameva vaṭṭati. Rogotiādīsu ābādhaṭṭhena rogo, antodosaṭṭhena gaṇḍo, anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sallaṃ. Muni santoti vuccatīti khīṇāsavamuni santo nibbutoti vuccati. Yattha ṭhitanti yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitaṃ. Saṃkhittenāti buddhānaṃ [V 4.0225] kira sabbāpi dhammadesanā saṃkhittāva, vitthāradesanā nāma natthi, samantapaṭṭhānakathāpi [P 5.0061] saṃkhittāyeva. Iti bhagavā desanaṃ yathānusandhiṃ pāpesi. Ugghāṭitaññūtiādīsu pana catūsu puggalesu pukkusāti kulaputto vipañcitaññū, iti vipañcitaññuvasena bhagavā imaṃ dhātuvibhaṅgasuttaṃ kathesi.

369. ‘This is what is conceived’ means: conceiving through craving, conceiving through conceit, and conceiving through views—all three kinds are applicable. However, in the phrase ‘I am this,’ only the one conceiving through craving is applicable. In ‘disease,’ and so on: ‘disease’ in the sense of affliction; ‘boil’ in the sense of internal corruption; ‘dart’ in the sense of having penetrated. ‘A sage is called peaceful’ means: a sage whose taints are destroyed is called peaceful, extinguished. ‘Where one is established’ means: in which state one is established. ‘Briefly’ means: indeed, all the Buddhas' Dhamma teachings are brief; there is no teaching called ‘detailed.’ Even the discourse on the Conditional Relations is brief. Thus the Blessed One delivered the teaching in accordance with the connection. Now, among the four types of individuals, such as the one who understands upon a brief utterance, the clansman Pukkusāti is one who understands after elaboration. Therefore, by way of teaching one who understands after elaboration, the Blessed One spoke this Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements.

370. Na kho me, bhante, paripuṇṇaṃ pattacīvaranti kasmā kulaputtassa iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ na nibbattanti. Pubbe aṭṭhannaṃ parikkhārānaṃ adinnattā. Kulaputto hi dinnadāno katābhinīhāro, na dinnattāti na vattabbaṃ. Iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ pana pacchimabhavikānaṃyeva nibbattati, ayañca punapaṭisandhiko, tasmā na nibbattanti. Atha bhagavā sayaṃ pariyesitvā kasmā na upasampādesīti. Okāsābhāvato. Kulaputtassa āyu parikkhīṇaṃ, suddhāvāsiko anāgāmī mahābrahmā kumbhakārasālaṃ āgantvā nisinno viya ahosi. Tasmā sayaṃ na pariyesi.

370. Regarding “Venerable sir, my bowl and robe are not complete”: Why did a bowl and robe created by psychic power not arise for the clansman? Because in a previous life, one of the eight requisites was not given. Indeed, the clansman had given gifts and had made an aspiration, so it should not be said that it was because he had not given. However, a bowl and robe created by psychic power arises only for those in their final existence, and this one was subject to rebirth; therefore, it did not arise. Then why did the Blessed One not ordain him after searching for the requisites Himself? Because there was no opportunity. The clansman's lifespan was exhausted. Having become a non-returner, a Great Brahmā to be reborn in the Pure Abodes, he had, as it were, come to the potter's shed and sat down, but was already reborn in the Pure Abodes. Therefore, the Blessed One did not search for the requisites Himself.

Pattacīvarapariyesanaṃ pakkāmīti kāya velāya pakkāmi? Uṭṭhite aruṇe. Bhagavato kira dhammadesanāpariniṭṭhānañca aruṇuṭṭhānañca rasmivissajjanañca ekakkhaṇe ahosi. Bhagavā kira desanaṃ niṭṭhapetvāva chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajji, sakalakumbhakāranivesanaṃ ekapajjotaṃ ahosi, chabbaṇṇarasmiyo jālajālā puñjapuñjā hutvā vidhāvantiyo sabbadisābhāge suvaṇṇapaṭapariyonaddhe viya ca nānāvaṇṇakusumaratanavisarasamujjale viya ca akaṃsu. Bhagavā “nagaravāsino maṃ passantū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Nagaravāsino bhagavantaṃ [P 5.0062] disvāva “satthā kira āgato, kumbhakārasālāya kira nisinno”ti aññamaññassa ārocetvā rañño ārocesuṃ.

Regarding “He set out in search of a bowl and robe”: At what time did he set out? He set out when the dawn was rising. It is said that the Blessed One's completion of the Dhamma teaching, the rising of the dawn, and the emission of rays occurred in a single moment. It is said that the Blessed One, upon completing the teaching, emitted the six-colored rays. The entire potter's dwelling became illuminated as if by a single lamp. The six-colored rays, becoming like nets and masses and darting about, made all directions appear as if wrapped in golden cloth and as if resplendent with the spreading glitter of various colorful flowers and jewels. The Blessed One resolved, “Let the city dwellers see me.” The city dwellers, upon seeing the Blessed One, informed one another, saying, “It seems the Teacher has come! It seems he is seated in the potter's shed!” and they reported it to the king.

Rājā [M 4.0216] āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā, “bhante, kāya velāya āgatatthā”ti pucchi. Hiyyo sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya mahārājāti. Kena kammena bhagavāti? Tumhākaṃ sahāyo pukkusāti rājā tumhehi pahitaṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā nikkhamitvā pabbajitvā maṃ uddissa āgacchanto sāvatthiṃ atikkamma pañcacattālīsa yojanāni āgantvā imaṃ kumbhakārasālaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi, ahaṃ tassa saṅgahatthaṃ āgantvā dhammakathaṃ kathesiṃ, kulaputto tīṇi phalāni paṭivijjhi mahārājāti. Idāni kahaṃ, bhanteti? Upasampadaṃ yācitvā aparipuṇṇapattacīvaratāya pattacīvarapariyesanatthaṃ [V 4.0226] gato mahārājāti. Rājā kulaputtassa gatadisābhāgena agamāsi. Bhagavāpi ākāsenāgantvā jetavanagandhakuṭimhiyeva pāturahosi.

The king came, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked, "Venerable sir, at what time did you arrive?" "Yesterday at sunset, great king." "For what reason, Blessed One?" "Your friend, King Pukkusāti, having heard the message sent by you, went forth, became a monk, and while coming with me as his object, he passed beyond Sāvatthī, traveled forty-five yojanas, entered this potter’s shed, and sat down. I came for the purpose of helping him and gave a Dhamma talk. The noble youth penetrated the three fruits, great king." "Where is he now, venerable sir?" "Having requested the higher ordination, but because his bowl and robes were incomplete, he has gone for the purpose of searching for a bowl and robes, great king." The king went in the direction the noble youth had gone. The Blessed One also, having come through the air, reappeared in the perfumed chamber of Jetavana itself.

Kulaputtopi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesamāno neva bimbisārarañño na takkasīlakānaṃ jaṅghavāṇijānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “na kho me kukkuṭassa viya tattha tattha manāpāmanāpameva vicinitvā pattacīvaraṃ pariyesituṃ yuttaṃ, mahantaṃ nagaraṃ vajjitvā udakatitthasusānasaṅkāraṭṭhānaantaravīthīsu pariyesissāmī”ti antaravīthiyaṃ saṅkārakūṭesu tāva pilotikaṃ pariyesituṃ āraddho.

The noble youth, while searching for a bowl and robes, went neither to King Bimbisāra nor to the foot-merchants from Takkasilā. It is said that this thought occurred to him: "It is not fitting for me to search for a bowl and robes like a chicken, investigating here and there for what is pleasing and unpleasing. I will avoid the great city and search at the water-landings, charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, and in the lanes.” Thus, he first began to search for a worn-out cloth among the rubbish heaps in the lanes.

Jīvitā voropesīti etasmiṃ saṅkārakūṭe pilotikaṃ olokentaṃ vibbhantā taruṇavacchā gāvī upadhāvitvā siṅgena vijjhitvā ghātesi. Chātakajjhatto kulaputto ākāseyeva āyukkhayaṃ patvā patito. Saṅkāraṭṭhāne adhomukhaṭṭhapitā suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya ahosi, kālaṅkato ca pana avihābrahmaloke nibbatti, nibbattamattova arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Avihābrahmaloke kira nibbattamattāva satta janā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Vuttañhetaṃ –

While he was looking for a worn-out cloth in that rubbish heap, an agitated cow with a young calf ran up, gored him with its horn, and killed him. Thus he was deprived of life. The noble youth, being afflicted by hunger internally, reached the exhaustion of his life-span in mid-air and fell. In the rubbish place, he was like a golden statue placed face down. And having passed away, he was reborn in the Avihā Brahmā world, and just upon being reborn, he attained Arahantship. It is said that seven persons attained Arahantship just upon being reborn in the Avihā Brahmā world. As it has been said:

“Avihaṃ [P 5.0063] upapannāse, vimuttā satta bhikkhavo;

Rāgadosaparikkhīṇā, tiṇṇā loke visattikaṃ.

Seven monks who arose in Avihā, freed, with lust and hatred exhausted, have crossed over attachment in the world.

Ke ca te ataruṃ paṅkaṃ, maccudheyyaṃ suduttaraṃ;

Ke hitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, dibbayogaṃ upaccaguṃ.

And who are they who crossed the mire, the realm of Death so very hard to cross? Who, having abandoned the human body, have attained the divine existence?

Upako [M 4.0217] palagaṇḍo ca, pukkusāti ca te tayo;

Bhaddiyo khaṇḍadevo ca, bāhuraggi ca siṅgiyo;

Te hitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, dibbayogaṃ upaccagu”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.50, 105);

Upaka and Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti, these three; Bhaddiya and Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi and Siṅgiya; they, having abandoned the human body, have attained the divine existence.

Bimbisāropi “mayhaṃ sahāyo mayā pesitasāsanamattaṃ vācetvā hatthagataṃ rajjaṃ pahāya ettakaṃ [V 4.0227] addhānaṃ āgato, dukkaraṃ kataṃ kulaputtena, pabbajitasakkārena taṃ sakkarissāmī”ti “pariyesatha me sahāyaka”nti tattha tattha pesesi. Pesitā taṃ addasaṃsu saṅkāraṭṭhāne patitaṃ, disvā āgamma rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā gantvā kulaputtaṃ disvā – “na vata, bho, labhimhā sahāyakassa sakkāraṃ kātuṃ, anātho me jāto sahāyako”ti. Paridevitvā kulaputtaṃ mañcakena gaṇhāpetvā yuttokāse ṭhapetvā anupasampannassa sakkāraṃ kātuṃ jānanābhāvena nhāpakakappakādayo pakkosāpetvā kulaputtaṃ sīsaṃ nhāpetvā suddhavatthāni nivāsāpetvā rājavesena alaṅkārāpetvā sovaṇṇasivikaṃ āropetvā sabbatāḷāvacaragandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ karonto nagarā nīharitvā bahūhi gandhakaṭṭhehi mahācitakaṃ kāretvā kulaputtassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā dhātuyo ādāya cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

King Bimbisāra too, saying, "My friend, having merely read the message sent by me, abandoned the kingdom that had come into his hands and came this long distance. A difficult thing has been done by the noble youth. I will honor him with the respect due to one gone forth," sent men here and there, saying, "Search for my friend." Those who were sent saw him fallen in the rubbish heap. Having seen him, they returned and informed the king. The king, having gone and seen the noble youth, lamented: "Alas, sirs, we did not get to pay respect to our friend. My friend has become without a protector." Having lamented, he had the noble youth taken on a stretcher and placed in a suitable spot. Due to not knowing how to perform the honors for one not fully ordained, he had bath attendants, barbers, and others summoned. He had the noble youth's head washed, had him dressed in clean clothes, and had him adorned in royal attire. Having placed him on a golden palanquin, and making offerings with all kinds of musical instruments, perfumes, garlands, and so on, he had him brought out of the city. He had a great pyre made with much fragrant wood, performed the bodily rites for the noble youth, took the relics, and established a cetiya. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Dhātuvibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

11. Saccavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta

371. Evaṃ [V 4.0228][P 5.0064] me sutanti saccavibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha ācikkhanāti idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ nāma…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ nāmāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Apicettha paññāpanā nāma dukkhasaccādīnaṃ ṭhapanā. Āsanaṃ ṭhapento hi āsanaṃ paññapetīti vuccati. Paṭṭhapanāti paññāpanā. Vivaraṇāti vivaṭakaraṇā. Vibhajanāti vibhāgakiriyā. Uttānīkammanti pākaṭabhāvakaraṇaṃ.

371. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta. Herein, “declaring” means: “This is the noble truth of suffering… This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” The same method applies to the remaining terms. Moreover, here, “designation” means the establishing of the truth of suffering, etc. For one setting up a seat is said to “designate a seat.” “Establishing” means designation. “Explanation” means making open. “Analysis” means the act of distinguishing. “Making plain” means making apparent.

Anuggāhakāti [M 4.0218] āmisasaṅgahena dhammasaṅgahenāti dvīhipi saṅgahehi anuggāhakā. Janetāti janikā mātā. Āpādetāti posetā. Posikamātā viya moggallānoti dīpeti. Janikamātā hi nava vā dasa vā māse loṇambilādīni pariharamānā kucchiyā dārakaṃ dhāretvā kucchito nikkhantaṃ posikamātaraṃ dhātiṃ paṭicchāpeti. Sā khīranavanītādīhi dārakaṃ posetvā vaḍḍheti, so vuddhimāgamma yathāsukhaṃ vicarati. Evameva sāriputto attano vā paresaṃ vā santike pabbajite dvīhi saṅgahehi saṅgaṇhanto gilāne paṭijagganto kammaṭṭhāne yojetvā sotāpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā apāyabhayehi vuṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya – “idāni paccattapurisakārena uparimagge nibbattessantī”ti tesu anapekkho hutvā aññe nave nave ovadati. Mahāmoggallānopi attano vā paresaṃ vā santike pabbajite tatheva saṅgaṇhitvā kammaṭṭhāne yojetvā heṭṭhā tīṇi [P 5.0065] phalāni pattesupi anapekkhataṃ na āpajjati. Kasmā? Evaṃ kirassa hoti – vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, appamattakopi gūtho duggandho hoti…pe… appamattakampi muttaṃ… kheḷo… pubbo… lohitaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, evameva kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, appamattakampi bhavaṃ na vaṇṇemi antamaso accharāsaṅghatamattampī”ti (a. ni. 1.320-321). Tasmā yāva arahattaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva tesu anapekkhataṃ anāpajjitvā arahattaṃ pattesuyeva āpajjatīti. Tenāha bhagavā – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, janetā evaṃ sāriputto. Seyyathāpi jātassa āpādetā, evaṃ moggallāno. Sāriputto, bhikkhave, sotāpattiphale vineti, moggallāno uttamatthe”ti. Pahotīti sakkoti.

“Supporters” means those who support through both material assistance and Dhamma assistance. “Producer” means the birth mother. “Nurturer” means one who raises; it is shown that Moggallāna is like a foster mother. For the birth mother carries the child in her womb for nine or ten months, avoiding salty and sour things, and then, after the child has come forth from the womb, she entrusts him to a foster mother or nurse. That nurse raises the child with milk, fresh butter, and so on, nurturing him until he grows and roams freely as he pleases. In the same way, Sāriputta supports those who have gone forth, whether in his own presence or that of others, through both forms of assistance. He tends to the sick, assigns them a meditation subject, and, knowing they have attained the state of a stream-enterer, from the time they have arisen from the fears of the lower realms, he thinks, “Now they will attain the higher paths through their own personal effort.” Thus, he becomes unconcerned with them and advises other newcomers. Mahāmoggallāna, too, supports those who have gone forth, whether in his own presence or that of others, in the same way. He assigns them a meditation subject, and even when they have attained the lower three fruits, he does not become unconcerned. Why? Because it occurs to him thus: the Blessed One has said: “Just as, monks, even a small amount of excrement is foul-smelling… so too, monks, I do not praise even the slightest existence, not even for the time of a finger-snap.” Therefore, as long as they do not attain Arahantship, he does not become unconcerned with them; only when they have attained Arahantship does he become so. For that reason, the Blessed One said: “Monks, Sāriputta is like a producer. Moggallāna is like a nurturer of one who is born. Sāriputta, monks, trains for the fruit of stream-entry, Moggallāna for the highest goal.” “Is capable” means he is able.

Dukkhe [V 4.0229] ñāṇanti savanasammasanapaṭivedhañāṇaṃ, tathā dukkhasamudaye. Dukkhanirodhe savanapaṭivedhañāṇanti vaṭṭati, tathā dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya. Nekkhammasaṅkappādīsu kāmapaccanīkaṭṭhena, kāmato nissaṭabhāvena vā, kāmaṃ sammasantassa uppannoti vā, kāmapadaghātaṃ kāmavūpasamaṃ karonto uppannoti vā, kāmavivittante uppannoti vā nekkhammasaṅkappo. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Sabbepi cete pubbabhāge nānācittesu, maggakkhaṇe ekacitte labbhanti. Tatra hi micchāsaṅkappacetanāya samugghātako ekova saṅkappo labbhati, na nānā labbhati[M 4.0219]. Sammāvācādayopi pubbabhāge nānācittesu, vuttanayeneva maggakkhaṇe ekacitte labbhanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena pana saccakathā visuddhimagge ca sammādiṭṭhisutte (ma. ni. 1.89 ādayo) ca vuttāyevāti.

Knowledge of suffering is knowledge through hearing, reflection, and penetration; likewise with the origin of suffering. Regarding the cessation of suffering, it is knowledge through hearing and penetration; likewise with the path leading to the cessation of suffering. The thought of renunciation is so called because it is opposed to sensual pleasure, or because it is detached from sensual pleasure, or because it arises for one who reflects on sensual pleasure, or because it arises while destroying the basis of sensual pleasure and pacifying sensual pleasure, or because it arises at the end of seclusion from sensual pleasure. The same method applies to the other two terms. All these are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the path, they are obtained in a single consciousness. For at that moment, only the one thought that uproots the volition of wrong thought is obtained, not various thoughts. Right speech and the others, too, are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage, but, by the method stated, they are obtained in a single consciousness at the moment of the path. This is the summary here; in detail, however, the account of the truths has been stated in the Visuddhimagga and in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Saccavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta is concluded.

12. Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta

376. Evaṃ [V 4.0230][P 5.0066] me sutanti dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha mahāpajāpati gotamīti gotamīti gottaṃ. Nāmakaraṇadivase panassā laddhasakkārā brāhmaṇā lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā – “sace ayaṃ dhītaraṃ labhissati, cakkavattirañño aggamahesī bhavissati. Sace puttaṃ labhissati, cakkavattirājā bhavissatīti ubhayathāpi mahatīyevassā pajā bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Athassā mahāpajāpatīti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Idha pana gottena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā mahāpajāpatigotamīti vuttaṃ. Navanti ahataṃ. Sāmaṃ vāyitanti na sahattheneva vāyitaṃ, ekadivasaṃ pana dhātigaṇaparivutā sippikānaṃ vāyanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā vemakoṭiṃ gahetvā vāyanākāraṃ akāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

376. “Thus have I heard” begins the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta. Therein, regarding “Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī,” “Gotamī” is the clan name. On her naming day, brahmins who had received honors saw the perfection of her characteristics and prophesied: “If she has a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a wheel-turning monarch. If she has a son, he will become a wheel-turning monarch. In either case, her progeny will be great.” Then they gave her the name Mahāpajāpatī.
