Here, however, it is stated as “Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī,” combining it with the clan name. “New” means unworn. “Woven by herself” does not mean it was woven entirely by her own hand; rather, one day, surrounded by a group of nurses, she went to the weavers’ workshop, took hold of the shuttle-tip, and made the motion of weaving. This is said in reference to that.

Kadā pana gotamiyā bhagavato dussayugaṃ dātuṃ cittaṃ uppannanti. Abhisambodhiṃ patvā paṭhamagamanena kapilapuraṃ āgatakāle. Tadā hi piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ satthāraṃ gahetvā suddhodanamahārājā sakaṃ nivesanaṃ pavesesi, atha bhagavato rūpasobhaggaṃ disvā mahāpajāpatigotamī cintesi – “sobhati vata me puttassa attabhāvo”ti. Athassā balavasomanassaṃ uppajji. Tato cintesi – “mama puttassa ekūnatiṃsa vassāni agāramajjhe vasantassa antamaso mocaphalamattampi mayā dinnakameva ahosi, idānipissa cīvarasāṭakaṃ dassāmī”ti. “Imasmiṃ kho pana rājagehe bahūni mahagghāni vatthāni atthi, tāni maṃ na tosenti, sahatthā katameva maṃ toseti, sahatthā katvā dassāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādesi.

When did the thought arise for Gotamī to give a pair of cloths to the Blessed One? It was on the occasion of his first visit to Kapilapura after attaining full enlightenment. At that time, King Suddhodana escorted the Teacher, who had entered for alms, into his own palace. Then, seeing the beauty of the Blessed One’s form, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī thought: “How splendid is my son’s being!” Then strong joy arose in her. Then she reflected: “For the twenty-nine years that my son lived in the household, I had not given him even so much as a banana. Now I will give him a robe-cloth.” She then thought: “In this royal household, there are many expensive cloths, but they do not please me. Only what is made by my own hands pleases me. I will make it with my own hands and give it.”

Athantarāpaṇā [M 4.0220] kappāsaṃ āharāpetvā sahattheneva [P 5.0067] pisitvā pothetvā sukhumasuttaṃ kantitvā antovatthusmiṃyeva sālaṃ kārāpetvā sippike pakkosāpetvā sippikānaṃ attano paribhogakhādanīyabhojanīyameva datvā vāyāpesi, kālānukālañca dhātigaṇaparivutā gantvā vemakoṭiṃ aggahesi. Niṭṭhitakāle sippikānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ katvā dussayugaṃ gandhasamugge pakkhipitvā vāsaṃ gāhāpetvā – “mayhaṃ puttassa cīvarasāṭakaṃ gahetvā gamissāmī”ti rañño ārocesi[V 4.0231]. Rājā maggaṃ paṭiyādāpesi, vīthiyo sammajjitvā puṇṇaghaṭe ṭhapetvā dhajapaṭākā ussāpetvā rājagharadvārato paṭṭhāya yāva nigrodhārāmā maggaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā pupphābhikiṇṇaṃ akaṃsu. Mahāpajāpatipi sabbālaṅkāraṃ alaṅkaritvā dhātigaṇaparivutā samuggaṃ sīse ṭhapetvā bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā idaṃ me, bhante, navaṃ dussayugantiādimāha.

Then, having had cotton brought from the inner market, she herself ground it, carded it, and spun fine thread. Having had a weaving shed built right within the palace grounds, she summoned weavers, and giving the weavers her own provisions of food, she had them weave. From time to time, surrounded by her retinue of nurses, she would go and take hold of the end of the shuttle. When it was finished, having honored the weavers with a great reward, she placed the pair of cloths in a scented casket, had it brought to her quarters, and informed the king, saying: 'I will take the robe-cloth for my son and go.' The king had the road prepared. Having had the streets swept, full water pots set up, and banners and flags raised, they prepared the road from the gate of the royal palace all the way to the Nigrodha monastery and scattered it with flowers. Mahāpajāpatī, too, having adorned herself with all her ornaments and surrounded by her retinue of nurses, placed the casket on her head, went to the Blessed One, and said: 'Venerable sir, this new pair of cloths...' and so on.

Dutiyampi khoti “saṅghe gotami dehī”ti vutte – “pahomahaṃ, bhante, dussakoṭṭhāgārato bhikkhusatassāpi bhikkhusahassassāpi bhikkhusatasahassassāpi cīvaradussāni dātuṃ, idaṃ pana me bhagavantaṃ uddissa sāmaṃ kantaṃ sāmaṃ vāyitaṃ, taṃ me, bhante, bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātū”ti nimantayamānā āha. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ yāci, bhagavāpi paṭikkhipiyeva.

And a second time, when it was said, 'Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha,' she, inviting him, said: 'Venerable sir, I am able to give robe-cloths from the cloth storehouse to a hundred bhikkhus, a thousand bhikkhus, or even a hundred thousand bhikkhus. But this, venerable sir, I have spun myself and woven myself, specifically for the Blessed One. May the Blessed One accept it from me.' Thus she requested up to the third time, and the Blessed One only refused.

Kasmā pana bhagavā attano diyyamānaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa dāpetīti? Mātari anukampāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “imissā maṃ ārabbha pubbacetanā muñcacetanā paracetanāti tisso cetanā uppannā, bhikkhusaṅghampissā ārabbha uppajjantu, evamassā cha cetanā ekato hutvā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya pavattissantī”ti. Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – “saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalanti tasmā evaṃ vutta”nti. So vattabbo – “kiṃ tvaṃ satthu dinnato saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalataraṃ vadasī”ti āma vadāmīti. Suttaṃ āharāti. Saṅghe gotami dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi saṅgho cāti. Kiṃ panassa suttassa ayameva atthoti[P 5.0068]? Āma ayamevāti. Yadi evaṃ “tena hānanda, vighāsādānaṃ pūvaṃ dehī”ti ca (pāci. 269) “tena hi tva, kaccāna, vighāsādānaṃ guḷaṃ dehī”ti (mahāva. 284) ca vacanato vighāsādānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphalatarañca bhaveyya. Evampi hi “satthā attano diyyamānaṃ [M 4.0221] dāpetī”ti. Rājarājamahāmattādayopi attano āgataṃ paṇṇākāraṃ hatthigopakādīnaṃ dāpenti, te rājādīhi mahantatarā bhaveyyuṃ. Tasmā mā evaṃ gaṇha –

But why does the Blessed One have what is being given to him given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus? Out of compassion for his mother. It seems it occurred to him thus: 'With me as the object, three volitions have arisen in her: pre-donative volition, donative volition, and post-donative volition. May they also arise in her with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as the object. In this way, her six volitions, having come together, will lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time.' A sophist, however, says: 'It is because “what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit” that it was said thus.' He should be told: 'Do you say that what is given to the Saṅgha is of greater fruit than what is given to the Teacher?' 'Yes, I do.' 'Bring forth the Sutta.' 'Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha. When it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.' 'But is this the only meaning of this Sutta?' 'Yes, this is the only meaning.' 'If so, then from the statements, “In that case, Ānanda, give the cake to one who eats leftovers,” and “In that case, Kaccāna, give the molasses to one who eats leftovers,” what is given to one who eats leftovers would be of greater fruit. For in this way too, the Teacher has what is being given to him given away. Kings, royal ministers, and others also have the presents that come to them given to elephant keepers and others; would those people then be greater than the kings? Therefore, do not take it in this way:

“Nayimasmiṃ loke parasmiṃ vā pana,

Buddhena seṭṭho sadiso vā vijjati;

Yamāhuneyyānamaggataṃ gato,

Puññatthikānaṃ vipulaphalesina”nti. –

“Not in this world nor in the next is there found one superior to or equal to the Buddha, who has reached the supreme state among those worthy of offerings, for those seeking merit and searching for abundant fruit.”

Vacanato [V 4.0232] hi satthārā uttaritaro dakkhiṇeyyo nāma natthi. Evamassā cha cetanā ekato hutvā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissantīti sandhāya yāvatatiyaṃ paṭibāhitvā saṅghassa dāpesi.

For, according to that saying, there is indeed no recipient of offerings more excellent than the Teacher. Thus, with the intention that her six volitions, having come together, would lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time, after refusing up to the third time, he had her give it to the Saṅgha.

Pacchimāya janatāya saṅghe cittīkārajananatthaṃ cāpi evamāha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ahaṃ na ciraṭṭhitiko, mayhaṃ pana sāsanaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe patiṭṭhahissati, pacchimā janatā saṅghe cittīkāraṃ janetū”ti yāvatatiyaṃ paṭibāhitvā saṅghassa dāpesi. Evañhi sati – “satthā attano diyyamānampi saṅghassa dāpesi, saṅgho nāma dakkhiṇeyyo”ti pacchimā janatā saṅghe cittīkāraṃ uppādetvā cattāro paccaye dātabbe maññissati, saṅgho catūhi paccayehi akilamanto buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā samaṇadhammaṃ karissati. Evaṃ mama sāsanaṃ pañca vassasahassāni ṭhassatīti. “Paṭiggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā”ti vacanatopi cetaṃ veditabbaṃ “satthārā uttaritaro dakkhiṇeyyo nāma natthī”ti. Na hi ānandattherassa mahāpajāpatiyā āghāto vā veraṃ vā atthi. Na thero – “tassā dakkhiṇā mā mahapphalā ahosī”ti icchati. Paṇḍito hi thero bahussuto sekkhapaṭisambhidāpatto[P 5.0069], so satthu dinnassa mahapphalabhāve sampassamānova paṭiggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavāti gahaṇatthaṃ yāci.

He also spoke thus for the sake of generating respect for the Saṅgha in future generations. Indeed, this thought occurred to him: 'I will not be long-lasting, but my Dispensation will be established in the community of monks. Let future generations generate respect for the Saṅgha.' Having refused up to the third time, he had it given to the Saṅgha. For in this way, the future generation—thinking, 'The Teacher had even that which was being given to himself given to the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha, indeed, is worthy of offerings'—will generate respect for the Saṅgha and will consider the four requisites as things that should be given. The Saṅgha, not becoming weary on account of the four requisites, will learn the Buddha's word and practice the ascetic's duties. Thus my Dispensation will last for five thousand years. And from the words, 'May the Blessed One accept, venerable sir,' it should be understood that 'there is no one worthy of offerings superior to the Teacher.' For the Venerable Ānanda had no grudge or enmity towards Mahāpajāpatī. The elder did not wish, 'May her offering not be of great fruit.' For the elder was wise, learned, and had attained the analytical knowledges of a learner. He, clearly seeing the great fruitfulness of that which is given to the Teacher, requested its acceptance, saying, 'May the Blessed One accept, venerable sir.'

Puna vitaṇḍavādī āha – “saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi saṅgho cā”ti vacanato satthā saṅghapariyāpanno vāti. So vattabbo – “jānāsi pana tvaṃ kati saraṇāni, kati aveccappasādā”ti jānanto tīṇīti vakkhati, tato vattabbo – tava laddhiyā satthu saṅghapariyāpannattā dveyeva honti. Evaṃ sante ca – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, imehi [M 4.0222] tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajjaṃ upasampada”nti (mahāva. 34) evaṃ anuññātā pabbajjāpi upasampadāpi na ruhati. Tato tvaṃ neva pabbajito asi, na gihi. Sammāsambuddhe ca gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinne bhikkhū uposathampi pavāraṇampi saṅghakammānipi karonti, tāni satthu saṅghapariyāpannattā kuppāni bhaveyyuṃ, na ca honti. Tasmā na vattabbametaṃ “satthā saṅghapariyāpanno”ti.

Again, the sophist says: 'Because of the statement, "When you give to the Sangha, I will be honored, and the Sangha too," the Teacher is included in the Sangha.' He should be told: 'Do you know how many refuges there are, how many unwavering faiths there are?' Knowing, he will say, 'Three.' Then he should be told: 'According to your view, because the Teacher is included in the Sangha, there are only two. And if this were so, the going forth and higher ordination permitted thus, "I allow, monks, the going forth and higher ordination by means of these three goings for refuge," would not be valid. Therefore, you are neither one who has gone forth nor a householder. Furthermore, while the Perfectly Enlightened One is seated in the fragrant chamber, the monks perform the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and other acts of the Sangha. Because the Teacher is included in the Sangha, those acts would be invalid, but they are not. Therefore, this should not be said: "The Teacher is included in the Sangha."

377. Āpādikāti saṃvaḍḍhikā, tumhākaṃ hatthapādesu hatthapādakiccaṃ asādhentesu hatthe ca pāde [V 4.0233] ca vaḍḍhetvā paṭijaggikāti attho. Posikāti divasassa dve tayo vāre nhāpetvā bhojetvā pāyetvā tumhe posesi. Thaññaṃ pāyesīti nandakumāro kira bodhisattato katipāheneva daharo, tasmiṃ jāte mahāpajāpati attano puttaṃ dhātīnaṃ datvā sayaṃ bodhisattassa dhātikiccaṃ sādhayamānā attano thaññaṃ pāyesi. Taṃ sandhāya thero evamāha. Iti mahāpajāpatiyā bahūpakārataṃ kathetvā idāni [P 5.0070] tathāgatassa bahūpakārataṃ dassento bhagavāpi, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha bhagavantaṃ, bhante, āgammāti bhagavantaṃ paṭicca nissāya sandhāya.

377. `Āpādikā` means a foster-mother; the meaning is that when your hands and feet were not accomplishing their functions, she tended to you, having caused your hands and feet to grow. `Posikā` means she nourished you, having bathed, fed, and given you drink two or three times a day. 'She gave you her milk to drink' refers to this: it is said that Prince Nanda was younger than the Bodhisatta by only a few days. When he was born, Mahāpajāpatī, having given her own son to wet nurses, herself accomplished the duties of a wet nurse for the Bodhisatta and gave him her own milk to drink. With reference to that, the elder spoke thus. Thus, having spoken of Mahāpajāpatī's great helpfulness, now, showing the Tathāgata's great helpfulness, he said, 'The Blessed One also, venerable sir...' and so on. Therein, 'on account of the Blessed One, venerable sir' means because of, depending on, and with reference to the Blessed One.

378. Atha bhagavā dvīsu upakāresu atirekataraṃ anumodanto evametantiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ hānanda, puggalo puggalaṃ āgammāti yaṃ ācariyapuggalaṃ antevāsikapuggalo āgamma. Imassānanda, puggalassa iminā puggalenāti imassa ācariyapuggalassa iminā antevāsikapuggalena. Na suppaṭikāraṃ vadāmīti paccūpakāraṃ na sukaraṃ vadāmi, abhivādanādīsu ācariyaṃ disvā abhivādanakaraṇaṃ abhivādanaṃ nāma. Yasmiṃ vā disābhāge ācariyo vasati, iriyāpathe vā kappento tadabhimukho vanditvā gacchati, vanditvā nisīdati, vanditvā nipajjati, ācariyaṃ pana dūratova disvā paccuṭṭhāya paccuggamanakaraṇaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Ācariyaṃ pana disvā añjaliṃ paggayha sīse ṭhapetvā ācariyaṃ namassati, yasmiṃ vā disābhāge so vasati, tadabhimukhopi tatheva namassati, gacchantopi ṭhitopi nisinnopi añjaliṃ paggayha namassatiyevāti idaṃ añjalikammaṃ nāma. Anucchavikakammassa pana karaṇaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ nāma. Cīvarādīsu cīvaraṃ dento na yaṃ vā taṃ vā deti, mahagghaṃ satamūlikampi pañcasatamūlikampi sahassamūlikampi detiyeva[M 4.0223]. Piṇḍapātādīsupi eseva nayo. Kiṃ bahunā, catūhi paṇītapaccayehi cakkavāḷantaraṃ pūretvā sinerupabbatena kūṭaṃ gahetvā dentopi ācariyassa anucchavikaṃ kiriyaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotiyeva.

378. Then the Blessed One, expressing even greater appreciation for the two helpful acts, said, 'So it is, Ānanda...' and so on. Therein, 'Ānanda, on account of which person another person...' means on account of which teacher-person a student-person... 'For this person, Ānanda, by this person...' means for this teacher-person, by this student-person. 'I do not say it is easy to repay' means I do not say a return of service is easy. `Abhivādana` is the name for seeing the teacher and making a salutation. Or, in whatever direction the teacher dwells, one faces that direction and pays homage before going, sitting, or lying down. But seeing the teacher from afar, rising, and going to meet him is called `paccuṭṭhāna`. And `añjalikamma` is this: seeing the teacher, one raises the joined hands, places them on the head, and pays homage. Or in whatever direction he dwells, one faces him and pays homage in the same way; whether walking, standing, or sitting, one raises the joined hands and pays homage. But the doing of a suitable action is called `sāmīcikamma`. Among robes and so on, when giving a robe, one does not give just any old thing; one gives a valuable one worth a hundred, five hundred, or even a thousand. This is the same method for almsfood and so on. What is the use of saying much? Even if one were to fill the space within the world-sphere with the four excellent requisites and give it, having taken a peak the size of Mount Sineru, one is still not able to perform a suitable action for the teacher.

379. Cuddasa kho panimāti kasmā ārabhi? Idaṃ suttaṃ pāṭipuggalikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ ārabbha samuṭṭhitaṃ. Ānandattheropi “paṭiggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā”ti pāṭipuggalikadakkhiṇaṃyeva [P 5.0071] samādapeti, cuddasasu ca ṭhānesu dinnadānaṃ pāṭipuggalikaṃ nāma hotīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Ayaṃ paṭhamāti ayaṃ dakkhiṇā guṇavasenapi paṭhamā jeṭṭhakavasenapi. Ayañhi paṭhamā aggā jeṭṭhikā, imissā dakkhiṇāya pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Dutiyatatiyāpi [V 4.0234] paramadakkhiṇāyeva, sesā paramadakkhiṇabhāvaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Bāhirake kāmesu vītarāgeti kammavādikiriyavādimhi lokiyapañcābhiññe. Puthujjanasīlavanteti puthujjanasīlavā nāma gosīladhātuko hoti, asaṭho amāyāvī paraṃ apīḷetvā dhammena samena kasiyā vā vaṇijjāya vā jīvikaṃ kappetā. Puthujjanadussīleti puthujjanadussīlā nāma kevaṭṭamacchabandhādayo paraṃ pīḷāya jīvikaṃ kappetā.

379. Why was the teaching beginning with 'These are the fourteen' undertaken? This discourse arose concerning an offering to an individual. The Elder Ānanda also caused him to accept only the offering to an individual, saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept.' And, to show that 'a gift given in the fourteen instances is called an individual offering,' he undertook this teaching. As for 'This is the first,' this offering is first by the power of virtue and also first by the power of seniority. For this first offering is supreme and eldest; for this offering, there is no measure. The second and third are also supreme offerings indeed, but the remaining ones do not reach the state of a supreme offering. As for 'one outside the Dispensation who is free from lust for sensual pleasures,' this refers to one who is a proponent of kamma and action and who has attained the five mundane higher knowledges. As for 'a virtuous worldling,' a virtuous worldling is one who has the nature of a cow's virtue, is not deceitful, not fraudulent, and earns a living without oppressing others, righteously and justly, by farming or trade. As for 'an immoral worldling,' immoral worldlings are those such as fishermen and hunters who earn a living by oppressing others.

Idāni pāṭipuggalikadakkhiṇāya vipākaṃ paricchindanto tatrānandātiādimāha. Tattha tiracchānagateti yaṃ guṇavasena upakāravasena posanatthaṃ dinnaṃ, idaṃ na gahitaṃ. Yampi ālopaaḍḍhaālopamattaṃ dinnaṃ, tampi na gahitaṃ. Yaṃ pana sunakhasūkarakukkuṭakākādīsu yassa kassaci sampattassa phalaṃ paṭikaṅkhitvā yāvadatthaṃ dinnaṃ, idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tiracchānagate dānaṃ datvā”ti. Sataguṇāti satānisaṃsā. Pāṭikaṅkhitabbāti icchitabbā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayaṃ dakkhiṇā āyusataṃ vaṇṇasataṃ sukhasataṃ balasataṃ paṭibhānasatanti pañca ānisaṃsasatāni deti, attabhāvasate [P 5.0072] āyuṃ deti, vaṇṇaṃ, sukhaṃ, balaṃ, paṭibhānaṃ deti, nipparitasaṃ karoti. Bhavasatepi vutte ayameva attho. Iminā upāyena sabbattha nayo netabbo.

Now, wishing to define the result of an offering to an individual, he spoke the words beginning with 'There, Ānanda...' Therein, as for 'to one born as an animal,' that which is given for the purpose of nourishment by way of virtue or by way of assistance, this is not taken here. Also, that which is given to the extent of a morsel or half a morsel, that too is not taken. But that which is given as much as desired to any animal that has arrived—such as a dog, pig, chicken, or crow—while desiring the fruit, it is with reference to this that it was said, 'having given a gift to one born as an animal.' 'One hundredfold' means one hundred benefits. 'To be expected' means to be desired. This is what is meant: this offering gives five hundred benefits—a hundredfold lifespan, a hundredfold beauty, a hundredfold happiness, a hundredfold strength, and a hundredfold wisdom. In one hundred existences, it gives long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom; it produces a result that has long life as its cause. Even when 'in one hundred existences' is said, this is the very meaning. By this method, the principle should be understood in all cases.

Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanneti ettha heṭṭhimakoṭiyā tisaraṇaṃ gato upāsakopi sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno nāma, tasmiṃ dinnadānampi asaṅkhyeyyaṃ appameyyaṃ. Pañcasīle patiṭṭhitassa tato uttari mahapphalaṃ, dasasīle patiṭṭhitassa tato [M 4.0224] uttari, tadahupabbajitassa sāmaṇerassa tato uttari, upasampannabhikkhuno tato uttari, upasampannasseva vattasampannassa tato uttari, vipassakassa tato uttari, āraddhavipassakassa tato uttari, uttamakoṭiyā pana maggasamaṅgī sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno nāma. Etassa dinnadānaṃ tato uttari mahapphalameva.

Herein, regarding 'one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry,' at the lower limit, even a lay follower who has gone to the three refuges is called 'one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.' A gift given to such a one is also incalculable and immeasurable. For one established in the five precepts, the fruit is greater than that. For one established in the ten precepts, it is greater still. For a novice who has gone forth that very day, it is greater still. For a fully ordained monk, it is greater still. For a fully ordained monk who is also accomplished in observances, it is greater still. For one practicing insight, it is greater still. For one who has undertaken insight meditation, it is greater still. But at the highest limit, one endowed with the path is called 'one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.' A gift given to this one is indeed of even greater fruit than that.

Kiṃ pana maggasamaṅgissa sakkā dānaṃ dātunti? Āma sakkā. Āraddhavipassako hi pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, tassa gehadvāre ṭhitassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ pakkhipanti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bhikkhuno maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, idaṃ dānaṃ maggasamaṅgino dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Atha vā panesa āsanasālāya nisinno hoti, manussā gantvā [V 4.0235] patte khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ ṭhapenti, tasmiṃ khaṇe tassa maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, idampi dānaṃ maggasamaṅgino dinnaṃ nāma. Atha vā panassa vihāre vā āsanasālāya vā nisinnassa upāsakā pattaṃ ādāya attano gharaṃ gantvā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ pakkhipanti, tasmiṃ khaṇe tassa maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, idampi dānaṃ maggasamaṅgino dinnaṃ nāma. Tattha [P 5.0073] soṇḍiyaṃ udakassa viya sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanne dinnadānassa asaṅkhyeyyatā veditabbā. Tāsu tāsu mahānadīsu mahāsamudde ca udakassa viya sotāpannādīsu dinnadānassa uttaritaravasena asaṅkhyeyyatā veditabbā. Pathaviyā khayamaṇḍalamatte padese paṃsuṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva mahāpathaviyā paṃsuno appameyyatāyapi ayamattho dīpetabbo.

But is it possible to give a gift to one endowed with the path? Yes, it is possible. Indeed, one who has undertaken insight meditation takes his bowl and robe and enters a village for alms. While he is standing at the door of a house, they take the bowl from his hand and place hard and soft food in it. At that moment, the arising from the path occurs for the monk. This gift is called 'one given to a person endowed with the path.' Or else, this monk is sitting in a dining hall, and people go and place hard and soft food in his bowl. At that moment, the arising from the path occurs for him. This gift, too, is called 'one given to a person endowed with the path.' Or else, while he is sitting in the monastery or in the dining hall, lay followers take his bowl, go to their own house, and place hard and soft food in it. At that moment, the arising from the path occurs for him. This gift, too, is called 'one given to a person endowed with the path.' Therein, just as the water in the ocean is incalculable, so the incalculability of a gift given to one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry should be known. Just as the water in those great rivers and in the great ocean is incalculable, so the incalculability of a gift given to stream-enterers and so on should be known by way of its being successively superior. This meaning should also be understood through the immeasurability of the dust, beginning with the dust in a place the size of a threshing floor up to the dust of the entire great earth.

380. Satta kho panimāti kasmā ārabhi? “Saṅghe gotami dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi saṅgho cā”ti hi vuttaṃ, tattha sattasu ṭhānesu dinnadānaṃ saṅghe dinnaṃ nāma hotīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha buddhappamukhe ubhatosaṅgheti ekato bhikkhusaṅgho, ekato bhikkhunisaṅgho, satthā majjhe nisinno hotīti ayaṃ buddhappamukho ubhatosaṅgho nāma. Ayaṃ paṭhamāti imāya dakkhiṇāya samappamāṇā dakkhiṇā nāma natthi. Dutiyadakkhiṇādayo pana etaṃ paramadakkhiṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti.

380. Why was the teaching beginning with 'These are the seven' undertaken? Indeed, it was said: 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha. When it is given to the Saṅgha by you, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.' Therefore, to show that 'a gift given in the seven instances is called a gift given to the Saṅgha,' this teaching was undertaken. Therein, as for 'to the twofold Saṅgha headed by the Buddha': on one side the Saṅgha of monks is seated, on one side the Saṅgha of nuns is seated, and the Teacher is seated in the middle. Therefore, this Saṅgha is called 'the twofold Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.' As for 'This is the first': there is no offering of equal measure to this offering. But the second offering and so on do not reach this supreme offering.

Kiṃ [M 4.0225] pana tathāgate parinibbute buddhappamukhassa ubhatosaṅghassa dānaṃ dātuṃ sakkāti? Sakkā. Kathaṃ? Ubhatosaṅghassa hi pamukhe sadhātukaṃ paṭimaṃ āsane ṭhapetvā ādhārakaṃ ṭhapetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ satthu paṭhamaṃ datvā ubhatosaṅghassa dātabbaṃ, evaṃ buddhappamukhassa ubhatosaṅghassa dānaṃ dinnaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha yaṃ satthu dinnaṃ, taṃ kiṃ kātabbanti? Yo satthāraṃ paṭijaggati vattasampanno bhikkhu, tassa dātabbaṃ. Pitusantakañhi puttassa pāpuṇāti, bhikkhusaṅghassa dātumpi vaṭṭati, sappitelāni pana gahetvā dīpā jalitabbā, sāṭakaṃ gahetvā paṭākā āropetabbāti. Bhikkhusaṅgheti [P 5.0074] aparicchinnakamahābhikkhusaṅghe. Bhikkhunisaṅghepi eseva nayo.

But is it possible, after the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, to give an offering to the twofold Saṅgha headed by the Buddha? It is possible. How? At the head of the twofold Saṅgha, having placed an image containing relics on a seat, having set up a bowl-stand, and beginning with the water of dedication, one should first give everything to the Teacher and then give to the twofold Saṅgha. In this way, an offering is said to be given to the twofold Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. In that case, what should be done with what was given to the Teacher? It should be given to a bhikkhu, accomplished in the duties pertaining to the shrine, who attends to the Teacher. For what belongs to the father reaches the son. It is also proper to give to the community of bhikkhus. Furthermore, taking ghee and oil, lamps should be lit; taking a cloth, banners should be raised. By 'community of bhikkhus' is meant the great, unrestricted community of bhikkhus. In the case of the community of bhikkhunīs too, this same method should be understood.

Gotrabhunoti gottamattakameva anubhavamānā, nāmamattasamaṇāti attho. Kāsāvakaṇṭhāti kāsāvakaṇṭhanāmakā. Te kira ekaṃ kāsāvakhaṇḍaṃ hatthe vā gīvāya vā bandhitvā vicarissanti[V 4.0236]. Gharadvāraṃ pana tesaṃ puttabhariyā kasivaṇijjādikammāni ca pākatikāneva bhavissanti. Tesu dussīlesu saṅghaṃ uddissa dānaṃ dassantīti ettha dussīlasaṅghanti na vuttaṃ. Saṅgho hi dussīlo nāma natthi. Dussīlā pana upāsakā tesu dussīlesu bhikkhusaṅghaṃ uddissa saṅghassa demāti dānaṃ dassanti. Iti bhagavatā buddhappamukhe saṅghe dinnadakkhiṇāpi guṇasaṅkhāya asaṅkhyeyyāti vuttaṃ. Kāsāvakaṇṭhasaṅghe dinnadakkhiṇāpi guṇasaṅkhāyeva asaṅkhyeyyāti vuttā. Saṅghagatā dakkhiṇā hi saṅghe cittīkāraṃ kātuṃ sakkontassa hoti, saṅghe pana cittīkāro dukkaro hoti.

'Gotrabhū' means those who partake only of the lineage of monks; the meaning is, they are samaṇas in name only. 'Kāsāvakaṇṭhā' means immoral persons named 'ochre-necked'. It is said they will wander about, having tied a piece of ochre cloth on their hand or neck. However, their households, wives and children, and activities such as farming and trade will be just like those of ordinary people. In the passage, 'They will give an offering to those immoral ones, dedicating it to the Saṅgha,' it is not said 'immoral Saṅgha'. Indeed, there is no such thing as an immoral Saṅgha. Rather, lay followers will give an offering to those immoral ones, dedicating it to the community of bhikkhus and saying, 'We give to the Saṅgha.' Thus, it was said by the Blessed One that an offering given to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is immeasurable by way of counting its merit. An offering given to the Kāsāvakaṇṭha-saṅgha is also said to be immeasurable in merit. For an offering directed to the Saṅgha is for one who is able to show reverence to the Saṅgha, but reverence for the Saṅgha is difficult to do.

Yo hi saṅghagataṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dassāmīti deyyadhammaṃ paṭiyādetvā vihāraṃ gantvā, – “bhante, saṅghaṃ uddissa ekaṃ theraṃ dethā”ti vadati, atha saṅghato sāmaṇeraṃ labhitvā “sāmaṇero me laddho”ti aññathattaṃ āpajjati, tassa dakkhiṇā saṅghagatā na hoti. Mahātheraṃ labhitvāpi “mahāthero me laddho”ti somanassaṃ uppādentassāpi na hotiyeva. Yo pana sāmaṇeraṃ vā upasampannaṃ vā daharaṃ vā theraṃ vā bālaṃ vā paṇḍitaṃ vā yaṃkiñci saṅghato labhitvā nibbematiko hutvā saṅghassa demīti saṅghe cittīkāraṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, tassa dakkhiṇā saṅghagatā nāma hoti. Parasamuddavāsino [P 5.0075] kira evaṃ karonti.

For a donor who, having prepared an offering with the thought, 'I will give an offering directed to the Saṅgha,' goes to the monastery and says, 'Venerable sirs, designating from the Saṅgha, please give me one thera,' and then, having received a sāmaṇera from the Saṅgha, falls into a different state of mind, thinking, 'I have received a sāmaṇera'—his offering is not one directed to the Saṅgha. Even for one who, having received a great thera, generates gladness thinking, 'I have received a great thera,' it is not so at all. But a donor who, having received from the Saṅgha a sāmaṇera or an ordained one, a junior or a thera, a foolish one or a wise one—anyone at all—becomes free from doubt and is able to show reverence to the Saṅgha, thinking, 'I am giving to the Saṅgha'—his offering is called one directed to the Saṅgha. It is said that those dwelling across the ocean do so.

Tattha [M 4.0226] hi eko vihārasāmi kuṭumbiko “saṅghagataṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dassāmī”ti saṅghato uddisitvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ dethāti yāci. So ekaṃ dussīlabhikkhuṃ labhitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ opuñjāpetvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā upari vitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhadhūmapupphehi pūjetvā pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā buddhassa nipaccakāraṃ karonto viya saṅghe cittīkārena deyyadhammaṃ adāsi. So bhikkhu pacchābhattaṃ vihārajagganatthāya kudālakaṃ dethāti gharadvāraṃ āgato, upāsako nisinnova kudālaṃ pādena khipitvā “gaṇhā”ti adāsi. Tamenaṃ manussā āhaṃsu – “tumhehi pātova etassa katasakkāro vattuṃ na sakkā, idāni upacāramattakampi natthi, kiṃ nāmeta”nti. Upāsako – “saṅghassa so ayyā cittīkāro, na etassā”ti āha. Kāsāvakaṇṭhasaṅghassa dinnadakkhiṇaṃ pana ko sodhetīti? Sāriputtamoggallānādayo asīti mahātherā sodhentīti. Apica therā ciraparinibbutā, there ādiṃ katvā yāvajja dharamānā khīṇāsavā sodhentiyeva.

For there, a householder who was the patron of a monastery, thinking, 'I will give an offering directed to the Saṅgha,' requested, 'Designating from the Saṅgha, give me one bhikkhu.' Having received an immoral bhikkhu, he had the sitting place smeared with wet cow-dung, prepared a seat, tied a canopy above, paid homage with perfumes, incense, and flowers, washed his feet, anointed them with oil, and, as if paying obeisance to the Buddha, gave the offering with reverence for the Saṅgha. After the meal, that bhikkhu came to the house door for the purpose of tending to the monastery and said, 'Give me a spade.' The upāsaka, while still seated, tossed the spade with his foot and said, 'Take it.' People said to him, 'The respect you showed him this morning is impossible to describe, but now there is not even the slightest courtesy. What is this?' The upāsaka replied, 'Sirs, that reverence was for the Saṅgha, not for him.' But who purifies an offering given to the Kāsāvakaṇṭha-saṅgha? The eighty great theras, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, purify it. Moreover, though the theras attained Parinibbāna long ago, starting from those theras up to the present day, the living Arahants still purify it.

Na tvevāhaṃ[V 4.0237], ānanda, kenaci pariyāyena saṅghagatāya dakkhiṇāyāti ettha atthi buddhappamukho saṅgho, atthi etarahi saṅgho, atthi anāgate kāsāvakaṇṭhasaṅgho. Buddhappamukho saṅgho etarahi saṅghena na upanetabbo, etarahi saṅgho anāgate kāsāvakaṇṭhasaṅghena saddhiṃ na upanetabbo. Tena teneva samayena kathetabbaṃ. Saṅghato uddisitvā gahitasamaṇaputhujjano hi pāṭipuggaliko sotāpanno, saṅghe cittīkāraṃ kātuṃ sakkontassa puthujjanasamaṇe dinnaṃ mahapphalataraṃ. Uddisitvā gahito sotāpanno pāṭipuggaliko sakadāgāmītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Saṅghe cittīkāraṃ kātuṃ sakkontassa hi khīṇāsave dinnadānato uddisitvā gahite dussīlepi dinnaṃ mahapphalatarameva[P 5.0076]. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “sīlavato kho, mahārāja, dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, no tathā dussīle”ti, taṃ imaṃ nayaṃ pahāya “catasso kho imānanda, dakkhiṇā visuddhiyo”ti imasmiṃ catukke daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding the passage, 'I do not say, Ānanda, that in any way an offering directed to the Saṅgha...': there is the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, there is the present Saṅgha, and there is the future Kāsāvakaṇṭha-saṅgha. The Saṅgha headed by the Buddha should not be compared with the present Saṅgha, and the present Saṅgha should not be compared with the future Kāsāvakaṇṭha-saṅgha. It should be spoken of according to its own time. For one who is able to show reverence to the Saṅgha, a gift given to a worldling monk designated by the Saṅgha is of greater fruit than a gift given to a stream-enterer as an individual recipient. This same method should be understood in cases such as a gift to a stream-enterer designated by the Saṅgha versus a gift to a once-returner as an individual recipient, and so on. Indeed, for one who is able to show reverence to the Saṅgha, a gift given to an immoral person designated by the Saṅgha is of greater fruit than a gift given to an Arahant. As for the statement, 'Great king, a gift given to a virtuous person is of great fruit, not so to an immoral one,' that should be understood by setting aside this method and viewing it within this fourfold discourse on the 'four purifications of offerings, Ānanda.'

381. Dāyakato visujjhatīti mahapphalabhāvena visujjhati, mahapphalā hotīti attho. Kalyāṇadhammoti sucidhammo, na pāpadhammo. Dāyakato visujjhatīti cettha vessantaramahārājā kathetabbo. So hi jūjakabrāhmaṇassa dārake datvā pathaviṃ kampesi.

381. 'It is purified by the donor' means it is purified by way of becoming of great fruit; the meaning is, it becomes of great fruit. 'Of wholesome nature' means of pure nature, not of evil nature. Here, regarding 'it is purified by the donor,' King Vessantara should be spoken of. For he, having given his children to the brahmin Jūjaka, caused the earth to tremble.

Paṭiggāhakato [M 4.0227] visujjhatīti ettha kalyāṇīnadīmukhadvāravāsikevaṭṭo kathetabbo. So kira dīghasomattherassa tikkhattumpi piṇḍapātaṃ datvā maraṇamañce nipanno “ayyassa maṃ dīghasomattherassa dinnapiṇḍapāto uddharatī”ti āha.

Here, regarding 'it is purified by the recipient,' the story of the fisherman living at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River should be told. It is said that having given alms-food to the Elder Dīghasoma three times, while lying on his deathbed, he said, 'The alms-food given to the noble Elder Dīghasoma delivers me.'

Neva dāyakatoti ettha vaḍḍhamānavāsiluddako kathetabbo. So kira petadakkhiṇaṃ dento ekassa dussīlasseva tayo vāre adāsi, tatiyavāre “amanusso dussīlo maṃ vilumpatī”ti viravi, ekassa sīlavantabhikkhuno datvā pāpitakāleyevassa pāpuṇi.

Here, regarding 'neither from the donor...,' the story of the hunter living in Vaḍḍhamāna should be told. It is said that while giving an offering dedicated to the dead, he gave to just one immoral person three times. On the third occasion, the non-human (the peta) lamented, 'The immoral one is robbing me!' Having given to one virtuous monk, it reached him (the peta) at the very time of dedication.

Dāyakato ceva visujjhatīti ettha asadisadānaṃ kathetabbaṃ.

Here, regarding 'it is purified by the donor as well...,' the Asadisadāna (Incomparable Gift) should be told of.

Sā dakkhiṇā dāyakato visujjhatīti ettha yathā nāma cheko kassako asārampi khettaṃ labhitvā samaye kasitvā paṃsuṃ apanetvā sārabījāni patiṭṭhapetvā rattindivaṃ ārakkhe [P 5.0077] pamādaṃ anāpajjanto [V 4.0238] aññassa sārakhettato adhikataraṃ dhaññaṃ labhati, evaṃ sīlavā dussīlassa datvāpi phalaṃ mahantaṃ adhigacchatīti. Iminā upāyena sabbapadesu visujjhanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“That offering is purified by the donor”—here, just as a skilled farmer, obtaining even a worthless field, plows it in season, removes the dust, plants good seeds, and guards it day and night without negligence, gaining more grain than from another's fertile field, so too a virtuous person, even giving to an immoral one, attains great fruit. By this method, purification should be understood in all instances.

Vītarāgo vītarāgesūti ettha vītarāgo nāma anāgāmī, arahā pana ekantavītarāgova, tasmā arahatā arahato dinnadānameva aggaṃ. Kasmā? Bhavālayassa bhavapatthanāya abhāvato. Nanu khīṇāsavo dānaphalaṃ na saddahatīti? Dānaphalaṃ saddahantā khīṇāsavasadisā na honti. Khīṇāsavena katakammaṃ pana nicchandarāgattā kusalaṃ vā akusalaṃ vā na hoti, kiriyaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, tenevassa dānaṃ aggaṃ hotīti vadanti.

Here, regarding '(a gift from) one free from lust to those free from lust': 'one free from lust' means a non-returner, but an Arahant is one completely free from lust. Therefore, a gift given by an Arahant to an Arahant is indeed the highest. Why? Because of the absence of craving for existence and aspiration for existence in both. Is it not so that one whose taints are destroyed does not believe in the fruit of giving? Those who believe in the fruit of giving are not like one whose taints are destroyed. However, for one whose taints are destroyed, an action done, being without desire and lust, is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; it stands in the category of a functional action. For that very reason, they say, their gift is the highest.

Kiṃ pana sammāsambuddhena sāriputtattherassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, udāhu sāriputtattherena sammāsambuddhassa dinnanti. Sammāsambuddhena sāriputtattherassa dinnaṃ mahapphalanti vadanti. Sammāsambuddhañhi ṭhapetvā añño dānassa vipākaṃ jānituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Dānañhi catūhi sampadāhi dātuṃ sakkontassa tasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Tatrimā sampadā – deyyadhammassa dhammena [M 4.0228] samena paraṃ apīḷetvā uppannatā, pubbacetanādivasena cetanāya mahattatā, khīṇāsavabhāvena guṇātirekatā, taṃdivasaṃ nirodhato vuṭṭhitabhāvena vatthusampannatāti.

Now, is a gift given by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One to the Elder Sāriputta of great fruit, or is a gift given by the Elder Sāriputta to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One? They say that the gift given by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One to the Elder Sāriputta is of great fruit. For apart from the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there is truly no one else capable of knowing the result of giving. A gift, indeed, given by one who is able to give with four accomplishments, yields its result in that very existence. Here are these accomplishments: the object to be given having arisen righteously, justly, without oppressing others; the greatness of intention due to preliminary intention and so on; the superiority of qualities due to the state of being one whose taints are destroyed; and the accomplishment of the recipient due to having arisen from cessation on that very day.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta is concluded.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is concluded.

5. Saḷāyatanavaggo

5. The Section on the Six Sense-Bases.

1. Anāthapiṇḍikovādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discourse of Admonition to Anāthapiṇḍika.

383. Evaṃ [V 4.0239][M 4.0229] me sutanti anāthapiṇḍikovādasuttaṃ. Tattha bāḷhagilānoti adhimattagilāno maraṇaseyyaṃ upagato. Āmantesīti [P 5.0078] gahapatissa kira yāva pādā vahiṃsu, tāva divase sakiṃ vā dvikkhattuṃ vā tikkhattuṃ vā buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ akāsi. Yattakañcassa satthu upaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi, tattakaṃyeva mahātherānaṃ. So ajja gamanapādassa pacchinnattā anuṭṭhānaseyyaṃ upagato sāsanaṃ pesetukāmo aññataraṃ purisaṃ āmantesi. Tenupasaṅkamīti bhagavantaṃ āpucchitvā sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya upasaṅkami.

383. Thus have I heard—this is the Discourse on the Admonition to Anāthapiṇḍika. Therein, bāḷhagilāno (severely ill) means: being excessively ill, he has approached the deathbed. Āmantesi (he addressed) means: it is said that as long as the householder's feet could carry him, he would attend upon the Buddha once, twice, or thrice a day without interruption. And his attendance upon the great elders was just as much as his attendance upon the Teacher. Today, because his ability to walk was cut off, having reached the bed from which he could not rise, that householder, wishing to send a message, addressed a certain man. Tenupasaṅkami (he approached him) means: the Elder Sāriputta, having taken leave of the Blessed One, approached at the time of sunset.

384. Paṭikkamantīti osakkanti, tanukā bhavanti. Abhikkamantīti abhivaḍḍhanti ottharanti, balavatiyo honti.

384. Paṭikkamanti (Do they retreat?) means: Do they recede? Do they become weak? Abhikkamanti (Do they advance?) means: Do they increase? Do they overwhelm? Do they become powerful?

Abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamoti yasmiñhi samaye māraṇantikā vedanā uppajjati, uparivāte jalitaggi viya hoti, yāva usmā na pariyādiyati, tāva mahatāpi upakkamena na sakkā vūpasametuṃ, usmāya pana pariyādinnāya vūpasammati.

As for Abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo (Their advance is discerned, not their retreat): Because at the time when feelings that have death as their end arise, it is like a burning lamp in an updraft. As long as the heat element born of kamma is not exhausted, it is not possible to appease the painful feeling, even with great effort. However, when the heat element is exhausted, it is pacified.

385. Athāyasmā sāriputto cintesi – “ayaṃ mahāseṭṭhissa vedanā māraṇantikā, na sakkā paṭibāhituṃ, avasesā kathā niratthakā, dhammakathamassa kathessāmī”ti. Atha naṃ taṃ kathento tasmātihātiādimāha. Tattha tasmāti yasmā cakkhuṃ tīhi gāhehi gaṇhanto uppannaṃ māraṇantikaṃ vedanaṃ paṭibāhituṃ samattho nāma natthi, tasmā. Na cakkhuṃ upādiyissāmīti cakkhuṃ [V 4.0240] tīhi gāhehi na gaṇhissāmi. Na ca me cakkhunissitaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāpi me cakkhunissitaṃ na bhavissati. Na rūpanti heṭṭhā āyatanarūpaṃ kathitaṃ, imasmiṃ ṭhāne sabbampi kāmabhavarūpaṃ kathento evamāha.

385. Then the Venerable Sāriputta thought: 'This feeling of the great merchant has death as its end; it cannot be prevented. Other talk is fruitless. I will give a Dhamma talk to him.' Then, wishing to deliver that talk to him, he spoke the words beginning with Tasmātiha. Therein, tasmā (therefore) means: because a person who grasps the eye with the three kinds of grasping is not able to prevent the arisen feeling that has death as its end, therefore... As for Na cakkhuṃ upādiyissāmi (I will not cling to the eye): I will not grasp the eye with the three kinds of grasping. As for Na ca me cakkhunissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ (And for me, there will be no consciousness dependent on the eye): My eye-consciousness will not be dependent on the eye-faculty. By the phrase Na rūpaṃ (not form): previously, form as a sense-base was spoken of; in this instance, wishing to speak of all form belonging to the kāma-sphere, the Elder spoke thus.

386. Na idhalokanti vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vā ghāsacchādanaṃ vā [P 5.0079] na upādiyissāmīti attho. Idañhi paccayesu aparitassanatthaṃ kathitaṃ. Na paralokanti [M 4.0230] ettha pana manussalokaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā paralokā nāma. Idaṃ – “asukadevaloke nibbattitvā asukaṭṭhāne bhavissāmi, idaṃ nāma khādissāmi bhuñjissāmi nivāsessāmi pārupissāmī”ti evarūpāya paritassanāya pahānatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tampi na upādiyissāmi, na ca me tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ tīhi gāhehi parimocetvā thero desanaṃ arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhapesi.

386. As for Na idhalokaṃ (Not this world): the meaning is, 'I will not cling to a place of residence or to food and clothing.' This was spoken for the purpose of not craving for requisites. As for Na paralokaṃ (Not the next world): here, setting aside the human world, the remaining worlds are called 'the next world'. This was spoken for the purpose of abandoning craving of this sort: 'Having been reborn in such-and-such a deva world, I will dwell in such-and-such a place; I will eat this hard food; I will consume this soft food; I will wear this lower garment; I will don this upper garment.' 'I will not cling to that next world either, and for me there will be no consciousness dependent on that.' Thus, causing liberation from the three kinds of grasping, the Elder concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

387. Olīyasīti attano sampattiṃ disvā ārammaṇesu bajjhasi allīyasīti. Iti āyasmā ānando – “ayampi nāma gahapati evaṃ saddho pasanno maraṇabhayassa bhāyati, añño ko na bhāyissatī”ti maññamāno tassa gāḷhaṃ katvā ovādaṃ dento evamāha. Na ca me evarūpī dhammīkathā sutapubbāti ayaṃ upāsako – “satthu santikāpi me evarūpī dhammakathā na sutapubbā”ti vadati, kiṃ satthā evarūpi sukhumaṃ gambhīrakathaṃ na kathetīti? No na katheti. Evaṃ pana cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni cha bāhirāni cha viññāṇakāye cha phassakāye cha vedanākāye cha dhātuyo pañcakkhandhe cattāro arūpe idhalokañca paralokañca dassetvā diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena arahatte pakkhipitvā kathitakathā etena na sutapubbā, tasmā evaṃ vadati.

387. As for Olīyasi (You are attached): the meaning is, 'Seeing your own prosperity, you are bound to and you cling to sense-objects.' Thus the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, 'Even this householder, so faithful and devoted, fears the danger of death; who else would not be afraid?', and wishing to give him a firm admonition, spoke thus. As for Na ca me evarūpī dhammīkathā sutapubbā (I have never before heard such a Dhamma talk): this upāsaka says, 'Even from the Teacher, I have not heard such a talk before.' Is it that the Teacher does not teach such a subtle and profound talk? It is not that he does not teach; he certainly does teach. However, a talk taught by showing the six internal sense-bases, the six external sense-bases, the six bodies of consciousness, the six bodies of contact, the six bodies of feeling, the six elements, the five aggregates, the four immaterial states, this world and the next world, and—by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—placing it in Arahantship, had not been heard by him before. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Apicāyaṃ upāsako dānādhimutto dānābhirato buddhānaṃ santikaṃ gacchanto [P 5.0080] tucchahattho na gatapubbo. Purebhattaṃ gacchanto yāgukhajjakādīni gāhāpetvā gacchati, pacchābhattaṃ sappimadhuphāṇitādīni. Tasmiṃ asati vālikaṃ gāhāpetvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe okirāpeti, dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā gehaṃ gato. Bodhisattagatiko kiresa upāsako, tasmā bhagavā catuvīsati saṃvaccharāni upāsakassa yebhuyyena dānakathameva kathesi – “upāsaka, idaṃ dānaṃ nāma bodhisattānaṃ gatamaggo, mayhampi gatamaggo, mayā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni [V 4.0241] dānaṃ dinnaṃ, tvaṃ mayā gatamaggameva anugacchasī”ti. Dhammasenāpatiādayo mahāsāvakāpi attano attano santikaṃ āgatakāle dānakathamevassa kathenti. Tenevāha na kho gahapati gihīnaṃ odātavasanānaṃ evarūpī dhammīkathā paṭibhātīti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – gahapati gihīnaṃ nāma khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇadāsīdāsaputtabhariyādīsu tibbo ālayo tibbaṃ nikantipariyuṭṭhānaṃ[M 4.0231], tesaṃ – “ettha ālayo na kātabbo, nikanti na kātabbā”ti kathā na paṭibhāti na ruccatīti.

Furthermore, this upāsaka was intent on giving and delighted in giving. When going to the presence of the Buddhas, he had never gone empty-handed. Going in the morning, he would have gruel, hard food, and so on brought; going in the afternoon, he would have ghee, honey, molasses, and so on brought. When these were not available, he would have sand brought and have it scattered in the precinct of the Gandhakuti. Having given gifts and observed the precepts, he would return home. It is said this upāsaka was one who followed the course of a Bodhisatta. Therefore, for twenty-four years, the Blessed One, for the most part, taught only the talk on giving to the upāsaka, saying: 'Upāsaka, this giving is the path trodden by Bodhisattas; it is my path too. For four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand great aeons, I have given gifts. You are following the very path I have trodden.' The great disciples, such as the General of the Dhamma, also spoke only the talk on giving to him when he came to their presence. For that very reason, it was said: 'Indeed, householder, for householders, wearers of white clothes, such a Dhamma talk does not come to mind.' This is what is meant: For householders, there is intense attachment, intense delight, and obsession with fields, land, silver, gold, female and male slaves, children, wives, and so on. For them, a talk saying, 'Attachment should not be made to these things; delight should not be taken,' does not come to mind and is not pleasing.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Tusitabhavane kirassa nibbattamattasseva tigāvutappamāṇaṃ suvaṇṇakkhandhaṃ viya vijjotamānaṃ attabhāvaṃ uyyānavimānādisampattiñca disvā – “mahatī ayaṃ mayhaṃ sampatti, kiṃ nu kho me manussapathe kammaṃ kata”nti olokento tīsu ratanesu adhikāraṃ disvā cintesi “pamādaṭṭhānamidaṃ devattaṃ nāma, imāya hi me sampattiyā modamānassa satisammosopi siyā, handāhaṃ gantvā mama jetavanassa ceva bhikkhusaṅghassa ca tathāgatassa ca ariyamaggassa ca sāriputtattherassa ca vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā tato āgantvā sampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”ti. So tathā [P 5.0081] akāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho anāthapiṇḍikotiādi vuttaṃ.

Why did he approach where the Blessed One was? It is said that, having just arisen in the Tusita realm, he saw his own body shining like a golden mass extending three gāvutas, as well as the splendor of pleasure gardens, celestial mansions, and so on. Reflecting, 'Great is this prosperity of mine! What meritorious deed did I perform in the human realm?' he looked and saw his great service to the Three Jewels. He thought, 'This state of being a deva is a basis for negligence. For, delighting in this prosperity, I might even experience a lapse of mindfulness. Come, let me go and speak in praise of my Jetavana, the community of monks, the Tathāgata, the Noble Path, and the Venerable Sāriputta, and then return here to experience this prosperity.' He acted accordingly. To show this, the passage beginning 'Then Anāthapiṇḍika...' was spoken.

Tattha isisaṅghanisevitanti bhikkhusaṅghanisevitaṃ. Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya jetavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni ariyamaggassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento kammaṃ vijjā cātiādimāha. Tattha kammanti maggacetanā. Vijjāti maggapaññā. Dhammoti samādhipakkhiko dhammo. Sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamanti sīle patiṭṭhitassa jīvitaṃ uttamanti dasseti. Atha vā vijjāti diṭṭhisaṅkappo. Dhammoti vāyāmasatisamādhayo. Sīlanti vācākammantājīvā. Jīvitamuttamanti etasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitassa jīvitaṃ nāma uttamaṃ. Etena maccā sujjhantīti etena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena sattā visujjhanti.

Therein, 'frequented by the community of seers' means frequented by the community of monks. Having thus spoken of the virtues of Jetavana in the first verse, now, wishing to speak of the virtues of the Noble Path, he speaks the passage beginning with 'action and knowledge.' Therein, 'action' is the volition associated with the path. 'Knowledge' is the wisdom associated with the path. 'Dhamma' is the factor belonging to the side of concentration. 'Virtue, the supreme life' shows that for one established in virtue, life is supreme. Alternatively, 'knowledge' means Right View and Right Resolve. 'Dhamma' means Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. 'Virtue' means Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood. 'The supreme life' means that for one established in this virtue, life is indeed supreme. 'By this mortals are purified' means by this eight-factored Noble Path, beings are purified.

Tasmāti yasmā maggena sujjhanti, na gottadhanehi, tasmā. Yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena samādhipakkhiyaṃ dhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tasmiṃ ariyamagge visujjhati[V 4.0242]. Atha vā yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena pañcakkhandhadhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tesu catūsu saccesu visujjhati.

The word 'Therefore' is used because they are purified by the path, not by lineage or wealth. 'One should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means one should investigate with skillful means the qualities conducive to concentration. 'Thus one is purified thereby' means thus, one is purified by that Noble Path. Alternatively, 'one should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means one should investigate with skillful means the dhamma of the five aggregates. 'Thus one is purified thereby' means thus, one is purified in those four truths.

Idāni sāriputtattherassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento sāriputto vātiādimāha. Tattha sāriputto vāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ. Etehi paññādīhi sāriputtova seyyoti vadati. Upasamenāti kilesaupasamena. Pāraṅgatoti [M 4.0232] nibbānaṃ gato. Yo koci nibbānaṃ patto bhikkhu, so etāvaparamo siyā, na therena uttaritaro nāma atthīti vadati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Now, speaking in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he speaks the passage beginning with 'Sāriputta...' Therein, 'Sāriputta...' is a word of emphasis. He says that with these qualities beginning with wisdom, Sāriputta alone is superior. 'By calm' means by the calming of the defilements. 'Gone to the far shore' means gone to Nibbāna. Any monk who has attained Nibbāna would be supreme only to that extent; there is none superior to the Elder, he says. The rest is clear throughout.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Anāthapiṇḍikovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anāthapiṇḍikovāda Sutta is finished.

2. Channovādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Channovāda Sutta

389. Evaṃ [V 4.0243][P 5.0082] me sutanti channovādasuttaṃ. Tattha channoti evaṃnāmako thero, na abhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantatthero. Paṭisallānāti phalasamāpattito. Gilānapucchakāti gilānupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma buddhavaṇṇitaṃ, tasmā evamāha. Satthanti jīvitahārakasatthaṃ. Nāvakaṅkhāmīti icchāmi.

389. 'Thus have I heard'—this is the Channovāda Sutta. Therein, 'Channa' refers to an elder of that name, not the elder who went forth at the Great Renunciation. 'From seclusion' means from the attainment of fruition. Regarding 'one who asks after the sick': attending to the sick is praised by the Buddha; therefore, he spoke thus. 'A weapon' means a life-taking weapon. 'I do not long for' means 'I do not desire.'

390. Anupavajjanti anuppattikaṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ.

390. 'Without fault' means without subsequent becoming, without relinking.

391. Etaṃ mamātiādīni taṇhāmānadiṭṭhigāhavasena vuttāni. Nirodhaṃ disvāti khayavayaṃ ñatvā. Netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na meso attāti samanupassāmīti aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti samanupassāmi.

391. The phrases beginning with ‘This is mine’ are spoken by the power of the grip of craving, conceit, and views. ‘Having seen cessation’ means knowing exhaustion and passing away. ‘I contemplate “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self”’ means I contemplate it as impermanent, suffering, and not-self.

393. Tasmāti yasmā māraṇantikavedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto satthaṃ āharāmīti vadati, tasmā. Puthujjano āyasmā, tena idampi manasi karohīti dīpeti. Niccakappanti niccakālaṃ. Nissitassāti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nissitassa. Calitanti [P 5.0083] vipphanditaṃ hoti. Passaddhīti kāyacittapassaddhi, kilesapassaddhi nāma hotīti attho. Natīti taṇhānati. Natiyā asatīti bhavatthāya ālayanikantipariyuṭṭhānesu asati. Āgatigati na hotīti paṭisandhivasena āgati nāma na hoti, cutivasena gamanaṃ nāma na hoti. Cutūpapātoti cavanavasena cuti, upapajjanavasena upapāto. Nevidha na huraṃ na ubhayamantarenāti nayidha loke, na paraloke, na ubhayattha hoti. Esevanto dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhakilesadukkhassa ayameva anto ayaṃ paricchedo [M 4.0233] parivaṭumabhāvo hoti. Ayameva hi ettha attho. Ye pana “na ubhayamantarenā”ti vacanaṃ gahetvā antarābhavaṃ icchanti, tesaṃ uttaraṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

393. Therefore: because, being unable to endure the feeling that ends in death, he says, 'I bring a weapon,' therefore... The venerable one is a worldling; for that reason, it is pointed out, 'Pay attention to this as well.' 'Niccakappaṃ' means at all times. 'Nissitassa' means of one dependent on craving and views. 'Calitaṃ' means agitated. 'Passaddhi' means tranquility of body and mind; it is called the pacification of defilements—this is the meaning. 'Nati' means the inclination of craving. 'When there is no inclination' means when there are no attachments, delights, or obsessions for the sake of existence. 'No coming or going' means there is no coming by way of rebirth-linking, nor going by way of decease. 'Passing away and reappearance' means decease by way of passing away, and reappearance by way of arising. 'Not here, nor beyond, nor in between' means not in this world, not in the next world, nor in both. 'This is the end of suffering' means this itself is the end, the limit, the non-recurrence of the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements. This indeed is the meaning here. But as for those who, taking the statement 'nor in between,' wish for an intermediate existence, their refutation has already been stated below.

394. Satthaṃ āharesīti jīvitahārakaṃ satthaṃ āhari, kaṇṭhanāḷiṃ chindi. Athassa tasmiṃ [V 4.0244] khaṇe maraṇabhayaṃ okkami, gatinimittaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So attano puthujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā saṃviggo vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅkhāre pariggaṇhanto arahattaṃ patvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi. Sammukhāyeva anupavajjatā byākatāti kiñcāpi idaṃ therassa puthujjanakāle byākaraṇaṃ hoti, etena pana byākaraṇena anantarāyamassa parinibbānaṃ ahosi. Tasmā bhagavā tameva byākaraṇaṃ gahetvā kathesi. Upavajjakulānīti [P 5.0084] upasaṅkamitabbakulāni. Iminā thero, – “bhante, evaṃ upaṭṭhākesu ca upaṭṭhāyikāsu ca vijjamānāsu so bhikkhu tumhākaṃ sāsane parinibbāyissatī”ti pucchati. Athassa bhagavā kulesu saṃsaggābhāvaṃ dīpento honti hete sāriputtātiādimāha. Imasmiṃ kira ṭhāne therassa kulesu asaṃsaṭṭhabhāvo pākaṭo ahosi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

394. 'Satthaṃ āharesi' means he brought a life-taking weapon and cut his throat. At that moment, the fear of death descended upon him, and the sign of his destination appeared. Realizing his own state as a worldling, he became stirred with urgency, established insight, and while comprehending the formations, he attained Arahantship. Having become a samasīsī, he attained Parinibbāna. 'Sammukhāyeva anupavajjatā byākatā' means that although this declaration was made during the elder's time as a worldling, through this declaration his Parinibbāna occurred without obstruction. Therefore, the Blessed One took that very declaration and spoke of it. 'Upavajjakulāni' means families that are to be attended upon. Through this, the elder asks: 'Venerable sir, with such male and female attendants available, how will that monk attain Parinibbāna in your dispensation?' Then the Blessed One, pointing out his lack of association with families, said the words beginning with, 'Honti hete, Sāriputta...' In this instance, it is said, the elder's lack of association with families became evident. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Channovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Channovāda Sutta is finished.

3. Puṇṇovādasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Puṇṇovāda Sutta

395. Evaṃ [V 4.0245] me sutanti puṇṇovādasuttaṃ. Tattha paṭisallānāti ekībhāvā. Taṃ ceti taṃ cakkhuñceva rūpañca. Nandīsamudayā dukkhasamudayoti nandiyā taṇhāya samodhānena pañcakkhandhadukkhassa samodhānaṃ hoti. Iti chasu dvāresu dukkhaṃ samudayoti dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ vasena vaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi. Dutiyanaye nirodho maggoti dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ vasena vivaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi. Iminā ca tvaṃ puṇṇāti pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Evaṃ tāva vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena desanaṃ arahatte pakkhipitvā idāni puṇṇattheraṃ sattasu ṭhānesu sīhanādaṃ nadāpetuṃ iminā ca tvantiādimāha.

395. The Puṇṇovāda Sutta begins with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ.' Therein, 'paṭisallāna' means from a state of being alone. 'Taṃ ce' means that eye and that form. 'Nandīsamudayā dukkhasamudayo' means: through the arising of delight, which is craving, there is the arising of the suffering of the five aggregates. Thus, at the six doors, concerning suffering and arising, by way of these two truths, he showed it, having brought the cycle to its culmination. In the second method, concerning cessation and the path, by way of these two truths, he showed it, having brought the reversal of the cycle to its culmination. 'Iminā ca tvaṃ puṇṇa' is a distinct connection. Thus, first, having included the teaching by way of the cycle and its reversal within Arahantship, now, in order to have the Elder Puṇṇa utter a lion's roar in seven instances, he said, 'Iminā ca tvaṃ,' and so on.

396. Caṇḍāti [M 4.0234] duṭṭhā kibbisā. Pharusāti kakkhaḷā. Akkosissantīti [P 5.0085] dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosissanti. Paribhāsissantīti kiṃ samaṇo nāma tvaṃ, idañca idañca te karissāmāti tajjessanti. Evametthāti evaṃ mayhaṃ ettha bhavissati.

396. 'Caṇḍā' means destructive and cruel. 'Pharusā' means harsh. 'Akkosissanti' means they will abuse with the ten grounds for abuse. 'Paribhāsissanti' means they will threaten, saying, “What kind of monk are you? We will do this and that to you.” 'Evamettha' means: thus it will be for me here.

Daṇḍenāti catuhatthena daṇḍena vā ghaṭikamuggarena vā. Satthenāti ekatodhārādinā. Satthahārakaṃ pariyesantīti jīvitahārakaṃ satthaṃ pariyesanti. Idaṃ thero tatiyapārājikavatthusmiṃ asubhakathaṃ sutvā attabhāvena jigucchantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ satthahārakapariyesanaṃ sandhāyāha. Damūpasamenāti ettha damoti indriyasaṃvarādīnaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. “Saccena danto damasā upeto, vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.195; su. ni. 467) ettha hi indriyasaṃvaro damoti vutto. “Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 191) ettha paññā damoti vutto. “Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166; ma. ni. 2.226) ettha uposathakammaṃ damoti vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte khanti damoti veditabbā. Upasamoti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

'Daṇḍena' means with a four-cubit staff or a club. 'Satthena' means with a single-edged weapon and so on. 'Satthahārakaṃ pariyesanti' means they seek a weapon that takes life. The Elder said this with reference to the story of the third pārājika offense, concerning the monks who, having heard the discourse on non-beauty, were disgusted with their own existence and sought a weapon-bringer. Herein, in 'damūpasamena,' 'dama' is a name for restraint of the senses and so on. In the verse, ‘Saccena danto damasā upeto, vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo,’ restraint of the senses is called 'dama.' In the verse, ‘Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjatī,’ wisdom is called 'dama.' In the phrase, ‘Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjenā,’ the Uposatha observance is called 'dama.' In this sutta, however, 'dama' is to be understood as patience. 'Upasama' is a synonym for that very word.

397. Atha kho āyasmā puṇṇoti ko panesa puṇṇo, kasmā panettha gantukāmo ahosīti[V 4.0246]. Sunāparantavāsiko eva eso, sāvatthiyaṃ pana asappāyavihāraṃ sallakkhetvā tattha gantukāmo ahosi.

397. Regarding 'Atha kho āyasmā puṇṇo': Who is this Puṇṇa, and why did he wish to go there? This is the question. He is a resident of Sunāparanta. However, having noted that dwelling in Sāvatthī was unsuitable for his practice, he wished to go there.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – sunāparantaraṭṭhe [P 5.0086] kira ekasmiṃ vāṇijakagāme ete dve bhātaro. Tesu kadāci jeṭṭho pañca sakaṭasatāni gahetvā janapadaṃ gantvā bhaṇḍaṃ āharati, kadāci kaniṭṭho. Imasmiṃ pana samaye kaniṭṭhaṃ ghare ṭhapetvā jeṭṭhabhātiko pañca sakaṭasatāni gahetvā janapadacārikaṃ caranto anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanassa nātidūre sakaṭasatthaṃ nivāsetvā bhuttapātarāso parijanaparivuto phāsukaṭṭhāne nisīdi.

Herein is the sequential account: In the Sunāparanta country, it is said, there were two brothers in a certain merchant village. Sometimes the elder would take five hundred carts, go to the country, and bring back goods; sometimes the younger would. At this time, however, the elder brother, having left the younger at home and taking five hundred carts, was traveling through the country. He gradually arrived at Sāvatthī and, having settled the caravan of carts not far from Jetavana, he ate his morning meal and, surrounded by his retinue, sat in a comfortable place.

Tena ca samayena sāvatthivāsino bhuttapātarāsā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya suddhuttarāsaṅgā gandhapupphādihatthā yena buddho yena dhammo yena saṅgho, tanninnā tappoṇā tappābbhārā hutvā dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā jetavanaṃ [M 4.0235] gacchanti. So te disvā “kahaṃ ime gacchanti”ti ekamanussaṃ pucchi. Kiṃ tvaṃ ayyo na jānāsi, loke buddhadhammasaṅgharatanāni nāma uppannāni, iccesa mahājano satthu santike dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ gacchatīti. Tassa buddhoti vacanaṃ chavicammādīni chinditvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi. Atha attano parijanaparivuto tāya parisāya saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā satthu madhurassarena dhammaṃ desentassa parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajjāya cittaṃ uppādesi. Atha tathāgatena kālaṃ viditvā parisāya uyyojitāya satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā svātanāya nimantetvā dutiyadivase maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā āsanāni paññapetvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā bhuttapātarāso uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya bhaṇḍāgārikaṃ pakkosāpetvā, ettakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vissajjitaṃ, ettakaṃ na vissajjitanti sabbaṃ ācikkhitvā – “imaṃ sāpateyyaṃ mayhaṃ kaniṭṭhassa dehī”ti sabbaṃ niyyātetvā satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaparāyaṇo ahosi.

At that time, the residents of Sāvatthī, having eaten their morning meal, undertaking the Uposatha observances, dressed in clean upper robes, and with perfumes, flowers, and so on in hand, were inclined, bent, and directed towards where the Buddha was, where the Dhamma was, and where the Saṅgha was. Leaving through the southern gate, they went to Jetavana. Seeing them, he asked a man, “Where are these people going?” “Sir, do you not know? In the world, the jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha have arisen. Therefore, this great crowd is going to hear a Dhamma talk in the Teacher’s presence.” For him, upon hearing the word “Buddha,” it cut through his outer skin, inner skin, and so on, struck the marrow of his bones, and there it stood. Then, surrounded by his retinue, he went with that assembly to the monastery. Standing at the edge of the assembly while the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice, he heard the Dhamma, and a desire for the going forth arose in his mind. Then, when the Tathāgata, knowing the time, had dismissed the assembly, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and invited him for the next day. On the second day, having had a pavilion built and seats prepared, he gave a great offering to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head. Having eaten his morning meal and undertaken the Uposatha observances, he had the treasurer summoned. Having explained everything, saying, “This much merchandise has been sold, and this much has not been sold,” he then said, “Give this property to my younger brother.” Having thus handed everything over, he went forth in the Teacher’s presence and became devoted to his meditation subject.

Athassa [P 5.0087] kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ na upaṭṭhāti. Tato cintesi – “ayaṃ janapado mayhaṃ asappāyo, yaṃnūnāhaṃ satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gaccheyya”nti. Atha pubbaṇhasamaye piṇḍāya caritvā sāyanhasamaye paṭisallānā vuṭṭhahitvā bhagavantaṃ [V 4.0247] upasaṅkamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā satta sīhanāde naditvā pakkāmi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā puṇṇo…pe… viharatī”ti.

Then, as he was attending to his meditation subject, the meditation subject did not become manifest to him. Then he thought: “This country is unsuitable for me. What if I were to receive a meditation subject from the Teacher and go to my own place?” Then, having wandered for alms in the morning and having arisen from seclusion in the evening, he approached the Blessed One, had him teach a meditation subject, uttered seven lion's roars, and departed. Therefore it was said: “Then the venerable Puṇṇa… and so on… dwells.”

Kattha panāyaṃ vihāsīti? Catūsu ṭhānesu vihāsi, sunāparantaraṭṭhaṃ tāva pavisitvā ajjuhatthapabbate nāma pavisitvā vāṇijagāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha naṃ kaniṭṭhabhātā sañjānitvā bhikkhaṃ datvā, “bhante, aññattha agantvā idheva vasathā”ti paṭiññaṃ kāretvā tattheva vasāpesi.

But where did he dwell? He dwelt in four places. First, having entered the Sunāparanta country, he entered a mountain named Ajjuhatthapabbata and then entered a merchant village for alms. Then his younger brother, recognizing him, gave him alms. Having had him make a promise—“Venerable sir, do not go elsewhere; dwell right here”—he had him dwell in that very place.

Tato samuddagirivihāraṃ nāma agamāsi. Tattha ayakantapāsāṇehi paricchinditvā katacaṅkamo atthi, taṃ koci caṅkamituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Tattha samuddavīciyo āgantvā ayakantapāsāṇesu paharitvā mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Theronaṃ – “kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontānaṃ phāsuvihāro hotū”ti samuddaṃ nissaddaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi.

Thence, he went to a monastery named Samuddagirivihāra. There is a promenade there, enclosed with rocks like iron spikes, and no one is able to walk on it. There, ocean waves come and strike against the rocks like iron spikes, making a great sound. The Elder, thinking, 'May there be a comfortable abiding for those attending to their meditation subject,' made a resolution, making the ocean silent.

Tato [M 4.0236] mātulagiriṃ nāma agamāsi. Tattha sakuṇasaṅgho ussanno, rattiñca divā ca saddo ekābaddhova hoti, thero imaṃ ṭhānaṃ aphāsukanti tato makulakārāmavihāraṃ nāma gato. So vāṇijagāmassa nātidūro naccāsanno gamanāgamanasampanno vivitto appasaddo. Thero imaṃ ṭhānaṃ phāsukanti tattha rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamanādīni kāretvā vassaṃ upagacchi. Evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu vihāsi.

Thence, he went to the place named Mātulagiri. There, the flock of birds was abundant; both by night and by day, the sound was continuous. The Elder, thinking, 'This place is uncomfortable,' went from that place to the monastery named Makulakārāma. That monastery was not too far from the merchant village and not too near; it was convenient for coming and going, secluded, and with little sound. The Elder, thinking, 'This place is comfortable,' had places for the night, places for the day, promenades, and so forth made there, and entered upon the rains-residence. Thus, he dwelt in four places.

Athekadivasaṃ [P 5.0088] tasmiṃyeva antovasse pañca vāṇijasatāni parasamuddaṃ gacchāmāti nāvāya bhaṇḍaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Nāvārohanadivase therassa kaniṭṭhabhātā theraṃ bhojetvā therassa santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā vanditvā gacchanto, – “bhante, mahāsamuddo nāma appameyyo anekantarāyo, amhe āvajjeyyāthā”ti vatvā nāvaṃ āruhi. Nāvā uttamajavena gacchamānā aññataraṃ dīpakaṃ pāpuṇi. Manussā pātarāsaṃ karissāmāti dīpake otiṇṇā. Tasmiṃ dīpe aññaṃ kiñci natthi, candanavanameva ahosi.

Then, on one day during that very rains-residence, five hundred merchants, thinking, 'We shall go to the other side of the ocean,' loaded their goods onto a ship. On the day of embarking, the Elder's younger brother, having fed the Elder, having taken the training precepts in the Elder's presence, and having paid homage, said as he was departing: 'Venerable sir, the great ocean is indeed immeasurable and has many dangers. May you be mindful of us.' Having spoken thus, he boarded the ship. The ship, traveling with supreme speed, reached a certain small island. The men, thinking, 'We shall make our morning meal,' disembarked on the small island. On that island, there was nothing else whatsoever; there was only a sandalwood forest.

Atheko vāsiyā rukkhaṃ ākoṭetvā lohitacandanabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “bho mayaṃ lābhatthāya [V 4.0248] parasamuddaṃ gacchāma, ito ca uttari lābho nāma natthi, caturaṅgulamattā ghaṭikā satasahassaṃ agghati, hāretabbakayuttaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ hāretvā candanassa pūremā”ti. Te tathā kariṃsu. Candanavane adhivatthā amanussā kujjhitvā – “imehi amhākaṃ candanavanaṃ nāsitaṃ, ghātessāma ne”ti cintetvā – “idheva ghātitesu sabbaṃ vanaṃ ekaṃ kuṇapaṃ bhavissati, samuddamajjhe nesaṃ nāvaṃ osīdessāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Atha tesaṃ nāvaṃ āruyha muhuttaṃ gatakāleyeva uppādikaṃ uṭṭhapetvā sayampi te amanussā bhayānakāni rūpāni dassayiṃsu. Bhītā manussā attano attano devatā namassanti. Therassa kaniṭṭho cūḷapuṇṇakuṭumbiko – “mayhaṃ bhātā avassayo hotū”ti therassa namassamāno aṭṭhāsi.

Then one man, having struck a tree with an adze and realized it was red sandalwood, said: 'Sirs, we go to the other side of the ocean for the sake of profit, and there is no profit greater than this. A piece the measure of four fingers is worth one hundred thousand. Having discarded the goods that should be discarded, let us fill the ship with sandalwood.' They did so. The non-humans dwelling in the sandalwood forest became angry and thought: 'Our sandalwood forest has been destroyed by these men; we shall kill them.' Then they said: 'If they are killed right here, the entire forest will become a single mass of corpses. We shall sink their ship in the middle of the ocean.' Then, having boarded their ship, just after they had traveled for a moment, the non-humans raised a great wave and displayed terrifying forms themselves. The frightened men paid homage to their respective deities. The Elder's younger brother, the householder Cūḷapuṇṇa, stood paying homage to the Elder, thinking: 'May my brother be my refuge.'

Theropi kira tasmiṃyeva khaṇe āvajjitvā tesaṃ byasanuppattiṃ [P 5.0089] ñatvā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā sammukhe aṭṭhāsi. Amanussā theraṃ disvā “ayyo puṇṇatthero etī”ti pakkamiṃsu, uppādikaṃ sannisīdi. Thero mā bhāyathāti te [M 4.0237] assāsetvā “kahaṃ gantukāmatthā”ti pucchi. Bhante, amhākaṃ sakaṭṭhānameva gacchāmāti. Thero nāvaṃ phale akkamitvā “etesaṃ icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Vāṇijā sakaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ puttadārassa ārocetvā “etha theraṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmā”ti pañcasatā attano pañcamātugāmasatehi saddhiṃ tīsu saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesuṃ. Tato nāvāya bhaṇḍaṃ otāretvā therassa ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā – “ayaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ koṭṭhāso”ti āhaṃsu. Thero – “mayhaṃ visuṃ koṭṭhāsakiccaṃ natthi, satthā pana tumhehi diṭṭhapubbo”ti. Na diṭṭhapubbo, bhanteti. Tena hi iminā satthu maṇḍalamāḷaṃ karotha, evaṃ satthāraṃ passissathāti. Te sādhu, bhanteti tena ca koṭṭhāsena attano ca koṭṭhāsehi maṇḍalamāḷaṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu.

The Elder also, it is said, at that very moment, having reflected and known of the arising of disaster for them, having flown up into the sky, stood at the bow of the ship. The non-humans, having seen the Elder, thought thus, 'The noble Elder Puṇṇa comes,' and departed. The great wave subsided. The Elder, having said, 'Do not be afraid,' and having reassured them, asked, 'Where do you wish to go?' They said, 'Venerable sir, we wish to go only to our own place.' The Elder, having stepped on a plank of the ship, resolved thus: 'Let it go to their desired place.' The merchants, having gone to their own place and related that event to their children and wives, said thus: 'Come, let us go for refuge to the Elder.' The five hundred men, together with their own five hundred women, having been established in the three refuges, declared their state as lay disciples. Thence, having unloaded the goods from the ship and having made one portion for the Elder, they said: 'Venerable sir, this is your portion.' The Elder said: 'For me, there is no need for a separate portion. But have you seen the Teacher before?' When it was said, 'Venerable sir, we have not seen him before,' he spoke thus: 'Then with this portion, make a circular pavilion for the Teacher. In this way, you will see the Teacher.' They, having said, 'Very well, venerable sir,' began to make the circular pavilion with that portion and with their own portions.

Satthāpi kira āraddhakālato paṭṭhāya paribhogaṃ akāsi. Ārakkhamanussā rattiṃ obhāsaṃ disvā “mahesakkhā devatā atthī”ti saññaṃ kariṃsu. Upāsakā maṇḍalamāḷañca bhikkhusaṅghassa ca senāsanāni niṭṭhapetvā dānasambhāraṃ sajjetvā – “kataṃ, bhante, amhehi attano kiccaṃ, satthāraṃ pakkosathā”ti therassa ārocesuṃ. Thero sāyanhasamaye iddhiyā sāvatthiṃ patvā, “bhante, vāṇijagāmavāsino tumhe daṭṭhukāmā, tesaṃ anukampaṃ karothā”ti bhagavantaṃ yāci. Bhagavā adhivāsesi. Thero bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā sakaṭṭhānameva paccāgato.

The Teacher also, it is said, from the time it was begun, made use of it. The watchmen, having seen a light at night, made the perception thus: 'There are deities of great power.' The lay disciples, having completed the circular pavilion and the lodgings for the community of monks, and having prepared the requisites for the offering, informed the Elder, saying thus: 'Venerable sir, our duty has been done by us. Please summon the Teacher.' The Elder, in the evening time, having reached Sāvatthī by means of psychic power, requested the Blessed One, saying thus: 'Venerable sir, the inhabitants of the merchant village are desirous of seeing you. Please show compassion towards them.' The Blessed One consented. The Elder, having known the Blessed One's consent, returned to his own place.

Bhagavāpi [V 4.0249] ānandatheraṃ āmantesi[P 5.0090], – “ānanda, sve sunāparante vāṇijagāme piṇḍāya carissāma, tvaṃ ekūnapañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ salākaṃ dehī”ti. Thero sādhu, bhanteti bhikkhusaṅghassa tamatthaṃ ārocetvā nabhacārikā bhikkhū salākaṃ gaṇhantūti āha. Taṃdivasaṃ kuṇḍadhānatthero paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ aggahesi. Vāṇijagāmavāsinopi “sve kira satthā āgamissatī”ti gāmamajjhe maṇḍapaṃ katvā dānaggaṃ sajjayiṃsu. Bhagavā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdi. Sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. So kiṃ idanti āvajjetvā [M 4.0238] satthu sunāparantagamanaṃ disvā vissakammaṃ āmantesi – “tāta ajja bhagavā timattāni yojanasatāni piṇḍācāraṃ karissati, pañca kūṭāgārasatāni māpetvā jetavanadvārakoṭṭhamatthake gamanasajjāni katvā ṭhapehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Bhagavato kūṭāgāraṃ catumukhaṃ ahosi, dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ dvimukhāni, sesāni ekamukhāni. Satthā gandhakuṭito nikkhamma paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitakūṭāgāresu dhurakūṭāgāraṃ pāvisi. Dve aggasāvake ādiṃ katvā ekūnapañcabhikkhusatānipi kūṭāgāraṃ gantvā nisinnā ahesuṃ. Ekaṃ tucchakūṭāgāraṃ ahosi, pañcapi kūṭāgārasatāni ākāse uppatiṃsu.

The Blessed One also addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying, “Ānanda, tomorrow we will wander for alms in the merchant village in the Sunāparanta country. You, give the ticket to the five hundred monks less one.” The Elder replied, “Very well, Venerable Sir,” and having informed the community of monks of that matter, said, “Let the sky-faring monks take the ticket.” On that day, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna took the ticket first. The inhabitants of the merchant village, having heard, “It is said the Teacher will come tomorrow,” made a pavilion in the middle of the village and prepared the excellent alms.
