The Blessed One, having attended to His body early in the morning, entered the Perfumed Chamber, entered into the fruition attainment, and sat. Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone seat became hot. He, reflecting, “What is the reason for this?” saw the Teacher’s journey to the Sunāparanta country and addressed Vissakamma, saying, “My dear, today the Blessed One will go on an alms-round of three hundred yojanas. Having created five hundred pinnacled mansions and having made preparations for the journey, place them above the gatehouse of Jetavana.” He did so accordingly. The Blessed One’s pinnacled mansion had four entrances, those of the two chief disciples had two entrances, and the remaining ones had one entrance. The Teacher, having departed from the Perfumed Chamber, entered the foremost pinnacled mansion among those placed in succession. Beginning with the two chief disciples, the five hundred monks less one also went to their pinnacled mansions and were seated. One pinnacled mansion was empty, and the five hundred pinnacled mansions rose up into the sky.

Satthā [P 5.0091] saccabandhapabbataṃ nāma patvā kūṭāgāraṃ ākāse ṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ pabbate saccabandho nāma micchādiṭṭhikatāpaso mahājanaṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ uggaṇhāpento lābhaggayasaggappatto hutvā vasati. Abbhantare cassa antocāṭiyaṃ padīpo viya arahattassa upanissayo jalati. Taṃ disvā dhammamassa kathessāmīti gantvā dhammaṃ desesi. Tāpaso desanāpariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, maggenevāssa abhiññā āgatā. Ehibhikkhu hutvā iddhimayapattacīvaradharo hutvā kūṭāgāraṃ pāvisi.

The Teacher, having reached the mountain named Saccabandha, halted the pinnacled mansion in the sky. On that mountain dwelt an ascetic with wrong view named Saccabandha, who, causing the great populace to take up wrong view, had reached the highest gain and fame. And within him, like a lamp inside a large pot, the supporting condition for Arahantship was shining. Seeing this, the Teacher thought, “I will teach him the Dhamma,” and having gone, He taught the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, the ascetic attained Arahantship. With the path itself, the supernormal knowledges came to him. Having become an Ehi-bhikkhu, a bearer of a bowl and robes created by psychic power, he entered the pinnacled mansion.

Bhagavā kūṭāgāragatehi pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vāṇijagāmaṃ gantvā kūṭāgārāni adissamānāni katvā vāṇijagāmaṃ pāvisi. Vāṇijā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā satthāraṃ makulakārāmaṃ nayiṃsu. Satthā maṇḍalamāḷaṃ pāvisi. Mahājano yāva satthā bhattadarathaṃ paṭipassambheti, tāva pātarāsaṃ katvā uposathaṅgāni samādāya bahuṃ gandhañca pupphañca ādāya [V 4.0250] dhammassavanatthāya ārāmaṃ paccāgamāsi. Satthā dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājanassa bandhanamokkho jāto, mahantaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ ahosi.

The Blessed One, together with the five hundred monks who were in the pinnacled mansions, went to the merchant village. Having made the pinnacled mansions invisible, He entered the merchant village. The merchants, having given a great alms-offering to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, led the Teacher to the Makulakārāma monastery. The Teacher entered the round pavilion. While the Teacher was allaying the fatigue from the meal, the great populace, having had their morning meal and undertaken the Uposatha precepts, took many perfumes and flowers and returned to the monastery in order to hear the Dhamma. The Teacher taught the Dhamma. For the great populace, release from the bondage of craving arose, and there was a great acclamation of the Buddha.

Satthā mahājanassa saṅgahatthaṃ katipāhaṃ tattheva vasi, aruṇaṃ pana mahāgandhakuṭiyaṃyeva uṭṭhapesi. Tattha katipāhaṃ vasitvā vāṇijagāme piṇḍāya caritvā “tvaṃ idheva vasāhī”ti puṇṇattheraṃ nivattetvā antare nammadānadī [M 4.0239] nāma atthi, tassā tīraṃ agamāsi. Nammadānāgarājā satthu paccuggamanaṃ katvā nāgabhavanaṃ pavesetvā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ sakkāraṃ akāsi. Satthā [P 5.0092] tassa dhammaṃ kathetvā nāgabhavanā nikkhami. So – “mayhaṃ, bhante, paricaritabbaṃ dethā”ti yāci, bhagavā nammadānadītīre padacetiyaṃ dassesi. Taṃ vīcīsu āgatāsu pidhīyati, gatāsu vivarīyati, mahāsakkārappattaṃ ahosi. Satthā tato nikkhamma saccabandhapabbataṃ gantvā saccabandhaṃ āha – “tayā mahājano apāyamagge otārito, tvaṃ idheva vasitvā etesaṃ laddhiṃ vissajjāpetvā nibbānamagge patiṭṭhāpehī”ti. Sopi paricaritabbaṃ yāci. Satthā ghanapiṭṭhipāsāṇe allamattikapiṇḍamhi lañchanaṃ viya padacetiyaṃ dassesi, tato jetavanameva gato. Etamatthaṃ sandhāya tenevantaravassenātiādi vuttaṃ.

The Teacher, for the sake of helping the great populace, dwelt right there for some days; however, He caused the dawn to arise right at the great Perfumed Chamber in Jetavana. Having dwelt there for some days and having wandered for alms in the merchant village, He said, “You stay right here,” and sent back the Elder Puṇṇa. On the way, there is a river named Nammadā; He went to its bank. The Nāga king of Nammadā went out to meet the Teacher, led Him into the nāga abode, and paid homage to the Three Jewels. The Teacher, having taught the Dhamma to him, departed from the nāga abode. The Nāga king requested, “Venerable Sir, give me an object of veneration.” The Blessed One showed a footprint shrine on the bank of the Nammadā river. When the waves come, it is covered; when they recede, it is revealed. It came to be greatly honored. The Teacher, departing from there, went to the Saccabandha mountain and said to Saccabandha, “By you, the great populace was cast down onto the path to the plane of misery. You, dwelling right here, having made them abandon their view, establish them on the path to Nibbāna.” He too requested an object of veneration. The Teacher showed a footprint shrine on a solid stone slab, like a seal on a lump of wet clay. From there, He went right to Jetavana. With reference to this meaning, “Therefore, during that same rains-retreat,” etc., was said.

Parinibbāyīti anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Mahājano therassa satta divasāni sarīrapūjaṃ katvā bahūni gandhakaṭṭhāni samodhānetvā sarīraṃ jhāpetvā dhātuyo ādāya cetiyaṃ akāsi. Sambahulā bhikkhūti therassa āḷāhane ṭhitabhikkhū. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

“Parinibbāyi” means: he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. The great populace paid homage to the Elder's body for seven days, collected much fragrant firewood, cremated the body, took the relics, and built a cetiya. “Sambahulā bhikkhū” means: the monks who were standing at the Elder's cremation ground. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Puṇṇovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Puṇṇovāda Sutta is finished.

4. Nandakovādasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nandakovāda Sutta

398. Evaṃ [V 4.0251] me sutanti nandakovādasuttaṃ. Tattha tena kho pana samayenāti bhagavā mahāpajāpatiyā yācito bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ uyyojetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātetvā – “therā bhikkhū vārena bhikkhuniyo ovadantū”ti saṅghassa bhāraṃ akāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha pariyāyenāti vārena. Na icchatīti attano vāre sampatte dūraṃ gāmaṃ vā gantvā sūcikammādīni vā ārabhitvā “ayaṃ nāmassa papañco”ti [P 5.0093] vadāpesi. Imaṃ pana pariyāyena ovādaṃ bhagavā nandakattherasseva kāraṇā akāsi. Kasmā? Imāsañhi bhikkhunīnaṃ theraṃ disvā cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti [M 4.0240] pasīdati. Tena tā tassa ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitukāmā, dhammakathaṃ sotukāmā. Tasmā bhagavā – “nandako attano vāre sampatte ovādaṃ dassati, dhammakathaṃ kathessatī”ti vārena ovādaṃ akāsi. Thero pana attano vāraṃ na karoti, kasmāti ce? Tā kira bhikkhuniyo pubbe therassa jambudīpe rajjaṃ kārentassa orodhā ahesuṃ. Thero pubbenivāsañāṇena taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā cintesi – “maṃ imassa bhikkhunisaṅghassa majjhe nisinnaṃ upamāyo ca kāraṇāni ca āharitvā dhammaṃ kathayamānaṃ disvā añño pubbenivāsañāṇalābhī bhikkhu imaṃ kāraṇaṃ oloketvā ‘āyasmā nandako yāvajjadivasā orodhe na vissajjeti, sobhatāyamāyasmā orodhaparivuto’ti vattabbaṃ maññeyyā”ti. Etamatthaṃ sampassamāno thero attano vāraṃ na karoti. Imāsañca kira bhikkhunīnaṃ therasseva desanā sappāyā bhavissatīti ñatvā atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ āmantesi.

Thus have I heard—the Nandakovāda Sutta. Therein, as for 'at that time': the Blessed One, having been requested by Mahāpajāpatī, dismissed the order of bhikkhunīs and assembled the order of bhikkhus, assigning the duty to the Saṅgha: 'Let the elder bhikkhus instruct the bhikkhunīs in turn.' This was said with reference to that. Therein, pariyāyena means 'by turn'. 'He does not wish to' means that when his turn came, he would either go to a distant village or take up needlework and the like, and the Blessed One would have it said, 'This is his delaying tactic.' However, the Blessed One arranged this rotational instruction for the sake of Venerable Nandaka alone. Why? Because when these bhikkhunīs saw the elder, their minds became one-pointed and serene. Therefore, they were eager to receive his instruction and listen to his Dhamma talk. Thus, the Blessed One arranged the instruction by turn, thinking, 'When Nandaka’s turn comes, he will give the instruction and deliver the Dhamma talk.' Yet, the elder would not take his turn. Why? It is said that these bhikkhunīs had previously been his consorts when he ruled in Jambudīpa. The elder, knowing this through his recollection of past lives, reflected: 'If I sit in the midst of this order of bhikkhunīs, giving a Dhamma talk while bringing up similes and reasons, another bhikkhu who has attained the recollection of past lives might observe this and think, “Venerable Nandaka has not given up his consorts even to this day—how splendid he looks surrounded by them!”' Foreseeing this matter, the elder would not take his turn. And knowing that for these bhikkhunīs, the Elder's teaching alone would indeed be suitable, the Blessed One then addressed Venerable Nandaka.

Tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ pubbe tassa orodhabhāvajānanatthaṃ idaṃ vatthuṃ – pubbe kira bārāṇasiyaṃ pañca dāsasatāni pañca dāsisatāni cāti jaṅghasahassaṃ ekatova kammaṃ katvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasi. Ayaṃ nandakatthero tasmiṃ kāle jeṭṭhakadāso hoti[P 5.0094], gotamī jeṭṭhakadāsī. Sā jeṭṭhakadāsassa pādaparicārikā ahosi paṇḍitā byattā. Jaṅghasahassampi puññakammaṃ karontaṃ ekato karoti. Atha vassūpanāyikasamaye pañca paccekabuddhā nandamūlakapabbhārato isipatane otaritvā nagare piṇḍāya caritvā isipatanameva gantvā – “vassūpanāyikakuṭiyā atthāya hatthakammaṃ [V 4.0252] yācissāmā”ti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā sāyanhasamaye nagaraṃ pavisitvā seṭṭhissa gharadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu. Jeṭṭhakadāsī kuṭaṃ gahetvā udakatitthaṃ gacchantī paccekabuddhe nagaraṃ pavisante addasa. Seṭṭhi tesaṃ āgatakāraṇaṃ sutvā “amhākaṃ okāso natthi, gacchantū”ti āha.

4. For the sake of knowing the former state of those bhikkhunīs as his consorts, this is the story: Formerly, it is said, in Bārāṇasī, five hundred male slaves and five hundred female slaves—thus a thousand people—lived in one place, working together. This Elder Nandaka was the chief male slave at that time, and Gotamī was the chief female slave. She was the wife of the chief male slave; she was wise and skilled. She also brought the thousand people together to perform meritorious deeds. Then, at the time for entering the rains-residence, five Paccekabuddhas descended from the Nandamūlaka mountain slope to Isipatana. After wandering for alms in the city and returning to Isipatana, they thought, 'We will request manual labor for a rains-residence hut.' Having donned their robes, they entered the city in the evening and stood at the wealthy merchant’s door. The chief female slave, taking a water pot and going to the water-landing place, saw the Paccekabuddhas entering the city. The wealthy merchant, hearing the reason for their arrival, said, 'We have no opportunity. Please go.'

Atha te nagarā nikkhamante jeṭṭhakadāsī kuṭaṃ gahetvā pavisantī disvā kuṭaṃ otāretvā vanditvā onamitvā mukhaṃ pidhāya – “ayyā nagaraṃ paviṭṭhamattāva nikkhantā, kiṃ nu kho”ti pucchi. Vassūpanāyikakuṭiyā hatthakammaṃ yācituṃ āgamimhāti. Laddhaṃ, bhanteti. Na laddhaṃ upāsiketi? Kiṃ panesā kuṭi issareheva kātabbā, duggatehipi sakkā kātunti. Yena kenaci sakkāti? Sādhu, bhante, mayaṃ karissāma. Sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathāti nimantetvā [M 4.0241] udakaṃ netvā puna kuṭaṃ gahetvā āgamma titthamagge ṭhatvā āgatā avasesadāsiyo “ettheva hothā”ti vatvā sabbāsaṃ āgatakāle āha – “amma kiṃ niccameva parassa dāsakammaṃ karissatha, udāhu dāsabhāvato muccituṃ icchathā”ti? Ajjeva muccitumicchāma ayyeti. Yadi evaṃ mayā pañca paccekabuddhā hatthakammaṃ alabhantā svātanāya nimantitā, tumhākaṃ sāmikehi ekadivasaṃ hatthakammaṃ dāpethāti. Tā sādhūti sampaṭicchitvā sāyaṃ aṭavito āgatakāle sāmikānaṃ ārocesuṃ. Te sādhūti jeṭṭhakadāsassa gehadvāre sannipatiṃsu.

Then, as they were leaving the city, the chief female slave, who was entering with her water pot, saw them. She lowered the pot, paid homage, bowed down, covered her mouth, and asked, 'Noble sirs, you have just entered the city and are already leaving. What, I wonder, is the matter?' 'We came to request manual labor for a rains-residence hut.' 'Did you receive it, venerable sirs?' 'We did not receive it, laywoman.' 'But must this hut be built by the powerful alone? Is it not also possible for the poor to build it?' They replied, 'It is possible for anyone at all.' 'Very well, venerable sirs, we will do it. Tomorrow, please accept my almsfood,' she invited. Having taken the water to her home, she took the pot again, returned, and stood on the path to the water-landing place. To the remaining slave women as they arrived, she said, 'Please wait right here.' When all had gathered, she said, 'Mothers, will you always do the work of a slave for another, or do you wish to be freed from the state of slavery?' 'Noble lady, we wish to be freed this very day!' 'If so, five Paccekabuddhas who did not receive manual labor have been invited by me for tomorrow. Have your husbands provide one day of manual labor.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and in the evening, when their husbands returned from the forest, they informed them. They said, 'Very well,' and gathered at the door of the chief male slave's house.

Atha ne jeṭṭhakadāsī sve tātā paccekabuddhānaṃ hatthakammaṃ dethāti ānisaṃsaṃ ācikkhitvā yepi [P 5.0095] na kātukāmā, te gāḷhena ovādena tajjetvā paṭicchāpesi. Sā punadivase paccekabuddhānaṃ bhattaṃ datvā sabbesaṃ dāsaputtānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi. Te tāvadeva araññaṃ pavisitvā dabbasambhāre samodhānetvā sataṃ sataṃ hutvā ekekakuṭiṃ ekekacaṅkamanādiparivāraṃ katvā mañcapīṭhapānīyaparibhojanīyabhājanādīni ṭhapetvā paccekabuddhe temāsaṃ tattha vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ kāretvā vārabhikkhaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. Yo attano vāradivase na sakkoti. Tassa jeṭṭhakadāsī sakagehato āharitvā deti. Evaṃ temāsaṃ jaggitvā jeṭṭhakadāsī ekekaṃ dāsaṃ ekekaṃ sāṭakaṃ vissajjāpesi. Pañca thūlasāṭakasatāni ahesuṃ. Tāni parivattāpetvā pañcannaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ ticīvarāni katvā adāsi. Paccekabuddhā yathāphāsukaṃ agamaṃsu. Tampi jaṅghasahassaṃ ekato kusalaṃ katvā kāyassa bhedā devaloke nibbatti. Tāni pañca mātugāmasatāni kālena kālaṃ tesaṃ pañcannaṃ purisasatānaṃ gehe honti, kālena [V 4.0253] kālaṃ sabbāpi jeṭṭhakadāsaputtasseva gehe honti. Atha ekasmiṃ kāle jeṭṭhakadāsaputto devalokato cavitvā rājakule nibbatto. Tāpi pañcasatā devakaññā mahābhogakulesu nibbattitvā tassa rajje ṭhitassa gehaṃ agamaṃsu. Etena niyāmena saṃsarantiyo amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle koliyanagare devadahanagare ca khattiyakulesu nibbattā.

Then the chief female slave, having explained the benefits, said to them, 'My dears, tomorrow, give manual labor to the Paccekabuddhas.' Having threatened even those who were unwilling with firm admonishment, she made them agree. The next day, after giving almsfood to the Paccekabuddhas, she gave a signal to all the male slaves. They immediately entered the forest, gathered building materials, and forming groups of a hundred each, built individual huts, each with a walking path and other appurtenances. They set up beds, seats, pots for drinking water and for general use, and other requisites, then made the Paccekabuddhas promise to stay there for the three months of the rains retreat and established a system of alms by rotation. If anyone was unable to provide on his assigned day, the chief female slave would bring provisions from her own house and give them. Thus, having looked after them for three months, the chief female slave had each slave contribute a single cloth. There were five hundred coarse cloths. Having had these exchanged, she made sets of three robes for the five Paccekabuddhas and gave them. The Paccekabuddhas departed as they pleased. That group of a thousand, having performed this meritorious deed together, were reborn in the heavenly realm after the breaking up of the body. Those five hundred women, from time to time, were in the households of those five hundred men, and at other times, all were in the household of the son of the chief male slave. Then at one time, the son of the chief male slave, having passed away from the heavenly realm, was reborn in a royal family. Those five hundred celestial maidens also, having passed away from the heavenly realm and been born into families of great wealth, came to his household when he was established in the kingdom. Following this pattern, wandering through saṃsāra, in the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn in the warrior clans in Koliyanagara and Devadahanagara.

Nandakattheropi pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto, jeṭṭhakadāsidhītā vayaṃ āgamma suddhodanamahārājassa aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhitā, itarāpi tesaṃ tesaṃ [M 4.0242] rājaputtānaṃyeva gharaṃ gatā. Tāsaṃ sāmikā pañcasatā rājakumārā udakacumbaṭakalahe satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitā, rājadhītaro tesaṃ ukkaṇṭhanatthaṃ [P 5.0096] sāsanaṃ pesesuṃ. Te ukkaṇṭhite bhagavā kuṇāladahaṃ netvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhapetvā mahāsamayadivase arahatte patiṭṭhāpesi. Tāpi pañcasatā rājadhītaro nikkhamitvā mahāpajāpatiyā santike pabbajiṃsu. Ayamāyasmā nandako ettāva tā bhikkhuniyoti evametaṃ vatthu dīpetabbaṃ.

The Elder Nandaka also, having gone forth, attained Arahantship. The princess who had been the chief female slave, having come of age, was established in the position of chief queen of King Suddhodana; the other princesses also went to the homes of those respective princes. Their husbands, the five hundred princes, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse during a quarrel over a water-pot head-coil, went forth. The princesses, in order to make them discontented, sent a message. When they were discontented, the Blessed One, taking them to Lake Kuṇāla, established them in the fruit of stream-entry, and on the day of the Mahāsamaya discourse, established them in Arahantship. Those five hundred princesses also, having renounced, went forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī. This is the Venerable Nandaka, and these are the bhikkhunīs. Thus this story should be explained.

Rājakārāmoti pasenadinā kārito nagarassa dakkhiṇadisābhāge thūpārāmasadise ṭhāne vihāro.

Rājakārāma means: the monastery caused to be built by King Pasenadi, situated in the southern part of the city in a place similar to the Thūpārāma.

399. Sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhanti hetunā kāraṇena vipassanāpaññāya yāthāvasarasato diṭṭhaṃ.

399. ‘Well seen with right wisdom’ means: seen with insight-wisdom, by way of reason and cause, according to its real nature.

401. Tajjaṃ tajjanti taṃsabhāvaṃ taṃsabhāvaṃ, atthato pana taṃ taṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca tā tā vedanā uppajjantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

401. ‘Corresponding to that, corresponding to that’ means that very nature, that very nature. In meaning, however, it is said thus: dependent on this or that condition, this or that feeling arises.

402. Pagevassa chāyāti mūlādīni nissāya nibbattā chāyā paṭhamataraṃyeva aniccā.

402. ‘How much more so its shadow’ means: the shadow, which has arisen in dependence on the roots and so on, is impermanent from the very first.

413. Anupahaccāti anupahanitvā. Tattha maṃsaṃ piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ katvā cammaṃ alliyāpento maṃsakāyaṃ upahanati nāma. Cammaṃ baddhaṃ baddhaṃ katvā maṃse alliyāpento maṃsakāyaṃ [V 4.0254] upahanati nāma. Evaṃ akatvā. Vilimaṃsaṃ nhārubandhananti sabbacamme laggavilīpanamaṃsameva. Antarākilesasaṃyojanabandhananti sabbaṃ antarakilesameva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

413. ‘Without damaging’ means without destroying. Herein, one who makes the flesh into lumps and makes the skin adhere to it is said to damage the mass of flesh. One who makes the skin into connected pieces and makes it adhere to the flesh is said to damage the mass of flesh. Not having done so. ‘The clinging flesh and sinew-bonds’ means all the clinging and smeared flesh on the skin. ‘The inner bond of defilements and fetters’ is said with reference to all inner defilements.

414. Satta kho panimeti kasmā āhāti? Yā hi esā paññā kilese chindatīti vuttā, sā na ekikāva attano dhammatāya chindituṃ sakkoti. Yathā pana kuṭhārī na [P 5.0097] attano dhammatāya chejjaṃ chindati, purisassa tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicceva chindati, evaṃ na vinā chahi bojjhaṅgehi paññā kilese chindituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā evamāha. Tena hīti yena kāraṇena tayā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, cha bāhirāni[M 4.0243], cha viññāṇakāye, dīpopamaṃ, rukkhopamaṃ, gāvūpamañca dassetvā sattahi bojjhaṅgehi āsavakkhayena desanā niṭṭhapitā, tena kāraṇena tvaṃ svepi tā bhikkhuniyo teneva ovādena ovadeyyāsīti.

414. Why was it said, ‘These seven, indeed’? Because this wisdom which is said to cut off the defilements cannot do so alone by its own nature. Just as an axe does not cut that which is to be cut by its own nature, but cuts only in dependence on a person's corresponding effort, so too, without the six factors of enlightenment, wisdom cannot cut off the defilements. Therefore, it was said thus. ‘Therefore’ means: for the reason that you, having shown the six internal sense bases, the six external sense bases, the six classes of consciousness, the simile of the lamp, the simile of the tree, and the simile of the butcher, concluded the discourse with the destruction of the taints by means of the seven factors of enlightenment—for that reason, you should instruct those bhikkhunīs tomorrow with that same instruction.

415. Sā sotāpannāti yā sā guṇehi sabbapacchimikā, sā sotāpannā. Sesā pana sakadāgāmianāgāminiyo ca khīṇāsavā ca. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ paripuṇṇasaṅkappāti. Ajjhāsayapāripūriyā. Yassā hi bhikkhuniyā evamahosi – “kadā nu kho ahaṃ ayyassa nandakassa dhammadesanaṃ suṇantī tasmiṃyeva āsane sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikareyya”nti, sā sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchākāsi. Yassā ahosi “sakadāgāmiphalaṃ anāgāmiphalaṃ arahatta”nti, sā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tenāha bhagavā “attamanā ceva paripuṇṇasaṅkappā cā”ti.

415. ‘She is a stream-enterer’ means: she who was the very last in terms of virtues, she is a stream-enterer. As for the rest, they are once-returners, non-returners, and those whose taints are destroyed. If so, how is it that they had ‘fulfilled aspiration’? Through the fulfillment of their inclination. For whichever bhikkhunī had this thought: ‘When, while listening to the Venerable Nandaka’s Dhamma discourse, might I realize the fruit of stream-entry on this very seat?’—she realized the fruit of stream-entry. Whichever had the thought for the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or Arahantship, she realized Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One said, ‘delighted and with fulfilled aspiration’.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Nandakovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Nandakovāda Sutta is finished.

5. Rāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Rāhulovāda Sutta

416. Evaṃ [V 4.0255] me sutanti rāhulovādasuttaṃ. Tattha vimuttiparipācanīyāti vimuttiṃ paripācentīti vimuttiparipācanīyā. Dhammāti [P 5.0098] pannarasa dhammā. Te saddhindriyādīnaṃ visuddhikāraṇavasena veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

416. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Rāhulovāda Sutta. Therein, `vimuttiparipācanīyā` means that which causes the fruit of Arahantship to ripen. As for `dhammā`, they are fifteen principles. These are to be understood by way of being the cause for the purification of the faculties of faith and so forth. For it has been said:

“Assaddhe puggale parivajjayato, saddhe puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato pasādanīye suttante paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi saddhindriyaṃ visujjhati. Kusīte puggale parivajjayato āraddhavīriye puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato sammappadhāne paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi vīriyindriyaṃ visujjhati. Muṭṭhassatī puggale parivajjayato upaṭṭhitassatī puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato satipaṭṭhāne paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi satindriyaṃ visujjhati[M 4.0244]. Asamāhite puggale parivajjayato samāhite puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato jhānavimokkhe paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi samādhindriyaṃ visujjhati. Duppaññe puggale parivajjayato paññavante puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi paññindriyaṃ visujjhati. Iti ime pañca puggale parivajjayato pañca puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato pañca suttantakkhandhe paccavekkhato imehi pannarasahi ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni visujjhantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.185).

“By avoiding individuals without faith, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon individuals with faith, and contemplating inspiring discourses, in these three ways the faculty of faith becomes purified. By avoiding lazy individuals, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon energetic individuals, and contemplating the right strivings, in these three ways the faculty of energy becomes purified. By avoiding unmindful individuals, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon mindful individuals, and contemplating the foundations of mindfulness, in these three ways the faculty of mindfulness becomes purified. By avoiding uncomposed individuals, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon composed individuals, and contemplating the meditative absorptions and liberations, in these three ways the faculty of concentration becomes purified. By avoiding unwise individuals, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon wise individuals, and contemplating the domain of profound knowledge, in these three ways the faculty of wisdom becomes purified. Thus, by avoiding these five kinds of individuals, associating, frequenting, and waiting upon these five kinds of individuals, and contemplating these five groups of discourses, through these fifteen ways, these five faculties become purified.” (Paṭis. Ma. 1.185)

Aparepi pannarasa dhammā vimuttiparipācanīyā – saddhādīni pañcimāni indriyāni, aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññāti, imā pañca nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā, meghiyattherassa kathitā kalyāṇamittatādayo pañcadhammāti. Kāya pana velāya bhagavato etadahosīti. Paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokentassa.

Furthermore, there are another fifteen principles conducive to the ripening of liberation: the five faculties beginning with faith; the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in that which is impermanent, the perception of non-self in that which is suffering, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion—these five perceptions being conducive to penetration; and the five principles taught to the Elder Meghiya, such as good friendship. Now, at what time did this occur to the Blessed One? At dawn, while surveying the world.

419. Anekānaṃ devatāsahassānanti āyasmatā rāhulena padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle pālitanāgarājakāle patthanaṃ [P 5.0099] paṭṭhapentena saddhiṃ patthanaṃ paṭṭhapitadevatāyeva. Tāsu pana kāci bhūmaṭṭhakā [V 4.0256] devatā, kāci antalikkhakā, kāci cātumahārājikā, kāci devaloke, kāci brahmaloke nibbattā. Imasmiṃ pana divase sabbā ekaṭṭhāne andhavanasmiṃyeva sannipatitā. Dhammacakkhunti upāliovāda- (ma. ni. 2.69) dīghanakhasuttesu (ma. ni. 2.206) paṭhamamaggo dhammacakkhunti vutto, brahmāyusutte (ma. ni. 2.395) tīṇi phalāni, imasmiṃ sutte cattāro maggā, cattāri ca phalāni dhammacakkhunti veditabbāni. Tattha hi kāci devatā sotāpannā ahesuṃ, kāci sakadāgāmī, anāgāmī, khīṇāsavā. Tāsañca pana devatānaṃ ettakāti gaṇanavasena paricchedo natthi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

419. “Many thousands of deities” refers to just those deities who made an aspiration together with the Venerable Rāhula at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during the time he was the Nāga king Pālita. Among them, some deities were terrestrial, some aerial, some belonged to the realm of the Four Great Kings, some were born in the deva world, and some in the Brahma world. On this day, all of them gathered together in one place in the Andhavana forest. “The eye of Dhamma” refers to the first path, as stated in the Upāliovāda and the Dīghanakhasutta. In the Brahmāyusutta, the three lower fruits are to be understood as such; while in this sutta, the four paths and the four fruits are to be understood as “the eye of Dhamma.” Indeed, among those deities, some were stream-enterers, some were once-returners, some were non-returners, and some were Arahants. And of those deities, there is no defined limit by way of counting. The rest is clear in every way.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Rāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rāhulovāda Sutta is finished.

6. Chachakkasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Chachakka Sutta

420. Evaṃ [V 4.0257][M 4.0245] me sutanti chachakkasuttaṃ. Tattha ādikalyāṇantiādimhi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ niddosaṃ katvā desessāmi. Majjhapariyosānesupi eseva nayo. Iti bhagavā ariyavaṃsaṃ navahi, mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sattahi, mahāassapuraṃ sattahiyeva padehi thomesi. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ navahi padehi thomesi.

420. The sutta beginning with `Evaṃ me sutaṃ` is the Chachakkasutta. Therein, as for `ādikalyāṇaṃ` (good in the beginning), it means: 'I shall teach, having made it good in the beginning, excellent, and faultless.' This same method should be understood for the middle and the end as well. Thus, the Blessed One praises the Ariyavaṃsa with nine terms, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna with seven, and the Mahā-assapura with seven terms indeed. This sutta, however, he praised with nine terms.

Veditabbānīti [P 5.0100] sahavipassanena maggena jānitabbāni. Manāyatanena tebhūmakacittameva kathitaṃ, dhammāyatanena bahiddhā tebhūmakadhammā ca, manoviññāṇena ṭhapetvā dve pañcaviññāṇāni sesaṃ bāvīsatividhaṃ lokiyavipākacittaṃ. Phassavedanā yathāvuttavipākaviññāṇasampayuttāva. Taṇhāti vipākavedanāpaccayā javanakkhaṇe uppannataṇhā.

As for `veditabbāni` (to be understood), they are to be known by the path together with insight. By `manāyatana` (mind-base), only consciousness of the three planes is taught. By `dhammāyatana` (phenomena-base), external phenomena of the three planes are also taught. By `manoviññāṇa` (mind-consciousness), having excluded the two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the remaining twenty-twofold mundane resultant consciousness is taught. Contact and feeling are only those associated with the aforementioned resultant consciousness. As for `taṇhā` (craving), it is the craving that has arisen at the impulsion moment due to resultant feeling as a condition.

422. Cakkhu attāti pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhā kathitānañhi dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ anattabhāvadassanatthaṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Tattha na upapajjatīti na yujjati. Vetīti vigacchati nirujjhati.

422. `Cakkhu attā` (the eye is self) is a separate connection. Indeed, this discourse was undertaken for the purpose of showing the state of non-self of the two truths taught below. Therein, `na upapajjati` (does not arise) means 'it is not fitting.' As for `veti` (passes away), it means it departs, it ceases.

424. Ayaṃ kho pana, bhikkhaveti ayampi pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Ayañhi desanā tiṇṇaṃ gāhānaṃ vasena vaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ āraddhā. Dukkhaṃ samudayoti dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ vasena vaṭṭaṃ dassetuntipi vadantiyeva. Etaṃ mamātiādīsu taṇhāmānadiṭṭhigāhāva veditabbā. Samanupassatīti gāhattayavasena passati.

424. `Ayaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave` (And this, monks) is also a separate connection. This discourse was undertaken to show the round by way of the three graspings. They also say that it was undertaken to show the round by way of the two truths, namely, suffering and its origin. In `etaṃ mama` (this is mine) and so on, the graspings of craving, conceit, and views should be understood. As for `samanupassati` (one contemplates), it means one sees by way of the three graspings.

Evaṃ vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni tiṇṇaṃ gāhānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena, nirodho maggoti imesaṃ vā dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ vasena vivaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ ayaṃ kho panātiādimāha. Netaṃ mamātiādīni taṇhādīnaṃ paṭisedhavacanāni. Samanupassatīti aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti passati.

Having thus shown the round, now, in order to show that which is not the round (vivaṭṭa) by way of the counterpart to the three graspings, or by way of these two truths, namely, cessation and the path, he said `Ayaṃ kho pana` (And this...), and so on. `Netaṃ mama` (This is not mine) and so on are words of negation for craving and so on. As for `samanupassati` (one contemplates), it means one sees as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

425. Evaṃ [V 4.0258] vivaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni tiṇṇaṃ anusayānaṃ vasena puna vaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ cakkhuñca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha abhinandatītiādīni taṇhādiṭṭhivaseneva vuttāni. Anusetīti appahīno hoti. Dukkhassāti [P 5.0101] vaṭṭadukkhakilesadukkhassa.

425. Having thus shown that which is not the round, now, in order to again show the round by way of the three latent tendencies, he said `Cakkhuñca, bhikkhave` (And the eye, monks), and so on. Therein, `abhinandati` (delights in) and so on are spoken only by way of craving and views. As for `anuseti` (lies latent), it means it is unabandoned. As for `dukkhassa` (of suffering), it means of the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements.

426. Evaṃ [M 4.0246] tiṇṇaṃ anusayānaṃ vasena vaṭṭaṃ kathetvā idāni tesaṃ paṭikkhepavasena vivaṭṭaṃ dassento puna cakkhuñcātiādimāha. Avijjaṃ pahāyāti vaṭṭamūlikaṃ avijjaṃ pajahitvā. Vijjanti arahattamaggavijjaṃ uppādetvā.

426. Having thus spoken of the round by way of the three latent tendencies, now, while showing that which is not the round by way of their counterpart, he again said `Cakkhuñca` (And the eye), and so on. As for `avijjaṃ pahāya` (having abandoned ignorance), it means having abandoned ignorance which is the root of the round. As for `vijjaṃ` (knowledge), it means having produced the knowledge of the path of Arahantship.

427. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti ettakeneva kathāmaggena vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena desanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā puna tadeva sampiṇḍetvā dassento evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Saṭṭhimattānaṃ bhikkhūnanti ettha anacchariyametaṃ, yaṃ sayameva tathāgate desente saṭṭhi bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā. Imañhi suttaṃ dhammasenāpatimhi kathentepi saṭṭhi bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā, mahāmoggallāne kathentepi, asītimahātheresu kathentesupi pattā eva. Etampi anacchariyaṃ. Mahābhiññappattā hi te sāvakā.

427. As for `Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati` (This is possible): Having brought the teaching to its culmination by way of the round and that which is not the round with just this much of a line of discourse, and then while showing that very thing summarized, he said `Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave` (Seeing thus, monks), and so on. Here, regarding `saṭṭhimattānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ` (sixty monks), it is no wonder that while the Tathāgata himself was teaching, sixty monks attained Arahantship. Indeed, even when this sutta was taught by the General of the Dhamma, sixty monks attained Arahantship; even when taught by Mahāmoggallāna, and even when taught by the eighty great elders, they attained it indeed. This too is no wonder, for those disciples were attainers of great supernormal knowledge.

Aparabhāge pana tambapaṇṇidīpe māleyyadevatthero nāma heṭṭhā lohapāsāde idaṃ suttaṃ kathesi. Tadāpi saṭṭhi bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā. Yathā ca lohapāsāde, evaṃ thero mahāmaṇḍapepi idaṃ suttaṃ kathesi. Mahāvihārā nikkhamitvā cetiyapabbataṃ gato, tatthāpi kathesi. Tato sākiyavaṃsavihāre, kūṭālivihāre, antarasobbhe, muttaṅgaṇe, vātakapabbate, pācinagharake, dīghavāpiyaṃ, lokandare, nomaṇḍalatale kathesi. Tesupi ṭhānesu saṭṭhi saṭṭhi [P 5.0102] bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā. Tato nikkhamitvā pana thero cittalapabbataṃ gato. Tadā ca cittalapabbatavihāre atirekasaṭṭhivasso mahāthero, pokkharaṇiyaṃ kuruvakatitthaṃ nāma paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ atthi, tattha thero nhāyissāmīti otiṇṇo. Devatthero tassa santikaṃ gantvā nhāpemi, bhanteti āha. Thero paṭisanthāreneva – “māleyyadevo nāma atthīti vadanti, so ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā tvaṃ devoti āha. Āma, bhanteti. Saṭṭhivassaddhānaṃ me, āvuso, koci sarīraṃ hatthena phusituṃ nāma na labhi, tvaṃ pana nhāpehīti uttaritvā tīre nisīdi.

In a later time, however, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, an elder named Māleyyadevatthera taught this sutta below the Lohapāsāda. At that time also, sixty monks attained Arahantship. And just as in the Lohapāsāda, so too the elder taught this sutta in the great pavilion. Having left the Mahāvihāra, he went to Cetiyapabbata and taught there also. From there, he taught at the Sākiyavaṃsa monastery, the Kūṭālī monastery, Antarasobbha, Muttaṅgaṇa, Vātakapabbata, Pācinagharaka, Dīghavāpiya, Lokandara, and Nomaṇḍalatala. In those places also, sixty monks each attained Arahantship. Having left there, the elder then went to Cittalapabbata. At that time, in the Cittalapabbata monastery, there was a great elder of over sixty vassas. At the pond, there is a secluded place named Kuruvakatittha; the elder went down into it, thinking, 'I will bathe.' The elder Deva, having gone to him, said, 'Venerable sir, I shall bathe you.' The elder, just by the friendly greeting, knowing, 'They say there is one named Māleyyadeva; this must be he,' said, 'Are you Deva?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'For a period of sixty years, friend, no one has had the chance to touch my body with their hand. You, however, may bathe me.' And getting out, he sat on the bank.

Thero [V 4.0259] sabbampi hatthapādādiparikammaṃ katvā mahātheraṃ nhāpesi. Taṃ divasañca dhammassavanadivaso hoti. Atha mahāthero – “deva amhākaṃ dhammadānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Thero sādhu, bhanteti sampaṭicchi. Atthaṅgate sūriye [M 4.0247] dhammassavanaṃ ghosesuṃ. Atikkantasaṭṭhivassāva saṭṭhi mahātherā dhammassavanatthaṃ agamaṃsu. Devatthero sarabhāṇāvasāne imaṃ suttaṃ ārabhi, suttantapariyosāne ca saṭṭhi mahātherā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tato tissamahāvihāraṃ gantvā kathesi, tasmimpi saṭṭhi therā. Tato nāgamahāvihāre kāḷakacchagāme kathesi, tasmimpi saṭṭhi therā. Tato kalyāṇiṃ gantvā tattha cātuddase heṭṭhāpāsāde kathesi, tasmimpi saṭṭhi therā. Uposathadivase uparipāsāde kathesi, tasmimpi saṭṭhi therāti evaṃ devatthereyeva idaṃ suttaṃ kathente saṭṭhiṭṭhānesu saṭṭhi saṭṭhi janā arahattaṃ pattā.

The elder, having done all the services such as rubbing the hands and feet, bathed the great elder. And that day was a day for listening to the Dhamma. Then the great elder said, 'Deva, it is fitting for you to give us the gift of the Dhamma.' The elder said, 'Good, venerable sir,' and accepted. When the sun had set, they announced the listening to the Dhamma. Sixty great elders, who had passed sixty vassas, came for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma. At the end of the chanting, the elder Deva began this sutta. And at the conclusion of the sutta, the sixty great elders attained Arahantship. From there, he went to Tissamahāvihāra and taught, and there too, sixty elders attained Arahantship. From there, he taught at Nāgamahāvihāra in the village of Kāḷakacchagāma, and there too, sixty elders attained Arahantship. From there, he went to Kalyāṇī and taught there in the lower pāsāda on the fourteenth day, and there too, sixty elders attained Arahantship. On the Uposatha day, he taught in the upper pāsāda, and there too, sixty elders attained Arahantship. Thus, while the elder Deva himself was teaching this sutta, in sixty places, sixty persons each attained Arahantship.

Ambilakāḷakavihāre pana tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthere [P 5.0103] imaṃ suttaṃ kathente manussaparisā gāvutaṃ ahosi, devaparisā yojanikā. Suttapariyosāne sahassabhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā, devesu pana tato tato ekekova puthujjano ahosīti.

At Ambiḷakāḷaka Monastery, when the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga was teaching this sutta, the human assembly extended for a gāvuta, and the deva assembly for a yojana. At the conclusion of the sutta, a thousand monks attained Arahantship, while among the devas, only one here and there remained an ordinary person.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Chachakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chachakka Sutta is concluded.

7. Mahāsaḷāyatanikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta

428. Evaṃ [V 4.0260] me sutanti mahāsaḷāyatanikasuttaṃ. Tattha mahāsaḷāyatanikanti mahantānaṃ channaṃ āyatanānaṃ jotakaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ.

428. Thus have I heard—this is the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta. Therein, 'Mahāsaḷāyatanika' refers to the Dhamma discourse that illuminates the six sense bases, which are 'great' in the sense of having great faults and great benefits.

429. Ajānanti sahavipassanena maggena ajānanto. Upacayaṃ gacchantīti vuḍḍhiṃ gacchanti, vasibhāvaṃ gacchantīti attho. Kāyikāti pañcadvārikadarathā. Cetasikāti manodvārikadarathā. Santāpādīsupi eseva nayo.

429. 'Not knowing' means not knowing by means of the path together with insight. 'They go to accumulation' means they go to growth; the meaning is that they attain mastery. 'Bodily' refers to the distresses of the five sense-doors. 'Mental' refers to the distresses of the mind-door. This same method should be understood for the terms beginning with 'burning' and so forth.

430. Kāyasukhanti pañcadvārikasukhaṃ. Cetosukhanti manodvārikasukhaṃ. Ettha ca pañcadvārikajavanena samāpajjanaṃ vā vuṭṭhānaṃ vā natthi, uppannamattakameva hoti. Manodvārikena sabbaṃ hoti. Ayañca maggavuṭṭhānassa paccayabhūtā balavavipassanā, sāpi manodvārikeneva hoti.

430. 'Bodily happiness' means happiness arising in the five-door impulsion. 'Mental happiness' means happiness arising in the mind-door impulsion. And herein, by means of five-door impulsion, there is neither entering into attainment nor emerging from it; it is merely a momentary arising. By means of the mind-door impulsion, all entering and emerging occurs. And this powerful insight, which is the cause for emerging from the path, also occurs solely through the mind-door impulsion.

431. Tathābhūtassāti [M 4.0248] kusalacittasampayuttacetosukhasamaṅgībhūtassa. Pubbeva kho panassāti assa bhikkhuno vācākammantājīvā pubbasuddhikā nāma ādito paṭṭhāya parisuddhāva [P 5.0104] honti. Diṭṭhisaṅkappavāyāmasatisamādhisaṅkhātāni pana pañcaṅgāni sabbatthakakārāpakaṅgāni nāma. Evaṃ lokuttaramaggo aṭṭhaṅgiko vā sattaṅgiko vā hoti.

431. 'For one who has become thus' means for one endowed with the mental happiness associated with wholesome consciousness, which occurs together with the insight knowledge leading to emergence. 'For him, even before' means that for that monk, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are called 'previously purified,' being indeed pure from the very beginning. The five factors, however, known as Right View, Right Intention, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration, are called the factors that accomplish the preliminary work for the entire path. Thus, the supramundane path is either eightfold or sevenfold.

Vitaṇḍavādī pana “yā yathābhūtassa diṭṭhī”ti imameva suttapadesaṃ gahetvā “lokuttaramaggo pañcaṅgiko”ti vadati. So – “evamassāyaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti iminā anantaravacaneneva paṭisedhitabbo. Uttari ca evaṃ saññāpetabbo – lokuttaramaggo pañcaṅgiko nāma natthi, imāni pana pañca sabbatthakakārāpakaṅgāni maggakkhaṇe virativasena pūrenti. “Yā catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati viratī”ti evaṃ vuttaviratīsu hi micchāvācaṃ pajahati, sammāvācaṃ bhāveti, evaṃ sammāvācaṃ [V 4.0261] bhāventassa imāni pañcaṅgikāni na vinā, saheva viratiyā pūrenti. Sammākammantājīvesupi eseva nayo. Iti vacīkammādīni ādito paṭṭhāya parisuddhāneva vaṭṭanti. Imāni pana pañca sabbatthakakārāpakaṅgāni virativasena paripūrentīti pañcaṅgiko maggo nāma natthi. Subhaddasuttepi (dī. ni. 2.214) cetaṃ vuttaṃ – “yasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti. Aññesu ca anekesu suttasatesu aṭṭhaṅgikova maggo āgatoti.

A sophist, however, taking just this phrase from the sutta, 'the view of one who has become thus,' says, 'The supramundane path is five-factored.' He should be refuted by this immediately following statement: 'Thus this Noble Eightfold Path goes to the perfection of its development.' Furthermore, he should be made to understand thus: There is no such thing as a five-factored supramundane path. Rather, these five factors that accomplish the preliminary work for the entire path are fulfilled at the moment of the path by the power of the abstinences. For, among the abstinences spoken of thus, 'the abstaining, the refraining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct,' one abandons wrong speech and cultivates Right Speech. For one cultivating Right Speech in this way, these five factors are not fulfilled without the abstinence; they are fulfilled only together with the abstinence. This same method should be understood in the case of Right Action and Right Livelihood. Thus, it is fitting that verbal actions and so on are pure from the very beginning. Since these five factors that accomplish the preliminary work are fulfilled by the power of the abstinences, there is no such thing as a five-factored path. Moreover, in the Subhadda Sutta this is stated: 'In whatever Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found…' And in many hundreds of other suttas, the path that has come down is only the eight-factored one.

433. Cattāropi satipaṭṭhānāti maggasampayuttāva cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Sammappadhānādīsupi eseva nayo. Yuganandhāti ekakkhaṇikayuganandhā. Etehi aññasmiṃ khaṇe samāpatti, aññasmiṃ vipassanāti. Evaṃ nānākhaṇikāpi honti, ariyamagge pana ekakkhaṇikā.

433. 'The four foundations of mindfulness' means the four foundations of mindfulness that are indeed associated with the path. This same method should be understood in the case of the Right Exertions and so forth. 'Yoked together' means serenity and insight yoked together in a single moment. For with these, there can be attainment in one moment and insight in another. Thus, they can also occur in different moments, but on the noble path, they occur in a single moment.

Vijjā ca vimutti cāti arahattamaggavijjā ca phalavimutti ca. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Knowledge and liberation' means the knowledge associated with the path of Arahantship and the liberation that is its fruit. The rest is plain in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāsaḷāyatanikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta is concluded.

8. Nagaravindeyyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Nagaravindeyya Sutta

435. Evaṃ [V 4.0262][P 5.0105][M 4.0249] me sutanti nagaravindeyyasuttaṃ. Tattha samavisamaṃ carantīti kālena samaṃ caranti, kālena visamaṃ. Samacariyampi hetanti samacariyampi hi etaṃ.

435. Thus have I heard. This is the Nagaravindeyya Sutta. Therein, 'they practice evenly and unevenly' means: sometimes they practice evenly, sometimes unevenly. The phrase `Samacariyampi hetanti` is to be divided as `samacariyam pi hi etaṃ` (this is indeed also even conduct).

437. Ke ākārāti kāni kāraṇāni? Ke anvayāti kā anubuddhiyo? Natthi kho pana tatthāti kasmā āha, nanu araññe haritatiṇacampakavanādivasena atimanuññā rūpādayo pañca kāmaguṇā atthīti? No natthi. Na panetaṃ vanasaṇḍena kathitaṃ, itthirūpādīni pana sandhāyetaṃ kathitaṃ. Tāni hi purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Yathāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekarūpampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, itthirūpaṃ. Itthirūpaṃ, bhikkhave, purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti (a. ni. 1.1) vitthāretabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

437. `Ke ākārā` means: what are the reasons? `Ke anvayā` means: what are the inferences? Why was it said, 'But there is nothing there'? Is it not that in the forest, by way of green grass, champak groves, and so on, there are the five strands of sensual pleasure—forms and so on—which are exceedingly delightful? It is not that they do not exist; they certainly do exist. However, this was not said with reference to the forest grove; rather, it was said with reference to a woman's form and so on. For those overwhelm and occupy a man's mind. As it was said: 'Monks, I do not see even one other form that so overwhelms and occupies a man's mind as this, monks, a woman's form. A woman's form, monks, overwhelms and occupies a man's mind' (AN 1.1). This should be elaborated upon. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle-Length Discourses.

Nagaravindeyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nagaravindeyya Sutta is concluded.

9. Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta

438. Evaṃ [V 4.0263] me sutanti piṇḍapātapārisuddhisuttaṃ. Tattha paṭisallānāti phalasamāpattito.

438. Thus have I heard. This is the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta. Therein, 'seclusion' refers to the attainment of fruition from which one has arisen.

Vippasannānīti okāsavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Phalasamāpattito hi vuṭṭhitassa pañcahi pasādehi patiṭṭhitokāso vippasanno hoti, chavivaṇṇo parisuddho. Tasmā evamāha. Suññatavihārenāti suññataphalasamāpattivihārena. Mahāpurisavihāroti [P 5.0106] buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatamahāsāvakānaṃ mahāpurisānaṃ vihāro. Yena cāhaṃ maggenātiādīsu vihārato paṭṭhāya yāva gāmassa indakhīlā esa paviṭṭhamaggo nāma, antogāmaṃ pavisitvā gehapaṭipāṭiyā caritvā yāva nagaradvārena nikkhamanā esa caritabbapadeso nāma, bahi indakhīlato paṭṭhāya yāva vihārā esa paṭikkantamaggo nāma. Paṭighaṃ vāpi cetasoti citte paṭihaññanakilesajātaṃ [M 4.0250] kiñci atthi natthīti. Ahorattānusikkhināti divasañca rattiñca anusikkhantena.

'Exceedingly clear' is said with reference to the physical basis of the senses. For one who has arisen from the attainment of fruition, the physical basis established by the five sensitive qualities becomes exceedingly clear, and the skin-complexion pure. Therefore, it was said thus. 'By the dwelling in emptiness' means by the dwelling that is the fruition attainment of emptiness. 'The dwelling of a great person' is the dwelling of the great persons—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the great disciples of the Tathāgata. In 'And by which path I...' and so on: starting from the monastery up to the village threshold, this is called the path of entry; having entered the village and walked from house to house up to exiting by the town gate, this is called the area to be walked; starting from outside the threshold up to the monastery, this is called the path of return. 'Or any aversion in mind' means: 'Is there or is there not any kind of defilement of the nature of impingement in my mind?' 'By one who trains day and night' means by one who trains continuously by day and by night.

440. Pahīnā nu kho me pañca kāmaguṇātiādīsu ekabhikkhussa paccavekkhaṇā nānā, nānābhikkhūnaṃ paccavekkhaṇā nānāti. Kathaṃ? Eko hi bhikkhu pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā vivittokāse nisinno paccavekkhati “pahīnā nu kho me pañcakāmaguṇā”ti. So “appahīnā”ti ñatvā vīriyaṃ paggayha anāgāmimaggena pañcakāmaguṇikarāgaṃ samugghāṭetvā maggānantaraṃ phalaṃ phalānantaraṃ maggaṃ tato vuṭṭhāya paccavekkhanto “pahīnā”ti pajānāti. Nīvaraṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Etesaṃ pana arahattamaggena pahānādīni honti, evaṃ ekabhikkhussa nānāpaccavekkhaṇā hoti. Etāsu pana paccavekkhaṇāsu añño bhikkhu ekaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ paccavekkhati, añño ekanti evaṃ nānābhikkhūnaṃ nānāpaccavekkhaṇā hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

440. In such passages as, 'Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?' the meaning should be understood thus: the reflection of a single bhikkhu is varied, and the reflection of different bhikkhus is varied. How so? A certain bhikkhu, having returned from the alms-round after the meal, having put away his bowl and robe, sits in a secluded place and reflects: 'Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?' He, knowing, 'They have not been abandoned,' rouses his energy and, by means of the path of non-returning, eradicates the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Immediately after the path he attains the fruit, and immediately after the fruit, the path. Rising from that, while reflecting, he understands, 'They have been abandoned.' This same method applies to the hindrances and so on. But the abandonment of these occurs by means of the path of Arahantship. In this way, the reflection of a single bhikkhu is varied. Furthermore, among these reflections, one bhikkhu reflects on one reflection, another on another. In this way, the reflection of different bhikkhus is varied. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta is concluded.

10. Indriyabhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Development of the Faculties

453. Evaṃ [V 4.0264] me sutanti indriyabhāvanāsuttaṃ. Tattha gajaṅgalāyanti evaṃnāmake nigame. Suveḷuvaneti [P 5.0107] suveḷu nāma ekā rukkhajāti, tehi sañchanno mahāvanasaṇḍo, tattha viharati. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ na passati, sotena saddaṃ na suṇātīti cakkhunā rūpaṃ na passitabbaṃ, sotena saddo na sotabboti evaṃ desetīti adhippāyena vadati.

453. Thus have I heard: This is the Discourse on the Development of the Faculties. Therein, 'at Gajaṅgalā' means in a market town of that name. 'In the Suveḷu Wood' means: suveḷu is a species of tree; there is a great forest thicket covered by them. Therein He dwelt. 'He does not see a form with the eye, he does not hear a sound with the ear'—the young man Uttara speaks with the intention that the Buddha teaches thus: 'A form should not be seen with the eye, a sound should not be heard with the ear.'

Aññathā ariyassa vinayeti iminā bhagavā attano sāsane asadisāya indriyabhāvanāya kathanatthaṃ ālayaṃ akāsi. Athāyasmā ānando – “satthā ālayaṃ dasseti, handāhaṃ imissaṃ parisati bhikkhusaṅghassa indriyabhāvanākathaṃ kāremī”ti satthāraṃ yācanto etassa [M 4.0251] bhagavātiādimāha. Athassa bhagavā indriyabhāvanaṃ kathento tena hānandātiādimāha.

'Otherwise than in the noble one's discipline'—by this, the Blessed One created an opportunity for speaking about the incomparable development of the faculties in His Dispensation. Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, 'The Teacher is creating an opportunity; come now, I shall have a discourse on the development of the faculties given for this assembly of bhikkhus,' requesting the Teacher, spoke the words beginning with, 'etassa bhagavā...' Then the Blessed One, speaking to him about the development of the faculties, spoke the words beginning with, 'Tena hānanda...'

454. Tatha yadidaṃ upekkhāti yā esā vipassanupekkhā nāma, esā santā esā paṇītā, atappikāti attho. Iti ayaṃ bhikkhu cakkhudvāre rūpārammaṇampi iṭṭhe ārammaṇe manāpaṃ, aniṭṭhe amanāpaṃ, majjhatte manāpāmanāpañca cittaṃ, tassa rajjituṃ vā dussituṃ vā muyhituṃ vā adatvāva pariggahetvā vipassanaṃ majjhatte ṭhapeti. Cakkhumāti sampannacakkhuvisuddhanetto. Cakkhābādhikassa hi uddhaṃ ummīlananimmīlanaṃ na hoti, tasmā so na gahito.

454. 'That is, equanimity'—this refers to insight-equanimity, which is peaceful, sublime, and unagitated; that is the meaning. Thus, this bhikkhu, at the eye-door, regarding a visible object—whether it is desirable and pleasing, undesirable and displeasing, or neutral and neither pleasing nor displeasing—does not allow the mind to become attached, repelled, or deluded, but having fully comprehended it, establishes insight in a neutral state. 'One with vision' means with a fully endowed eye, with purified vision. For one with an eye disease, there is no opening and closing of the eyelids; therefore, such a one is not taken as the example.

456. Īsakaṃpoṇeti rathīsā viya uṭṭhahitvā ṭhite.

456. 'Slightly bent' means standing raised like a chariot pole.

461. Paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññītiādīsu paṭikūle mettāpharaṇena vā dhātuso upasaṃhārena vā appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Appaṭikūle asubhapharaṇena vā aniccato upasaṃhārena vā paṭikūlasaññī viharati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvāti [V 4.0265] majjhatto hutvā viharitukāmo [P 5.0108] kiṃ karotīti? Iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu āpāthagatesu neva somanassiko na domanassiko hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

461. In the phrases beginning with 'perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,' one dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive by pervading it with loving-kindness or by attending to it in terms of elements. In the unrepulsive, one dwells perceiving the repulsive by pervading it with the perception of foulness or by attending to it as impermanent. The same method should be understood in the remaining passages. 'Having avoided both'—what does one do who wishes to dwell having become neutral? This is the question. When desirable and undesirable objects come into range, one is neither joyful nor sorrowful. For this has been said:

“Kathaṃ paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharati? Aniṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ mettāya vā pharati, dhātuto vā upasaṃharati, evaṃ paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Kathaṃ appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī viharati? Iṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ asubhāya vā pharati, aniccato vā upasaṃharati, evaṃ appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī viharati. Kathaṃ paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī viharati? Aniṭṭhasmiñca iṭṭhasmiñca vatthusmiṃ mettāya vā pharati, dhātuto vā upasaṃharati. Evaṃ paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Kathaṃ appaṭikūle ca paṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī viharati? Iṭṭhasmiñca aniṭṭhasmiñca vatthusmiṃ asubhāya vā pharati, aniccato vā upasaṃharati, evaṃ appaṭikūle ca paṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī viharati[M 4.0252]. Kathaṃ paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno? Idha bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno”ti.

'How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive? In a disagreeable object, one pervades it with loving-kindness or attends to it in terms of elements. Thus, one dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive? In an agreeable object, one pervades it with the perception of foulness or attends to it as impermanent. Thus, one dwells perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive? In both disagreeable and agreeable objects, one pervades them with loving-kindness or attends to them in terms of elements. Thus, one dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive? In both agreeable and disagreeable objects, one pervades them with the perception of foulness or attends to them as impermanent. Thus, one dwells perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive. How does one dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the unrepulsive? Here, a bhikkhu, seeing a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending… cognizing a mental object with the mind, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Thus, one dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the unrepulsive.'

Imesu ca tīsu nayesu paṭhamanaye manāpaṃ amanāpaṃ manāpāmanāpanti saṃkilesaṃ vaṭṭati, nikkilesaṃ vaṭṭati. Dutiyanaye saṃkilesaṃ, tatiyanaye saṃkilesanikkilesaṃ vaṭṭati. Puna vuttaṃ – “paṭhamaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vaṭṭati, dutiyaṃ saṃkilesampi nikkilesampi, tatiyaṃ nikkilesameva vaṭṭatī”ti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

And in these three methods: in the first method, the pleasing, the displeasing, and the pleasing-and-displeasing pertains to defilement and pertains to non-defilement. In the second method, it pertains to defilement. In the third method, it pertains to defilement and non-defilement. Again, it is said: 'The first pertains to defilement; the second pertains to both defilement and non-defilement; the third pertains only to non-defilement.' The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Indriyabhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Development of the Faculties is concluded.

Pañcamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fifth Chapter is concluded.

Uparipaṇṇāsaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Uparipaṇṇāsa is concluded.

Yo [V 4.0266][P 5.0109] cāyaṃ “sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desissāmī”ti āraddhattā ādikalyāṇo, majjhe “suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ gāthā udānaṃ itivuttakaṃ jātakaṃ abbhutadhammaṃ vedalla”nti vacanato majjhekalyāṇo, sanniṭṭhāne “ariyo bhāvitindriyo”ti vacanato pariyosānakalyāṇoti tividhakalyāṇo majjhimanikāyo “mahāvipassanā nāmāya”nti vutto, so vaṇṇanāvasena samatto hoti.

And this Majjhima Nikāya, which is called 'Mahāvipassanā' (Great Insight), is good in the beginning because it was begun with, 'Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Discourse on the Root of All Phenomena'; it is good in the middle because it was taught with the ninefold division of 'Discourses, mixed prose and verse, explanations, verses, inspired utterances, thus-saids, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical teachings'; and it is good in the end because it was taught with, 'a noble one with developed faculties.' Thus it is good in three ways. That Majjhima Nikāya is brought to completion by means of the commentary.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Verses

Ettāvatā [M 4.0253] ca –

Thus far:

Āyācito sumatinā therena bhadantabuddhamittena,

Pubbe mayūradūtapaṭṭanamhi saddhiṃ nivasantena.

Requested by the wise elder, the venerable Buddhamitta, who formerly dwelt with me in Mayūradūtapaṭṭana,

Paravādavidhaṃsanassa majjhimanikāyaseṭṭhassa,

Yamahaṃ papañcasūdanimaṭṭhakathaṃ kātumārabhiṃ.

I began to compose the commentary named Papañcasūdanī for the supreme Majjhima Nikāya, the destroyer of others' doctrines.

Sā hi mahāaṭṭhakathāya sāramādāya niṭṭhitā esā,

Sattuttarasatamattāya pāḷiyā bhāṇavārehi.

Indeed, this was completed by extracting the essence from the Great Commentary, for the Pāḷi text consisting of one hundred and seven recitation sections.

Ekūnasaṭṭhimatto visuddhimaggopi bhāṇavārehi,

Atthappakāsanatthāya āgamānaṃ kato yasmā.

Since the Visuddhimagga, too, consisting of fifty-nine recitation sections, was composed to illuminate the meaning of the Āgamas,

Tasmā tena sahā’yaṃ gāthāgaṇanānayena aṭṭhakathā,

Samadhikachasaṭṭhisatamiti viññeyyā bhāṇavārānaṃ.

Therefore, along with that, this commentary should be understood as consisting of one hundred and sixty-six recitation sections with a surplus, by the reckoning of verses.

Samadhikachasaṭṭhisatapamāṇamiti bhāṇavārato esā,

Samayaṃ pakāsayantī mahāvihārādhivāsīnaṃ.

This, being of the measure of one hundred and sixty-six with a surplus by way of recitation sections, proclaims the doctrine of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

Mūlaṭṭhakathāsāraṃ [V 4.0267][P 5.0110] ādāya mayā imaṃ karontena,

Yaṃ paññamupacitaṃ tena hotu loko sadā sukhitoti.

By the merit that has been accumulated by me in composing this, having taken the essence of the root commentary, may the world always be happy.

Paramavisuddhasaddhābuddhivīriyappaṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjavamaddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhanasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattippabhede sāṭṭhakathe satthu sāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena mahāveyyākaraṇena karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāre chaḷabhiññādippabhedaguṇappaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme suppatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyena therena katā ayaṃ papañcasūdanī nāma majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathā –

Adorned with supreme, pure faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a collection of virtues such as morality, good conduct, honesty, and gentleness; capable of plunging into the thickets of his own and others' doctrines; possessing the brilliance of unimpeded knowledge in the Teacher’s dispensation, which is comprised of the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries; a great exegete; endowed with faultless and clear speech, sweet and noble, born of the bliss that comes from perfect articulation; a speaker of what is fitting and freely spoken; a foremost debater; a great poet; attended by the analytical knowledges; adorned with qualities such as the six higher knowledges; whose wisdom is well-established in the supramundane states; a lamp to the lineage of the elders; an ornament to the lineage of the elders who are residents of the Mahāvihāra; of vast and pure wisdom; by the elder who was given the name Buddhaghosa by his teachers—this commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, named the Papañcasūdanī, was composed.

Tāva [M 4.0254] tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassentī kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhiyā.

For so long may it endure in the world, showing to sons of good family who seek escape from the world the method for the purification of view,

Buddhoti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesinoti.

as long as the very name 'Buddha'—of the pure-minded, the Steadfast One, the world's foremost, the great sage—continues in the world.

Papañcasūdanī nāma

The Papañcasūdanī,

Majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathā sabbākārena niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed in every aspect.
